### [25] [LLPR: Location-aware learning and physics-based reconstruction for raindrop removal from a single image](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30758)
*Zewei He,Xingyu Liu,Xing Luo,Guizhong Fu,Zixuan Chen,Yu Chen,Jinlei Li,Zhe-Ming Lu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LLPR (Location-aware Learning and Physics-based Reconstruction) integrates a training-time location-aware branch with a physics-based reconstruction module for raindrop removal from a single image. It avoids extra inference costs by removing the location branch at test time, learns a transparency matrix and raindrop layer under a physical model, and demonstrates strong performance on a real-world raindrop-degraded dataset with code to be released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Raindrops on windows or lenses cause occlusion and distortion that degrade background recovery. Existing methods rely on CNN/Transformer architectures with dedicated mask subnets, increasing parameters and computation. The authors propose adding a location-aware training branch and physics-based modeling to improve restoration while keeping inference cost low.

Method: Introduce a location-aware learning branch during training to teach encoders to perceive raindrop positions; remove this branch during inference. Employ a physics-based reconstruction scheme to learn a transparency matrix and the raindrop layer, then derive the latent background via the physical model. Integrate these components into the LLPR framework and evaluate on a real-world raindrop-degraded image dataset.

Result: Extensive experiments show LLPR achieves superior performance over state-of-the-art single-image raindrop removal (SIRR) methods and demonstrates generality across scenarios. A real-world raindrop-degraded image dataset was collected to evaluate robustness.

Conclusion: LLPR effectively leverages location information and a physics-based reconstruction to tackle raindrop removal, providing high-quality restoration with a cost-free inference branch and strong generalization. The authors also provide a real-world dataset and plan to release the code.

Abstract: Raindrops can cause occlusion and distortion in the background scenes due to their adherence to windows or camera lenses. Existing raindrop removal methods concentrate on designing sophisticated CNN or Transformer architectures to recover distorted and missing texture. In this paper, we try to integrate location information and physical model into off-the-shelf CNN or Transformer architectures to help improve their performance. Specifically, we notice that existing methods deploy a preprocessing sub-network to generate a binary or soft mask to indicate the raindrop location, which will increase the network parameters and computational complexity. In contrast, a location-aware learning branch is embedded to teach the encoder in the training phase with the capability of perceiving the position of the raindrops. Note that this location-aware learning branch can be removed during the inference process (achieving performance improvements at no cost). Furthermore, instead of directly reconstructing the raindrop-free image (i.e., background scene), we devise a physics-based reconstruction scheme to first learn the transparency matrix and the raindrop layer. The latent background layer is then reversely derived based on the physical model. By combining the above-mentioned components, we propose our location-aware learning and physics-based reconstruction (LLPR) framework for this challenging ill-posed problem. We also collect a real-world raindrop-degraded image dataset, which is challenging for single-image raindrop removal (SIRR) methods. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of our LLPR framework, achieving superior performance against state-of-the-art SIRR methods. The code will be made available upon acceptance.

</details>


### [26] [Timo: $\textbf{T}$aming Mult$\textbf{i}$modal Diffusion Transformer for Human $\textbf{Mo}$tion Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30761)
*Zhao Wang,Jiangtao Hu,Jack Yu,Tao Yu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Timo introduces a kinematics-aware multimodal diffusion transformer (MMDiT) for human motion generation (HMG) that enables bidirectional text–motion modeling, with flow matching and geometry/rotational-kinematics supervision, plus a two-stage curriculum. It reports large-scale benchmarking (40,025 clips across six datasets) and outperforms state-of-the-art (Kimodo on 5/6 dims, ~40.8% relative average improvement).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limitation of cross-attention-only approaches in HMG that neglect bidirectional text–motion coupling and the mismatch of applying generic MMDiT with flow matching to articulated, temporally coherent, multi-joint motion.

Method: Propose Timo: a kinematics-aware MMDiT with (1) fully shared multimodal attention for bidirectional text–motion modeling, (2) flow matching paired with geometric and rotational-kinematics supervision (actual rotations and their temporal changes), and (3) a two-stage curriculum from broad motion learning to fine caption alignment. Construct a large held-out benchmark (40,025 clips) across six datasets with a unified evaluator.

Result: Timo substantially outperforms SOTA methods on both quantitative and qualitative metrics, surpassing Kimodo on five of six evaluation dimensions and achieving a 40.8% relative improvement in the average benchmark score.

Conclusion: A bidirectional, kinematics-aware MMDiT with curriculum learning and strong supervision signals yields significant gains for HMG and is validated on a large, diverse benchmark.

Abstract: Most existing human motion generation (HMG) methods use cross-attention modules to inject text semantics, but ignore the importance of bidirectional modeling between motion and text tokens, which limits text comprehension. A straightforward idea is introducing multimodal diffusion transformers (MMDiT), which have shown effective joint text--visual modeling in vision generation, into HMG. However, we find that articulated motion is temporally coherent but weakly correlated across joints, in which directly applying an MMDiT with flow matching produces poorly coordinated and jerky motion. In this work, we propose Timo, a novel kinematics-aware MMDiT framework tailored for HMG. Timo combines fully shared multimodal attention for bidirectional text--motion modeling with flow matching, geometric and rotational-kinematics supervision that compares actual rotations and their changes over time, and a two-stage curriculum progressing from broad motion learning to detailed caption alignment. Further, we construct a benchmark of $40{,}025$ held-out clips from six public datasets spanning diverse actions, assessing six complementary dimensions under a common evaluator and scoring protocol. Our model substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. Remarkably, Timo surpasses Kimodo on five of six dimensions, achieving a $40.8$% relative improvement in the average benchmark score. Project page: https://kyfafyd.wang/projects/timo. Demo page: https://timo.kyfafyd.wang.

</details>


### [27] [Query-Conditioned Prototype Adaptation for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning: Single-Query Inference, Controlled Comparisons, and Failure Modes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30769)
*Rushab Rasik Karania,Tomas Maul*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WIPT introduces one-shot test-time prototype adaptation by jointly transforming one query with support embeddings to form query-specific class means, yielding dataset- and shot-dependent gains that are not universally better than ProtoNet.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Isolate the contribution of joint query-support adaptation to prototype construction under a fixed global representation in cross-domain few-shot learning.

Method: Freeze a ViT-S/16 encoder. Train on miniImageNet; evaluate on CUB, EuroSAT, ISIC across 1-shot and 5-shot. Compare Within-Instance Prototypical Transformer (WIPT) against ProtoNet. Explore joint processing of up to five queries, head-only vs full, and efficiency metrics (attention-token pairs, memory, latency). Include rescue/break decomposition, source-shift, and scorer controls to analyze when benefits arise.

Result: 1-shot: WIPT improves ProtoNet on CUB (+0.21pp) and EuroSAT (+2.07pp) but drops on ISIC (-0.22pp). 5-shot: ProtoNet remains strongest overall; WIPT only improves a capacity-matched support-only Transformer on ISIC (+0.99). Joint processing of up to five queries yields no reliable accuracy gain. In head-only 5-shot, g=5 reduces attention-token pairs by 73% and peak memory by 29% versus g=1, with non-monotonic latency. Across target/shot, WIPT shifts uncertain ProtoNet decisions more than confident ones; rescue/break decomposition explains gains/losses. Source-shift and scorer controls indicate the benefit is not universal. Conclusion: WIPT provides a streaming-compatible form of test-time prototype adaptation that can aid difficult low-shot cross-domain decisions without target-time optimization, but benefits are dataset- and setup-dependent.

Conclusion: WIPT offers a streaming, test-time prototype adaptation mechanism that can help select low-shot cross-domain decisions without updating target-time parameters, though its advantages are not universal and depend on data and evaluation controls.

Abstract: Cross-domain few-shot learning requires adapting a classifier to a new visual domain from very few labelled examples without target-time parameter updates. We isolate one question: under a fixed global representation, what does joint query-support adaptation contribute to prototype construction? The Within-Instance Prototypical Transformer (WIPT) implements single-query test-time prototype adaptation by jointly transforming one unlabelled query and the labelled support embeddings, then forming query-specific class means. Using a shared frozen ViT-S/16 encoder, miniImageNet source training, and CUB, EuroSAT and ISIC targets, we replicate the key comparisons across five independent training seeds. In 1-shot evaluation, WIPT improves frozen ProtoNet in every run on CUB (+0.21 percentage points) and EuroSAT (+2.07), but decreases ISIC (-0.22). In 5-shot evaluation, ProtoNet remains strongest overall, while WIPT consistently improves a capacity-matched support-only Transformer on ISIC (+0.99). Joint processing of up to five queries yields no reliable accuracy gain; in a head-only 5-shot benchmark, g = 5 reduces analytical attention-token pairs by 73% and peak allocated memory by 29% relative to g = 1, although latency is non-monotonic. Across all target/shot conditions, WIPT changes uncertain ProtoNet decisions far more than confident ones, and rescue/break decomposition accounts for the observed gains and losses. Source-shift and scorer controls further show that the benefit is not universal. Overall, WIPT provides a streaming-compatible form of test-time prototype adaptation that can improve difficult low-shot cross-domain decisions without target-time optimization.

</details>


### [28] [Skip the Talk, Re-Focus on Vision: Latent Reasoning for Reasoning Segmentation in Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30783)
*Tianhang Guo,Yulin He,Wei Chen,Wenjuan Zhou,Yuhang Li,Xinbiao Gan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LIRSeg replaces explicit chain-of-thought reasoning with a compact set of learnable latent tokens for reasoning-based segmentation, achieving superior segmentation accuracy with substantially fewer reasoning tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explicit CoT in multimodal reasoning introduces attention interference and longer effective token distances, hindering fine-grained visual segmentation. A latent-token-based reasoning approach aims to preserve interpretability and reasoning capacity while reducing token overhead.

Method: Two-stage training: (1) spatial alignment grounds latent tokens in object-relevant visual evidence; (2) GRPO (a policy-gradient-like optimization) refines tokens with segmentation rewards. Three information-theoretic mechanisms enhance learning: extreme-advantage sampling to select informative signals; decoupled exploration-stability updates to learn complementary representations; latent diversity amplification to avoid representational collapse.

Result: On ReasonSeg, MUSE, and MMR benchmarks, LIRSeg yields absolute gIoU improvements of 4.9%, 7.1%, and 4.7% respectively over VisionReasoner, and reduces reasoning tokens by ~16×. Code is provided in supplementary materials.

Conclusion: LIRSeg demonstrates that compact latent reasoning tokens can replace explicit CoT to improve both segmentation performance and reasoning efficiency, suggesting broad applicability to reasoning-centric vision tasks with reduced token overhead.

Abstract: Reasoning segmentation aims to interpret implicit textual queries and enable fine-grained visual perception, which is critical for applications such as human-computer interaction and embodied agents. Existing methods typically generate explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) by multimodal large language models (MLLMs) before localizing the target. Although intuitive, such explicit verbal reasoning introduces substantial attention interference: redundant textual tokens disrupt attention during perception-token generation and also increase the effective distance between visual tokens. To address this issue, we propose LIRSeg, which fully replaces explicit CoT with a compact set of learnable latent tokens for reasoning segmentation. LIRSeg is trained in two stages: spatial alignment grounds the latent tokens in object-relevant visual evidence, and GRPO further optimizes them with segmentation rewards. To make these compact latent tokens more informative, we introduce three complementary mechanisms from an information perspective: extreme-advantage sampling for selecting informative training signals, decoupled exploration-stability updates for learning complementary representations, and latent diversity amplification for preventing representational collapse. Extensive experiments on benchmarks demonstrate that LIRSeg consistently improves both segmentation accuracy and reasoning efficiency. Compared with the VisionReasoner baseline, LIRSeg achieves absolute gIoU improvements of 4.9% on ReasonSeg, 7.1% on MUSE, and 4.7% on MMR, while achieving a approximately 16x reduction in reasoning tokens. Code is available in supplementary materials.

</details>


### [29] [Motion Style Slider: Endpoint-Supervised Continuous Style Control for Human Motion Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30795)
*Chen-Chieh Liao,Yichen Peng,Yiyi Cai,Yûi Ono,Hiroki Hanaoka,Erwin Wu,Hideki Koike,Shuichi Kurabayashi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes Motion Style Slider: a diffusion-based motion-to-motion style transfer with a monotonic, endpoint-supervised, continuous intensity control for style transfer, built from a style-direction in a learned embedding space and trained with denoising plus latent intensity regularization; compatible with pretrained backbones and heterogeneous datasets, with an out-of-range extension to test extreme intensities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a need for fine-grained, monotonic, continuous control of motion style intensity in animation pipelines, as current style transfer methods offer subjective, discrete cues and lack a reliable scale across artists and directors.

Method: Introduce Motion Style Slider: compute a style direction in a motion-style embedding space from content and style motions, condition diffusion generation with a scalar intensity, and train with denoising loss plus latent intensity regularization to ensure smooth, monotonic style scaling without intermediate ground-truths. The framework is endpoint-supervised, backbone-compatible, and evaluated on multi-actor and heterogeneous style datasets, with an additional real-capture extension for large intensities.

Result: Experiments assess controllability, interpolation/extrapolation, content preservation, and realism, with ablations on direction construction and loss design, demonstrating smooth, monotonic style scaling, compatibility with pretrained backbones, and robustness to unseen extreme targets.

Conclusion: Motion Style Slider enables practical, monotonic, continuous control of motion style in diffusion-based generation, leverages a learned style-direction embedding, and remains compatible with existing backbones and diverse datasets; it includes an out-of-range extension to probe extreme intensity behavior.

Abstract: Existing human motion diffusion methods provide strong motion generation quality, and recent style transfer models can inject target style cues, but fine-grained continuous control of style intensity remains underexplored. In production, style intensity is subjective across artists and directors, so the practical requirement is not a universal absolute unit, but a reliable monotonic control axis. We propose Motion Style Slider, a motion-to-motion style transfer framework for endpoint-supervised continuous control. Given a content motion and a style motion, we construct a style direction in a learned motion-style embedding space and condition diffusion generation with a scalar intensity. The training objective combines diffusion denoising with latent intensity regularization to encourage smooth and monotonic style scaling without requiring intermediate-intensity ground-truth motions. Our framework is compatible with pretrained motion diffusion backbones and supports heterogeneous style datasets, including the multi-actor style motion dataset. To test out-of-range usability, we additionally introduce a small real-capture over-reaction extension and evaluate large-intensity behavior against these unseen targets. Experiments measure controllability, interpolation/extrapolation behavior, content preservation, and motion realism, with ablations on direction construction and loss design.

</details>


### [30] [MDSkin-Net: Multi-Task Skin Lesion Analysis Driven by Pattern Analysis Priors and Spatial Alignment Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30855)
*Yijian Li,Saad Bedros,Paul Bigliardi,Mei Bigliardi Qi,Vassilios Morellas,Nikolaos Papanikolopoulos*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MDSkin-Net integrates Pattern Analysis priors into a hybrid CNN-Transformer for joint segmentation/classification; it uses a Pattern Analysis-Guided Attention Module with iECA, MSSA, and BAA, plus multi-scale spatial alignment regularization to leverage segmentation masks as soft supervision; achieves strong zero-shot transfer and competitive/in-domain performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dermoscopic diagnosis benefits from microscopic Pattern Analysis cues; existing multi-task or macroscopic-prior approaches lack clinical grounding. Incorporating dermoscopic feature-based priors aims to improve segmentation and classification robustness and cross-cohort generalization.

Method: A hybrid CNN-Transformer architecture (MDSkin-Net) with a Pattern Analysis-Guided Attention Module (PAGAM) consisting of three priors: improved Efficient Channel Attention (iECA), Multi-Scale Spatial Attention (MSSA), and Biased Asymmetry Attention (BAA). Includes a multi-scale spatial alignment regularization (MSAR) that uses segmentation masks as hierarchical soft supervision to constrain the classification head and couple tasks via a shared spatial prior. Trained only on ISIC 2017; ensemble evaluated zero-shot on PH2 and ISIC2018 Task 1, and in-domain on ISIC 2017.

Result: Zero-shot: DSC 92.38% and melanoma AUC 97.84% on PH2; DSC 88.92% on ISIC2018 Task 1. In-domain: mean AUC 91.60% across melanoma and seborrheic keratosis vs. rest; DSC 84.72% for segmentation. Classification competitive with baselines; segmentation slightly behind single-task specialists but priors/regularization promote cross-cohort generalization.

Conclusion: Incorporating Pattern Analysis priors and MSAR yields representations that generalize across cohorts of varying scale, achieving robust zero-shot transfer and competitive in-domain performance for joint dermoscopic segmentation and classification.

Abstract: Reliable skin lesion segmentation and classification are central to dermoscopic computer-aided diagnosis. Existing multi-task frameworks couple the two tasks architecturally without clinical knowledge, while knowledge-injecting approaches rely on the macroscopic ABCD rule, which was not designed for dermoscopy. Dermoscopic diagnosis is grounded in Pattern Analysis, a microscopic framework structured around dermoscopic features. We propose MDSkin-Net, which incorporates cue-level Pattern Analysis priors into a hybrid CNN-Transformer architecture. At its core is a Pattern Analysis-Guided Attention Module (PAGAM) comprising three priors motivated by distinct dermoscopic cues: an improved Efficient Channel Attention (iECA), a Multi-Scale Spatial Attention (MSSA), and a Biased Asymmetry Attention (BAA). We further introduce a multi-scale spatial alignment regularization (MSAR) that uses the segmentation ground-truth mask as hierarchical soft supervision, confining the classification head to lesion-localized evidence and coupling both task pathways through a shared spatial prior. Trained exclusively on the ISIC 2017 training split without external dermoscopy data, the MDSkin-Net ensemble transfers robustly under zero-shot evaluation, reaching a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 92.38% and a melanoma AUC of 97.84%on PH2, and a DSC of 88.92% on the ISIC 2018 Task 1 test set. On the in-domain ISIC 2017 benchmark, the ensemble attains a mean Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 91.60% across the two classification tasks (melanoma and seborrheic keratosis vs. rest), and a DSC of 84.72% for segmentation. Classification remains competitive with baselines; in-domain segmentation trails single-task specialists, yet the proposed priors and alignment regularization yield representations that generalize consistently across cohorts of different scales.

</details>


### [31] [Reliability-Regulated Trajectory Optimization for Progressive COLMAP-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30865)
*Zijian Wu,Jinliang Wang,Zidian Lin,Ying Song,Ziqian Lu,Hanjie Ma,Zhen Ye,Mingfeng Jiang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A self-supervised reliability-regulated trajectory optimization framework (RRTO-CF3DGS) improves COLMAP-free 3D Gaussian Splatting by mitigating drift via bidirectional cycle-consistency, using Forward Motion Propagation and Retrospective Trajectory Correction, without external priors. It yields better camera trajectories and novel-view rendering on Tanks and Temples and CO3D-V2; code available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Progressive camera pose tracking in COLMAP-free 3DGS is susceptible to error accumulation that corrupts future initializations and becomes baked in; a unified solution that regulates both initialization and trajectory consolidation without heavy priors or offline preprocessing is needed.

Method: Introduce a self-supervised reliability regulator with two modules: Forward Motion Propagation that gates first-order motion warm-starts into pairwise registrations to provide directional priors and block untrusted transitions, and Retrospective Trajectory Correction that weights relative-pose constraints in a sliding window based on reliability signals; both rely on cycle-consistency across forward and backward temporal horizons.

Result: Extensive evaluation on Tanks and Temples and CO3D-V2 shows substantial improvements in camera trajectory accuracy and novel-view rendering quality, outperforming unposed baselines; code released.

Conclusion: A unified reliability-regulated trajectory optimization framework can resolve progressive drift in COLMAP-free 3DGS without external priors or offline preprocessing, improving robustness and rendering quality; potential applicability to other unposed SfM-free pipelines.

Abstract: COLMAP-free 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) bypasses computationally expensive structure-from-motion (SfM) pipelines, yet progressive camera pose tracking remains fundamentally vulnerable to error compounding---early pairwise tracking inaccuracies both corrupt subsequent frame initializations and remain permanently frozen in the scene representation. Rather than relying on heavyweight external neural priors or treating progressive tracking through isolated heuristic fixes, we propose a unified reliability-regulated trajectory optimization framework for progressive COLMAP-free 3DGS. At its core, our framework establishes an intrinsic, self-supervised bidirectional cycle-consistency mechanism that systematically regulates progressive camera trajectory estimation across two complementary temporal horizons: (1) Forward Motion Propagation, where the online reliability signal adaptively gates first-order kinematic warm-starts of rigid motion into upcoming pairwise registrations, supplying informed directional search priors while safely intercepting untrusted transitions; and (2) Retrospective Trajectory Correction, where the same reliability signal dynamically weights relative-pose consistency constraints within a sliding window of neighboring camera poses. By governing both prospective state initialization and retrospective trajectory consolidation through a unified reliability regulator, our self-contained framework resolves progressive drift without external priors or offline preprocessing. Extensive evaluations on Tanks and Temples and CO3D-V2 benchmarks show that our method substantially improves camera trajectory accuracy and novel-view rendering quality, outperforming existing unposed baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/Zijian1026/RRTO-CF3DGS.

</details>


### [32] [UltraG-Bench: A Multi-task Benchmark for assessing Large Vision-Language Models on Pixel-level Evidence Grounding in Ultrasound](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30928)
*Quanhao Zhu,Bo Xu,Rui Lin,Chenyuan Wang,Yu Shao,Boling Zhu,Jiuyan Sun,Liang Zhao,Hongfei Lin,Feng Xia*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: UltraG-Bench is a large-scale, multi-task benchmark for pixel-level evidence grounding in ultrasound, filling a gap between semantic predictions and fine-grained localization.



<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate and improve the pixel-level visual grounding abilities of vision-language models (VLMs) in ultrasound, where semantic predictions often lack corresponding visual evidence.

Method: Assembles 40 public ultrasound segmentation datasets across 13 anatomical categories into a single benchmark and defines three tasks: instruction-guided segmentation, evidence-grounded VQA, and evidence-grounded report generation, with large-scale annotations (331,125; 666,779; 138,832).

Result: 14 state-of-the-art models reveal a substantial gap between semantic understanding and pixel-level grounding. UltraG-Agent, which fuses VLM semantic reasoning with Ultrasound-specific segmentation (UltraSAM3), significantly improves both semantic predictions and pixel-level grounding.

Conclusion: UltraG-Bench provides a comprehensive platform to assess and close the gap between high-level predictions and pixel-perfect localization in ultrasound, and UltraG-Agent demonstrates the benefit of integrating ultrasound-aware segmentation with semantic reasoning.

Abstract: Ultrasound is one of the most widely used medical imaging modalities, and recent large vision-language models(VLMs) have shown increasing capabilities in ultrasound image understanding. However, these models fail to provide pixel-level visual evidence aligned with their semantic predictions, and their fine-grained grounding capability in ultrasound remains largely unclear. We introduce UltraG-Bench, a large-scale multi-task benchmark for evaluating pixel-level evidence grounding in ultrasound. UltraG-Bench is built by annotating 40 public ultrasound segmentation datasets spanning 13 anatomical categories, and comprises three progressive tasks: instruction-guided segmentation, evidence-grounded VQA, and evidence-grounded report generation, with 331125, 666779, and 138832 annotations, respectively. Comprehensive evaluation of 14 state-of-the-art models reveals a substantial gap between semantic understanding and fine-grained pixel-level localization. We further propose UltraG-Agent, which combines the semantic reasoning capabilities of a VLM with the ultrasound-specific segmentation capability of UltraSAM3. Experiments show that UltraG-Agent substantially improves both semantic prediction and pixel-level visual grounding. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/zhuqh19/UltraG-Bench.

</details>


### [33] [ManiVid: Unified and Explainable Forensic Analysis of Manipulated Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30934)
*Hengrui Kang,Zhonghao Yan,Yuxuan Yang,Ruoyan Jing,Yuncheng Guo,Hao Chen,Kongming Liang,Zhanyu Ma,Conghui He,Weijia Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ManiVid introduces ManiVid-38K dataset and ManiVidLens framework for unified forensic analysis of manipulated videos, addressing detection, artifact grounding, and anomaly explanation; achieves notable gains on grounding and explanation tasks, with competitive detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rising AI-generated video manipulation poses forgery risks; existing datasets and methods lack open-vocabulary, pixel-level grounding and unified analysis across detection, grounding, and explanation.

Method: Construct ManiVid-38K dataset with ~19K real-fake pairs, open-vocabulary localized manipulations, authenticity labels, forgery masks, anomaly explanations; sample ManiVidBench (~1K pairs) for fair evaluation; propose ManiVidLens with Forensic Evidence Router and Prompt Distill Module for grounding and full-video propagation.

Result: Artifact grounding gains: +21.1% mIoU; +21.3% J&F. Anomaly explanation gains: +131.3% ROUGE-L; +9.9% CSS. Forgery detection accuracy 0.914 and F1 0.913, comparable to dedicated classifiers.

Conclusion: Provides a unified, explainable framework for video forgery analysis; dataset enables comprehensive evaluation; demonstrates significant improvements in grounding and explanation, with competitive detection.

Abstract: Rapid advances in AI-generated video (AIGV) have increased the risks posed by deceptive video manipulation. Unlike fully synthetic videos, manipulated videos retain most source content and alter only localized regions, making forensic analysis particularly challenging. Existing video forgery research faces two limitations in both data and methodology: (1) High-quality datasets and benchmarks tailored for manipulated videos remain scarce. (2) Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) extend forgery analysis beyond binary classification but struggle to use low-level forensic cues and provide precise pixel-level grounding. Specifically, we introduce ManiVid, a unified forensic analysis task covering forgery detection, artifact grounding, and anomaly explanation for manipulated videos. We construct ManiVid-38K, the first dataset to combine paired, open-vocabulary localized manipulations of general videos with authenticity labels, forgery masks, and anomaly explanations. It comprises about 19K manually verified real-fake video pairs, mostly at 1080P resolution, generated under 2 paradigms with 15 powerful generation models. We sample 1K pairs for ManiVidBench, balanced across six manipulation types and generation models for fair evaluation. We further propose ManiVidLens, a unified framework for explainable video forgery analysis. Its Forensic Evidence Router supplies shared low-level forensic evidence for multimodal reasoning and video segmentation. Its Prompt Distill Module converts grounding states into semantic and geometric prompts and distills spatial priors for mask decoding and full-video propagation. ManiVidLens achieves relative gains over the strongest comparison methods in artifact grounding (+21.1% mIoU; +21.3% J&F) and anomaly explanation (+131.3% ROUGE-L; +9.9% CSS). Its forgery detection remains comparable to dedicated classifiers (0.914 Acc; 0.913 F1).

</details>


### [34] [Spackle: Completing Large View Single Image NVS with Adaptive Gaussians](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30941)
*Xuanzhi Liu,Yuhe Zhou,Xinyi Wu,Zhenyao Wu,Jinghao Chen,Ruize Han,Song Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Spackle mitigates capacity competition in hybrid 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) + diffusion NVS by learning a lightweight residual 3DGS only for poorly reconstructed regions, combined with a base 3DGS. It achieves state-of-the-art results on large-view-deviation NVS while remaining efficient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hybrid 3DGS+diffusion NVS suffers from capacity competition: a fixed Gaussian budget shifts resources away from visible to disoccluded regions, degrading fidelity as the target view diverges from the input. A residual refinement focused on error-prone areas promises better reconstruction without sacrificing efficiency.

Method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) predict base 3DGS attributes from the given views; (2) automatically identify poorly reconstructed regions; (3) train a residual 3DGS specialized for those regions. At inference, combine baseline Gaussians with augmented Gaussians to render novel views, enabling efficient large-view-deviation NVS.

Result: Comprehensive experiments report state-of-the-art performance on large-view-deviation NVS scenarios, demonstrating improved reconstruction fidelity in disoccluded areas while maintaining efficiency through selective residual augmentation.

Conclusion: Spackle offers a lightweight, targeted residual refinement for 3DGS-based NVS, addressing capacity competition and enabling superior performance in challenging view deviations without compromising efficiency.

Abstract: Single-image novel view synthesis (NVS) enables photorealistic rendering of un- observed viewpoints from a single input. Practical NVS systems require two key capabilities: robust reconstruction of occluded regions and high inference effi- ciency. While hybrid decoupled frameworks combining feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and diffusion models show promise for large-view-deviation NVS, they suffer from capacity competition: a fixed number of Gaussians forces resource shifts from visible to newly disoccluded areas, degrading original scene fidelity when the target view deviates significantly from the input. To address this, we propose Spackle, a lightweight residual learning framework that mit- igates capacity competition without sacrificing efficiency. Spackle operates in three stages: predicting base 3DGS attributes from given views, automatically identifying poorly reconstructed regions, and learning a residual 3DGS optimized exclusively for these areas. At inference, we combine the baseline and aug- mented Gaussians for NVS. We conduct comprehensive experiments and show that Spackle achieves state-of-the-art performance on large-view-deviation cases.

</details>


### [35] [OneWorld: Learning Consistent Physics Across Actions in World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30946)
*Ke He,Yichen Ding,Bin Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OneWorld jointly models multiple action-conditioned futures using a shared latent physical mechanism, aligning their latent explanations via a mechanism interpreter and shared-world evidence, and evaluates via a multi-intervention protocol; it improves cross-intervention physical consistency while maintaining single-rollout accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Futures generated from the same initial scene can be individually plausible yet imply conflicting physical parameters, undermining reliability for planning; need a consistent underlying physics across interventions.

Method: Infer latent mechanism distributions per action-outcome branch with a physical mechanism interpreter; aggregate into shared-world evidence that captures common physical explanations and uncertainty; use evidence to constrain flow training and guide sampling; introduce multi-intervention evaluation protocol mirroring ACWM-Phys to assess joint explainability of futures.

Result: Empirical results show improved cross-intervention physical consistency without sacrificing competitive single-rollout prediction quality.

Conclusion: Jointly modeling multiple futures under a shared physical mechanism yields more coherent world models that are better suited for planning under action interventions.

Abstract: Action-conditioned video world models aim to predict scene evolution under different actions, a capability that is essential for reliable planning, decision-making, and interaction in dynamic environments. However, futures generated independently from the same initial scene may each appear plausible while implying incompatible physical properties, such as friction or mass. This inconsistency can lead to contradictory predictions across interventions, making it difficult for the model to maintain a coherent understanding of the underlying world and limiting its reliability for planning and decision-making. To address these issues, we propose OneWorld, a shared-mechanism counterfactual generation framework that jointly models multiple action-conditioned futures under a common latent physical mechanism. A physical mechanism interpreter first infers a distribution over latent mechanisms from each action-outcome branch. These distributions are then aggregated into shared-world evidence, which captures whether the branches admit a common physical explanation while accounting for uncertainty in less informative branches. This evidence constrains flow training and guides sampling, encouraging consistency in the underlying physical mechanism while preserving the distinct outcomes induced by different actions. We further introduce a multi-intervention evaluation protocol in controlled environments, following the interaction settings of ACWM-Phys, to assess whether generated futures can be jointly explained by the same physical parameters, alongside standard measures of single-rollout prediction quality. Experiments in these environments show that OneWorld improves cross-intervention physical consistency while maintaining competitive single-rollout prediction quality.

</details>


### [36] [DAPEVO: Deep Adaptive Patch Frame-Event Visual Odometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30947)
*Luca Gandolfi,Simone Nascivera,Roberto Pellerito,Rong Zou,Chiara Plizzari,Davide Scaramuzza*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DAPEVO fuses image and event cues per patch with a learned gating mechanism to robustly estimate VO under degraded RGB inputs, including event-only tracking, and shows major robustness gains over DPVO, RAMP-VO, and DEVO on UZH-FPV and TartanEvent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RGB-based visual odometry struggles with motion blur, challenging illumination, and dropped frames. Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and dynamic range, but asynchronous data complicates correspondence. Integrating both modalities aims to improve robustness and continuity.

Method: DAPEVO computes image and event descriptors independently at shared patch locations, learns a per-patch scalar gate to fuse modality-specific correlation embeddings before a shared recurrent refinement and bundle-adjustment stage. Each tracked patch stores per-modality descriptors; event-only observations are supported; modality-aware keyframe culling preserves frame constraints.

Result: When RGB frames are reduced to one in six, mean ATE on UZH-FPV increases from 1.00m to 1.36m for DAPEVO (a 36% rise) while DPVO and RAMP-VO worsen by ~3.7x and ~3.1x respectively. On TartanEvent, DAPEVO remains below 1m ATE at 3Hz RGB; DPVO and RAMP-VO exceed 9m. Under degraded RGB, DAPEVO achieves 0.60m ATE vs >4m for DPVO/RAMP-VO, and outperforms event-only DEVO at 0.87m.

Conclusion: DAPEVO delivers robust VO by fusing per-patch image and event cues with a learned gate, enabling strong performance under sparse RGB frames and in event-rich scenarios. The approach demonstrates clear advantages over state-of-the-art RGB-only and event-aware baselines, though potential trade-offs include computational load from per-patch descriptors and the need for broader validation across datasets.

Abstract: Visual odometry is essential for autonomous navigation in GPS-denied environments, yet RGB-based methods remain vulnerable to motion blur, challenging illumination, and dropped frames. Event cameras complement conventional cameras with high temporal resolution and dynamic range, but their asynchronous measurements complicate reliable correspondence estimation. We present DAPEVO, a learned visual odometry system that estimates image and event correspondences independently at shared patch locations and fuses their correlation evidence before motion refinement. Each tracked patch maintains image and event descriptors, and a learned scalar gate combines modality-specific correlation embeddings for each patch--frame edge before a shared recurrent refinement and bundle-adjustment update. DAPEVO also supports event-only observations, enabling continued tracking when RGB frames are sparse or unavailable, while modality-aware keyframe culling preserves scarce frame constraints. On UZH-FPV, when retaining only one in six RGB frames, DAPEVO's mean absolute trajectory error (ATE) increases by only 36%, from 1.00 to 1.36m, whereas the ATE of DPVO and RAMP-VO rises by factors of $3.7\times$ and $3.1\times$, respectively. On TartanEvent, DAPEVO similarly remains below 1m ATE at 3Hz RGB input, while DPVO and RAMP-VO exceed 9m. Under degraded RGB input on TartanEvent, DAPEVO achieves an ATE of 0.60m, compared with more than 4m for both DPVO and RAMP-VO, while also outperforming event-only DEVO at 0.87m.

</details>


### [37] [MVVBench: Benchmarking 4D Reasoning in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30952)
*Hyungjin Chung,Byeongjun Park,Joonseok Lee,Hojun Kim,Jaeho Choi,Byung-Hoon Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MVVBench introduces a benchmark for cross-view, cross-time 4D multi-view reasoning in video, using monocular-ambiguous questions across multiple camera streams; it analyzes LLMs and proposes elicitation scaffolds and reinforcement-based training cues to improve latent cross-view competence without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the gap in evaluating and training models for 4D multi-view reasoning in embodied perception, where evidence must be integrated across views and time, and single-view or single-frame reasoning is insufficient.

Method: Construct MVVBench from real multi-camera datasets with monocular-ambiguous QA designed so answers require joint cross-view and cross-time reasoning; define six capabilities (attribute identification, relative distance, relative pose, counting); provide human-authored QA and verification; analyze LLM success/failure; propose task-specific chain-of-thought scaffolds and structured cross-view evidence aggregation; explore reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards to elicit latent competence.

Result: Key observations: failures due to temporal mis-localization, cross-view identity breaks, and brittle multi-hop reasoning; elicitation strategies significantly improve performance without retraining; preliminary evidence that RL with verifiable rewards can elicit some latent multi-view competence; benchmark offers a robust evaluation framework and baseline for future work.

Conclusion: MVVBench provides a rigorous 4D multi-view reasoning benchmark and lays groundwork for future progress toward reliable embodied perception, including training-time directions via elicitation and RL-based approaches.

Abstract: Multi-view video understanding requires integrating spatial and temporal evidence across multiple, often non-overlapping camera streams: tracking entities as they transition between viewpoints, aligning events across time, and reasoning about latent 4D continuity rather than any single visible frame. We introduce MVVBench, a benchmark for multi-view video reasoning built from real world multi camera datasets. Questions are curated to be monocular-ambiguous along both the view and the temporal axis: each question is unanswerable from any single view in the designated input set, and the majority are further unanswerable from any single moment. Each question becomes uniquely solvable only by jointly reasoning across views and across time. MVVBench spans diverse dynamic scenes and probes six capabilities: implicit/explicit attribute identification, implicit/explicit relative distance, relative camera pose, and compositional counting, with human-authored QA and rigorous verification. Beyond benchmarking, we provide an extensive analysis of when and why current vision language models succeed or fail, characterizing errors due to temporal mis-localization, cross-view identity breaks, and brittle multi-hop reasoning. We then study inference-time elicitation strategies that unlock latent multi-view competence---task-specific chain-of-thought scaffolds and structured cross-view evidence aggregation---yielding substantial gains without retraining. Finally, we present preliminary evidence that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can elicit some latent multi-view competence in the base model, pointing to training-time approaches as a promising direction for future work. Together, MVVBench offers a rigorous evaluation of 4D multi-view reasoning and a foundation for future progress toward reliable embodied perception.

</details>


### [38] [IDM-Net: A Lightweight Illumination-Decoupled Modulation Network for Low-Light Image Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30962)
*Cheng-Yen Hsiao,Jing-Ming Guo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: IDM-Net is a lightweight LLIE framework that uses illumination-decoupled modulation via a dual-encoder design and an Illumination-Guided Modulation (IGM) module to inject luminance priors into reconstruction, achieving favorable restoration-quality and efficiency trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Joint optimization of illumination restoration and color fidelity in RGB is challenging for lightweight models; existing color-decoupled approaches decouple luminance but underutilize luminance as an explicit guidance prior in feature reconstruction.

Method: A dual-encoder architecture with a structure encoder for multi-scale RGB appearance features and a lightweight illumination encoder that learns priors from the luminance (Y) channel; an Illumination-Guided Modulation (IGM) module applies multi-scale illumination cues to the decoder via spatially adaptive affine modulation; a lightweight Feature Refinement Block (FRB) progressively suppresses artifacts and recovers details.

Result: On standard LLIE benchmarks, IDM-Net achieves competitive performance among lightweight methods while maintaining an excellent restoration-quality–efficiency balance.

Conclusion: IDM-Net demonstrates effective illumination-guided, decoupled modulation for LLIE, enabling natural color fidelity and brightness restoration with low computational cost.

Abstract: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) remains challenging for lightweight models because illumination restoration and color fidelity are difficult to optimize simultaneously in the RGB color space. Although recent color-decoupled methods separate luminance and chrominance representations, they primarily optimize luminance as an enhancement target, leaving its potential as an explicit guidance prior largely unexplored during feature reconstruction. To address this limitation, we propose IDM-Net, a lightweight Illumination-Decoupled Modulation Network for low-light image enhancement. IDM-Net adopts a dual-encoder architecture consisting of a structure encoder that extracts multi-scale appearance features from the RGB image and a lightweight illumination encoder that learns illumination priors from the decoupled luminance (Y) channel. To effectively exploit these priors, we introduce an Illumination-Guided Modulation (IGM) module that injects multi-scale illumination cues into the decoder through spatially adaptive affine modulation, enabling accurate brightness restoration while preserving natural color consistency. Furthermore, we design a lightweight Feature Refinement Block (FRB) to progressively suppress degradation artifacts and recover fine-grained image details during reconstruction. Extensive experiments on multiple standard low-light image enhancement benchmarks demonstrate that IDM-Net achieves competitive performance among lightweight LLIE methods while maintaining an excellent balance between restoration quality and computational efficiency.

</details>


### [39] [Where and When to Force: Routed Forcing for Streaming Avatars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30963)
*Zihan Su,Siwen Lu,Junhao Zhuang,Zeyue Xue,Haoyang Huang,Guanghao Li,Xiaofeng Tan,Chun Yuan,Nan Duan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Routed Forcing reduces mode collapse in audio-driven avatar diffusion by region- and stage-aware distillation, improving dynamics and diversity while keeping lip-sync and visual quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reverse KL-based Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) in Self Forcing tends to be mode-seeking, collapsing dynamics and diversity in generated videos, with region-heterogeneous losses (pose/gestures most affected).

Method: Introduce semantic-region routing (Data-Forcing Distillation on the most diverse region, i.e., person) and noise-stage routing (apply DFD at high noise stages; use DMD at low noise stages) to balance realism, synchronization, and diversity.

Result:  empirically, Routed Forcing yields up to 45% gains in dynamics and 7–25% gains in diversity over Self Forcing, while maintaining video quality and lip synchronization.

Conclusion: Region- and stage-aware distillation (Routed Forcing) effectively mitigates mode collapse and preserves synchronization, offering a practical improvement for real-time audio-driven avatar generation.

Abstract: Audio-driven streaming avatar generation requires real-time synthesis of speech-synchronized videos with dynamic and diverse motion. Self Forcing uses Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) to distill bidirectional video diffusion models into causal, few-step generators for real-time streaming. However, DMD minimizes a reverse KL divergence, which is inherently mode-seeking: it causes the student to discard high-dynamic modes and collapse onto static outputs, compressing both dynamics and diversity of generated videos. We find that this collapse is region-heterogeneous: person regions involving pose and gesture variations suffer the largest diversity loss, the audio-driven mouth region shows a small loss, and the background remains nearly stable. Based on this observation, we propose Routed Forcing, which routes the distillation objective by semantic region and noise stage to improve dynamics and diversity while preserving visual quality. Specifically, (1) Where to Force: Semantic-Region Routing applies Data-Forcing Distillation (DFD), which supervises the student with real videos, to the person region where diversity collapse is most severe, while retaining DMD for the mouth and background to preserve lip synchronization and scene stability. (2) When to Force: Noise-Stage Routing activates DFD at high noise stages, where real video serves as effective supervision to inject diverse and dynamic motion patterns. At low noise stages, DMD is used to refine details, avoiding blur and artifacts from spatial differences between real video and student-generated video. Experiments show that Routed Forcing improves dynamics by up to 45% and diversity by 7-25% over Self Forcing, while preserving video quality and lip synchronization.

</details>


### [40] [CCRV-Bench: Constraint-Based Evaluation of Causal Reasoning in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30979)
*Linyuan Gao,Yuan Wu,Yi Chang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CCRV-Bench is a constraint-driven visual causal reasoning benchmark for single-image physical scenarios that assesses four causal tasks under controlled constraints, revealing that robustness to constraints varies by task and model and that aggregate scores can mask specific failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current VLM evaluations often conflate causal reasoning with reliance on statistical correlations, failing to distinguish true causal understanding from shortcuts; there is a need for a standardized, constraint-based evaluation framework to diagnose image-grounded causal reasoning.

Method: An orthogonal framework evaluating four causal task dimensions (causal relation discovery, state prediction, causal diagnosis, intervention) with constraint mechanisms including entity symbolization, spatial grounding, factual adversarial constraint, and minimalist output constraints; evaluates 15 multimodal models to study constraint sensitivity across tasks.

Result: Constraint sensitivity is task- and model-dependent: intervention shows the largest average degradation; spatial grounding is the most damaging constraint on average; factual adversarial constraint improves DCR for all models; unconstrained performance does not guarantee constrained robustness; a single aggregate score can mask distinct failures in causal identification, spatial grounding, and constraint-compliant expression.

Conclusion: CCRV-Bench provides a standardized framework for diagnosing image-grounded causal reasoning under controlled constraints and offers code for reproducible evaluation.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated excellent performance in visual tasks, but their visual causal reasoning capabilities still lack reliable evaluation. Existing evaluations struggle to distinguish whether a model is performing causal reasoning based on visual evidence or relying on statistical correlations for shortcut learning, thereby potentially overestimating their actual capabilities. This paper proposes CCRV-Bench, a constraint-driven visual causal reasoning benchmark for single-image physical scenarios. We construct an orthogonal framework that evaluates four causal task dimensions: causal relation discovery, state prediction, causal diagnosis, and intervention. We further introduce entity symbolization, spatial grounding, the factual adversarial constraint, and minimalist output constraints to reduce shortcut cues while preserving the physical commonsense required by the task. Experiments across 15 multimodal models show that constraint sensitivity is task- and model-dependent: intervention has the largest average effective degradation among the four causal tasks, spatial grounding is the most damaging constraint on average, and the factual adversarial constraint improves DCR for all evaluated models. These results show that unconstrained performance does not determine constrained robustness and that a single aggregate score can obscure distinct failures in causal identification, spatial grounding, and constraint-compliant expression. CCRV-Bench provides a standardized framework for diagnosing image-grounded causal reasoning under controlled constraints. The code is available at https://github.com/0815linyuan/CCRV-Bench-Constraint-Based-Evaluation-of-Causal-Reasoning-in-Vision-Language-Models

</details>


### [41] [STORM-Bench: Evaluating Online Video QA under Evolving and Incomplete Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30981)
*Siru Zhong,Shenghan Tan,Rihong Yan,Xiaohui Lv,Yuzheng Zhuang,Shuai Tao,Wulong Liu,Haohuan Fu,Yuxuan Liang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A benchmark suite (STORM-Bench) for reliable online video question answering with state tracking and abstention; introduces STORM-BR metrics to expose epistemic reliability gaps; demonstrates overconfidence and need for reliable tracking in 14 video LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess coupled capabilities of state-transition tracking and uncertainty abstention under evolving and incomplete evidence in video QA; existing benchmarks emphasize static recognition or long-range retrieval.

Method: 5,736 questions across 630 episodes in STORM-Real and STORM-Sim at 1 FPS; questions stratified by change intensity (Low/Medium/High) and answerability (Known/Uncertain); evaluate 14 video LLMs; introduce STORM-BR (harmonic accuracy over answer-status) and STORM-BR-ATTR for uncertainty attribution.

Result: Online accuracy peaks at 60.3% (mean 51.7%); STORM-BR ranges 5.7%–35.6% (mean 18.8%), indicating pervasive overconfidence on uncertain queries; reveals gaps between task accuracy and epistemic reliability/state tracking; benchmark and code available.

Conclusion: High aggregate accuracy masks epistemic unreliability and poor state tracking; STORM-Bench provides a nuanced framework to evaluate online VQA with abstention, prompting improved model reliability and uncertainty handling.

Abstract: Reliable online video question answering requires tracking state transitions while selectively abstaining when visual evidence is insufficient. Existing benchmarks focus on static recognition or long-range retrieval, rarely evaluating these coupled capabilities under evolving and incomplete evidence. We present STORM-Bench, comprising 5,736 questions across 630 compact, change-dense episodes spanning five egocentric domains (STORM-Real) and two controlled simulation subsets (STORM-Sim) at 1 FPS. Questions are stratified by a proxy for accumulated change intensity (Low, Medium, High) and query-time answerability (Known, Uncertain). To measure reliability, we introduce STORM-BR, a harmonic metric over joint answer-status correctness that exposes abstention failures masked by aggregate accuracy, alongside STORM-BR-ATTR for uncertainty attribution. Across 14 video LLMs, online accuracy peaks at 60.3\% (mean 51.7\%), whereas STORM-BR ranges from 5.7\% to 35.6\% (mean 18.8\%), driven by pervasive overconfidence on uncertain queries. STORM-Bench shows that task accuracy masks these gaps in epistemic reliability and state tracking. Benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/siruzhong/STORM-Bench.

</details>


### [42] [FARE: Forensic Acceptance Region Estimation for Catching Bait-and-Switch Image Generators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30982)
*Kai Yao,Marc Juarez*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FARE enables deployment-time integrity auditing for AI image generators: it learns a generator-specific acceptance region from enrolled images and detects swaps (including model variants) using only a single test image; it outperforms baselines under strict operating points and is robust to exact-model and decision-only attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Opaque generator APIs risk silent substitutions after certification, undermining trust and safety. A lightweight, deployment-time audit can verify that the deployed generator matches the certified one.

Method: Enroll a certified generator by training FARE on samples from that generator to learn generator-specific forensic features. At inference, compare a new image against the enrolled region using only that image. Enhance features via hard-sample mining to tighten the acceptance region and increase sensitivity to subtle model changes.

Result: FARE consistently outperforms existing baselines at strict operating points across generator swaps, including substitutions with similar model versions/variants. It remains effective under exact-model and decision-only attacks evaluated in the work.

Conclusion: FARE provides a practical, deployment-time integrity auditing approach for image generators, enhancing public trust and safety in high-stakes deployments by detecting unauthorized swaps.

Abstract: Modern AI image generators are increasingly deployed as opaque APIs, where customers can query the deployed service, but cannot inspect model weights or architecture. This creates a practical challenge: a provider may pass governance certification with one generator and later silently switch to a cheaper and lower-quality one for deployment, compromising public trust or even safety in high-stakes domains. We study integrity auditing at deployment time and propose FARE (Forensic Acceptance Region Estimation). A certified generator is enrolled by training FARE on images sampled from that generator. After deployment, FARE can determine whether a generated image is consistent with the enrolled generator---using only that image. FARE's features are based on image generator-specific artifacts that have been proposed for forensic applications. FARE amplifies these features during training by finding hard samples that tighten the acceptance region and increase sensitivity to subtle changes in the certified generator. Across generator swaps, including substitutions with similar model versions and model variants, FARE is effective at detecting swaps, consistently outperforming existing baselines at strict operating points, and remains effective under the exact-model and decision-only attacks evaluated in this work.

</details>


### [43] [Self-Supervised Perceptually Interpretable Monocular Depth Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30987)
*Zain Ul Abidin,George Dimas,Dimitris K. Iakovidis*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PIMDE introduces perceptual feature maps (PFMs) and multi-branch depth estimators with explicit fusion to achieve interpretable, self-supervised monocular depth estimation with KITTI-level accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the lack of interpretability in self-supervised monocular depth estimation, where depth is inferred from RGB representations; aims to relate depth predictions to distinct perceptual cues for better failure analysis and safety.

Method: Decompose input images into perceptual feature maps (PFMs) encoding specific visual cues; deploy separate depth estimation branches (PIDEs) for each PFM; fuse the outputs through an explicit fusion mechanism to obtain final depth while enabling cue-level analysis.

Result: On KITTI, achieves performance comparable to established self-supervised MDE methods while providing insights into how different perceptual cues influence depth estimation.

Conclusion: Perceptual decomposition enables interpretable depth estimation without sacrificing accuracy, offering a framework to analyze contributions of visual cues and potentially diagnose failures.

Abstract: Self-supervised monocular depth estimation (MDE) enables depth prediction from monocular images without requiring ground-truth supervision, making it attractive for large-scale and real-world applications. Despite steady improvements in accuracy, most existing methods remain difficult to interpret, as depth is inferred from RGB representations that obscure the impact of individual perceptual image components. This lack of transparency limits systematic analysis of failure cases and reduces confidence in safety-critical settings. This paper presents a self-supervised framework for perceptually interpretable monocular depth estimation (PIMDE), designed to associate depth predictions with distinct perceptual components of the input image. Rather than operating directly on RGB inputs, the proposed method decomposes each image into a set of perceptual feature maps (PFMs), each encoding a specific visual cue. Distinct depth estimation branches process these PFMs independently to produce depth estimates (PIDEs), which are subsequently combined through an explicit fusion strategy. This formulation allows us to examine directly the contribution of each perceptual cue to the final depth prediction. Experiments conducted on the KITTI benchmark dataset demonstrate that PIMDE achieves performance comparable to established self-supervised MDE methods while providing additional insight into how different perceptual cues influence depth estimation. These results indicate that perceptual decomposition can support interpretability without sacrificing depth estimation accuracy.

</details>


### [44] [PhoenixSR: Generative Heterogeneous Distillation Unleashes Efficient Models for Real-World Super-Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30988)
*Xin Di,Mingyu Shi,Yuanfei Bao,Long Peng,Yue Zhao,Jiaming Guo,Renjing Pei,Xueyang Fu,Yang Cao,Zheng-Jun Zha*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Transfers diffusion priors to diffusion-free SR networks via score-based distribution matching, enabling perceptual gains with no inference-time diffusion overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world SR benefits from strong generative priors but diffusion methods are costly; efficient feed-forward SR struggles to recover high-frequency, perceptually realistic details.

Method: PhoenixSR uses score-based distribution matching with heterogeneous distribution adaptation to align the diffusion prior with SR domains, while paired supervision anchors reconstruction. Directional Reliability Weighting stabilizes training. After training, diffusion components are removed, leaving the original SR backbone unchanged.

Result: Across three SR benchmarks and six backbones (e.g., SwinIR, HAT, Real-ESRGAN, SeeMoRe), PhoenixSR yields consistent perceptual improvements with largely preserved reconstruction fidelity.

Conclusion: Diffusion priors can be effectively transferred to diffusion-free SR networks through distribution-level supervision and hetero adaptation, achieving better perceptual quality without increasing inference cost; the approach preserves the original architecture and runtime.

Abstract: Real-world image super-resolution (SR) requires recovering perceptually realistic high-resolution images from complex low-resolution observations while preserving faithful content. Diffusion-based SR benefits from strong generative priors but incurs substantial computational overhead, whereas feed-forward CNN and Transformer SR models are efficient yet often struggle to recover realistic high-frequency details. This motivates a natural question: can diffusion priors be transferred to existing diffusion-free SR networks without introducing diffusion components at inference time? To this end, we propose PhoenixSR, a generative heterogeneous distillation framework that transfers diffusion priors to independently designed feed-forward SR networks through score-based distribution matching. Rather than aligning heterogeneous features or imitating sampled diffusion outputs, PhoenixSR uses the pretrained diffusion model as distribution-level supervision, while paired SR supervision preserves reconstruction fidelity. To make distribution matching effective for fidelity-sensitive SR, we introduce Heterogeneous Distribution Adaptation, which adapts the target score to the SR domain, improves tracking of the evolving student distribution, and anchors training with paired supervision. We further employ Directional Reliability Weighting, a lightweight residual-consistency-based reweighting strategy that reduces unstable distributional guidance. All diffusion-related components are removed after training, leaving the original student architecture and inference cost unchanged. Experiments on three SR benchmarks and six feed-forward backbones, including SwinIR, HAT, Real-ESRGAN, and SeeMoRe, show consistent perceptual improvements with largely preserved reconstruction fidelity.

</details>


### [45] [PICO: Projection-Informed Consistency Optimisation for 6DoF Surgical Tool Pose Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30989)
*Lucy Fothergill,Pietro Valdastri,Dominic Jones,Duygu Sarikaya*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: End-to-end, multi-task 6DoF pose estimation for surgical tools (PICO) using segmentation, depth, and regression with geometry-aware proxy losses (projection and point-to-point) to improve robustness under occlusion; evaluated on SurgRIPE with strong rotation accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome accumulated errors in kinematics ( cable-driven robots ) and dependency on external markers in vision pipelines; achieve real-time, robust, 6DoF pose estimation without staged processing by leveraging geometry-aware training signals.

Method: An end-to-end network (PICO) that jointly predicts segmentation, depth maps, translations, and rotations, augmented with two proxy tasks: a projection loss enforcing 2D/3D geometric consistency and a point-to-point loss enforcing correspondence between predicted and true 3D points.

Result: On SurgRIPE across four subsets, PICO achieves consistently strong performance, with particularly strong rotation accuracy, ranking second under occlusion, and competitive translational accuracy even in occluded scenarios.

Conclusion: Multi-task learning with geometry-aware proxy tasks improves robustness and reliability of surgical tool pose estimation, especially under occlusion; suitable for real-time applications and future integration into robotic assistance systems.

Abstract: Purpose: Accurate 6 DoF pose estimation of surgical tools is critical for automa- tion, robotic proprioception, and safe interaction with the tissue operated on. Kinematics-based approaches suffer from accumulated errors due to the cable- driven nature of robotic arms, while vision-based methods often rely on external markers or trackers. Although more recent vision-based advances have been pro- posed, these two-stage pose estimation methods often lack real-time robustness due to accumulated errors and computational overhead. Methods: We propose a novel end-to-end trainable model, PICO. Our model employs a multi-task learning architecture to predict segmentation and depth maps, alongside regression of translation and rotation parameters. We define two proxy tasks that enforce geometric consistency in both 2D and 3D spaces, improving accuracy and robustness. For this, we propose a projection loss, and a point-to-point loss. Results: We evaluate our method on the SurgRIPE dataset, benchmarking its performance against state-of-the-art approaches using standard 6DoF pose esti- mation metrics. Our results demonstrate consistently strong performance across all four subsets, specifically in rotation, ranking second even under occlusion. It also demonstrates comparable translational performance, remaining competitive, especially in occluded cases. Conclusion: PICO demonstrates the effectiveness of multi-task learning and geometry-aware proxy tasks for robust and reliable surgical tool pose estimation, especially in occluded scenarios, highlighting potential for future applications.

</details>


### [46] [FLIP: Final Layer Inference-Time Probing for Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30993)
*Drandreb Earl O. Juanico,Rowel O. Atienza*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FLIP is a final-layer, inference-time probe that tests whether a logit-facing intervention in open-weight vision-language models induces structured task-linked computation rather than generic perturbation; it introduces a four-criterion protocol and a three-region response to a controlled detection/counting probe; results show robustness across same-site operators and multiple VLMs, with raw decoder-layer interventions failing to reproduce the signature; concludes it's a validation step for mechanistic interpretability, not a steering method.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To disambiguate the mechanism behind behavioral changes caused by internal interventions and provide a principled, testable protocol for intervention-based mechanistic interpretability.

Method: Apply elementwise flooring to the final normalized hidden state prior to logit computation; sweep intervention strength on a detection/counting probe; formalize a four-criterion probe-and-sweep protocol: regime structure, grounding-proxy alignment, feature-coherence dependence, and failure to reproduce positive regime on negative control; compare post-normalization state with logit-facing instantiation; test across same-site operators, raw decoder-layer interventions, and multiple VLMs.

Result: Observed three regions: negligible change, a bounded interior regime with improved detection recall at IoU 0.50 and reduced counting error, and over-suppression; on the test, the post-normalization state passes the protocol; raw decoder-layer interventions and the last-block pre-normalization outputs fail to reproduce the signature, while same-site operators and multiple VLMs reproduce it.

Conclusion: FLIP provides a validation step for intervention-based mechanistic interpretability, rather than a method to steer model outputs.

Abstract: We present FLIP, a final-layer inference-time probe for testing whether a logit-facing intervention site in an open-weight vision-language model (VLM) supports structured, task-linked computation rather than generic perturbation. Behavioral change under internal intervention is otherwise mechanistically ambiguous: it may reflect improved use of visual evidence, generic output instability, or outright degradation. FLIP applies elementwise flooring to the final normalized hidden state before logit computation, leaving parameters, prompts, and decoding unchanged. On a controlled detection/counting probe, sweeping intervention strength reveals three regions: negligible change, a bounded interior regime in which detection recall at IoU 0.50 ($R_{50}$) improves while tolerant counting error ($\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{count}}$) falls, and over-suppression. We formalize a four-criterion probe-and-sweep protocol for disciplining the interpretation of intervention effects: regime structure, grounding-proxy alignment, feature-coherence dependence, and failure to reproduce the same positive regime on a performance-based negative control. The post-normalization state passed to the output head is the logit-facing instantiation of this test; under a non-targeted flooring sweep it satisfies the full protocol. Raw decoder-layer interventions, including the last-block output before final normalization, and the singleton-pair left/right control fail to reproduce the Final-site signature, while same-site operators and multiple VLMs replicate it. FLIP is therefore a validation step for intervention-based mechanistic interpretability, not a steering method.

</details>


### [47] [TRACKGRAPH: Online Open-Vocabulary 3D Scene Graphs via Image-Space Tracking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31005)
*Peder Borge Hellesylt,Albert Gassol Puigjaner,Kostas Alexis,Annette Stahl*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Online open-vocabulary 3D mapping (TRACKGRAPH) maintains short-term 2D mask identities in the image stream, then fuses into a 3D scene graph for efficient open-vocabulary segmentation and retrieval, achieving faster speed and lower memory than prior methods while enabling real-world deployments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the high computational cost and latency of open-vocabulary 3D mapping by avoiding per-frame Vision-Language inference. Track 2D masks across frames with sparse keyframe processing and propagate between frames to enable real-time, open-vocabulary 3D mapping and retrieval.

Method: Maintain short-term 2D mask identities in the image stream. Compute FastSAM masks and CLIP features at sparse keyframes. Propagate masks between frames using dense DINOv3 features. Fuse masks into a class-agnostic 3D segment layer within a hierarchical scene graph. Use 3D association to handle tracking interruptions and long-term revisits. Employ compact multi-view CLIP embeddings for open-vocabulary retrieval.

Result: Competitive open-vocabulary segmentation and retrieval across Replica, ScanNet++, HM3D. Highest synonym frequency on Replica (0.50). On NVIDIA A100, 1.7x faster and 3.3x less GPU memory than ViT-H OVI-MAP. Real-world quadruped deployments show onboard scene graph construction and object search at 7.5 Hz; drone data used to test under aerial viewpoints.

Conclusion: TRACKGRAPH provides an efficient, scalable online open-vocabulary mapping approach that integrates short-term 2D mask tracking with 3D scene graphs, enabling real-time open-vocabulary reasoning for real-world robotics.

Abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D maps enable robots to reason about previously unknown environments using natural language. However, existing systems typically segment every incoming image, associate detections with persistent 3D segments, and frequently perform costly Vision-Language (VL) inference. We present TRACKGRAPH, an online open-vocabulary system that maintains short-term 2D mask identity directly in the image stream before fusing segments into 3D. FastSAM masks and CLIP features are computed at sparse keyframes, while dense DINOv3 features are used to propagate masks at a high rate in between. The resulting tracked masks are fused into a class-agnostic 3D segment layer within a hierarchical scene graph, with 3D association handling tracking interruptions and long-term revisits. Compact multi-view CLIP embeddings enable open-vocabulary retrieval. Across Replica, ScanNet++, and HM3D, TRACKGRAPH achieves competitive open-vocabulary segmentation and retrieval against state-of-the-art mapping methods, including the highest synonym frequency on Replica (0.50). On the same NVIDIA A100, it is 1.7x faster and uses 3.3x less GPU memory than ViT-H OVI-MAP. Real-world quadruped deployments demonstrate onboard scene graph construction and object search at 7.5Hz, while recorded drone data is used to test the method under aerial viewpoints.

</details>


### [48] [Refining Cytology Predictions with Conditional Random Fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31028)
*Manon Dausort,Tiffanie Godelaine,Karim El Khoury,Maxime Zanella,Christophe De Vleeschouwer,Benoît Macq*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CytoCRF tailors CRF refinement to cytology by designing chromatin- and staining-aware pairwise terms and enriching neighborhoods with multi-backbone ensembles; it yields robust gains across ten cytology datasets, surpassing all baselines and zero-shot performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLMs excel on histology but underperform on cytology due to differences in staining and cell morphology; existing CRF methods, designed for histopathology, fail to transfer to cytology datasets with independent patch pools from multiple stains.

Method: Adapt CRF pairwise terms to cytology by focusing on chromatin and cytology-specific staining; combine multiple backbones to enrich the neighborhood used in CRF refinement, enabling cross-stain patch propagation across independent patch pools.

Result: CytoCRF outperforms existing CRF frameworks at every annotation budget across ten cytology datasets, achieving up to +13.6 percentage points over the best baseline and +33.7 over zero-shot using only 50 annotations; multi-backbone ensembles provide further gains, indicating neighborhood topology more critical than the exact pairwise potential.

Conclusion: CytoCRF demonstrates effective transfer of CRF refinement to cytology, with neighborhood topology and multi-backbone ensembles driving performance; results support extending CRF-based refinement to diverse cytology datasets and staining protocols.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) achieve strong zero-shot (ZS) classification on histology images but do not perform as well on cytology, whose stains and cell morphology differ markedly compared to histology.
