Conditional random fields (CRFs) can refine noisy VLM predictions by propagating information across patches, but existing CRF frameworks were designed for histopathology and do not transfer to cytology datasets, released as independent patch pools spanning multiple staining protocols. We introduce CytoCRF, which adapts the pairwise terms to cytology by targeting chromatin and cytology-specific staining, and further enrich the neighborhood of each potential term by combining multiple backbones. Across ten cytology datasets, CytoCRF outperforms existing CRF frameworks at every annotation budget, reaching +13.6 percentage points over the best baseline and +33.7 over ZS with only 50 annotations. Combining information from multiple backbones brings further gains, showing that the neighborhood topology matters more than the pairwise potential computed over it.

</details>


### [49] [Exploiting Spatial Structure for Transductive Few-Shot Classification of Whole-Slide Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31040)
*Tiffanie Godelaine,Manon Dausort,Karim El Khoury,Benoît Gérin,Benoît Macq,Christophe De Vleeschouwer*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SlideTIM adapts transductive TIM to whole-slide images by enforcing spatial–latent consistency and a patch-class prior, yielding strong 1-shot gains in macro-F1 across four histology datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Zero-shot vision–language patch classification on whole-slide images is noisy for fine-grained tasks; there is a need for a transductive refinement tailored to WSIs that accounts for spatial layout and severe class imbalance.

Method: Adapt LC-TIM to WSIs by introducing a joint spatial–latent regularizer that promotes agreement among spatially and semantically similar patches, plus a prior on patch class distribution to calibrate class proportions.

Result: SlideTIM consistently outperforms TIM variants, achieving +8.1 percentage points macro-F1 over the best TIM baseline at 1 shot, and +19.4pp macro-F1 over zero-shot at 1 shot, tested on four histology datasets; code to be released after submission.

Conclusion: The proposed transductive refinement effectively tackles WSIs’ spatial structure and class imbalance, delivering substantial performance gains and demonstrating practical viability with a forthcoming code release.

Abstract: Automating the analysis of whole-slide images (WSIs), a key step in cancer diagnosis, has high clinical value, as it can reduce pathologist's workload while improving diagnosis accuracy. Recently, vision-language models have shown promising performance for patch-level classification without requiring any annotation, yet these zero-shot (ZS) predictions remain noisy on fine-grained tasks and must be further refined. A promising direction is to refine all predictions jointly, i.e., a transductive approach. However, most existing methods are not tailored to WSIs. We thus propose SlideTIM, an adaptation to WSIs of the recent transductive approach LC-TIM, which introduces a combined spatial--latent regularizer together with a prior on the patch class distribution. The former enforces spatially and semantically close patches to receive the same predictions, while the prior calibrates the predicted class proportions. Together, they address the complex spatial organization and the strong class imbalance of WSIs. Evaluated on four histology datasets, SlideTIM consistently outperforms all TIM variants, improving the macro-F1 by +8.1pp over the best competing baseline at 1 shot. Compared to the ZS, it raises the macro-F1 by +19.4pp at 1 shot. The code will be made available after submission.

</details>


### [50] [Where Compute Matters: Heterogeneous Attention for Efficient Video Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31050)
*Olga Zatsarynna,Denis Korzhenkov,Juergen Gall,Amir Habibian,Mohsen Ghafoorian*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: HetA-DiT introduces heterogeneous attention for video diffusion models, routing tokens by estimated denoising difficulty to balance quality and efficiency, achieving ~20% dense-attention usage while maintaining competitive quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficient video generation requires reducing quadratic self-attention costs; denoising difficulty varies across space, time, and during generation, so a fixed attention pattern is suboptimal. A method that adapts computation to token difficulty can reduce cost without sacrificing quality.

Method: Compute a lightweight uncertainty branch to predict token-wise denoising difficulty; route uncertain tokens through dense global attention; process reliable tokens with efficient local attention; content- and timestep-adaptive routing; uses a single parameter to control quality-efficiency trade-off; reuses uncertainty from previous step to avoid extra inference; compatible with few-step distribution-matching distillation; evaluated on Wan2.2-5B and Wan2.1-1.3B; no additional inference complexity beyond reusing uncertainty.

Result: Maintains competitive generation quality across VBench, VBench-2.0, and human preferences; routes about 20% of tokens through dense attention; demonstrates effective balance between efficiency and quality.

Conclusion: HetA-DiT provides an adaptive, practical approach to reduce self-attention costs in video generation without sacrificing quality, scalable to large diffusion models, and compatible with distillation workflows.

Abstract: Efficient video generation requires reducing the quadratic cost of self-attention over long spatio-temporal token sequences. Existing efficient-attention methods typically apply the same computation pattern to every token, even though denoising difficulty varies substantially across video regions and evolves throughout the generation process. We introduce HetA-DiT, a heterogeneous attention mechanism that adaptively allocates computation according to token difficulty. A lightweight uncertainty branch predicts a token-wise estimate of denoising difficulty, which is used to route uncertain tokens through dense global attention while processing more reliable tokens with efficient local attention. The resulting routing is content- and timestep-adaptive, retains global context where it matters most, and provides a single parameter for controlling the quality-efficiency trade-off. HetA-DiT is compatible with few-step distribution-matching distillation and introduces no additional Transformer evaluation at inference time by reusing uncertainty estimates from the preceding denoising step. We evaluate the method on DMD-distilled Wan2.2-5B and Wan2.1-1.3B models. Across VBench, VBench-2.0, and human preference evaluation, HetA-DiT maintains competitive generation quality while routing only approximately 20% of tokens through dense attention.

</details>


### [51] [Band-Selection Stability and Semantic Segmentation Performance: A Study on Hyperspectral City](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31074)
*Jiarong Li,Imad Ali Shah,Enda Ward,Martin Glavin,Edward Jones,Brian Deegan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A cross-method evaluation of six band-selection approaches on hyperspectral City V2 shows intra-method stability is method-dependent and not a reliable predictor of segmentation performance; top-K band subsets can closely match baselines with substantial speedups, but performance does not monotonically improve with K and should be tested across repeated samples and models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hyperspectral imaging suffers from high dimensionality; band selection aims to reduce data dimensionality while preserving semantic segmentation quality. Understanding stability of band-selection methods and their interaction with semantic segmentation models is essential for robust, efficient perception.

Method: Use ten independently sampled, class-balanced ROI sets from Hyperspectral City V2 (128 bands, 450–950 nm) to generate 60 top-25 band subsets across six band-selection methods. Evaluate top-K bands (K in {3,5,...,13}) from the first three ROI sets with three semantic segmentation models against the 128-band baseline. Report intra-method stability via pairwise Jaccard similarity, segmentation performance (e.g., mIoU, mF1), and CPU inference speed (for K=9).

Result: Sim-LP produced the highest intra-method stability; together with JMIM+CSNR, it yielded the best segmentation results. Top-K subsets were competitive with the full 128-band baseline, achieving gains up to 2.01 mIoU points and 1.72 mF1 points, with 18–22× faster CPU inference for K=9. However, increasing K did not monotonically improve performance, and stability did not consistently correlate with segmentation performance across methods and models.

Conclusion: Intra-method stability provides useful information but is not a reliable indicator of downstream segmentation performance. Robust evaluation requires multiple samples, varying subset sizes, and multiple semantic segmentation models to guide band-selection choices.

Abstract: Resource constraints make high-dimensional hyperspectral imaging challenging in autonomous perception, motivating the use of band selection methods. However, the sensitivity of band-selection methods to sampled data and their relationship to semantic segmentation models (SSMs) remain underexplored. This study evaluates six band selection methods on ten independently sampled, class-balanced region-of-interest (ROI) sets, yielding 60 top-25 band subsets from the Hyperspectral City V2 (128 bands: 450-950nm) dataset. Top-$K$ bands ($K\in\{3,5, ... 13\}$) from the first three ROI sets are evaluated with three SSMs against the corresponding 128-band baseline. Experiments show that intra-method stability is method-dependent: Sim-LP shows the highest stability (pairwise Jaccard similarity) and, together with JMIM+CSNR, yields the best segmentation results. Top-$K$ based SSMs remain competitive with baselines, with gains of up to 2.01 mIoU and 1.72 mF1 points, and 18-22x faster CPU inference for $K=9$. However, performance does not improve monotonically with $K$, and stability shows no consistent association with SSM performance. These findings suggest that intra-method stability is informative but an unreliable indicator of downstream segmentation performance, highlighting the need to evaluate band-selection methods across repeated samples, subset sizes, and SSMs.

</details>


### [52] [DepthEvidence: Unifying Metric Depth Prediction and Geometric Reasoning in Multimodal Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31103)
*Jiangning Wei,Yuan Yao,Miaomiao Cui,Mingsheng Li,Humen Zhong,Shuai Bai,Zhibo Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DepthEvidence is a 4B vision-language model that grounds language in dense metric depth predictions, using a dense-to-language interface and geometric supervision to preserve metric information during reasoning. It achieves leading performance on a Depth-VQA benchmark and competitive results with specialized estimators, while maintaining general VQA ability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To bridge geometric measurements (depth) with language reasoning, preserving numerical content during reasoning and enabling object-grounded, metric-aware interactions for spatial queries.

Method: A camera-conditioned decoder predicts full-resolution metric depth from multi-scale visual features with RGB refinement. Predicted depths and decoder features are converted into object-aligned continuous geometry tokens via a dense-to-language interface anchored to object IDs. Geometric supervision enforces recoverability of metric information before and after language interaction; instruction tuning supports object measurement and compositional reasoning. Evaluated on a Depth-VQA benchmark across nine datasets.

Result: DepthEvidence attains the highest average dense δ1 among evaluated methods, is competitive with specialized estimators, and leads in instance-level metric depth estimation and overall accuracy on both relative and metric reasoning tracks, while preserving general VQA performance and improving spatial understanding relative to the base model.

Conclusion: Explicitly integrating metric depth as object-grounded, tokenized geometry within a language model, guided by geometric supervision, yields strong metric-spatial reasoning capabilities and robust performance across VQA tasks.

Abstract: Spatial reasoning with metric constraints requires linking objects to geometric measurements and preserving their numerical content during language reasoning. We present DepthEvidence, a 4B model that uses its own dense metric predictions as object-grounded evidence for language generation. A camera-conditioned decoder predicts full-resolution metric depth using multi-scale visual features and high-resolution RGB refinement. A dense-to-language interface converts predicted depths and decoder features into object-aligned continuous geometry tokens anchored to object identifiers. Geometric supervision encourages metric information to remain recoverable before and after language-context interaction, while instruction tuning supports object measurement and compositional reasoning. We introduce a Depth-VQA benchmark evaluating object-depth queries, relative comparisons, and decisions combining spatial and numerical constraints. Across nine datasets, DepthEvidence achieves the highest average dense $δ_1$ among evaluated methods, competitive with specialized estimators. It also leads the evaluated methods in instance-level metric depth estimation and overall accuracy on both relative and metric reasoning tracks, while broadly preserving general VQA performance and improving spatial understanding relative to the base model.

</details>


### [53] [Double-stream registration with pyramid fusion for HDR video with alternating exposures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31108)
*Onofre Martorell,Ivan Pereira-Sánchez,Antoni Fuentes,Antoni Buades*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Dual-stream HDR reconstruction from three-frame sequences using center-frame optical flow and midpoint displacement, with pyramid fusion; shown to outperform state-of-the-art methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: HDR video reconstruction from alternating-exposure sequences struggles in regions with extreme luminance variation; robust registration and fusion are needed to produce high-quality HDR frames.

Method: Three consecutive frames are used; optical flow is computed using the central frame. A dual-stream registration framework is employed, along with a complementary midpoint displacement strategy to handle severe overexposure. A pyramid fusion stage merges the radiance and LDR images into a final HDR output.

Result: Experiments indicate the proposed approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art HDR reconstruction methods.

Conclusion: The dual-stream registration with midpoint displacement and pyramid fusion effectively addresses extreme luminance variation in HDR video reconstruction, yielding superior results.

Abstract: High dynamic range (HDR) video reconstruction from al\-ter\-na\-ting-exposure sequences remains challenging, especially in regions with extreme luminance variation. We propose a novel HDR reconstruction framework based on dual-stream registration and accurate pyramid fusion. Given three consecutive frames, our method computes optical flow directly with the central frame, while introducing a complementary midpoint displacement strategy to handle cases with severe overexposition. A pyramid fusion stage then merges the resulting radiance and LDR images into a final HDR output. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [54] [Pocket-STVG: lightweight architecture for Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31135)
*Alberto Presta,Michal Byra,Grzegorz Stefański,Karol Szurkowski,Eryk Kołodziejczyk,Krzysztof Arendt*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Pocket-STVG (P-STVG) is a lightweight, precomputed-feature cascade for spatio-temporal video grounding that uses a MobileViCLIP-based temporal encoder, an MDETR-like spatial encoder-decoder, and a shared text encoder; it supports weakly supervised and zero-shot settings with simple temporal localization (1D U-Net or thresholding) and precomputed video representations for efficient large-scale inference, achieving competitive performance with under 90M parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce reliance on heavy end-to-end architectures and multimodal large language models, lowering memory and computation, while enabling scalable, indexing-friendly STVG on large video collections.

Method: Construct a cascade with a temporal encoder based on MobileViCLIP, a spatial encoder-decoder derived from MDETR, and a shared aligned text encoder. Precompute video representations independent of queries for efficiency. Localize temporal extent via a lightweight 1D U-Net or a simple thresholding strategy. The framework supports weakly supervised and zero-shot settings without relying on large end-to-end models.

Result: Achieves performance on par with weakly supervised methods and improves on earlier zero-shot approaches at a fraction of their memory and computational cost; uses fewer than 90M parameters, indicating a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off for STVG.

Conclusion: Demonstrates a practical, resource-efficient STVG framework that matches or surpasses previous zero-shot baselines while remaining significantly lighter than end-to-end large-model approaches, enabling scalable deployment on large video datasets.

Abstract: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding (STVG) aims to localize the spatio-temporal tube in a video corresponding to a natural language query. While recent methods achieve strong performance in fully supervised, weakly supervised, and zero-shot settings, they typically rely on computationally expensive architectures, complex training pipelines, or multimodal large language models. We present Pocket-STVG (P-STVG), a lightweight cascade architecture that addresses STVG by combining efficient pre-trained components instead of large end-to-end models. P-STVG integrates a temporal-aware video encoder based on MobileViCLIP, a spatial encoder-decoder derived from MDETR, and a shared aligned text encoder. Temporal localization is performed through either a lightweight 1D U-Net or a simple thresholding strategy, enabling the same framework to operate in both weakly supervised and zero-shot settings. Furthermore, video representations are precomputed independently of the query, yielding an indexing-friendly pipeline for efficient inference and large-scale video collections. Despite requiring fewer than 90M parameters, P-STVG performs on par with weakly supervised methods and improves on earlier zero-shot approaches at a fraction of their memory and computational cost, establishing a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off for STVG.

</details>


### [55] [Seeing Semantic Shift: Difference-Aware Sentence-Level Temporal Segmentation of Sign Language Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31148)
*Bowen Guo,Shiwei Gan,Yafeng Yin,Xiao Liu,Kuizhuang Liu,Zhiwei Jiang,Lei Xie*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A difference-aware, two-module framework (SignShift) for Vis-SSLS that uses temporal frame differences and segment-count guidance to segment long sign-language videos into sentence-level units without captions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long, continuous sign-language videos suffer from performance drops; sentence boundaries are visually ambiguous without explicit pauses, making static frames insufficient. Vis-SSLS is a realistic, caption-free prerequisite task for downstream translation/recognition.

Method: SignShift comprises (1) Temporal Difference Module that uses inter-frame differencing with full-frame, facial, and hand cues to learn multi-scale temporal variations; (2) Segment Count Prediction module that estimates the number of sentences to guide boundary selection and reduce over-/under-segmentation.

Result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show SignShift substantially outperforms existing methods, demonstrating strong effectiveness for Vis-SSLS.

Conclusion: The proposed approach effectively leverages temporal differences and sentence-count cues to improve sentence-level segmentation in sign language videos, addressing the challenges of smooth, ambiguous sentence transitions and non-captioned data.

Abstract: Recent advances in sign language understanding have achieved impressive success on short, single-sentence videos, yet their performance drops sharply when applied to long, continuous sign language videos. To bridge this gap, we focus on a challenging and realistic setting: Visual-only Sentence-level Sign Language Segmentation (Vis-SSLS), which aims to partition continuous sign language videos into non-overlapping sentence-level segments without any caption assistance, serving as a crucial prerequisite for downstream recognition and translation tasks. However, sentence transitions in sign language are often smooth and visually ambiguous, lacking explicit pauses or posture resets. As a result, static frame representations may fail to capture the subtle temporal changes that indicate sentence boundaries. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{SignShift}, a difference-aware segmentation framework that explicitly models frame-to-frame feature variation as semantic cues for sentence boundary detection. First, to model the feature variation, we design a Temporal Difference Module, which incorporates full-frame, facial, and hand cues, and employs inter-frame differencing to learn multi-scale temporal variations that capture both fine-grained local kinematics and global semantic transitions. Second, to mitigate over- and under-segmentation issues, we design a Segment Count Prediction module, which predicts the number of sentences to guide boundary selection. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SignShift substantially outperforms existing methods, validating its effectiveness.

</details>


### [56] [FedHisto-PAST: Parameter-Efficient Stain-Aware Federated Learning for Cross-Site Lung Histopathology Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31150)
*Muhammad Muhtasim Shahriar,M. M. Golam Hafiz,Saad Aloteibi,Mohammad Ali Moni*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Federated, stain-aware histopathology classification using FedHisto-PAST v2 shows near-CEIL internal performance but limited external discriminability; it uses a frozen foundation model with lightweight adapters, stain-conditioned views, and prototype-based learning with adaptive aggregation; external gains attributed mainly to prediction-level consistency; small parameter update (~1.25%), but no formal privacy, independence, deployment, or clinical validation established.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tackle stain variation, non-IID client data, missing classes, and high cost of adapting large pathology encoders in cross-site histopathology classification; evaluate FedHisto-PAST v2 under realistic federated conditions.

Method: Five-client, non-IID, raw-data-local simulation; frozen HIBOU-B foundation model with parameter-efficient adapters; stain-conditioned paired-view prediction and feature consistency; reliability-aware prototype learning; adaptive federated aggregation; inclusion of LungHist700 cohort for development-influenced external assessment; analysis includes component ablations and calibration assessment.

Result: Macro-F1 = 0.728560; balanced accuracy = 0.730454 on LungHist700. Higher recognition of Normal and SCC, lower ACA recall; calibration imperfect. Prediction-level consistency is the only component with a clearly supported independent contribution in external ablation. Feature consistency and prototype regularization show no conclusive independent gains. The framework updated ~1.25% of model parameters. Findings provide exploratory cross-dataset evidence for stain-aware, parameter-efficient federation but do not establish privacy, patient-level independence, prospective deployment, or clinical validation.

Conclusion: The study provides exploratory evidence that stain-aware, parameter-efficient federated learning can approach strong internal performance in cross-site lung histopathology, with limited external discrimination and mostly attributed gains to prediction-level consistency. Nonetheless, it stops short of proving privacy, independence, deployment readiness, or clinical validity; further work needed on balancing class recall (notably ACA) and calibration, along with rigorous prospective and privacy-preserving evaluations.

Abstract: Cross-site lung histopathology classification must account for stain variation, non-IID client data, missing classes, and the cost of adapting large pathology encoders. This study evaluates FedHisto-PAST v2 for three-way classification of adenocarcinoma (ACA), Normal, and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). FedHisto-PAST v2 combines a frozen HIBOU-B foundation model with parameter-efficient adaptation, stain-conditioned paired-view prediction and feature consistency, reliability-aware prototype learning, and adaptive federated aggregation. Experiments used a five-client, non-IID, raw-data-local simulation with fixed internal evaluation, client-level analysis, component ablations, communication accounting, and a development-influenced exploratory LungHist700 cohort. All principal methods achieved near- ceiling internal performance, which limited discrimination on the fixed split. On LungHist700, FedHisto- PAST v2 achieved a Macro-F1 of 0.728560 and a balanced accuracy of 0.730454. Higher recognition of Normal and SCC was accompanied by lower ACA recall, and calibration remained imperfect. Prediction-level consistency was the only component with a clearly supported independent contribution in the external ablation analysis. Feature consistency and prototype regularization showed no conclusive independent overall gains in Macro-F1. The framework updated 1.253841% of the model parameters. The results provide exploratory cross-dataset evidence for stain-aware, parameter-efficient federation; they do not establish formal privacy, patient-level independence, prospective deployment, or clinical validation.

</details>


### [57] [HyperErase: Scale-Calibrated Hypernetwork for Multi-Concept Erasure in Text-to-Image Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31154)
*Yi Sun,Xinhao Zhong,Zhiqi Zhang,Yimin Zhou,Junhao Li,Yuxia Qiao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: HyperErase uses a hypernetwork to synthesize prompt-conditioned LoRA updates for concept erasure in text-to-image models, with a decoupled rectification strategy to improve stability and alignment, enabling per-prompt specialized LoRAs in a single forward pass without gradient updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static erasure adapters are inflexible for diverse prompts and exhibit parameter interference when scaling to multiple concepts; a scalable, prompt-aware mechanism is needed to maintain image quality and semantic alignment while erasing targeted concepts.

Method: Train a hypernetwork that maps textual descriptions to prompt-specific LoRA updates (concept erasure) without per-prompt gradient optimization. Introduce decoupled rectification that separates LoRA tokens into pattern and scale subspaces, applies a square-root transform to curb multiplicative over-scaling, and uses teacher-derived canonical priors for inference-time correction. Inference yields specialized LoRAs in a single forward pass per input prompt.

Result: HyperErase improves the trade-off among erasure effectiveness, image quality, and semantic alignment, achieving performance comparable to gold-standard single-concept baselines. It enables specialized LoRAs for each prompt variation without gradient updates during inference.

Conclusion: A principled, flexible framework that extends concept erasure to multiple concepts with prompt-conditioned parameter synthesis, offering a new paradigm for safe and controllable T2I generation.

Abstract: Recent advances in text-to-image (T2I) generation have substantially improved visual synthesis, but have also raised increasing safety concerns due to their potential to generate harmful or undesirable content. Existing concept erasure methods predominantly follow a static weight paradigm, producing a single frozen adapter that struggles to adapt to diverse prompt variations and suffers from parameter interference when scaling to multiple concepts. We propose \textbf{HyperErase}, a framework for concept erasure based on hypernetwork-driven prompt-conditioned parameter synthesis. Our approach first reframes concept erasure as prompt-conditioned parameter amortization and trains a hypernetwork to map textual descriptions to prompt-specific LoRA updates, eliminating the need for per-prompt gradient optimization or manual LoRA merging. To further improve the stability and precision of synthesized adapters, we develop a decoupled rectification strategy, which disentangles LoRA tokens into pattern and scale subspaces, applies a square-root transform to curb multiplicative over-scaling, and leverages teacher-derived canonical priors for inference-time correction. Extensive experiments across major concept categories demonstrate that HyperErase consistently improves the trade-off between erasure effectiveness, image quality, and semantic alignment, achieving performance comparable to gold-standard single-concept baselines. Furthermore, the resulting models can provide specialized LoRAs for each input prompt variation in a single forward pass without requiring gradient updates during inference. These principled and flexible framework offers a new paradigm for concept erasure in T2I models.

</details>


### [58] [ReG-SAM: Reference Graph-Driven SAM for 2D Foundational Vessel Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31160)
*Donghang Lyu,Zichen Zhang,Oleh Dzyubachyk,Marius Staring*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A SAM-based framework (ReG-SAM) improves 2D vessel segmentation by using a modality-aware reference graph approach to generate global (GPEs) and fine-grained (VPEs) vascular representations without ground-truth masks, enabling cross-dataset generalization across anatomies and modalities; evaluated on 19 datasets, it outperforms strong baselines, especially for thin vessels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To achieve generalizable vessel segmentation across anatomies and imaging modalities, addressing SAM’s limited exploitation of vascular morphology and its difficulty with fine vessels.

Method: Construct modality-wise vascular database and two reference graph-guided representation learning schemes to derive GPEs from graphs and VPEs from multi-scale feature maps and vascular masks. Use samples from the database, not ground-truth masks, to estimate GPEs and VPEs during inference.

Result: Extensive experiments over 19 datasets show ReG-SAM consistently outperforms existing baselines, including those with manual prompts, with notable gains on challenging thin vessels.

Conclusion: ReG-SAM demonstrates improved generalization and performance for 2D vessel segmentation by leveraging graph-based global cues and fine-grained vascular prototypes through modality-aware representations.

Abstract: Vessel segmentation in medical images is essential for many clinical tasks, ranging from diagnosis to treatment planning. However, it remains challenging due to complex vascular morphology and diverse imaging conditions. Existing deep learning methods rarely aim at building a generalizable vessel segmentor across anatomies and modalities. While the Seg- ment Anything Model (SAM) has shown promise for med- ical image segmentation, its original design does not fully exploit vascular morphology and struggles with fine-grained vascular structures, leading to suboptimal performance. In this paper, we propose ReG-SAM, a SAM-based framework tailored to 2D vessel segmentation that leverages reference graph set for enhancing vascular representations. Specifically, we introduce two modality-aware representations derived from the reference masks: graph prompt embeddings (GPEs) that encode global spatial features from graphs, and vascu- lar prototype embeddings (VPEs) that capture fine-grained modality-specific vessel characteristics from multi-scale fea- ture maps and vascular masks. Since both require vascular masks that are unavailable during inference and require robust modality-aware vascular feature representations, we construct a modality-wise vascular database and develop two reference graph-guided representation learning schemes for estimating GPEs and VPEs using samples from the database rather than ground-truth masks. Extensive experiments across 19 datasets demonstrate that ReG-SAM consistently outperforms existing baselines, even those using manual prompts, particularly on challenging thin vessels.

</details>


### [59] [TaskIR: Task-Driven Image Restoration via Degradation Adaptation and Task Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31170)
*Yanjie Tu,Qingsen Yan,Axi Niu,Wenxuan Cai,Tao Hu,Wei Dong,Haokui Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TaskIR: a two-stage, task-driven image restoration framework that unifies degradation-adaptive restoration with task feedback refinement to handle diverse real-world degradations and improve both restoration quality and downstream task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world degradations are diverse; single-degradation restoration fails to preserve object boundaries and semantic cues, leading to residual artifacts that impair downstream task performance.

Method: Stage I: DRM extracts degradation representations; DGTB dynamically modulates feature transformations for adaptive restoration. Stage II: TRFG converts heterogeneous task features into restoration feedback by modeling task-representation discrepancies; STFR selectively refines restoration features to mitigate interference with well-restored content.

Result: Extensive experiments show TaskIR achieves competitive restoration quality and downstream task performance across diverse degradations and tasks.

Conclusion: TaskIR effectively integrates degradation-aware restoration with task feedback refinement, offering robust performance across varied degradations and downstream tasks.

Abstract: Task-driven image restoration aims to improve both image quality and downstream task performance. However, existing methods predominantly focus on single degradation type and struggle to handle the diverse degradations encountered in real-world scenarios. Different degradations impose distinct restoration demands, and insufficient restoration may leave residual degradations and artifacts that impair object boundaries and semantic cues, thereby compromising downstream task performance. To address these challenges, we propose TaskIR, a two-stage task-driven unified image restoration framework that integrates degradation-adaptive restoration with task feedback refinement. In Stage I, a Degradation Representation Module (DRM) extracts degradation representations, enabling a Degradation-Guided Transformer Block (DGTB) to dynamically modulate feature transformations for adaptive restoration. In Stage II, a Task-to-Restoration Feedback Generation module (TRFG) transforms heterogeneous task features into restoration feedback by modeling task-representation discrepancies associated with the current restoration. Subsequently, a Selective Task Feedback Refinement module (STFR) assesses feedback relevance and selectively refines intermediate restoration features to mitigate interference with well-restored content. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TaskIR achieves competitive restoration quality and downstream task performance across diverse degradations and tasks.

</details>


### [60] [Who Says What: Symbolic Trimodal Binding Mechanisms in Audio-Visual LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31193)
*Jihoo Jung,Youngjoon Jang,Joon Son Chung*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper reveals emergent symbolic trimodal binding in AVLLMs using modality-specific variables for audio and visual streams; identifies audio-visual misalignment as a key bottleneck; proposes a training-free ASD-based prompting by overlaying active speaker boxes to boost performance, with further gains from small-scale fine-tuning on ASD-prompted videos; shows gains on several AV benchmarks, suggesting generalizability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AVLLMs lag in reasoning for videos with multi-speaker dialogues; accurate 'who says what' requires tight trimodal alignment among text, audio, and vision.

Method: Identify symbolic variables capturing temporal utterances (audio) and spatial entities (visual); analyze cross-modal binding in this abstract space; propose an audio-visual prompting approach using an off-the-shelf Active Speaker Detection model by overlaying boxes on active speakers; minimal training; limited fine-tuning on ASD-prompted videos to extend gains.

Result: Training-free ASD prompting yields immediate improvements across four conversation-centric benchmarks; sub-300-step fine-tuning on ASD-prompted videos extends gains to three general AV benchmarks; results indicate generalizability.

Conclusion: Trimodal binding in AVLLMs can be grounded in symbolic representations per modality; misalignment between audio-visual channels is a primary failure point; ASD-based prompting is an effective, training-free booster with good generalizability; the approach points toward robust trimodal reasoning via symbolic cross-modal spaces.

Abstract: Current Audio-Visual LLMs (AVLLMs) struggle with reasoning over videos featuring multi-speaker dialogues. In such videos, resolving "who says what" is crucial, which necessitates trimodal (text-audio-visual) binding. Motivated by these challenges, we systematically investigate how this trimodal binding is achieved in AVLLMs. Specifically, we identify emergent symbolic trimodal binding mechanisms in AVLLMs that utilize modality-specific symbolic variables. By encoding auditory and visual components into symbolic variables-capturing temporal utterance sequences and spatial entity coordinates, respectively-the model establishes cross-modal linking within this abstract space. Crucially, we reveal that when trimodal binding fails, the breakdown predominantly stems from misaligned audio-visual connections. To overcome this bottleneck, we introduce an audio-visual prompting method utilizing an off-the-shelf Active Speaker Detection (ASD) model. By simply overlaying visual bounding boxes on active speakers, this training-free approach yields immediate performance gains across four conversation-centric benchmarks. Moreover, lightweight fine-tuning of fewer than 300 steps on these ASD-prompted-videos extends these gains to three general AV benchmarks, suggesting the generalizability of our method.

</details>


### [61] [Light Field Primitive for Novel View Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31198)
*Liang Chen,Jiahui Ning,Xun Jiang,Xing Xu,Jimmy Ren,Fenglei Fan,Heng Tao Shen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A compact set of differentiable primitives in 4D ray space replaces dense ray databases for novel view synthesis, enabling real-time rendering and built-in support for optical/appearance effects via a shared renderer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce memory and computation from dense ray databases while enabling differentiable optimization and flexible rendering effects by operating directly in light-field (4D ray) space.

Method: Introduce differentiable primitives that group rays in the 4D two-plane parameterization. Each primitive yields a response based on query similarity; a camera ray is rendered by compositing the responses of relevant primitives. The system is optimized from posed images and renders in real time, with minimal changes to an existing renderer to support multi-scale anti-aliasing, defocus/refocusing, fisheye, and refraction. 

Result: Achieves competitive performance on standard benchmarks; provides a structural advantage by living in 4D ray space, enabling optical/appearance operations to be handled by a single shared renderer. Real-time rendering and broad support for varied optical effects are demonstrated.

Conclusion: Light Field Primitives offer a compact, differentiable, ray-space representation that integrates seamlessly with a shared renderer to deliver flexible, real-time novel view synthesis and advanced optical effects without requiring specialized pipelines.

Abstract: We present Light Field Primitives (LFP), a formulation for novel view synthesis that replaces the dense ray database with a compact set of differentiable primitives in the classical two-plane parameterization. Each primitive condenses a group of rays into one learned record, and its response to a query is governed by how closely that query belongs to the group. Rendering a camera ray then reduces to compositing all responses it elicits, and a scene can be optimized directly from posed images and rendered in real time with rays. Beyond its competitive performance on standard benchmarks, the main advantage of LFP is structural: its primitives reside directly in the 4D ray space, so optical and appearance effects that are already operations on the light field become behaviors of a single shared renderer. With minimal changes to that renderer, LFP supports multi-scale anti-aliasing, defocus deblurring with refocusing, rendering for fisheye cameras, and even transparent object reconstruction with ray refraction, matching specialized frameworks that devote substantial machinery to these effects.

</details>


### [62] [Preserve-and-Compose Training for Composed Image Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31202)
*Sehyun Kwon*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Zero-shot composed image retrieval (CIR) using Preserve-and-Compose Training (PACT) with ITT triplets and Chord scoring; aligns composed queries to target captions while preserving source image evidence; strong results on four ZS-CIR benchmarks; code at GitHub.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CIR seeks to retrieve images modified as per user guidance while preserving source content; zero-shot supervision via target captions may lose source details. There is a need to leverage source image evidence to preserve content while aligning with target captions.

Method: Propose Preserve-and-Compose Training (PACT) that learns from image--text--text (ITT) triplets without target images or gallery updates. It aligns composed queries with target captions and preserves source evidence through visual supervision. Introduce Chord scoring, which combines target similarity with source-relative directional agreement in the frozen image space.

Result: Empirical evaluation across four zero-shot CIR benchmarks shows strong retrieval performance when combining target-caption supervision with source-image evidence, robust across datasets, backbone scales, and external galleries.

Conclusion: PACT effectively leverages source-image evidence in conjunction with target captions to improve zero-shot CIR. Code is available at the provided GitHub URL.

Abstract: Composed image retrieval (CIR) aims to retrieve images that satisfy a user-specified modification while preserving relevant visual content from a reference image. Collecting target images for this purpose is costly, motivating zero-shot CIR methods that instead use target captions as supervision. However, target captions may omit source details that should be preserved. We therefore propose, Preserve-and-Compose Training, which complements target-caption supervision with visual evidence from the source image. PACT learns from image--text--text (ITT) triplets without target images or gallery updates, aligning composed queries with target captions while preserving source evidence through visual supervision. We further introduce Chord scoring, which combines target similarity with source-relative directional agreement in the frozen image space. Results across four ZS-CIR benchmarks show that combining target-caption supervision with source-image evidence leads to strong retrieval performance across datasets, backbone scales, and external galleries. The code is available on https://github.com/sehyunkwon/PACT.

</details>


### [63] [WeaveAgent: A Two-Stage Tool-Routing Agent for Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing Imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31234)
*Zhongyu Pang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WeaveAgent proposes a two-stage tool-routing framework for ultra-high-resolution remote sensing with vague intents, decoupling routing from perception. Stage A trains emission routing; Stage B conditionally executes intrinsic (visual) vs extrinsic (tool) queries. Training uses alignment SFT followed by GRPO with reward. Results show substantial improvement in extrinsic routing (up to 80.75%) and reduced intrinsic mis-emissions, but overall a 2B model underperforms a zero-shot 8B baseline. Oracle analysis highlights the impact of incorporating observations and multi-turn SFT; ablations indicate visually grounded emission suppression and the cost of query rewriting. Dataset is from VagueUHR; runtime ~7.3s per image on RTX 4090; code and data to be released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address two bottlenecks in ultra-high-resolution remote sensing with vague user intents: (1) expensive visual token processing and (2) fragile tool-call behavior in zero-shot setups. A decoupled, two-stage routing-perception architecture with a fixed-budget evidence interface aims to improve tool usage reliability and robustness.

Method: Two-stage design: Stage A (routing-first) trains the emission policy; Stage B performs conditional execution: intrinsic queries use a visual answering path (full-scene thumbnail and a fixed-budget evidence board), while extrinsic queries trigger tool calls on original full-resolution imagery; outputs are integrated in a second round. Training uses Alignment SFT followed by GRPO with a reward R_WA2. The system is evaluated on the VagueUHR corpus (600 intrinsic, 400 tool-requiring; 5k/3.2k/1k split). Single-pass evidence construction runs at 7.31 s per image on an RTX 4090; code and protocols to be released.

Result: Alignment SFT lifts extrinsic routing from near-zero to 80.75% (323/400); GRPO reduces 9 intrinsic mis-emissions without changing tool selection. The 2B system does not surpass the zero-shot 8B baseline overall (0.263 vs 0.250). Oracle attribution shows: loading observation into context increases extrinsic answer accuracy from 0.025 to 0.425 under marker-free cross-mode returns; a two-turn SFT stage adds +9.3 points to 0.518 with modest routing cost. Ablations indicate emission suppression is visually grounded; query-register matrix shows LLM-rewritten queries subtract 2–11 points at trained checkpoints. Scope: experiments on the specified VagueUHR subsets; single-pass evidence; reproducibility planned with released code and data.

Conclusion: The approach delivers meaningful gains in routing fidelity and mitigation of intrinsic mis-emissions, but a smaller 2B model does not outperform a larger zero-shot baseline, suggesting routing improvements alone are insufficient to beat strong, pre-trained baselines. Key contributions include the observation-loading mechanism and the two-turn SFT stage, which substantially boost extrinsic accuracy. The work provides reproducible protocols and highlights the value of fixed-budget visual interfaces for precise tool use; future work could scale model size, refine evidence interfaces, and enhance tool reliability.

Abstract: Problem. Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing with vague user intents has two bottlenecks: visual tokens are expensive, and tool calling must be format-reliable (pretrained models emit zero tool calls zero-shot). Method. WeaveAgent, a two-stage tool-routing agent, decouples routing from visual perception. Stage A is routing-first: emission is trained, not elicited. Stage B executes conditionally: intrinsic queries enter visual answering (full-scene thumbnail; a WeaveEarth-style evidence board as an optional fixed-budget, approx. 5k-token compression interface); extrinsic queries execute tool call on original full-resolution imagery, answering from tool observations in a second, observation-masked round. Training: alignment SFT, then GRPO under reward R_WA2. Results. Alignment SFT lifts extrinsic routing from 0% to 80.75% (323/400); GRPO suppresses 9 intrinsic mis-emissions while tool selection is unchanged. The trained 2B system does not beat the zero-shot 8B baseline overall (0.263 vs. 0.250), a diagnostic contribution. Oracle attribution separates two repair ingredients: loading the observation into context lifts extrinsic answer accuracy from 0.025 to 0.425 under marker-free cross-mode returns, and the two-turn SFT stage adds a further +9.3 points to 0.518 at a small routing cost. A +/- image ablation shows emission suppression is visually grounded, and a query-register matrix shows LLM-rewritten queries cost trained checkpoints 2-11 points. Scope. All training and evaluation use the 5,000 / 3,273 / 1,000-record VagueUHR corpus (600 intrinsic + 400 tool-requiring; the base seeds synthesis and is not used for optimization). Single-pass evidence construction runs at 7.31 s per image on an RTX 4090. Code, data, and evaluation protocols will be released.

</details>


### [64] [Geometric Inconsistency Localization in Multi-View Image Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31247)
*Xander Staelens,Albéric Loos,Bert Ramlot,Hannes Mareen,Peter Lambert,Glenn Van Wallendael*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes DeformView dataset for wide-baseline multi-view consistency with pixel-level annotations; reveals that NVS-based MV metrics poorly transfer to forensic localization; introduces DEFECt3R, a lightweight cross-view feature classifier for pixel-level geometric inconsistency localization that reduces false positives; provides code and dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable forensic localization of geometric inconsistencies in wide-baseline MV image pairs by leveraging multi-view consistency, addressing the gap where NVS evaluation metrics do not translate to pixel-level localization in forensics and lacking annotated datasets.

Method: Create DeformView dataset with pixel-level annotations of geometric inconsistencies; evaluate existing MV consistency scoring methods; propose DEFECt3R, a lightweight classifier that leverages cross-view feature relationships and training with explicit supervision including hard negatives from geometrically consistent deformations; conduct ablations on feature representations and correspondence quality.

Result: DEFECt3R achieves improved localization accuracy and lower false-positive rates compared to existing MV consistency baselines; ablations show both feature representation and correspondence quality contribute to performance; establishes a new benchmark for geometric inconsistency localization on wide-baseline MV image pairs; code and dataset released.

Conclusion: MV geometric consistency is a promising forensic signal; this work establishes a benchmark and a strong baseline (DEFECt3R) for localizing geometric inconsistencies in wide-baseline multi-view images, with DeformView enabling future research.

Abstract: Novel view synthesis (NVS) models can produce realistic new views of the same scene from different viewpoints. However, these generated views are not always geometrically consistent with one another. Multi-view (MV) consistency has shown promise as a tool for evaluating these NVS models. Its potential for multimedia forensics, however, remains largely unexplored, particularly for localizing geometric inconsistencies across wide-baseline image pairs. To enable research in this direction, we introduce DeformView, a wide-baseline MV dataset with pixel-level annotations of geometric inconsistencies. Using DeformView, we evaluate state-of-the-art MV consistency-scoring methods and show that approaches developed for NVS evaluation transfer poorly to the forensic task of geometric inconsistency localization. To address this limitation, we propose DEFECt3R, a lightweight learning-based classifier that uses cross-view feature relationships to localize geometric inconsistencies at the pixel level. By learning from explicit supervision, including hard negatives from geometrically consistent yet deformed views, DEFECt3R improves localization performance and substantially reduces false positives compared to existing consistency-scoring methods. Ablation experiments further show that both feature representations and correspondence quality contribute to localization performance. Overall, our findings demonstrate that MV geometric consistency is a promising yet underexplored signal for multimedia forensics and establish a benchmark and baseline for geometric inconsistency localization in wide-baseline MV image pairs. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/IDLabMedia/DeformView-DEFECt3R

</details>


### [65] [Gauss What You Need: Compact Gaussian Splatting Across Scene Scales](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31248)
*Afif Boudaoud,Jiayi Liu,Alexandru Calotoiu,Torsten Hoefler*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TangoGS adaptively sizes 3D Gaussian Splatting models by combining capture-derived scale with training-feedback density control, achieving state-of-the-art quality with significantly fewer Gaussians.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automatic selection of the number of Gaussian primitives for 3D scene representations across captures is underdetermined; fixed-size baselines either underfit large captures or waste resources on standard benchmarks. A scalable, data-driven sizing strategy is needed to balance reconstruction quality, storage, and rendering cost.

Method: Capture-derived learning allowance sets an initial scale by computing available pixel budget (excluding repeatedly observed points). During training, reconstruction quality on training views guides dynamic growth or reduction of Gaussian count; the surface extent/resolution fixes the model’s scale while content complexity is revealed through training performance.

Result: On 13 standard benchmark scenes, TangoGS matches the mean PSNR of the best baseline (LeGS) with 48% fewer Gaussians. On eight large captures, it automatically scales to larger models, achieving the highest mean PSNR among evaluated methods, 0.54 dB above the runner-up with 2.3× as many Gaussians.

Conclusion: Capture-derived allowances plus training-quality-guided density control yield a robust quality–size trade-off across scene scales without retuning, enabling state-of-the-art results for both standard and large captures.

Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructs a scene as a collection of Gaussian primitives from a set of posed photographs called the capture. The number of primitives used to represent the scene affects reconstruction quality, storage, and rendering cost. How to select this number automatically across capture scales remains unresolved: configurations effective on standard benchmarks can leave larger captures with too few Gaussians to reconstruct fine details. We observe that the surface to represent, given by the capture's extent and resolution, is known before training, whereas its content complexity becomes apparent during training, through the reconstruction quality on the training views. We introduce TangoGS, which combines capture-derived model sizing with training-based adaptation: the capture determines the scale of the model, and training feedback determines its final size within that scale. Before training, TangoGS derives a learning allowance for model growth from the capture's total pixels after discounting views that re-observe the same scene points. During training, reconstruction quality guides how many Gaussians to add and remove. On 13 standard benchmark scenes, TangoGS matches the mean PSNR of the best-performing evaluated baseline, LeGS, with $48\%$ fewer Gaussians. On eight large captures, the same configuration automatically scales to larger models when necessary, achieving the highest mean PSNR among evaluated methods: $0.54$ dB above the runner-up with $2.3\times$ as many Gaussians. Together, capture-derived learning allowances and training-quality guided density control enable a state-of-the-art quality--size compromise across scene scales without retuning.

</details>


### [66] [MoTop: Motion-Topological Model For Micro AU Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31285)
*Huai-Qian Khor,Mengting Wei,Yante Li,Chu Kiong Loo,Guoying Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A motion-topological framework (MoTop) with learnable motion context, enhanced micro-landmark dynamics, and anatomical clusters yields state-of-the-art micro AU detection on CD6ME.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AU detection is challenging due to brief, subtle micro-expressions and AU ambiguity; finer representations (AUs) are valuable upstream in facial analysis, requiring multi-scale, topological modeling.

Method: Introduce MoTop, a motion-topological model augmented with learnable motion context for regional soft guidance; extract micro facial landmarks to capture fine-scale topological changes; apply linear extrapolation to amplify landmark transitions and increase spatial proximity; design anatomical facial clusters to enable hierarchical, multi-scale modeling of facial geometry.

Result: State-of-the-art performance on the CD6ME protocol for micro AU detection.

Conclusion: MoTop advances micro AU detection by integrating motion topology, contextual guidance, enhanced landmark dynamics, and anatomical clustering to form robust, multi-scale representations of micro-expressions.

Abstract: Facial micro-expressions are spontaneous, brief, and subtle facial movements that reveal suppressed emotions in high-stakes environments. In contrast to classic expression analysis, detecting action unit (AU) yields a finer representation of facial movements, serving as a preliminary step before defining expression classes and other downstream tasks. Therefore, it represents a crucial upstream task in facial analysis, and improving an AU detection module increases the precision of facial analysis. Despite that, detecting AU is challenging because of the constrictive nature of the AU activation regions, leading to confusion among different AUs known as AU ambiguity. To model the fine-scale changes, we propose \textbf{MoTop}, a motion-topological model that is augmented with a learnable motion context, yielding regional soft guidance for facial activity, followed by facial landmarks that capture the fine-scale topological changes of micro AUs. To increase the micro facial landmark representations, we amplify the encoded facial landmark transitions via linear extrapolation, thereby increasing the spatial proximity of landmarks and enhancing the low-intensity landmark dynamics. In addition, we design anatomical facial clusters that enhance the hierarchical representation, facilitating multi-scale modelling of facial geometry and improving micro-topological representations. With these contributions, we have achieved state-of-the-art performance on the CD6ME protocol for the micro AU detection task.

</details>


### [67] [UniAR: A Unified Framework for Autism Recognition Enhanced by Multi-View Prompt Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31298)
*Lei Xin,Zeheng Wang,Jiayin Zhu,Shihong Huang,Fanhu Zeng,Changjiang Jiang,Dengbo He,Yutao Yue,Zhenglun Kong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: UniAR is a unified multimodal framework for ASD recognition under semantic scarcity, using a large multimodal model to generate hierarchical diagnostic semantics and a Mixture-of-Experts module to align visual prototypes with semantic levels, achieving improvements on MRI and facial benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scarcity of diagnostic text data hampers semantic-rich ASD recognition; existing methods rely heavily on visuals and struggle with semantic reasoning tied to clinical reports.

Method: 1) Hierarchical diagnostic description generation at word/phrase/sentence levels via a large multimodal model; 2) Mixture-of-Experts-based Multi-Scale Alignment Module to dynamically match vector-quantized visual prototypes with semantic representations at corresponding granularities.

Result: Across four benchmarks (brain MRI and facial expressions), UniAR achieves 75.9% average accuracy on MRI and 91.6% on facial benchmarks, with improvements of 1.5 and 1.2 percentage points in average accuracy over strong baselines.

Conclusion: UniAR provides a robust, interpretable framework for ASD screening under semantic scarcity, leveraging multi-granularity prompts and cross-modal alignment to improve performance across heterogeneous data.

Abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder for which early and accurate diagnosis is critical to improving long-term developmental outcomes. However, existing ASD recognition methods are often constrained by the scarcity of diagnostic text data, forcing them to rely mainly on visual analysis and limiting their ability to model clinically meaningful semantic reasoning. To address this challenge, we propose UniAR, a unified framework enhanced by multi-granularity prompt learning for robust ASD recognition under heterogeneous data variations. Specifically, UniAR leverages a large multimodal model to generate hierarchical diagnostic descriptions at the word, phrase, and sentence levels, compensating for the lack of paired clinical reports. To align the generated semantics with visual evidence, we further design a Mixture-of-Experts-based Multi-Scale Alignment Module, which dynamically matches vector-quantized visual prototypes with semantic representations at corresponding granularities. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks covering brain MRI and facial expression scenarios show that UniAR consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving average accuracies of 75.9\% on MRI benchmarks and 91.6\% on facial benchmarks, while improving average Accuracy on MRI benchmarks by 1.5 percentage points and average Accuracy on facial benchmarks by 1.2 percentage points over baselines. These results demonstrate that UniAR offers a robust and interpretable framework for ASD screening under semantic scarcity.

</details>


### [68] [CytoSPM: Open-Vocabulary Cytopathology Detection with Structured Prompt Bank](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31314)
*Wenjie Li,Zishan Xu,Jinyang Huang,Zhengxin Nie,Shichao Kan,Yixiong Liang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PentaCyto provides a multi-domain open-vocabulary cytopathology benchmark (24 base + 9 novel categories) with structured cytomorphology prompts, and CytoSPM a decoupled two-stage detector that uses class-agnostic visual features followed by prompt-based class matching; it achieves state-of-the-art performance on novel categories and open-vocabulary detection with efficient inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cytopathology requires open-vocabulary recognition due to fine-grained, long-tailed, and evolving cell types across organ systems, and there is no unified benchmark for open-vocabulary cytopathology detection.

Method: Introduce PentaCyto benchmark across cervical, urinary, respiratory, serous fluid, and thyroid cytology with 24 base categories and 9 held-out novel categories, each paired with structured cytomorphology prompts. Propose CytoSPM, a decoupled two-stage detector that first extracts reusable class-agnostic visual representations, then performs class-aware structural prompt matching using class names and cytomorphology prompts.

Result: CytoSPM outperforms existing methods in novel-category detection and open-vocabulary detection on PentaCyto while maintaining efficient inference.

Conclusion: PentaCyto offers a unified, multi-domain benchmark and a scalable open-vocabulary cytopathology detector (CytoSPM) that leverages prompt-based knowledge to handle novel categories with efficient inference.

Abstract: Cytopathology detection requires open-vocabulary recognition because cellular categories are fine-grained, long-tailed, and continuously evolving across different organ systems. However, existing cytology detectors are mostly single-domain and closed-set, and there is still no unified benchmark for evaluating open-vocabulary cytopathology detection. We present PentaCyto, a multi-domain benchmark covering cervical, urinary, respiratory, serous fluid, and thyroid cytology, with 24 base categories and 9 held-out novel categories. Each category is associated with structured cytomorphology prompts that describe diagnostic morphological attributes and provide clinically grounded textual knowledge. We further propose CytoSPM, an efficient detector based on a decoupled two-stage design. It first extracts reusable class-agnostic visual representations, and then performs class-aware structural prompt matching with class names and cytomorphology prompts. On PentaCyto, CytoSPM outperforms existing methods in novel-category detection and open-vocabulary detection while maintaining efficient inference.

</details>


### [69] [CG-HAF: An Interpretable Global-Local Lesion-Burden Fusion Framework for Ordinal Acne Severity Grading in Agentic Skincare Support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31326)
*Muhammad Muhtasim Shahriar,Md. Naimur Asif Borno,Saad Aloteibi,Mohammad Ali Moni*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces CG-HAF, a global-local fusion framework for ordinal acne severity grading that preserves global evidence (holistic severity) and local lesion burden (count, area, confidence) via an object detector, yielding improved accuracy over global-only baselines and showing interpretability; cross-dataset transfer is limited by criterion misalignment rather than detection failure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To avoid the collapse of ordinal acne grading into a single opaque representation by preserving explicit global and local cues, enabling more interpretable and potentially more robust grading.

Method: Train independent classifiers to predict holistic severity probabilities; use an object detector to extract structured lesion descriptors (count, detection confidence, area); fuse these into a compact representation; apply a lightweight, interpretable classifier to predict the final ordinal grade.

Result: On a widely used benchmark, the global-local fusion yields statistically significant improvement over global-evidence baselines, with the largest gains for the most severe cases. Cross-dataset testing reveals that strong in-dataset performance does not automatically transfer; much of the gap is due to mismatched grading criteria rather than detection failure.

Conclusion: Global-local fusion provides an interpretable, effective approach for ordinal acne grading, but cross-dataset portability requires careful alignment of grading criteria; the resulting severity signal can support transparent, non-diagnostic decision-making in skincare.

Abstract: Ordinal acne severity grading requires distinguishing visually similar neighboring grades while jointly weighing holistic facial appearance and localized lesion burden - evidence that most existing approaches collapse into a single opaque representation. We introduce CG-HAF, a global-local fusion framework that instead keeps this evidence explicit: averaged holistic severity probabilities from independently trained classifiers are combined with structured lesion-burden descriptors from an object detector (lesion count, detection confidence, lesion area) into a compact representation, from which a lightweight, interpretable classifier produces the final grade. On a widely used benchmark, this fusion yields a clear, statistically supported improvement over global-evidence-only baselines, with the largest gains on the most severe cases. Testing on an independent dataset with a different grading standard shows that strong within-dataset performance does not transfer automatically, and a follow-up diagnostic attributes much of this gap to mismatched grading criteria rather than detection failure alone. These findings support interpretable global-local fusion as an effective strategy for ordinal acne grading while highlighting criterion alignment as key to cross-dataset portability, with a further illustration of how the resulting severity signal can support transparent, non-diagnostic decision-making in skincare applications.

</details>


### [70] [DyMD: Preserving Interaction Dynamics through Distribution Matching Distillation in Few-Step Video World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31349)
*Haojun Xu,Jie Huang,Xin Lu,Mingchen Zhong,Zihao Fan,Linjiang Huang,Si Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DyMD distills a 14B teacher into a four-step 1.3B student for video diffusion, using adaptive teacher supervision and dynamics-aware critic training to balance motion restoration and appearance, achieving strong downstream task performance with four-step generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large video diffusion models yield expressive priors but require costly multi-step sampling. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) helps with few-step generation but can suppress motion. There is a need for adaptive supervision and dynamic-aware training to preserve motion while maintaining visual quality.

Method: DyMD introduces temporal affinity conditioned re-noise sampling that mixes a base timestep schedule with a teacher prior based on local posterior variation to adapt to each rollout's interaction fidelity. It also uses dynamics-guided fake-score tracking with a noise-conditioned predictor to estimate hardness from latent dynamics and upweight hard rollouts in the critic loss. It distills a 14B teacher into a four-step 1.3B student with no inference-time modules and evaluates on embodied-video benchmarks.

Result: The student achieves 9.6 percentage points higher R-Bench task adherence and 5.1 points higher PAI-Bench-G Domain score than Base DMD. It attains 34% mean success on two WorldArena tasks versus 16% for Base DMD, demonstrating improved downstream performance while maintaining comparable visual quality.

Conclusion: Adaptive teacher supervision and dynamics-aware critic fitting enable efficient four-step video diffusion with strong motion and interaction dynamics, enabling effective embodied-video planning and downstream tasks.

Abstract: Large video diffusion models offer expressive priors for embodied prediction and learning, yet their many-step sampling remains costly for interactive downstream use. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) enables few-step video generation, but can suppress robot--object motion while preserving visual quality. Examining DMD's teacher and fake-score signals, we find that weak re-noising keeps the teacher posterior concentrated near motion-deficient rollouts, limiting motion-restoring guidance. Meanwhile, stronger-motion rollouts tend to incur larger fake-score fitting errors, which can hinder the generator's learning of interaction dynamics. We propose DyMD, a DMD framework that adapts both teacher supervision and critic fitting to the evolving student. Temporal affinity--conditioned re-noise sampling adapts the timestep distribution to each rollout's current interaction fidelity by mixing the base schedule with a teacher prior motivated by local posterior variation, thereby balancing motion recovery and appearance refinement. To better track stronger-motion rollouts, dynamics-guided fake-score tracking uses a noise-conditioned predictor to estimate noise-relative fitting difficulty from latent temporal dynamics, then upweights predicted-hard rollouts in the critic loss. Using DyMD, we distill a 14B teacher into a four-step 1.3B student with no auxiliary modules at inference. On embodied-video benchmarks, the student improves R-Bench task adherence by $9.6$ percentage points and PAI-Bench-G Domain score by $5.1$ points over Base DMD while maintaining comparable visual quality. As a backbone for downstream action planning, our student achieves 34% mean success across two WorldArena tasks, compared with 16% for Base DMD.

</details>


### [71] [Open Vocabulary Domain Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31356)
*Sumanth Udupa,Mehrtash Harandi,Yadan Luo,Mahsa Baktashmotlagh*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Open-Vocabulary Domain Unlearning (OVDU) formalizes class-agnostic domain forgetting and introduces a surgical parameter-editing framework (Fisher mask + Targeted Manifold Scattering) to erase domain-specific styles while preserving zero-shot generalization; achieves improved open-vocabulary generalization across PACS, OfficeHome, DomainNet with high sample efficiency (4-shot vs 8-shot).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Approximate Domain Unlearning (ADU) uses a closed-vocabulary setup, causing domain forgetting to overfit to seen class-domain pairs and fail to erase the domain for unseen classes. A truly robust solution requires class-agnostic, open-vocabulary forgetting that transfers to held-out classes.

Method: 1) Fisher Information mask identifies and protects domain-sensitive weights to preserve foundational zero-shot capabilities. 2) Targeted Manifold Scattering (TMS) objective, via preference-based mining, locally scatters the forget domain's stylistic geometry to disrupt recognition across domains.

Result: Across PACS, OfficeHome, and DomainNet, the method significantly improves open-vocabulary generalization over baselines and demonstrates exceptional sample efficiency, outperforming an 8-shot baseline with only 4 shots.

Conclusion: OVDU with a surgical parameter-editing approach enables true, class-agnostic domain erasure that transfers to unseen classes, addressing the limitations of closed-vocabulary ADU and delivering stronger, more efficient open-vocabulary generalization.

Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit remarkable zero-shot generalization, yet they often encode unwanted or hazardous stylistic domains such as idealized textbook diagrams in medical AI or cartoon vehicles in autonomous driving. Approximate Domain Unlearning (ADU) aims to selectively erase a model's recognition of a target visual domain while preserving accuracy on the remaining domains. However, existing ADU methods operate under a flawed closed-vocabulary assumption: they evaluate unlearning solely on the specific object classes seen during the unlearning fine-tuning phase. Consequently, these methods do not unlearn the domain itself; they merely overfit to seen class-domain pairs, leaving the domain easily recognizable for unseen classes and providing a false sense of removal. We argue that true domain erasure must be class-agnostic. To address this, we formalize Open-Vocabulary Domain Unlearning (OVDU), a rigorous protocol that mandates domain forgetting must transfer to held-out classes. To solve the OVDU challenge, we propose a surgical parameter-editing framework. First, a Fisher Information mask isolates domain-sensitive weights, mathematically protecting foundational zero-shot generalization. Second, our Targeted Manifold Scattering (TMS) objective uses preference-based mining to locally scatter the forget domain's stylistic geometry. Evaluated across PACS, OfficeHome, and DomainNet, our method vastly improves open-vocabulary generalization over existing baselines. Crucially, it delivers exceptional sample efficiency, outperforming peak 8-shot baseline results with only 4 shots.

</details>


### [72] [OpenVAM: Open-World Visual Attention Modeling with VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31364)
*Kiana Hooshanfar,Amirhossein Kazerouni,Alireza Hosseini,Michael Brudno,Babak Taati*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OpenVAM: a unified, domain-robust visual attention model that combines dense saliency localization with language-grounded explanations, using a decoupled architecture and a three-stage training regime to handle natural scenes, commercial imagery, and UI/web layouts with multi-domain annotations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Move beyond dense saliency maps to discrete scene elements (what) and context-driven explanations (why) and to maintain robustness under domain shift across diverse image types and layouts.

Method: Decoupled architecture: a dense visual pathway for precise localization plus an instruction-following vision–language head for grounded what/why explanations. Three-stage training preserves localization priors, introduces language grounding, and aligns explanations via parameter-efficient adaptation without perturbing the saliency branch. A scalable pipeline generates multi-domain saliency–reason annotations for training and evaluation.

Result: Experiments on diverse datasets show improved robustness to domain shift and generation of image-grounded explanations, making saliency predictions more interpretable without sacrificing localization accuracy.

Conclusion: OpenVAM achieves universality and explainability across heterogeneous domains while preserving accurate saliency localization, demonstrated via a scalable annotation pipeline and cross-domain evaluations.

Abstract: Predicting human gaze is a core capability for applications ranging from web/UI design analysis to robotics and human-computer interaction. Yet, most visual attention modeling methods output only a dense saliency map, which is often insufficient for action: practitioners need to connect attention peaks to discrete elements in the scene (what) and understand the drivers of those peaks in context (why), while remaining robust to domain shift across natural images, commercial content, and UI/web layouts. We, therefore, introduce OpenVAM (Open-world Visual Attention Modeling with VLMs), a unified framework that jointly addresses universality and explainability across heterogeneous domains (natural scenes, commercial imagery, and UI/web layouts) and supervision modalities. OpenVAM adopts a decoupled-but-aligned design: a dedicated dense visual pathway provides stable, spatially precise localization, while an instruction-following vision--language semantic head generates grounded what/why explanations conditioned on the same image and data-type prompts. A three-stage training strategy preserves strong localization priors while progressively introducing language grounding and improving explanation alignment via parameter-efficient adaptation without perturbing the saliency branch. We further propose a scalable pipeline to generate multi-domain saliency-reason annotations for training and systematic evaluation. Experiments across diverse datasets show that OpenVAM improves robustness under domain shift while producing image-grounded explanations that make saliency predictions more interpretable.

</details>


### [73] [ContraFM-S2O: Flow Matching-Based One-step SAR-to-Optical Image Translation Model with Contrastive Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31378)
*Mingqian Yu,Wei-kuan Chiang,Qiurui Wang,Peilin Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A flow-matching-based SAR-to-optical translation method, ContraFM-S2O, with velocity-field prediction, ODE-based inference, one-step translation using average velocity, and contrastive learning. Claims state-of-the-art on SAR2Opt and QXS with lower latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
