Motivation: Address the limitations of diffusion- and GAN-based SAR-to-optical translation: high inference latency and blurred edges/fine textures in generated optical images.

Method: Predict velocity field via flow matching; solve ODE during inference instead of SDE; use average velocity along an interpolation path for one-step translation; apply contrastive learning to enhance image quality.

Result: Reported state-of-the-art performance on SAR2Opt and QXS datasets; reduced inference latency due to one-step generation.

Conclusion: ContraFM-S2O offers faster, higher-quality SAR-to-optical translation by combining flow matching with one-step generation and contrastive learning, surpassing baselines on the evaluated datasets.

Abstract: In recent years, diffusion models and GAN-based models have become the mainstream approaches for SAR-to-optical image translation, owing to their advantages, such as high-quality generation and stable training. However, they have shortcomings such as high inference latency and the generated optical images suffer from low detail fidelity, often resulting in blurred edges and loss of fine textures. Thus, we propose ContraFM-S2O, which is a flow matching-based model for SAR-to-optical image translation. Unlike conventional diffusion models, ContraFM-S2O learns to predict the velocity field in training and solves ODE instead of SDE during inference to improve the sampling efficiency. In addition, ContraFM-S2O replaces instantaneous velocity with average velocity along the interpolation path to realize one-step SAR-to-optical image translation and uses contrastive learning to improve the quality of the generated optical images. Experiments show our model achieves state-of-the-art on SAR2Opt and QXS datasets, outperforming baselines, and reduces inference latency via one-step generation.

</details>


### [74] [AxonSynth: Domain-Randomized Synthetic Data for Zero-Shot 3D Axon Segmentation in Light-Sheet Microscopy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31431)
*Edward Gaibor,Kyriaki-Margarita Bintsi,Carmen Luz Leiva Ureta,Zayneb Bellatif,Chiara Maffei,Wenze Li,Elizabeth Hillman,Yaël Balbastre,Anastasia Yendiki*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Synthetic-data domain randomization enables zero-shot 3D axon segmentation with competitive performance on held-out LSM patches, reducing manual annotation needs and improving topology metrics, across macaque and human brain samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual axon annotations are expensive and fragile under domain shifts (tissue type, species, modality, acquisition). A synthetic-label, domain-randomized approach aims to train robust segmentation without real annotations.

Method: AxonSynth creates dense synthetic axon labels with orientation priors and renders them with randomized density, contrast, bias fields, blur, and noise. A three-class 3D U-Net is trained to predict background, axon sheath, and intra-axonal space. Zero-shot transfer is evaluated on 10 held-out LSM patches from macaque and human brains using three axonal markers, compared to calibrated thresholding and Frangi. Metrics include overlap, corrected detection, false positives, topology metrics (component-count, Euler characteristic).

Result: Macaque: corrected Dice 0.826 (AxonSynth) vs 0.765 (thresholding) and 0.685 (Frangi); corrected precision 0.851 vs 0.754 (thresholding) and 0.762 (Frangi). Human: corrected Dice 0.857 vs 0.868 (thresholding); component-count error reduced from 22,504 to 3,377. Across all patches: AxonSynth reduces component-count error in 10/10 patches and Euler-characteristic error in 8/10 patches.

Conclusion: Synthetic-label domain randomization can reduce reliance on manual axon annotations and enable effective synthetic-to-real 3D axon segmentation across species, with strong gains in topology metrics and competitive Dice on held-out real data.

Abstract: Accurate segmentation of axons in 3D microscopy data is important for analyzing white-matter organization, but dense ground truth labels are expensive to obtain. Existing supervised axon segmentation methods rely on target-domain annotations and can be brittle when tissue type, species, modality, or acquisition conditions change. We present AxonSynth, a domain-randomized synthetic-data framework for training 3D axon segmentation models without manually annotated real training volumes. AxonSynth generates dense synthetic axon labels with orientation priors that reflect realistic fiber configurations and renders them with randomized density, contrast, bias fields, blur, and noise. A three-class 3D U-Net is trained to predict background, axon sheath and intra-axonal space. We evaluate zero-shot transfer on 10 held-out light-sheet microscopy (LSM) patches from macaque and human brain samples labeled with one of three axonal markers, comparing against calibrated thresholding and Frangi filtering using overlap, corrected detection, false-positive, and topology metrics. On macaque samples, AxonSynth achieved the best corrected Dice and corrected precision (0.826 and 0.851), compared with 0.765 and 0.754 for thresholding and 0.685 and 0.762 for Frangi. On human samples, corrected Dice was comparable to thresholding (0.857 vs. 0.868), while component-count error decreased from 22,504 to 3,377. Across all held-out patches, AxonSynth reduced component-count error in 10/10 patches and Euler-characteristic error in 8/10. These results show that synthetic-label domain randomization can reduce dependence on manual axon annotation while supporting synthetic-to-real 3D segmentation.

</details>


### [75] [Implicit Neural Representation for Hyperspectral Video Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31435)
*Alfredo Scalera,Paul Murray,Jaime Zabalza*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Implicit neural representations are extended from an RGB video compression model to hyperspectral video, yielding substantial rate–distortion gains and improved downstream task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hyperspectral video data are high-dimensional and expensive to compress. Frame-by-frame HS compression methods underutilize spectral redundancy and may hinder downstream tasks. A continuous, learned representation could better capture spectral/spatiotemporal correlations.

Method: Extend an existing RGB video compression model to hyperspectral video using implicit neural representation. Compare against traditional hyperspectral image compression applied frame-by-frame and evaluate downstream tracking performance. Use HOT2026 dataset for object tracking metrics in low data regimes.

Result: Reconstruction quality improvements: BD-PSNR gains of +4.99 dB and BD-rate reductions of -88.88% relative to frame-by-frame HS compression. Downstream task gains: tracking area under the curve (AUC) up to +23.42% and distance precision up to +35.56% compared to PCA+JPEG2000 baselines in low data regimes on HOT2026.

Conclusion: Implicit neural representations are a promising approach for hyperspectral video compression, delivering large gains in both reconstruction quality and downstream task performance, and warrant further investigation into efficiency, generalization across datasets, and real-time applicability.

Abstract: With the advent of snapshot cameras, hyperspectral video is becoming more readily available. In recent years, new applications have emerged which have led to increasingly larger datasets. However, hyperspectral video compression remains in the early stages. In this study, we explore the use of implicit neural representation as a candidate solution. We propose a novel extension of an existing RGB video compression model, achieving Bjøntegaard Delta PSNR gains of +4.99 dB and Bjøntegaard Delta rate of -88.88% compared to traditional hyperspectral image compression methods applied frame-by-frame. In addition to reconstruction quality, the effects on downstream task performance are measured in the form of object tracking success. Compared to video compressed with methods based on principal component analysis and JPEG2000 in low data regimes, our proposed method improves tracking area under the curve by up to 23.42% and distance precision by up to 35.56% on examples from the HOT2026 dataset.

</details>


### [76] [From Reward Signal to Visual Utility: A Controlled Audit of Medical VLM Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31450)
*Wang Jingxin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Post-training strategies for medical VLMs yield mixed effects on image-conditioned decisions; LoRA on the LM provides small accuracy gains but reduces visual-benefit and image-sensitivity; broader multimodal adaptation and GRPO show unstable gains; an audit reveals path-dependent evidence signals and misalignment with held-out visual behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To quantify how accuracy changes and training objectives translate into image-conditioned decision performance, and to identify gaps between optimization signals and actual visual behavior across SFT, LoRA, broader multimodal adaptation, GRPO, and counterfactual objectives.

Method: Controlled study on Qwen2.5-VL-3B using PMC-VQA with 2,000 clean-test questions; compare SFT, LM-only LoRA, expanded multimodal adaptation, standard answer-only GRPO, and a counterfactual evidence objective; evaluate correct-image accuracy, visual-benefit events, image-sensitivity; perform generation audits to compare option scores along generation paths; conduct sample-level analyses of evidence scores, decision margins, and generated answers.

Result: Key findings: +1.10 percentage points in correct-image accuracy with LM LoRA SFT (95% CI: -0.85 to +3.05); visual-benefit events decrease by 2.40 points; image-sensitivity decreases by 5.60 points; 155 acquired versus 203 lost visual-benefit events. Broader adaptation yields lower correct-image accuracy than LM LoRA SFT. Standard GRPO shows mixed reward groups and inconclusive accuracy changes. A generation audit reveals canonical option scores can follow different token paths from generated answers; greedy-path evidence targets improve on training data, but gains over GRPO are inconsistent on validation. Sample-level analyses trace how evidence scores, decision margins, and generated answers evolve during post-training. Overall, the study exposes gaps between optimization activity, target acquisition, and useful held-out visual behavior.

Conclusion: The empirical audit reveals misalignment between optimization signals and actual image-conditioned behavior in medical VLM post-training, highlighting the need to align training objectives with true visual decision-making and to adopt robust, path-aware evaluation of generation and evidence signals.

Abstract: Medical vision-language model (VLM) post-training is commonly evaluated through answer accuracy. We examine how changes in accuracy and training objectives relate to image-conditioned decisions in a controlled Qwen2.5-VL-3B study on PMC-VQA. We compare supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) restricted to the language model, expanded multimodal adaptation scopes, standard answer-only Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and a counterfactual evidence objective. On 2,000 clean-test questions, language model LoRA SFT changes correct-image accuracy by +1.10 percentage points (95% paired bootstrap CI:-0.85 to +3.05), while visual-benefit events decrease by 2.40 points and image sensitivity decreases by 5.60 points. Paired records reveal 155 acquired and 203 lost visual-benefit events. Broader adaptation yields lower correct-image accuracy than language-model LoRA SFT. Standard GRPO produces mixed-reward groups and parameter updates, with an uncertain clean test accuracy change. A generation audit reveals that canonical option scores can follow a different token path from generated answers. With scores taken along the greedy generation path, the evidence target improves on the training set; its gains over standard GRPO remain inconsistent on validation data at matched training doses. Sample-level analyses trace how evidence scores, decision margins, and generated answers change during post-training. This empirical and measurement audit identifies gaps between optimization activity, target acquisition, and useful held-out visual behavior.

</details>


### [77] [Diagnosing the Sources of Compositional Failure in Vision-Language Models: A Controlled Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31456)
*Mona Gandhi,Cenk Merih Olcay,Kuan-Chieh Lo,Santiago Castro,Christopher W. Myers,Srinivasan Parthasarathy*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: COMPASS provides a controlled framework to quantify compositional integration costs in VLMs and finds that degradation stems from separable factors, with self-load driving errors and cross-load context often helpful across architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To directly quantify the cost of compositional binding in vision-language models and disentangle joint reasoning from component recognition, addressing limitations of benchmarks that only evaluate composed captions.

Method: Introduce COMPASS to compare composed captions with decomposed counterparts using 87K image-caption pairs; assess by skill (object detection, attribute binding, relation reasoning) with 274K perturbations; evaluate across standard contrastive encoders, explicitly trained compositional models, and non-contrastive architectures.

Result: The compositional gap exists but is only partial; degradation is not solely due to joint reasoning. Self-load effects drive deterioration per primitive type, while cross-load effects are predominantly positive, and patterns hold across diverse model families.

Conclusion: Compositional degradation arises from multiple separable factors; the problem cannot be reduced to joint reasoning alone, motivating finer-grained analyses and targeted interventions.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often struggle with compositional reasoning tasks, but the reasons for this underperformance remain unclear. A common hypothesis is that models struggle to integrate multiple components, leading to training interventions to improve compositional binding. However, this assumption has never been directly quantified. Existing benchmarks evaluate captions only in their composed form, making it impossible to separate the cost of joint reasoning from the cost of recognizing individual components under increasing load. We introduce COMPASS (COMPositional Analysis of SkillS), a controlled evaluation framework designed to isolate and measure the distinct factors underlying compositional failure. By comparing performance on composed captions with their decomposed counterparts , we directly quantify the cost of compositional integration across 87K image-caption pairs. Across multiple VLMs, this gap is real but partial, accounting for only part of the observed degradation. This motivates a finer-grained investigation into what additional factors govern model behavior. We analyze performance at the level of individual skills: object detection, attribute binding, and relation reasoning, using skill-targeted perturbations across 274K image-caption pairs. We find a consistent skill-specific pattern: each skill degrades primarily with the count of its own primitive type (self-load), while cross-load effects are predominantly positive, suggesting that primitives of different types provide useful grounding context. This pattern holds across standard contrastive encoders, explicitly trained compositional reasoning models, and non-contrastive architectures. These findings show that compositional degradation reflects multiple separable factors that cannot be reduced to joint reasoning alone.

</details>


### [78] [KneePreM: Towards 3D Knee MRI Foundation Models via Large-Scale Unlabeled Pretraining and Label-Efficient Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31461)
*Xinxin Wang,Liam Hazan,Jing Li,Simona Rabinovici-Cohen,Xiaojuan Li,Mingrui Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: KneePreM, a 3D self-supervised model trained on 19k unlabeled knee MRIs, improves label-efficient transfer for knee MRI classification and segmentation, outperforming baselines (including SuPreM), especially with limited labeled data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Exploit abundant unlabeled knee MRI data to boost transfer learning and reduce annotation effort across multiple downstream knee-imaging tasks.

Method: Pretrain a 3D U-Net masked autoencoder on 19,011 unlabeled OAI MRI series (4,791 participants). Fine-tune downstream with full and reduced training sets for tasks: fastMRI+ two-label classification (1,172 exams), APM eight-target classification (1,716 exams), SKM-TEA segmentation (155 exams), and APM segmentation (25 exams). Baselines: random initialization and SuPreM. Evaluation used balanced accuracy, F1, ROC AUC, PR AUC, and Dice; bootstrap/CIs and nonparametric tests.

Result: KneePreM achieved higher full-data macro ROC AUC than baselines for fastMRI+ and APM (p<0.001). In fastMRI+ classification, 0.722 ROC AUC with 50% of data, surpassing full-data baselines. In APM classification, 0.740 ROC AUC with 70% data, matching full-data random baseline and outperforming SuPreM. For SKM-TEA segmentation, 70% data yielded Dice 0.838, exceeding full-data random baseline (0.835). In APM segmentation, 75% data Dice 0.746, exceeding full-data random baseline (0.731).

Conclusion: KneePreM enhances transfer learning and label efficiency across knee MRI classification and segmentation tasks, particularly when labeled data are scarce.

Abstract: Background: Large volumes of unlabeled knee MRI scans are available across repositories but remain insufficiently leveraged. We developed KneePreM, a knee-specific 3D self-supervised model, and evaluated transfer and label efficiency for classification and segmentation. Methods: A 3D U-Net masked autoencoder was pretrained on 19,011 unlabeled Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) MRI series from 4,791 participants. Downstream fine-tuning used full and reduced training sets for fastMRI+ two-label classification (1,172 examinations), Arthroscopic Partial Meniscectomy (APM) eight-target classification (1,716 examinations), SKM-TEA segmentation (155 examinations), and APM segmentation (25 examinations). Baselines were random initialization and SuPreM. Deployment workflow was implemented with a Model Context Protocol interface. Evaluation metrics included balanced accuracy, F1 score, ROC AUC, PR AUC, and Dice score. Statistical analysis used bootstrap confidence intervals and paired bootstrap tests for classification and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for segmentation. Results: KneePreM achieved higher full-data macro ROC AUC than both baselines for fastMRI+ and APM (all p < .001). For fastMRI+ classification, KneePreM achieved a ROC AUC of 0.722 using 50% of the training data, exceeding both full-data baselines. In APM classification, KneePreM reached a ROC AUC of 0.740 with 70% of the data, matching the full-data random baseline and outperforming SuPreM. For SKM-TEA segmentation, its 70%-data Dice of 0.838 exceeded the full-data random baseline (0.835) and both same-budget comparators. In APM segmentation, its 75%-data Dice of 0.746 exceeded the full-data random baseline (0.731) and both same-budget comparators. Conclusion: KneePreM improves transfer performance and label efficiency across knee MRI classification and segmentation tasks, particularly when labeled training data are limited.

</details>


### [79] [SatNav: A Scalable Benchmark for Long-Horizon UAV Vision-Language Navigation from Satellite Imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31507)
*Jiajun Jiang,Chunliang Hua,Zichun Chen,Yanxing Wu,Zeyuan Yang,Jie Song,Xiao Hu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SatNav is a scalable UAV VLN benchmark built from high-resolution satellite imagery to enable long-horizon, city-scale navigation without costly 3D reconstructions; it provides 118k episodes across 18 cities to stress memory and geospatial grounding, introduces SwiftVLN for memory-ablation studies, and demonstrates satellite-to-UAV transfer of navigation models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations in existing VLN benchmarks caused by dependence on costly reconstructed 3D assets, which constrain geographic diversity and episode scale; enable city-level, long-horizon UAV navigation with varied memory and grounding challenges.

Method: Construct SatNav from satellite crops as nadir observations, automate cue-to-episode pipeline to yield 118k episodes from 59 scenes across 18 cities (avg trajectory ~379 m); define three task families (Boundary, Landmark, Route) to stress loop tracking, landmark grounding, and route following with counting cues; benchmark classical VLN and LVLM-based agents; introduce SwiftVLN modular framework with switchable memory components and perform memory-design ablations; conduct satellite-to-UAV transfer experiments to validate practicality.

Result: City-scale VLN remains challenging for both classical and LVLM-based agents, indicating substantial room for memory and geospatial grounding improvements; SwiftVLN reveals effects of memory components; satellite-trained models can transfer to real UAV observations, suggesting practical applicability.

Conclusion: SatNav provides a scalable, long-horizon UAV VLN benchmark that emphasizes memory and geospatial grounding, enabling systematic memory design research (via SwiftVLN) and cross-domain transfer from satellite to UAV imagery; it expands geographic diversity and episode scale beyond 3D asset–dependent benchmarks.

Abstract: Urban uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) vision-language navigation (VLN) requires agents to follow instructions across extended urban spaces, inherently demanding long-term memory and geospatial grounding. However, scaling existing benchmarks remains difficult because of their reliance on costly reconstructed 3D assets, limiting geographic diversity and episode scale. To address this, we introduce SatNav, a scalable, long-horizon UAV VLN benchmark built from high-resolution satellite imagery. SatNav targets city-level navigation missions and uses satellite crops as approximations of UAV nadir views for visual observations. Through an automated cue-to-episode pipeline, SatNav constructs 118K episodes from 59 scenes across 18 cities, with an average trajectory length of 379 m. To stress-test long-horizon memory and geospatial reasoning, SatNav defines three task families: Boundary, Landmark, and Route, targeting loop progress tracking, landmark-based spatial grounding, and route following with counting cues. Benchmarking classical VLN agents and recent agents based on large vision-language models (LVLMs) on SatNav shows that city-scale navigation remains challenging. We further introduce SwiftVLN, a modular framework with switchable memory components, and conduct systematic memory-design ablations. Finally, satellite-to-UAV transfer experiments show that satellite-trained navigation models can operate on real-flight UAV observations, showing the practical relevance of SatNav. Our project page: https://eku127.github.io/SatNav/

</details>


### [80] [ClearGS: Reliability-Aware Gaussian Splatting from Handheld Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31509)
*Xuanzhi Liu,Xinyi Wu,Hang Pan,Wensi Huang,Zhenyao Wu,Ruize Han,Song Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ClearGS: reliability-aware frame weighting, in-video restoration, and trajectory repair for 3D Gaussian Splatting from handheld videos, achieving SOTA without clean references.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address uneven viewpoint coverage and mixed frame quality in handheld video sequences for 3DGS, where weighting alone cannot recover details lost to blur or distortion.

Method: RVA assigns graded weights to raw frames; RIVR uses a pose-aligned render, a no-reference restoration module, and no-reference perceptual scores to select among render, restored observation, and high-frequency fusion; Full-Trajectory Repair Consolidation revisits repairs.

Result: State-of-the-art on GS2E and GSOTM; consistent CLIP-IQA and MUSIQ gains; LPIPS reductions across most degradations; no paired sharp supervision or clean references.

Conclusion: The combination of graded supervision, no-reference restoration, and trajectory consolidation yields robust 3DGS quality under degraded handheld inputs and generalizes without clean references.

Abstract: We present ClearGS for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) from handheld videos with uneven viewpoint coverage and mixed frame quality. Rather than selecting frames with binary decisions, ClearGS uses Reliability-aware View Allocation (RVA) to assign graded raw-supervision weights based on appearance reliability, degradation risk, and geometric utility, while weakly reactivating useful suppressed frames to maintain trajectory coverage. Since weighting cannot restore details lost to blur or distortion, ClearGS further introduces Render-Guided In-Video Restoration (RIVR). The current 3DGS render provides a pose-aligned structural candidate, a frozen no-reference restoration expert restores the corresponding raw video observation without any clean reference image, and no-reference perceptual scores select among the render, restored observation, and high-frequency fused candidate. ClearGS then applies Full-Trajectory Repair Consolidation to revisit accepted repairs and preserve details introduced early. On GS2E and GSOTM, ClearGS achieves state-of-the-art overall performance, with consistent CLIP-IQA and MUSIQ gains and LPIPS reductions in most degradation settings, without paired sharp supervision or matched clean references.

</details>


### [81] [Forensic Twins: Self-Supervised Residual Learning for AI-Generated Image Forensics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31514)
*Javier Muñoz-Haro,Ruben Tolosana,Ruben Vera-Rodriguez,Aythami Morales,Julian Fierrez*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Forensic Twins presents a self-supervised residual-learning framework trained only on real images to detect AI-generated images. It uses a frozen forensic residual extractor to create two crops per image and learns via a redundancy-reduction objective that preserves a common acquisition fingerprint. It achieves 56.61% generator attribution accuracy (6.13% above prior zero-shot) with very low latency, and a downstream GMM on real-image embeddings achieves 97.99% AUC on 27 unseen generators, suggesting strong zero-shot generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Detectors trained on known AI architectures struggle to generalize to new, unseen generators. Standard self-supervised pretraining can conflict with forensic signals due to augmentations that erase micro-statistics. A real-data-only, self-supervised approach that preserves intrinsic acquisition fingerprints could offer robust, zero-shot detection of new generators.

Method: A frozen, off-the-shelf forensic residual extractor is applied to images to obtain residuals. For each image, two spatially disjoint crops are sampled; they share no pixels but retain minimal semantic content. A redundancy-reduction objective aligns the two views, emphasizing the common, stationary fingerprint of the image acquisition pipeline. Training uses only real images; no AI-generated images are observed. The approach yields direct attribution via a classifier and enables strong zero-shot detection when a Gaussian Mixture Model is fitted offline on the real-image embeddings.

Result: Attribution accuracy of 56.61% for identifying AI generator sources, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot method by 6.13% with 375x lower latency. An offline GMM on real-image embeddings achieves 97.99% AUC across 27 unseen generators (GANs, diffusion models, and commercial systems).

Conclusion: Forensic Twins offers a robust, low-latency, zero-shot path for AI-generated image detection by leveraging real-image self-supervision and a residual-based forensic signal. The strong unseen-generator performance via the GMM suggests practical generalization, with code and weights to be released.

Abstract: Detectors of AI-generated images are typically trained using samples from all Generative AI architectures they must catch, and struggle as soon as a new architecture emerges. Recent approaches have explored self-supervised pre-training as an alternative solution, yet standard frameworks work against the forensic task, e.g., their augmentations overwrite the micro-statistics of image formation. This paper introduces Forensic Twins, a Self-Supervised Residual Learning (SSRL) framework whose pretext task suppresses macroscopic content availability. Each image is mapped through a frozen, off-the-shelf forensic residual extractor, from which two spatially disjoint crops are drawn. Sharing no pixel, the two views retain minimal semantic structure to align, leaving a redundancy-reduction objective with a predominant common signal: the stationary fingerprint of the image acquisition pipeline. Additionally, Forensic Twins is trained exclusively on real images; no AI-generated image is observed at any stage. Experiments show that Forensic Twins attributes AI generator sources with 56.61% accuracy, i.e., 6.13% above the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot method at 375x lower latency. We also demonstrate that fitting a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) offline using only the real image embeddings extracted from Forensic Twins turns it into a state-of-the-art zero-shot detector, reaching 97.99% AUC across 27 unseen AI generators, including GANs, diffusion models and commercial systems. Code, weights and exact splits will be made publicly available

</details>


### [82] [Structured Reasoning Agentic Framework for Interpretable Critical View of Safety Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31524)
*Qing Xu,Yuxiang Luo,Zhen Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A structured reasoning framework for CVS assessment (ReasonCVS) that uses Anatomical Scene Graph Abstraction and a rationale-aware LLM to verify sub-criteria via VLMs, yielding interpretable decisions with strong mAP on Endoscapes-CVS201.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address lack of interpretability and poor compositional generalization in holistic CVS assessment by encoding anatomical relations and explicit sub-criterion verification.

Method: Construct Anatomical Scene Graph Abstraction (ASGA) of anatomical entities and spatial relations; employ a Rationale-Aware Reasoning Agent (LLM fine-tuned via rationale distillation) as central decision-maker; use VLM-driven Sub-criterion Verifiers to parse the graph and verify individual sub-criteria; synthesize observations with calibrated soft reasoning to produce final verdict and traceable rationale.

Result: Achieves 68.1% mAP on Endoscapes-CVS201, outperforming state-of-the-art methods and providing interpretable, criterion-level explanations for surgical assessment.

Conclusion: Structured, interpretable reasoning with explicit anatomical relations and dedicated perceptual tools enhances CVS assessment performance and interpretability, with potential for better generalization and clinical trust.

Abstract: Surgical scene understanding is critical for computer-assisted intervention, yet laparoscopic cholecystectomy remains challenged by the complex anatomy of the hepatocystic triangle and the risk of bile duct injury. Existing methods for Critical View of Safety (CVS) assessment typically treat it as a holistic prediction task, mapping visual features directly to criterion-level labels. This black-box paradigm lacks explicit reasoning about anatomical relationships, limiting both interpretability and compositional generalization. To address this, we propose ReasonCVS, a structured reasoning agentic framework empowered by Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that decomposes CVS assessment into explicit, fine-grained anatomical verification. Specifically, we devise an Anatomical Scene Graph Abstraction (ASGA) that organizes anatomical entities and their spatial relationships into a structured representation. To operationalize this, we introduce a Rationale-Aware Reasoning Agent, powered by a Large Language Model (LLM) fine-tuned via rationale distillation. Functioning as a strict central decision-maker, it invokes VLM-driven Sub-criterion Verifier as a specialized perceptual tool to parse the graph and independently evaluate individual sub-criteria. Through calibrated soft reasoning, this agent synthesizes the tool-gathered distributed observations, yielding a final verdict alongside a traceable clinical rationale. Extensive experiments on the Endoscapes-CVS201 benchmark demonstrate that ReasonCVS achieves superior performance (68.1\% mAP) over state-of-the-art while providing interpretable, criterion-level explanations for reliable surgical assessment.

</details>


### [83] [Region-Level Black-Box Defense Against Stealthy Embedding-Space Backdoors in CLIP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31558)
*Ahmed Abdelnaby,Mohamed Elmahallawy*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A black-box defense, CLIPGuard, detects and purifies embedding-space backdoors in CLIP encoders by segment-wise perturbation analysis and semantic inpainting, achieving strong robustness with minimal impact on clean accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Embedding-space backdoor attacks on CLIP are highly effective and hard to detect, especially in black-box deployments where access to gradients or model parameters is unavailable.

Method: CLIPGuard measures segment-wise embedding perturbations to identify suspicious regions and purifies only those segments via semantic inpainting, preserving benign content and alignment quality without requiring model parameters, gradients, or clean validation data.

Result: On STL-10, ImageNet, and diverse trigger families (BadCLIP, BadNets, blended, patch-based, typographic), CLIPGuard reduces attack success rates to as low as 1.05% while maintaining clean accuracy up to 86.34%, outperforming existing black-box defenses such as CleanCLIP and CleanerCLIP.

Conclusion: CLIPGuard is a lightweight, fully black-box defense that effectively mitigates embedding-space backdoors in CLIP encoders while preserving alignment quality and scalability across datasets and trigger types.

Abstract: Contrastive Language--Image Pretraining (CLIP) has emerged as a dominant vision backbone due to its strong transferability and zero-shot capabilities. However, recent studies reveal a critical vulnerability: embedding-space backdoor attacks. By poisoning only a tiny fraction of image--text pairs, adversaries can implant stealthy triggers that induce targeted shifts in CLIP's joint embedding space. Unlike conventional backdoors that manipulate classifier logits, these attacks corrupt representations directly, making them highly effective under extremely low poisoning ratios and difficult to detect. Existing defenses require access to model parameters, gradients, logits, or clean validation data---assumptions that rarely hold in realistic black-box deployments. Moreover, current black-box methods struggle to accurately localize small or out-of-distribution triggers. We propose CLIPGuard, a lightweight and fully black-box defense specifically designed to mitigate embedding-space backdoors in CLIP encoders. CLIPGuard identifies malicious regions by measuring segment-wise embedding perturbations and selectively purifies only suspicious segments via semantic inpainting, preserving benign visual content and alignment quality. Extensive experiments on STL-10, ImageNet, and diverse trigger families---including BadCLIP, BadNets, blended, patch-based, and typographic attacks---demonstrate that CLIPGuard reduces attack success rates to as low as 1.05% while maintaining clean accuracy up to 86.34%, consistently outperforming existing black-box defenses, including CleanCLIP and CleanerCLIP. Our code is available https://github.com/wsu-cyber-security-lab-ai/CLIPGuard.git

</details>


### [84] [OC-GS: Gaussian Splatting for Irregular Turntable Capture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31572)
*Jae Joong Lee,Bedrich Benes*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OC-GS refines per-image angles under a shared camera/motion model for sparse, irregular turntable captures, improving object reconstruction with Gaussian splatting and yielding higher PSNR than pose-free baselines; real data shows modest gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uneven rotation and dropped frames violate equal-angle assumptions in turntable reconstruction, making angle estimates unreliable; a joint optimization that refines angles within a shared motion model can improve geometry and rendering quality.

Method: Orbit-consistent refinement jointly optimizes image-derived geometry and per-image angles under a shared camera, rotation axis, and pivot; uses object-centric Gaussian splatting; includes a shared trainer and ablation studies on angle initialization and motion model; evaluated on rendered objects with irregular view counts and on real captures.

Result: Rendered tests: with 12, 8, 6 irregular views, mean foreground PSNRs of 21.26, 19.36, 15.83 dB, respectively, beating four pose-free Gaussian splatting baselines. Under a shared trainer, angle refinement adds 7.88 dB over fixed estimates. Ablation confirms contributions from angle initialization and motion model. Real captures: mean foreground PSNR increases by 0.70 dB with refinement.

Conclusion: Refining uncertain per-image angles within a shared motion framework improves reconstruction from sparse, irregular turntable data.

Abstract: Uneven rotation and dropped frames make equal-angle assumptions unreliable for turntable reconstruction. We present OC-GS, an object-centric Gaussian splatting that refines each image's angle while maintaining a shared camera, rotation axis, and pivot. This orbit-consistent refinement jointly optimizes image-derived geometry and angles to reconstruct objects from sparse, irregular captures. On rendered objects with 12, 8, and 6 irregularly spaced views, OC-GS achieves mean foreground PSNR scores of 21.26, 19.36, and 15.83dB, respectively, exceeding all four evaluated pose-free Gaussian splatting baselines in each condition. Under a shared trainer, refining image-estimated angles improves mean foreground PSNR by 7.88dB over keeping those estimates fixed. An ablation study shows that both image-derived angle initialization and the shared motion model contribute to the improvement. On real captures, OC-GS's refinement increases mean foreground PSNR by 0.70dB. Results show that refining uncertain angles within a shared motion model improves reconstruction from sparse, irregular turntable captures.

</details>


### [85] [How Far Can INRs Go? Cross-Domain Parameter-efficient INR-Based Semantic Segmentation for Brain MRI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31573)
*Ziyao Shang,Pouya Sadeghi,Letian Jiang,Alexander Wong,Sirisha Rambhatla*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: HierINRSeg, a hierarchical INR-based segmentation model, improves cross-domain brain MRI segmentation by aggregating multi-layer INR representations, outperforming MetaSeg especially in out-of-domain settings; INRs show strongest gains under low-parameter regimes and limited augmentation, while U-Nets benefit from larger capacity and standard augmentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) behave for semantic segmentation, particularly their mechanisms, scaling, and domain generalization, in cross-domain brain MRI. The study also aims to identify when INR-based segmentation is most advantageous and how to design robust architectures.

Method: Systematic analysis of INR-based segmentation across low-parameter budgets and limited augmentation, comparison with U-Net-based pipelines, probing how semantic information is distributed across INR layers, and development of HierINRSeg that aggregates multi-layer representations. Extensive experiments on in-domain and out-of-domain brain MRI segmentation, comparing to MetaSeg (a strong INR-based baseline).

Result: INRs are not simply better with more parameters; their advantages appear primarily in low-parameter, limited-augmentation regimes. The hidden features encode complementary, multi-layer semantic information. HierINRSeg, which aggregates multiple layer representations, yields consistent improvements over MetaSeg: +5.6 Dice points in-domain and +8.2 Dice points out-of-domain.

Conclusion: INR-based segmentation has regime-dependent benefits. For cross-domain brain MRI, HierINRSeg provides robustness and generalization by multi-layer representation aggregation, guiding model selection toward low-parameter INR designs in constrained settings, while conventional U-Nets excel with higher capacity and standard augmentations.

Abstract: Biomedical image segmentation is central to medical image analysis, but practical deployment often faces limited annotations, memory constraints, and cross-site distribution shifts. Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) have recently emerged as a lightweight alternative for semantic segmentation, achieving competitive performance with substantially fewer parameters than conventional architectures. However, the mechanisms, scaling behavior, and domain generalization abilities of INR-based segmentation remain insufficiently understood. In this work, we study these questions in the context of cross-domain brain MRI segmentation. We analyze INR-based segmentation across low-parameter regimes, comparing it with conventional pipelines in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings. Surprisingly, we find that INR-based models do not simply improve with increasing parameter budget. Their advantage is most pronounced under low-parameter and limited-augmentation settings, while U-Net-based models benefit more from larger capacity and standard augmentation. We also investigate how INRs encode semantic information in their hidden features and show that complementary segmentation-relevant structure is distributed across multiple INR layers. Building on this insight, we introduce HierINRSeg, a hierarchical INR-based architecture that aggregates multi-layer representations for improved robustness and generalization. Extensive experiments show that HierINRSeg consistently outperforms MetaSeg, a strong recent INR-based segmentation baseline, with an average improvement of 5.6 percentage points in Dice for the in-domain test set and 8.2 percentage points out-of-domain. Overall, our analysis identifies the conditions under which INR-based segmentation is most effective, providing concrete guidance for model selection and future research.

</details>


### [86] [GraphWrit3R: End-to-End 3D Scene Graph Writing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31595)
*Luka Milivojevic,Nikola Popovic,Sayan Deb Sarkar,Sebastian Koch,Iro Armeni,Luc Van Gool,Danda Pani Paudel*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: End-to-end 3D scene graph generation (GraphWrit3R) using multimodal inputs (point clouds via Sonata or Gaussian splats via Chorus) fused on a shared voxel grid with per-voxel contrastive alignment, decoded by an LLM to produce a JSON scene graph. It achieves state-of-the-art recall on 3DSSG without requiring ground-truth annotations at inference and supports open-vocabulary querying.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address core drawbacks of existing 3D scene graph pipelines: fragility from multi-stage processing and error propagation, reliance on ground-truth annotations during inference, proprietary dependencies, and slow inference. The goal is an end-to-end, open, efficient pipeline that can operate on diverse inputs and still output structured graphs.

Method: Process 3D inputs (point clouds via Sonata, Gaussian splats via Chorus, or both) and project to a shared voxel grid. Fuse modalities using a novel per-voxel contrastive alignment loss. Decode the fused representation with a large language model to produce a complete scene graph in JSON, enabling open-vocabulary querying.

Result: On the 3DSSG benchmark, GraphWrit3R achieves state-of-the-art recall for object classes, predicates, and triplets, outperforming methods that rely on ground-truth object annotations during inference. The work also provides qualitative results and analyzes different modality configurations, contrastive loss formulations, and token fusion strategies.

Conclusion: An end-to-end, multimodal 3D scene graph generator that eliminates intermediate representations and restrictive assumptions, offers open-vocabulary querying via the LLM, and delivers strong performance on standard benchmarks—facilitating versatile, open deployment without ground-truth-inference dependencies.

Abstract: 3D scene graphs provide a structured representation of complex environments by encoding objects, their semantic attributes, and the spatial and functional relationships between them. Current approaches for 3D scene graph generation suffer from several fundamental limitations. They rely on complex multi-stage pipelines with explicit intermediate representations, making systems fragile and prone to error propagation. They assume access to ground-truth object annotations during inference, which deviates from real-world scenarios. They depend on proprietary models, hindering open-source deployment, or incur prohibitively slow inference. We present GraphWrit3R, a simple end-to-end method that takes a 3D point cloud, Gaussian Splats, or a combination of both as input, and directly outputs a complete scene graph as a structured JSON script. The graph lists all objects, their semantic attributes, and the relationships between them, while avoiding all of the above mentioned limitations. The choice of multiple input modalities is purely for versatility, allowing a single set of weights to handle diverse scenarios. Point cloud inputs are encoded via Sonata and Gaussian Splat inputs via Chorus, with both modalities projected onto a shared voxel grid and fused through a novel per-voxel contrastive alignment loss before being decoded by a large language model. As a natural consequence of the LLM, GraphWrit3R also supports open-vocabulary querying. On the 3DSSG benchmark, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on object class, predicate, and triplet recall, outperforming methods that rely on ground-truth object annotations during inference. We further provide qualitative results and analyze different input modality configurations, contrastive loss formulations, and token fusion strategies.

</details>


### [87] [FuseReg: Regularizing Layer Fusion Mitigates the Reconstruction-Generation Gap in Representation Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31620)
*Hongyang Du,Yunfei Xie,Junjie Ye,Jiawei Yang,Xiaoyan Cong,Haodong Zhang,Yongchao Huang,Haiyu Wu,Zongxia Li,Shihang Gui,Dawei Liu,Runhao Li,Jingcheng Ni,Chen Wei,Randall Balestriero,Yue Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FuseReg trains downstream models on random subsets of encoder layers to robustly fuse representations, replacing fixed heuristic fusion with layer-subset regularization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed, hand-picked layer fusion in representation autoencoders trades off fine pixel details (shallow layers) against strong generation metrics (deep layers); a robust approach should perform well across layer choices without retraining the encoder.

Method: Train downstream decoders (and diffusion stages) on random encoder-layer subsets to penalize cross-layer disagreement; provide theoretical justification for subset sampling; evaluate on ImageNet-256 with DINOv3-L, testing full/sparse/single-layer fusions without retraining; apply joint regularization for diffusion training.

Result: Single FuseReg decoder reconstructs well across full, sparse, and single-layer fusions, outperforming decoders fixed to specific fusions (PSNR gains); reduces unguided gFID by 27% in generation with unchanged generator; joint regularization during diffusion reduces unguided gFID by 29%; overall narrows reconstruction-generation gap without altering the pretrained encoder.

Conclusion: Training for layer-fusion robustness yields flexible, encoder-agnostic reconstruction and generation improvements, demonstrating that downstream regularization can supplant fixed fusion heuristics without encoder modification.

Abstract: Representation autoencoders (RAEs) reuse features from a pretrained visual encoder as reconstruction and diffusion latents, integrating strong visual representations into image generation. However, RAEs still need to decide which encoder layers form the shared latent space for the generator and pixel decoder. This choice involves a trade-off. Shallower layers tend to preserve fine pixel details better, while deeper layers tend to yield better generation metrics. A fixed heuristic layer fusion therefore couples two stages that benefit from different information. We introduce FuseReg, which replaces heuristic feature selection with training over random subsets of encoder layers. We theoretically analyze the underlying mechanism: subset sampling explicitly penalizes sensitivity to cross-layer disagreement. On ImageNet-256 with DINOv3-L, a single FuseReg decoder reconstructs from full, sparse, and single-layer fusions without retraining, achieving higher PSNR than decoders specialized to fixed fusions. This flexibility also benefits generation: decoder replacement alone reduces unguided gFID by 27% with an unchanged RAEv2 DiT-XL generator. The same regularization principle extends to diffusion training, with joint regularization of both stages reducing unguided gFID by 29% on DiT-Base. These results show that training downstream models for layer-fusion robustness narrows the reconstruction-generation gap without modifying the pretrained encoder.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [88] [HybridInfer: Thermal-Aware Reinforcement-Learning Tier Routing for On-Device, Edge, and Cloud LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30270)
*Simran Koul*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A thermal-aware RL router (HybridInfer) dynamically selects among on-device, edge, and cloud LLMs to balance quality, latency, cost, and thermal constraints on mobile hardware; it uses on-device thermal headroom and query complexity as state, with an offline Q-learning policy, showing improvements over heuristic baselines on an Android benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mobile on-device LLM inference is thermally constrained and can fail during long generations; existing routing approaches ignore thermal headroom. A motivation to design a thermostat-aware, tiered inference system to improve reliability and efficiency.

Method: A three-tier hierarchy (on-device Llama 3.2 3B, edge Llama 3.1 8B with retrieval, cloud GPT-4o) is managed by a Q-learning policy trained offline. State includes thermal headroom and query complexity. Reward trades quality, latency, cost, and a thermal penalty, plus a locality bonus for on-device execution. Evaluation on 210 prompts on Android, comparing to two hand-tuned heuristics.

Result: The learned router achieves significantly higher quality than heuristics (paired Wilcoxon, p < 0.02) at the lowest cost among adaptive configurations. Always-on-device yields servable-query quality but is 3–6x slower and fails on long queries. Routing reduces latency, improves reliability, and increases coverage. This is the first reported use of on-device thermal headroom to select among LLM tiers on real hardware.

Conclusion: Thermal-aware, RL-based tier routing can outperform heuristic baselines in a three-tier LLM setup, leveraging on-device headroom to improve latency, reliability, and coverage; the approach demonstrates the feasibility and novelty of thermal-aware decision-making in mobile AI systems.

Abstract: On-device inference with small language models keeps user data local, works offline, and incurs no per-query cost, so the on-device tier is preferred when it is adequate. It is thermally constrained, however, and I find the constraint is sharper than a slowdown: on a flagship Snapdragon device, sustained on-device generation destabilizes the GPU inference runtime, which crashes or silently wedges after a few consecutive queries. The failure lies in the current toolchain (OpenCL kernel compilation and long-prompt prefill on the mobile GPU), recurs even when the device is cool, and is worst for long generations. Multi-tier routers across on-device, edge, and cloud models can relieve this pressure, but existing routers are thermal-blind and typically evaluated in simulation or on non-mobile hardware. I present HybridInfer, a thermal-aware reinforcement-learning router for a three-tier hierarchy (on-device Llama 3.2 3B, edge Llama 3.1 8B with retrieval, cloud GPT-4o) that uses the phone's thermal headroom and a query-complexity estimate as state and selects a tier by an offline-trained Q-learning policy. Its reward trades quality against latency, cost, and a thermal penalty, plus a locality bonus crediting on-device execution. I show this bonus is a precondition for thermal-aware routing: without it the optimal policy offloads every query. On a real Android benchmark of 210 prompts, the learned router attains significantly higher quality than two hand-tuned heuristics (paired Wilcoxon, p < 0.02) at the lowest cost of any adaptive condition. Always-on-device conditions match per-query quality on servable queries but are three to six times slower and fail on long queries, so routing wins on latency, reliability, and coverage rather than quality. To my knowledge this is the first use of on-device thermal headroom to select among LLM inference tiers of differing capability on real hardware.

</details>


### [89] [When the Preconditioning Exponent Turns Negative: Learning-Rate Coupling and Cross-Environment Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30271)
*Gongyue Zhang,Honghai Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Examines how the exponent p of the second-moment preconditioner interacts with learning rate η in adaptive optimizers across four environments; finds p*(η) decreases roughly linearly with log10 η; shows source-validation can select different preconditioning than what maximizes cross-environment robustness; negative p is not universally optimal and reflects a high-step-size regime.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand the coupled influence of preconditioning exponent and learning rate on cross-environment robustness and spurious feature handling in partially adaptive optimizers.

Method: Empirical study across 21 preconditioning exponents p in [-0.5,0.5] and five learning rates η in [1e-4,1e-2], using a paired four-environment classification task with varying feature regimes; evaluate using source-validation, cross-environment, and worst-environment criteria; perform checkpoint decomposition to analyze weight ratios; report regression of optimal p vs log10 η and robustness metrics across environments.

Result: Optimal p decreases almost linearly with log10 η (slopes -0.270 to -0.300, R^2 0.972–0.996). At η=1e-2, source-validation prefers positive p, but cross-environment and worst-environment criteria prefer negative p. Lower p reduces spurious-to-stable and noise-to-stable weight ratios, and under reversed correlation also reduces the harmful spurious margin. Negative p is not universally optimal; p acts as a high-step-size allocation regime via joint η and preconditioning. A model-selection conflict exists: source-domain validation selects a regime different from the one maximizing robustness to environmental change. The study is a single-seed, finite-budget exploration rather than a broad benchmark.

Conclusion: Practitioners should consider joint tuning of preconditioning exponent p and learning rate η; rely on robustness-focused criteria rather than source-validation alone; negative p is not universally best and the optimal choice depends on the interaction with η and the evaluation criterion.

Abstract: Adaptive optimizers are commonly parameterized by a fixed power of the second-moment estimate. Existing partially adaptive methods study exponents between momentum-like updates and the standard Adam square root, while the interaction between this exponent and the global learning rate is less understood. We perform a controlled cross-environment study using a paired four-environment classification problem with stable sparse features, environment-dependent spurious sparse features, dense features, and high-dimensional noise. Across \NumRuns{} source-training runs covering 21 preconditioning exponents $p\in[-0.5,0.5]$ and five learning rates $η\in[10^{-4},10^{-2}]$, we find that the exponent maximizing cross-environment accuracy decreases almost linearly with $\log_{10}η$. The fitted slopes range from $-0.270$ to $-0.300$, with $R^2$ between $0.972$ and $0.996$. At $η=10^{-2}$, source-validation selection still prefers positive exponents in all four environments, whereas cross-environment and worst-environment criteria prefer negative exponents. Checkpoint decomposition shows that lower $p$ reduces the learned spurious-to-stable and noise-to-stable weight ratios; under reversed correlation, it also reduces the magnitude of the harmful spurious margin. Negative $p$ is therefore not a universally optimal setting. It is a high-step-size allocation regime produced by the joint action of learning rate and preconditioning. The study also exposes a model-selection conflict: source-domain validation systematically selects a different preconditioning regime from the one that maximizes robustness to environmental change. The results are a single-seed, finite-budget mechanism study rather than a broad benchmark claim.

</details>


### [90] [ENAS: An Efficient Hardware-Aware Neural Architecture Search Framework for TinyML on Resource-Constrained Microcontrollers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30272)
*Mohd Moin Khan,Naman Srivastava,Pandarasamy Arjunan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GPU-free, hardware-aware NAS (ENAS) for microcontrollers with a three-stage search and caching, achieving fast search and memory-efficient architectures; open-source.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need for efficient NAS that runs on resource-constrained devices without GPUs. Microcontroller deployment imposes RAM and compute constraints; existing NAS often rely on GPUs and large memory, limiting TinyML deployment. ENAS targets reduced peak activation RAM and practical search on constrained hardware.

Method: Static feasibility check; cell-based search space including standard, depthwise-separable, and bottleneck blocks with optional skip connections; three-stage hybrid search (random → top-K → mutation) with persistent cross-run caching; hardware-aware evaluation on TinyML benchmarks (Visual Wake Words, Melanoma Cancer) across eight microcontrollers (20 KB–1 MB SRAM) and nine input resolutions; comparison to NanoNAS; metrics include search-time speedups, peak activation RAM, and test accuracy.

Result: Mean search-time speedups: 2.41× on Visual Wake Words and 1.70× on Melanoma Cancer vs baselines; ENAS models exhibit substantially lower peak activation RAM, enabling deployment under memory constraints; 79.4% test accuracy on an STM32H743, outperforming a greedy CPU-only baseline by 2.6 percentage points; competitive test accuracy relative to NanoNAS.

Conclusion: ENAS demonstrates effective GPU-free, hardware-aware NAS for microcontrollers, delivering faster searches, lower RAM footprint, and competitive/high accuracy. Open-source release provided.

Abstract: We present \textbf{ENAS}, a hardware-aware Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework that combines a static feasibility check, a cell-based search space supporting standard, depthwise-separable, and bottleneck blocks with optional skip connections, and a three-stage hybrid search strategy (random $\rightarrow$ top-$K$ $\rightarrow$ mutation) with persistent cross-run caching. Unlike many existing NAS frameworks that rely on GPU acceleration, ENAS is designed to operate efficiently without requiring GPUs, making it suitable for resource-constrained development environments. We evaluate ENAS on two TinyML benchmarks, Visual Wake Words and Melanoma Cancer, across eight microcontrollers with memory footprints ranging from 20\,KB to 1\,MB SRAM and nine input image resolutions. Our experimental results show that ENAS achieves mean search-time speedups of $2.41{\times}$ and $1.70{\times}$ on the Visual Wake Words and Melanoma Cancer datasets, respectively, while maintaining competitive test accuracy compared with the recent NanoNAS framework. A measured resource analysis further shows that ENAS-selected models use substantially lower peak activation RAM, the binding constraint for microcontroller deployment at matched accuracy. Additionally, ENAS achieves $79.4\%$ test accuracy on an STM32H743-based microcontroller, outperforming the greedy CPU-only baseline by $2.6$ percentage points. We release the ENAS framework as open-source at: https://github.com/EdgeIntelligenceLab/ENAS

</details>


### [91] [Offline Policy Evaluation as a decision support tool for designing Adaptive Experiments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30273)
*João Victor Ferreira Alves,Eduardo Rocha Laurentino,Gustavo de Oliveira Kanno,Thiago Costa Rizuti da Rocha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a framework to reuse historical fixed-allocation A/B test data to evaluate and select adaptive, context-aware policies via off-policy evaluation (OPE) and warm-start simulations; finds adaptive policies outperform fixed allocations when treatment heterogeneity exists, otherwise little gain; validated on benchmarks and synthetic trials; offers a practical methodology to decide when to deploy adaptive experimentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To decide whether adaptive experiments informed by contextual bandits should be deployed, using only data from static A/B tests.

Method: Estimate nuisance components from logged data with heterogeneity; apply doubly robust OPE to rank a portfolio of adaptive and non-adaptive policies; use controlled warm-start simulation reusing actual reward probabilities for offline-to-online study; test on synthetic data with known heterogeneity and on open benchmarks Hillstrom, Criteo Uplift, LaLonde; reinterpret results with policy value and regret.

Result: Adaptive policies improve over fixed allocations when meaningful heterogeneity is present; minimal benefit when heterogeneity is absent; consistent results across benchmarks; provides methodology for when and how to deploy adaptive experiments and how to choose among policies.

Conclusion: Offers a practical framework to decide when adaptive experimentation is warranted and how to select among competing adaptive policies using historical A/B test data.

Abstract: We investigate how historical data from fixed randomized experiments (A/B tests) can be used to inform the deployment of adaptive experiments based on contextual bandits. Given data collected under a static allocation, our goal is to assess which adaptive policies, if any, would have outperformed the original design and under what conditions. To this end, we combine off-policy evaluation (OPE) with a controlled warm-start simulation. From logged A/B test data exhibiting heterogeneous treatment effects, we estimate nuisance components and use doubly robust estimators to rank a portfolio of pre-specified adaptive and non-adaptive policies. When ground truth is available, we then deploy the same offline-trained policies in a simulator that reuses the exact data-generating reward probabilities, providing a safe, ground-truth-anchored environment to study the offline-to-online transition under warm starting. Using synthetic randomized controlled trials with known heterogeneity structures and an oracle policy, our results indicate that adaptive, context-aware policies improve upon fixed allocations when meaningful heterogeneity is present, while providing little benefit in its absence. We reinforce our findings on standard open benchmarks (Hillstrom, Criteo Uplift, and LaLonde), reinterpreted through a policy-value and regret perspective. Overall, our results provide a practical methodology for deciding when adaptive experimentation is worth deploying and how to select among competing adaptive policies using existing A/B test data.

</details>


### [92] [Cosine Similarity Is Not Evidence: Measuring the Noise Floor of Interpretability Transfer Under Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30275)
*Pranav Varshney*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Interpreting scale-invariant similarity metrics across full-precision vs quantized models requires reporting the sample size and class separation; without these, cosine similarities can’t be interpreted as evidence of preservation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve reproducibility and safety of AI interpretability artifacts, show how calibration against full-precision weights and transfer to quantized weights can mislead if noise floors aren't reported.

Method: Analytical derivation of split-half behavior of the difference-in-means direction estimator; use κ = nρ^2/d; revisit classical E[cos] = (1+4/κ)^{-1}; augment with empirical measurements of ρ on real activations; apply to Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct; compare two independent estimator runs; evaluate cosine between full-precision and quantized directions against appropriate nulls; test translation vs attenuation using scale-invariant stats; provide reporting guidelines and code.

Result: Without n, cosine 0.996 cannot be read as preservation; for INT4, direction rotates beyond estimator noise; for INT8, no movement detected; scale-invariant stats cannot distinguish translation from attenuation; two runs show 0.978–0.994 agreement; ρ in range 33–61; concludes that claims require reporting n and nulls; release code and one-cell reproduction.

Conclusion: Adopt reporting practices: always specify the effective sample size n, the class-separation ρ, and compare to a model-specific null; prefer low-cost forward-pass reporting; carry out quantized-null checks to avoid misinterpreting invariances.

Abstract: A statistic reported without the quantity needed to interpret it is not evidence. We develop that thesis for a concrete practice in AI safety. Interpretability artifacts are calibrated on full-precision weights, deployed on quantized ones, and certified as surviving the change by scale-invariant statistics (cosine similarity, correlation, AUROC) that are reported without their noise floor. For the difference-in-means direction estimator, the split-half floor is governed by one dimensionless number, $κ= nρ^2/d$. The closed form $\mathbb{E}[\cos] \approx (1+4/κ)^{-1}$ is classical; the missing input is the class separation $ρ$, which we measure on real activations; no compression-transfer study we know of reports it. On Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, $ρ= 33$--$61$ across depth, so two independent runs of the estimator agree to $0.978$--$0.994$ by sampling alone. A published cosine of $0.996$ between full-precision and quantized refusal directions therefore cannot be read as preservation without the $n$ it was computed at, which is not reported. Where $n$ is known, we judge each low-bit cosine against the split-half null measured within that quantized model, because a full-precision null assumes the low-bit estimator has the same variance. That assumption is exactly what a null exists to test. The result is plain: at INT4 the direction rotated, and the deficit exceeds the estimator's own noise. At INT8 we detect no movement, which is not an equivalence claim. We also show that a scale-invariant statistic cannot distinguish translation from attenuation of a transferred decision variable, although the two call for opposite remedies. We close with reporting recommendations that cost one forward pass. Code, data, and a one-cell reproduction are released at https://github.com/pvarshh/quantinterp

</details>


### [93] [Why Clipping Matters in AdaGrad? Toward a High-Probability Theory under Generalized Smoothness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30276)
*Alokendu Mazumder,Ayaan Mohd,Harshit Rawat,Arnab Roy,Mayank Baranwal,Punit Rathore*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Clipping AdaGrad under heavy-tailed noise prevents anisotropic miscalibration and yields finite-horizon high-probability convergence with O~(ε^-2) complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand stability and convergence of AdaGrad when gradients are heavy-tailed and local curvature grows sub-quadratically, and assess the role of gradient clipping.

Method: Analytical study of the original same-step coordinate-wise AdaGrad under generalized smoothness with heavy-tailed noise (bounded conditional second moments). Show that the adaptive denominator learns the geometry of rare noise shocks, causing directional distortion and hindering progress. Introduce clipping to repair this failure mode. Derive a finite-horizon high-probability guarantee for the non-lagged AdaGrad update and obtain a rate of (1/T)∑||∇f(x_t)||^2 = O(d(√log T + log(1/δ))/√T), yielding tilde O(ε^-2) complexity.

Result: Clipping stabilizes the adaptive geometry, converting a potential failure mode into a provable convergence guarantee. The analysis yields a finite-horizon high-probability bound and quantifies the benefit of clipping beyond robustness.

Conclusion: In AdaGrad under heavy-tailed noise, gradient clipping is a structural stabilizer that preserves meaningful adaptive geometry and enables provable convergence with near-optimal (ε^-2) complexity.

Abstract: We analyze the original same-step coordinate-wise AdaGrad under generalized smoothness and heavy-tailed noise with bounded variance. In this setting, local curvature may grow sub-quadratically with the gradient norm, and stochastic gradients are assumed to have only bounded conditional second moments. We show that unclipped AdaGrad can become \emph{anisotropically miscalibrated}: under heavy-tailed noise, the adaptive denominator can learn the geometry of rare noise shocks rather than the local curvature of the objective, leading to a persistent directional distortion that blocks finite-horizon Euclidean progress. We then prove that clipping repairs this failure mode. Our main result is a finite-horizon high-probability guarantee for the original non-lagged AdaGrad update, yielding $\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\|\nabla f(x_t)\|^2=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{d\big(\sqrt{\log T} + \log \frac{1}δ\big)}{\sqrt{T}}\right),$ and hence $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ complexity. This shows that, for AdaGrad under heavy-tailed noise, clipping is a structural stabilizer of the adaptive geometry rather than merely a robustness heuristic.

</details>


### [94] [Fixed Points Without Fixed Diffusion: Implicit Neural Sheaves for Convergent Test-Time Computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30277)
*Rémi Bourgerie,Šarūnas Girdzijauskas,Viktoria Fodor*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SheafDEQ introduces a subhomogeneous deep-equilibrium GNN with adaptive neural-sheaf propagation, achieving a unique globally convergent fixed point and improved performance on nonlocal aggregation and heterophilic graphs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To increase IGNN expressiveness via edge-dependent, matrix-valued transformations while preserving the equilibrium guarantees that IGNNs rely on, enabling richer message passing without sacrificing convergence.

Method: Propose SheafDEQ, a subhomogeneous deep-equilibrium architecture with neural-sheaf propagation using learned matrix-valued restriction maps that can align, mix, or reverse neighboring representations. Prove existence and uniqueness of a fixed point under mild regularity; establish contractivity leading to convergence under bounded communication staleness; evaluate on distributed-inference tasks requiring nonlocal aggregation and on community detection with increasing cross-community rewiring.

Result: The framework admits a unique equilibrium reachable by fixed-point iteration from any positive initialization; contraction guarantees convergence under bounded staleness; empirically outperforms fixed-propagation implicit baselines on Sums, MNIST Terrain, and Coordinates, and improves community-detection performance as heterophily increases; diagnostics show decreasing residuals and low sensitivity up to 100 iterations; delayed-update experiments show robustness to bounded communication delays.

Conclusion: SheafDEQ demonstrates that IGNN expressiveness can be enhanced via adaptive neural-sheaf transformations while preserving equilibrium properties, yielding robust, scalable performance in nonlocal and heterophilic settings and opening avenues for richer, edge-aware implicit graph models.

Abstract: Implicit Graph Neural Networks (IGNNs) define node representations as fixed points of message-passing operators, enabling effectively infinite-depth propagation, iteration-independent parameterization, and flexible test-time computation. Yet these benefits depend on the equilibrium being unique and attainable by fixed-point iteration. Existing constructions often impose constraints on recurrent updates to obtain these guarantees, limiting the transformations available at equilibrium. This raises a central question: can IGNNs gain expressiveness through richer, edge-dependent transformations while retaining the inherent strengths of their equilibrium formulation? We introduce SheafDEQ, a subhomogeneous deep-equilibrium architecture with adaptive neural-sheaf propagation. Its learned, matrix-valued sheaf restriction maps can align, mix, or reverse neighbouring representations. Under mild regularity conditions, we prove that SheafDEQ admits a unique equilibrium reached globally by fixed-point iteration from any positive initialization. Contractivity further guarantees convergence under bounded communication staleness. We evaluate SheafDEQ on distributed-inference tasks requiring repeated nonlocal aggregation and on community detection whose rewiring increasingly favours cross-community interactions. SheafDEQ improves over fixed-propagation implicit baselines on Sums, MNIST Terrain, and Coordinates, and on community detection as connectivity becomes increasingly heterophilic. Continued-iteration diagnostics show decreasing residuals and low prediction sensitivity after 100 iterations for initialization scales from $0.001$ to $10$, while delayed-update experiments show low sensitivity to bounded communication staleness.

</details>


### [95] [Neural Ideals and Neural Codes: An Algebraic Framework for Neural Network Classification and Feature Interpretation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30279)
*Venkata Subbaiah Yerrapati,Rahul Dixit,Ajay Kumar Shukla*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces an algebraic framework based on neural ideals to analyze features captured by hidden layers of neural networks for classification; provides computation and stabilization results, per-neuron feature identification, MNIST validation, and a visualization tool.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To better understand what hidden-layer neurons learn by providing a rigorous algebraic representation and actionable algorithms for feature interpretation.

Method: Formalize a correspondence between neural networks and neural ideals; develop algorithms to compute neural ideals; prove a stabilization theorem for approximating ideals; design per-neuron feature identification algorithms; implement interactive visualization tool.

Result: Algorithms enable identification and interpretation of features per hidden neuron; empirical demonstration on MNIST; neural ideals highlighted as a useful mathematical/computational framework; released visualization software.

Conclusion: The neural-ideals framework offers a principled approach to analyze and visualize neural representations in classification networks, with practical tools and demonstrated effectiveness on MNIST.

Abstract: Understanding the features captured by the hidden layers of neural networks is a fundamental challenge in machine learning, despite their widespread success across various classification problems. In this work, we propose an algebraic framework for examining neural networks that model classification problems. Certain results, such as the correspondence between the neural network and neural ideals, algorithms for computing the neural ideals, and a stabilization theorem that enables approximation of the neural ideals, are first established. As an application to the framework, we present algorithms to identify and interpret the features captured by each hidden-layer neuron. Along with these theoretical developments, the practical performance has been demonstrated on the MNIST digit dataset, and the results highlight the pivotal role of neural ideals as a mathematical and computational tool for analyzing the features captured by neural networks. Further, we develop an interactive software that builds on the presented framework to visualize the features captured by each neuron. This tool is available at https://github.com/yvs1967/neural-network-representation-explorer

</details>


### [96] [Seasonal and Quantum-inspired Models for Neutron Monitor Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30281)
*Krishna Bhatia,Shalini Devendrababu,Srinjoy Ganguly*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Focused multi-horizon forecasting study for the Lomnicky Stit neutron monitor time series evaluating seasonal baselines, deep sequence models, and quantum-inspired architectures; QiKAN achieves the lowest aggregate error, while Seasonal Naive remains competitive, underscoring the value of strong seasonal priors for periodic scientific signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether modern sequence models improve forecasts for highly periodic scientific time series and explore whether parsimonious, low-dimensional function approximators can match or outperform more complex architectures.

Method: Dataset: Lomnicky Stit neutron monitor (LMKS) time series. Evaluated models include Seasonal Naive, LSTM, Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN), N-BEATS, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), and two quantum-inspired variants, QiLSTM and QiKAN. Describes dataset characteristics, preprocessing pipeline, and training procedures. Performance evaluated on multi-horizon forecasts using mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE).

Result: QiKAN achieves the lowest aggregate forecasting error among the evaluated configurations; Seasonal Naive baseline remains remarkably competitive. Overall, strong seasonal or low-dimensional priors can match or outperform more complex sequence architectures for highly periodic scientific monitoring time series.

Conclusion: The findings motivate further investigation of parsimonious and decomposable function approximators for forecasting periodic scientific signals and support focusing on models that embed strong seasonal priors for periodic data.

Abstract: We present a focused and reproducible study of multi-horizon forecasting on the Lomnicky Stit neutron monitor (LMKS) time series.
