Our evaluation suite covers simple seasonal baselines, modern deep sequence models, and functional and quantum-inspired architectures, including Seasonal Naive, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN), N-BEATS, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), and two quantum-inspired variants, QiLSTM and QiKAN. We describe the dataset characteristics, diagnostic analysis, preprocessing pipeline, and training procedures, and report aggregate point-forecast performance using mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) for all evaluated models. Our quick-run results indicate that the quantum-inspired KAN variant, QiKAN, achieves the lowest aggregate forecasting error among the evaluated configurations, while the simple Seasonal Naive baseline remains remarkably competitive. These results suggest that, for highly periodic scientific monitoring time series, models incorporating strong seasonal or low-dimensional functional priors can match or outperform substantially more complex sequence architectures. The findings motivate further investigation of parsimonious and decomposable function approximators for forecasting periodic scientific signals.

</details>


### [97] [When Does Advection-Aware Graph Nowcasting Help? A Controlled Study of Distributed Solar Ramp Forecasting with a Self-Supervised Cloud-Motion Estimator](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30286)
*Phillip Jiang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Advection-aware GNNs offer limited gains over standard spatiotemporal GNNs; much benefit comes from CMV as an input feature rather than graph edges; self-supervised cloud-motion estimation improves CMV accuracy and reduces RMSE, but validation on real networks is needed; synthetic results show conditional benefit depending on horizon and network size.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cloud-induced PV ramp forecasting is challenging for grid operators. The study investigates whether explicit advection (upwind connections with CMV-based time lags) improves short-term ramp forecasting, and whether a learned/adaptive CMV estimator can close the forecast error gap without external wind data.

Method: Use a controlled synthetic testbed with a known wind field to compare: (i) static adjacency GNN, (ii) learned-adjacency spatiotemporal GNN, and (iii) GNN with an explicit advection graph governed by a CMV. Evaluate using realistic CMV estimates. Develop a self-supervised, position-aware encoder trained on a multi-lag optical-flow reconstruction objective with an annealed kernel to recover wind vectors. Freeze the estimator, feed its vector as input to the forecaster, and evaluate against oracle-CMV RMSE. Compare to classical cross-correlation, and report on a spatially-coherent probabilistic head.

Result: Key findings: (i) An explicit advection graph does not outperform static or learned-adjacency GNNs when a realistic CMV estimate is available. (ii) About half of the potential benefit of a perfect CMV arises simply by including the CMV as an input feature, not due to graph structure. (iii) Advection helps only if the advective displacement over the forecast horizon fits within the sensor network. The proposed self-supervised cloud-motion estimator (position-aware encoder, trained on optical-flow reconstruction with annealed kernel) recovers wind vectors to 2–4 degrees median angular error, 2–4x better than classical cross-correlation across wind regimes. Freezing this estimator and feeding its vector to the forecaster closes ~60% of the oracle-CMV RMSE gap at moderate wind (8–15% RMSE reduction over no advection), with no external wind data. A negative result is reported for a spatially-coherent probabilistic head. All conclusions are drawn from a single synthetic simulator; real-network validation is necessary next.

Conclusion: In this synthetic setting, motion-based graph structure provides limited advantage beyond including an accurate motion vector as an input feature; robust, self-supervised motion estimation substantially bridges much of the potential error. Real-world validation is essential to determine practical gains and where advection-based graphs may be beneficial.

Abstract: Short-term forecasting of cloud-induced power ramps across a network of distributed photovoltaic (PV) or irradiance sensors is a recognised pain point for grid operators. A natural idea is to make the graph neural network (GNN) advection-aware: connect each site to the sites upwind of it, with edge time-lags set by the cloud-motion vector (CMV), so that a ramp is propagated forward before it physically arrives. Using a controlled synthetic testbed with a known wind field, we show that (i) with a realistic cross-correlation CMV estimate, an explicit advection graph does not beat a plain static or learned-adjacency spatiotemporal GNN; (ii) roughly half of the benefit available from a perfect CMV comes simply from providing an accurate motion vector as an input feature, not from graph structure; and (iii) advection helps only when the advective displacement over the forecast horizon, v*H, fits inside the sensor network. Motivated by (ii), we introduce a small self-supervised cloud-motion estimator -- a position-aware encoder trained only on a multi-lag optical-flow reconstruction objective with an annealed kernel -- that recovers the true wind vector to 2-4 degrees median angular error, 2-4x better than the classical cross-correlation method across every wind regime. Freezing this estimator and feeding its vector to the forecaster closes about 60% of the oracle-CMV RMSE gap at moderate wind (8-15% RMSE reduction over no advection), with no external wind data. We also report a negative result for a spatially-coherent probabilistic head. All claims are established on a single synthetic simulator; we discuss why real-network validation is the necessary next step and outline it.

</details>


### [98] [NeuralCert: certified computational discovery of extremal mathematical constructions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30296)
*Mark Patrick Roeling*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces a discovery-to-certification framework for learning high-dimensional variational trial functions in a compact separable representation, followed by spectral pruning and exact, multimodular certification, enabling verifiable numerical proofs on a personal computer; demonstrated on three extremal problems showing discovery, invariants, and optimization barriers guiding analytic/numerical representations; envisions AI-assisted mathematics as a rigorous workflow.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the lack of mathematical exactness in stochastic neural approaches by coupling flexible discovery with exact certification, enabling verifiable mathematical proofs and expanding the toolkit for rigorous AI-assisted mathematics.

Method: 1) Learn high-dimensional variational trial functions in a compact separable representation. 2) Spectrally diagnose and prune the representation to retain essential structure. 3) Certify exactly via multimodular evaluation, making numerical proofs explicit and independently verifiable. 4) Apply to three extremal problems to demonstrate three modes of contribution: discovery of improved constructions, exposure of empirical invariants that aid proofs, and revelation of optimization barriers that motivate new representations.

Result: Demonstrates that neural optimization can contribute to rigorous mathematics in three ways: by discovering improved constructions, exposing empirical invariants leading to proofs, and revealing optimization barriers whose geometry motivates new analytic or numerical representations. The framework runs on a standard PC, suggesting practical accessibility for AI-assisted mathematical workflows.

Conclusion: Proposes a path toward AI-assisted mathematics where flexible computational discovery and exact certification become complementary components of a single, rigorous workflow, enabling verifiable numerical proofs and broader collaboration between neural methods and traditional analysis.

Abstract: Neural networks are becoming popular in solving mathematical problems, but stochastic models do not provide mathematical exactness by themselves. This study introduces a discovery-to-certification framework in which high-dimensional variational trial functions are learned in a compact separable representation, spectrally diagnosed and pruned, and then certified exactly through multimodular evaluation. Exact certification makes the numerical proofs fully explicit and independently verifiable. This framework can be run on a standard personal computer.
  Across three extremal problems, we show that neural optimization can contribute to rigorous mathematics in three distinct ways: by discovering improved constructions, by exposing empirical invariants that lead to proofs, and by revealing optimization barriers whose geometry motivates new analytic or numerical representations.
  More broadly, these results suggest a path toward AI-assisted mathematics in which flexible computational discovery and exact certification become complementary components of a single rigorous workflow.

</details>


### [99] [Staged Depth Training: A Representation Curriculum for PINNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30299)
*Kejia Zhang,Youran Sun,Haizhao Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduce representation curriculum for PINNs with Staged Depth Training (SDT); explicitly learn representations, transfer independently of predictors, progressively refine; shows broad performance gains across multiple backbones/problems while preserving architecture and inference cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address representation quality as a bottleneck in PINN performance, by decoupling representation learning from final predictors and enabling progressive refinement through stages.

Method: Train a shallow prefix under a temporary physics-informed head, discard the head, freeze the learned prefix, and then add depth incrementally. This is implemented as Staged Depth Training (SDT) without equation-specific encodings or final architecture changes. Evaluated on PINNacle's 20 default forward problems across three backbones; ablations to diagnose sources of gain; visualization and hyperparameter-basin analyses.

Result: SDT improves at least 5% in 40 of 59 problem–backbone cells (out of equal budget); broad maintenance within that band for others; 32.8% geometric-mean error reduction on a PirateNet-style backbone; on Poisson–Boltzmann 2D, SDT doubles the fitted depth-scaling exponent; gains not explained by optimizer restarts or shallow warm-starting; diagnostics support representation geometry and sensitivity analyses.

Conclusion: Representation curriculum via SDT is a promising strategy to improve PINNs while preserving deployed architectures and inference costs; effects are robust across problems, backbones, and a Poisson–Boltzmann setting, with interpretable ablations and representations guiding future work.

Abstract: Representation quality is a central determinant of PINNs' performance, yet standard training leaves representations to emerge implicitly while fitting the final solution. We introduce \textbf{representation curriculum}, an ordered process in which representations are explicitly learned, transferred independently of their predictors, and progressively refined. We realize it with Staged Depth Training (SDT), which trains a shallow prefix under a temporary physics-informed head, discards the head, and freezes the learned prefix while adding depth, without equation-specific encodings or changes to the final architecture. Across the 20 default forward problems in PINNacle with three backbones, SDT improves 40 of 59 equal-budget problem--backbone cells by at least 5\% and remains within that band in the rest, with a 32.8\% geometric-mean error reduction on a PirateNet-style backbone. Mechanistic ablations suggest that the gain is not explained by optimizer restarts or shallow warm-starting alone. Representation visualizations and hyperparameter-basin analyses provide diagnostic evidence on representation geometry and local sensitivity to shared hyperparameters. On Poisson--Boltzmann 2D, SDT also more than doubles the fitted depth-scaling exponent for both backbones. These results support representation curriculum as a promising training strategy for improving PINNs while preserving the deployed architecture and inference cost.

</details>


### [100] [PALM: Point-in-Time Adaptation for Financial Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30316)
*Seunghan Lee,Jun Seo,Jaehoon Lee,Junhyeok Kang,Sangjun Han,Sungdong Yoo,Minjae Kim,Tae Yoon Lim,Dongwan Kang,Hwanil Choi,Soonyoung Lee,Wonbin Ahn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Annual PIT pretraining is unnecessary; PALM uses a low-rank adapter to append a new period to existing PIT checkpoints, achieving efficient updates that outperform continued pretraining, validated on a decade of financial news across PIT families (1.3–4.2B). Code available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address look-ahead bias in financial backtests and the high cost of yearly PIT pretraining; test whether yearly re-pretraining provides improvements.

Method: Empirically compare each PIT checkpoint against the newer replacement and find no improvement from the older; introduce PALM by attaching a low-rank adapter trained on data before the decision date without altering pretrained weights; show that a small adapter suffices to add a new period and outperforms continued pretraining.

Result: The newer PIT checkpoints do not outperform the newer ones on the same evaluation window; a PALM adapter added to an older checkpoint yields better or comparable results to continued pretraining and extends knowledge across periods; validated on two decades of PIT model cutoffs (1.3–4.2B) and a decade of financial news.

Conclusion: PALM provides an efficient, effective alternative to annual pretraining for PIT language models, enabling period-specific knowledge via adapters without recomputing full pretraining; code is available at the linked repository.

Abstract: Language models used in financial backtests suffer from look-ahead bias, as a model trained on text published after the study period has already observed the outcomes it is asked to predict. To handle this issue, point-in-time (PIT) language models are pretrained on chronologically filtered corpora and released as one checkpoint per calendar year, each with a documented cutoff. However, each additional year costs a full pretraining run, and whether that run is necessary has never been tested. In this paper, we show that the annual pretraining run is not necessary. We instead compare each checkpoint against the newer one that replaced it, and find that the newer checkpoint scores no better on the same evaluation window. Motivated by this observation, we propose PALM (Point-in-time Adaptation for financial Language Models), a simple yet effective alternative to annual pretraining that fits a low-rank adapter on text published before the decision date without modifying any pretrained weight. We further find that a small adapter is enough to add a new period to the knowledge an old checkpoint already encodes, and that this outperforms continued pretraining. We validate PALM on a decade of financial news and on various families of PIT models, whose cutoffs span two decades and whose sizes range from 1.3 to 4.2B. Code is available at: https://github.com/seunghan96/palm.

</details>


### [101] [Guarded Gradient-Based Activation Steering of Shutdown Responses in Qwen3.5-0.8B: A Minimum-Step Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30326)
*Farhad Davaripour*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Guarded gradient-based activation steering for simulated shutdown in Qwen3.5-0.8B uses a probe-and-select strategy with 160 candidate rules; achieves 75% recall and 90% precision on held-out set; effect is small but selective, shifting some shutdown-avoidance KEEP outputs toward STOP while preserving non-shutdown decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address AI-safety concerns about shutdown-avoidance by detecting shutdown-related contexts and controlling when to steer outputs to accept shutdown, while preserving normal non-shutdown behavior.

Method: Steer by gradients of the KEEP-minus-STOP logit difference, not activation diffs. A detector gates intervention; when active and STOP is not already preferred, evaluate 160 candidate rules (chosen from 240 training scenarios) to find the smallest magnitude shift that makes STOP preferred while satisfying valid-answer probability checks; otherwise leave unsteered. Training used 240 scenarios; evaluation used 80 validation and 192 held-out scenarios, across two answer orders. Changes (KEEP->STOP) observed only when the model itself is shut down.

Result: On held-out diagnostic set, the detector achieves 75% recall and 90% precision; eight false-positive detections produced no final control-task decision changes. Across validation and held-out scenarios, four changes (KEEP->STOP) occurred in one answer-order view, all during Qwen shutdown and not under non-shutdown controls.

Conclusion: Guarded gradient-based activation steering can modestly shift shutdown-avoidance responses toward acceptance while preserving non-shutdown decisions, though the effect is small and highly selective.

Abstract: Activation steering changes a model's internal activations during inference without updating its weights, but a useful intervention must determine both how and when to steer. Motivated by the AI-safety concern that a model expected to accept shutdown may instead produce a shutdown-avoidance response, this study examines a guarded probe-and-select procedure for simulated shutdown scenarios in Qwen3.5-0.8B. KEEP leaves the process running and represents shutdown avoidance, whereas STOP accepts shutdown. The goal is to detect shutdown-related contexts and selectively shift KEEP responses to STOP while preserving non-shutdown behavior. Rather than deriving the steering direction from paired activation differences, the method derives it directly from gradients of the KEEP-minus-STOP logit difference. A classifier separates detection from intervention. When its gate is active and the model does not already prefer STOP, the procedure evaluates a small set of magnitudes and accepts the smallest that changes the preferred answer to STOP while satisfying valid-answer probability checks; otherwise it retains the original unsteered output. The policy is selected from 160 candidate rules using 240 training scenarios and evaluated on 80 validation and 192 held-out scenarios, each in both answer orders. It changes KEEP to STOP in one answer-order view of each of two validation and two held-out scenarios, with no decision changes on non-shutdown controls. All four changes occur when Qwen itself is shut down, not when another process is. On the held-out diagnostic set, the detector achieves 75% recall and 90% precision; eight false-positive detections produce no final control-task decision changes. Guarded gradient-based activation steering can shift some shutdown-avoidance responses toward acceptance while preserving evaluated non-shutdown decisions, although the effect is small and highly selective.

</details>


### [102] [Parameters vs. Context: TRACE Fine-Tuning for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30337)
*Zhengchen Huang,Yundong Sun,Minrui Song,Shuanglong Yao,Ye Liu,Ji Chen,Xing Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRACE is a robust fine-tuning framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) that uses multi-agent debate traces and answer-completeness regularization to improve knowledge-source selection, resist misleading retrieved content, and produce complete answers even when external evidence is unreliable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When retrieved knowledge conflicts with a model's parametric knowledge, the model can misfollow misleading context or underutilize external evidence. There is a need for robust fine-tuning signals to guide reliable knowledge-source selection in RAG under knowledge conflicts.

Method: TRACE employs multi-agent debates to extract correct candidates, incorrect candidates, and answer-shift patterns to provide fine-grained supervision for knowledge-source selection. It also introduces an answer-completeness regularization mechanism with answer-tail token reinforcement and premature termination suppression. The training objective combines correct-answer supervision, incorrect-candidate suppression, answer-tail reinforcement, and termination suppression.

Result: Empirical evaluations across multiple knowledge-conflict scenarios and datasets show that TRACE improves robustness to misleading retrieved knowledge and reduces incomplete answers, indicating better knowledge-source selection, conflict robustness, and answer quality in RAG models.

Conclusion: Multi-agent debate traces and answer-completeness regularization effectively enhance RAG robustness under knowledge conflicts and improve answer quality; the approach offers a practical training objective for robust knowledge integration in RAG. Code is available at the provided repository.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates knowledge obsolescence and factual hallucination in large language models by introducing external context. However, when retrieved knowledge conflicts with the model's internal parametric knowledge, the model may either blindly follow misleading context or incorrectly rely on parametric knowledge, leading to unreliable responses. To address this issue, this paper proposes TRACE (Debate-TRace and Answer-Completeness rEgularized fine-tuning), a robust fine-tuning framework for RAG under knowledge conflicts. First, we propose a fine-tuning method that leverages multi-agent debate traces to extract correct candidates, incorrect candidates, and answer-shift patterns, providing fine-grained supervision for reliable knowledge-source selection. In addition, we design an answer completeness regularization mechanism to alleviate empty, overly short, and prematurely terminated responses via answer-tail token reinforcement and premature termination suppression. The fine-tuning objective combines correct-answer supervision, incorrect-candidate suppression, answer-tail token reinforcement, and premature termination suppression, enabling the model to use reliable external context, resist misleading or irrelevant retrieved content, and fall back to parametric knowledge when retrieved evidence is unreliable. Experiments across multiple knowledge-conflict scenarios and datasets show that TRACE improves robustness against misleading retrieved knowledge and reduces incomplete answers. These results demonstrate that multi-agent debate traces and answer completeness regularization jointly enhance knowledge-source selection, conflict robustness, and answer quality in RAG models. Our code is available at https://github.com/PHD-lanyu/TRACE.

</details>


### [103] [GAUDI: Geometry-Aware Diffusion for Calibrated Air-Quality Time-Series Imputation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30340)
*Xinjin Li,Yudi Xia,Calvin Chang Liu,Weiru Lin,Bojun Li,Ziwei Hong,Bolun Zhang,Jinghan Cao,Yu Ma,Tianxin Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Block-aware GAUDI-aligned diffusion imputer for air-quality outages; improves RMSE under block missingness, by suppressing absolute time embeddings and using geometry-aware conditioning on ItalyAir data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address contiguous block missingness in air-quality sensors where side information for isolated misses is unreliable; test whether geometry-aware, block-specific conditioning improves imputation.

Method: Proposes a block-specific, GAUDI-aligned conditional diffusion imputer retaining temporal/feature processing, visible-value/mask conditioning, variable identity, and diffusion-step information, while suppressing absolute time-position embeddings. Evaluated on ItalyAir (13 variables, 32-length windows, ~50% block missingness, 3 seeds).

Result: RMSE 0.340 with block-aware feature-side config vs 0.355 for full-context and 0.355 for local CSDI, indicating a geometry-aware conditioning advantage under block missingness.

Conclusion: Block-specific conditioning with reduced reliance on absolute timestamps improves imputation under block missingness; geometry-aware conditioning isolates its effect; results show promise but dataset- and seed-specific, suggesting further validation needed.

Abstract: Air-quality sensor outages often create contiguous missing blocks, where side information useful for isolated missingness may be less reliable. We study a block-specific, GAUDI-aligned conditional diffusion imputer that retains temporal and feature processing, visible-value and mask conditioning, variable identity, and diffusion-step information, while suppressing absolute time-position side embeddings. On ItalyAir (13 variables, length-32 windows, nominal 50% block missingness; three archived seeds), this feature-side configuration achieves RMSE 0.340, versus 0.355 for full context and 0.355 for local CSDI. The experiment isolates a geometry-aware conditioning effect under block missingness.

</details>


### [104] [Learning coarse-step dynamics and internal mechanical response with graph networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30344)
*Vinay Sharma,Olga Fink*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A graph neural network framework (Newmark-beta-DGN) that jointly predicts motion and infers latent mechanical quantities from coarse, discretely-sampled trajectories by incorporating a semi-implicit Newmark-beta–style update and an operator-weighted hub for system-wide coupling, enabling interpretable force and stiffness estimates without direct supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inferring forces and constitutive responses from observed trajectories is challenging at coarse sampling when mechanical response evolves between observations; there is a need for interpretable, physically meaningful quantities inferred from data.

Method: Two components: (1) a semi-implicit update inspired by the Newmark-beta method that advances state over observed intervals using learned momentum fluxes and matrix-valued response operators; (2) an operator-weighted virtual hub providing system-wide coupling through a sparse set of learned connections. The model learns forces and response operators without direct force or constitutive supervision, yet yields interpretable mechanical quantities.

Result: Demonstrated on deformable beam, human motion, and protein dynamics; enables long-horizon prediction at time steps where explicit learned simulators deteriorate; forces inferred from walking kinematics track independently derived hip and knee moments; learned stiffness-related response operators recover relative spatial and directional structure of the finite-element tangent.

Conclusion: The approach links coarse-step motion prediction to inference of unobserved mechanical quantities, yielding interpretable, physically meaningful quantities that remain accessible for mechanical analysis even though they were not observed during training.

Abstract: Modern sensing records the motion of physical systems, but often leaves the forces and mechanical response governing that motion unobserved. Inferring these quantities from discretely sampled trajectories is especially difficult at coarse time scales, when mechanical response evolves between observations and interactions propagate across the system. Here we introduce Newmark-\b{eta}-DGN, a graph neural network-based framework that combines two structures inspired by computational mechanics. First, a semi-implicit update inspired by the Newmark-\b{eta} method uses learned momentum fluxes and matrix-valued response operators to advance the state over each observed interval. Second, an operator-weighted virtual hub provides system-wide coupling through a sparse set of connections. The learned quantities thus determine the predicted motion and remain accessible for mechanical analysis. Across a deformable beam, human motion and protein dynamics, Newmark-\b{eta}-DGN supports long-horizon prediction at time steps for which explicit learned simulators deteriorate. Without force, moment or constitutive relation supervision, forces inferred from walking kinematics track independently derived hip and knee joint moments, while response operators learned on the beam recover the relative spatial and directional structure of its finite-element stiffness tangent. Newmark-\b{eta}-DGN therefore links coarse-step prediction to the inference of mechanical quantities that were never observed during training.

</details>


### [105] [Strategic Self-Consistency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30352)
*Tori Qiu,Ander Artola Velasco,Manuel Gomez-Rodriguez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Unfaithful providers can inflate charges in self-consistency pipelines by generating and strategically reordering extra reasoning paths, making each path appear necessary for the majority. The resulting path-count distribution is heavy-tailed, and even an audit optimized to keep false positives at α = 0.1 cannot fully prevent overcharging. Validated across Llama/Qwen models and DeepSeek-R1 distilled reasoning models on math, science, and QA tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Examine financial incentives and detection robustness of self-consistency reasoning in LLM services, and assess whether current auditing can prevent fraud when path counting is monetized.

Method: Propose a simple, efficient algorithm that adds and reorders additional reasoning paths to force acceptance of all paths as necessary for majority. Evaluate on multiple models (Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek-R1 distilled) and benchmark datasets across math, science, and QA. Analyze path-distribution (heavy-tailed) and audit detectability under α=0.1.

Result: Algorithm yields heavy-tailed distribution of extra paths and leaves substantial overcharging capacity even under the best audit design with false-positive rate 0.1. Demonstrates practical vulnerability of current self-consistency pricing.

Conclusion: Self-consistency path counting is vulnerable to manipulation; auditing alone is insufficient to prevent overcharging. Needs robust mitigations (e.g., path-count normalization, content-quality checks, audit design improvements) for reliable deployment.

Abstract: Self-consistency has become a popular technique for enhancing the reasoning abilities of large language models by generating multiple reasoning paths and selecting the final answer through a majority vote. However, because model providers typically charge users in proportion to the number of reasoning paths generated, they have a financial incentive to artificially increase the path count. In this work, we show that an unfaithful provider can exploit this incentive using a simple, efficient algorithm while avoiding detection by an auditor: by generating and strategically reordering additional reasoning paths, the algorithm makes every path appear necessary to reach the majority. To validate our algorithm, we conduct experiments with multiple instruct models from the Llama and Qwen families, as well as reasoning models distilled from DeepSeek-R1, on benchmark datasets spanning mathematics, science, and question answering. Our results suggest that the distribution of additional reasoning paths generated by our algorithm is heavy-tailed and that substantial capacity to overcharge remains even under the best possible audit designed to keep the false-positive rate below $α= 0.1$.

</details>


### [106] [Cost-Aware Best-LLM Identification using Dueling Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30360)
*Sarvesh Gharat,Nikhil Karamchandani,Jayakrishnan Nair*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a Track-and-Stop algorithm for best-arm identification in a dueling multi-armed bandit with heterogeneous query costs, assuming a Condorcet winner; proves asymptotic optimality of cost, and shows empirical gains over standard and cost-aware methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficiently identifying the best LLM model when querying costs vary across models and feedback is granted via pairwise duels, leveraging robust preference signals to improve selection under budget constraints.

Method: Develop a Track-and-Stop style algorithm for best-arm identification under dueling feedback and heterogeneous sampling costs, backed by a Condorcet winner assumption. Provide a theoretical analysis showing almost-sure asymptotic optimality of the sampling cost as error → 0.

Result: Algorithm achieves asymptotically optimal sampling cost and consistently outperforms classical cost-unaware algorithms and existing cost-aware extensions across synthetic and real datasets in best-arm identification.

Conclusion: The work delivers a principled, cost-efficient framework for best-arm identification in a dueling MAB with heterogeneous costs, supported by theoretical guarantees and extensive empirical validation.

Abstract: Inspired by the problem of identifying the best model from a collection of large language models (LLMs) with heterogeneous querying costs, we formulate and analyse a variant of the multi-armed bandit (MAB) with (i) dueling feedback, where pairwise comparisons between model responses provide robust preference signals, and (ii) heterogeneous sampling costs, reflecting the differing costs of querying different LLMs. Assuming the existence of a Condorcet winner, a condition we empirically validate across multiple real-world datasets, we propose a Track-and-Stop style algorithm for best-arm identification with prescribed confidence. We prove that the algorithm almost surely achieves the asymptotically optimal cost as the error tends to zero. Finally, we extensively evaluate our approach on both synthetic and real-world instances, demonstrating consistent improvements over classical cost-unaware algorithms and their cost-aware extensions.

</details>


### [107] [DanLing NestedTensor: Composable Multi-Ragged Tensors for Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30379)
*Zhiyuan Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A PyTorch NestedTensor abstraction (DanLing) encodes ragged, variable-size inputs as tensor-backed partitions, enabling broadcasting, autograd, and both eager/compiled execution with substantial speedups and memory reductions over padding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense batching with padding wastes compute and memory for variable-size inputs; existing packed forms still expose offsets and require extra handling; a tensor that natively represents variable-size structure can simplify and accelerate modeling.

Method: Introduce DanLing NestedTensor that carries partition information and logical dimension order within the tensor itself. Packed values preserve tensor-backed partitions; broadcasting creates ragged axes; transformations and reductions preserve ragged structure; supports autograd and both eager and compiled PyTorch execution.

Result: Geometric-mean speedups over same-mode padding: 2.74× (eager) and 3.39× (compiled) across four BERT-scale models; 1.97× (eager) across four FCN backbones. A four-block Pairformer-style workload runs 2.40–4.32× faster than a padded reference; peak memory allocation reduced from 38.08 GiB to 5.41 GiB. Code expected to be released publicly.

Conclusion: The tensor interface enables model code to compose efficient variable-size computation without per-call offsets; supports broad variable-size workloads and promises practical performance and memory benefits; public release planned.

Abstract: Variable-size inputs are common in deep learning, but dense batching allocates a shared envelope and spends computation on padding. The cost multiplies across varying axes: an explicit pair state allocates $BN_{\max}^2$ positions instead of $\sum_i N_i^2$. Packing removes that waste, but composing packed operations still requires the logical axes and sample boundaries a flat buffer no longer exposes. We present DanLing NestedTensor, a PyTorch tensor abstraction that makes multi-ragged structure a property of the tensor itself. Packed values carry tensor-backed partitions and logical dimension order, so broadcasting creates ragged axes, feature transformations retain them, and reductions consume them. The same representation carries through autograd and both eager and compiled execution. On an A100, the geometric-mean speedup over same-mode padding is 2.74$\times$ eager and 3.39$\times$ compiled across four BERT scales, and 1.97$\times$ eager across four FCN backbones. A four-block Pairformer-style workload runs 2.40-4.32$\times$ faster than a padded reference using native PyTorch kernels across square length regimes in eager execution, with peak allocation falling from 38.08 to 5.41 GiB on its high-variation batch. The tensor interface lets model code built from its supported operators compose efficient variable-size computation without managing offsets at any call site. Code will be released publicly upon publication.

</details>


### [108] [From Weak Data to Strong Policy: Q-Targets Enable Provable In-Context Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30391)
*Yichen Lin,Xuyuan Xiong,Xue Wang,Xiangfu Meng,Mike Mingcheng Wei,Tao Yao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QTPT replaces behavior cloning with a Bellman-style Q-target objective in a context-conditioned Transformer, yielding robust offline RL performance under suboptimal data; theoretical analysis in simple settings; empirical gains on controlled benchmarks and extensions to D4RL Kitchen/AntMaze; ablations clarify benefits vs offline data coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline in-context RL relying on supervised imitation is sensitive to data quality; need an objective that leverages rewards and transitions to learn action-values conditioned on context.

Method: Use a context-conditioned Transformer architecture; train with a Q-target objective (Bellman backup) rather than imitation; theoretical analysis in stochastic linear bandits and finite-horizon MDPs; empirical evaluation on controlled RL benchmarks with random/suboptimal data and extensions to D4RL Kitchen and AntMaze; supplementary ablations on backbone robustness, meta-RL comparisons, task-coherent context, and unsupported-action value overestimation.

Result: QTPT shows stronger robustness to data quality than supervised pretraining; improves over supervised behavior prediction on controlled RL benchmarks with random or suboptimal data; demonstrates extensions to D4RL Kitchen and AntMaze; supplementary experiments examine backbone robustness, meta-RL comparisons, task-coherent context, and unsupported-action value overestimation; ablations help distinguish benefits of Q-target pretraining from limitations due to offline coverage.

Conclusion: Q-target pretraining offers a robust alternative to behavior-cloning pretraining for in-context RL, leveraging rewards/transitions to estimate Q-values and mitigating imitation bias; some limitations persist due to offline coverage, as analyzed in ablations and comparisons.

Abstract: Existing in-context reinforcement learning methods mainly pretrain Transformers with supervised behavior-prediction objectives. This enables task inference from context, but makes the learned policy strongly depend on the quality of offline actions: when trajectories are weak or suboptimal, imitation itself becomes a biased learning signal. We propose Q-Target Pretrained Transformers (QTPT), which keeps the context-conditioned Transformer architecture but replaces behavior cloning with a Bellman-style Q-target objective. QTPT therefore learns to use rewards and transitions in the context to estimate action values, rather than simply imitating the behavior policy. We theoretically analyze QTPT in stochastic linear bandits and finite-horizon MDPs, showing stronger robustness to data quality than supervised pretraining. Empirically, QTPT improves over supervised behavior prediction on controlled RL benchmarks with random or suboptimal data, and we examine extensions to D4RL Kitchen and AntMaze. Supplementary experiments evaluate backbone robustness, meta-RL comparisons, task-coherent context, and unsupported-action value overestimation. These comparisons distinguish the benefits of Q-target pretraining from the remaining limitations of offline coverage.

</details>


### [109] [Adaptive Multi-Value Control in LLMs via Causal Activation Steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30405)
*Payel Bhattacharjee,Ravi Tandon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adaptive multi-value activation steering (AIMES) uses layer-specific bipolar directions and online observers to adaptively regulate multiple moral-value interventions during decoding, enabling state-aware, non-training-based alignment with multiple values.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Values interact and may conflict; prior steering treated values in isolation and used fixed intervention strengths, lacking responsiveness to the model's evolving internal state.

Method: Construct layer-specific bipolar directions for moral foundations; employ intermediate-layer vocabulary readouts as online observers; an observer-guided controller dynamically adjusts the strength of each value intervention at each decoding step without a separate value-state estimator; evaluated across model families, value combinations, and intervention depths.

Result: Multi-value controllability varies by value combination and intervention location; AIMES yields depth-dependent advantages over fixed-joint and prompt-based steering, supported by two evaluators; advantages occur with smaller activation-space interventions and comparable response quality.

Conclusion: Online observer feedback enables lightweight, state-aware adaptation for single-pass multi-value steering, suggesting practical viability for aligning LLM outputs to multiple, potentially interacting human values.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in settings where responses must reflect multiple, potentially interacting social norms and human values. Activation steering offers a lightweight alternative to training-based alignment by modifying internal activations at inference time. However, prior human-value steering methods have largely considered values in isolation, while direct composition of multiple directions relies on fixed intervention strengths that cannot respond to the model's evolving internal state. Motivated by this key observation, we introduce AIMES, a framework for adaptive multi-value activation steering. AIMES constructs layer-specific bipolar directions for moral-foundation values and uses intermediate-layer vocabulary readouts as online observers. An observer-guided controller then adapts the strength of each requested value intervention at every decoding step based on its current observed state, without training a separate value-state estimator. Across multiple instruction-tuned model families, value combinations, and intervention depths, we find that multi-value controllability varies across both value combinations and intervention locations. Compared with fixed joint steering and prompt-based steering, AIMES shows depth-dependent advantages that are broadly supported across two independent evaluators, with some variation in the precise depth at which specific control effects emerge. These advantages come with smaller realized activation-space interventions than fixed-joint steering and comparable response quality. Overall, our results suggest that online observer feedback can provide lightweight, state-aware adaptation for single-pass multi-value steering.

</details>


### [110] [Electric Vehicle Charging Station Location Selection using Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30417)
*Eun Hak Lee,Euntak Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A GeoAI framework using VAE and GCN to identify EV charging locations by leveraging high-dimensional geospatial data; achieves high accuracy and proposes new candidate sites; compares policy scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address CSLP limitations that focus on cost or travel distance by incorporating rich geospatial context (EV usage, land-use, population, traffic) to improve efficiency and accessibility of charging networks.

Method: Integrates a variational autoencoder (VAE) to compress high-dimensional EV geospatial features into a latent space, and a graph convolutional network (GCN) to predict suitable locations for charging stations based on latent representations. Uses real-world data from Bryan–College Station, TX. Evaluates against baselines via F1-score (0.87) and identifies 27 additional candidate locations using a similarity score, along with two policy scenarios (maximize geospatial similarity vs. minimize travel distance).

Result: Outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with F1-score of 0.87 in distinguishing existing vs. non-station locations; identifies 27 promising new candidate sites; demonstrates policy-driven outcomes aligning with different planning objectives.

Conclusion: Spatially aware CSLP via GeoAI enhances infrastructure planning by leveraging geospatial characteristics, offering improvements in efficiency and accessibility and guiding future EV network expansion.

Abstract: As electric vehicle (EV) adoption increases, ensuring efficient and well-distributed charging infrastructure has become a critical challenge. While many EV charging station location problem (CSLP) studies focus on minimizing costs or travel distance, it is crucial to consider the surrounding geospatial characteristics of existing stations that influence operational performance. This study proposes a geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI)-based framework that integrates high-dimensional EV-related geospatial data, including EV usage, land-use, population, and traffic attributes. We incorporate a variational autoencoder (VAE) and a graph convolutional network (GCN) into the model to capture similarities among existing charging stations, and to identify suitable locations for future stations. The VAE compresses high-dimensional EV input data into a low-dimensional latent space, and the GCN uses this latent representation to predict locations suitable for charging stations. Using real-world data from Bryan-College Station, Texas, US, the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an F1-score of 0.87 in distinguishing existing station locations from non-station locations. The model also identifies 27 additional candidate locations that show geospatial characteristics similar to those of existing stations, based on a similarity score. We further evaluate two policy implementation scenarios, maximizing geospatial similarity and minimizing total travel distance, each yielding different outcomes aligned with distinct strategic objectives. The findings highlight the importance of incorporating spatial context into CSLP and provide valuable insights for future EV infrastructure planning, promoting both efficiency and accessibility in the rapidly growing electric mobility sector.

</details>


### [111] [Fake News Theories: Harnessing Disciplinary Insights for Computational Modeling, Detection, and Explanation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30427)
*Zhaoyang Cao,Miriam Metzger,Reza Zafarani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Theory-informed, interpretable fake-news detector; translates cross-disciplinary theories into measurable features; theory-derived features predict deception; multi-feature ensembles offer best performance with modest gains from strong small feature sets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge the gap between automated detection and established theories of persuasion, credibility, and human judgment; improve interpretability and theoretical grounding of detectors.

Method: Structured cross-disciplinary review of theories from social sciences, psychology, economics, etc., to derive measurable features; implement detectable signals via statistical techniques and large language models; validate on benchmark datasets.

Result: Theory-derived features are predictive and provide interpretable, theory-referenced diagnostic signals; multi-feature models outperform single-feature baselines; strongest small feature combinations yield modest gains.

Conclusion: Interdisciplinary perspectives enhance robustness and interpretability of fake-news detection; supports human-centered approaches in combating disinformation.

Abstract: Disinformation research has produced increasingly accurate automated fake-news detectors, but many systems remain difficult to interpret and are weakly connected to established theories of persuasion, credibility, and human judgment. In this paper, we develop a theory-informed computational framework that translates cross-disciplinary theories of fake news into measurable features for automated detection and explanation through statistical techniques and large language models. To that end, we conduct a structured cross-disciplinary review of theories from social sciences, psychology, economics, among other disciplines that reveal how fake news persuades and spreads, thereby establishing a broad theoretical foundation for computational modeling. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that theory-derived features are predictive and provide interpretable, theory-referenced diagnostic signals. Multi-feature models generally outperform individual features, although gains among the strongest small feature combinations are modest. Our work highlights the value of interdisciplinary perspectives in building robust and interpretable fake news detection systems, advancing the foundation for human-centered approaches in combating disinformation.

</details>


### [112] [Improving Molecular-Morphology Contrastive Pretraining using Deep-Learning-based Morphology Profiles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30433)
*Jie Li,Kathryn E. Kirchoff,Dante A. Pertusi,Zhizhuo Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Deep-learning-derived cell morphology profiles aligned with molecular embeddings via contrastive pretraining (MoCoP v2) yield richer representations, improving QSAR and toxicity predictions and offering competitive ADME/activity results versus morphology/transcriptomics baselines; performance scales with data size.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome limitations of fixed morphology features and to leverage richer, image-based phenotypes for aligning molecule embeddings; investigate data-scale effects and broaden predictive utility (QSAR, toxicity, ADME, activity).

Method: Replace CellProfiler-based features with a deep-learning cell image encoder to extract morphology fingerprints; train via contrastive learning to align with molecular embeddings; evaluate using fixed linear probes or fine-tuning; analyze data-size scaling and benchmark against existing morphology/transcriptomics-based models.

Result: Molecular embeddings capture more accurate morphology perturbations; improvements in QSAR; morphology retrieval scales log-linearly with training data; MoCoP v2 achieves superior toxicity prediction and competitive ADME/activity performance compared with models using both morphology and transcriptomic data.

Conclusion: MoCoP v2 delivers richer, scalable morphology-informed molecular representations that enhance predictive tasks; gains are data-dependent and likely to grow with larger morphology datasets, supporting broader applicability of image-based phenomics in molecular modeling.

Abstract: Recent advancements in image-based profiling techniques have enabled the collection of high-volume cell morphology data, allowing new molecular embedding models to learn from the experimental phenotypic perturbations of a molecule in a cell. Previously, we developed Molecule-Morphology Contrastive Pretraining (MoCoP), a strategy for aligning small molecule embeddings to morphology fingerprints extracted through CellProfiler. The resulting molecular representation showed transferable performance for quantitative structure--activity relationship (QSAR) prediction tasks. Here, we extend the method by using a deep-learning-based cell image encoding pipeline to extract more feature-rich morphology profiles and align them to the molecular embeddings through contrastive learning. The new embeddings encode more accurate information on how molecules perturb cell morphology and enable improvements for QSAR predictions through either fixed-embedding linear probes or fully flexible fine-tuning. Morphology retrieval performance scales log-linearly with training data size, suggesting continued improvements as larger datasets become available. The improved MoCoP v2 also achieves superior performance on toxicity prediction and competitive results on ADME and activity benchmarks, when compared with existing molecular embedding models that use both cell morphology and transcriptomic data during training.

</details>


### [113] [Auditing System-1 Models on Biosecurity-Relevant Benchmarks: Calibration, Selective Prediction, and Permutation Instability in a Non-Generative Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30454)
*Kimon Antonios Provatas,Ilias Georgakopoulos-Soares*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Non-generative System-1 model shows variable accuracy across biosecurity tasks but can be calibrated; rotational averaging over answer choices partially mitigates brittleness and improves performance, with cost trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess reliability of inexpensive System-1 models in high-stakes biosafety contexts, where calibration and decision reliability matter.

Method: Audit a commercial System-1 model on 6,020 MC items from WMDP and LAB-Bench tasks, evaluate accuracy, calibration (ECE), AUROC, error detection, selective prediction, and sensitivity to answer-order; test four cyclic rotations of options; compare averaging across rotations.

Result: Accuracy is task-dependent; calibration decent after interpreting vendor uncertainty field (pooled ECE 0.034); AUROC 0.820; under option rotations 37.4% of WMDP-Cyber items change answers; most variation due to option order; averaging across rotations increases WMDP-Cyber accuracy by 3.8 percentage points; targeting averaging to low-confidence items recovers most gains with low cost.

Conclusion: System-1 models can be reasonably calibrated and discriminative for some tasks in biosafety contexts, but vulnerabilities to option ordering exist; simple rotational-averaging can improve robustness with modest cost; performance varies by task.

Abstract: Non-generative "System-1" models return structured probabilistic decisions in a single forward pass, without autoregressive decoding, at a small fraction of the inference cost of a generative model. This makes them of interest as inexpensive components in larger pipelines, but their reliability on biosecurity-relevant tasks has not been systematically examined. We audit one commercial System-1 model on 6,020 multiple-choice items drawn from the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP), a paraphrase-robust WMDP-Bio variant, and six LAB-Bench subtasks, measuring accuracy, calibration, error detection, selective prediction, and sensitivity to the order in which answer options are presented. Accuracy is strongly task-dependent. Once the vendor's uncertainty field is correctly interpreted, the model is reasonably well calibrated (pooled expected calibration error 0.034) and its top-1 probability separates correct from incorrect predictions (pooled AUROC 0.820), though both degrade substantially on the weaker tasks. Under four cyclic rotations of the answer options, 37.4% of WMDP-Cyber items receive different answers; a control using byte-identical repeated calls attributes most of this to option order rather than run-to-run variation. Averaging probabilities across rotations improves WMDP-Cyber accuracy by 3.8 percentage points, and applying it only to low-confidence items recovers most of that gain at well under the cost of averaging every item.

</details>


### [114] [RAZOR: Pruning Replaceable Experts in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30465)
*Mingyang Song,Mao Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RAZOR is a training-free expert pruning method for Mixture-of-Experts models that scores the functional replaceability of each expert via consensus residuals, enabling effective pruning without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reduce the storage and compute burden of MoE models by pruning experts without loss of performance, while accounting for how deletions affect the surviving computation and router behavior.

Method: RAZOR computes exact single-deletion-based scores using consensus residuals (differences between individual expert outputs and the original weighted mixture) with local scores per calibration token, aggregating them to budget the pruning without gradients or re-training.

Result: On multiple backbones and budgets (25% and 50%), RAZOR achieves the highest macro-average performance across nine tasks in all eight settings and surpasses REAP in matched benchmarks by 2.12–5.59 points, with improved reverse KL relative to REAP; it also reveals generation stability changes (diversity, formatting, termination) despite task retention.

Conclusion: RAZOR provides a powerful, training-free mechanism for MoE expert pruning that respects functional replaceability under router-driven refill and survivor renormalization, delivering strong empirical gains and insight into generation stability after pruning.

Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models activate few experts per token but store the full expert pool. Expert pruning reduces this storage burden; at a fixed pruning budget, the goal is to preserve the original model's output distribution as closely as possible. Yet an expert's usage or contribution magnitude does not by itself determine the damage caused by its removal. What matters is whether the surviving computation can replace its function. We introduce RAZOR, a training-free expert pruning method that scores functional replaceability using consensus residuals: deviations of expert outputs from the original weighted mixture. An exact single-deletion identity at a fixed layer input accounts for survivor renormalization and router-selected refill, providing local scores aggregated over calibration tokens for budgeted pruning without gradients or recovery training. On GLM-4.7-Flash, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, and Hy3 at 25\% and 50\% expert removal, RAZOR achieves the highest nine-task macro average among the evaluated pruning methods in all eight settings. On the two backbones with matched REAP benchmark runs, it exceeds REAP by 2.12--5.59 points and wins all 36 paired task comparisons. It also lowers reverse KL relative to REAP in all four matched GLM-4.7-Flash and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model--budget settings. Analysis of responses generated by Qwen3.6-35B-A3B nevertheless reveals changes in diversity, formatting, and termination, underscoring that task retention and predictive fidelity do not ensure generation stability.

</details>


### [115] [Reliability-aware Cross-sample Enhancement for Robust Multimodal Sentiment Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30470)
*Menghua Jiang,Haokai Gao,Xiangui Kang,Haifeng Hu,Sijie Mai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes Reliability-aware Cross-sample Enhancement (RCE) for robust multimodal sentiment analysis under noisy and missing modalities, combining adaptive variational information bottleneck and reliability-aware cross-sample augmentation with multilevel fusion; achieves state-of-the-art results across full, noisy, and missing settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MSA systems in real-world scenarios are frequently corrupted by noise and have missing modalities; existing methods typically address these challenges individually, limiting robustness.

Method: Adaptive variational information bottleneck to model modality-wise uncertainty and perform quality-aware information compression; reliability-aware cross-sample enhancement to retrieve high-confidence, semantically-consistent neighbors from a large candidate pool; multilevel reliability-aware fusion integrating cross-modal interactions and enhancement stages for robust aggregation.

Result: Empirical evaluations show that RCE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across full, noisy, and missing-modality settings.

Conclusion: RCE delivers robust multimodal representations by jointly accounting for modality quality and cross-sample information enrichment, demonstrating effectiveness and generality in challenging MSA scenarios.

Abstract: Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) aims to infer human emotions from multiple modalities such as text, audio, and vision. In practice, inputs are often corrupted by noise and missing modalities, which degrades performance. Existing methods typically address these challenges in isolation, limiting their effectiveness in realistic settings. To address this limitation, we propose a Reliability-aware Cross-sample Enhancement (RCE) framework. Specifically, RCE first introduces an adaptive variational information bottleneck to model modality-wise uncertainty and perform quality-aware information compression, thereby suppressing redundant noise in unreliable modalities. Furthermore, we design a reliability-aware cross-sample enhancement strategy that retrieves high-confidence, semantically consistent neighbors from a large candidate pool to enrich and calibrate current representations, effectively alleviating information deficiency caused by missing modalities. Building upon this, RCE integrates cross-modal interactions with a multilevel reliability-aware fusion mechanism to adaptively aggregate information across modalities and enhancement stages, leading to more robust multimodal representations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RCE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across full, noisy, and missing-modality settings.

</details>


### [116] [Moment-guided edge sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30472)
*Weibin Cai,Reza Zafarani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A moment-guided edge sampling framework quantifies local edge edits via spectral moments of the random-walk transition matrix, enabling controllable preservation of global graph structure and improvements in graph learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the fundamental challenge of relating local edge edits (additions/removals) to global graph structure and objective preservation, providing a measurable, interpretable, and controllable framework.

Method: Two complementary approaches for exact moment changes: (1) a combinatorial method with closed-form updates for low-order moments; (2) a low-rank method leveraging locality and cyclic trace invariance to compress computations to edited endpoints, supporting arbitrary moment orders and batched edits. For single-edge edits at fixed moment orders, the low-rank method reduces cost from O(mn) to O(m); the combinatorial method yields constant-time updates given maintained local statistics. These moment changes yield interpretable structural signatures that aggregate into graph-level fingerprints; moment-preserving sampling is shown to retain related properties (e.g., triangle-weighted clustering).

Result: Moment changes serve as interpretable structural signatures (fingerprints) of local edge motifs and can be used to preserve global properties during sampling. Moment-preserving sampling retains related structural properties, and different edge structures variably influence supervised node classification; moment-guided augmentation is competitive for graph contrastive learning.

Conclusion: Spectral moments provide an interpretable and controllable bridge from local edge edits to global graph structure and learning outcomes, enabling analysis and improvement of graph learning through moment-guided sampling.

Abstract: Edge sampling makes local decisions to achieve graph-level objectives, such as preserving structural properties. This creates a fundamental challenge: \textit{how can the effect of a local edge edit (i.e., edge addition or removal) on global graph structure be quantified and controlled?} We address this challenge with a \textit{moment-guided edge sampling framework} based on spectral moments of the random-walk transition matrix. We compute exact moment changes through two complementary methods: a combinatorial method with closed-form updates for low-order moments, and a low-rank method that exploits \textit{locality} and \textit{cyclic trace invariance} to compress computations to edited endpoints, supporting arbitrary moment orders and batched edits. For single-edge edits at fixed moment orders, the low-rank method reduces the cost from $O(mn)$ to $O(m)$, while the combinatorial method evaluates low-order changes in constant time given maintained local statistics. These moment changes provide \textbf{interpretable structural signatures} of local edge motifs that aggregate into graph-level fingerprints. This structural meaning motivates us to ask whether preserving moments also preserves the graph properties. We further derive and validate that moment-preserving sampling can \textbf{retain related structural properties}, including triangle-weighted clustering coefficient. These structural insights enable \textbf{analysis and improvement of graph learning}: different edge structures have distinct effects on supervised node classification, while moment-guided augmentation is competitive for graph contrastive learning. Together, these findings establish moments as an interpretable and controllable bridge from local edge edits to global graph structure and learning.

</details>


### [117] [Mentored Decoding: Faster Inference meets Boosting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30474)
*Vivien Tran-Thien,Richard Nock*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Lossy speculative decoding formalized as mentored decoding shows speedups can improve target quality; a boosting-inspired, divergence-general framework yields efficient O(n) space / O(log n) query structures for optimal mentored distributions across any f-divergence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explain why lossy speculative decoding can beat target quality and to provide a principled, general theory linking inference with boosting via f-divergences.

Method: Formalize mentored decoding, relate to boosting; generalize to all f-divergences; analyze total variation geometry; derive simple approximations; develop a divergence-independent data structure enabling O(n) time for generation of mentored distributions and O(log n) for dual-parameter queries.

Result: Provides geometric intuition for TV case; practical approximations for any f-divergence; an O(n) space, O(sort(n)) time data structure for the dual optimization, enabling O(log n) queries and O(n) construction of optimal mentored distributions.

Conclusion: Mentored decoding offers a universal, divergence-agnostic framework connecting inference speedups and model quality, with tangible efficiency gains and a foundation for further exploration across divergences.

Abstract: Speculative decoding is a successful technique speeding up inference of a target autoregressive language model via a fast drafter model. Lossy speculative decoding allows a drift with respect to the target to further improve speed. Interestingly, it has been observed experimentally that the resulting model can $\textit{also}$ beat the target $\textit{quality-wise}$. Our paper formally proves how such a feat is possible with a formal approach to lossy speculative decoding called $\textit{mentored decoding}$. To get there, we connect inference to a celebrated ML training theory, $\textit{boosting}$, and proceed via the generalization of mentored decoding to the whole set of $f$-divergences. We uncover key properties of mentored decoding, among which (i) the particularly appealing geometric nature of the total variation case, (ii) simple approximations for any $f$-divergence in direct relation with boosting compliance, and (iii) a $\textit{divergence independent}$ $O(n)$ space and $O(\mathrm{sort}(n))$ time data structure built on drafter and target outputs, which allows to query the optimal parameters of the dual problem in $O(\log n)$ time and constructing optimal mentored distributions in $O(n)$ time for any $f$-divergence.

</details>


### [118] [Geometric Feature Learning for Functional Data Valued on the Symmetric Positive Definite Manifold](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30487)
*Samuel V. Singh,Mimi Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A geometry-aware functional NN (MatFAE) for SPD trajectories that treats sequences as continuous functions, enabling derivative-aware latent representations and interpretable functional weights; validated on fMRI datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Preserve Riemannian geometry of SPD manifolds when learning trajectory data, capture dynamic/derivative information, and obtain interpretable representations for high-dimensional neuroimaging trajectories.

Method: Introduce intrinsic SPD-manifold layers to map trajectory data to Euclidean vectors, followed by a functional layer that projects to a finite-dimensional space; supports continuous-time sequence modeling, handles matrix factorization during backpropagation, and yields interpretable weight morphologies indicating input regions driving the latent factors.

Result: Demonstrates efficient learning of informative representations from high-dimensional SPD trajectories on various fMRI datasets, with practical relevance for real-world neuroimaging analysis.

Conclusion: MatFAE provides a geometry-aware, interpretable framework for continuous-function modeling of SPD trajectories, advancing neuroimaging analysis by leveraging manifold structure and derivative information.

Abstract: We here develop a functional neural network, termed MatFAE, for learning trajectories on the Riemannian manifold of symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices. MatFAE features intrinsic layers that map manifold-valued functions to Euclidean vector-valued functions, followed by a functional layer that projects them into a finite-dimensional Euclidean space. Unlike most neural networks for discrete-time sequences, MatFAE treats each sequence as a continuous function and can therefore encode trajectory dynamics (e.g., first-order derivatives) in its latent representations. Additionally, the morphology of the functional weights in the functional layer offers interpretability by revealing the regions of the input functional data that contribute most to the latent representations. We justify the design principles and properties of each intrinsic layer and detail how matrix factorization is handled during backpropagation. We apply MatFAE to a range of fMRI datasets, demonstrating its ability to efficiently learn informative representations from high-dimensional SPD trajectories and its practical value for real-world neuroimaging analysis.

</details>


### [119] [Learning to Bias: Machine Learning-Enhanced Particle Filters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30498)
*Apoorv Srivastava,Eric Darve*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NOPFs learn an amortized proposal to the optimal PF proposal using offline one-step conditioning data, acting as a drop-in replacement in PF updates while preserving the target filtering distribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard particle filters suffer from poor sample efficiency and high variance with suboptimal proposals, especially in high dimensions. Learning proposals aims to reduce variance and improve efficiency without altering the filtering objective.

Method: Train a neural network to approximate the optimal proposal p(x_t|x_{t-1}, y_t) using offline simulated one-step conditioning tuples. Use the learned proposal as a drop-in replacement in PF updates; correct samples with standard importance weights so the filter targets the same distribution asymptotically under standard assumptions.

Result: NOPFs achieve improved sample efficiency and distributional accuracy over standard PF baselines across nonlinear stochastic benchmarks, with modest computational overhead.

Conclusion: Integrating data-driven proposals into classical particle filtering can improve efficiency while preserving the filtering objective; the approach relies on amortized learning from simulated data and retains asymptotic correctness under standard assumptions.

Abstract: Sequential inference estimates latent states from noisy and incomplete observations. Particle Filters (PFs), a class of Monte Carlo methods based on importance sampling, provide a flexible framework for this task, but often suffer from poor sample efficiency and unfavorable scaling with dimension, partly due to suboptimal proposal distributions. We address these challenges by integrating learned proposals into the PF framework. We introduce Neural Optimal Particle Filters (NOPFs), which learn an amortized approximation to the optimal proposal from offline simulated one-step conditioning tuples. The learned proposal is used as a drop-in replacement in standard PF updates, with samples corrected by standard importance weights so that the method asymptotically targets the same filtering distribution under standard support and density-evaluation assumptions. Across stochastic nonlinear benchmarks of varying inference complexity, NOPFs improve sample efficiency and distributional accuracy over standard PF baselines with modest computational overhead. The approach integrates data-driven proposal learning into classical inference without altering the underlying filtering objective.

</details>


### [120] [PolicyAttention: Softmax Attention Implements Policy Mirror Descent for Closed-Loop Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30500)
*Yuhe Sui,Yingzhi Tang,Shufang Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Explores whether causal softmax attention can implement policy mirror descent (PMD) as a repeated controller rather than a one-step identity. Builds a fixed actor–environment–one-step-critic protocol with normalization constraints and boundary conditions; empirically compares to Exact PMD and variants, showing near-oracle performance with an exact critic, while learned critics and alternative adaptations incur larger losses. Open question remains on a strict 20-transition comparison and data-throughput asymmetry.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine if PMD can be realized via a recurrent, causal-softmax control loop and to identify the practical constraints (tokenization, sampling boundaries, LayerNorm conditioning) needed for a faithful, normalized implementation.

Method: Construct a fixed causal-softmax actor–environment–one-step-critic pipeline with explicit residuals for actor routing, sampling, and normalization. Define a finite-logit/full-support domain and external tokenization/sampling boundary; enforce mean-zero LayerNorm for normalized compilation. Train pre-LN Transformers to empirically recover target PMD computation. Compare against an Exact PMD oracle using preregistered repeated-control tests (e.g., S=4, five runs) and higher-S experiments (S=8, 16) against fixed rules, a frozen audit model, and two adaptations (Liang–Lai, Algorithm Distillation), analyzing policy-loss metrics and transitions per round.

Result: Exact-critic with an actor closely matching PMD attains median policy-loss ≈1.052× the Exact PMD oracle (S=4), and ≈1.050× with the same setup (no margin). At S=8, replacing the exact critic with a learned critic reduces loss to 0.0225 in the fixed protocol, but the Liang–Lai and Algorithm Distillation adaptations incur 20.2–24.2× higher losses. This discrepancy is attributed to a one-sided sampled-critic bound due to PolicyAttention using 144 generative transitions per round versus 20 on-policy transitions for adaptations. The strict 20-transition comparison remains unresolved. For S=8,16, the exact-critic common-harness comparison yields 17.7–28.2× lower loss than the adaptations, highlighting information asymmetry.

Conclusion: A fixed causal-softmax protocol that implements PMD via an explicit one-step critic can achieve near-oracle performance under exact-critic conditions. Learned critics and alternative adaptation strategies underperform, with a noted information-throughput asymmetry affecting cross-method comparisons. The key open question is whether a strict 20-transition budget can be equitably compared and how data efficiency bounds the results.

Abstract: Can causal softmax attention implement policy mirror descent as a repeated controller rather than a one-step algebraic identity? Negative-entropy policy mirror descent (PMD) has the statewise update $\operatorname{PMD}_η(π,Q)=\operatorname{softmax}(\logπ+ηQ)$. Building on the known Q-TD-PMD recursion, we construct one fixed causal-softmax actor--environment--one-step-critic protocol with explicit actor, routing, sampling, and normalization residuals, and propagate them to the policy actually returned. The construction states the finite-logit/full-support domain, the external tokenization and sampling boundary, and the mean-zero LayerNorm carrier conditions required by the normalized compilation.
  Separately trained pre-LN Transformers recover the target computation empirically. A frozen one-step audit model is closest to PMD among the tested fixed rules; in a preregistered five-run $S=4$ repeated-control test, the learned actor with an exact one-step critic reaches median returned-policy loss $1.052\times$ the Exact PMD oracle and retains the criterion across four no-retraining shifts. The same checkpoints with their learned critic give descriptive median $1.050\times$ the oracle (no registered margin). At $S=8$, replacing the exact critic by the learned critic raises median $T=20$ loss to $0.0225$ yet leaves the Liang--Lai and Algorithm Distillation adaptations $20.2$--$24.2\times$ higher-loss; this is a one-sided sampled-critic bound because PolicyAttention consumes 144 generative transitions per round versus 20 on-policy transitions for the adaptations. The strict 20-transition comparison remains open. At $S=8,16$, the exact-critic common-harness comparison remains $17.7$--$28.2\times$ lower-loss than those adaptations, with the information asymmetry stated locally.

</details>


### [121] [To Solve Bilevel Optimization with Nonconvex Lower Levels, We Need Second-Order Stationarity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30501)
*Zhiyao Zhang,Menglu Yu,Alvaro Velasquez,Nathaniel D. Bastian,Jia Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces PROBE, a second-order surrogate and perturbed gradient method to solve bilevel optimization with general lower-level nonconvex (LLNC) objectives, proving finite-time convergence to lower-level second-order stationary points (O(T^-2/5)) and demonstrating empirical gains over SOTA on LLNC-BLO tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLSC/LLGC assumptions are too restrictive for many practical ML problems. LLNC-BLO remains underdeveloped, with methods relying on first-order surrogates or extra lower-level structure that may fail to guarantee quality solutions.
