There is a need for methods that achieve lower-level second-order stationary solutions without restrictive assumptions.

Method: Reformulate the LLNC lower-level problem using a second-order stationarity-based surrogate and introduce PROBE (Perturbed gradient algorithm for bilevel problem). PROBE perturbs the gradient path to escape lower-level saddle points and delivers a finite-time convergence rate to a lower-level 2nd-order stationary solution.

Result: Theoretical: PROBE achieves finite-time convergence to lower-level second-order stationary solutions in general LLNC-BLO with rate O(T^-2/5). Empirical: On LLM-based data curation and meta-learning tasks, PROBE outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: This work is the first to establish finite-time convergence to lower-level second-order stationary solutions in general LLNC-BLO, expanding the applicability of bilevel optimization to nonconvex lower levels and showing practical performance improvements.

Abstract: Although bilevel optimization (BLO) has emerged as a powerful framework for addressing many complex and nested machine learning problems in recent years, most existing studies are confined to the lower-level strongly convex (LLSC) or lower-level generally convex (LLGC) settings (i.e., the lower-level objective function is assumed to be, at least, convex). While the LLSC/LLGC assumptions render more tractable algorithmic design and theoretical analysis, they are too rigid to encompass many machine learning problems in practice. The limitations of LLSC/LLGC assumptions in BLO motivate us to investigate solving the BLO problem in the general lower-level nonconvex (LLNC) settings, which remains in its infancy. In the literature on LLNC-BLO, most of the existing works either require additional structures in the lower-level objective function for tractable theoretical analysis, or adopt the first-order stationarity reformulation as a lower-level surrogate problem, which is inherited from the LLSC/LLGC settings but could lose their effectiveness in the LLNC setting. To bridge this gap, we propose to reformulate the nonconvex lower-level problem using a second-order stationarity-based surrogate, the solution of which guarantees a local optimal solution at the lower level. Based on this reformulation, we propose the PROBE (Perturbed gradient algorithm for bilevel problem) and show that it overcomes the limitations of prior works by probing and escaping lower-level saddle points. We prove that PROBE achieves a finite-time convergence rate of $O(T^{-2/5})$, where T denotes iterations. To our knowledge, this work is the first to establish the finite-time convergence for achieving lower-level second-order stationary solutions in general LLNC-BLO. Our experiments on both a large language model-based data curation task and a meta-learning task also show that PROBE outperforms SOTA methods.

</details>


### [122] [Federated Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30503)
*Diyang Li,Fei Wang,Kyra Gan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces two federated TMLE algorithms (FedTMLE-G and FedTMLE-L) enabling targeting in cross-silo settings with finite-precision communication, achieving accuracy close to centralized TMLE while exposing tradeoffs in privacy guarantees and convergence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the barrier that critical evidentiary data are siloed in hospitals, banks, or registries, preventing pooling of individual observations. TMLE is powerful but centralized; need federated TMLE to perform efficient, valid inference without raw-data pooling.

Method: Two complementary frameworks: FedTMLE-G aggregates local gradients to reproduce the centralized targeting step (step-by-step equivalence); FedTMLE-L allows each institution to complete its own fluctuation fit and then exchanges fitted updates (favors local autonomy). A finite-precision, change-based gradient protocol transmits increments rather than values with explicit bounds on exchanges and bits. A description-length analysis shows accepted updates yield negligible targeting error compared to sampling uncertainty. A personalized local-averaging variant keeps institutions’ own estimates, exiting after local targeting. A nonconvex convergence bound links the improvement lost due to averaging to disagreement among local fits, highlighting a tradeoff between equal institutional influence and small-silo variability.

Result: The federated approach preserves targeting accuracy with limited communication; numerical targeting error is negligible against sampling uncertainty; computation cost is separable from model/target selection complexity; identifying privacy guarantees is not straightforward because local data retention alone does not prevent sensitive attribute recovery; provides a bounded framework for trading synchronization with autonomy and a formal convergence bound to quantify tradeoffs.

Conclusion: Federated TMLE is feasible and well-characterized: local computation can replace centralized targeting under explicit communication and convergence guarantees; practitioners gain privacy-aware, scalable inference without pooling raw data, but must account for privacy limitations and tradeoffs between institutional influence and sampling variability.

Abstract: The evidence behind a scientific or operational decision is often held by hospitals, banks, or registries that cannot pool individual observations. Cross-silo federated learning moves computation to the data and exchanges agreed summaries. Targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) refines a flexible initial fit, yielding plug-in estimators that respect the model and support efficient inference. TMLE itself, however, has remained a fully centralized procedure. To fill this gap, our paper introduces the first federated TMLE algorithm. We federate targeting itself, for an arbitrary target, loss, and fluctuation family, through two complementary frameworks. FedTMLE-G aggregates local gradients and reproduces centralized targeting step for step. FedTMLE-L lets each institution complete its own fluctuation fit before a single exchange of fitted updates, trading synchronized fidelity for local autonomy. For gradient aggregation, we develop a finite-precision protocol that transmits changes rather than values and certifies targeting accuracy within explicit bounds on exchanges and bits. A description-length analysis of the accepted updates then shows that this finite communication leaves numerical targeting error negligible against sampling uncertainty. The cost of computing an estimator is thus distinct from the complexity of selecting it. Our analysis also indicates that keeping data local is not itself a privacy guarantee of TMLE, since instability of full-record reconstruction need not prevent recovery of a specified sensitive attribute. For a personalized version of local averaging, institutions retain their own estimates and leave once local targeting is complete. A nonconvex convergence bound charges the improvement forfeited through averaging to disagreement among local fits and exposes a tradeoff between equal institutional influence and the sampling variability of small silos.

</details>


### [123] [Benchmarking the Connectomes of Caenorhabditis elegans within the Reservoir Computing Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30508)
*Felix S. Reimers,Ola Huse Ramstad,Aliaksandr Hubin,Stefano Nichele*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Reservoir computing on C. elegans connectomes shows that biology-inspired wiring does not inherently outperform randomized networks; performance strongly depends on reservoir configuration and data derivation (age and measurement method).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether whole-organism connectomes of C. elegans, across ages and measurement methods, act as effective reservoirs for echo state networks, and to benchmark how biological wiring compares to random baselines under various configurations.

Method: Represent connectomes as reservoirs (echo state networks) with minimal preprocessing. Use multiple connectomes (different ages and three measurement methods) as substrates. Train/test using neuro-inspired tasks. Compare with equally sized randomized null models. Explore different reservoir configurations and input/output node schemes.

Result: Biological wiring and bio-informed input/output configurations do not necessarily yield better performance. Randomized null models often outperform the original connectomes on the chosen benchmarks. Outcomes depend on reservoir configuration and how the connectome was derived; connectomes from different ages yield varying results with no clear trend.

Conclusion: Structural wiring alone is not a guaranteed predictor of reservoir performance in these benchmarks; results are sensitive to data derivation (age and measurement method) and reservoir setup. Care is needed when using organism connectomes as benchmarks, and comparisons should include well-medaled random nulls and standardized configurations.

Abstract: The aim of this work is to examine the connectomes of Caenorhabditis elegans through a computational lens using the reservoir computing framework. Connectomes are mappings of biological neural networks; C. elegans is the first organism for which physical connectomes covering the whole nervous system have been published. The connectomes of C. elegans used in this paper have been derived at different ages of the organism and are based on three different ways of measuring inter-cellular connections. They have, with minimal preprocessing, been implemented as reservoirs in the form of echo state networks, which are recurrent neural networks. In reservoir computing, the reservoir itself is not trained, rather the output of the reservoir is passed to a comparatively small read-out module in which training takes place. Training and testing is conducted in different neuro-inspired tasks, with the aim of using these tasks as a benchmark for the connectomes. This process has been repeated with different configurations of the reservoir and equally sized but randomized null models have been used for comparison. The results show that the biological wiring and a bio-informed configuration of input and output nodes of the reservoirs do not necessarily lead to better performance. Contrarily, the randomized null models are often outperforming the original connectomes on the chosen benchmarks. At the same time it becomes clear that the results depend a lot on the configuration of the reservoir and the way the connectome has been derived from the organism. Connectomes from different ages may produce varying outcome, without a clear trend becoming visible.

</details>


### [124] [AutoResearch at Production Scale: Failure Modes and a Multi-Agent Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30541)
*Aparajith Chandran,Juwon Kim,Saurav Jha,Pablo Castells,Florian Hottier*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AutoResearch-driven exploration applied to production-scale embedding systems yields performance gains but reveals five recurring failure modes; a three-principle scaffolding design (prevent, persist, redirect) mitigates them, achieving ~1.8x Recall@6, ~2.1x coherence gains, and 5.8x catalog expansion via a text-only fallback across diverse iteration costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production recommendation pipelines require expensive, large-scale exploration of training configurations. Automating this with an LLM-based agent that edits training scripts can accelerate research while operating under real-world constraints. The study seeks to identify failure modes that emerge in production-scale autonomous research and to validate a design that scales with iteration cost.

Method: Implemented Karpathy's AutoResearch paradigm: an LLM iteratively edits a training script; kept edits that improve a held-out scalar metric. Conducted 12 weeks of production-scale experiments across two representation-learning systems for book recommendations, totaling 220+ runs. Evaluations involved multiple criteria and long campaign lifecycles. Analyzable failure modes were identified, leading to a three-principle scaffolding design (prevent, persist, redirect) with remedies mapped to each mode. Outputs included automated text-only fallbacks and cross-system generalization across orders of magnitude variation in per-iteration cost.

Result: Observed five recurrent failure modes not present in the original setting: infrastructure fragility, agent memory decay, search-direction stagnation, iteration-cost asymmetry, and metric fixation. The scaffolding design mitigates these, yielding 1.82x Recall@6 and 2.1x coherence improvements over hand-tuned baselines, and a 5.8x expansion in catalog coverage via a text-only fallback. The findings suggest these failure modes are structural to production-scale autonomous research rather than application-specific.

Conclusion: Production-scale autonomous research exhibits consistent failure modes across large cost variations. A three-principle scaffold—prevent, persist, redirect—provides scalable remedies that enable meaningful metric gains and broader coverage, indicating these design principles may generalize to other production AI pipelines.

Abstract: Optimizing embedding systems for production recommendation pipelines demands systematic exploration that consumes disproportionate engineering effort at scale. We apply Andrej Karpathy's AutoResearch paradigm -- a large language model that iteratively edits a training script and retains modifications that improve a held-out scalar metric -- to automate this exploration. We report on twelve weeks of running this paradigm at production scale, where iterations consume hours of multi-GPU compute, evaluation involves competing criteria, and campaigns span weeks across many training jobs. Across two independently developed representation-learning systems for a book recommendation pipeline, we ran 220+ experiments and observed five recurring failure modes absent from the original setting: infrastructure fragility, agent memory decay, search-direction stagnation, iteration-cost asymmetry, and metric fixation. We contribute a three-principle scaffolding design -- prevent, persist, redirect -- that maps each failure mode to a structural remedy and whose instantiation scales with iteration cost. The framework produced a 1.82x Recall@6 lift and a 2.1x coherence lift over hand-tuned baselines, and the agent autonomously designed a text-only fallback that expanded catalog coverage by 5.8x. The two systems span nearly three orders of magnitude in per-iteration cost yet exhibit the same failure modes, suggesting these are structural properties of production-scale autonomous research rather than artifacts of either application.

</details>


### [125] [GyroNovo: Error-Guided Fragment Imputation with Mass-Aware Attention for \textit{De Novo} Peptide Sequencing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30542)
*Abdellah El Mekki,Laks V. S. Lakshmanan,Muhammad Abdul-Mageed*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GyroNovo aligns missing-fragment imputation with decoder behavior and adds mass-aware inductive bias via rotary embeddings, yielding substantial de novo peptide sequencing gains without extra inputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: De novo peptide sequencing suffers from sparse/noisy spectra with missing informative b- and y-ions. Existing latent imputation ignores which missing fragments most affect decoding errors and peak representations lack mass-difference modeling.

Method: 1) Decoder-error-guided imputation: adapt the imputation objective to fragments linked to frequent decoder errors and create easy/hard augmented views from the error distribution. 2) Mass-aware self-attention: incorporate rotary embeddings to encode pairwise mass differences between peaks, biasing attention by mass relationships. 3) Use standard encoder–imputer–decoder at inference with no extra inputs.

Result: On NovoBench, GyroNovo achieves ~9 percentage-point gains in peptide-level precision and ~7 percentage-point gains in amino-acid-level precision over the state-of-the-art baseline.

Conclusion: Mass-aware bias and error-driven imputation align missing-fragment recovery with decoder behavior, improving de novo sequencing accuracy while preserving a standard architecture and requiring no extra inference steps.

Abstract: De novo peptide sequencing from tandem mass spectra is essential for identifying peptides without relying on reference databases. Despite advances in deep learning, accurate sequencing remains challenging because experimental spectra are often sparse, noisy, and incomplete, leaving informative b- and y-ion fragments unobserved. Existing methods attempt to recover this missing evidence via latent-space imputation before autoregressive decoding. However, they typically treat imputation as a fixed reconstruction task, without considering which missing fragments are most relevant to decoder errors. Moreover, existing peak representations do not explicitly model mass differences between peaks, despite their fundamental importance.
  We introduce GyroNovo, a framework with two main contributions. First, we use decoder errors observed during training to adapt the imputation objective, prioritizing fragments associated with frequent decoding errors. We further use the decoder error distribution to construct easy and hard augmented views of each spectrum, enabling the decoder to learn under varying degrees of spectral corruption and missing-fragment severity. Second, we introduce a mass-aware inductive bias into self-attention by using rotary embeddings to encode pairwise mass differences between spectral peaks. Together, these components align missing-fragment recovery with decoder behavior while explicitly incorporating the mass relationships that underlie peptide fragmentation. At inference time, GyroNovo retains a standard encoder-imputer-decoder architecture and requires neither additional inputs nor auxiliary search procedures. Experiments on NovoBench show gains of about 9 percentage points in peptide-level precision and 7 percentage points in amino-acid-level precision over the state-of-the-art baseline. Code: https://github.com/UBC-NLP/gyronovo.

</details>


### [126] [Dynamic Regret in Online Convex Optimization with Indicator Switching Costs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30556)
*Naram Mhaisen,George Iosifidis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A meta-learning framework with randomized lazy FTRL base learners and a movement-aware master achieves minimax-optimal dynamic regret with indicator switching costs, without prior knowledge of comparator properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Indicator switching costs model startup overheads (server activation, deployment, cache updates) and make static-comparator methods insufficient. Existing techniques fail to extend to dynamic regret with these costs, especially under unknown S_T and P_T; a robust dynamic-regret guarantee is needed.

Method: Randomized lazy Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (FTRL) base learners restarted at dyadic time scales; their proposals are mixed by a movement-aware master, and actions are sampled via maximal coupling of consecutive mixtures.

Result: E[R^1_T] ≤ ~O(min{√(T(S_T+1)), T^{2/3}(P_T+1)^{1/3}}) in expectation, where R^1_T is the dynamic regret plus cumulative indicator switching cost. The bound holds for all comparator sequences, is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors for piecewise-constant comparators, and also handles frequently moving comparators with small total path length.

Conclusion: The proposed meta-learning algorithm provides robust, prior-free guarantees for dynamic regret with indicator switching costs, effectively unifying static and dynamic objectives and adapting to varying comparator behavior.

Abstract: We study dynamic regret in online convex optimization with an \emph{indicator switching cost}: a fixed penalty incurred whenever two consecutive decisions differ. This captures startup overheads such as server activation, model deployment, and cache updates, and on a bounded domain it recovers norm-based movement costs as a special case. Existing guarantees for indicator costs handle only static comparators. We show that a direct extension of these techniques to dynamic regret provably fails, motivating a different approach. We propose a meta-learning framework: a set of randomized lazy FTRL base learners restarted at dyadic time scales, aggregated by a movement-aware master that mixes their proposal densities and samples actions via maximal coupling of consecutive mixtures. The resulting algorithm satisfies, in expectation, $\mathcal{R}^{\mathbf{1}}_T \le \tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\min\{\sqrt{T(S_T{+}1)},T^{2/3}(P_T+1)^{1/3}\})$, where $\mathcal{R}^{\mathbf{1}}_T$ is the dynamic regret plus the cumulative indicator switching cost, $S_T$ counts comparator switches, and $P_T$ is the comparator path length. The bound holds simultaneously for all sequences and requires no prior knowledge of $S_T$ or $P_T$: it is minimax-optimal (up to logarithmic factors) for tracking piecewise-constant comparators, and also captures frequently moving comparators with small total path length.

</details>


### [127] [Entropy Regularization: A Free Correction to Cross-Entropy for Verified Demonstrations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30572)
*Mihir Dhanakshirur,Adam Ousherovitch,Ambuj Tewari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CE training can misalign with verifier risk in tasks with multiple correct outputs; introduces entropy-regularized cross-entropy (ER-CE) to constrain policy support via token-level entropy, yielding better verifier accuracy on math reasoning and code generation benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard cross-entropy (CE) optimization may yield identical demonstration likelihoods for distinct policies while placing mass on incorrect outputs, which is misaligned with the verifier's acceptance criteria in verifiable domains with multiple valid solutions.

Method: 1) A learning-theoretic counterexample showing CE minimization can select a suboptimal policy. 2) Propose controlling policy support to avoid spreading probability to unsupported outputs. 3) Introduce ER-CE as a tractable proxy using token-level Shannon entropy. 4) Empirical evaluation on mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks comparing CE vs ER-CE.

Result: ER-CE consistently improves verifier accuracy over standard CE across mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, indicating better alignment with producing correct outputs.

Conclusion: Imitation-based post-training in verifiable tasks has a simple failure mode. A practical objective (ER-CE) that regulates output support via entropy improves alignment with verifier correctness.

Abstract: Large language models are often post-trained on expert demonstrations using cross-entropy (CE), even when the downstream objective is not to imitate the demonstrated solution but to produce any output accepted by a verifier. This mismatch is seen in verifiable domains with multiple correct solutions, such as mathematical reasoning and code generation, where training data may contain only one expert solution per problem. We show that minimizing cross-entropy can be misaligned with minimizing verifier risk; two policies can assign identical likelihood to the observed demonstrations while placing different probability mass on incorrect outputs. This is formalized through a learning-theoretic counterexample in which CE minimization selects a suboptimal policy. We identify that controlling the support of the learned policy can solve this problem by preventing probability mass from spreading to unsupported outputs. Since support size is non-differentiable and computationally intractable, we propose entropy-regularized cross-entropy (ER-CE), using token-level Shannon entropy as a tractable proxy. Finally, across mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, we find that entropy-regularized training consistently improves verifier accuracy over standard cross-entropy. Our results identify a simple failure mode of imitation-based post-training in verifiable tasks and provide a practical objective that is better aligned with producing correct outputs.

</details>


### [128] [Reinforcement Learning of Communication in a Mesh of Small Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30578)
*Mehmet Kerem Turkcan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TalkMesh enables collaboration among small language model agents through learned, decentralized communication; gossip-like consensus and confidence-guided hints/revisions improve accuracy beyond self-consistency, but are vulnerable to coordinated poisoning unless defenses are applied.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce reliance on a single large model and improve reasoning accuracy by enabling agents to share key steps; avoid a central coordinator by using a decentralized communication mesh.

Method: A mesh of small LMs each samples a proposal and scores it with a trained confidence head. The most confident agent broadcasts a hint; agents below a threshold revise, keeping revisions that outscore their own proposal. Gossip consensus approximates the weighted vote by confidence without a central coordinator. A talk policy is trained via group relative policy optimization on the change in correctness after revisions. Evaluation scales from 3 to 8 agents, comparing against self-consistency on datasets GSM8K and MATH-500.

Result: With 3 agents (up to 6 outputs) the mesh matches majority voting over 32 samples. With up to 8 agents and 32 evaluations, accuracy rises from 0.568 (self-consistency) to 0.705 on Qwen3.5-0.8B GSM8K and from 0.492 to 0.722 on SmolLM3-3B MATH-500. A 4-of-8 poisoning attack with colluding agents collapses accuracy to 0.000; a defended mesh that re-scores with individual confidence heads maintains 0.507. Across domains, messaging helps when agents lack necessary information and others can supply it.

Conclusion: Decentralized agent communication can boost decision quality in reasoning tasks and control domains, provided defenses against poisoning are in place; the benefit generalizes to tasks where information is distributed and no single agent has full observability.

Abstract: Language models gain accuracy from more compute at test time, but majority voting over independent samples saturates: as samples grow, the vote converges to the model's most frequent answer. Communication can add what sampling cannot: an agent that solves a problem can pass the key step to the others. We present TalkMesh, a decentralized mesh of small language model agents that learns when and what to communicate. Each agent samples a proposal and scores it with a trained confidence head. The most confident agent broadcasts a hint; agents below a confidence threshold revise, keeping each revision that outscores its proposal. Gossip consensus approximates the vote weighted by confidence without a coordinator. A talk policy, trained with group relative policy optimization on the change in correctness after revision, writes hints and revisions. With three agents, which together generate at most six outputs, the mesh reaches the accuracy of majority voting over 32 samples with each of three models. Trained with at most 8 agents and evaluated with 32, it raises accuracy from 0.568 under self-consistency to 0.705 (Qwen3.5-0.8B, GSM8K) and from 0.492 to 0.722 (SmolLM3-3B, MATH-500). When 4 of 8 agents collude on a wrong answer with fabricated confidence and poisoned hints, majority vote accuracy falls to 0.000 (Qwen3.5-0.8B, GSM8K). A defended mesh, whose agents rescore solutions with their own confidence heads, retains 0.507. Across reasoning, embodied coordination, and traffic signal control, messages improve a decision when the acting agent cannot observe the information it requires and another agent can send it.

</details>


### [129] [Energy-efficient operation of neural operators for virtual sensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30580)
*Jason Yoo,Samrendra Roy,Souvik Chakraborty,Syed Bahauddin Alam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Energy savings from computation reuse in virtual sensing are demonstrated, with gains dependent on update frequency and execution lifetime; DeepONet/FNO controls separate reusable arithmetic from launch overhead; prep/artifact costs persist; results link operator structure to energy efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce energy consumption of virtual sensing pipelines for physical fields by exploiting shared spatial computation and repeated inferences on fixed geometries.

Method: Empirical study using a heat-exchanger service. Compare standard compiler freezing and trunk reuse against graph replay and eager execution. Measure energy at different update rates (1/s and 40/s) and in 15 W mode with fixed clocks. Use DeepONet and Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) as controls to separate reusable arithmetic effects from launch overhead; account for preparation, artifact construction, and worker replacement as overheads.

Result: Energy reductions: ~1% at 1 request/s and ~20% at 40 requests/s when using reuse with graph replay vs graph replay? relative to graph replay? The abstract states: 1% at 1/s and 20% at 40/s. In 15 W mode with fixed clocks, reuse with graph replay achieves 22.0–22.5% less energy than eager execution, including prep and waiting. DeepONet/FNO controls help separate reusable arithmetic from launch overhead; prep, artifact construction, and worker replacement add costs outside repeated inference.

Conclusion: Operator structure and update frequency/execution lifetime govern the energy benefits of computation reuse in physical-field virtual sensing. Reuse yields meaningful energy savings at higher update rates; design must consider preparation and launcher overheads to realize full benefits.

Abstract: Virtual sensing repeatedly reconstructs physical fields from changing observations, often on a fixed geometry. We investigate how shared spatial computation reduces the energy of these updates while retaining the selected checkpoint and its evaluated predictions. In a heat-exchanger service, standard compiler freezing and explicit trunk reuse give similar operating energy reductions relative to graph replay: approximately 1% at one request per second and 20% at forty requests per second. In 15 W mode with fixed clocks, reuse with graph replay completes the same request sequence with 22.0 to 22.5% less energy than eager execution, including preparation and waiting. DeepONet and Fourier neural operator (FNO) controls distinguish the effects of reusable arithmetic and launch overhead. Preparation, artifact construction, and worker replacement add costs outside repeated inference. These results connect operator structure to operating energy and show how update frequency and execution lifetime govern the benefit of computation reuse in physical-field virtual sensing.

</details>


### [130] [QSV: Quat-Sphere-Vision for Coupled Quaternion Attention on Spherical Lattices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30592)
*Nicholas Foley,Devin Marinelli,Donny Moore,Diego Enriquez,Amanda Fernandez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A quaternion-based sparse spherical vision model (QSV) replaces the standard projection trio (Q, K, V) with a per-token unit quaternion. The relative quaternion r_{ij} provides both the attention logit (Re(r_{ij})) and a feature transport (x -> r_{ij} ⊗ x ⊗ r_{ij}^*) on sparse kNN graphs on concentric Fibonacci spheres. Ablations show the transport component is essential and geometry helps but does not always outperform standard attention on the same graph. On CIFAR datasets, removing transport hurts accuracy (~4 pp); replacing learned weights with uniform weights has little effect. Parameter-matched controls reveal standard attention on the same graph exceeds QSV, while a flat 2D lattice is competitive but still below the best graph-based attention. Most learned pairwise computation resides in the transport channel.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To unify the attention projection triplet into a single learnable unit (a quaternion per token) and to leverage spherical geometry for sparse attention on graphs, while investigating how much of the computation comes from attention weights versus the transport mechanism.

Method: Use a per-token unit quaternion q_i; define r_{ij} = q_i^* ⊗ q_j as the relative quaternion. The attention logit is Re(r_{ij}) and a message transport is performed as x -> r_{ij} ⊗ x ⊗ r_{ij}^*. Messages are passed on sparse kNN graphs laid on concentric Fibonacci spheres. Ablations include removing the transport term and using uniform attention weights. Parameter-matched controls compare standard attention on the same graph and a flat 2D lattice.

Result: Removing the transport reduces CIFAR-10/100 accuracy by about four percentage points (single CIFAR-100 variant). Replacing learned attention weights with uniform averaging leaves performance essentially unchanged. On a geometry-preserving graph, standard attention outperforms QSV (mean 87.3% vs 85.9%). The same model on a flat 2D lattice reaches 91.1%, within 2.1 points of a ResNet-20 trained in the same pipeline. In the coupled kernel, nearly all learned pairwise computation resides in the transport channel.

Conclusion: The geometry and especially the transport channel dominate the learned pairwise computation in QSV. The transport mechanism encodes most of the learned interactions, while the attention weights contribute less when the geometry and transport are fixed. Geometry provides a meaningful but not always superior alternative to standard attention on the same graph.

Abstract: In standard attention, three separately learned projections decide how strongly a token attends to each neighbor ($W_Q$, $W_K$) and how the attended features are transformed before aggregation ($W_V$). We study Quat-Sphere-Vision (QSV), a sparse spherical vision model that replaces this projection triple with a single learned unit quaternion per token: the relative quaternion $r_{ij} = q_i^{*} \otimes q_j$ supplies both the attention logit $\operatorname{Re}(r_{ij})$ and a sandwich-product feature transport $x \mapsto r_{ij} \otimes x \otimes r_{ij}^{*}$, with messages passed over sparse kNN graphs on concentric Fibonacci spheres. Ablations that change only the targeted component show the two roles to be asymmetric. Removing the transport reduces test accuracy by about four percentage points on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (single runs per CIFAR-100 variant), while replacing the learned attention weights with uniform averaging leaves it essentially unchanged. Parameter-matched controls then remove the geometry itself: standard attention on the same graph exceeds QSV (mean $87.3\%$ vs. $85.9\%$), and the same model on a flat 2D lattice reaches $91.1\%$, within $2.1$ points of a ResNet-20 trained under the same pipeline (single run). In the coupled kernel, nearly all of the learned pairwise computation resides in the transport channel.

</details>


### [131] [Probabilistic Robustness-driven Universal Adversarial Perturbations with Explainability against Deep Reinforcement Learning-based Intrusion Detection System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30605)
*Hongsen Zhang,Lu Zhang,Mingjing Xu,Yi Zhang,Gregory Epiphaniou,Carsten Maple*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a probabilistic robustness (PR) driven universal adversarial perturbation (UAP) against DRL-based IDS, named PX-UAP, with XAI-guided perturbation shaping; shows superior attack effectiveness and provides theoretical analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DRL-based intrusion detection is vulnerable to universal perturbations; PR offers a principled population-level metric aligned with universality, enabling PR-driven UAP generation; aim to craft more effective attacks under domain constraints.

Method: Formulates PR-based UAP objective; develops PX-UAP leveraging explainable AI to shape perturbations under realistic network-domain constraints; provides theoretical reasoning for design.

Result: Extensive experiments show PX-UAP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art UAP methods in attack effectiveness against DRL-based IDS.

Conclusion: Integrating a PR-driven objective and XAI-guided perturbation improves UAP effectiveness; offers a principled framework for evaluating and designing attacks on DRL-based IDS and motivates robust defense research.

Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) enables adaptive intrusion detection in dynamic network environments but also exposes intrusion detection systems (IDS) to adversarial threats such as universal adversarial perturbations (UAPs), which apply a single input-agnostic perturbation to degrade detection performance across traffic. Probabilistic Robustness (PR), as a post-hoc evaluation metric, provides a principled, population-level measure of adversarial impact that conceptually aligns with the universality objective of UAPs, i.e., PR quantifies the prevalence of misclassification in the input space, making it a natural signal for guiding UAP generation. Hence, we propose PR-based UAP, which represents the first integration of an explicit PR-driven objective into generating UAPs against DRL-based IDS. Building on this formulation, we introduce PX-UAP, which leverages explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to guide perturbation shaping under realistic domain constraints, and provides a rigorous theoretical analysis of its design. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PX-UAP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art UAP methods in attack effectiveness.

</details>


### [132] [OpenHail: An Event-Driven Gymnasium Environment for Electric Ride-Hailing Fleet Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30628)
*Tommaso Schettini,Nicholas D. Kullman,Jorge E. Mendoza*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OpenHail is an open-source Gymnasium environment for joint control of electric ride-hailing fleets, enabling RL research with an event-driven simulator that handles requests, vehicle operations, and charging constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide a realistic, flexible simulation platform for training and evaluating reinforcement learning policies for electric ride-hailing fleets, capturing stochastic demand, vehicle dynamics, and capacitated charging.

Method: Design of a fixed-size observation-action interface exposing assignment, repositioning, and charging; an event-driven simulator with pickup deadlines, vehicle queues, battery dynamics, and FIFO charging; configurable decision epochs enabling event-driven, periodic, hybrid, or policy-requested control; includes seeds, feasible-action utilities, evaluators, metrics, and baseline policies; implemented in Gymnasium and released publicly.

Result: A reproducible, modular testbed for evaluating RL policies in electric fleet control; provides evaluation tools and baseline policies; ready for benchmarking and research.

Conclusion: OpenHail offers a versatile, open-source platform that standardizes RL experimentation for joint fleet control under stochastic demand and charging constraints, encouraging rigorous development and comparison of policies.

Abstract: Machine-learning policies have attracted increasing interest for ride-hailing fleet control in recent years. Reinforcement learning, in particular, requires a structured simulation environment that specifies observations, actions, rewards, and decision epochs for training and evaluation. For electric fleets, this environment must also capture the interaction among stochastic demand, vehicle operations, and capacitated charging infrastructure. We present OpenHail, an open-source Gymnasium environment for joint control of electric ride-hailing fleets. Its fixed-size observation--action interface exposes request assignment, repositioning, and charging to a single policy. The event-driven simulator represents requests with pickup deadlines, vehicle job queues, battery dynamics, and finite-capacity charging facilities with first-in--first-out queues. A configurable decision-epoch mechanism separates internal simulator events from policy interactions, supporting event-driven, periodic, hybrid, and policy-requested control within the same operational model. The software provides seeded instances, feasible-action utilities, evaluation tools, operational metrics, and baseline policies. The source code is available at https://github.com/tommaso-schettini/openhail.

</details>


### [133] [Stable initialization without the CLT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30633)
*Simon Kuang,Kyle Chickering,Xinfan Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduce uniform-phase initialization for sine-activated networks to fully decouple layers and avoid distributional approximation errors, achieving improved neural representation performance even without extensive tuning and supporting width scaling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address instability and inter-layer dependencies in deep random networks stemming from classical CLT-based approximations; exploit sine's periodic symmetry to decouple layers and enable stable initialization.

Method: Derive uniform-phase initialization tailored to sine activation functions to eliminate distributional approximation and inter-layer coupling; demonstrate decoupled layer behavior and compare with state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines on image and audio fitting tasks; assess untuned models against tuned baselines and μP width scaling.

Result: Uniform-phase initialization yields improved performance on neural representation tasks, with untuned models competitive with tuned baselines and support for μP width scaling; outperforms prior art in image and audio fitting.

Conclusion: Sine activation's periodic symmetry enables a novel initialization that fully decouples layers, removing distributional approximation errors inherent in CLT-based analyses; this stable, untuned approach can rival tuned methods and scales with width via μP.

Abstract: Successful training of deep neural networks is highly dependent on the distribution of the initial weights. If the weights are too large, network training blows up; if they are too small, the model fails to learn features. Stable initialization is the optimal moderation between these two extremes. The conventional theory of random networks uses the Central Limit Theorem to control inter-neuron dependencies, which introduces distributional approximation error and coupling between layers. For networks with sine activations, we derive the uniform-phase initialization, which obviates distributional approximation and fully decouples the layers. Ours is the first work to use the sine function's periodic symmetry. Models trained with the uniform-phase initialization outperform the state of the art in neural representation tasks like image and audio fitting. We find that our untuned models are competitive with the best-tuned baselines from previous work and support $μ$P width scaling.

</details>


### [134] [In-Context Binding Capacity in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30634)
*Manas Venkata Sai Ravulapalli,Samrath Singh Chadha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Memory recall capacity of language models scales with model size; a load threshold K50 for recall follows K50 = c N^α with α ≈ 0.820 (R^2 = 0.73). Pretraining recipe introduces an eightfold range, but after controlling for scale its effect is small. Interference can lower capacity by reducing single-binding recall. Direct task training can exceed zero-shot predictions, but the measurement criteria complicate claims of capacity gain. Formation times follow a power-law in two codebases, conditional on successes. Overall, the study links capacity to the model's query interface, connecting to working memory and instruction following rather than alignment, and establishes a baseline for testing binding limits and world-state tracking; it does not measure state updates or downstream transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Define and quantify the capacity of language models to maintain correct value bindings (entities to values) during recall tasks, and relate this capacity to model scale, training recipes, interference, and task training, with implications for working memory and instruction following.

Method: Evaluate recall across 12 models ≤3B and a 30-model sweep up to 12B; use continuous recall curves and a threshold sweep; fit a power-law for K50 as a function of model size; analyze effects of pretraining recipe and scale; model interference and its impact on single-binding recall; compare direct task training to zero-shot extrapolation; measure formation times of recall binding across two codebases; derive bounds on joint recall and decompose policy errors; discuss relation to world-state tracking and alignment.

Result: K50 follows K50 = c N^α with α = 0.820 and R^2 = 0.73. Eightfold variation linked to pretraining recipe; after controlling for scale, recipe effect largely undetectable. Interference lowers measured capacity by reducing single-binding recall without changing the load-dependent profile. Direct task training surpasses extrapolated zero-shot predictions, but differing measurement criteria prevent claiming a capacity gain. Formation times exhibit a power-law form across two codebases, conditional on successes. The work bounds joint recall and decomposes policy errors, tying recall capacity to working memory and instruction following; the controlled task provides a baseline for testing binding limits in world-state tracking, though it does not measure state updates or downstream transfer.

Conclusion: Capacity at a model’s query interface can be characterized by a scale-dependent K50 bound with sublinear growth, influenced largely by scale rather than training recipe; interference and binding constraints are central to recall performance and relate to working memory and instruction following. The controlled task establishes a baseline for world-state tracking tests, while acknowledging the measurement does not address state updates or transfer. The framework connects recall to cognitive constructs rather than alignment.

Abstract: How many assignments can a language model recall before it loses track of which value belongs to which entity? We measure this limit using continuous recall curves for 12 models at or below 3B parameters and a threshold sweep over 30 open models up to 12B. On the continuous curves, the load at which recall falls halfway to chance follows $K_{50}=cN^α$, with $α=0.820$ and $R^2=0.73$. The broader sweep shows an eightfold range associated with pretraining recipe, although the continuous curves show no detectable recipe effect after controlling for scale, with few modern models in the fit. We derive why interference can lower measured capacity by reducing single-binding recall even when the load-dependent recall profile is unchanged. Direct task training also exceeds the extrapolated zero-shot law, but different measurement criteria prevent interpreting that comparison as a capacity gain. Its formation times follow a power-law form in two independent codebases, conditional on runs that succeed. Together, these results characterize capacity at the model's query interface. Bounds on joint recall and a decomposition of policy errors connect this measurement to working memory and instruction following, without treating recall as a measure of alignment. The controlled task also provides a baseline for testing whether binding limits constrain world-state tracking; the present experiments do not measure state updates or downstream transfer.

</details>


### [135] [Causal Retention in Interactive Agents: Interface Factorization and Selective Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30650)
*Shengjun Zhang,Tingyi Liu,Dong Xie,Yunlong Dong,Xiang Wang,Cheng Zeng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Task performance need not determine which intervention mechanism an agent retains. We study causal retention: whether a frozen learned state answers a mechanism-probe map fixed independently of training, including action, context, direct target, value, and delay. For finite structural causal model classes, the optimal probe error is a Bayes decision risk. It vanishes exactly when every learning-interface fiber lies within one probe-answer fiber; any state obtained by post-processing that interface inherits the same lower bound. A posterior-coverage theorem characterizes budgeted retesting, while an exact edit decomposition shows that the shifted set is the unique support of an error-free target update. Causal Core implements these conditions through evidence-gated writing, readout filtering, temporal credit, hidden-context setup, and local diagnostic updates. Experiments cover finite causal systems, continuous simulators, an official TD-MPC2 world model, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. A frozen Qwen last-layer probe reaches 0.958 balanced accuracy on source mechanisms but 0.583 on changed delays; the gated mechanism state reaches 1.000 and accepts only 0.056 of synchronized-readout candidates. In TD-MPC2, five target states per actuator recover effect-sign accuracy from 0.057 to 0.948 without degrading stable responses. Causal retention is therefore distinct from task sufficiency and source-domain decodability.

</details>


### [136] [Population loss in shallow ReLU networks: Bias & families of critical points](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30661)
*Michael Field*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A closed-form population loss for biased shallow ReLU student-teacher kernel is derived, extending previous results; the formula relies on Owen's T-function and is complemented by high-precision computations; bias reduces loss and only mildly alters landscape geometry; analysis is currently for equal input and hidden-layer sizes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand how bias affects the loss landscape and spurious minima in shallow ReLU networks within the student-teacher kernel framework, and generalize prior unbiased results to biased networks.

Method: Derivation of a population-loss formula using Owen's T-function; presentation of T-function theory; high-precision MPFR computations for the T-function following Komelj (2023); analysis of spurious-minima families (Arjevani et al.) extended to biased networks; use of analytic geometry tools (analytic/subanalytic sets, Curve Selection Lemma).

Result: Obtains a closed-form population loss formula for biased shallow ReLU student-teacher kernel; demonstrates that spurious minima extend to biased networks and that the loss decreases strictly with the introduction of bias; landscape changes caused by bias are mild; analysis is restricted to the equal-input-equals-neuron setting; includes a review of prior unbiased results.

Conclusion: Biased shallow ReLU student-teacher kernel networks exhibit a comparable loss landscape to the unbiased case, with a consistent bias-induced decrease in loss and only mild geometric changes; the work provides a rigorous, computable framework (via Owen’s T-function and MPFR) and sets the stage for extensions beyond the equal-size setting.

Abstract: The main result presented is a formula for the population loss in the student-teacher kernel model that is applicable to shallow ReLU networks with bias. This extends previous work of Choo and Saul (2009) and Brutzkus and Globerson (2017). The formula makes essential use of Owen's T-function. The necessary theory of the T-function is given and a high precision coding using MPFR for the T-function, based on an algorithm of Komelj (2023), is available on request. It is shown that various families of spurious minima described in past papers of Arjevani and the author extend to biased networks and that the loss is always strictly decreased when bias is added. The change in landscape geometry caused by adding bias appears to be relatively mild. Only the simplest examples are described in this paper where it is assumed that the number of inputs is equal to the number of neurons (this restriction is for reasons of length). A review of relevant previous results on unbiased networks is included. Aside from Gaussian statistics, the main mathematical tools and ideas come from analytic geometry (analytic and subanalytic sets, the Curve Selection Lemma).

</details>


### [137] [PixSim: a calibrated open-source simulator of instant-payment fraud, recovery and interdiction under analyst capacity constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30684)
*Bashir Zeimarani,Alireza Khatib,Somayeh Mousavinasr,Carlos Maurício Serodio Figueiredo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PixSim is an open-source, calibrated simulator of Brazil's Pix irreversible settlement with a regulated recovery mechanism, downstream fund dispersal, and capacity-constrained human review, enabling policy evaluation under multiple scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need to jointly model irreversible settlement, regulated recovery, fund dispersal, and reviewer capacity to assess interdiction effectiveness and policy choices in the Pix system.

Method: PixSim is an open-source simulator calibrated to Banco Central do Brasil data. It models irreversible settlement, a Med-like recovery mechanism, downstream fund dispersal, and a limited, team-based review with a regulatory hold window. Parameters are sourced from public data, published observables, or explicit assumptions. The model is frozen and used for full-scale runs, comparing simulated recovery to observed values and exploring policy variants across a payer-side scorer, four reference policies, and ten scenarios. A mule model is used, with a synthetic scorer achieving AUC 0.82.

Result: Calibration reproduces the 2025 recovery rate within about 0.6 percentage points and decompositions within about 2 percentage points. February–April 2026 is a misfit; May 2026 tracing regime is a projection. Under various policies and staffing, results show: (1) dispersal speed constrains post-settlement recovery; (2) staffing aligned to arrival profile drastically reduces alert expiry from 52% to 2% under a fixed-rule; (3) halving the team eliminates the advantage of a fixed-threshold-and-block rule over a queue-aware rule; (4) a reversal at two-thirds of the team is not consistently supported across seeds; (5) a synthetic scorer with AUC 0.82 reduces lost value by ~25% on average. Code and data are available at the provided DOI.

Conclusion: PixSim provides a transparent, data-calibrated platform to study attack-interdiction dynamics in the Pix system, illustrating how staffing, policy rules, and scoring influence recovery outcomes and lost value. While calibration is strong for 2025 and some 2026 aspects, certain windows (Feb–Apr 2026) show misfit and forward-looking projections depend on assumptions; the approach enables scenario analysis but requires more data for robust external validation and policy guidance.

Abstract: Brazil's Pix settles about 5.9 billion instant, irreversible transfers a month. A fraudulent transfer can be recovered only while the funds remain in a traceable account, and in 2025 the Central Bank's recovery mechanism (MED) returned 9% of accepted contested value. Interdiction therefore has to happen before settlement, by routing each transaction to pass, human review or block, under a finite analyst team and a regulatory hold window. To our knowledge no public simulator jointly models irreversible settlement, a regulated recovery mechanism, downstream fund dispersal and capacity-constrained review. We present PixSim, an open-source simulator of the Pix rail with these elements, calibrated to Banco Central do Brasil open data, with every parameter sourced, calibrated to one published observable, or registered as an assumption. With the model frozen, full-scale runs reproduce the 2025 recovery rate within 0.006 and its decomposition within 0.02; the February-April 2026 window is reported as a misfit and the May 2026 tracing regime as a projection. On a benchmark with a payer-side scorer, four reference policies and ten scenarios, within the simulated mule model: recovery after settlement is constrained by dispersal speed; staffing by the arrival profile cuts a fixed rule's alert expiry from 52% to 2% at constant hours; halving the team removes a fixed threshold-and-block rule's advantage over a queue-aware rule, on loss and on loss plus false-block harm (+0.106 of victim value, positive on all twenty paired seeds), while a reversal at two thirds of the team was not confirmed on independent seeds; and a synthetic scorer of held-out AUC 0.82 cuts lost value by about a quarter. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22948895

</details>


### [138] [LUMO (Lightweight Unified Multilingual Orchestrator): A Privacy Preserving Offline Voice Assistant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30692)
*Md. Mehedi Hasan Naeem,Mst. Kamrunnahar Ruma,Nafiza Anjum,Shakila Sultana,Md. Sujan Ali*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Offline, privacy-preserving multilingual voice assistant (LUMO) for edge devices; uses 4-bit GGUF quantized LLM, local ASR/TTS on Raspberry Pi 5; competitive latency and low power; supports Bangla; enables offline operation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need for reliable, privacy-preserving voice assistants in low-connectivity settings; cloud-based systems raise latency, privacy concerns, and dependency on internet access.

Method: Integrates local ASR, 4-bit GGUF quantized LLM, and offline TTS into a fully offline pipeline on Raspberry Pi 5; evaluates performance (WER, latency, power) and multilingual capability; compares with Mycroft and Rhasspy.

Result: WER 6.8% for short English utterances in low noise; end-to-end latency 2.0-4.0 s; peak power ~9.0 W; effective offline recognition for Bangla; supports multilingual accessibility in low-resource settings; privacy-preserving with no cloud dependency.

Conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of privacy-preserving, offline, multilingual voice assistant on constrained hardware with competitive latency and energy; enables edge deployment in rural/education/healthcare/disaster contexts; reduces cloud reliance.

Abstract: Reliable voice interaction is essential in environments with limited internet connectivity and strong privacy. However, most existing voice assistants depend on cloud-based services, which leads to latency issues, dependency on internet access, and privacy vulnerabilities. This research presents LUMO (Lightweight Unified Multilingual Orchestrator), a privacy preserving offline voice assistant designed for edge computing environments. This system integrates local Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), locally deployed quantized Large Language Model (LLM), and Text-to-Speech (TTS) synthesis into a fully offline pipeline running on a Raspberry Pi 5 with 8 GB RAM.
  To enable efficient operation on resource constrained hardware, the language model is compressed using 4-bit GGUF quantization, which reduces memory usage while preserving practical conversational capability. Existing edge based voice assistants Mycroft provides partial offline functionality without a generative LLM, with an approximate latency of ~5 s and power consumption of ~12 W, while Rhasspy supports full offline operation but lacks generative capabilities, with ~3 s latency and ~11 W power usage. In contrast, LUMO achieves a Word Error Rate (WER) of 6.8% for short English utterances in low noise conditions, an end-to-end response latency of 2.0-4.0 s, and a lower peak power consumption of approximately 9.0 W. The system also achieves effective offline recognition for Bangla speech, supporting multilingual accessibility in low resource settings. By operating entirely offline, LUMO provides strong data privacy, reduced need for cloud connectivity, and suitability for privacy sensitive edge execution such as rural healthcare, education, and disaster response scenarios.

</details>


### [139] [NEMSim: Learning Control-Conditioned Multi-Event Physical Dynamics via Executable Event-Mechanism Priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30718)
*Junsong Yu,Junjie Xie,Pengwei Liu,Dong Ni*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NEMSim integrates executable event-attribute rules into a neural simulator for control-conditioned multi-event systems, using a 3D KMC benchmark; achieves large RMSE reductions and data-efficiency gains, attributed to rule-based prior integration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-fidelity simulation of control-conditioned multi-event systems with discrete events is computationally expensive. Data-driven surrogates struggle to generalize to unseen control regimes; explicit event-rule priors offer a route to better generalization and efficiency.

Method: Compile predefined event-attribute descriptions into an executable transition structure linking control-dependent event intensities, prior-guided mechanism attribution, and state-dependent responses. Develop a 3D KMC-based benchmark with explicit event rules, standardized splits, and evaluation protocols. Evaluate across three settings, with data-efficiency tests down to 10% training data.

Result: Avg RMSE reductions of 58.9%-81.3% relative to the strongest baseline in each setting. Best in data-efficiency study with 10% training data. Mechanism analyses show gains arise from executable rule integration rather than prior access or architecture alone.

Conclusion: Executable integration of event-rule priors yields substantial accuracy and data-efficiency gains; future work could extend rule expressivity, scalability, and interpretability of the mechanism attribution.

Abstract: High-fidelity simulation of control-conditioned multi-event physical systems is computationally expensive, especially across broad control spaces and long trajectories. In these systems, macroscopic evolution emerges from localized discrete events whose intensities and effects depend on process controls and evolving local states, while the available system knowledge is typically expressed as event-attribute descriptions. Purely data-driven surrogates must infer these event effects from limited trajectory coverage, which can hinder generalization to unseen control regimes. Physics-guided methods instead primarily build on equation-level constraints or differentiable solvers rather than discrete event-rule priors. We therefore propose NEMSim (Neural Event-Mechanism Simulator), which compiles predefined event-attribute descriptions into an executable transition structure linking control-dependent event intensities, prior-guided mechanism attribution, and state-dependent responses. To enable evaluation of control-conditioned multi-event dynamics with explicit system knowledge, we construct a 3D KMC-based benchmark pairing high-fidelity trajectories with explicit event rules, standardized splits, and evaluation protocols. Across three settings, NEMSim reduces Avg. RMSE by 58.9%-81.3% relative to the strongest baseline in each setting. It also remains best in the data-efficiency study with training-data fractions down to 10%. Mechanism analyses further show that these gains arise from executable rule integration rather than prior access or architecture alone.

</details>


### [140] [When 10,000 Windows Are Not 10,000 Tests: Auditing Statistical Confidence in Sliding-Window Time-Series Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30721)
*Xinze Shi,Litian Zhang,Binrui Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Auditing sliding-window evaluations under overlap using dependence-robust inference reveals substantial miscalibration and informative loss; proposes an audit workflow to separate added predictions from added evidence across observed, future, and unseen subjects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mitigate leakage and dependence among overlapping test windows in subject-disjoint evaluations; provide explicit aggregation rules and robust inference across data-splits.

Method: Map three claims to aggregation rules; run controlled simulations at various overlap; apply Bartlett-HAC; audit frozen WISDM and HARTH predictions; compare information growth vs test rows; report interval widths and inclusion of zero; implement independent recomputation and calibration seeds.

Result: Type-I error: 16.9% IID observed-record; 7.2% session-centered; fourfold increase in test rows yields only 1.75-1.94x information; paired Accuracy-diff intervals inflated by 1.22-1.66x; zero-overlap case not universal; HARTH shows zero included in Accuracy-diff intervals across overlaps; Macro-F1 vs MiniROCKET rankings vary.

Conclusion: The audit workflow makes predictions vs evidence separable and auditable; independent recomputation and calibration improve interpretability; results suggest dependence-robust inference is essential for sliding-window benchmarks.

Abstract: Sliding-window classifiers are often evaluated on thousands of overlapping test windows, even though neighboring predictions share observations and remain nested within recordings and subjects. Subject-disjoint evaluation prevents one form of leakage but does not make those test windows independent. We present a practical audit that maps three claims - performance on observed recordings, future recordings from observed subjects, and unseen subjects - to explicit aggregation rules and established dependence-robust inference. At 75% overlap, controlled simulations give 16.9% Type-I error for IID observed-record inference and 7.2% for session-centered Bartlett-HAC: a substantial improvement with residual miscalibration. Audits of frozen WISDM and HARTH predictions show that nearly fourfold growth in test rows yields only 1.75-1.94-fold variance-equivalent information growth. At that overlap, fixed-record paired Accuracy-difference intervals are 1.22-1.66 times the IID widths; this inflation is not universal at zero overlap. On HARTH, paired Accuracy-difference intervals include zero across three overlap settings, whereas Macro-F1 favors MiniROCKET. Independent recomputation, common-session checks, class-level results, and separately seeded calibration make the audit's scope and limitations inspectable. The resulting workflow distinguishes additional predictions from additional independent evidence.

</details>


### [141] [Mechanism-Aware Ensemble Conditioning for Data-Limited Emulation of Extreme Events](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30746)
*Isabella S. Thiel,Juan Bello-Rivas,Yannis G. Kevrekidis,Themistoklis P. Sapsis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A mechanism-aware conditioning framework uses ensemble geometry as a Jacobian-free proxy to inject local instability information via FiLM into a backbone model, improving rare-event emulation in chaotic systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extreme events in chaotic systems stem from transient finite-time instability; learning from short trajectories is hard because bulk dynamics miss rare-event drivers.

Method: Compute ensemble covariance from a nudged coarse ensemble to proxy local amplification (Jacobians) without explicit Jacobians. Inject this geometry via a small FiLM module into a backbone predictor (Transformer-style residual-attention corrector or FiLM-STORN corrector). Demonstrated on a low-dimensional chaotic system and a topographic quasi-geostrophic (QG) flow; a fixed ensemble trained on limited data substantially improves long-horizon rare-event statistics.

Result: Low-dimensional case: FiLM conditioning aligns ensemble directions with OTD modes and reduces 99th-percentile exceedance errors versus a context-free Transformer baseline. QG case: with only 50 time units of training, ensemble-conditioned FiLM-STORN markedly improves long-horizon rare-event statistics (density tails, exceedance frequencies, spatial exceedance-area distributions) compared to an unconditioned STORN trained on the same data; even surpasses a baseline STORN trained on 20x more high-resolution data.

Conclusion: Local instability geometry is not only interpretable post hoc but can be used as an actionable conditioning signal to enable data-efficient rare-event emulation across different backbone architectures.

Abstract: Extreme events in chaotic systems are difficult to learn from short trajectories because they are controlled by transient finite-time instability rather than by frequently observed bulk dynamics. We propose a mechanism-aware conditioning plug-in framework that turns a nudged coarse ensemble into a non-intrusive sensor of local instability geometry. In the small-noise regime, the ensemble covariance aggregates the same finite-time deformation kernels that govern local instability, providing a Jacobian-free proxy for the local amplification structure around a synchronized coarse trajectory. A small FiLM module injects statistics of this ensemble geometry into an otherwise unchanged backbone while leaving the coarse simulator unchanged. We demonstrate this interface in two distinct pipelines: a Transformer-style residual-attention corrector for a controlled low-dimensional chaotic system and a probabilistic recurrent STORN corrector for topographic two-layer quasi-geostrophic (QG) flow. In the low-dimensional benchmark, ensemble covariance directions co-activate with OTD modes and FiLM conditioning improves 99th-percentile exceedance-frequency errors over an identical no-context Transformer baseline. In QG, a fixed ensemble-conditioned FiLM-STORN model trained on only \(50\) time units substantially improves long-horizon rare-event statistics in the data-limited regime, including density-tail errors, exceedance frequencies, and spatial exceedance-area distributions relative to an unconditioned STORN trained on the same data; on averaged high-threshold exceedance diagnostics, it also outperforms the baseline STORN trained with $20$ times more high-resolution data. These results show that local instability geometry is not merely interpretable post hoc, but an actionable conditioning signal for data-efficient rare-event emulation.

</details>


### [142] [Differentiable RNA Secondary Structure Extraction for Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30752)
*Tyler Illman,Max Ward,Marcell Szikszai,Ryan K. Krueger*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Examines training-extraction congruence in RNA secondary structure prediction from base-pair weight matrices; finds that a differentiable symmetric doubly stochastic matrix (SDSM) normalization yields strongest performance and can bypass traditional extraction steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Structure extraction from weight matrices is an ad hoc, critical step in RNA structure prediction; improving alignment between training and extraction could improve accuracy and consistency.

Method: Compare four extraction algorithms (Nussinov-like DP, maximum-weight graph matching, SPOT-RNA greedy, RiNALMo greedy) using outputs from the RiNALMo model and three toy models (differentiable Nussinov-like, BCE baseline, SDSM-normalized model). The SDSM approach outputs base-pairing probability matrices directly and is differentiable, allowing inline training/evaluation.

Result: Performance depends on training-extraction congruence. The SDSM model shows the strongest overall performance, outperforming the BCE baseline under all four extraction methods and producing pre-extraction outputs closest to ground truth.

Conclusion: Aligning training with the intended extraction method improves predictive accuracy; the SDSM normalization provides a tractable, differentiable alternative to conventional structure extraction that can be integrated into training pipelines.

Abstract: Many deep learning approaches to RNA secondary structure prediction have recently been proposed. They typically output a weight matrix $W$ where $W_{ij}$ is an arbitrary weight for base $i$ pairing with base $j$. Converting this matrix to a predicted secondary structure or base-pairing probability matrix typically involves ad hoc and problematic downstream algorithms. Despite the importance of this conversion step, which we refer to as structure extraction, it has received relatively little attention in the literature. In this work, we analyze how the congruence between training and extraction methods affects prediction performance. To do this, we compare four extraction algorithms: a Nussinov-like dynamic programming method, maximum-weight graph matching and the greedy extraction algorithms used by SPOT-RNA and RiNALMo. These are evaluated on outputs from the pretrained RiNALMo model and three toy models trained in this paper: a differentiable Nussinov-like model, a binary cross-entropy (BCE) baseline, and a model that incorporates a novel symmetric doubly stochastic matrix (SDSM) normalization algorithm during training which allows it to output base-pairing probability matrices directly, without a separate extraction step. This SDSM normalization algorithm is differentiable and can be added inline to any deep learning model during training and evaluation. We find that the performance of each extraction method depends strongly on how the corresponding model was trained. Considering the toy models themselves, the SDSM model showed the strongest overall performance: it outperformed the BCE baseline under all four extraction algorithms and produced pre-extraction outputs closest to the ground truth. These results suggest that SDSM normalization is a tractable alternative to traditional structure extraction.

</details>


### [143] [Missingness-Aware Conformal Prediction Under Cross-Hospital Distribution Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30781)
*Liang You,Dongwen Ou,Hengyu Shi,Siyuan Dai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Missingness-aware conformal calibration for cross-hospital mortality prediction reduces worst-group calibration gaps relative to pooled calibration, but benefits are not uniform and pooling can misrepresent within-hospital performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hospitals exhibit different missingness patterns; marginal calibration does not guarantee coverage within groups defined by missingness; addressing distribution shift and fairness in clinical calibration is needed.

Method: Select a measurement on an independent sample, split patients by whether that measurement is recorded, and apply Mondrian calibration within each group; do not reuse calibration outcomes; evaluate across eICU hospitals and across care units in one MIMIC-IV hospital using three predictors.

Result: Reduces the average worst-group coverage gap on the selected groups relative to pooled calibration, with a median reduction of 1.9 percentage points; five of six paired site-bootstrap intervals exclude zero; gains are not uniform across settings or predictors; hospital-level decomposition explains discrepancies: pooling reweights hospitals via covariance between group shares and coverage errors and can allow opposing-error cancellation; within-hospital vs pooled evaluations can rank methods differently even without sampling noise.

Conclusion: Pooling improvement does not guarantee better within-hospital coverage; calibration groups fixed; missingness-aware calibration shows promise but must be evaluated within hospitals; decisions based solely on pooled calibration can be misleading.

Abstract: Clinical measurements are recorded for some patients but not others, at rates that differ across hospitals, and marginal conformal coverage does not ensure coverage within groups defined by missingness. We propose a missingness-aware conformal calibration procedure for mortality prediction under cross-hospital distribution shift. It selects a measurement on an independent sample, groups patients by whether that measurement is recorded, and applies Mondrian calibration within each group, so no calibration outcome is reused. We evaluate the procedure across hospitals in eICU and across care units within one MIMIC-IV hospital, using three predictors. Relative to pooled calibration, it reduces the average worst-group coverage gap on its selected groups in all six settings, with a median reduction of 1.9 percentage points; paired site-bootstrap intervals exclude zero in five. These gains do not extend uniformly. Calibration by predicted risk achieves smaller gaps on a broader panel of missingness groups, and when eICU hospitals are evaluated separately, the gain shrinks for all three predictors and reverses in sign for one. We explain this discrepancy with a hospital-level decomposition. Pooling reweights hospitals through a covariance between group shares and coverage errors, and lets errors of opposite sign cancel: weighting explains the reversal, and cancellation accounts for most of the attenuation for the other two predictors. Constructed population distributions show that pooled and within-hospital evaluations can rank calibration methods oppositely even without sampling noise. Pooled improvement alone therefore cannot establish better coverage within hospitals, even when the calibration groups are fixed.

</details>


### [144] [Interpretable-by-Design Descriptor Portfolios Match a 2048-Dimensional Foundation Embedding on Low-Data Molecular Assays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30789)
*Yiqi Yao,Miquel Duran-Frigola*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A compact, auditable descriptor portfolio nearly matches a 2048‑D CheMeleon embedding on ADME/Tox tasks, achieving mean AUC close to CheMeleon while preserving per‑feature provenance; parity holds at the pooled level but not for all individual assays.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether lean, semantically named descriptor blocks with provenance auditing can reach high-dimensional embedding accuracy while enabling feature-level auditability; benchmark against CheMeleon and Mordred across multiple ADME/Tox assays and evaluation cells.

Method: Start from an 11‑dim physicochemical base; greedily concatenate provenance-screened descriptor blocks using labelled context alone; evaluate across nine ADME/Tox assays and 50 evaluation cells restricted to molecules covered by all representations; compare mean AUC to CheMeleon (0.764) and Mordred (0.756); test pooled parity gate and per‑assay gate; vary context labels (25 or 10); test predeclared candidate-selection rules; perform post-freeze checks on ten seeds and three unseen assays; include a same-width random-bundle control.

Result: Mean test AUC = 0.762; CheMeleon = 0.764; Mordred = 0.756; pooled gap to CheMeleon = +0.003 AUC (task-bootstrap 95% CI [−0.020, +0.030]), satisfying the pooled parity gate but not the per‑assay gate; at 25 context labels the pooled gate is satisfied, at 10 labels it is not; four predeclared candidate-selection rules were falsified; post-freeze checks across ten seeds and three unseen assays support pooled competitiveness; a random-bundle control does not demonstrate that greedy membership adds accuracy; assay-level differences remain unresolved.
