Conclusion: Compact, auditable descriptor representations can approach the accuracy of a 2048‑D CheMeleon embedding on aggregate ADME/Tox tasks, indicating potential for interpretable, provenance-traceable models; however, consistent per‑assay parity is not achieved, and further work is needed to resolve assay-level differences and validate selection rules.

Abstract: In low-data structure-activity prediction, the choice of molecular representation can matter more than the choice of predictor, and tabular foundation models sharpen that effect. We ask whether a portfolio of compact, semantically named descriptor blocks can reach the accuracy of a 2048-dimensional CheMeleon embedding while staying auditable at the feature level, meaning that every input dimension carries a model name and a recorded training provenance. Starting from a fixed 11-dimensional physicochemical base, we greedily concatenate provenance-screened blocks using the labelled context alone. Across nine ADME/Tox assays and 50 evaluation cells, scored on common-coverage subsets restricted to the molecules that every representation covers, the portfolio reaches a mean test AUC of 0.762, against 0.764 for CheMeleon and 0.756 for Mordred. The pooled gap to CheMeleon is +0.003 AUC (task-bootstrap 95% CI [-0.020, +0.030]), which satisfies our predeclared pooled parity gate but not the per-assay gate. At 25 context labels the headline rule again satisfies the pooled gate; at 10 labels it does not. We also report four predeclared candidate-selection rules that we falsified. Post-freeze checks over ten seeds and three previously unseen assays support pooled competitiveness for compact, auditable representations; a same-width random-bundle control does not establish that greedy membership itself adds accuracy. Assay-level differences remain unresolved.

</details>


### [145] [Towards Universal Representation-Based Process Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30790)
*Jinmyeong Choi,Taesup Kim,Artur Dubrawski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A nonparametric, reference-based window-level monitoring framework for time series that uses pretrained encoders, kernel density estimation, and conformal calibration to draw finite-sample valid inferences in a learned representation space, with nulls defined by empirical reference distributions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical parametric tests restrict flexibility for window-level monitoring; an empirical-reference, representation-based approach enables robust, data-driven decision rules and broad applicability to time-series process control.

Method: Map windows into a learned representation via pretrained time-series encoders; estimate the reference distribution in the representation space using kernel density estimation; apply conformal calibration to obtain finite-sample valid p-values under the empirical reference null; treat the null as the empirical reference set and perform hypothesis testing.

Result: Experiments show sensitivity to distributional deviations in window-level statistics while maintaining well-calibrated inference under stable reference regimes; demonstrates applicability to a broad class of time-series process control and monitoring tasks; links to stationarity/cyclostationarity as natural instantiations of empirical reference sets.

Conclusion: A flexible, nonparametric framework unifying window-level process control with empirical-reference hypothesis testing in learned representations; enables robust detection of distributional shifts while preserving valid inference under reference stability, broadening the scope of time-series monitoring tasks.

Abstract: Many temporal process learning and monitoring pipelines operate in local windows, making window-level decisions unavoidable in practice. In such settings, classical statistical tests can be applied to individual windows, but they typically evaluate predefined parametric hypotheses-such as unit-root or moment-based conditions-thereby limiting flexibility when reference behavior is defined empirically from task- or domain-specific data. In this work, we view window-level monitoring as a process control problem and reformulate it as reference-based hypothesis testing, where the null hypothesis is specified by an empirical reference distribution rather than a fixed parametric model. We operationalize this perspective through a representation-based, nonparametric framework that combines pretrained time series encoders, kernel density estimation, and conformal calibration, yielding finite-sample valid inference in learned representation space. Classical notions such as stationarity and cyclostationarity arise as natural instantiations of empirical reference sets within this framework. Through experiments, we demonstrate sensitivity to window-level distributional deviations while maintaining well-calibrated inference under stable reference regimes, highlighting the applicability of the proposed approach to a broad class of time series process control and monitoring tasks.

</details>


### [146] [Counterfactual Online Conformal Prediction Under Adaptive Logging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30811)
*Xinyu Qiao,Yichen Lin,Kaihong Ji,Xue Wang,Tao Yao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces Propensity-Weighted Online Conformal Prediction (PW-OCP) and a doubly robust variant (DR-OCP) to fix counterfactual coverage failures in online conformal prediction when actions influence outcomes. The methods provide near-optimal coverage under positivity, improve counterfactual calibration and downstream regret without sacrificing set sharpness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Online conformal prediction can fail to provide valid counterfactual coverage when predictions influence actions and rare actions bias which outcomes are observed. There is a need for debiased calibration that yields correct counterfactual coverage under adaptive data collection.

Method: Propose an inverse-propensity-weighted recursion to debias calibration (PW-OCP). Introduce a doubly robust variant that combines an outcome model with propensity weights to further reduce nuisance bias.

Result: Under a positivity assumption, the resulting coverage matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Empirically, PW-OCP and DR-OCP improve counterfactual coverage and downstream regret on synthetic decision tasks, open-bandit data, and financial rebalancing, while preserving prediction-set sharpness.

Conclusion: PW-OCP and DR-OCP provide robust, well-calibrated counterfactual coverage in online decision settings with action-dependent outcomes, supported by theoretical guarantees and empirical gains.

Abstract: Online conformal prediction can fail when predictions shape actions and actions determine which outcomes enter calibration. Standard adaptive methods may retain marginal coverage while systematically miscovering the counterfactual outcomes of rarely selected actions. This paper formalizes the failure through counterfactual coverage and introduces Propensity-Weighted Online Conformal Prediction, an inverse-propensity-weighted recursion that debiases calibration. A doubly robust variant further reduces nuisance bias to the product of outcome-model and propensity errors. Under positivity, the resulting coverage rate matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Experiments on synthetic decision tasks, open bandit data, and financial rebalancing show that PW-OCP and DR-OCP improve counterfactual coverage and downstream regret without sacrificing prediction-set sharpness.

</details>


### [147] [Learning Provable Neural Network Observer for Uncertain Dynamical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30819)
*Zhangyi Wang,Jiaxu Liu,Chen Song,Chao Xu,Shengze Cai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Two-stage training for provably stable neural network observers that decouples Lyapunov stability certification from global training. Stage 1 pre-trains with point-guided Lyapunov estimates for local stability; Stage 2 uses LMI-based fine-tuning to enforce a global Lyapunov certificate. The approach aims to overcome LMI scalability bottlenecks, with theoretical guarantees on local stability radii and probabilistic coverage, and empirical validation shows faster training and robust generalization. Code available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Certifying Lyapunov stability for neural network observers via LMIs yields large-scale SDPs that do not scale well with network size. There is a need for scalable, provably stable observer training that preserves estimation accuracy across disturbances and uncertainties.

Method: A two-stage training framework: (1) point-guided Lyapunov pre-training to achieve high estimation accuracy and local stability over sampled states; (2) LMI-based fine-tuning to satisfy a strict global Lyapunov stability certificate. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for local stability radii and probabilistic coverage over a prescribed compact error-domain under regularity and sampling assumptions.

Result: Demonstrates significantly faster training than direct LMI-based methods and robust generalization across diverse systems (nonlinear benchmarks and X-29 aircraft ablations). Achieves improved tracking accuracy over observer baselines.

Conclusion: The framework offers a scalable approach to certifiably stable neural network observers, combining data-driven pre-training with formal LMI-based stability guarantees, validated by theory and experiments; code is publicly available.

Abstract: In many safety-critical applications, control of uncertain dynamical systems relies on observers that estimate states and external disturbances. Neural network observers can improve estimation accuracy, but certifying their Lyapunov stability via Linear Matrix Inequality (LMI) constraints leads to large-scale semidefinite programs (SDPs) that are difficult to solve for large networks. To overcome this scalability bottleneck, we propose a novel two-stage training framework for provably stable neural network observers. Our approach decouples the optimization into a point-guided Lyapunov pre-training phase, which rapidly achieves high estimation accuracy and local stability over sampled states, followed by an LMI fine-tuning phase that efficiently satisfies a strict global Lyapunov stability certificate. We provide formal theoretical guarantees for local stability radii and probabilistic coverage over a prescribed compact error-state domain under specified regularity and sampling assumptions. Experiments on nonlinear control benchmarks and X-29 aircraft ablations show that our LMI-certified neural network observers train significantly faster than direct LMI-based methods and generalize robustly across diverse systems, achieving improved tracking accuracy over a range of observer baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/Berry-Myon/LearningNeuralNetworkObserver.

</details>


### [148] [Quantizing Looped Transformers: Feedback Exposure and Calibration Blindness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30820)
*Nux Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Two PTQ failure modes in looped models: 1) feedback exposure where hashed quantization perturbs recurrent state lacking an identity path, and 2) calibration blindness where one-step Hessian-based GPTQ ignores later recurrence directions. Across multiple looped architectures, one-step GPTQ underperforms RTN, while accumulating GPTQ Hessians across steps recovers bf16-level accuracy on Huginn, clarifying when and what to calibrate in looped models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Looped transformers reuse weights across recurrence steps, making low-bit quantization attractive but prone to unique failure modes. The work aims to disentangle where quantization errors enter the recurrence and which states the calibration method actually uses, to guide PTQ design for looped architectures.

Method: Empirical study across HuggingFace Huginn-3.5B and other looped architectures. Evaluate per-channel INT4 PTQ, identifying failure at non-residual loop-entry adapters vs residual cores. Extend experiments to linear filters and Mamba state-space models to show feedback exposure outside transformers. Analyze calibration blindness via a one-step GPTQ baseline that builds a Hessian from step-0 activations and neglects later recurrence input directions. Compare nine checkpoints from seven looped architectures. Test grouped INT4 and accumulate GPTQ Hessians across recurrence steps; compare against one-step GPTQ and RTN.

Result: Identified two distinct PTQ failure modes for looped models: 1) feedback exposure (quantized layer perturbs recurrent state without an identity path, impacting later steps) and 2) calibration blindness (one-step GPTQ Hessian misses directions used later in recurrence). One-step GPTQ underperforms RTN on most checkpoints; accumulating the GPTQ Hessian across steps yields better accuracy than both baselines on all nine checkpoints, achieving bf16-level accuracy on Huginn. Demonstrates that PTQ for looped models should separately consider where error enters the recurrence and which states calibrators observe.

Conclusion: PTQ for looped models must address two orthogonal aspects: the entry point of quantization error in the recurrence and the set of states visible to calibration. Accumulating curvature information across recurrence steps and using grouped quantization mitigate both failure modes, enabling bf16-level accuracy on challenging looped architectures and clarifying PTQ design principles for recurrent models.

Abstract: Looped transformers reuse weights across recurrence steps, making low-bit quantization especially attractive. We identify two distinct failure modes of standard post-training quantization. On Huginn-3.5B, per-channel INT4 fails primarily at the non-residual loop-entry adapter, while quantizing the residual core is much less damaging. We call this feedback exposure: a quantized layer perturbs the recurrent state without an identity path, and the resulting error is fed back at later steps. Controlled experiments on linear filters and Mamba state-space models show that feedback exposure also occurs outside transformers. Grouped INT4 reveals a separate failure, calibration blindness: our one-step GPTQ baseline builds its Hessian from step-0 activations, leaving input directions used later in the recurrence nearly unweighted. Across nine checkpoints from seven looped architectures, one-step GPTQ is worse than round-to-nearest (RTN) on the primary task metric for five checkpoints. Accumulating the GPTQ Hessian across recurrence steps outperforms both one-step GPTQ and RTN on all nine checkpoints and recovers bf16-level accuracy on Huginn. These results separate two questions for PTQ on looped models: where quantization error enters the recurrence, and which states calibration sees.

</details>


### [149] [Adaptive Interaction Graphs for Particle Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30822)
*Aiden Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adaptive graphs via per-particle uncertainty improves long-horizon accuracy in learned particle simulators; yields Pareto gains, especially where spatial complexity concentrates (WaterDrop), with modest gains elsewhere (Sand).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed interaction topology (kNN or static radius) in learned particle simulators causes error accumulation; enabling adaptive neighborhoods guided by particle uncertainty aims to allocate modeling capacity where needed.

Method: Train a per-particle variance head alongside the acceleration head using a heteroscedastic Gaussian NLL loss. Use the previous step's uncertainty to adapt the particle's neighborhood dynamically, expanding the neighborhood for high-uncertainty particles. The variance head learns meaningful uncertainty (high variance near splash zones/free surfaces). The adaptation is integrated with the GNS framework (AdaptGNS); evaluation on WaterDrop and Sand. Code at the provided GitHub.

Result: Achieves a strict Pareto improvement on WaterDrop and a modest gain on Sand, indicating adaptive graphs outperform fixed topology where complexity is spatially localized.

Conclusion: Adaptive graphs are particularly beneficial when runtime complexity is concentrated in space, enabling improved long-horizon accuracy with minor inference overhead.

Abstract: Learned particle simulators based on graph neural networks achieve strong one-step accuracy, but errors compound over long horizons. An underexplored variable is the interaction graph: existing methods fix its topology via k-nearest neighbors or a static radius rule, regardless of local model confidence. We propose making this graph adaptive: a per-particle variance head, trained jointly with the acceleration head under a heteroscedastic Gaussian NLL loss, drives a trajectory in which high-uncertainty particles receive an expanded neighborhood. This is done at little extra inference cost by using the previous step's uncertainty estimate. A key discovery is that the variance head learns a meaningful notion of uncertainty: high-variance particles concentrate near complex regions, such as splash zones or free surfaces. When this signal drives graph topology, the resulting AdaptGNS simulator achieves a strict Pareto improvement on WaterDrop and a modest gain on Sand. Given the model's stronger performance on WaterDrop, we hypothesize that adaptive graphs are most useful when complexity is concentrated in space. Our code can be found at https://github.com/aidenzhou8/AdaptGNS.

</details>


### [150] [MOPD-Router: Rethinking Teacher Routing in Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30837)
*Tianze Xu,Yanzhao Zheng,Zhentao Zhang,Yuanqiang Yu,Chao Ma,Jihuai Zhu,Lelun Wu,Lyumanshan Ye,Pengfei Liu,Baohua Dong,Hangcheng Zhu,Ruohui Huang,Gang Yu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MOPD-Router enables token-level routing among multiple domain-specialized teachers without prompt-domain labels, using ExpertAlign and alternative metrics to weight signals; yields consistent gains across unlabeled and domain-labeled data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To remove the dependency on prompt-level domain labels in multi-teacher on-policy distillation and to leverage cross-teacher signals from unlabeled mixtures.

Method: Introduce MOPD-Router with a plug-in interface for selecting and weighting teacher OPD signals; propose ExpertAlign scoring based on whether a teacher’s token-level corrections align with the teacher’s post-training specialization, and compare against Entropy and Novelty baselines.

Result: ExpertAlign achieves the strongest performance across four settings (unlabeled and domain-labeled mixtures; strong-to-weak and same-size distillation). On unlabeled data, +5.88 points (+12.3%) over Mean aggregation; on domain-labeled data, +3.95 points (+7.8%) over standard MOPD. Code is released.

Conclusion: Token-level routing enables exploitation of cross-domain complementary supervision and reduces reliance on prompt-level domain assignments.

Abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates specialized capabilities into a single student, but existing practice typically hard-routes each prompt to a domain-matched teacher for the entire rollout. This dependence on prompt-level domain labels restricts using unlabeled training mixtures and leaves complementary signals from other teachers unused. We introduce MOPD-Router, a framework that routes supervision over the full teacher pool at each token, without domain labels or training a separate routing model. Its plug-in interface supports different metrics for selecting and weighting teacher-specific OPD signals. Within this interface, we propose ExpertAlign, which scores each teacher by whether its correction to the student at the current token expresses the specialization that teacher acquired during post-training, and compare it against two reference metrics built on teacher confidence (Entropy) and teacher-student discrepancy (Novelty). Experiments on unlabeled and domain-labeled training mixtures under strong-to-weak and same-size distillation scenarios show that ExpertAlign achieves the strongest overall performance in all four settings. On unlabeled data, it improves the overall score by 5.88 (+12.3%) points over Mean aggregation; on domain-labeled data, it outperforms standard MOPD by 3.95 (+7.8%) points without using available domain labels. These results demonstrate token-level routing can exploit cross-domain complementary supervision, and reduce exclusive reliance on prompt-level domain assignment. Code is available at: https://github.com/TURLEing/MOPD-Router.

</details>


### [151] [Peer-Grounded Counterfactual Path Planning for Chronic Health Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30838)
*Saman Khamesian,Hassan Ghasemzadeh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: POROS constructs a Behavioral Progression Graph to decompose monotone, peer-supported health improvements into minimal, incremental steps; it uses minimum-cost paths to guide behavior change, and is validated in two diabetes cohorts showing large reductions in per-step gain and high social-boundary crossing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Counterfactual explanations that imply a direct target state lack a feasible route and may require non-monotone progress; there is a need for actionable, monotone guidance grounded in social learning theory.

Method: Build a directed acyclic graph over observed patient states where edges encode both peer-grounded behavioral proximity and strict health-improvement; edges correspond to single-period, achievable changes. Find minimum-cost paths to bridge gaps. Framework is domain-agnostic and grounded in Bandura's self-efficacy and Festinger's social comparison theories. Evaluate on two diabetes cohorts.

Result: In patients below 70% TIR, the mean required per-step gain drops from 26.3 pp to 5.5 pp (cohort 1) and from 31.1 pp to 5.7 pp (cohort 2). Across cohorts, 97–98% of multi-hop paths cross patient boundaries, embedding social comparison into the progression.

Conclusion: POROS effectively decomposes large behavioral gaps into incremental, peer-grounded steps, enhancing self-efficacy and feasibility of behavior change; demonstrated performance in two diabetes cohorts suggests promise for domain-agnostic chronic-disease guidance, with potential for broader application and further validation.

Abstract: Effective behavioral intervention in chronic disease management requires not a single prescription but a sequence of incremental steps, each grounded in what real, similar individuals have demonstrably achieved. Counterfactual explanation offers a natural computational route to such guidance, answering what change in behavior would have produced a better outcome. But existing methods return a target state without a route to it, guarantee no monotone health improvement along the way, and draw no evidence from peer behavior -- asking a patient to close a wide gap in one move, which is precisely the recommendation structure least likely to be attempted. We propose POROS (Peer-Grounded Optimal Routes Over States), a domain-agnostic framework rooted in Bandura's self-efficacy theory and Festinger's social comparison theory that constructs a Behavioral Progression Graph -- a directed acyclic graph over observed patient states in which every edge requires both peer-grounded behavioral proximity and strict health outcome improvement. Every edge is therefore a behavioral change that individuals in the cohort have demonstrated is achievable within a single period. Minimum-cost paths through this graph decompose otherwise inactionable behavioral gaps into incremental, peer-grounded steps. We evaluate POROS on two independent longitudinal cohorts of patients with diabetes. For patients below the 70% clinical threshold for time in range (TIR, blood glucose within 70-180 mg/dL), it reduces the mean gain required per step from 26.3 percentage points (pp) to 5.5 pp on one cohort and from 31.1 pp to 5.7 pp on the other, decomposing large behavioral jumps into the incremental steps that self-efficacy requires. Across both cohorts, 97-98% of multi-hop paths cross patient boundaries, embedding social comparison by construction.

</details>


### [152] [Attention-Based Adaptive Policies for Simultaneous Speech-to-Text Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30839)
*Filip Tăşădan,Ema Tomanová,Ondrej Lopuch,Paweł Bilko,Anders Søgaard*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Cross-attention based policies RFAP and DCAP enable streaming S2TT with offline-trained models, improving latency-quality trade-offs without extra training; RFAP yields up to 4.0 BLEU and ~1s latency reduction; DCAP maintains quality at very low latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Alleviate the latency-accuracy trade-off in simultaneous speech-to-text translation by deciding optimal translation emission moments using attention alignments, reusing offline models without retraining.

Method: Introduce RFAP and DCAP that leverage the encoder-decoder cross-attention to align input speech frames with target tokens. They operate in streaming mode without additional training; RFAP uses recent frame attention; DCAP uses dual conditions to govern emission.

Result: Empirical evaluation on CVSS-C corpus across three language pairs shows RFAP outperforms other policies with up to 4.0 BLEU improvement and ~1-second delay reduction; DCAP maintains high translation quality at very low latency.

Conclusion: RFAP and DCAP demonstrate effective, training-free adaptation of offline S2TT models to streaming settings, achieving favorable latency-quality trade-offs; potential for broader applicability and further refinement.

Abstract: Simultaneous speech-to-text translation (Simul-S2TT) consists of generating partial translations while the incoming audio frames are processed by the system. However, the streaming nature of this setup creates the challenge of deciding the best moment to perform an accurate translation while minimizing the delay. To address this challenge, we utilize the cross-attention mechanism of the encoder-decoder architecture to find the right alignment between the input speech frames and the target text tokens. In this paper, we propose the Recent Frame Attention Policy (RFAP) and the Dual-Condition Attention Policy (DCAP) that allow offline trained speech-to-text translation models to be used in streaming scenarios without requiring additional training. Results on three different language translation pairs over the CVSS-C corpus show that the RFAP is able to surpass other policies with gains of up to 4.0 BLEU while reducing the translation delay by almost 1 second. Moreover, the DCAP is able to preserve a high translation quality when the latency is very low.

</details>


### [153] [Aligning One-Step Generative Models with Reward-Weighted Transport Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30840)
*Austin Wang,Ziheng Cheng,Lexing Ying*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RWTD is a post-training method for one-step generators that uses reward-weighted transport distillation to adapt models using only generated samples and scalar rewards. It blends tilted current and reference distributions via feature-space optimal transport and fixed-point regression, balancing reward adaptation with retention of prior knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training for implicit one-step generators lacks tractable likelihoods and differentiable rewards; there is a need to adapt to rewards while preserving pretrained capabilities, circumventing non-differentiable rewards and poor likelihoods.

Method: RWTD constructs an adaptive target as a mix between a tilted current distribution and a tilted reference distribution. It leverages feature-space optimal transport and fixed-point regression to realize this target, using only generated samples and scalar rewards.

Result: RWTD substantially improves GenEval score of the one-step SANA Sprint 1.6B backbone from 0.73 to 0.80; shows cross-reward generalization in preference alignment experiments, balancing improvements with preservation of compositional capabilities.

Conclusion: RWTD provides a principled post-training approach that interpolates between off-policy reward tilting of the reference and on-policy tilting of the current model, enabling effective reward adaptation while retaining prior knowledge for large implicit generators.

Abstract: One-step generators enable high-quality visual generation with a single network evaluation, but their post-training is difficult: general implicit generators provide neither tractable likelihoods nor denoising trajectories, and many rewards are non-differentiable. We introduce Reward-Weighted Transport Distillation (RWTD), a post-training method that requires only generated samples and scalar reward evaluations. Rather than aligning solely to the conventional reward-tilted reference distribution, RWTD constructs an adaptive target that mixes separately tilted current and reference distributions. The current component incorporates improvements discovered during training, while the reference component anchors the target to the pretrained generator. RWTD realizes this target through feature-space optimal transport and fixed-point regression. Theoretical analysis shows that the fixed-point distributions of RWTD interpolate between off-policy reward tilting of the reference and on-policy tilting of the current model, providing a principled approach to balancing reward adaptation with retention of prior knowledge. Empirically, RWTD substantially improves the GenEval score of the one-step SANA Sprint 1.6B backbone from 0.73 to 0.80, while separate preference alignment experiments demonstrate strong cross-reward generalization that yields balanced improvements and preservation of compositional capabilities.

</details>


### [154] [Learning Chance-Constrained MDPs with Bellman Distributional Certificates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30856)
*Chenbei Lu,Hongyu Yi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Establishes near-tight sample complexity bounds for tabular discounted CCMDPs with a planning oracle, via a Bellman distributional certificate that recurses constraint violation probabilities and can be reused across policies; extends to model-free, variance-reduced policy gradient with finite-sample KKT guarantees; demonstrated on synthetic CCMDPs and an IEEE energy storage benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chance constraints in MDPs target probabilistic safety under high-cost events, but are computationally hard due to nonconvex trajectory-dependent constraints. The work investigates whether this computational hardness translates to a worse statistical price (sample complexity) and provides both theoretical bounds and practical algorithms.

Method: Introduce Bellman distributional certificate to compute trajectory-violation probabilities before policy selection; enables policy-uniform trajectory-KL transfer using shared reverse-KL confidence sets without a union bound over policies/time; derive a model-based upper bound and a matching lower bound (up to log terms); develop a model-free, variance-reduced policy-gradient algorithm with finite-sample KKT-residual guarantees and independent validation of accepted policies; validate through experiments on synthetic CCMDPs and an IEEE 14-bus energy storage control benchmark.

Result: Model-based upper bound and near-matching lower bound for tabular discounted CCMDPs with bounded successor support and planning oracle; a reusable Bellman distributional certificate enabling policy evaluation independent of candidate policies; a variance-reduced, model-free policy gradient with finite-sample KKT guarantees; empirical demonstrations showing safety outcomes and mechanism behavior under CC constraints.

Conclusion: Computational difficulty of CCMDPs does not inherently imply a larger statistical price; the Bellman distributional certificate and shared confidence-sets enable tractable, policy-agnostic certification of constraint violations and practical safe RL algorithms with theoretical guarantees, applicable to domains like energy storage management.

Abstract: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) commonly enforces expected-cost constraints, but such expectation safety may fail to control the probability of rare high-cost trajectories. Chance-constrained MDPs (CCMDPs) impose a stronger probability-level requirement, but are widely viewed as harder because the chance constraint is nonconvex and depends on the full trajectory rather than a Bellman-linear expectation. In this paper, we reveal that this computational difficulty does not necessarily imply a higher statistical price. For tabular discounted CCMDPs with fixed bounded successor support and access to a certified planning oracle, we establish a model-based upper bound, with a matching lower bound up to logarithmic terms. Technically, our key idea is the \emph{Bellman distributional certificate}, which constructs a Bellman recursion for constraint violation probabilities before policy selection. The certificate can be reused across candidate policies; combined with shared row-wise reverse-KL confidence sets, it gives a policy-uniform trajectory-KL transfer without a union bound over policies or time--budget Bellman tables. For stochastic policies, we give a model-free variance-reduced policy-gradient algorithm with a finite-sample expected KKT-residual guarantee and independent validation of every accepted policy. Numerical experiments on synthetic CCMDPs and an IEEE 14-bus energy storage control benchmark illustrate the safety and mechanism behavior of the proposed algorithms.

</details>


### [155] [CacheReforge: Bounded Recovery for Stale KV Caches under Evolving Adapters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30884)
*Yuhang Cao,Yanzhou Mu,Chunrong Fang,Zhenyu Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CacheReforge introduces a layerwise mixed-version cache representation to recover current adapter behavior with bounded recomputation, achieving high fidelity with minimal recomputation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Stale KV caches arise when lightweight adapters update; reuse from earlier versions distorts outputs, and full recomputation is costly. A version-aware recovery strategy is needed.

Method: Represent caches as layerwise mixed-version objects; use per-layer adapter anchors, calibrated sensitivity, drift accumulation, and executable restart boundaries to choose direct reuse, bounded recomputation, or full affected-suffix recovery. Distinguish dependency depth from recomputation horizon and use cumulative tail influence to decide bounded recovery.

Result: Evaluated on Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B with continual LoRA updates, including 16K HotpotQA and 2WikiMQA workloads. Achieved 92.4% reduction in mean KL divergence relative to stale reuse; recomputed only 5.44% of layers; reduced cache-maintenance time by 93.2% relative to fresh full prefill.

Conclusion: Version-aware recovery preserves current-model fidelity while retaining most KV caching gains and avoiding large-scale recomputation.

Abstract: Large language models rely on KV caching to reduce repeated prefill computation in long context and interactive applications. As lightweight adapters evolve, cached states reflect earlier versions, so stale reuse distorts current model outputs, while complete affected suffix recomputation restores fidelity at substantial cost. We seek minimal recomputation that recovers current adapter behavior. Existing systems track token, context, or stable adapter identity, but neither represent caches from earlier adapter versions nor distinguish update propagation from the recomputation required for behavioral recovery. To address these gaps, we introduce CacheReforge, which represents stale KV caches as layerwise mixed-version objects. It combines per-layer adapter anchors, calibrated sensitivity, accumulated drift, and executable restart boundaries to select direct reuse, bounded recomputation, or complete affected-suffix recovery. We distinguish dependency depth from the functional recomputation horizon and use cumulative tail influence to characterize when bounded recovery preserves current-model behavior. We evaluate CacheReforge on Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B with continual LoRA updates, including 16K HotpotQA and 2WikiMQA workloads. CacheReforge reduces mean KL divergence by 92.4% relative to stale reuse, while recomputing only 5.44% of layers and reducing cache-maintenance time by 93.2% relative to fresh full prefill. These results show that version-aware recovery preserves model fidelity and most KV caching gains.

</details>


### [156] [Robust to Which Model Change? A Unified Evaluation of Robust Counterfactual Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30918)
*Marcin Kostrzewa,Maciej Zięba*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A cross-family evaluation protocol for robust counterfactual explanations (RobX) benchmarks robustness across eight model-change types on four tabular datasets, revealing varying robustness and underscoring the need for standardized evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing robustness scores for counterfactual explanations are not directly comparable because they reflect different kinds of model changes. A unified protocol is needed to assess true robustness under realistic model updates and to separate generation quality from robustness.

Method: Propose a unified cross-family evaluation protocol that fixes factual instances and generated counterfactuals, tests methods against eight model-change types, and compares six robust CFE methods plus two baselines on four tabular datasets. Each changed classifier is characterized by its outputs; the study reports empirical robustness along with coverage, base validity, and proximity.

Result: The robustness landscape varies by change family; perturbing model parameters changes about 0.95% of test predictions, bootstrap retraining changes about 4.9%. Methods with guarantees for the tested perturbations do not necessarily transfer to other changes. RobX transfers most consistently, though achieving greater stability may require larger interventions.

Conclusion: A unified protocol that specifies model changes, quantifies their behavioral magnitude, and separates generation quality from robustness is essential for meaningful comparison of robust CFE methods.

Abstract: Robust counterfactual explanations promise recourse that still works after the model behind it changes. Whether they keep that promise depends on what the change is. A small perturbation of the parameters, retraining on new data, and a new architecture are different events, and each existing method is evaluated against the one it was built for. Reported robustness scores, therefore, answer different questions and cannot be compared. We propose a unified cross-family evaluation protocol that holds factual instances and generated counterfactuals fixed while testing every method against the same eight types of model change. The benchmark compares six robust methods and two standard baselines on four tabular datasets. It characterizes every changed classifier through its outputs and reports empirical robustness together with coverage, base validity, and proximity. We find that relative performance and failure modes vary across change families. Bounded parameter perturbations change 0.95\% of test predictions on average, compared with 4.9\% for bootstrap retraining. Methods with guarantees for these perturbations do not necessarily transfer to other changes. RobX transfers most consistently in our experiments, although greater stability can require larger interventions. We argue that robust CFE methods should be evaluated through a common protocol that specifies the model changes, measures their realized behavioral magnitude, and keeps generation performance separate from robustness.

</details>


### [157] [EPOC: Endpoint-Preserving Online Correction With Compressed Residual State for Multi-Horizon Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30929)
*Takumi Fujimoto,Hiroaki Nishi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EPOC compresses residual state with DCT coefficients and endpoint value, enabling online ridge corrections that blend with the base forecast, achieving notable MSE/MAE reductions with far lower auxiliary state than alternatives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retaining full residual blocks for multi-horizon forecasts yields large auxiliary state; need a compact representation to provide residual feedback without memory bloat.

Method: Store low-order DCT coefficients and the endpoint of the preceding residual; per-channel endpoint shared across online ridge regressions using current forecast coefficients; blend DCT correction with base forecast; evaluate on eight multivariate series with DLinear and PatchTST across seeds/training variants (96 fixed-base conditions, 24-step horizon).

Result: Mean MSE/MAE reductions of 15.40%/9.35% vs uncorrected base; median retained state ~6.35 KB; outperforms δ-Adapter, COSA, FAC, OMPB in many conditions; Full ELF yields larger MSE reduction but far larger state; increasing DCT components from 4 to 8 adds ~1% MSE reduction for 5.7 KB; on jointly trained bases, EPOC reduces MSE by 16.69-20.15% vs TEFL-style adapters; code at GitHub.

Conclusion: EPOC offers a compact, effective residual-correction mechanism for multi-horizon forecasting, balancing accuracy gains with low memory footprint, and clarifying the endpoint's role as a shared input; scalable with more DCT components; practical for fixed-base online correction settings.

Abstract: Completed multi-horizon forecasts provide residual feedback for a fixed forecaster, but retaining full residual blocks increases auxiliary state. We propose Endpoint-Preserving Online Correction (EPOC) with a compressed residual state. It stores low-order discrete cosine transform (DCT) coefficients and the final value of the preceding residual block. Within each channel, the endpoint is shared across component-wise online ridge regressions that also use current-forecast coefficients. The fitted DCT correction is blended with the base forecast. We evaluate eight multivariate series with DLinear and PatchTST, three seeds, and two training variants, yielding 96 matched fixed-base conditions at a 24-step horizon. EPOC achieves mean condition-wise reductions in mean squared error (MSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) of 15.40% and 9.35% from the uncorrected base, respectively, with a median of 6,352 B in retained auxiliary arrays. It has lower paired MSE than the $δ$-Adapter, COSA, FAC, and OMPB in a majority of conditions and uses less state than each. Full ELF achieves the largest mean MSE reduction, 19.29%, but its median retained state is 474,048 B ($\times$75 relative to EPOC). Equal-size summary controls favor the endpoint by 1.65--2.20% in paired MSE; a coefficient-reconstructed endpoint yields similar accuracy to the observed endpoint, highlighting its role as a shared input. Increasing the retained DCT component count from 4 to 8 adds 1.00 percentage point of MSE reduction for 5,728 B. On jointly trained bases, EPOC lowers MSE by 16.69--20.15% relative to globally blended TEFL-style adapters applied to the same base. The code and numerical records are available at https://github.com/keiotakmin/endpoint-preserving-residual-correction.

</details>


### [158] [PORL: Pretrained Offline Reinforcement Learning for the Job Shop Scheduling Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30948)
*Mateo Toro Diz,Jonathan Hoss,Noah Klarmann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hybrid pretrained-online RL for JSSP: first online pretraining to learn general policies, then offline fine-tuning with KL-constraint; achieves lower optimality gaps under distribution shift than offline RL and baselines, especially with poorer offline data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge exploration and data-driven adaptation in industrial scheduling; mitigate sim-to-real gap and sensitivity to offline data quality and coverage.

Method: Two-stage approach: (1) online reinforcement learning to learn a general scheduling policy; (2) offline fine-tuning on production-specific data with a KL-divergence constraint to limit deviations from the pretrained policy; evaluated on JSSP instances with distribution shift using datasets from heuristic, noisy-expert, and random policies.

Result: PORL consistently achieves lower optimality gaps than standalone offline RL and general scheduling baselines; advantage over offline RL increases as offline data quality decreases, indicating reduced sensitivity to data quality/coverage.

Conclusion: Offline adaptation of pretrained policies is a promising strategy for industrial scheduling where direct online exploration is impractical; suggests broader applicability to real-world production environments with distribution shifts.

Abstract: The Job Shop Scheduling Problem (JSSP) is a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem in industrial optimization. This work introduces Pretrained Offline Reinforcement Learning (PORL), a hybrid approach that combines simulation-based online pretraining with offline fine-tuning on production-specific data.
  Reinforcement learning through online interaction enables exploration of general scheduling strategies, but typically relies on simulation environments and may suffer from a simulation-to-reality gap. In contrast, offline RL avoids direct interaction with the environment by learning from historical data, but its performance is strongly influenced by dataset quality and coverage. PORL combines the strengths of both paradigms by first learning a general scheduling policy through online interaction and subsequently adapting it offline to a target distribution. A KL-divergence-based policy constraint is introduced to limit deviations from the pretrained policy during fine-tuning.
  The approach is evaluated on JSSP instances with distribution shift and datasets generated from heuristic, noisy-expert, and random behavioral policies. The results show that PORL consistently achieves lower optimality gaps than standalone offline RL and the considered general scheduling baselines. Furthermore, its advantage over standalone offline RL increases as dataset quality decreases, indicating reduced sensitivity to the quality and coverage of the available offline data. The results suggest that offline adaptation of pretrained policies is a promising approach for industrial scheduling environments where direct online exploration is impractical.

</details>


### [159] [Low-Bit Recurrent States in Hybrid Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30950)
*Hongren Chen,Jiayang He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Mixed-precision, state-space quantization for hybrid language models using observability Gramian distortion weights; achieves substantial NLL gains at 4–6 bits without calibration or training, with gains sensitive to write-back frequency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce memory/bitwidth overhead of fixed-size recurrent states in hybrid LMs while preserving performance, without calibration data or retraining.

Method: Derive distortion weights from the observability Gramian; combine with normalized state ranges for mixed-precision bit allocation; quantize decay rates logarithmically; per-token state quantization; no calibration data, rotation, or training; ablations to isolate gains; evaluate across three hybrid models.

Result: Four-bit mean payload reduces excess negative log-likelihood by factors of 3.3–27.9 relative to seven baselines across three models; metadata costs vary. At six bits, negative log-likelihood differs from the FP32-state baseline by <0.005 nats. Ablations separate gains from variable bit widths, decay weighting, and range normalization. With less frequent write-backs, gains diminish and depend on model and budget.

Conclusion: Observability-informed, distortion-weighted mixed-precision quantization enables substantial retention of model performance at low bitwidth for hybrid language models, with caveats regarding write-back cadence and model/budget interactions.

Abstract: Hybrid language models maintain fixed-size recurrent states, but existing quantizers typically use eight bits or more. Quantization errors persist according to channel decay rates. We derive distortion weights from the observability Gramian and combine them with normalized state ranges for mixed-precision bit allocation, without calibration data, rotation, or training. We also quantize decay rates logarithmically. With per-token state quantization, a four-bit mean payload reduces excess negative log-likelihood by factors of 3.3--27.9 relative to the best of seven baselines across three hybrid models; metadata costs vary. At six bits, negative log-likelihood differs from the FP32-state baseline by less than 0.005 nats. Ablations separate gains from variable bit widths, decay weighting, and range normalization. With less frequent write-backs, gains diminish and depend on the model and budget.

</details>


### [160] [Towards Understanding Momentum Acceleration in River-Valley Loss Landscape](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30957)
*Miao Lu,Zeyu Bian,Kaiyue Wen,Beining Wu,Siyu Chen,Tianhao Wang,Zhiyuan Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Momentum in river-valley loss landscapes enables large learning rates to accelerate progress along the river, with LR dynamics contributing more to acceleration than momentum itself when the river is very flat/slow-spinning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand the role of momentum in non-convex loss landscapes characterized by a river-valley structure and explain empirical success of warmup-stable-decay schedulers.

Method: Theoretical analysis of gradient descent with momentum in a simplified river-valley landscape; derive stability conditions for large LR; compare to vanilla GD; examine the interplay between momentum and LR schedule; discuss special cases with flat river.

Result: Momentum stabilizes large learning rates, enabling faster progress along the river; the primary acceleration arises from admissible larger LR rather than the momentum term itself, particularly when the river is flat/slow-spinning.

Conclusion: Momentum accelerates optimization in river-valley landscapes by enabling stable large LRs; LR dynamics are the main driver of long-term progress; in flat rivers, momentum contributes little directly to river tracking; practical implication for LR schedules like WSD.

Abstract: The empirical success of pretraining large language models has inspired a deeper investigation into the underlying loss landscapes and the optimization dynamics. Recent empirical and theoretical study suggest that the training loss landscape often exhibits a "river-valley" structure, which features a low-loss manifold (river) flanked by sharp orthogonal directions with higher loss (mountains). In the long term, the optimization progress is determined primarily by the progress along the river. Within such a landscape, gradient descent with large learning rates can move faster along the river despite high apparent loss due to vertical oscillations, while a subsequent sharp decay in the learning rate suppresses these oscillations, revealing genuine optimization progress. This explains the recent success of warmup-stable-decay (WSD) learning rate scheduler which, unlike cosine scheduling, keeps stable high learning rate and decays before producing intermediate checkpoints. Building on this foundation, in this work we take a step further and study the role of momentum within such a loss landscape. We establish theoretical analysis that characterizes how momentum accelerates optimization by stabilizing large learning rates that can not be tolerated by vanilla GD without deviating significantly from the river. The enabled large learning rate in-turn gives greater speed along the river and makes faster essential progress in the long run. Another intriguing observation from theory is that for a river-valley landscape with very flat and slow-spinning river, the momentum itself does not contribute directly to acceleration in terms of the speed of tracking the river, while the main acceleration comes from the admissible larger learning rate.

</details>


### [161] [Gradient Surgery for Physics-Informed Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30966)
*Thomas Borsani,Giuseppe Di Fatta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PAM-GS introduces physics-aware gradient surgery for PINNs to adaptively mitigate inter-task gradient interference, addressing three phase-dependent gradient conflicts observed during training, leading to balanced optimization and improved performance across PDE benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PINNs optimize a composite objective spanning data and physics constraints, creating imbalanced multi-task learning where conflicting gradients impede convergence, especially for stiff/high-frequency PDEs. A robust method to balance tasks during training is needed.

Method: Identify three distinct gradient-conflict phases (varying angle- and magnitude-based conflicts) that alternate during PINN training. Develop PAM-GS, a gradient-surgery mechanism that adaptively mitigates task interference based on the current conflict type, leveraging physics-awareness to guide updates.

Result: PAM-GS achieves competitive accuracy while consistently delivering strong task-balanced performance across four PDE benchmarks, outperforming existing methods on most problems.

Conclusion: Adaptive, physics-aware gradient surgery effectively mitigates inter-task interference in PINNs, enabling stable, efficient training and improved performance across challenging PDE problems.

Abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are trained by optimising a composite objective that combines data fitting with physics-based constraints, typically resulting in a highly imbalanced multi-task optimisation problem. Under these conditions, existing optimisation strategies are affected by conflicting task gradients, leading to slow convergence and unstable training, particularly for stiff and high-frequency partial differential equations. We analyse gradient conflicts throughout training of PINNs with standard optimiser and investigate Multi-Task Deep Learning (MTDL) optimisation methods. In our analysis across four benchmark problems we observed that PINN optimisation exhibits three distinct phases in which angle- and magnitude-based gradient conflicts alternate, with only one present at a time. Building on these observations, we propose PAM-GS, a physics-aware gradient surgery method that adaptively mitigates task interference during training according to the observed conflict types. Experiments on four representative PDE benchmarks demonstrate that PAM-GS combines competitive solution accuracy with consistently strong task-balanced performance, outperforming existing methods on most problems.

</details>


### [162] [LipSSM: Structurally Lipschitz-Bounded Cascaded State-Space Model via Metric Transfer between Consecutive SSM Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30973)
*Natsuki Yoshino,Ren Uchida,Kazuki Matsumoto,Kohei Yatabe*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Extends LipKernel's tight Lipschitz bound to cascaded state-space models (LipSSM) to build Lipschitz-continuous DNNs capable of longer-term dependencies, with theoretical justification and empirical evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Layer-wise Lipschitz bounds are overly conservative, limiting expressivity and empirical robustness. A tighter global bound is needed for certifiable robustness in deep sequential models.

Method: Transfer inter-layer LipKernel information to cascaded SSMs, constructing LipSSM architecture that enforces Lipschitz continuity overall, with theoretical analysis of the bound and its tightness; empirical experiments on benchmarks demonstrating robustness-performance improvements.

Result: LipSSM is theoretically justified and empirically evaluated, showing a tighter global Lipschitz bound and improved performance over conventional layer-wise approaches in sequential settings.

Conclusion: LipSSM enables longer-term dependency modeling while maintaining tight Lipschitz bounds, enabling certifiable robustness for sequential DNNs.

Abstract: Lipschitz continuity is a fundamental principle in the design of certifiably robust deep neural networks (DNNs), wherein adjusting the Lipschitz constant, which quantifies network robustness, is of central theoretical importance. A standard approach to enforcing Lipschitz continuity requires each layer of a DNN to be Lipschitz continuous, thereby guaranteeing overall Lipschitz continuity. However, this layer-wise approach typically imposes overly conservative restrictions by producing a loose estimate of the overall Lipschitz constant, which limits the expressive capacity of the DNN and degrades empirical performance at a prescribed level of robustness. To overcome this loose estimation, the recently proposed LipKernel transfers information across layers to yield a much tighter overall Lipschitz bound than conventional layer-wise construction. In this paper, we extend this concept to cascaded state-space models (SSMs) to construct Lipschitz-continuous DNNs capable of modeling longer-term dependencies. The proposed architecture, named LipSSM, is theoretically justified and empirically evaluated.

</details>


### [163] [Does Uniform Discrete Diffusion Need Time?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30977)
*Chunsan Hong,Chieh-Hsin Lai,Satoshi Hayakawa,Yuhta Takida,Jong Chul Ye,Yuki Mitsufuji*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Time conditioning in uniform discrete diffusion models (UDMs) may be unnecessary in practice. The population-optimal predictor depends on time, but in finite-data regimes common in language tasks, the empirical predictor is nearly time-insensitive across most of the diffusion trajectory, with sensitivity and guarantees weakening only near the high-noise endpoint. Time-agnostic predictors often compete with or outperform time-conditioned ones across datasets and objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reassess the necessity of explicit time conditioning in UDMs, particularly for language modeling where data is finite and noisy. Understand when time information actually drives performance and when it can be ignored to simplify models.

Method: Theoretically show that the population-optimal UDM predictor depends on time. Empirically evaluate language UDMs under finite-data conditions, analyzing corrupted versus clean sequences to assess time sensitivity. Compare time-conditioned and time-agnostic predictors across multiple datasets and training objectives, examining performance across the diffusion trajectory, especially toward high-noise endpoints.

Result: Population-optimal predictors are time-dependent, but empirical predictors in finite data are largely insensitive to time over most of the trajectory. Time-agnostic predictors perform competitively or better than time-conditioned models across datasets and objectives; the insensitivity degrades near the high-noise endpoint.

Conclusion: Explicit time conditioning in UDMs may be unnecessary in practice for language tasks, despite the population optimum depending on time. Omitting time conditioning can simplify models without sacrificing performance in typical finite-data settings.

Abstract: Uniform discrete diffusion models (UDMs) commonly use explicit time conditioning, but we find that it can often be unnecessary in practice. In this paper, we first show that the population-optimal UDM predictor generally depends on time: time controls how much the model should trust the observed context. We then show that this dependence can become negligible in finite-data settings relevant to language. When a corrupted training sequence remains much closer to its original clean sequence than to competing training sequences, the empirical-optimal predictor is nearly insensitive to time over most of the diffusion trajectory, where the guarantee weakens toward the high-noise endpoint. Empirically, trained language UDMs exhibit limited time sensitivity over most of the trajectory, while time-agnostic predictors remain competitive with, and often outperform, time-conditioned models across datasets and training objectives. These results challenge the use of explicit time conditioning in UDMs: although the population optimum depends on time, explicitly conditioning on it may often be unnecessary in practice.

</details>


### [164] [Learning Hierarchical Causal Representations of the Effects of Forcings on Temperature in Climate Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30995)
*Shan Zhao,Ilija Trajkovic,Julia Kaltenborn,Yaniv Gurwicz,Peer Nowack,David Rolnick,Julien Boussard*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hierarchical causal representation learning framework for sea surface temperature emulation that captures both internal climate variability and forced responses, enabling accurate long-term projections and physically realistic reactions to greenhouse gas and aerosol perturbations on unseen scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the lack of interpretability and causal attribution in ML-based climate emulators by disentangling internal dynamics from external forcings to enable trustworthy extrapolation.

Method: Proposes a hierarchical causal representation learning framework that models atmospheric dynamical interactions from internal variability and explicit forced responses due to greenhouse gas and aerosol changes; trained on future climate change scenarios using sea surface temperature fields from a state-of-the-art global climate model.

Result: Accurate predictions of long-term global mean and regional SST evolution; physically realistic responses to perturbations in greenhouse gas and aerosol concentrations when evaluated on unseen scenarios.

Conclusion: Demonstrates the potential of causal representation learning to improve climate model emulation, offering better interpretability and extrapolation under changing forcings.

Abstract: Machine learning (ML) emulators provide a fast and cost-effective method to simulate climate change scenarios after being trained on Earth System Models projections. However, the black-box nature of those data-driven approaches limit the usability and trustworthiness of their outputs and in particular their use as causal attribution tools. Here, we develop a hierarchical causal representation learning framework applied to sea surface temperature fields from a state-of-the-art global climate model. As a key advance over previous work, our framework explicitly models both atmospheric dynamical interactions arising from internal climate variability and forced responses due to changes in atmospheric greenhouse gas and aerosol concentrations. When trained on future climate change scenarios, our method accurately predicts the long-term global mean and regional temperature evolution and shows physically realistic responses to perturbations in greenhouse gas and aerosol concentrations when evaluated on unseen scenarios. Our results underline the potential of causal representation learning frameworks for advancing climate model emulation.

</details>


### [165] [The Linear Representation Hypothesis for Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30996)
*Minseok Jeong,Hyewon Choi,Hiroyasu Tsukamoto,SooJean Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Extends the linear representation hypothesis to vision-language-action (VLA) systems by a signature-based framework that unifies representations and policies, proving linear recoverability of a QoI under actions and monotonic steering along linear paths, with an explicit oracle in planar navigation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LRH has been successful in static semantic attributes within LLMs; embodied VLA introduces a dynamic coupling between representations, actions, and the physical state. A theory is needed to relate internal representations to future QoI evolution in the presence of a policy.

Method: On the representation side: prove existence of representations from which the future QoI evolution under a candidate action trajectory can be recovered via linear probing. On the policy side: propose a signature generalized linear model for stochastic action chunks, yielding monotonic expected QoI change along linear parameter paths. Empirically validate with an explicit oracle representation in a planar control-affine navigation setup, demonstrating linear probing and steering.

Result: A theoretical framework that unifies representations and policies under a signature-based LRH for VLA. It establishes (i) existence of linear-probe-able representations for QoI evolution, (ii) a signature G-LM for action sequences that induces monotone QoI advancement along linear trajectories, and (iii) an explicit oracle example in planar navigation validating the predicted mechanisms.

Conclusion: The LRH can be extended to embodied settings using signatures to connect representations with policy decisions, enabling linear probing and steering of QoI in VLA, and providing a concrete plan for verifying the mechanisms in a controlled planar experiment.

Abstract: The linear representation hypothesis (LRH) has become a standard lens for measuring and intervening on semantic information through the internal representations of large language models (LLMs). A growing body of work has begun extending this perspective to vision-language-action (VLA) models, but the dynamical nature of embodied interaction introduces an additional challenge. Unlike semantic attributes commonly studied in LLMs, such as gender or language, a physical quantity of interest (QoI) in a VLA evolves jointly with the system dynamics: the representation influences the actions selected by the policy, which alter the physical state and, in turn, the next representation.
  In this paper, we develop a theoretical, signature-based formulation of the LRH for VLA that unifies representations and policies. On the representation side, we establish the existence of representations from which the future evolution of a QoI under a candidate action trajectory can be recovered via linear probing. On the policy side, we introduce a signature generalized linear model for stochastic action chunks. This structure yields a monotonic change in the expected future QoI along linear paths in natural parameter space, enabling linear steering. We construct an explicit oracle representation in a planar control-affine navigation experiment and verify the predicted linear probing and steering mechanisms.

</details>


### [166] [Robust Successor Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31016)
*Erik Nikulski,Yamen Habib,Vicenç Gomez,Anders Jonsson,Rubén Moreno-Bote,Javier Segovia-Aguas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A unified robust successor features framework for generalization across rewards and transitions in linear MDPs; derives a Generalized Policy Improvement (GPI) bound with transition-mismatch and validates on grid benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generalization in RL and robustness to model uncertainty are central challenges. Prior work handles either reward variation or dynamics uncertainty separately; a unified approach across both is desirable.

Method: Introduce robust successor features (RSF) that generalize across reward functions and transition kernels under Linear MDP assumptions. Derive a bound on Generalized Policy Improvement that explicitly accounts for mismatch in dynamics, recovering standard SF guarantees when dynamics are shared.

Result: Theoretical bound quantifying performance degradation due to transition kernel mismatch; empirical validation on several grid-based benchmarks showing improved generalization over methods focusing solely on rewards or transitions.

Conclusion: RSF unifies transfer and robustness in RL for linear MDPs, enabling generalization across both rewards and dynamics; offers theoretical guarantees and practical benefits on benchmark grid tasks, with potential for extension beyond linear settings.

Abstract: Generalization in Reinforcement Learning (RL) refers to the ability to execute close-to-optimal policies in unseen tasks after the agent has been trained on a different set of tasks. Building on the seminal work of the successor representation and further adaptations with function approximation, Transfer in RL has traditionally focused on generalizing to tasks that only differ in the reward function. A decade after the introduction of the successor representation, Robust RL emerged simultaneously from several articles in the field of operations research. In Robust RL, the transition kernel is unknown, and the goal is to maximize the expected reward under this uncertainty. Our work unifies these two paradigms through robust successor features, which generalize across both the reward function and the transition kernel, under the assumption that tasks are linear Markov Decision Processes. We derive a bound on Generalized Policy Improvement (GPI) that explicitly quantifies how performance degrades with the mismatch between transition kernels, recovering existing successor-feature guarantees when dynamics are shared. Finally, the generalization capabilities of robust successor features are validated on several grid-based benchmarks and compared to previous alternatives that focus solely on either the reward or the transition kernel.

</details>


### [167] [Metacognitive Selective Ensemble for Mobile Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31031)
*Sungmin Lee,Kichang Lee,Joonhee Lee,JaeYeon Park,Songkuk Kim,JeongGil Ko*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MetaSE is an active ensemble framework for mobile sensing that maintains a small active set of models across windows, uses post-execution evidence to prune unreliable members, and performs lightweight routing only when replacement is needed. It achieves accuracy close to larger, more expensive ensembles with lower runtime and memory, demonstrated on HAR tasks and embedded hardware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep ensembles improve robustness but are costly for continuous sensor streams. Repeated full-pool evaluation and adaptive selection incur substantial computation and memory. There is a need to access the diversity of a large pool with reduced evaluations.

Method: MetaSE keeps a small, stateful active set of models across time windows. It uses post-execution evidence to reject unreliable members and only performs lightweight routing to replace members when needed, avoiding repeated full-pool evaluation while leveraging diversity from a larger pool.

Result: Across four HAR datasets and four model architectures, MetaSE consistently outperforms a fixed three-model ensemble and achieves accuracy on par with more expensive adaptive and full-ensemble inference. On a Raspberry Pi 4B, it is 2.7x faster and uses 69% less memory than full ten-model inference.

Conclusion: MetaSE provides a practical, resource-efficient active ensemble approach for mobile sensing by exploiting short-term persistence in model reliability and avoiding unnecessary evaluations, achieving strong accuracy with reduced compute and memory.

Abstract: Deep ensembles improve robustness in mobile sensing, but repeatedly executing many models over continuous sensor streams is costly. Selecting only a few members reduces this cost, yet adaptive selection often requires additional model execution to obtain reliable evidence about inactive candidates. We present MetaSE, an active ensemble framework that exploits short-term persistence in per-model reliability. MetaSE maintains a small active set across windows, uses post-execution evidence to reject unreliable members, and invokes lightweight routing only when replacement is needed. This stateful design accesses the diversity of a larger pool without repeated full-pool evaluation. Across four HAR datasets and four model architectures, MetaSE consistently improves over a fixed three-model ensemble and achieves accuracy comparable to substantially more expensive adaptive and full-ensemble inference. On a Raspberry Pi 4B, MetaSE is 2.7x faster and uses 69% less memory than full ten-model inference.

</details>


### [168] [Robust Graph Clustering Network for Multiple Missing Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31033)
*Keyuan Qiu,Renda Han,Zhen Tang,Qiang He,Xingwei Wang,Wenxin Zhang,Guangzhen Yao,Junxin Chen,Qingjian Ni*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RGCN robustly clusters graphs with simultaneous missing node attributes and structure by decoupled dual-branch imputation, a directional hyperspherical latent prior for tight clusters, and a boundary-aware contrastive objective, outperforming baselines under various missing patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing works impute or cluster on incomplete graphs in a single view, leading to cross-view error propagation and blurred cluster boundaries when both attributes and structure are missing. A robust method that jointly handles multiple missing data in graphs is needed to preserve cluster structure and separation.

Method: 1) View-decoupled dual-branch imputation to recover missing attributes and links without mutual interference. 2) Multi-hyperspherical mixture prior on a directional latent manifold to promote intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster separability. 3) Boundary-aware contrastive enhancement objective to reduce imputation-bias induced cluster boundary blurring.

Result: Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets show RGCN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse missing data patterns.

Conclusion: RGCN provides a robust framework for graph clustering under multiple missing data, achieving stronger cluster cohesion and distinction through decoupled imputation, a directional latent prior, and boundary-aware contrastive learning.

Abstract: Clustering on graphs where both node attributes and structural links are partially missing remains a challenging task. Existing methods typically rely on imputation-then-clustering on single-view missingness incomplete graphs, which are vulnerable to cross-view error propagation and cluster-boundary blurring under simultaneous attribute and structure missingness. To address these limitations, we propose a Robust Graph Clustering Network for Multiple Missing Data (RGCN), which is designed to handle simultaneous node attribute and graph structure incompleteness. RGCN introduces three key innovations: First, we design a view-decoupled dual-branch imputation to mitigate interference and enable mutual enhancement in recovering missing data. Second, we employ a multi-hyperspherical mixture prior to enhance intra-cluster compactness and inter-cluster separability on a directional latent manifold. Third, a boundary-aware contrastive enhancement objective mitigates the blurring of clusters caused by imputation bias. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that RGCN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under various missing patterns.

</details>


### [169] [Aurora-X: Built for Extreme Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31038)
*Xingjian Wu,Chenjuan Guo,Xiangfei Qiu,Zhigang Hu,Hanyin Cheng,Peng Chen,Yang Shu,Jilin Hu,Bin Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Aurora-X introduces a billion-scale time-series foundation model with a progressive curriculum and a unified architecture, enabling cross-variable modeling, covariate conditioning, variable-resolution post-training, and test-time scaling. It features a pattern-guided mixture-of-experts for sparse activation and an implicit quantile head for probabilistic forecasting, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations in current TSFMs: limited training potential, insufficient architectural versatility, and difficulty achieving true general-purpose forecasting across diverse domains and variables.

Method: A progressive curriculum training regime starting with channel-independent pretraining to learn temporal patterns, followed by midtraining to incorporate cross-variable dependencies, varied context/horizon lengths, and available covariates; variable-resolution post-training to adjust temporal span per token at inference; a fixed-weight, test-time scalable architecture enabling longer histories or fewer tokens; a versatile architecture supporting cross-variable modeling, covariate conditioning, and parallel decoding of future patches; a novel pattern-guided mixture-of-experts with sparse activation and shallow patch-similarity guided routing; an implicit quantile network head for predicting arbitrary quantiles to characterize predictive distributions.

Result: Comprehensive experiments on GIFT-Eval, TIME, FEV-Bench, TFB, and DAG-Bench show state-of-the-art forecasting performance compared to pretrained TSFMs and task-specific supervised models.

Conclusion: Aurora-X demonstrates that a curriculum-driven, unified TSFM with architecture supporting cross-variable modeling and probabilistic forecasting can achieve strong general-purpose forecasting performance across diverse datasets, while enabling test-time scaling and flexible horizon handling through component innovations like pattern-guided mixture-of-experts and an implicit quantile head.

Abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) enable cross-domain forecasting, but their development as general-purpose forecasters remains constrained by underexplored training potential and limited architectural versatility. To address these challenges, we introduce Aurora-X, a billion-scale TSFM with a progressive curriculum and a unified architecture. We first use channel-independent pretraining to learn temporal patterns, then introduce cross-variable dependencies, varied context and horizon lengths, and future covariates if available during midtraining. Variable-resolution post-training further enables an adjustable temporal span per token at inference. With fixed model weights, this supports longer histories under a fixed token budget or fewer tokens for the same history, enabling test-time scaling. With a versatile architecture, Aurora-X supports cross-variable modeling, covariate conditioning, and parallel decoding of future patches for probabilistic forecasting. These are supported by a novel pattern-guided mixture-of-experts that expands model capacity through sparse activation and uses shallow patch similarities to constrain deep-layer routing, guiding expert specialization across heterogeneous time series. Furthermore, we propose an implicit quantile network head that predicts arbitrary quantiles to characterize predictive distributions, enhancing probabilistic forecasting flexibility. Comprehensive experiments on GIFT-Eval, TIME, FEV-Bench, TFB, and DAG-Bench demonstrate state-of-the-art forecasting performance against pretrained TSFMs and task-specific supervised models.

</details>


### [170] [Distributed Learning as a Service: The Developer's Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31061)
*Tianyue Chu,Filippo Vannella,Dimitra Tsigkari,Paula Delgado-Santos,Fernando López,Pablo Gomez Guerrero,Sotirios Spantideas,David Solans Noguero*

Main category: cs.LG
