TL;DR: DLaaS enables developer-centric distributed learning with declarative DP, Split Learning, Hierarchical Aggregation, and Knowledge Distillation options, orchestrated via a single admin dashboard, demonstrated on an on-device Wake Word task with no client code changes; source and video released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address privacy risks from model updates, resource constraints of edge devices, scalability limits of a single aggregator, and high bandwidth costs in federated learning by providing a developer-friendly, end-to-end DL-as-a-Service platform.

Method: A middleware/admin-dashboard controls and deploys distributed/federated learning jobs across Android clients and Dockerized helper aggregators. DP, SL, HA, and KD are exposed as declarative options with no changes required to client code. The workflow includes local client training, aggregation, and serving the resulting model to a consumer Android app for on-device Wake Word detection, tested live with the Ok Aura WuW dataset.

Result: Demonstrations run across configurations with live monitoring of per-class confidence and inference latency. The trained model is delivered to the consumer app for real-time WuW detection on a microphone stream. Source code and short configuration walkthroughs are released.

Conclusion: DLaaS is feasible for edge-centric, privacy-preserving distributed learning, enabling developers to orchestrate DP, SL, HA, and KD without touching client code. The approach is validated on an industrial WuW task, suggesting applicability to similar edge ML scenarios and paving the way for broader adoption with open-source resources.

Abstract: Application developers of distributed learning services face challenges that a typical federated learning loop does not address. Specifically, the model updates can still leak private data, devices might not be able to participate in the training due to limited resources, a single aggregator might not be able to scale, and the transmissions of model weights induce a considerable bandwidth cost. This paper demonstrates DLaaS (Distributed Learning as a Service) from the developer's vantage point. Using a single admin dashboard, the developer initiates a distributed/federated learning job and is able to activate Differential Privacy (DP), Split Learning (SL), Hierarchical Aggregation (HA), and Knowledge Distillation (KD) as declarative options, with no change to the clients' code. We demonstrate the complete service lifecycle on an industrial smart-home Wake-up Word (WuW) task, using the "Ok Aura" dataset. Once the developer initiates a distributed learning job by toggling DP, SL, HA, and KD in the admin dashboard, the system dispatches the job to a set of Android clients and Dockerized helper aggregators. In the demonstration, these mechanisms run live across configurations. Then, the clients train the model locally and return their updates. The trained model is served to a consumer-side Android application that performs on-device WuW detection on a live microphone stream. In particular, the conference attendees will be invited to speak the trigger phrase and monitor in real time the per-class confidence and inference latency. Finally, we release the source code and short video walkthroughs of these configurations.

</details>


### [171] [SAGE: A sampling-aware global evaluation benchmark for species distribution modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31082)
*Emilia Arens,Nina van Tiel,Robin Zbinden,Damien Robert,Lukas Drees,Chiara Vanalli,Benjamin Kellenberger,Niklaus E. Zimmermann,Loïc Pellissier,Devis Tuia,Jan Dirk Wegner*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAGE introduces a sampling-aware benchmark for multi-species SDMs using GBIF training data and sPlotOpen presence-absence evaluation across 5771 plant species; findings show no universal winner—Random Forests and DeepSDMs perform best overall, with deep models aiding rare species only when bias-correction (e.g., thinning, reweighting) is applied.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address substantial species-level variability and data bias in large-scale, multi-species SDMs; current evaluations may mislead due to rare species and observation bias, hindering reliable ecological inference and conservation decisions.

Method: Develop Sampling-Aware Global Evaluation (SAGE) framework that stratifies species by sampling effort and relative prevalence; train models on GBIF data and evaluate with sPlotOpen presence-absence plots for 5,771 plant species; compare single-species SDMs with multi-species DeepSDMs; apply and assess bias-correction practices such as spatial thinning and reweighting.

Result: Random Forests and DeepSDMs perform best overall; DeepSDMs outperform single-species SDMs for infrequently recorded species but not for well-sampled ones; the advantage of DeepSDMs emerges only when bias-correction is applied in the deep-learning context.

Conclusion: SAGE clarifies when different SDM approaches are advantageous, under what data conditions, and underscores the importance of incorporating bias-correction in deep learning SDMs to yield ecologically credible predictions; provides data and code for reproducibility.

Abstract: Knowing where species occur is fundamental for biodiversity research and conservation. Species distribution models (SDMs) link species observations to environmental conditions to estimate their spatial distribution. However, accuracy varies with the underlying data and models, making it essential to know for which species models can be trusted. Deep-learning-based SDMs ("DeepSDMs") now jointly model thousands of species, drawing on hundreds of millions of community-science records. At this scale, averaging performance hides substantial species-level variability, particularly for rare species, often of greatest conservation concern. Records are also strongly biased, making occurrence counts misleading. Accounting for these factors is essential for a reliable and informative evaluation of multi-species SDMs. Here, we introduce a Sampling-Aware Global Evaluation (SAGE) benchmark, combining GBIF records for training with sPlotOpen vegetation plots for presence-absence evaluation across 5771 plant species. We propose an evaluation framework that groups species based on two properties, sampling effort and relative prevalence, which describe how densely a species' range is sampled and how frequently the species is recorded. Evaluating single-species SDMs and multi-species DeepSDMs, we find that Random Forests and DeepSDMs perform best overall, but neither dominates: DeepSDMs outperform single-species SDMs for infrequently recorded species while offering no consistent advantage for well-sampled ones. Crucially, this advantage emerges only when established bias-correction practices, such as spatial thinning and reweighting, are carried over to the deep-learning setting. SAGE helps identify the species and data conditions for which a given approach is beneficial, thereby supporting the development of more transparent and ecologically credible SDMs. Data and code: https://earens.github.io/sage/

</details>


### [172] [Block Sparse Attention with Log-Linear Complexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31093)
*Bohao Tang,Zhen Qin,Yuqi Pan,Zheng Li,Pengfei Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PISA introduces a pyramid Top-K block-sparse attention that uses a coarse-to-fine key hierarchy to select relevant blocks, achieving O(N log N) complexity with hardware-aware Triton kernels, and comparable or better performance than baselines on reasoning and retrieval tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context language modeling is constrained by quadratic self-attention. Block-sparse attention helps but requires expensive block scoring. A scalable, efficient, top-k selection strategy is needed to maintain performance while reducing computation.

Method: Construct a coarse-to-fine pyramid of keys via pooling across O(log N) levels. At each level apply LogSumExp scoring on a bounded candidate set to select keys for the next finer level, progressively narrowing candidates until the finest level. This yields O(N log N) complexity. Implement hardware-aware Triton kernels that fuse hierarchical routing and LogSumExp scoring without materializing the full query-key score matrix and evaluate on language modeling tasks.

Result: Compared to a baseline, PISA achieves comparable performance on commonsense reasoning benchmarks and shows improved results on retrieval-oriented tasks, while providing substantial efficiency gains due to the O(N log N) complexity and fused kernels.

Conclusion: PISA offers an effective, hardware-friendly block-sparse attention mechanism that reduces attention complexity from quadratic to near-linear-log, with competitive or superior performance across evaluated tasks, particularly excelling in retrieval scenarios.

Abstract: Scaling language models to long contexts is limited by the quadratic cost of self-attention. Block sparse attention offers an efficient alternative, but selecting the retained blocks remains a bottleneck. Conventional block selection requires scoring all query-block pairs and therefore remains quadratic in sequence length. To address this issue, we propose PISA, a block-sparse attention mechanism that employs a pyramid Top-$K$ selection strategy. The main idea is to gradually narrow down the candidates across different levels, making it more efficient to find the most relevant keys. Specifically, we construct a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of keys and perform selection from the coarsest level. At each level, LogSumExp scoring is applied to a bounded candidate set to select candidates for the next finer level, continuing until the finest level is reached. Through pooling, we construct $O(\log N)$ levels of keys, yielding an overall complexity of $O(N\log N)$, where $N$ denotes the sequence length. We develop hardware-aware Triton kernels for both training and inference, fusing hierarchical routing and LogSumExp scoring without materializing the query-key score matrix. We further evaluate our method on language modeling tasks. Compared with the baseline, our method achieves comparable performance on benchmarks such as commonsense reasoning while delivering better results on retrieval tasks.

</details>


### [173] [The Residual Stream's Effective Depth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31098)
*Barak Gahtan,Ido Galil,Alex M. Bronstein*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces effective depth Deff, a scalar that captures how quickly layer-wise residual signals decorrelate in a transformer’s residual stream, and shows across 16 decoder-only LMs that Deff typically falls below a theoretical reference, indicating a global accumulated-state regime due to correlated residual updates rather than depth being unused.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The goal is to disentangle structural consequences of residual accumulation from empirical update effects and to provide a single, global diagnostic of depth usage in Transformer decoders.

Method: Define Deff by treating the layer-wise residual stream as a discrete-time process, measuring representation similarity decay across layer distance, and aggregating this profile into one scalar. Compare against the closed-form reference F_L = 2L/(L+1). Apply symmetric and normalization controls (position-0 symmetry, token normalization, top-PC) and evaluate across sixteen decoder-only models (e.g., Qwen3.5, OLMo-2, Pythia). Inspect intermediate checkpoints to assess temporal stability, and perform a controlled residual-carry intervention to test mechanism.

Result: Default Deff measurements lie below the reference F_L in 15 of 16 models, with a single outlier above F_L. The gap is not caused by persistent initial states or update-size imbalance but is largely a calibrated signature of correlated residual updates. Symmetric position-0, token-normalization, and top-PC controls rule out BOS or top-PC artefacts; the regime remains sub-reference after these controls. Early establishment in OLMo-2 and stability through 5T tokens, whereas Pythia-1.4B follows a distinct decreasing trajectory. A controlled residual-carry intervention supports the proposed mechanism.

Conclusion: Deff should be interpreted as a global accumulated-state diagnostic rather than a capability score or pruning metric. It reveals a depth-related regime driven by correlated residual updates, not simply depth usage. The finding appears robust across models and persists under several controls, suggesting a meaningful signature of residual dynamics in decoder-only transformers; further work should clarify links to training dynamics and potential ways to exploit this diagnostic.

Abstract: We introduce \emph{effective depth} ($\Deff$), a scalar diagnostic that treats the layer-wise residual stream of a transformer as a discrete-time process, measures how representation similarity decays with layer distance, and aggregates that profile into one number. Across sixteen decoder-only language models, $\Deff$ separates a structural consequence of residual accumulation from an empirical one: even maximally diverse orthogonal updates have the closed-form reference $F_L = 2L/(L+1)<2$, yet fifteen of sixteen default measurements lie below $F_L$ (Qwen3.5: 32--44\%, OLMo-2: 40--41\%, Pythia: 23--28\%). Matched references show that the gap is not caused by the persistent initial state or update-size imbalance, but is largely a calibrated signature of correlated residual updates rather than evidence that depth is unused. Symmetric position-0, token-normalisation, and top-PC controls show the regime is not reducible to BOS or top-PC artefacts: the lone above-reference default outlier joins the same regime, and all sixteen models are sub-reference after token-normalisation or top-1-PC removal. Intermediate checkpoints show that the regime is established early in OLMo-2 and stable through 5T tokens, while Pythia-1.4B follows a distinct decreasing trajectory. A controlled residual-carry intervention supports the mechanism, and $\Deff$ is best read as a \emph{global} accumulated-state diagnostic, not as a capability score or pruning method.

</details>


### [174] [Bayesian Optimization with Fisher Information Geometry: Gradient Bounds and Trust-Region Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31107)
*Saksham Kiroriwal,Julius Pfrommer,Jürgen Beyerer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Fisher-information pullback framework for Bayesian optimization yields a local sensitivity measure and a gradient bound, enabling a new trust-region BO method (FITR) that uses local pullback-Fisher weights; shows competitive results on SE-GP benchmarks and can handle non-isotropic surrogates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explain gradient behavior and heuristics in Bayesian optimization through information geometry; address vanishing gradients in high dimensions; unify heuristics such as RAASP and dimension-scaled lengthscales.

Method: Derive a local sensitivity tensor by pulling back the Fisher information metric through the surrogate posterior map; obtain an upper bound on the gradient of reparameterizable acquisition functions; develop FITR, a trust-region-based BO that replaces lengthscale scaling with local pullback-Fisher weights; applicable beyond kernels with explicit lengthscales; empirical evaluation on GP benchmarks with SE kernel; extension to non-isotropic surrogates.

Result: The framework provides insight into vanishing-gradient phenomena in high-dimensional BO; FITR achieves competitive performance on SE-kernel GP benchmarks; non-isotropic surrogates can be supported with task-dependent gains.

Conclusion: An information-geometric view yields both conceptual unification and a practical algorithm (FITR) for BO; the approach generalizes beyond standard isotropic kernels, with gains influenced by task characteristics.

Abstract: We study Bayesian optimization (BO) through the lens of information geometry. Pulling back the Fisher information metric through the surrogate posterior map yields a local sensitivity tensor on the input space, which leads to an upper bound on the gradient of reparameterizable acquisition functions. This view explains vanishing-gradient behavior in high-dimensional BO and provides a common interpretation of heuristics such as RAASP and dimension-scaled lengthscales. Building on this analysis, we propose FITR, a trust-region-based BO method that replaces lengthscale-based scaling by local pullback-Fisher weights. FITR is not restricted to GP kernels with explicit lengthscales. On GP benchmarks with an SE kernel, experiments show competitive performance using FITR. The proposed method also easily generalizes to non-isotropic surrogates, although the gains are more task-dependent in that setting.

</details>


### [175] [From Shortcut Learning to Discrete Neural Insertion Sort](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31114)
*Konstantinos Mylonas,Thrasyvoulos Spyropoulos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Discrete Neural Insertion Sort achieves strong length generalization by discretizing execution and separating concerns, but requires global inner-loop supervision and problem-specific inductive bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether Neural Algorithmic Reasoning models truly implement algorithms vs. exploiting shortcuts, and assess their generalization to longer input lengths.

Method: Analyze the CLRS30 baseline NAR, identify weaknesses in hint optimization and potential shortcut representations; introduce Discrete Neural Insertion Sort (DNIS) with a chain representation, separation of scalar exchanges from control-state transitions, and discretization of states after each processor step; train on length-16 sequences and test on lengths 64 and 128; perform ablations on discretization, graph structure, and inner-loop supervision.

Result: DNIS achieves 100% sorted-sequence accuracy on lengths 64 and 128 when trained on length 16; ablations show that discretization and graph structure alone are insufficient without supervision of the global inner-loop state; model learns a strong length generalization with discrete execution but requires problem-specific inductive bias to faithfully execute the algorithm.

Conclusion: Discrete execution can enable robust length generalization in neural algorithmic reasoning, but faithful algorithmic execution hinges on inducing appropriate inductive biases and providing supervision for the global inner-loop state beyond local discretization and graph structure.

Abstract: Neural algorithmic reasoning aims to train neural networks to follow known algorithms and generalize beyond the input sizes seen during training. However, correct final outputs and intermediate supervision do not necessarily show that a model follows the intended execution. We study this problem using insertion sort. Our analysis of the CLRS30 baseline NAR shows that the hint objective is weakly optimized and that hint accuracy remains low. Moreover, many intermediate representations can already be decoded into sorted sequences before the reference insertion-sort execution terminates, suggesting that the model learns a shortcut to the final output. Motivated by these findings, we introduce Discrete Neural Insertion Sort. Our model represents the sequence as a chain, separates scalar exchanges from control-state transitions, and projects node representations back to discrete states after every processor step. When trained only on sequences of length 16, the model achieves $100\%$ sorted-sequence accuracy on sequences of length 64 and 128. However, an ablation shows that discretization and graph structure alone are insufficient: without additional supervision of the global inner-loop state, the model fails even at the training length. Our results show that discrete execution can support strong length generalization, while also highlighting the problem-specific inductive bias required to learn a faithful algorithmic execution.

</details>


### [176] [Frame the adversary: a structure-aware attack methodology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31128)
*Vicky Kouni,Stelios Perrakis,Francis Bach,Pascal Frossard,Yann Chevaleyre*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A principled optimization-based framework for frequency-domain adversarial attacks using a structured perturbation set from non-orthogonal transforms, yielding weighted L2 projections and transferable effectiveness across unseen architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transform-domain vulnerabilities are systematic across neural models; existing attacks lack an optimization-consistent perturbation constraint, hindering principled analysis and robust evaluation of safety-critical systems.

Method: Define a perturbation constraint set tied to structured non-orthogonal transforms. Show that attacks emerge as weighted L2 projections onto this set, providing a geometric and optimization-aligned attack generation mechanism. Validate on standardized datasets for pretrained and adversarially robust models.

Result: Attacks, as solutions to the constrained optimization, are highly effective and transfer to unseen architectures, offering a general, principled baseline for transform-based adversarial attacks.

Conclusion: Provides a general framework for designing and analyzing transform-based attacks, aligning optimization objectives with transform-domain perturbation constraints, aiding robust evaluation beyond architecture-specific artifacts.

Abstract: Frequency-based adversarial attacks have recently grown popular by exploiting spectral sensitivities shared across neural architectures. Unlike spatial perturbations, frequency-based attacks expose deeper vulnerabilities, making them especially valuable for robust evaluation of safety-critical and security-sensitive applications. Yet, existing approaches are typically not derived as solutions to an optimization problem that explicitly captures transform-domain structure. In this paper, we propose a methodology for crafting principled frequency-based adversarial attacks, via a dedicated optimization framework. A cornerstone of our method hinges on the introduction of a perturbation constraint set, tied to highly structured non-orthogonal transforms, well-known for their flexible, non-predefined frequency handling. We prove that the attacks emerge as weighted $\ell_2$-projections onto this set, yielding a general and controlled attack generation mechanism. By this, we provide a clear geometric attack characterization, ensuring alignment between the optimization objective and the perturbation constraint. We assess our framework on standardized datasets, for pretrained and adversarially robust models. Results highlight that our attacks, being solutions to an optimization problem, over a structured perturbation set, are highly effective, even across different, unseen architectures. Our methodology could serve as a theoretical baseline for designing and analyzing transformed-based attacks, targeting fundamental model vulnerabilities, instead of mere architecture-specific artifacts typically studied in the robustness literature.

</details>


### [177] [CRNDiff: Count-Native Diffusion Framework via Chemical Reaction Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31149)
*Yuxuan Qiu,Praful Gagrani,Tetsuya J Kobayashi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CRNDiff introduces a count-native diffusion framework for stochastic CRNs that enables tractable forward noising, FFBS-based reverse sampling, and steering to efficiently generate rare subpopulations in scRNA-seq data with high conditional fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To model discrete count data from scRNA-seq within a diffusion framework while preserving count structure, and to enable efficient, targeted generation of rare cell subpopulations without retraining.

Method: A birth–death instantiation of stochastic chemical reaction networks yields a closed-form forward-noising kernel. Inference uses reverse sampling via forward-filtering backward-sampling (FFBS); terminal noising time is selected data-drivenly. Introduces tilted Feynman–Kac steering to sample rare target subpopulations from a frozen generator by tilting posterior marginals before FK correction. Validated on human heart scRNA-seq data with three target populations.

Result: CRNDiff achieves the highest conditional fidelity among evaluated models across all three target populations, with larger mean purity margins for rarer populations. Generated cells preserve marker-level differential-expression structure, and substituting real target-class cells with generated cells yields downstream classification performance close to the real-data reference.

Conclusion: Count-native diffusion with inference-time conditioning and steering enables tractable modeling of scRNA-seq counts, accurate generation of cell-type-specific distributions, and effective data augmentation for rare subpopulations without retraining.

Abstract: Scientific measurements such as single-cell RNA (scRNA) sequencing often take the form of nonnegative integer counts, whereas continuous-state diffusion models approximate this discrete structure using continuous coordinates. Building on stochastic chemical reaction networks (CRNs), a class of count-native Markov jump processes, we introduce CRNDiff, a structured framework that combines count-space diffusion with inference-time conditioning on rare subpopulations. An independent birth--death instantiation yields a closed-form transition kernel for forward noising. This kernel enables reverse sampling via forward-filtering backward-sampling (FFBS) and supports data-driven selection of the terminal noising time, eliminating the need for a validation sweep. This tractability also lets us introduce tilted Feynman--Kac (FK) steering, a method for sampling target subpopulations from a frozen generator without retraining. By tilting posterior marginals before FK particle correction, steering mitigates importance-weight concentration when the target population is rare. Using scRNA-seq data from the human heart cell atlas, we test the ability of CRNDiff to generate cell-type-specific distributions. Across the three evaluated target populations, CRNDiff achieves the highest conditional fidelity among the evaluated generative models, with larger mean purity margins for rarer target populations. Generated cells preserve marker-level differential-expression structure. Replacing real training cells for the target classes with generated cells yields downstream classification performance approaching that of the real-data reference.

</details>


### [178] [Teacher-Anchored Selection of Post-Training Quantized Models under Domain Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31155)
*Alejandro Rodriguez Dominguez,Muhammad Shahzad,Xia Hong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Under label-free deployment, select among many compressed model candidates after training. Minimum teacher distortion yields a nearly fixed eight-bit, per-channel, unclipped config; common estimators misbehave under overconfidence. Anchoring to the teacher reduces regret at small label budgets across 134 candidate families, with fading advantage beyond ~25 labels. The work provides exact quadratic identities and analysis of criterion components under symmetry-corrupted and label-limited settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how to select among a family of compressed models for deployment when target labels are scarce or absent, especially under domain shift, and to characterize robust scoring criteria.

Method: The study analyzes candidate families defined by different compression levels and per-channel configurations. It evaluates distortion-based and distribution-based estimators, derives quadratic identities for a canonical quadratic analogue, analyzes symmetry-based corruption, and conducts large-scale empirical evaluation (134 candidate families across CNNs and vision transformers) with anchoring to the teacher as a baseline.

Result: Minimum teacher distortion consistently favors an eight-bit, per-channel, unclipped configuration across runs. Confidence-based estimators can order the family in the reverse of desired under overconfident regimes; output-distribution estimators can align with the teacher anchor and outperform it on some architectures. Distortion remains stable, allowing a supervised term to shift selection away. The authors derive exact quadratic identities for a canonical analogue and show a common factor effect under symmetric corruption for a certain class of linear-in-label-indicator criteria. Anchoring reduces mean regret at small label budgets (≤25 labels) across 134 teacher families; the advantage fades beyond 25 labels.

Conclusion: In label-scarce deployment scenarios, anchoring to the teacher provides robust regret reduction for model selection with limited labels, though benefits attenuate as label availability grows. The work also offers theoretical tools (quadratic identities, factor analyses) to understand score components and the behavior of selection criteria under domain shift and corruption.

Abstract: Compressing a trained model yields a family of deployment candidates, and under domain shift the most compressed one need not be the one to deploy. We study selection over such a family, with candidates and teacher fixed and target labels absent or scarce. Two findings organize the label-free case. Minimum teacher distortion behaves almost as a constant rule, selecting the same eight-bit, per-channel, unclipped configuration in every run, which does not minimize empirical target cross-entropy. Established estimators divide sharply: in the overconfident-collapse regime of the CNN families, confidence-based estimators order the family close to backwards, and the diagnostics that identify it need the labels the setting denies, while output-distribution estimators match the teacher-relative anchor and on one architecture beat it. Distortion is nonetheless stable, so a supervised term can move selection away from it. Combining the two, we give exact quadratic identities for a canonical quadratic analogue of the family. We also show that under symmetric corruption the label-dependent part of a criterion linear in the label indicator is multiplied by one common factor whenever its coefficient sums are candidate-invariant, a class holding teacher contrasts and accuracy but not cross-entropy. These characterize the score's components without bounding selection regret. Across one hundred and thirty-four candidate families, one per independently trained convolutional or Vision Transformer teacher, anchoring reduces mean regret at the smallest label budget in every setting, an advantage that fades beyond twenty-five labels.

</details>


### [179] [Bayesian Tensor Autoencoder with Physics-informed Predictive Prior for Multi-dimensional Time Series Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31157)
*Jianan Liu,Chunguang Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Physics-informed Predictive Prior Tensor Autoencoder (PPPTAE) integrates a predictive prior into a tensor autoencoder via Bayesian fusion and tensor low-rank constraints to improve anomaly detection in multi-dimensional time series, preserving intrinsic correlations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-dimensional time series are inherently tensorial. Existing time-series AEs (reconstruction- or prediction-based) struggle to leverage both types of information without disrupting correlations, and can over-generalize. A unifying approach that preserves tensor structure and fuses predictive information is needed for better anomaly detection.

Method: Employ a tensor autoencoder backbone to preserve multi-dimensional correlations. Introduce a Bayesian predictive prior that fuses reconstruction-based AE with historical/predictive information. Impose physics-informed constraints via tensor low-rank decomposition rules within the network to regularize learning and reduce over-generalization, forming the PPPTAE framework.

Result: Experimental results on real-world datasets show the proposed approach effectively models normal data and enhances anomaly detection performance compared to baselines.

Conclusion: PPPTAE demonstrates that integrating a predictive prior with physics-informed, tensor-structured autoencoding yields improved modeling of normal behavior and improved anomaly detection for multi-dimensional time series.

Abstract: Multi-dimensional time series, inherently tensorial, are common in practice. Despite great progress in time series anomaly detection, most existing methods are confined to uni-/multi-variate time series. When handling multi-dimensional time series using these methods, reshaping operations are required, which inevitably break the intrinsic correlations and thus lead to performance degradation. In uni-/multi-variate time series anomaly detection, AutoEncoders (AEs) are widely adopted and generally categorized into reconstruction-based and prediction-based AEs. The reconstruction-based AE utilizes the current observation for reconstruction, while the prediction-based AE utilizes the historical information to predict the current observation. Thus, the two AEs utilize different information. To bridge the gap between reconstruction-based and prediction-based AEs, so as to fully leverage the available information and thus further enhance performance, we propose a predictive prior and incorporate it into the reconstruction-based AE. It may not be very difficult to conceive this idea, but designing the predictive prior so that it can work for tensor anomaly detection is non-trivial. Specifically, to avoid breaking the intrinsic correlations within the multi-dimensional time series, we use the tensor AE as the backbone. To incorporate the predictive prior into the reconstruction-based AE, we propose a Bayesian fusion approach and our analysis reveals that this approach can enhance the modeling capability of the model for normal data. To mitigate the over-generalization problem of AE, we incorporate physical laws, i.e. tensor low-rank decomposition rules, into the neural networks in the predictive prior, leading to the Physics-informed Predictive Prior Tensor AE (PPPTAE) framework. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

</details>


### [180] [I Act Therefore I Am: When Is JEPA's Action-Conditioning Enough to Learn Causal Mechanisms?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31161)
*Yuhang Liu,Zhuo Huang,Javen Qinfeng Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes an information-theoretic objective for joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) to recover latent causal states in action-conditioned dynamics, deriving identifiability conditions that require action-induced variation; introduces an instantiation (A-JEPA) with action-modulated Gaussian noise; validates theory on synthetic data and demonstrates improved state recovery and transfer on visual benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge the gap between predictive accuracy and recovery of latent causal states in action-conditioned environments, enabling interpretable, transferable world-model representations.

Method: Propose a latent variable model where high-dimensional observations are generated from latent causal states with action-conditioned transition dynamics. Develop a general objective combining conditional likelihood for transition dynamics and entropy maximization to preserve latent information. Derive identifiability conditions under which learned representations recover latent states up to component-wise invertible transformations and permutation; instantiate with an action-modulated Gaussian additive-noise model (A-JEPA).

Result: Identifiability is proven under sufficient action-induced variation; experiments on synthetic environments verify the theoretical identifiability and robustness to moderate violations; visual benchmarks show improved latent-state recovery and transfer to unseen transition mechanisms.

Conclusion: Under the proposed objective and identifiability conditions, JEPA representations can recover latent causal states up to invertible transformations and permutation. The A-JEPA instantiation provides a practical approach, highlighting JEPAs as viable pathways to learn interpretable, transferable world-model representations.

Abstract: Recent empirical and theoretical advances suggest that joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) may learn meaningful representations for action-conditioned prediction of future outcomes, thus becoming one of the foundational structures for world models. However, accurate prediction does not, in general, necessarily imply recovery of underlying causal states that give rise to the observed dynamics. This work investigates when and how JEPAs can recover the underlying causal states from observations. We first introduce a latent variable model, in which high-dimensional observations are generated from latent causal states whose dynamics are governed by action-conditioned transition mechanisms. Based on this formulation, we develop a general information-theoretic objective that combines conditional likelihood maximization for learning transition dynamics with entropy maximization for preserving latent state information. We then establish identifiability conditions under which representations learned by this general objective recover the underlying latent causal states up to component-wise invertible transformations and permutation. One key condition for such identifiability is sufficient action-induced variation in the transition mechanisms. Guided by this finding, we instantiate the general objective with an action-modulated Gaussian additive-noise model, yielding action-modulated JEPA (A-JEPA). Experiments on synthetic environments verify the theoretical findings under the identifiability conditions and robustness to moderate violations, while visual benchmarks demonstrate improved state recovery and transfer to unseen transition mechanisms.

</details>


### [181] [WorldTS: World Modeling for Multimodal Covariate-aware Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31162)
*Yuhan Zhu,Xiangfei Qiu,Hanyin Cheng,Wangmeng Shen,Chenjuan Guo,Bin Yang,Jilin Hu,Christian S. Jensen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Two-stage world-modeling with multimodal covariates improves forecasting by learning latent dynamics conditioned on external inputs and then decoding to observations, validated on 21 real-world datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Forecasting in observation space is limited because future observations are shaped by latent dynamics and external factors; existing latent-space forecasts underutilize multimodal covariates that could shape latent-state formation and evolution.

Method: Train forecasting-relevant latent state dynamics conditioned on multimodal covariates to produce encoded future states; freeze these dynamics and train an observation decoder to map predicted states to future observations.

Result: Extensive experiments on 21 real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach, with improved forecasting performance and insights into WorldTS.

Conclusion: WorldTS shows that integrating multimodal covariates within a world-modeling framework enhances forecasting by shaping latent-state dynamics, offering a robust approach for multimodal time-series forecasting.

Abstract: Time series forecasting is typically framed as learning a direct mapping from historical to future observations in the observation space. However, sequences of observations generally provide only a partial view of the dynamics of the underlying system, with future observations being shaped by latent dynamics. Recent latent-space forecasting methods thus achieve improved performance by predicting future observations from latent-space representations of historical observations rather than directly forecasting future observations in the observation space. Next, while future observations are also shaped by external factors, how to incorporate external, often multimodal, information into forecasting, so that it can shape latent-state formation and evolution directly, remains underexplored. We propose WorldTS, a world-modeling based forecasting framework that integrates multimodal covariates directly into the forecasting to further improve forecasting performance. Specifically, WorldTS employs a two-stage training strategy. First, it learns forecasting-relevant latent state dynamics conditioned on multimodal covariates, yielding encoded future states. Next, the learned state dynamics are frozen, and an observation decoder is trained to map the predicted future states back to future observations. Extensive experiments on 21 real-world datasets offer insight into WorldTS and its effectiveness.

</details>


### [182] [Audio emotion recognition for atypical hearing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31168)
*Ulysse Roussel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A doctoral project on Audio Emotion Recognition (AER) for atypical listening in autism, using transfer from neurotypical affective data by fine-tuning CLAP with LoRA on valence/arousal annotations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Auditory hypersensitivity in autism makes AER difficult to evaluate and highly individualized. The work aims to generalize affective responses from limited annotated data by leveraging a robust foundation model.

Method: Fine-tune the Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP) model using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), trained on a valence/arousal dataset collected from neurotypical listeners.

Result: No empirical results are provided in the abstract; the text describes the planned approach as the first step of the doctoral work.

Conclusion: If successful, this approach could enable cross-domain transfer of affective representations from neurotypical data to atypical listening contexts, though careful evaluation is required given individual variability in autism.

Abstract: My doctoral work aims to explore Audio Emotion Recognition (AER) in the context of atypical listening. This research focuses on auditory hypersensitivity in people with autism, a phenomenon that is often difficult to evaluate and unique to each individual. Our core idea is to leverage our understanding of affect from acoustic traits, relying on the possibility of generalizing affective responses from a small amount of annotated data. As a first step, we fine-tune a large foundation model, Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP) using low-rank adaptation (LoRA), trained on a valence and arousal dataset of neurotypical listeners.

</details>


### [183] [ALF: An Active Learning Framework for Scientific Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31197)
*Shikha Surana,Alex Hawkins-Hooker,Olivia Gallup,Christoph Brunken,Jules Tilly,Paul Duckworth*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A modular active-learning framework (ALF) that supports the full data acquisition loop for both offline and online settings, enabling end-to-end AL experiments in science.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data labeling/experimentation is costly; current tools cover only parts of the loop; a unified, reusable framework facilitates efficient data collection and reproducible benchmarking.

Method: Five modular components implementing the end-to-end data acquisition loop; a single API for offline evaluation against existing datasets and online acquisition against an oracle; open-source.

Result: No empirical results reported; framework description and open-source availability.

Conclusion: ALF provides a reusable, open-source platform to streamline active learning in scientific discovery, bridging offline benchmarking and online deployment.

Abstract: Machine learning for scientific discovery is almost systematically data bound. Producing relevant high quality data, under budget constraints, is amongst the most promising ways to advance the field. Active learning (AL) offers promise wherever labelling requires expensive experiment, measurement, or simulation. Most existing tools cover only part of the data acquisition loop, and typically focus on either offline benchmarking or online deployment, but not both. We present ALF, a modular AL Framework that runs the full data acquisition loop via five modular components. One clear API for both settings: offline, against an existing dataset for controlled and reproducible experimentation; and online, against an oracle for acquiring new candidates in real-world deployments. ALF is open-source and available at https://github.com/instadeepai/alf.

</details>


### [184] [Self-Supervised Representation Learning: From Spectral Foundation Models to Auroral Emission Spectra](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31206)
*Matthieu Le Lain,Gaël Cessateur,Sébastien Lefèvre*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Self-supervised 1D ViT with masked autoencoder on 223k unlabeled auroral spectra learns physics-relevant representations (emission-line ratios) and strong downstream performance, with limited gains from cross-domain spectral pretaining depending on spectral window.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Labeling hundreds of thousands of auroral spectra is labor-intensive; leverage unlabeled data to learn representations that capture diagnostic emission features and improve downstream tasks.

Method: Pretrain a 1D Vision Transformer using masked autoencoding on 223,000 unlabeled spectra. Evaluate via linear probes and fine-tuning. Compare to a supervised auroral classifier. Analyze feature attribution. Test transfer from two spectral foundation models (SpectraFM, SpecFormer) trained in different wavelength regimes.

Result: The hidden representations recover emission-line intensity ratios with R^2=0.91 (vs. 0.77 for an untrained model). A linear probe matches the diagnostic features designed by experts. Fine-tuned model achieves macro-AP 88.5 (vs. 77.8 baseline) and 0.870 mAP; achieves +0.159 mAP over training from scratch with only 10% labels. Attribution indicates reliance on N2+ bands. In cross-domain transfer, SpectraFM underperforms the untrained control, while SpecFormer approaches in-domain pretraining but does not surpass it.

Conclusion: Self-supervised, domain-relevant pretraining with a 1D MAE ViT is effective for auroral spectroscopy, enabling strong representations for both linear diagnostics and downstream classification. Cross-domain spectral backbones show partial transfer benefit that depends on spectral window; in-domain or closely related pretraining remains superior.

Abstract: Auroral spectrographs such as the Auroral Spectrograph In Skibotn (ASIS) record hundreds of thousands of emission spectra, but only a few hundred can be labelled by an expert. To exploit the rest, we pretrain a 1D Vision Transformer with a masked autoencoder on 223,000 unlabelled spectra. Without labels, its representation recovers the emission-line intensity ratios that physicists use to diagnose the precipitating particles (R^2 0.91 vs. 0.77 for an untrained control) and, under one linear probe, classifies as well as 13 features designed by experts. Fine-tuned, the model outperforms the previous supervised auroral classifier on its own benchmark (macro-AP 88.5 vs. 77.8), reaches 0.870 mAP, and exceeds the same architecture trained from scratch by +0.159 with 10% of the labels; attribution shows that it uses both N2+ bands. Could an existing pretrained model replace it? Two astronomical spectral foundation models and a time-series model transfer according to their spectral window: SpectraFM, trained in the infrared, falls below the untrained control, whereas SpecFormer, trained in the optical, approaches in-domain pretraining without reaching it.

</details>


### [185] [Budgeted Quotient-Residual Guidance for Frozen Pocket-Conditioned Molecular Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31222)
*Xinyu Wang,Jinbo Bi,Minghu Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Budgeted quotient-residual guidance (QRG) enables quotient objectives in diffusion-based molecular generation at inference time without retraining. It lifts quotient covectors into ambient directions and uses the sampler's step norm as a trust budget to scale updates, yielding quotient-aware generation with runtime accounting on frozen backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quotient features (distances, contacts, anchored substructures) are highly relevant for lead-optimization yet challenging to optimize with frozen generators. QRG provides a lightweight runtime correction to activate quotient objectives without retraining the model.

Method: Derive horizontal lift of quotient covectors to ambient coordinates; provide a closed-form sampler-budget update; offer KL/kinetic interpretation around a frozen reverse step; establish equivariance and a product-budget split for budgeted quotient and residual controls; apply on TargetDiff backbones with CBGBench expansions (fragment growing, scaffold hopping, linker design); compare Local-QRG and PredNext-QRG.

Result: Quantitative gains in validity: fragment growing 0.815→0.864; scaffold hopping 0.664→0.707; linker design 0.681→0.712 (Local-QRG). PredNext-QRG improves fragment/scaffold and is near-neutral for linker. Novelty remains 1.000 and diversity preserved in matched multi-seed slices; no retraining or backbone modification required.

Conclusion: QRG provides a lightweight, runtime-only mechanism to render quotient objectives active in frozen molecular samplers, with explicit budget accounting and task-dependent performance gains.

Abstract: Pocket-conditioned molecular diffusion updates ambient atom coordinates, but many lead-optimization objectives are expressed on quotient features such as distances, contacts, and anchored substructures. We introduce budgeted quotient-residual guidance (QRG), an inference-time correction that makes these quotient objectives active without retraining the molecular generator. QRG lifts quotient covectors to metric-horizontal ambient directions and delivers them through a trust budget set by the frozen sampler's own step norm: quotient geometry chooses the direction, while sampler motion bounds the scale. We derive the horizontal lift, closed-form sampler-budget update, KL/kinetic interpretation around a frozen reverse step, equivariance conditions, and a product-budget split for budget-capped section and residual controls. Controlled quotient tasks confirm that sampler-relative delivery activates signals that raw local quotient gradients leave dormant. On frozen TargetDiff backbones, official seed-0 CBGBench ligand-generation/editing sweeps show practical quality-runtime gains: Local-QRG improves validity from 0.815 to 0.864 on fragment growing, 0.664 to 0.707 on scaffold hopping, and 0.681 to 0.712 on linker design, while PredNext-QRG improves fragment/scaffold and remains near-neutral on linker. Novelty remains 1.000 and diversity is preserved in the matched multi-seed molecular slice, giving task-dependent improvements without sampler retraining or backbone modification. Overall, QRG provides a lightweight route to quotient-aware inference for frozen molecular samplers with explicit runtime accounting.

</details>


### [186] [Deterministic Regime Switching and Feasibility Inversion in Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31250)
*Mahesh Reddy Pagadala*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The abstract reports fine-grained, deterministic instability in Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization (DTR) under memory budgets, showing regime shifts, recurrence of evictions, and a deterministic infeasibility window in ResNet-32, with ablations pointing to a joint size-staleness term as a key driver; two distinct budget-sensitive pathologies are identified and differentiations between demonstrated results and hypotheses are made; study uses the reference simulator (simrd) and traces, with future production-runtime reproduction pending.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address memory-constrained DNN training via online eviction (DTR) and understand why small budget changes cause large, deterministic performance differences, aiming to improve robustness and guidance for memory management in training systems.

Method: Empirical study using the reference DTR simulator (simrd) with public execution traces from LSTM and ResNet-32 training. Perform fine budget sweeps (0.10% memory differences; 0.101–0.107 ratios) and analyze eviction patterns (repeated re-evictions, pinned rematerialization frontier). Conduct ablations using the DTR authors’ variants to identify contributing scoring terms (size-staleness) and separate distinct budget-sensitive pathologies. Compare fast/slow regimes, observable feasibility/oom boundaries, and Jaccard overlap of evicted storage sets.

Result: Identifies deterministic instability in memory budgeting for DTR, including: (1) LSTM: two execution regimes with up to 7.3x overhead difference; repeated evictions of the same storages; (2) ResNet-32: a narrow feasibility window with an OOM inversion (feasible at 0.101, infeasible 0.102–0.106, feasible again at 0.107). The OOM is traced to a fully pinned recursive rematerialization frontier exceeding the budget after evictable tensors are evicted. Ablations implicate the joint size-staleness scoring term as a driver; conclusion posits two distinct budget-sensitive pathologies rather than a single mechanism; broader claim of reproducibility pending in production runtimes; artifacts available with the preprint.”

Conclusion: The study uncovers precise, budget-sensitive instabilities in DTR, arguing for at least two separate mechanisms driving feasibility/OOM behavior and highlighting the need for further validation in production settings. It emphasizes separating demonstrated results from hypothesized mechanisms and suggests improvements to DTR scoring terms and robustness of memory-management policies.

Abstract: We report fine-grained, deterministic instability in Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization (DTR), an online eviction policy for memory-constrained DNN training, measured on the reference DTR simulator (simrd) using public execution traces. On an LSTM trace, memory budgets differing by 0.10% of unconstrained peak memory select fast and slow execution regimes whose overheads differ by as much as 7.3x; the slow regime is driven by broadly repeated re-eviction of the same storages (evictions per storage rise from 1.33 to 8.27 while the set of distinct evicted storages is essentially unchanged: 5,233 vs 5,236, with the two sets overlapping at Jaccard 0.999). On a ResNet-32 trace, a fine budget sweep reveals a deterministic feasibility inversion: the run is feasible at ratio 0.101, infeasible (OOM) across 0.102-0.106, and feasible again from 0.107. We trace the immediate cause of the OOM to a fully pinned recursive rematerialization frontier that exceeds the budget after every evictable tensor has been evicted. Ablations using the DTR authors' own variants implicate the joint size-staleness scoring term in the observed LSTM instability. We argue these are at least two distinct budget-sensitive pathologies rather than one mechanism, and we separate what is demonstrated from what remains hypothesised. All results concern the reference simulator; reproduction in a production runtime is future work. Code, instrumentation, and raw results accompany this preprint.

</details>


### [187] [Softmax Reparameterization for Output-Head Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31291)
*Asim Kadav,Christian Flores,Chirag Arora,Varun Kotte,Hongbo Zheng,Lan Yan,Priya Shanmugasundaram,Tracy Holloway King*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Softmax reparameterization is a post-training head reparameterization technique that improves quantization fidelity of large vocabularies in small LMs by centering vocabulary rows and selecting a single scalar to optimize logit behavior, preserving the softmax distribution and enabling minimal or no inference overhead for shift-compatible heads; gains transfer across models and quantizers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large output vocabularies cause substantial inference cost and accuracy loss when quantizing small LMs. The goal is to reduce the head’s sensitivity to quantization while maintaining exact softmax behavior and decoder compatibility, enabling improved generation quality and latency without retraining.

Method: Post-training reparameterization: apply fixed-mean centering by subtracting a scalar multiple of the vocabulary-row mean from every output row. Choose the scalar coefficient via a one-dimensional search that optimizes validation KL divergence, evaluated separately for RTN, activation-weighted MSE, and full-Hessian GPTQ. Include the original head and a rank-one correction for nonlinear logit paths (soft-capping). The approach preserves the full-precision softmax distribution, leaves the trained decoder unchanged, and, for shift-compatible heads, incurs no extra inference cost and preserves packed W4 execution.

Result: Substantial improvements in quantization fidelity and generation quality across multiple heads and quantizers. Example: Phi-4-mini AW-MSE KL drops from 0.936 to 0.256. Gains persist under stronger GPTQ calibration and complement exact per-channel scaling and affine quantization. Coefficients selected on WikiText generalize to C4 and OpenWebMath, outperforming mean-centering in 18 of 24 comparisons where the frozen coefficient differs from 1, and match it in the remaining six. In W2, benefits extend across nearly the full model-quantizer matrix. Residual analysis shows higher logit fidelity can accompany higher logit reconstruction error but reduces Fisher-weighted residual cost. For shift-compatible heads, there is no added inference cost and a 10.8% reduction in batch-one generation latency when quantizing the Phi head with the decoder in BF16.

Conclusion: A simple, effective post-training head reparameterization method preserves the softmax structure, improves quantization fidelity of large vocabularies, and provides transferability across models and quantizers with potential latency benefits for shift-compatible heads; it complements existing scaling and affine quantization techniques.

Abstract: Large vocabularies make output heads a substantial inference cost in small language models. We propose softmax reparameterization, a post-training method that selects a functionally equivalent output head before quantization. The method subtracts a scalar multiple of the vocabulary-row mean from every output row and selects the coefficient by validation KL separately for RTN, activation-weighted MSE, and full-Hessian GPTQ. This one-dimensional search includes the original head and fixed mean-centering, preserves the full-precision softmax distribution, and leaves the trained decoder unchanged; a rank-one correction handles nonlinear logit paths such as soft-capping. Across seven heads, W4 gains concentrate where baseline quantization substantially distorts predictions: on Phi-4-mini, AW-MSE KL falls from 0.936 to 0.256. The gains survive stronger GPTQ calibration and remain complementary to exact per-channel scaling and affine quantization. Across four heads and three W4 quantizers, frozen WikiText-selected coefficients also transfer to C4 and OpenWebMath, outperforming mean-centering in all 18 comparisons where the frozen coefficient differs from $1$ and matching it in the remaining six. At W2, used as a compression stress test, benefits broaden across nearly the full model--quantizer matrix. Matched residual analysis shows that improved fidelity can accompany greater logit reconstruction error while reducing the residual's Fisher-weighted cost. For shift-compatible heads, reparameterization adds no inference operation and preserves packed W4 execution: with the decoder held in BF16, quantizing the Phi output head reduces batch-one generation latency by 10.8% relative to the BF16-head baseline.

</details>


### [188] [Different Corruptions, Different Signals: Uncertainty and Loss in Federated Data Quality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31454)
*Bradley Scott,Zeqi Luo,Edmond S. L. Ho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper compares input-conditional uncertainty and prediction-label loss as corruption-detection signals in federated learning, finding that they detect different corruption modes; loss detects persistent label flips while uncertainty detects image noise; robust data-quality assessment should match signal to corruption type and not rely on uncertainty alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess which corruption-detection signal (uncertainty vs loss) is effective in FL under non-IID data and different corruption modes, addressing potential misalignment between detected uncertainty and actual label corruption.

Method: Experiment with ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 and SVHN under Dirichlet non-IID partitions. Simulate two corruption types: additive image noise and persistent random label flips. Compute input-conditional uncertainty using learned aleatoric variance, MC-dropout variance, and entropy; compute loss against the supplied label. Evaluate per-sample within-client AUC for corruption detection.

Result: Persistent random label flips: AUC(loss) ≈ 0.85 (CIFAR-10) and 0.95 (SVHN); AUC(uncertainty) ≈ 0.49–0.50 (chance). Image noise: AUC(entropy) ≈ 0.67 (CIFAR-10) and 0.66 (SVHN); AUC(loss) ≈ 0.64 (both). Conclusion: each signal is a stronger detector for a different corruption type; loss signals better for label flips, entropy better for image noise, with the advantage growing with higher federation-wide corruption prevalence.

Conclusion: Robust FL data-quality assessment should pair the signal with the corresponding corruption type and avoid relying solely on uncertainty; consider combining signals for comprehensive detection.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) data corruption can affect either inputs or labels, but it remains unclear whether input-conditional uncertainty and prediction-label loss expose these corruption modes equally. This paper compares two corruption-detection signals in FL: input-conditional uncertainty and prediction-label loss. The uncertainty signal is characterised using a learned aleatoric variance estimate together with Monte Carlo (MC) dropout variance and entropy measures, while the loss is computed against the supplied label. We test these signals against additive image noise and persistent random label flips. On ResNet-20 with CIFAR-10 and SVHN under Dirichlet partitions with data that are not independent and identically distributed (non-IID), the two corruption types behave differently. For persistent random label flips, the within-client per-sample area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) is 0.85 on CIFAR-10 and 0.95 on SVHN for prediction-label loss, while every uncertainty estimator stays at chance (0.49--0.50). This pattern is consistent with the model remaining confident in the underlying image despite the supplied label being wrong. For image noise, expected-entropy uncertainty rises above chance (0.67 on CIFAR-10 and 0.66 on SVHN), while loss responds comparably (0.64 on both). Each signal is therefore the stronger detector for a different corruption: the prediction-label loss for persistent label flips, and expected-entropy uncertainty for image noise, with its advantage becoming apparent as federation-wide corruption prevalence increases. Robust FL data-quality assessment should match the signal to the corruption rather than rely on uncertainty alone across corruption types.

</details>


### [189] [Benchmarking Attention for Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31306)
*Maximilian Schambach,Clemens Biehl,Sam Thelin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Benchmarking 2D tabular attention backends across hardware shows backend choice depends on row vs column attention; FlashAttention is typically best but CuDNN can win for long column attention; SageAttention suits long row sequences; provides open-source benchmark to advance table-native attention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tabular in-context learners (e.g., TabPFN, Mitra, ConTextTab) use 2D attention with longer row sequences and shorter column sequences, creating 2D memory challenges and inefficiencies not well addressed by 1D-attention optimizations. A reproducible, cross-backend, cross-hardware benchmark is needed to identify optimal attention backends and guide future optimizations for tabular data.

Method: Develop a self-contained, reproducible benchmarking setup to evaluate 2D tabular attention across multiple backends (Torch SDPA, FlashAttention-2/3/4, vLLM, SageAttention) on realistic tabular shapes. Measure forward and backward throughput for row vs column attention across GPUs (A100, H100, B200) and varying head dimensions.

Result: Findings vary by attention mode and hardware. FlashAttention implementations tailored to each GPU generally perform best, but CuDNN can outperform in column attention at longer sequences, with cross-over points depending on head dimension. SageAttention performs well for row attention and very long sequences (>16k rows).

Conclusion: The work establishes a reproducible baseline for evaluating table-native attention and highlights that backend selection is context-dependent (2D attention type, sequence length, head size, and hardware). This benchmark enables directed improvements to 2D tabular attention and provides open-source code for community use.

Abstract: Tabular in-context learners such as TabPFN, Mitra, or ConTextTab rely on alternating row and column attention over 2D sequences of latent embeddings. These attention patterns differ markedly from the one-dimensional case in language models: row attention involves longer sequences while column attention operates on much shorter ones, and the strided memory layout of tabular data makes producing contiguous tensors costly. Moreover, the hidden dimensions used in current models are small compared to recent language models. Yet efficient attention has been studied mostly for one-dimensional sequences, leaving the two-dimensional tabular setting unexplored. To this end, we create a reproducible benchmarking setup and study the unique characteristics of tabular attention across several backends -- Torch SDPA (efficient and cuDNN), FlashAttention-2/3/4, and the inference-only backends vLLM and SageAttention -- measuring forward and backward throughput across realistic tabular shapes on three GPU generations (A100, H100, B200). We find that the optimal backend choice differs between column and row attention and varies across hardware as well as model specifics: While the FlashAttention implementations tailored for each GPU generation perform overall best, they are at times outperformed by CuDNN in the case of column attention at longer sequences with cross-over points depending on the head dimension. Among inference-only backends, SageAttention performs well for row attention and large sequences beyond 16\,k rows. Our reproducible benchmark lays the foundation for future improvements to table-native attention. The self-contained benchmarking and evaluation code is openly available at: https://github.com/SAP-samples/tabular-attention-benchmark

</details>


### [190] [Uncertainty-Aware Federated Learning for Infant Movement Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31463)
*Edmond S. L. Ho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Federated learning with uncertainty-aware aggregation (UA-FedAvg) for infant movement analysis using skeletal data; achieves near-centralized performance and outperforms local training, with MC-Dropout-based predictive uncertainty guiding aggregation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Privacy, governance, and data-sharing constraints impede centralized training of infant movement assessment models across institutions; federated learning offers a privacy-preserving alternative.

Method: Introduce the first federated learning framework for infant movement analysis and General Movement Assessment (GMA) using skeletal motion data. Employ Monte Carlo Dropout to estimate predictive uncertainty during inference. Propose UA-FedAvg, which uses predictive entropy from MC-Dropout to weight client contributions during FedAvg aggregation. Evaluate on a three-client cross-subject FL setting for fidgety movement classification.

Result: Federated learning substantially improves over independently trained local models and approaches centralized training performance. UA-FedAvg and its validation-loss variant generally outperform conventional FedAvg across data-split configurations.

Conclusion: Uncertainty-aware federated learning is effective for privacy-preserving infant movement analysis, enabling performance close to centralized training and better robustness than standard FedAvg.

Abstract: Infant movement analysis provides valuable biomarkers for the early identification of neurodevelopmental disorders. Recent advances in deep learning have enabled automated analysis of infant movements from video-derived skeletal representations, achieving performance comparable to expert assessment for tasks such as General Movement Assessment (GMA). However, most existing approaches rely on centralized training, requiring data from multiple institutions to be collected and stored at a single site. Such assumptions are often impractical in clinical settings due to privacy, governance, and data-sharing constraints. To address these challenges, we present, to the best of our knowledge, the first federated learning framework for automated infant movement analysis and General Movement Assessment using skeletal motion data. As a clinically relevant use case, the proposed framework is evaluated on fidgety movement classification. To quantify model confidence, Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout is employed to estimate predictive uncertainty during inference. Building upon this, we propose an Uncertainty-Aware Federated Averaging (UA-FedAvg) strategy that incorporates predictive entropy derived from MC-Dropout into the federated aggregation process, enabling client contributions to be adjusted according to their predictive uncertainty. Experiments were conducted using a cross-subject evaluation protocol under a three-client federated learning setting. Results demonstrate that federated learning substantially improves classification performance compared with independently trained local models while achieving performance approaching that of centralized training. Furthermore, UA-FedAvg and its variant incorporating validation loss generally outperform conventional FedAvg across the evaluated data-split configurations.

</details>


### [191] [LUCID: Learning Under Confounding for Inference and Discovery in Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31315)
*Mohammad Fesanghary*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LUCID is a regime-adaptive deconfounding layer for time-series causal discovery that detects the confounding regime via a Marčenko–Pastur spectral router, attenuates factor-driven variation under pervasive confounding, and recovers lag-0 structure from the resulting innovations; it can wrap existing discovery engines and delivers robust improvements on synthetic out-of-distribution benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unobserved common causes induce spurious associations in causal discovery for real-world time series. The method aims to be robust across varying confounding strength/sparsity and spectral regimes, providing accurate contemporaneous (lag-0) edges while controlling for confounding.

Method: A regime-adaptive deconfounding layer (LUCID) that (1) estimates the confounding regime from data using a Marčenko–Pastur spectral router, (2) applies a deconfounding strategy matched to that regime (attenuating factor-dominated variation when pervasive confounding is detected), (3) recovers contemporaneous structure from the resulting innovations, with edge selection calibrated against a data-driven edge-free null, and (4) is wrapper-compatible with existing discovery engines.

Result: On a diverse synthetic out-of-distribution benchmark spanning changes in confounder strength and sparsity, loading density, lag structure, volatility dynamics, edge heterogeneity, persistence, intermittency, and tail behavior, LUCID achieves the best family-weighted directed, lag-resolved graph F1 (0.60), improving over the strongest baseline by 0.19 absolute (≈46% relative). The advantage widens for looser lag-collapsed scoring and remains robust under intermittent and heavy-tailed confounding.

Conclusion: LUCID provides robust, regime-adaptive deconfounding for causal discovery in time series and can wrap existing discovery engines, achieving substantial improvements across diverse confounding regimes; code and benchmarks are publicly available.

Abstract: Unobserved common causes are pervasive in real-world time series and can induce spurious associations that causal discovery methods mistake for direct edges. We propose LUCID (Learning Under Confounding for Inference and Discovery, a regime-adaptive deconfounding layer that first estimates the confounding regime from data using a Marčenko--Pastur spectral router, then applies a deconfounding strategy matched to that regime. When the spectrum indicates pervasive factor confounding, LUCID attenuates factor-dominated variation and recovers contemporaneous (lag-$0$) structure from the resulting innovations, with edge selection calibrated against a data-driven edge-free null. Rather than being tied to a particular discovery algorithm, it can wrap existing discovery engines; we demonstrate consistent improvements across three such methods. On a diverse synthetic out-of-distribution benchmark spanning changes in confounder strength and sparsity, loading density, lag structure, volatility dynamics, edge heterogeneity, persistence, intermittency, and tail behavior, LUCID achieves the best family-weighted directed, lag-resolved graph $F_1$ ($0.60$), improving over the strongest baseline by $0.19$ absolute ($\approx\!46\%$ relative). Its advantage widens relative to looser lag-collapsed scoring, and remains robust under intermittent and heavy-tailed confounding. Code reproducing the method, the benchmark generators, and every reported experiment is available at https://github.com/bloomberg/causal-ts.

</details>


### [192] [More Sensors Only One Field: Rethinking Continual Spatio-Temporal Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31325)
*Lewei Xie,Haoyu Zhang,Jiajun Zhou,Yulong Chen,Guanxing Chen,Yu-An Huang,Hau-San Wong,Yifan Zhang,Zhi-An Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: STFO introduces a universal Spatio-Temporal Field Operator to decouple forecasting knowledge from sensor layouts, enabling continual learning under sensor expansion and evolving dynamics. It achieves state-of-the-art average forecasting on multiple streams with notable MAE improvements, and provides code for reproducibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional graph-based continual learning ties forecasting representations to the current sensor layout, which hampers reuse when sensors are added or removed. There is a need to separate the dynamics to be learned from the observation layout to support expanding sensor networks and concept drift.

Method: STFO parameterizes forecasting as a shared field-evolution operator with observation and query interfaces to handle layout changes. It uses normalized coordinate-based aggregation to map irregular sensor histories to a fixed latent grid, enabling reuse of spatial maps. A spectral descriptor summarizes spatial-scale variation and, with Fourier propagation and attention, adapts operator responses to the current spatial regime. Coordinate-based decoding queries the evolved field at sensor locations, combining spatial corrections with local-history predictions.

Result: Empirical evaluation on PEMS-Stream, CA-Stream, and AIR-Stream shows state-of-the-art average forecasting performance. STFO-Large reduces average MAE over DOL by 8.4% on PEMS-Stream and 4.7% on CA-Stream.

Conclusion: STFO provides a transferable, parameter-efficient operator for continual spatio-temporal forecasting under changing sensor layouts and process drift, enabling reuse of spatial maps across observation sets. Code is released at the provided GitHub URL.

Abstract: Continual spatio-temporal forecasting supports traffic management and environmental monitoring under evolving dynamics and expanding sensor networks. However, conventional graph-based continual learning methods tie forecasting representations to the current sensor layout, so sensor expansion can alter the representation of learned spatial relationships. Our key insight is that sensor expansion changes the evidence available about a process without necessarily changing the dynamics to be learned. We propose STFO (Spatio-Temporal Field Operator), which parameterizes forecasting knowledge as a shared field-evolution operator and handles changing sensor layouts through observation and query interfaces. Normalized coordinate-based aggregation lifts irregular sensor histories onto a fixed latent grid, enabling reuse of learned spatial maps across observation sets without sensor-specific parameters. To accommodate process drift, a spectral descriptor summarizes variation across spatial scales and conditions Fourier propagation and attention to adapt operator responses to the current spatial regime. Coordinate-based decoding queries the evolved field at sensor locations and combines spatial corrections with local-history predictions. Experiments on PEMS-Stream, CA-Stream, and AIR-Stream demonstrate state-of-the-art average forecasting performance. STFO-Large reduces average MAE over DOL by 8.4% on PEMS-Stream and 4.7% on CA-Stream. Our code is available at https://github.com/Xielewei/Spatio-Temporal-Field-Operator.

</details>


### [193] [Bridging Body and Brain: Gene-Driven Morphology--Control Co-Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31329)
*Fu Feng,Ruixiao Shi,Yucheng Xie,Jing Wang,Xin Geng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Morphogene is a compact latent blueprint that ties body and brain, enabling coordinated morphology and controller generation at the limb level via AdaConcat; GeCode explores in Morphogene space with local anchors and performance-guided updates, yielding faster convergence and better performance than prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current morphology-control co-design often uses separate, loosely coupled networks, hindering explicit high-level coordination between body and controller. A unified latent representation can enable coordinated, scalable design of embodied agents.

Method: Propose Morphogene, a latent blueprint that jointly conditions morphology and control at the limb level using AdaConcat. Build GeCode as an exploration framework in Morphogene space, where each Morphogene defines a local design region; anchors are updated by performance-guided signals to balance local refinement with global exploration while maintaining body–brain compatibility.

Result: Empirical evaluation across diverse 2D and 3D co-design tasks shows GeCode outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with substantially faster convergence and higher final performance.
