Conclusion: A compact Morphogene latent space, combined with AdaConcat conditioning and anchored exploration (GeCode), enables efficient, coordinated co-design of morphology and control, yielding improved performance and sample efficiency.

Abstract: Morphology--control co-design jointly optimizes an agent's body structure and control policy as an integrated embodied system. However, existing methods typically model morphology design and control with separate networks coupled only indirectly through a shared task objective, limiting explicit high-level coordination. Inspired by natural genes that coordinate biological development, we introduce \textbf{Morphogene}, a compact latent blueprint that bridges an agent's body and brain. Through AdaConcat, Morphogene jointly conditions morphology and control generation at the limb level, allowing its variations to induce coordinated changes in both components. Building on this representation, we propose \textbf{GeCode}, which formulates co-design as exploration in the compact Morphogene space. Each Morphogene anchors a local design region in which nearby body--brain designs are explored, while performance-guided updates move these anchors toward promising regions for more efficient exploration of the broader design space. This process combines local refinement with global exploration while preserving body--brain compatibility. Extensive experiments across diverse 2D and 3D co-design tasks demonstrate that GeCode consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving substantially faster convergence and higher final performance.

</details>


### [194] [Progressive Memory Transformer: Memory-Aware Attention for Time-Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31351)
*Tord Sture Stangeland,Andreas Köhler,Steffen Mæland,Adín Ramíres Rivera*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes Progressive Memory Transformer (PMT) to enforce a three-scale time-series hierarchy via independent local, mid-range, and global objectives; memory-augmented transformer exposes mid-range representations for better multi-scale self-supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Time-series data exhibit structure at multiple scales (local, mid-range motifs, global properties). Most SSL methods supervise only globally or with limited temporal context, failing to explicitly exploit hierarchical structure.

Method: Introduce Progressive Memory Transformer (PMT): a transformer augmented with writable, window-aligned memory that exposes a mid-range scale alongside token and sequence representations; three independent objectives: local token continuity, mid-range window motifs, and global sequence agreement.

Result: Evaluated on seven UCR/UEA/UCI benchmarks, plus a cue-retention probe and forecasting tasks. PMT yields strong performance for low-label classification (1–5% labels), competitive forecasting across horizons, and evidence that memory states capture mid-range motifs.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling a hierarchical time-series structure with multi-scale representations improves downstream performance and interpretability; PMT demonstrates the feasibility and benefits of exposing and supervising across local, mid-range, and global scales.

Abstract: Time-series carry structure simultaneously at multiple scales (fine-grained variation, mid-range motifs, and global properties) and downstream tasks operate at correspondingly different scales. Most existing self-supervised learning approaches supervise representations globally via instance-level contrastive losses and limited temporal neighborhood supervision, but do not explicitly exploit the structural hierarchy. We propose a learning framework that explicitly enforces a structural hierarchy across three scales independently: a local objective for token continuity, a mid-range objective for window-level motifs, and a global objective for sequence-level agreement. Realizing this framework requires the backbone to expose a representation at each scale; we introduce \textbf{Progressive Memory Transformer} (PMT), which augments a transformer with writable, window-aligned memory that exposes the mid-range scale alongside the token and sequence-level representations conventional transformers already provide. Across seven UCR/UEA/UCI classification benchmarks, a cue-retention probe, and forecasting benchmarks, PMT learns representations that probe well at the global, mid-range, and local scales---strong low-label classification (1--5\% labels), competitive forecasting performance across multiple horizons, and quantitative and qualitative evidence that memory states capture mid-range motifs.

</details>


### [195] [Brenier Meets Adversarial Training: Optimal Transport Geometry for Robust Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31363)
*Alireza Abdollahpoorrostam,Ehsan Sharifian,Buse Şen,Marco Cuturi,Daniel Kuhn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Penalized DRO with Wasserstein penalty can be reformulated as transport-map optimization; optimal maps are cyclically monotone; standard adversarial training violates this and wastes transport costs; remedies are multi-start particle ascent and ICNN-gradient maps; experiments show improved robustness and generalization under distribution shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the difficulty of evaluating worst-case risk for nonconvex losses under distribution shift; ensure the adversary operates within a structured, cost-aware framework via Wasserstein penalties; leverage cyclic monotonicity for tractable worst-case analysis.

Method: Reformulate the DRO adversary as an optimization over transport maps that push empirical samples to adversarial ones; prove optimal maps are cyclically monotone; show that standard per-sample adversarial training violates cyclic monotonicity and wastes transport costs unless the adversary is heavily restricted; propose two remedies: (i) multi-start particle ascent—alternating parallel gradient ascent with reassignment to enforce cyclic monotonicity across samples; (ii) adversarial maps parameterized as gradients of input-convex neural networks (ICNNs) to guarantee monotonicity by construction.

Result: Experiments on robust regression, image classification, and robust control show the proposed methods consistently outperform standard adversarial training and state-of-the-art baselines, achieving improved robustness and better generalization under distribution shift.

Conclusion: Framing DRO via transport maps and enforcing cyclic monotonicity yields principled, tractable worst-case analysis; the proposed remedies provide practical gains across tasks by ensuring monotone, cost-aware adversaries.

Abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) provides a principled framework for learning under distribution shift, but its practical use is hindered by the difficulty of evaluating worst-case risks for nonconvex loss functions. We study a penalized DRO formulation in which the adversary may choose any distribution but incurs a Wasserstein penalty for deviating from the empirical distribution. We show that the adversary's problem can be reformulated as an optimization problem over transport maps that push empirical samples to adversarial ones, and we prove that optimal maps are cyclically monotone. We also show that standard adversarial training---based on per-sample local optimization---violates cyclical monotonicity and wastes transport costs unless the adversary is severely restricted. We propose two remedies. First, we introduce multi-start particle ascent, which alternates parallel gradient ascent with reassignment to enforce cyclical monotonicity across samples. Second, we parameterize adversarial maps as gradients of input-convex neural networks, which guarantees cyclical monotonicity by construction. Experiments on robust regression, image classification, and robust control show that our methods consistently outperform standard adversarial training and state-of-the-art baselines, achieving improved robustness and better generalization under distribution shift.

</details>


### [196] [Towards Understanding LLM-Based Log Anomaly Detection: An Empirical Study of Performance, Efficiency, and Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31371)
*Bin Li,Dongdong Wang,Siyang Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLMs for log anomaly detection show strong sensitivity to adaptation strategy, architecture, and deployment settings; scaling and quantization effects are dataset-dependent; efficiency and robustness are as important as accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: to understand how adaptation strategies, architectures, and deployment configurations influence detection performance and to provide practical guidance.

Method: systematic empirical analysis over three public log datasets; compare adaptation strategies, model architectures, parameter counts, and quantization levels; evaluate detection accuracy, computational cost, and robustness under structural, semantic, and label noise at varying perturbation levels.

Result: adaptation strategy choices lead to substantial performance differences; scaling yields dataset-dependent gains; models with similar accuracy can have different computational costs; low-bit quantization largely preserves performance across configurations; robustness varies under different perturbations but remains measurable.

Conclusion: provide empirical insights into performance, efficiency, and robustness for LLM-based log anomaly detection; emphasize practical deployment considerations beyond accuracy.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising performance in log anomaly detection, yet how their adaptation strategies, architectures, and deployment configurations affect detection effectiveness remains insufficiently understood. To investigate these factors, we conduct a systematic empirical analysis across three public log datasets, examining different adaptation strategies, model architectures, parameter scales, and quantization settings. Our results reveal substantial performance differences across adaptation strategies, while model scaling yields varying detection gains across datasets. We further observe that models with comparable detection accuracy can exhibit markedly different computational costs, and that low-bit quantization largely preserves detection performance in the evaluated configurations. Finally, we examine detection robustness under structural, semantic, and label noise at different perturbation levels. These findings provide empirical insights into the performance, efficiency, and robustness of LLM-based log anomaly detection, highlighting practical considerations beyond conventional accuracy-oriented evaluation.

</details>


### [197] [Differential Attention Unlocks Complementary EEG and Speech Fusion for Emotion Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31399)
*Philip H. Lee,Shreeram Suresh Chandra,John H. L. Hansen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Noise suppression is essential for effective EEG–speech fusion; EmoSpeechBrain uses differential attention and a gating adapter to align modalities, achieving notable gains on PME4/EAV.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MER with EEG and speech is hampered by EEG artifacts that corrupt shared representations. Effective fusion requires noise suppression as a precondition.

Method: EEG encoder employs differential attention (difference of two attention maps to cancel shared noise). An attention-based gating adapter aligns EEG and speech into a common space and weighs each modality's contribution.

Result: On PME4 and EAV, EmoSpeechBrain yields up to 12.9% absolute improvement over SOTA EEG encoders and up to 13.1% (speech) and 23.1% (EEG) over unimodal baselines.

Conclusion: By suppressing EEG noise before fusion, multimodal fusion becomes advantageous over naive combination, as demonstrated by substantial MER gains on two datasets.

Abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition (MER) increasingly pairs EEG with speech, treating internal neural signals and external vocal expression as informative views of affect. In practice, naive fusion underperforms the stronger single modality, because EEG artifacts inject noise that corrupts the shared representation. We introduce EmoSpeechBrain, a multimodal framework built on the insight that noise suppression is a precondition for effective fusion. Its EEG encoder uses differential attention, taking the difference between two attention maps to cancel shared noise and isolate discriminative neural activity. An attention-based gating adapter aligns both modalities in a shared space and weights each one's contribution to the prediction. On two datasets - PME4 and EAV, EmoSpeechBrain improves MER accuracy by up to 12.9% over other state-of-the-art (SOTA) EEG encoders, and surpasses unimodal speech and EEG baselines by up to 13.1% and 23.1%. These results show that once EEG noise is suppressed, fusion delivers gains that naive combination cannot.

</details>


### [198] [Decodable In-Context State and Model Output Across Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31401)
*Manas Venkata Sai Ravulapalli,Samrath Singh Chadha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Probe accuracy improves with pretraining; probe-guided steering yields larger benefits at certain sizes. Decodability on errors alone is insufficient to infer discarded information; oracle steering repairs many early errors, but saved aggregates confound target quality with intervention sensitivity. No final-state advantage detected for late-checkpoint errors; the link to downstream omissions remains unresolved.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how probe-based diagnostics and steering interventions relate to model errors across training, and to assess whether decodability of in-context bindings predicts discarded output information and downstream omissions.

Method: Track probe accuracy, model outputs, and steering responses across publicly available Pythia pretraining and post-training checkpoints. Compare model sizes for steering benefit; use saved scores to differentiate error types; perform an oracle-target steering baseline; compare decoders trained on final-state vs candidate logits; provide an information-theoretic counterexample to decodability conclusions.

Result: Probe accuracy rises during pretraining; probe-guided steering transitions from negligible per-trial benefit to a notable benefit at two model sizes. Saved scores separate probe-correct errors by the probability mass of the correct candidate. Oracle-target steering repairs many early errors, but saved aggregates fail to separate target quality from intervention sensitivity. Decoders trained on final state vs candidate logits show no detected final-state advantage on late-checkpoint errors. An information-theoretic counterexample demonstrates why decodability on errors alone cannot establish discarded output information. The relation to downstream omissions remains unresolved.

Conclusion: Decodability of errors alone is insufficient to infer discarded information or predict downstream omissions; steering can help, but disentangling target quality from intervention effects is challenging.

Abstract: Prior work established that a probe can decode an in-context binding on model errors and that probe-guided steering can repair some of them. We follow probe accuracy, model output, and steering response across public pretraining and post-training checkpoints. Probe accuracy rises during Pythia pretraining, while probe-guided steering moves from negligible all-trial benefit to a larger benefit at two model sizes. Saved scores distinguish probe-correct errors with low and above-uniform model probability for the correct candidate. Oracle-target steering already repairs many early errors, but saved aggregates cannot separate target quality from intervention sensitivity. A held-out comparison of decoders trained on the final state or candidate logits finds no detected final-state advantage on late-checkpoint model errors. An information-theoretic counterexample explains why decodability on errors alone cannot establish discarded output information. The connection to downstream omissions remains open.

</details>


### [199] [Evaluating the accuracy of KV cache reuse techniques](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31415)
*Samuel Cestola,Tianxiang Xia,Pengfei Zheng,Weiyan Zheng,Bo Wang,Yi Zhao,Diego Didona*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A study on position-independent KV cache reuse highlights biased accuracy measurements and inadequate datasets; introduces a robust evaluation methodology and Boxoffice tool to generate challenging KV cache reuse datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To obtain faithful assessment of accuracy loss due to KV cache reuse in retrieval-augmented generation and to ensure evaluation datasets exhibit the required reuse dynamics.

Method: Proposes a measurement framework that quantifies accuracy loss from reuse without ambiguity and presents Boxoffice, a dataset-generation tool that programmatically creates challenging KV cache reuse scenarios.

Result: Argues that current evaluations inflate effectiveness and that existing datasets lack reuse dynamics; provides a methodology and a data-generation tool to enable thorough evaluation.

Conclusion: A rigorous evaluation framework and Boxoffice tooling are needed to faithfully assess position-independent KV cache reuse, potentially revising perceived gains and guiding future dataset design.

Abstract: Position-independent KV cache reuse aims to reduce latency in retrieval-augmented generation by reusing chunk-level KV caches across prompts. We show that current evaluations of KV cache reuse techniques rely on measurements that fail to faithfully capture the loss of accuracy attributable to reuse, often artificially inflating the reported effectiveness. We also show that existing datasets do not exhibit the reuse dynamics needed to thoroughly evaluate such techniques. To address these issues, we propose an evaluation methodology that measures this accuracy loss without ambiguity and we introduce Boxoffice, a tool that programmatically generates evaluation datasets that exercise challenging KV cache reuse patterns.

</details>


### [200] [Scaffold: Support Graph Theory Based Sparsification for Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31466)
*Siddhartha Shankar Das,Sai Karthik Navuluru,S M Ferdous,Ryan A. Rossi,Baris Coskunuzer,Lakshman Tamil,Edoardo Serra,Alex Pothen,Robert Rallo,Mahantesh M Halappanavar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Scaffold presents a topology-based unsupervised graph sparsification framework for GNNs that jointly optimizes support-path dilation and congestion to preserve short communication paths while avoiding bottlenecks. It achieves strong performance with only 10–50% of edges across 19 benchmarks, reducing memory and training time, and is open-source.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GNNs incur high compute and memory costs on dense graphs via message passing. Unstructured edge removal can distort communication structure and degrade accuracy. There is a need for principled, scalable sparsification that preserves essential graph routes.

Method: Develop Scaffold, a topology-based sparsification framework rooted in support graph theory preconditioners. It explicitly controls dilation (lengthening of rerouted paths) and congestion (concentration of rerouted paths on retained edges) to jointly preserve short paths and avoid bottlenecks. The framework is unsupervised and scalable, and evaluated on 19 homophilic/heterophilic benchmarks.

Result: Scaffold achieves the best aggregate rank among sparsification methods across 19 benchmarks, with 10–50% of the original edges recovering or closely matching full-graph GNN performance while using less than half the memory and reduced end-to-end training time (including sparsification overhead). Open-source implementation available.

Conclusion: This work introduces the first scalable GNN sparsification framework using a joint dilation–congestion criterion on support paths, demonstrating broad effectiveness and practical efficiency for reducing graph density without sacrificing accuracy.

Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) rely on message passing over graph edges, making their computational and memory costs strongly dependent on graph density. Graph sparsification offers a natural way to reduce these costs, but removing edges indiscriminately can distort important communication structure and degrade predictive performance. We introduce Scaffold, a topology-based, unsupervised graph sparsification framework derived from support graph theory preconditioners. Scaffold explicitly controls two complementary structural quantities: dilation, which measures the length of rerouting paths induced by removed edges, and congestion, which measures how strongly these rerouted paths concentrate on the retained support. By jointly controlling dilation and congestion, Scaffold preserves short communication paths while avoiding structural bottlenecks. To our knowledge, Scaffold is the first scalable GNN sparsification framework to use a joint supporting-path dilation-congestion criterion. Across 19 homophilic and heterophilic benchmarks spanning small to large graphs, Scaffold achieves the best aggregate rank among the evaluated sparsification and related methods. Using only 10%-50% of the original edges per sparse support, Scaffold recovers or closely approaches full-graph GNN performance while using less than half the memory of full-graph training and reducing end-to-end training time, including sparsification overhead. We provide an open-source software package at https://github.com/siddhartha047/Scaffold.

</details>


### [201] [HySTAR: Anchored Hypergraphs for Stable Credit Assignment in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31531)
*Xinglong Luo,Yuding Zhang,Yuheng Kuang,Shuxuan Yuan,Zhenni Zeng,Weiqiang Zhu,Zhenhai Ji,Zhengning Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HySTAR is a MAPPO-based MARL framework that decouples adaptive representation learning from a temporally consistent, high-order value-decomposition basis using an overlapping sparse hypergraph scaffold and a spatiotemporal encoder, addressing structural target drift under partial observability and shared rewards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In cooperative MARL with partial observability and shared rewards, assigning team outcomes to individuals and higher-order coalitions leads to structural target drift when topology or active agents change. MAPPO-style critics collapse joint behavior into a single global value, causing inconsistent value mappings as interactions evolve.

Method: HySTAR anchors an overlapping sparse hypergraph as a uniformly covered decomposition scaffold, employs a spatiotemporal encoder to capture physical and task-dependent interactions, and combines temporal and structural relevance to produce agent-specific advantages. The framework separates adaptive representation learning from a consistent high-order value-decomposition basis for stable credit assignment.

Result: Empirical validation on SMAC, GRF, Traffic Junction, and MPE shows HySTAR consistently outperforms MAPPO-style, value-factorization, and dynamic-grouping baselines. On challenging SMAC settings, HySTAR yields relative gains of 16.7% over MAPPO and 15.6% over HYGMA; ranks first on all six GRF scenarios; reduces Traffic Junction convergence epochs by up to 40.2% relative to MAGIC; achieves the highest MPE episode rewards. Ablations with controlled topology, agent-death, neighborhood, and parameter analyses support the benefit of a fixed decomposition scaffold coupled with adaptive representations.

Conclusion: Anchoring a temporally consistent high-order decomposition scaffold while adaptively learning representations improves stability and performance in cooperative MARL under partial observability and shared rewards. HySTAR demonstrates robust gains across diverse benchmarks and supports the importance of fixed decomposition structure for reliable credit assignment.

Abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning under partial observability and shared rewards requires assigning team outcomes to individual agents and high-order coalitions. A MAPPO-style critic compresses joint behavior into one global value, while critics that dynamically reconstruct the grouping topology change the mapping from agents and coalitions to value components as interactions or active agents evolve. We refer to this inconsistency as structural target drift. We introduce HySTAR, a MAPPO-based framework that separates adaptive representation learning from a temporally consistent high-order value-decomposition basis. HySTAR anchors an overlapping sparse hypergraph as a uniformly covered decomposition scaffold, uses a spatiotemporal encoder to represent physical and task-dependent interactions, and combines temporal and structural relevance to construct agent-specific advantages. Experiments on SMAC, GRF, Traffic Junction, and MPE demonstrate consistent improvements over MAPPO-style, value-factorization, and dynamic-grouping baselines. On the hardest SMAC settings, HySTAR achieves relative gains of 16.7\% over MAPPO and 15.6\% over HYGMA, ranks first on all six GRF scenarios, reduces Traffic Junction convergence epochs by up to 40.2\% relative to MAGIC, and obtains the highest MPE episode rewards. Controlled topology, agent-death, neighborhood, and parameter analyses support the benefit of anchoring the decomposition scaffold while adapting the propagated representations.

</details>


### [202] [NEXT: Physics-Informed Neuro-Spectral Exponential Time Differencing Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31539)
*Márcio Marques,Leonardo Mendonça,Leonardo M. Moreira,Christian Júnior de Oliveira,Vitor Balestro,Tiago Novello,Daniel Yukimura,Pavel Petrov,Lucas Nissenbaum*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NEXT combines NeuSA's spectral PDE representation with high-order exponential time differencing to solve stiff PDEs; it stabilizes and accurately learns both forward and inverse problems, outperforming NeuSA in stiffness scenarios; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PINNs and NeuSA struggle with spectral bias, causality, and stiffness. There is a need for stable, high-order integration for stiff PDEs and reliable parameter/boundary learning from sparse data.

Method: Decompose the PDE's vector field into a linear stiff part and a nonlinear remainder. Integrate the linear part exactly via matrix exponentials; approximate the nonlinear part with a neural network within a high-order exponential integrator framework. Use NeuSA-style spectral representation for the solution and extend with exponential time differencing (NEXT). Validate on benchmark stiff PDEs and inverse problems; provide open-source code.

Result: NEXT remains stable and accurate for stiff PDEs where NeuSA diverges; demonstrates applicability to inverse problems with sparse data; code available at GitHub.

Conclusion: Exponential-time integration combined with spectral PDE representation effectively mitigates stiffness and spectral-biased learning, extending NeuSA's approach to a broader class of problems, including inverse learning; potential for wider adoption with further benchmarking.

Abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) build neural representations of time-dependent PDE solutions, naturally incorporating physics knowledge and observational data, which makes them well suited to both forward and inverse PDE problems. PINNs, however, are known to suffer from spectral bias and lack of causality. Neuro-Spectral Architectures (NeuSA), a recently proposed alternative to PINNs, mitigate both issues, but their numerical integration becomes unstable for stiff differential equations arising in many relevant physical problems. This study proposes Neuro-Spectral Exponential Time Differencing Architectures (NEXT), which combines the spectral representation of the PDE solution in NeuSA with high-order exponential integrators. Within this approach, the linear stiff part of the vector field induced by the PDE is integrated exactly through matrix exponentials, while the possibly nonlinear remainder is modeled by a neural network. The effectiveness of NEXT is verified through benchmark experiments on a set of stiff PDEs, in which NEXT is stable and accurate while NeuSA diverges numerically. It is also shown that NEXT can be applied to inverse problems, where the model has to learn unknown parameters or boundary conditions from sparse data. All code used in this work is publicly available at: https://github.com/marcioh2m/next.git .

</details>


### [203] [BeatGraph: Self-Supervised Heartbeat Graphs for Infant ECG Representations from the Home Environment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31546)
*Mohammad Nur Hossain Khan,M. S. Krafczyk,Beverly G. Bolster,Nancy McElwain,Mark A. Hasegawa-Johnson,Bashima Islam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BeatGraph uses beat-level graph representations for infant ECG, addressing high heart rates and pediatric differences by modeling beats as units with a beat encoder, temporal Transformer, and graph attention. Trains on unlabeled infant data with masked-beat pretraining and fine-tunes for diverse tasks, achieving consistent gains and cross-age transfer; releases a large public infant ECG corpus.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard ECG foundation models tokenize signals into fixed-length patches, which can split heartbeats and ignore cardiac structure. This is problematic for infants with higher heart rates and infant-specific ECG morphology. A beat-centric representation is proposed to preserve cardiac structure and improve downstream tasks.

Method: Represent 30-second windows as graphs of beats. Use a shared beat encoder to embed each heartbeat from waveform and inter-beat intervals. Apply a Transformer with positional encoding to order beats in time. Use residual graph attention layers to relate beats to all others, then attention pooling for a window embedding. Pretrain by predicting masked-beat embeddings on unlabeled infant ECG; fine-tune for tasks. A single backbone supports sleep-wake detection, infant-state classification, movement source identification (infant- vs caregiver-initiated), and affect recognition. Transfer across age groups demonstrated on ZZU-pECG pediatric benchmark (0-14 years) and adult PTB-XL benchmark under linear evaluation. Data release includes the first public infant ECG corpus collected in homes, classrooms, and labs: 3,408 hours, 143 infants (3–11 months), single-channel ECG, unlabeled pretraining data, benchmark tasks, subject-level splits.

Result: Macro-F1 improvements for all tasks range from 0.076 to 0.158 over strongest baselines. AUROC of 0.892 on ZZU-pECG pediatric benchmark (0–14 years) within 0.001 of the best published self-supervised ECG model. Matches the best model under linear evaluation on PTB-XL (adult) despite infant-only pretraining. Dataset release: 3,408 hours from 143 infants; includes unlabeled data and benchmarks with subject-level splits.

Conclusion: BeatGraph demonstrates beat-centric ECG modeling as an effective backbone for infant and cross-age ECG tasks, delivering consistent performance gains and enabling large-scale data release to support future research.

Abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) foundation models typically tokenize the signal into fixed-length patches that ignore cardiac structure, so a patch may split a heartbeat and the number of beats in each patch shifts with heart rate. This matters most for infants, whose heart rates are higher and whose ECG differs from the adult, clinic-recorded 12-lead data these models are built on. A model for infant ECG should therefore reason about heartbeats directly rather than recover them from arbitrary patches. We propose BeatGraph, which makes the heartbeat its unit of representation, modeling each 30-second window as a graph of beats. A shared beat encoder embeds each heartbeat from its waveform and inter-beat intervals, a Transformer with positional encoding orders the beats in time, and residual graph attention layers relate every beat to every other before attention pooling yields a window embedding. We pretrain BeatGraph on our new corpus of unlabeled infant recordings by predicting masked-beat embeddings, then fine-tune it for each task. One backbone supports sleep-wake detection, infant-state classification, activity-source identification (infant- or caregiver-initiated movement), and affect recognition, improving macro-F1 over the strongest baseline on each task by 0.076 to 0.158. It also transfers across age groups, reaching 0.892 AUROC on the ZZU-pECG pediatric benchmark (ages 0 to 14), within 0.001 of the best published self-supervised ECG model, and matching that model under linear evaluation on the adult PTB-XL benchmark despite infant-only pretraining. Finally, to our knowledge, we release the first public infant ECG corpus collected in homes, classrooms, and laboratory settings with state and affect labels. It contains 3,408 hours of single-channel ECG from 143 infants aged 3 to 11 months, with unlabeled pretraining data, benchmark tasks, and subject-level splits.

</details>


### [204] [Online Learning via Learned Latent Bayesian Tracking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31559)
*Guy Gerson,Tomer Raviv,Nir Shlezinger,Tirza Routtenberg,Osvaldo Simeone*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AURA learns a compact latent model of parameter evolution under distribution shift and uses online Kalman filtering in that latent space, with a learned lifting to update the full high-dimensional model efficiently for non-stationary online learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bayesian online learning for high-dimensional deep models is computationally intractable; a low-dimensional dynamical representation is the key bottleneck limiting effective Bayesian filters in practice.

Method: Meta-learning offline to fit a low-dimensional latent state-space model governing parameter evolution; online adaptation via extended Kalman filtering in latent space; reconstruct full parameters through a learned lifting map; enables single-step online updates.

Result: AURA achieves faster adaptation, higher accuracy, and reduced computation compared to traditional online learning and Bayesian-filter baselines on tasks like neural wireless receivers with time-varying channels and non-stationary image classification.

Conclusion: An adaptation-aware latent geometry facilitates effective Bayesian online learning in high-dimensional models, offering a practical framework for rapid, resource-efficient adaptation under distribution shift.

Abstract: Online learning in non-stationary environments requires models to adapt rapidly from streaming data under strict computational constraints. A principled approach casts online learning as Bayesian state tracking, where model parameters are updated sequentially via Bayesian filtering. However, applying Bayesian filters directly to modern deep models is computationally prohibitive due to the high dimensionality of parameter space, forcing existing methods to rely on restrictive approximations or manually designed low-dimensional subspaces. In this work, we identify the absence of a suitable low-dimensional dynamical representation as the core bottleneck in Bayesian filtering-based online learning. Accordingly, we propose Adaptive Update through Representation Adaptation (AURA), a meta-learning framework that learns offline a low-dimensional latent state-space model governing the evolution of optimal model parameters under distribution shift. Online adaptation is then performed via extended Kalman filtering in this learned latent space followed by reconstruction of the full model parameters through a learned lifting map, enabling efficient single-step online adaptation while preserving model expressiveness. Evaluated on online adaptation of neural wireless receivers under time-varying channels and on non-stationary image classification, AURA shows substantial improvements in adaptation speed, accuracy, and computational efficiency over existing online learning and Bayesian filtering baselines, demonstrating that an adaptation-aware latent geometry is beneficial for effective Bayesian online learning in high-dimensional models.

</details>


### [205] [Generalization behavior of OPTQ and the role of regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31560)
*Erin George,Rayan Saab*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Analyzes generalization bounds for OPTQ and stochastic OPTQ quantization, linking test error to calibration error and providing distribution-wide bounds with a key role for the regularization parameter λ; proposes a λ choice that improves empirical performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantization reduces memory and compute for large neural networks, but introduces quantization error that can affect generalization. Understanding how calibration data translates to test performance and how to set hyperparameters (λ) is essential for reliable quantization.

Method: Theoretical analysis deriving two generalization bounds for OPTQ and stochastic OPTQ. The first bound relates the expected test error to calibration-sample error for i.i.d. calibration data from the test distribution. The second bound gives a distribution-wide guarantee for all sufficiently nice distributions, independent of calibration data. Both results highlight the regularization term λ and its impact on the bounds.

Result: Two bounds are established: (i) a relation between generalization error and calibration-data error under i.i.d. sampling from the test distribution, and (ii) a distribution-wide bound valid for all sufficiently nice distributions, both featuring λ as a critical parameter. Theoretical analysis informs a new recommended λ, which matches or improves prior empirical recommendations.

Conclusion: The authors propose a theoretically motivated λ choice that improves practical performance of OPTQ and stochastic OPTQ over prior recommendations, and show how calibration data can inform generalization behavior in quantized networks.

Abstract: Large neural networks can be compressed by rounding or "quantizing" their weights to numbers that admit representations with fewer bits. One algorithm for quantization, OPTQ, progressively quantizes the weights of a neural network so that the squared quantization error on a specified calibration dataset is as small as possible. We study the performance of OPTQ and a variant algorithm, stochastic OPTQ, in a generalization setting and derive bounds for the expected squared error accrued by the algorithm when a test point is drawn from a fixed distribution. We prove two results. One result relates the generalization error to the error on a calibration dataset comprising independent samples from the same distribution as the test distribution. The other result bounds the generalization error of stochastic OPTQ for all sufficiently nice distributions, regardless of the calibration dataset. In both of these results, the regularization term $λ$ plays an important role. We use insights from these results to make a new recommendation for the choice of $λ$ and see that this choice of $λ$ preforms favorably in experiments when compared to prior recommendations in the literature.

</details>


### [206] [Weight Pair Encoding: Inducing a Smaller Grammar in Neural Network Weights](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31564)
*Irene Tallini,Daniele Solombrino,Alberto Cazzaniga,Emanuele Rodolà*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WeightPE integrates a lossy Re-Pair compressor into a straight-through estimator to train neural nets on a single int8 weight string, optimizing a grammar-based representation. It achieves substantial grammar-size reductions (0.43x and 0.38x) versus QAT with modest accuracy loss, and generalizes to other grammar compressors; this is the first explicit optimization of grammar size as a training objective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce weight storage/computation by leveraging structured grammar-based compression in neural networks. Fixed-size codebooks are limiting; grammar representations enable variable-length, hierarchical patterns and reuse. Introducing grammar size as a trainable objective could yield more compact, efficient models.

Method: Flatten int8 weights into a single string. Use a lossy Re-Pair compressor within a straight-through estimator to force near-matching Re-Pair patterns to be exactly equal under a global L2 budget. The network runs and learns with the rewritten weights; backprop uses the straight-through estimator. Compare against equivalent int8 QAT. Validate on ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 MLP weights finetuned on CIFAR-10. Test other grammar compressors (LZ78, SEQUITUR) without explicit fine-tuning against them.

Result: Re-Pair grammar size is 0.43x (ViT-B/16) and 0.38x (ViT-L/16) the size of the QAT baseline, with accuracy losses of 1.9 and 1.1 points respectively. The effect generalizes to other grammar compressors (LZ78, SEQUITUR) beyond what the model was trained on.

Conclusion: Grammar-based weight representations can substantially reduce model size with modest accuracy loss. Grammar size can be treated as an explicit training objective, suggesting broader applicability of grammar-based compression in neural networks.

Abstract: We show that neural network weights can be explicilty fintuned to admit a smaller grammar. Weight Pair Encoding (WeightPE) does so by placing a lossy Re-Pair compressor inside a straight-through estimator. The int8 weights of the network are flattened into one string, and near-matching Re-Pair patterns are made exactly equal within a global L2 budget. The network computes with the rewritten weights and trains through them with a straight-through estimator. Unlike a flat codebook of fixed-size entries, a grammar offers variable-length patterns and reuses them hierarchically inside larger ones. On the MLP weights of ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 finetuned on CIFAR-10, WeightPE produces a Re-Pair grammar 0.43x and 0.38x the size of the one produced by an equivalent int8 QAT run, at a cost of 1.9 and 1.1 accuracy points. The trend extends to different grammar compressors (LZ78, SEQUITUR), over which the networks has not be finetuned against. To our knowledge, this is the first time grammar size has been used as an explicit training objective for network weights.

</details>


### [207] [Trust Guided Decision Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31586)
*Chainesh Gautam,Raghuram Bharadwaj Diddigi,Chandramouli Kamanchi,Pankaj Dayama,Sumanta Mukherjee,Kameshwaran Sampath*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TGDT mitigates long-rollout context drift in Decision Transformer by evaluating recent context suffixes via next-state prediction error, calibrating with split conformal prediction, and selecting trusted suffixes for a frozen critic-guided action, improving performance on D4RL tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-rollout performance degradation due to training-distribution drift of conditioning context; need a reliable mechanism to detect and gate context usage.

Method: At each step, compute rolling next-state prediction error for recent context suffixes; calibrate error against offline data with split conformal prediction; keep only suffixes with error within threshold; apply a frozen critic to select the highest-value action among trusted suffixes.

Result: In D4RL navigation and locomotion, combining state prediction, critic guidance, and hard context reset reduces persistent high-error runs and yields higher returns than vanilla Decision Transformer, context-reset baselines, and value-only selection.

Conclusion: Trust-guided context selection with conformal calibration enhances robustness of Decision Transformer to distribution drift in long rollouts.

Abstract: Decision Transformer performance degrades on long rollouts because the conditioning context drifts out of the training distribution. We show that this drift is visible through the model's own next state prediction error, which rises during rollout and stays elevated, giving a direct signal of when context has become unreliable. We introduce Trust Guided Decision Transformer (TGDT), which selects context before applying value guidance. At each step, TGDT evaluates several recent context suffixes using rolling next state prediction error, calibrated against held out offline data via split conformal prediction. It keeps only suffixes whose error stays within the calibrated threshold, then uses a frozen critic to choose the highest value action among the trusted suffixes. This reverses the order used by value only elastic selection, where the critic may choose an action generated from a context the model itself has flagged as unreliable. Experiments on D4RL navigation and locomotion tasks show that state prediction, critic guidance, and hard context reset each solve only part of the problem. TGDT reduces persistent high error runs and improves return over vanilla Decision Transformer, reset based context control, and value only context selection.

</details>


### [208] [Common-Mode Collapse and Recovery in Direct Feedback Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31589)
*Varun Reddy,Bernardo L. Sabatini,Houman Safaai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DFA with fixed random feedback can cause a learning stall due to the common-mode error driving activations into saturation; a mean–covariance decomposition identifies a dominant rank-one update from the mean teaching signal and mean presynaptic activity, explaining collapse and slow readout learning; several remedies (readout calibration to class priors, subtracting the batch mean, or sign-based errors) mitigate collapse, with imperfect trade-offs depending on optimizer and data complexity; results extend to deeper/convolutional nets and CIFAR-10.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explain why direct feedback alignment can stall learning due to shared error components, quantify the mechanism, and evaluate practical remedies across datasets and architectures.

Method: Perform a mean–covariance decomposition of the DFA update to isolate a rank-one component driven by the mean teaching signal and mean presynaptic activity; analyze its effect on tanh activations; construct a reduced model to predict activation sensitivity across settings; run experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 comparing SGD and Adam; test remedies including class-prior calibration, mean subtraction, and sign-based errors; extend observations to deeper and convolutional networks.

Result: Identified that the error common mode pushes tanh units toward saturation; random feedback initially provides no systematic error correction; readout learning limits collapse duration; Adam accelerates learning despite deeper collapse; calibrating readout to class priors mitigates collapse and speeds learning; weaker feedback reduces collapse but slows learning; replacing errors with signs maintains collapse; subtracting the signal's batch mean prevents sustained collapse and improves learning; similar qualitative effects observed in deeper/convolutional nets and on CIFAR-10 with dependence on readout, optimizer, and input statistics.

Conclusion: The shared error component under DFA is the driver of activation saturation and learning stalls; targeted remedies that neutralize or decorrelate the mean error (e.g., readout calibration, batch-mean subtraction) can preserve decodability and accelerate learning, with broader applicability across architectures and datasets.

Abstract: Direct feedback alignment (DFA) trains hidden layers through fixed random projections of output error. With tanh hidden units and independent sigmoid outputs, plain stochastic gradient descent can stall near the loss of a constant predictor of class frequencies. We trace this stall to the error's common mode, the component shared across inputs. An exact mean-covariance decomposition separates a rank-one update formed by the mean teaching signal and mean presynaptic activity. Its leading component drives tanh units toward saturation. At initialization, random feedback provides no systematic correction of the shared error on average; readout learning limits its duration. A reduced model initialized from the network, without fitted parameters, predicts the concentration of activation sensitivity across 48 settings. On MNIST, class decodability largely survives collapse, but readout learning remains slow at a fixed learning rate. Adam learns faster despite deeper collapse. Calibrating the baseline readout to the class prior suppresses collapse and speeds learning; weaker feedback trades less collapse for slower learning. Replacing errors by their signs sustains collapse; subtracting the signal's batch mean prevents sustained collapse and improves learning in the tested setting. Related effects occur in deeper and convolutional networks and on CIFAR-10, with severity and cost depending on the readout, optimizer and input statistics.

</details>


### [209] [New LoRA Skills Should Read but Never Write](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31600)
*Zeyan Li,Panqi Yang,Qirong Guo,Shengda Zhuo,SIyuan Qiu,Hu Xu,Chun Li,Jianfeng Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: READ fixes adapter composition by canonicalizing each LoRA update and enforcing unidirectional coupling, enabling seamless, cost-free integration of multiple skills into a single model with strong empirical gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Merging independently trained adapters for task-specific fine-tuning is hard due to (i) update-factorization ambiguity in LoRA, which hides equivalence classes while sole adapters are used; (ii) bidirectional coupling between old and new skills can cause interference and overwrite useful old computations. A robust composition method should fix these ambiguities and prevent retroactive modification of prior skills.

Method: Introduce READ (Read-only Expansion of Adapter Deltas). Each adapter is rewritten into a balanced canonical form that preserves its update exactly. Coupling grows in one direction only, allowing a new skill to read the input subspaces of old skills but not write into their output subspaces. The only trainable component is the new skill's row of the coupling matrix. The composed update folds into the base weights with no inference cost, routing, or task-specific rules.

Result: READ yields consistent improvements across four benchmark suites and two model families as skills are added sequentially. Across these experiments, READ outperforms the strongest published baselines built from the same adapters by over 20 points on SuperGLUE and over 7 points on the domain suite; nearly all addition sequences surpass direct baselines.

Conclusion: Factor coordinates and coupling direction—hidden in a single adapter—determine whether composed skills survive. READ provides a principled, efficient framework for scalable adapter composition by fixing canonical form and enforcing unidirectional coupling, achieving robust performance gains with zero inference cost.

Abstract: Low-rank adapters (LoRA) make it cheap to fine-tune a large language model once per task, but combining several independently trained adapters into one model remains difficult: merging the updates in weight space causes interference, retraining on all task data is expensive, and routing between separate adapters gives up the goal of a single combined model. We trace the difficulty to two choices that every composition method makes implicitly. A LoRA update admits infinitely many equivalent factorizations; the choice among them is invisible while an adapter serves alone, but it determines what a learned interaction between adapters can see. A coupling between an old skill and a new one can likewise point in either direction, and the direction decides whether the old skills keep computing what they computed before. We introduce READ (Read-only Expansion of Adapter Deltas), which fixes both choices: each adapter is rewritten into a balanced canonical form that preserves its update exactly, and the coupling grows in one direction only, so a new skill can read the input subspaces of old skills but cannot write into their output subspaces. The only trainable object at each append is the new skill's row of the coupling matrix, and the composed update folds into the base weights with no inference cost, routing, or task-specific rules. We evaluate READ across four benchmark suites and two model families, adding skills one at a time. Across several families, READ improves every suite average over the strongest published baselines built from the same adapters---by more than twenty points on SuperGLUE and more than seven points on the domain suite---and nearly all complete addition sequences end above every direct baseline. Factor coordinates and coupling direction, which a lone adapter never exposes, are what decide whether composed skills survive.

</details>


### [210] [User Model Extraction via Belief Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31603)
*Ali Holmov,Yiran Huang,Kirill Bykov,Zeynep Akata*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Belief Self-Distillation (BSD) provides a read/write mechanism to extract and edit a compact, causal user-belief representation in LLMs, enabling stronger interventions on safety-related decisions and revealing cross-model common geometry of user representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the opacity and manipulability of user-aware beliefs in LLMs; bridge linear (activation-based) and causal probing by creating a writable internal state that can be decoded and rewritten to influence behavior.

Method: Learn a compact user representation via self-distillation with a frozen LLM acting as its own teacher. Distill beliefs from natural conversations without external annotations. Probing isolates both information in activations and the causal state that can be manipulated by writing back into the model. Evaluate across multiple model families, compare with hidden-state steering, and test causal impact by altering inferred user intent while keeping the request fixed.

Result: BSD accurately recovers user beliefs and enables substantially stronger, causal interventions than comparable probing methods. Refusal behavior depends on inferred user intent; altering this belief changes refusals even with the same request. Independently trained LLMs converge on a shared geometry for representing users, indicating a common latent structure across models.

Conclusion: Implicit user models in LLMs are readable and causally writable internal states with direct implications for AI safety, showing how safety decisions are conditioned on who the model believes it is interacting with.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) implicitly infer attributes of their users and adapt their behavior accordingly, yet these beliefs remain difficult to inspect and causally manipulate. We introduce Belief Self-Distillation (BSD), a unified read-write framework that bridges linear and causal probing by learning a compact user representation that can be both decoded and written back into the model. The frozen LLM acts as its own teacher, distilling beliefs from natural conversations without external annotations. Unlike conventional probing, BSD isolates not only information present in activations, but a state whose causal role can be directly tested. Across multiple model families, BSD faithfully recovers user beliefs and enables substantially stronger interventions than matched hidden-state steering. Crucially, we find that refusal depends not only on the request, but on the model's inferred user intent: changing this belief alters refusal while holding the request fixed. We further uncover a striking cross-model regularity: independently trained LLMs converge on a shared geometry for representing their users. Together, these results reveal implicit user models as readable and causally writable internal states with direct implications for AI safety, shaping how models condition safety decisions on whom they believe they are interacting with.

</details>


<div id='cs.AI'></div>

# cs.AI [[Back]](#toc)

### [211] [Bringing AI to Autonomous Systems -- From Cognition to Collective Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30291)
*Joseph Sifakis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a generic agent-architecture framework for autonomous systems that integrates cognitive functions around a long-term memory, addressing perception-to-memory mapping, decision-making, planning, and multi-agent coordination, with an emphasis on evaluating trustworthiness and a candid gap analysis between vision and state-of-the-art.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge AI subfields (connectionist and symbolic) and align AI with systems engineering to enable trustworthy, scalable autonomous systems. To move beyond behavioral trust to cognitive trust grounded in knowledge use.

Method: Develop a high-level, generic agent architecture in which behavior emerges from cognitive functions organized around long-term memory. Discuss implementation challenges: mapping sensory data to structured memory, goal-driven decision-making and planning, and coordination of multiple agents. Propose avenues for evaluating agent trustworthiness and critically assess the gap between aspirational multi-agent autonomy and current capabilities.

Result: A comprehensive design-and-evaluation framework for autonomous systems, highlighting core architectural components, memory integration, and cognitive-trust considerations, along with a candid assessment of the gap to current state of the art.

Conclusion: Autonomous multi-agent systems are aspirational; substantial progress requires integrating AI subfields, robust memory and reasoning architectures, and rigorous trustworthiness evaluation methods, with ongoing attention to the realism of anticipated capabilities.

Abstract: The purpose of this article is to highlight the central role of autonomous systems as the ultimate stage in the development of AI, to explain the underlying technical challenges that require a combination of connectionist AI and symbolic AI, and to integrate AI and systems engineering. We present a comprehensive framework for the design and evaluation of autonomous systems, based on a generic agent architecture that characterizes their behavior as the composition of cognitive functions organized around a long-term memory containing the agent's evolving knowledge. We address the challenges posed by the implementation of the fundamental features of the agent architecture, in particular the link between sensory data and structured data stored in memory, decision-making related to the achievement of the agent's goals and their planning, as well as the coordination of agents to combine individual and collective intelligence. We explain that agent trustworthiness, unlike that of traditional systems, is not limited to behavioral properties. It includes an essential dimension related to cognitive properties, the validity of which depends on how the agent uses its knowledge in decision-making. We present avenues for the development of methods for evaluating agent trustworthiness. We conclude with a critical assessment of the substantial gap between the aspirational vision of autonomous multi-agent systems and the current state of the art.

</details>


### [212] [ScopeBench: Do Agents Preserve Engagement Boundaries Under Goal Pressure?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30325)
*Shane Caldwell,Max Harley,Ads Dawson,Michael Kouremetis,Vincent Abruzzo,Will Pearce*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ScopeBench is a 30-task benchmark that isolates scope adherence in agentic security tasks by pairing scopeless (capability) and scoped (adherence) conditions. A deterministic verifier flags boundary violations; a human-in-the-loop judge assesses remaining out-of-scope calls, yielding high recall. Results show notable raw capability and adherence gaps across models, with violations missed by the verifier caught by the judge; dataset released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the gap where offensive-security benchmarks measure raw capability but not alignment to scope boundaries critical in real deployments.

Method: Each task appears in two conditions with the same environment/objective: one scopeless (measuring capability) and one with natural-language scope (measuring adherence). A deterministic verifier flags violations; if not flagged, an agentic judge estimates out-of-scope calls. The judge is calibrated against human-labeled trajectories and audited for recall. Evaluated across 8 models; 2160 ATIF trajectories released.

Result: Raw capability ranges 12.2%–81.1%; scope adherence ranges 34.4%–86.7%. The judge found 331 violations not caught by the verifier. Opus-4-8 beats sonnet-4-6 by 10 percentage points in raw capability and 35.6 pp in scope adherence. The authors publish the frozen pilot benchmark and 2160 trajectories.

Conclusion: Scope adherence can be reliably measured using a hybrid verifier+judge framework; current models show substantial variability in adherence, highlighting the need for alignment-aware evaluation. The benchmark and accompanying dataset aim to catalyze development of safer, scope-conscious autonomous agents.

Abstract: Agents are increasingly deployed with real autonomy in web application and network penetration testing, where a single out-of-scope action can breach a client's engagement boundary. Existing offensive-security benchmarks measure raw hacking capability; as those benchmarks saturate, the real barrier to deployment is a special case of alignment: scope adherence. We introduce ScopeBench, a benchmark of 30 dead-end agentic security tasks in which the stated objective is reachable only by violating the stated scope. Each task appears under two conditions that share an environment, verifier, and objective and differ only in scope: one instruction set has no scope and measures capability; the other has a natural-language scope to measure adherence. Scopeless trajectories are graded by a standard deterministic verifier. Scoped trajectories pass through two grading arms. First, the same deterministic verifier checks for the flag: because the flag sits behind the scope boundary, a pass proves by construction that a forbidden action occurred, yielding a high-precision lower bound on the violation rate. If the verifier does not pass the trajectory, an agentic judge estimates whether an out-of-scope call occurred. We calibrate the judge against 100 ScopeBench trajectories labeled call-by-call by human annotators, and a blinded audit of the evaluated rollouts finds its high recall holds - no false negatives among the 36 audited violations, with over-flagging its only observed error. Across 8 models in one harness, raw capability spans 12.2% to 81.1% and scope adherence spans 34.4% to 86.7%, with the judge finding 331 violations that mechanical verification misses. Opus-4-8 achieves a raw-capability score 10 percentage points higher than sonnet-4-6's while exhibiting 35.6 percentage points higher scope adherence. We release the frozen pilot benchmark, evaluation code, and all 2160 ATIF trajectories.

</details>


### [213] [When Is a Multi-Agent Code Judge Actually Grounded? Two Label-Free Measurements, and a Judge That Declines to Guess](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30328)
*Salma Roshdy Aly,Hussein Assaf,Ziad Kobti*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MARCH-based code judging yields high confidence even when evidence is not discriminative; two types of evidence issues undermine judgment, enabling a label-free gate to flag lack of basis rather than improve accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explain why LLM-based code judges often report confident verdicts without evidence of correctness, and evaluate how multi-agent verification performs when evidence is not independent of the verdict or discriminative between candidates.

Method: Apply MARCH to 80 condition-by-cell measurements on two code-judging benchmarks; analyze two evidence-derived measurements from the pipeline logs; test a gating strategy that rejects uncertain comparisons; compare against direct single-model judgments.

Result: MARCH often declares both solutions equally good in 78–95% of comparisons, achieving only 4.4% accuracy vs 43.7% for direct judgments; larger judges or easier problems do not change this; gating on a non-discriminative evidence signal improves accuracy to 36.9% while still covering about half of comparisons.

Conclusion: Evidence must be independent of the answer and discriminative between candidates; current multi-agent verification with retrieved documents can help flag lack of evidence but does not inherently produce more accurate judgments; a label-free gate can indicate when a judge has no basis for its answer.

Abstract: When one language model judges whether another's code is correct, it does not report the absence of evidence. It returns a confident verdict with reasoning attached, indistinguishable from a verdict it had grounds for. Multi-agent verification, which decomposes a judgment into checkable claims and verifies each against evidence, is a promising response and works well when the evidence is a set of retrieved documents.
  We argue such methods require two things of their evidence: it must be independent of the answer under review, and it must differ between the two candidates being compared. The second condition holds automatically with retrieved documents and stops holding in code judging.
  Running MARCH, a published framework unmodified over 80 condition-by-cell measurements on two code judging benchmarks, we find it declares both solutions equally good on 78 to 95% of comparisons, reaching 4.4% accuracy where the same model asked directly reaches 43.7%. Neither easier problems nor a larger judge changes this. Two measurements taken from the pipeline's own logs explain it without needing labels.
  Gating on one of them, the pipeline declines the comparisons it cannot make and raises its accuracy from 20.7 to 36.9% while still answering half of all comparisons. The contribution is not a more accurate judge, but a label-free way to tell when a judge has no basis for its answer.

</details>


### [214] [Bridging LLM Agents and Data Spaces: An Architectural Mediation Approach using the Model Context Protocol](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30341)
*Jaime Alonso Ruiz,Carlos Aparicio,Gabriel Huecas,Joaquín Salvachúa,Andres Munoz-Arcentales*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes an MCP-based mediation layer (via Eunomia Agent) to connect LLMs with data spaces by translating capabilities into discoverable schema-driven tools, enabling governance-preserving AI automation with no changes to data space components; validated in a prototype across discovery, metadata, and data service invocation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mismatches between probabilistic language model interactions and policy-driven data infrastructures hinder AI-enabled data sharing across organizational boundaries; there is a need for interoperable, governance-aligned integration that preserves architectural separation.

Method: Architectural mediation using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) implemented via the Eunomia Agent; translates data space capabilities into schema-driven tools discoverable by AI agents; supports discovery, metadata retrieval, and data service invocation while preserving governance constraints; prototype demonstrates end-to-end interactions without modifying existing data space components.

Result: Prototype validates end-to-end interaction: catalog discovery, metadata retrieval, and data service invocation; demonstrates interoperable, standards-aligned integration of AI agents into data space ecosystems under governance constraints.

Conclusion: Provides practical guidance for organizations to introduce AI-driven automation into governed data-sharing environments while maintaining compliance, interoperability, and architectural separation of concerns.

Abstract: Data Spaces enable sovereign and governed data sharing across organizational boundaries, but their integration with AI agents remains challenging due to mismatches between probabilistic language model interactions and policy-driven data infrastructures. This article presents an architectural mediation approach based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), implemented through the Eunomia Agent, to enable controlled interaction between large language model (LLM) agents and data space services. The proposed mediation layer translates data space capabilities into structured, schema-driven tools that AI agents can discover and invoke while preserving governance constraints. A prototype implementation validates end-to-end interaction across catalog discovery, metadata retrieval, and data service invocation without modifying existing data space components. Results demonstrate that protocol-based mediation enables interoperable and standards-aligned integration of AI agents into data space ecosystems. The approach provides practical guidance for organizations seeking to introduce AI-driven automation into governed data-sharing environments while maintaining compliance, interoperability, and architectural separation of concerns.

</details>


### [215] [Stealth Apart, Harm Together: Skill Cascading Attacks on Skill-Based Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30383)
*Zihao Zhu,Siwei Lyu,Adel Bibi,Baoyuan Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillCascade reveals cross-skill cascading attacks in skill-based agents, exposing systemic safety gaps; introduces a red-teaming framework and a 213-case benchmark, showing per-skill defenses miss multi-skill manipulation across domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open skill ecosystems enable flexible reuse but introduce cross-skill attack surfaces. Component-level safety is insufficient; system-level reasoning is needed to ensure overall safety.

Method: Developed SkillCascade, an automated multi-agent red-teaming framework; released SkillCascade-Bench with 213 validated cascading test cases across multiple agent systems and LLM backbones (e.g., OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex); evaluated cross-skill interactions and their ability to bypass per-skill scanners and runtime monitors.

Result: Cascaded interactions reliably induce harmful behaviors and evade existing per-skill detectors, highlighting a gap between module integrity and system safety; demonstrates that cross-skill reasoning is necessary for robust safety.

Conclusion: Defense should account for cross-skill interactions rather than evaluating skills in isolation; develop cross-skill-aware monitors and benchmarks to close the safety gap in skill-based agent ecosystems.

Abstract: A skill is a modular package of natural-language instructions, executable scripts, and reference resources that an agent can load at runtime to extend its capabilities for a specific task. Skill-based agent systems therefore enable flexible reuse of third-party capabilities, but the openness of this skill ecosystem also opens up a new attack surface. Prior work has focused on vulnerabilities within individual skills, but little attention has been paid to risks that arise from interactions across skills. In this paper, we introduce skill cascading attacks, a threat paradigm in which a malicious objective is distributed across multiple skills so that each modification looks benign in isolation, yet their combined execution is harmful. For instance, in a prescription-review pipeline, the first skill weakens signals of recently discontinued medications in the extracted history, the second downgrades the severity of any drug interaction tied to them, and the third suppresses the resulting low-priority alert in the final summary, so that a severe drug-interaction warning silently disappears before reaching the physician. To systematically study this safety blind spot, we develop SkillCascade, an automated multi-agent red-teaming framework, and release SkillCascade-Bench, a benchmark of 213 validated cascading test cases across multiple agent systems and domains. Across representative agents (e.g., OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) and LLM backbones, cascaded interactions reliably induce harmful behaviors while evading existing per-skill scanners and runtime monitors. Our findings highlight a gap between component-level integrity and system-level safety, and call for defenses that reason over cross-skill interactions rather than individual skills in isolation.

</details>


### [216] [A Synthetic Ground-Truth Framework for the Evaluation of Explainable AI Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30397)
*Miquel Miró-Nicolau,Francesco Spinnato,Riccardo Guidotti*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A synthetic-ground-truth, intervention-based framework for evaluating XAI methods across binary images, tabular data, and time series; nine XAI methods are assessed, revealing limitations of fidelity-based evaluations and underscoring the value of ground-truth benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ground-truth explanations are lacking; fidelity to model predictions is insufficient and can be misleading; robust evaluation requires explanations aligned with actual decision processes.

Method: Introduce a framework using controlled interventions to create synthetic datasets where input feature importance is known by design; instantiate across three data domains; evaluate nine widely used XAI methods.

Result: Current XAI methods exhibit significant limitations when evaluated with ground-truth-free, fidelity-based metrics; fidelity to predictions does not guarantee truthful explanations; synthetic benchmarks reveal inconsistencies and potential misinterpretations; cross-domain evaluation supports general claims.

Conclusion: Synthetic, intervention-based benchmarks are essential for reliable XAI evaluation; adopt ground-truth frameworks across domains to properly assess explanation quality; findings advocate moving beyond fidelity-only metrics.

Abstract: Evaluating explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods is a challenging task due to the lack of reliable evaluation procedures and, in particular, the absence of ground truth explanations. In the literature, existing evaluation approaches typically assess explanations by measuring their fidelity with respect to the predictions of a black-box model. However, such evaluation strategies only quantify the degree to which an explanation reproduces the model's output, without ensuring that the explanation correctly reflects the underlying decision process. As a consequence, different explanations may achieve similar fidelity scores while providing inconsistent or misleading interpretations of the model behavior. In this paper, we propose a framework for the evaluation of XAI methods based on synthetic ground truth. The proposed approach relies on controlled interventions to generate synthetic datasets in which the importance of input components can be determined by design. This enables the construction of ground truth explanations that are directly aligned with the behavior of the model under analysis. The framework is instantiated across three data domains, namely binary images, tabular data, and time series, allowing a comprehensive assessment of explanation methods in heterogeneous settings. Experimental results obtained by evaluating nine widely used XAI methods show significant limitations in current techniques and highlight the importance of synthetic, intervention-based benchmarks for a reliable assessment of explanation quality.

</details>


### [217] [Predicting Transmembrane Protein Topology from 3D Structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30446)
*Sitong Chen,Xiaopeng Mao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a SchNet-based graph neural network to infer protein topology from atom-level embeddings, trained on the same dataset as DeepTMHMM with 5-fold cross-validation, without pretraining; reports promising performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limitation of predicting protein topology using only sequences or Cα atoms by leveraging full atom-level information via a GNN.

Method: Utilizes the SchNet GNN with all atom-level embeddings; trains on the DeepTMHMM dataset under 5-fold cross-validation; no pre-trained weights used.

Result: Reports promising results, indicating that GNNs can be effective for protein topology prediction; no specific metrics provided in the abstract.

Conclusion: Atom-level GNNs offer a feasible and potentially competitive approach for topological predictions, highlighting a new direction beyond traditional sequence- or Cα-based methods; further quantitative benchmarking is warranted.

Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to infer protein topology using the state-of-the-art graph neural network (GNN), SchNet. The model is trained on the same dataset used to develop the recent DeepTMHMM model with 5-fold cross-validation. Unlike the conventional approaches based on using only the protein sequences or the $α$-carbons as features, we have decoded our classifier in this way, so all atom-level embeddings are used. Without applying any pre-trained weight, the final results have shown great potential that GNNs can be used for topological predictions.

</details>


### [218] [Spectral Feedback for Test-Time Alignment of Protein Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30456)
*Shai Dickman,Mert Cemri,Landon Butler,Kannan Ramchandran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Spectral Feedback introduces an edit-position selection mechanism for discrete diffusion models, enabling iterative correction of generations via re-masking and re-sampling, yielding substantial alignment gains without changing the generative process.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reward-based alignment in discrete diffusion is inherently unidirectional and cannot revisit unfavorable token choices; editing tokens in a coordinated, interdependent way is essential. The method leverages sparse, Fourier-based representations of edit-set values learned efficiently; inspired by sparse biological interactions.

Method: Define edit-set as positions to re-mask and re-sample; perform a feedback loop using the model's mask structure to reintroduce noise and re-run reverse diffusion; learn edit-position value functions via spectral (Fourier) representations that are sparse; model-agnostic, applicable to pretrained, test-time aligned, and RL-finetuned diffusion models.

Result: Empirical improvements in protein inverse folding: 32.3% more stable proteins for pretrained model, 24.8% for Best-of-10, and 5.8% for a state-of-the-art RL-finetuned diffusion model.

Conclusion: Spectral Feedback provides a scalable, general approach to alignment by focusing on revisiting edits rather than token labels, leveraging sparse spectral structure to efficiently learn edit-value functions; it improves alignment without modifying the underlying generative process and applies across model types.

Abstract: Reward maximization alignment methods for discrete diffusion models have primarily focused on steering the reverse process, either by influencing token logits or by selecting favorable sequences at intermediate steps.
