These approaches largely treat inference as a unidirectional process, lacking mechanisms for revisiting undesirable token selections. We introduce Spectral Feedback, an algorithm that selects edit-positions in a feedback loop, allowing the model to iteratively correct its own generations. This approach leverages the mask structure of discrete diffusion models by re-masking and re-sampling tokens, analogous to image editing methods that reintroduce noisy latents and re-run the reverse process. While prior alignment methods focus on what token labels to assign to maximize a target reward, we instead treat which tokens to revisit as the central alignment problem. Selecting edit-positions is challenging because edit effects are interdependent: the impact of modifying one token depends on which others are edited simultaneously. We define an edit-set as a set of token positions to re-mask and re-sample. Motivated by prior work on sparse interactions in biological systems, we find empirically that edit-set value functions for protein inverse folding admit sparse Fourier representations. This structure enables Spectral Feedback to efficiently learn and optimize the value functions for edit-position selection. Spectral Feedback is model-agnostic and can be applied to pretrained, test-time aligned, and fine-tuned diffusion models. For all of these models, the algorithm improves alignment performance without modifying the underlying generative process. Applied to inverse folding with a protein stability reward oracle, it achieves a 32.3% increase in stable proteins for a pretrained model, 24.8% for Best-of-10, and 5.8% for a state-of-the-art RL fine-tuned diffusion model.

</details>


### [219] [Pretrained ASR Pseudo-labeling for Noisy Police Audio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30469)
*Kaavya Chaparala,Su Huang,Stephen L. Miller,Rhiannon N. Miller,Anjalie Field*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Systematic study of pseudo-labeling for adapting Whisper and Qwen3-ASR to very noisy Broadcast Police Communication (BPC) data from Baltimore and Chicago. Internal confidence metrics (log-probabilities, STAR) fail to distinguish pseudo-label quality; an external LLM-based judge filtering paradigm reduces WER on pseudo-labeled data, though an oracle filter remains superior; introduces a cross-model pseudo-labeling paradigm as a promising avenue.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable accurate transcription of noisy, domain-specific BPC data to support police decision-making, by leveraging unsupervised pseudo-labeling without costly human labeling.

Method: Evaluate foundation ASR models (Whisper and Qwen3-ASR) on Baltimore/Chicago BPC corpora; compare internal confidence metrics; develop LLM-based judging filters; assess cross-model pseudo-labeling where one model is finetuned on pseudo-labels from another.

Result: LLM-based judging filters outperform internal metrics, significantly reducing WER of pseudo-labeled training sets across both cities; performance approaches but does not reach an oracle filter; cross-model pseudo-labeling identified as a promising future direction.

Conclusion: LLM-driven quality filtering is effective for domain adaptation via pseudo-labeling in noisy BPC, but gaps remain; cross-model pseudo-labeling offers a promising path for future work.

Abstract: Pretrained ASR systems perform poorly on noisy Broadcast Police Communication (BPC), hindering efforts to understand police decision-making. Pseudo-labeling offers an unsupervised path to improve ASR without expensive human labels, but the efficacy of this approach on very noisy domains is not known. In this work, we systematically assess the opportunities and limits of pseudo-labeling to adapt foundation ASR models (Whisper and Qwen3-ASR) to noisy BPC domain corpora from Baltimore and Chicago. We demonstrate that existing internal confidence metrics (log-probabilities and STAR scores) fail to distinguish between high and low quality BPC pseudo-labels, and we introduce an external LLM-as-a-judge filtering paradigm that leverages parametric knowledge to discard contextually implausible transcripts. Our LLM-judging filters more aggressively than internal metrics and significantly reduces WER of the pseudo-labeled training sets across the Baltimore and Chicago BPC corpora, though a substantial gap remains relative to an oracle filter. We also introduce a new cross-model pseudo-labeling paradigm where one model is finetuned with pseudo-labels from the other, and we identify this method as a promising direction for future pseudo-labeling work.

</details>


### [220] [Do LLMs Understand Context? A Knowledge Graph-Based Evaluation Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30484)
*Subavarshana Arumugam,Mamta Nallaretnam,Kithuni Wickramasinghe,Chamath Gunapala,Pragatheeswaran Vipulanandan,Kamal Premaratne,Uthayasanker Thayasivam*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces S3KG, a knowledge-graph-based evaluation framework for LLM contextual understanding in QA, with a diagnostic triplet-level error analysis; shows up to +7.6 F1 and AUROC 0.973 across nine benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current QA evaluation often relies on surface-level metrics (e.g., BLEU, perplexity) that miss context-grounded reasoning. There is a need for a KG-based, structurally informed evaluation that can assess whether LLMs reason over context and produce factually grounded answers.

Method: Define Semantic Structural Similarity for KGs (S3KG) as a hybrid score combining structural signals from the KG with semantic signals from entities/relations; apply it to QA outputs to measure contextual understanding. Develop a diagnostic analysis framework to categorize reasoning errors at the triplet level for fine-grained failure analysis. Evaluate across nine benchmarks with metrics such as F1 and AUROC.

Result: S3KG achieves up to +7.6 points in F1 over the strongest baseline and AUROC up to 0.973.

Conclusion: S3KG provides a more granular and robust evaluation of LLM contextual understanding in QA, enabling precise diagnosis of errors and improved benchmarking across multiple datasets.

Abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable linguistic capabilities, a profound question lingers at their core: do these models truly comprehend context or simply excel at pattern matching on an unprecedented scale? Contextual understanding in LLMs refers to the ability to correctly extract relevant information from a given context, integrate it into a coherent internal representation, and reason over it to produce factually consistent and contextually grounded responses. However, traditional methods such as BiLingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) and perplexity simply measure surface-level performance. This reveals a critical gap in question answering (QA), where responses must be contextually grounded rather than simply being memorized associations. To fill this void, we propose a novel knowledge graph (KG) based evaluation framework for LLM contextual understanding in QA. Central to this is Semantic Structural Similarity for KGs (S3KG), a hybrid similarity measure combining structural and semantic signals into a single score. In addition, a diagnostic analysis framework is developed to identify and categorize reasoning errors at the triplet level, enabling fine-grained analysis of model failures. Together, across nine benchmarks, S3KG achieves F1 gains of up to $+7.6$ points over the strongest baseline and AUROC up to $0.973$.

</details>


### [221] [BioEVAL: A global, multi-institutional benchmark of large language and multimodal models for bioengineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30489)
*Shun Ye,Vinny Chandran Suja,Chenlong Li,Chongming Jiang,Reza Zamani,Xiang Li,Christopher Bain,Yuqi Zhou,Walker Peterson,Huidong Wang,Chenglang Hu,Jongchan Park,Xiao Cheng,Benjamin Swedlund,Sandra Murillo,Anjali Sivanandan,Shiyu Sun,Liang Lanfeng,Mohammad Tariqul Islam,Baju C. Joy,Ishaq N. Khan,Sreedhar S. Kumar,Gabriel Mercado-Vásquez,James V. Vizzard,Jonathan M. Matthews,Helen Huang,Xiaolu Guo,Ethan Nicklow,Guorui Chen,Ryan A. Neff,Surjendu Maity,Hyeonjin Park,Han-ho Joo,Katherine Dong,Yuyan Cai,Weihang Huang,Yichen Zou,Rui Yan,Raphael Figueroa,Artem Goncharov,Bella Rose Schremmer,Lian Elsa Linton,Keisuke Goda,Liang Gao,Ke Cheng,Leonardo Morsut,Jennifer L. Wilson,Jianping Fu,Lim Chwee Teck,Deblina Sarkar,Andreas Hierlemann,Savaş Tay,Alexander Hoffmann,Donald Richieri Griffin,Jun Chen,Shana O. Kelley,Shyni Varghese,Jinwoo Cheon,Wilbur A. Lam,James J. Moon,Wilson W. Wong,Samir Mitragotri,Dino Di Carlo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BioEVAL is a global BE benchmark assessing experimental reasoning across subfields via 359 retained MCQs, literature synthesis tasks, and 10 multimodal problems; shows up to 90% MCQ accuracy, 0.72 literature similarity, and 80% multimodal accuracy; built with expert QC, blinded audits, and extensible protocols; useful for benchmarking but limited by subfield variability and relatively few multimodal items.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the gap in bioengineering AI evaluation by moving beyond factual recall to experimental reasoning and multimodal interpretation; provide a scalable, exam-style benchmark across BE subfields.

Method: Global, multi-institutional collaboration (22 groups) across 11 BE subfields plus uncategorized items. 608 evaluation items: 380 MCQs (359 retained after audit), 218 literature synthesis tasks, 10 multimodal problems. Expert-reviewed item authoring, centralized QC, blinded consensus audit to flag high/low-accuracy MCQs for revision/removal. Evaluation of diverse cloud-scale and local models. Standardized protocols for ongoing item contribution and evaluation.

Result: Top-performing models achieve up to ~90% on MCQs, a 0.72 similarity on literature synthesis, and ~80% accuracy on a small set of multimodal tasks; notable performance variation across subfields; a leaderboard summarizes capabilities and gaps.

Conclusion: BioEVAL provides an extensible, standardized benchmark to quantify experimental-reasoning and multimodal capabilities in BE LLMs, guiding development priorities and future iterations; includes robust QA processes and ongoing item maintenance.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated historic breakthroughs in general reasoning with early successes in biomedical science. However, existing LLM benchmarking emphasizes factual recall, offering limited insight into model performance on frontier and multimodal tasks. We assembled BioEVAL (BioEngineering Validation of AI and LLMs), a global, multi-institutional initiative designed to assess experimental reasoning capability across bioengineering (BE) subfields. BioEVAL spans 11 major BE subfields plus a set of uncategorized items, bringing together 22 research groups to create a PhD-level benchmark comprising 608 evaluation items: 1) 380 multiple-choice questions (MCQs, 359 retained after audit), 2) 218 literature synthesis tasks, and 3) 10 multimodal problems with experimental image interpretation. Benchmark items underwent authoring-group expert review and centralized quality control before evaluation. Following evaluation, a blinded cross-group consensus audit of the highest- and lowest-accuracy MCQ items flagged 21 questions for revision or removal; these were withheld, and all reported MCQ results are computed on the 359 retained items. We evaluated diverse cloud-scale foundation/multimodal models (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok) and locally deployable models suitable for inference on consumer-grade GPUs. Models achieved the highest accuracy of up to 90% on MCQs, similarity score of 0.72 on literature synthesis, and accuracy of 80% on a small sample of multimodal reasoning questions, with substantial performance variation across subfields. Leaderboard rankings characterize current capabilities, limitations, and development priorities across the evaluated BE task categories. BioEVAL is maintained as an extensible benchmark with standardized protocols for continuing expert item contribution and model evaluation.

</details>


### [222] [Benchy: towards a universal language for task-oriented AI benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30550)
*Francis F Daniel,Mauro Ibañez,Francis Perelman,Marian Basti*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Benchy presents a semantic language and engine to define, compile, and execute benchmarks for AI programs. Benchmarks are B=(P,S,D) specified in canonical YAML, deterministically compiled to a JSON IR, and run against an AI system via a universal runtime contract; semantics are decoupled from integration mechanics. The paper provides the semantic object model, ontology, validation rules, scoring/failure semantics, and the compilation/execution architecture, plus an appendix fixing the engine contract.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To achieve reproducible, architecture-agnostic AI benchmarking by separating benchmark semantics from AI implementations and mandating a canonical representation and execution contract.

Method: Define a semantic object model and ontology; specify a task-to-program validation rule; establish scoring and failure semantics; design a compilation step (YAML to canonical JSON) that changes representation but not meaning; implement a universal runtime contract with fixed input/output schemas; outline the compilation/execution architecture and current language scope; provide an appendix documenting the normative engine contract.

Result: Provides a formal specification and architecture for Benchy, detailing the semantic model, ontology, validation rules, scoring and failure semantics, compilation/execution pipeline, and the scope of the language, along with an appendix that fixes the engine contract.

Conclusion: The work delivers a decoupled, formal benchmarking framework that enables reproducible AI evaluations by enforcing a canonical representation, a strict boundary between benchmarks and AI systems, and a normative engine contract, while outlining current language scope and future engineering commitments.

Abstract: Benchy is a semantic language and execution engine for benchmarking AI programs. A benchmark is completely specified by a program, a scoring function, and a dataset, B=(P,S,D), and is separate from the AI-system taking it; a run binds the two, R=(B,AI). Benchmarks are authored as canonical YAML in which each semantic concept has one valid syntax, classified by a shared task/domain/language ontology, and deterministically compiled into a canonical JSON intermediate representation that the engine executes. Compilation changes representation, not meaning: it does not repair invalid definitions or inject hidden defaults. Programs use fixed schemas of named input and output fields, the leaf output fields are the scoring dimensions, and the engine exposes one universal runtime contract --- a named-field input object in, a named-field output object out --- to which external AI-systems adapt at the boundary, so integration mechanics never propagate into benchmark semantics. This paper gives the semantic object model, the ontology and task-to-program validation rule, the scoring and failure semantics, the compilation and execution architecture, and the scope of the current language. An appendix fixes the normative engineering contract for the first engine implementation.

</details>


### [223] [Rank-Reliable Teacher-Guided Fitness Approximation for Expensive Evolutionary Optimization: A TinyML Architecture Search Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30553)
*Soumen Garai,Suman Samui*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TGL-NSGA-II is a low-fidelity NAS framework for constrained TinyML that uses a teacher-guided stratified evaluation, KD-Lite distillation on a small training set, and a GP surrogate to cheaply rank candidates. It achieves better rank correlation, reduces proxy-score variance, and accelerates search (2.2x) under budget, though it does not guarantee convergence of the full evolutionary trajectory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Expensive evolutionary search for neural architectures requires reliable relative ranking rather than exact fitness for every candidate, especially in TinyML where evaluation is costly. A low-fidelity, guided evaluation framework is needed.

Method: A pretrained teacher stratifies samples by difficulty and class. Each candidate undergoes KD-Lite distillation on a compact training set, followed by scoring on a stratified evaluation set. The teacher-guided score is fused with a Gaussian-process surrogate to select candidates for full evaluation. The framework includes a variance-aware fusion weight and a capacity-adaptive distillation rule.

Result: Kendall-τ values: 0.74 (skill 1) and 0.62 (skill 2), above lower bounds 0.60 and 0.46. Joint stratification reduces proxy-score variance by 41%. Selective teacher mismatch worsens differential bias, lowering Kendall-τ to 0.41. Under budget constraints, TGL-NSGA-II achieves the largest mean hypervolume and smallest generational distance on keyword spotting, and the lowest mean false-positive rate on BirdCLEF, with a 2.2× speedup over full NSGA-II. These guarantees apply to population-level low-fidelity evaluation; they do not ensure convergence of the complete evolutionary trajectory.

Conclusion: TGL-NSGA-II provides an effective, budget-conscious approach for NAS in TinyML, delivering strong rank correlations, reduced variance, and speedups, while acknowledging that full convergence of the evolutionary process remains unguaranteed.

Abstract: Expensive evolutionary search does not always need an exact fitness estimate for every candidate. It often needs a reliable answer to a simpler question: which candidate is better? We address this need through Teacher-Guided Learning NSGA-II (TGL-NSGA-II), a low-fidelity framework for constrained Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) neural architecture search. A pretrained teacher organizes samples into strata defined jointly by difficulty and class. Each candidate then undergoes KD-Lite, a short and capped knowledge-distillation procedure on a compact training set, before being scored on a separate stratified evaluation set. This teacher-guided score is fused with a Gaussian-process surrogate to select candidates for full evaluation. For a fixed candidate population, we analyse evaluation variance, score concentration, pairwise rank inversion, expected Kendall-$τ$, first-front identification, and hypervolume perturbation. We also derive a variance-aware fusion weight and a capacity-adaptive distillation rule. On keyword spotting and bird-call classification, the measured Kendall-$τ$ values are 0.74 and 0.62, exceeding the corresponding predicted lower bounds of 0.60 and 0.46. Joint stratification reduces proxy-score variance by 41% relative to random evaluation. Selective teacher mismatch, in contrast, increases differential bias and reduces Kendall-$τ$ to 0.41. Under a constrained evaluation budget, TGL-NSGA-II achieves the largest mean hypervolume and smallest generational distance on keyword spotting, records the lowest mean false-positive rate on BirdCLEF, and runs 2.2x faster than full NSGA-II. These guarantees apply to population-level low-fidelity evaluation and do not establish convergence of the complete evolutionary trajectory.

</details>


### [224] [Thinking Less to Simulate Better: Intuitive Prompting Improves LLM Agents Simulating Individual Social Media Reactions, Including Unfamiliar Content](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30563)
*Ljubisa Bojic,Tijana Stanic,Joerg Matthes,Agariadne Dwinggo Samala,Bojana Dinic,Jue Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Intuition-focused, profile-aligned prompts yield high fidelity in simulating user reactions to social media posts; language models can act as general-purpose simulated users, outperforming human self-report fidelity and analytics-based prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address concerns that platform policies relying on artificial users may misrepresent public opinion; validate whether agents align to given profiles and examine how instruction style affects fidelity.

Method: Profiling eight Serbian participants via questionnaire, deep interview, and self-presentation; exposing reactions to 68 posts; four language models predict reactions under five prompt conditions varying profile content and instruction style.

Result: Attitudinal content boosts prediction accuracy over demographic backstories; agents align with stated profiles more closely than participants do with their own survey answers; fidelity is not tied to consistency once profile data exists; intuitive/immediate (rather than analytic) prompts yield highest fidelity, reducing individual difference compression; outperforms crowd baseline, even on topics not covered by the questionnaire.

Conclusion: Intuition-based prompting can enhance predictive fidelity and enable general-purpose simulated users, with implications for model development and evaluation strategies; emphasis on profile-informed, intuitive prompts may be advantageous over traditional reasoning-based prompts.

Abstract: Platform policies are increasingly tested on artificial users, making agent fidelity important. Yet convincing fake profiles could also manipulate perceived public opinion before elections. Validation has concentrated on agreement with human behaviour and has paid little attention to whether an agent behaves in line with the profile it was given. The present study profiled eight Serbian participants through a questionnaire, a deep interview, and a written self-presentation, recorded their reactions to sixty-eight social media posts, and asked four language models to predict those reactions under five prompt conditions varying profile content and instruction style. Attitudinal content improved prediction over demographic backstories by a wide margin. Agents matched their stated profiles more closely than participants matched their own survey answers, and consistency proved unrelated to fidelity once profile information was present. Instructing models to respond intuitively and immediately rather than analytically gave the highest fidelity of any condition and cut the compression of individual differences from seven times the human level to three. The advantage held on posts about topics the questionnaire never raised, where that condition reached the highest fidelity of any setup and beat a crowd baseline by a wide margin, which suggests that agents prompted this way could serve as general-purpose simulated users rather than specialists on the topics they were profiled for. Results may bear implications for the development of language models, because intuition-based setups appear better suited to some tasks than reasoning-based ones.

</details>


### [225] [Atelier: Learning Local Self-Supervised Features for CryoEM Volumes via Hypernetworks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30569)
*Phillip Lo,Sudarshan Babu,Dari Kimanius,Aly A. Khan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Amortizes implicit neural representations for cryoEM map interpretation using a transformer-based hypernetwork (Atelier) that produces coordinate-conditioned features, improving voxel-level predictions and enabling scale-agnostic, geometry-aware analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current DL map annotation relies on fixed voxel grids; INRs offer coordinate-conditioned, scale-agnostic representations but per-map fitting is expensive and not aligned across samples. There is a need for scalable, cross-sample aligned representations that provide local features at arbitrary coordinates.

Method: Train a transformer-based hypernetwork pretrained on 5,439 EM maps to generate INRs for cryoEM maps. The resulting INR yields continuous feature fields via intermediate activations at query points. Use these features as auxiliary channels to a 3D nested U-Net annotation head trained from scratch to predict voxel-level properties; evaluate on eight tasks and across large assemblies.

Result: The pretrained Atelier can reconstruct high-fidelity maps across diverse protein structures; the INR features improve voxel-level property prediction over a volume-only baseline across eight tasks.

Conclusion: Amortized INRs are effective for geometry-aware cryoEM analysis, enabling scale-agnostic, local feature representations that improve downstream annotation tasks.

Abstract: CryoEM map interpretation requires features that are spatially localized, consistent across samples, and informative across spatial scales. Most deep learning methods for map annotation extract features from fixed voxel grids. However, implicit neural representations (INRs) are able to model volumetric data as scale-agnostic, coordinate-conditioned functions. INRs are therefore attractive for cryoEM, but fitting a separate INR for each map is too expensive for large-scale feature extraction and produces representations that are not aligned across samples. We introduce Atelier, a self-supervised framework that amortizes INR fitting for reconstructed cryoEM maps. Pretrained on 5,439 Electron Microscopy Data Bank maps, Atelier is a transformer-based hypernetwork that generates high-fidelity reconstructions across a wide range of protein structures, including large multi-subunit assemblies. Beyond reconstruction, the INR generated by the pretrained transformer exposes a continuous, local feature field through its intermediate activations at any spatial query point, a property that voxel grid and patch-tokenizer architectures do not naturally provide. Used as auxiliary channels to a 3D nested U-Net annotation head trained from scratch, these coordinate-conditioned features improve performance on eight voxel-level property prediction tasks over a volume-only baseline. Our results demonstrate that amortized implicit neural representations are an effective primitive for geometry-aware analysis of cryoEM data.

</details>


### [226] [HARDEN: Constrained Evolutionary Search for Harder, Answer-Preserving Evaluation Cases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30571)
*Aditya Kumaran,Rahul Singhal,Karime Maamari,Amine Mhedhbi,Pradyumna Tambwekar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HARDEN uses constrained evolutionary search to create harder, semantically preserved evaluation variants, revealing larger falls in model accuracy than single-pass baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks often miss the complexity of real enterprise deployments; there is a need to generate harder, yet feasible, evaluation cases to more accurately gauge model robustness.

Method: HARDEN searches along domain-specific complexity axes while enforcing feasibility constraints (preserving task semantics, realism, and execution validity) to mutate inputs without changing expected outputs.

Result: Across FinQA, PubMedQA, and ContractNLI on three Qwen3.5 scales (35B, 122B, 397B), HARDEN reduces task-model accuracy by 22.7% on average and up to 49.9% relative to single-pass baselines using the same feasibility checks.

Conclusion: Constrained evolutionary search can yield substantially harder valid evaluation cases, highlighting a need for richer adversarial variants in evaluation suites and providing a practical method to stress-test model performance without altering ground-truth outputs.

Abstract: Language models are often evaluated on curated benchmarks that underrepresent the complexity of enterprise deployments. We introduce HARDEN, a constrained evolutionary search method to adapt the input of existing evaluation cases into more challenging variants while keeping their expected outputs fixed. HARDEN searches along generated domain-specific complexity axes while enforcing feasibility constraints such as preserving task semantics, realism, and execution validity. Across FinQA, PubMedQA, and ContractNLI and three Qwen3.5 model scales (35B-A3B, 122B-A10B, and 397B-A17B), HARDEN reduces task-model accuracy by 22.7% on average and by up to 49.9% relative to single-pass baselines using the same feasibility checks. These results show that evolutionary search can produce substantially harder valid evaluation cases.

</details>


### [227] [T-RoPE: Time-Aware Rotary Position Embedding for Sequential Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30576)
*Yang Liu,Noel Loo,Ali Khanafer,Shuying Sun,Akshay Soni,Zhong Wu,Linjun Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes T-RoPE, a time-aware RoPE for sequential generative recommendation that injects timestamp-based angles and temporal components into Rotary Position Encoding, achieving state-of-the-art results across benchmarks with efficient forward/backward methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RoPE in recommender systems currently encodes only interaction order via index rotations, ignoring elapsed time, cycles, and calendar phase. This limits the model's ability to capture temporal dynamics and seasonality in user behavior.

Method: Introduce T-RoPE with timestamp-based angles, learnable temporal coefficients, multiscale frequency banks, shifted query alignment, and non-stationary key rotation; prove time-translation invariance of standard RoPE on timestamps and non-invariance of T-RoPE; provide forward/backward algorithms with linear cost in sequence length and head dimension; integrate into sequential generative recommenders while preserving RoPE interface.

Result: Empirical validation on five public benchmarks shows T-RoPE achieves the best metrics on every dataset, with +78–130% improvement in HR@10 on PixelRec and +8–12% across metrics on Amazon Books. On a 6B-interaction industrial dataset, gains range 13–82% over a strong backbone, with ablations highlighting multiscale frequencies (+56% NDCG@50) and non-stationary keys (+4%). Online A/B test reports conversions up +0.33% and orders +0.63%. The added cost remains linear in sequence length and head dimension.

Conclusion: Time-aware RoPE effectively encodes temporal dynamics in sequential generative recommenders, surpassing standard RoPE while preserving interface and maintaining practical efficiency.

Abstract: Large-scale recommenders increasingly adopt the sequential generative recipe behind large language models, bringing the Transformer into recommendation along with design choices made for text, including Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE). In language models, RoPE encodes token indices for relative position reasoning, but in recommendation, an interaction index records only event order, saying nothing about elapsed time, behavioral cycles across scales, or calendar phase. We revisit this choice and propose T-RoPE, a time-aware RoPE for sequential generative recommendation that replaces index-only rotation with timestamp-based angles, learnable temporal coefficients, multiscale frequency banks, shifted query alignment, and non-stationary key rotation. We prove that standard RoPE, even on timestamps, remains time-translation invariant and cannot distinguish seasonal contexts, and that T-RoPE breaks this invariance while preserving the RoPE interface. Across five public benchmarks, T-RoPE achieves the best result on every metric on every dataset, improving over the strongest baseline by 78--130\% in HR@10 on the sparse PixelRec data and 8--12\% across metrics on Amazon Books. On an industrial-scale e-commerce dataset with more than 6B interactions, it improves every metric over the HSTU + Time RAB backbone by 13--82\%, with ablations attributing the largest gains to multiscale frequencies ($+56\%$ NDCG@50) and non-stationary keys ($+4\%$). An online A/B test in the Shop app yields positive lifts in conversion rate ($+0.33\%$) and order count ($+0.63\%$). We also provide forward and backward algorithms whose added cost is linear in sequence length and head dimension, keeping time-aware RoPE practical for large generative recommenders.

</details>


### [228] [Audio LLMs Know When They Can't Hear You](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30625)
*Amirhosein Javadi,Richa Dixit,Mehrdad Farajtabar,Minsik Cho,Devang Naik,Mohammad Samragh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Lightweight reliability predictor using frozen audio-encoder representations detects transcription reliability in Audio LLMs, enabling clarifications for unreliable queries without changing the LLM; strong macro-F1 and cross-domain transfer across LLM families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Audio LLMs can misinterpret degraded inputs due to erroneous transcriptions; there is a need for a model-conditional signal that can flag unreliable transcriptions before generation.

Method: Train a lightweight classifier on representations from the frozen audio encoder to predict transcription reliability before generation. Evaluate in-domain and cross-domain performance, compare to speech quality predictors, generation uncertainty, and transcript-conditioned WER; test transfer across Audio LLM families and analyze alignment of their reliability boundaries.

Result: Achieves 81.10% in-domain and 78.09% cross-domain macro-F1, outperforming strongest baselines by 10.33 and 11.93 percentage points. The predictor can trigger clarification requests for unreliable queries while leaving reliable queries unaffected; reliability labels transfer across Audio LLM families, with transfer performance linked to alignment of model-specific reliability boundaries.

Conclusion: Reliability signals reside in frozen audio-encoder representations; a lightweight predictor suffices to determine transcription reliability before generation, enabling efficient clarification without modifying the LLM, with promising cross-LLM transfer dependent on alignment of reliability boundaries.

Abstract: Audio large language models allow users to interact with the model through speech. When an input recording is too degraded, the model may misinterpret the user's query and respond based on an incorrect transcription. In this paper, we study model-conditional transcription reliability: whether an Audio LLM can recognize when its own transcription is unreliable. We first prompt the Audio LLM to assess whether its own transcription would be reliable, and find that the model is a poor judge of its own transcription reliability: in most cases, it predicts that its transcription will be reliable. We find that existing approaches, including speech quality predictors, audio LLM generation uncertainty, and transcript-conditioned WER estimation, provide limited signals for detecting transcription failures. In contrast, we discover that transcription reliability is strongly represented in the model's audio-encoder representations. Based on this observation, we devise a lightweight reliability predictor that operates on representations extracted by the frozen audio encoder and predicts the reliability class before generation. The reliability predictor can trigger a clarification request from the user when their voice query is predicted to be unreliable, while allowing reliable queries to proceed without modifying the underlying Audio LLM. Our predictor achieves 81.10% in-domain and 78.09% cross-domain macro-F1 scores, outperforming the strongest baselines by 10.33 and 11.93 points, respectively. Finally, we show that reliability labels can transfer across Audio LLM families, and that transfer performance is closely related to the alignment of their model-specific reliability boundaries.

</details>


### [229] [LLM Parkinsonism: Executive-Control Failure, Token-Inefficient Persistence, and an Uncertainty-Aware Global Executive Control Architecture for Autonomous Language-Model Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30662)
*Dongsheng Xiao,Zeyuan Wang,Xuzhe Xia,Bo Zhao,Yankai Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Global Executive Control (GEC) v0.2 introduces a governance layer that separates action generation from project-level control to curb LLM Parkinsonism, achieving near-state performance with reduced token usage in a large-scale simulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can achieve strong local competence but often fail at project-level executive control, continuing actions despite diminishing value (LLM Parkinsonism). The problem is not just next-token prediction but the entanglement of proposal generation, scope interpretation, progress assessment, and stopping within a single loop; hence a governance mechanism is needed.

Method: Propose Global Executive Control (GEC) v0.2, an uncertainty-aware governance architecture that separates action generation from project-level control. Evaluate on a 24,000-episode matched-candidate benchmark under a 40,000-token ceiling, comparing a first-candidate baseline, a candidate-set local control, and GEC.

Result: Hard-goal success: 1st candidate 67.42%, candidate-set local control 96.53%, GEC 96.57%. Access to multiple candidate actions accounts for most gains. GEC reduced mean token use from 19,782 to 12,574 (36.4%) and reduced mean tokens to completion within the ceiling from 16,136 to 13,114 (18.7%), while eliminating pre-completion drift and reducing gross complexity. Governance-overhead sensitivity remains favorable with additional 500 synthetic governance tokens per cycle.

Conclusion: Mechanistic simulations support explicit governance of scope, evidence, resource use, and stopping, indicating project-level control improves efficiency without sacrificing success; however, live-model validation is still necessary.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can plan, use tools, write code, and execute long-horizon workflows, yet strong local competence does not guarantee project-level executive control. Agents may continue acting after the original objective is satisfied, producing low-value refinements, repeated verification, and repairs to self-created complexity. We use LLM Parkinsonism as a narrowly defined, non-clinical metaphor for this pattern of persistent action despite diminishing task-level value. We argue that the problem is not explained by autoregressive next-token prediction alone, but more directly by concentrating proposal generation, scope interpretation, progress assessment, and stopping authority within the same self-conditioned loop. We therefore introduce Global Executive Control (GEC) v0.2, an uncertainty-aware governance architecture that separates action generation from project-level control. In a 24,000-episode matched-candidate benchmark under a common 40,000-token ceiling, a first-candidate baseline achieved 67.42% hard-goal success, a candidate-set local control achieved 96.53%, and GEC achieved 96.57%. The candidate-set control shows that access to multiple candidate actions explains most of the success gain; relative to that control, GEC preserved success while reducing mean token use from 19,782 to 12,574 (36.4%) and restricted mean tokens to completion at the 40,000-token ceiling from 16,136 to 13,114 (18.7%), while eliminating measured pre-completion drift and sharply reducing gross complexity. Governance-overhead sensitivity remained favorable through an additional 500 synthetic governance tokens per cycle. These mechanistic simulations support explicit governance of scope, evidence, resource use, and stopping, while live-model validation remains necessary.

</details>


### [230] [The Price of Thought: Does Test-Time Reasoning Pay in LLM Trading?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30705)
*Jiayi Chen,Guiling Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Adding more reasoning steps in LLM outputs does not reliably boost net portfolio returns; effects are nonmonotonic and unstable; validation required per task before deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether reasoning via LLMs is economically beneficial as an intervention in portfolio decision-making, beyond linguistic accuracy.

Method: Controlled cross-family study (DeepSeek, GPT, Gemini); manipulate reasoning effort while fixing information, prompts, outputs, and portfolio construction; test on a full year of US equities under three input regimes (numerical, identifiable news, masked news); ~800k asset predictions; multiple generations.

Result: No consistent improvement in net portfolio returns from increased reasoning across all families; DeepSeek shows nonmonotonic performance; repeated generations yield unstable treatment effects.

Conclusion: Reasoning depth alone does not guarantee economic value; validate prompts/tasks; implement economic-focused evaluation when deploying LLM-based trading aids.

Abstract: While inference-time reasoning in large language models (LLMs) promises better decision making, its higher computational cost may not yield better economic outcomes. Yet reasoning controls are rarely evaluated as economic interventions, where changes in model outputs must translate into better portfolios after trading costs. We conduct a controlled study of representative LLMs from the DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini families. We vary reasoning effort while holding information available at each formation date, prompts, output formats, and portfolio construction fixed. Our evaluation covers a full year of U.S. equities under three input conditions: numerical, identifiable news, and masked news. It includes more than 800,000 asset predictions and repeated model generations. Across all three model families, additional reasoning does not produce a reliable improvement in net portfolio returns. For DeepSeek, where we examine the full progression from no reasoning to maximum reasoning, performance is nonmonotonic. Repeated generations also produce unstable treatment effects and portfolio selections, even when overall scores remain similar. These findings show that additional reasoning can change financial decisions without reliably improving their economic value, motivating validation for each task before deployment.

</details>


### [231] [LAVOIR: Teaching a Single-Pass Decision Encoder When and What to Ask with Amortized Value of Information](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30706)
*Furkan Yilmaz,Habibe Aleyna Tasdemir,Muhammed Faruk Gozay*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LAVOIR adds Value-Of-Information routing to single-pass decision models by inserting candidate missing-information slots beside answers, enabling a forward pass to yield both decisions and per-slot VOI estimates, achieving near-Bayes performance with efficient, limited questioning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: System One models (e.g., Jev/Laya) answer in a single forward pass but cannot solicit missing information, leading to suboptimal decisions. LAVOIR aims to route information gathering via VOI to improve accuracy while minimizing questions.

Method: Insert candidate missing-information slots next to answer options. A forward pass outputs the decision distribution and, for each slot, the expected gain in P(correct decision) if the user is queried about it. VOI targets require no hand-labeled data: gold outcomes derive from schema rules; an LLM verbalizes messages/answers; a separate model checks text; pairing messages with multiple profiles enables regression on realized gains to estimate expected gain. A Gini-impurity cap bounds predicted VOI to what a calibrated model can still gain. Training and evaluation use seen schemas, real ABCD conversations, SGD, and Laya benchmarks. The final policy matches a greedy oracle VOI on seen schemas (AUC 0.799 vs 0.797).

Result: Controlled study: decisions on seen schemas are indistinguishable from Bayes ceiling. With ≤0.5 questions per conversation, the policy is 14.1 points more accurate than never asking. Real data: a single exchange raises accuracy by 8.3 points when LAVOIR asks; unchanged when not. SGD: VOI-cap reduces asking rate from 93% to 8.6%. Laya benchmarks: LAVOIR exceeds Laya on 7 of 12 benchmarks; median response time 31 ms (GH200).

Conclusion: LAVOIR provides a scalable VOI-driven slot-routing mechanism for System One models, approaching Bayes-optimal decisions with limited queries and broad cross-domain effectiveness, while maintaining fast inference.

Abstract: "System One" decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev and its open counterpart Laya answer typed questions about a text in a single forward pass with calibrated probabilities, but they cannot ask for missing information: when a first message does not say what separates two departments, they guess. We present LAVOIR (Laya with Value-Of-Information Routing), which places the candidate pieces of missing information (slots) in the input next to the answer options, so that one forward pass returns both the decision distribution and, for every slot, the expected gain in the probability of the correct decision if the user were asked about it. VOI targets need no human labels: gold decisions come from schema rules, an LLM only verbalizes messages and answers, a model from another family checks every text, and pairing each message with several profiles makes regression on realized gains estimate the expected gain. A Gini-impurity cap bounds the predicted value by what a calibrated model can still gain. In a controlled study, decisions on seen schemas are statistically indistinguishable from the Bayes ceiling. The final model's question policy matches a greedy oracle VOI policy on seen schemas (AUC 0.799 vs. 0.797), and with at most 0.5 questions per conversation it is 14.1 points more accurate than never asking. On real ABCD conversations, one real exchange raises accuracy by 8.3 points where LAVOIR asks and leaves it unchanged where it does not; on SGD the cap lowers the asking rate from 93% to 8.6%. On Laya's twelve benchmarks LAVOIR is above Laya's reported scores on seven, and it answers a question in 31 ms (median, GH200).

</details>


### [232] [CRC-Router: Risk-Constrained Routing for Medical Agentic AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30714)
*Xueyang Li,Mingze Jiang,Gelei Xu,Jun Xia,Ching-Hao Chiu,Mengzhao Jia,Danny Z. Chen,Yiyu Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CRC-Router is a risk-constrained, uncertainty-aware routing module for medical AI that calibrates when autonomous predictions should proceed or be escalated, using multiple uncertainty signals and a per-finding risk model within Conformal Risk Control (CRC). It is demonstrated on chest X-ray triage with NIH ChestX-ray14, showing superior risk–coverage trade-offs and modular compatibility with existing pipelines like MedRAX; code is released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safe deployment of agentic medical AI requires reliable, calibrated routing to prevent autonomous errors from propagating into downstream decisions. Existing models focus on predictive performance but lack robust mechanisms to decide when to trust an autonomous decision vs. escalate.

Method: Compute a per-finding routing feature vector by fusing predictive score with multiple uncertainty signals; map this vector to an estimated wrong-accept risk using a lightweight per-finding risk model; apply Conformal Risk Control (CRC) to calibrate acceptance thresholds toward a user-specified risk target. Evaluated as a standalone routing layer and as a plug-in with the MedRAX agent on chest X-ray multi-finding triage using NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset.

Result: CRC-Router yields the strongest empirical risk–coverage trade-off among evaluated baselines, both as a standalone routing layer and as a plug-in to MedRAX, demonstrating effective selective medical automation and model-agnostic compatibility.

Conclusion: CRC-Router provides a modular, uncertainty-aware, risk-controlled routing solution for both conventional and agentic medical AI systems, enabling safer autonomous deployment with calibrated acceptance thresholds and ready integration with existing predictive pipelines.

Abstract: Agentic AI systems are increasingly being explored in medical imaging to improve throughput and reduce clinician workload; however, safe deployment remains challenging because autonomous errors may propagate into downstream clinical decisions. A central requirement is therefore not only strong predictive performance, but also a reliable routing mechanism that determines when the system should proceed autonomously and when a case should be escalated for further review. To address this gap, we propose CRC-Router, a risk-constrained, uncertainty-aware routing module that is applicable to both conventional medical prediction models and agentic medical AI systems. CRC-Router combines multiple complementary uncertainty signals with the predictive score to construct a per-finding routing feature vector, maps this vector to an estimated wrong-accept risk using a lightweight per-finding risk model, and then applies Conformal Risk Control (CRC) to calibrate acceptance thresholds under a user-specified risk target. Instantiated on chest X-ray multi-finding triage using the NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset, CRC-Router achieves the strongest empirical risk--coverage trade-off among the evaluated baselines, both as a standalone routing layer and as a plug-in module integrated with the state-of-the-art MedRAX agent. These results demonstrate both the effectiveness of CRC-Router in selective medical automation and its modular, model-agnostic compatibility with existing predictive and agentic medical pipelines. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/XLIAaron/CRC-Router

</details>


### [233] [Analyzing and Mitigating Cost-Inefficient Behaviors in Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30725)
*Yiran Hu,Nan Jiang,Shanchao Liang,Anik Dey,Yi Wu,Lin Tan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: First study of behavioral cost inefficiencies in coding agents; identifies three inefficiencies and shows developer-designed skills yield largest cost reductions, with mixed results from retrieval-based mitigations and agent-synthesized skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantify recurring monetary costs due to cost-inefficient behaviors in code-generation agents and evaluate mitigation strategies to reduce task cost.

Method: Analyzed 1,200 trajectories from Claude Code and Mini-SWE-Agent across four configurations on SWE-bench Verified; identify three inefficiencies (subsumed retrieval, similar script generation, test re-execution); evaluate three mitigations (structure-aware retrieval, agent-synthesized skills, developer-designed skills) on 10k trajectories across held-out SWE-bench Verified and Pro tasks.

Result: Inefficiencies affect 79.00%-98.00% of coding tasks and account for up to 22.75% of task cost; structure-aware retrieval can introduce overhead and cause retrieval efficiency variations, with cost increases up to 28.14%; agent-synthesized skills tend to produce low-level, trace-specific guidance, limiting effectiveness and generality; developer-designed skills provide high-level, trace-agnostic guidance, reducing cost by up to 41.73%, roughly twice the maximum gain from agent-synthesized skills.

Conclusion: Developer-designed skills emerge as the most effective mitigation, offering substantial cost reductions and better generalization; retrieval-aware strategies yield mixed results with potential overhead; agent-synthesized skills are less effective due to scope limitations.

Abstract: Although effective, coding agents often incur substantial monetary costs. Their recurring cost-inefficient behaviors remain underexplored. We conduct the first study of behavioral cost inefficiencies in coding agents, analyzing 1,200 trajectories from Claude Code and Mini-SWE-Agent across four configurations on SWE-bench Verified. We identify three cost-inefficient behaviors: subsumed retrieval, similar script generation, and test re-execution. We then evaluate three mitigation strategies: structure-aware retrieval, agent-synthesized skills, and developer-designed skills, over 10k trajectories on held-out SWE-bench Verified and Pro tasks. Our main findings are: (1) The three behaviors affect 79.00\%--98.00\% of coding tasks and account for up to 22.75\% of task cost. (2) Structure-aware retrieval can introduce retrieval overhead and alter agent delegation, causing inconsistent improvements in retrieval efficiency and cost increases of up to 28.14\%. (3) Agent-synthesized skills tend to produce low-level, trace-specific guidance, limiting their effectiveness and generality. (4) In contrast, developer-designed skills provide high-level, trace-agnostic guidance, reducing cost by up to 41.73\%, roughly twice the maximum gain from agent-synthesized skills.

</details>


### [234] [Learning What to Skip: Counterfactual Credit Assignment for Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30734)
*Jinfeng Xu,Zheyu Chen,Ziyue Peng,Zheng Lin,Shuo Yang,Jinze Li,Zheng Xing,Mengran Li,Victor C. M. Leung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LW2S learns when to skip components in multi-agent LLM workflows by modeling the conditional utility of each step via counterfactual interventions, reducing cost while preserving or improving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve efficiency of multi-agent LLM workflows by avoiding unnecessary computation without sacrificing correctness; leverage observed trajectories and their counterfactual omissions to estimate component value.

Method: Train action-specific safety models using full-workflow logs and skip interventions (counterfactuals); combine held-out calibration with domain-native guards to decide skips; allow early skip rejection to continue and revisit later components; evaluate across math reasoning, MCQA, and code generation with two instruction-model families; perform scale-up and topology experiments and analyze shared-error cases.

Result: LW2S reduces recorded token cost while matching or improving aggregate full-workflow accuracy across tasks and model families; redundancy of components observed; agreement alone is insufficient for skip decisions.

Conclusion: Efficient workflow execution can be achieved by learning the conditional utility of individual components; LW2S provides a practical framework for selective execution in complex LLM workflows and highlights the need to consider component interactions and uncertainties.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM workflows use planning, execution, verification, and summarization to improve task performance, yet the value of each component depends on the state already produced. Executing every component can waste computation or overwrite a correct intermediate answer. We formulate component omission as counterfactual credit assignment: full-workflow logs reveal the executed trajectory's reward, while controlled skip interventions reveal the consequences of omitting a future step. We introduce Learning What to Skip (LW2S), which learns action-specific safety models from these interventions and combines held-out calibration with domain-native guards to select skips. When an early skip is rejected, the controller can continue execution and reconsider a later component. Across mathematical reasoning, multiple-choice QA, and code generation with two instruction-model families, LW2S reduces recorded token cost while matching or improving aggregate full-workflow accuracy in the evaluated settings. Scale-up and second-topology experiments further examine component redundancy, while shared-error cases reveal why agreement alone is insufficient for skip selection. These findings connect efficient workflow execution to learning the conditional utility of individual components.

</details>


### [235] [From S3Q Theory to Implementation: Towards an Architecture for Machine Qualia](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30743)
*Tetiana Grinberg,Katrina Schleisman,Patryk Laurent,Bogdan Udrea,Minda Myers,Brian Aufderheide,Luis El Srouji,Doyle Groves,Kevin Schmidt*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Five-layer pipeline architecture for S3Q that composes existing computational primitives to realize grounded sensorimotor situatedness, internal world-model simulation, and structural coherence; yields falsifiable predictions and self-like behavior patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge theoretical models of machine consciousness to concrete computational implementations and provide testable predictions by combining three necessary conditions for qualia.

Method: Design a five-layer architecture operating on continuous, differentiable per-object slot vectors; map each S3Q tenet to compatible machinery; specify interfaces in a single representation pipeline; incorporate developmental bootstrap; generate falsifiable predictions.

Result: Demonstrates a unified pipeline that integrates all three conditions (groundedness, internal simulation, coherence); predicts self-like sense through action-outcome coupling; behavior profiles (hesitation, curiosity, avoidance) based on surprise and valence; each prediction falsifiable.

Conclusion: Offers a testable framework for machine consciousness; provides a concrete plan to validate predictions and advance understanding; future work to empirically validate bootstrap and mapping to primitives.

Abstract: A key challenge in machine consciousness research is translating theoretical models into computational-level implementations. In this paper, we address this challenge by proposing a five-layer implementation architecture for the S3Q (Simulated, Situated, Structurally Coherent) theory of consciousness. Rather than introducing novel formalisms, the architecture composes published computational primitives into a single pipeline. S3Q identifies three jointly necessary conditions for qualia: (1) grounded sensorimotor situatedness, (2) internal simulation via a world model, and (3) structural coherence between predictions and observations. No existing computational system implements all three simultaneously. We map each S3Q tenet to specific, compatible computational machinery and specify how these components interface within a single representation pipeline that operates on continuous, differentiable, per-object slot vectors, along with a developmental bootstrap sequence and falsifiable predictions for the composed system that no subset of the architecture produces in isolation. The model suggests that a basic sense of "self" develops by linking actions to their outcomes, and that behavior falls into three patterns (hesitation, curiosity, or avoidance) depending on how unexpected an outcome is and whether it is experienced as positive or negative. Each prediction is individually falsifiable, providing the field with a testable framework to advance our understanding of machine consciousness.

</details>


### [236] [ORCA: Evaluating LLMs on Data Science Code Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30749)
*Xiaolong Li,Jinyang Li,Bowen Qin,Ge Qu,Nan Huo,Xiaohan Xu,Shipei Lin,Reynold Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A new DSCT benchmark (ORCA) reveals DSCT remains challenging for LLMs; introduces MAIN (1,600 grounding tasks) and PROJECT (200 project tasks) with annotated references and test cases; includes a quality-verification pipeline and an intent-augmented translation method that yields modest gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the lack of robust, functionally validated benchmarks for data science code translation across libraries, complementing progress in data science code generation (DSCG) by focusing on translation and interoperability.

Method: ORCA-MAIN: 1,600 tasks across three domains (Data Querying, Data Manipulation, Deep Learning). ORCA-PROJECT: 200 tasks across 7 DS task types. Each task has annotated reference translations and test cases to validate functional equivalence. A multi-stage quality-verification process ensures task correctness and test robustness. Proposes an intent-augmented method that first infers source-code intent before translation.

Result: Claude-Opus-4.6 achieves 56.92% success on ORCA-MAIN and 33.67% on ORCA-PROJECT. The intent-augmented method yields average absolute success-rate gains of 4.80% on ORCA-MAIN and 5.33% on ORCA-PROJECT.

Conclusion: DSCT remains challenging for current LLMs; translation is easier when source expresses tasks via explicit, fine-grained operations; intent-augmented translation provides consistent improvements, indicating a viable direction for DSCT research but leaving substantial room for improvement.

Abstract: Data Science Code Translation (DSCT) is the process of converting code between data science libraries while preserving functional equivalence and enabling interoperability across data science ecosystems. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable progress in Data Science Code Generation (DSCG), their performance in DSCT remains insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we introduce ORCA, a comprehensive benchmark with two complementary settings: ORCA-MAIN, which comprises 1,600 carefully curated grounding-level tasks across 3 representative domains: Data Querying, Data Manipulation, and Deep Learning; and ORCA-PROJECT, which contains 200 translation tasks over complete data science projects across 7 data science task types. Each task is accompanied by annotated reference translations and test cases for validating functional equivalence. We further incorporate a multi-stage quality verification process that thoroughly verifies task correctness and test case robustness. Experimental results demonstrate challenges in DSCT, with even frontier LLMs showing limited performance. Specifically, Claude-Opus-4.6 achieves a success rate of 56.92% on ORCA-MAIN and 33.67% on ORCA-PROJECT, indicating considerable room for improvement in DSCT. We also observe a clear directional preference in DSCT, where translation is consistently easier when the source code expresses the task through more explicit, fine-grained operations. Motivated by this, we propose an intent-augmented method, in which the model first infers source-code intent and then uses it as additional context for translation, achieving average absolute success-rate gains of 4.80% and 5.33% on ORCA-MAIN and ORCA-PROJECT, respectively.

</details>


### [237] [Backbone-Adaptive Evidence Routing for Robust Pairwise LLM Judging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30751)
*Zeyan Li,Jing Peng,Jianfeng Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BAER introduces backbone-adaptive evidence routing for pairwise language-model judging, using three symmetric heads to gather evidence: evidence stacking, reliability-based expert routing, and candidate-blind reference verification. Development data select and freeze a head per benchmark-backbone condition; BAER achieves top test accuracy across eight conditions (four benchmarks x two 8B backbones) with full coverage and sizable gains over baselines, suggesting adaptive evidence collection outperforms a fixed protocol.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: No single judging protocol (e.g., direct comparison, reasoning, or reference-based verification) consistently dominates across benchmarks and base models. The paper argues for adapting evidence gathering to the backbone and benchmark, while preserving candidate symmetry to prevent biased comparisons.

Method: BAER constructs three symmetric heads: evidence stacking, reliability-based expert routing, and candidate-blind reference verification. It decouples the expert's signed preference from the candidate-invariant reliability, and enforces symmetry so swapping responses flips preference but not its strength. Development data selects one head for each benchmark-backbone condition, and this choice is frozen at test time. The approach aims to adaptively route evidence based on backbone and benchmark.

Result: Empirical evaluation on four benchmarks and two 8B judge backbones shows BAER achieves the highest test accuracy among compared methods in all eight conditions, with full prediction coverage and gains of 0.87–7.32 points over the strongest external baseline.

Conclusion: Adapting how evidence is gathered (via backbone-adaptive routing) is more reliable than fixing a single judging protocol across benchmarks and backbones.

Abstract: Pairwise language-model judges can gather evidence through direct comparison, reasoning, or reference-based verification, but no single protocol is best across benchmarks and judge backbones. We introduce Backbone-Adaptive Evidence Routing (BAER), which adapts the evidence mechanism while preserving candidate symmetry: swapping the two responses may reverse the preference but cannot change its strength. BAER separates each expert's signed preference from candidate-invariant reliability and builds three symmetric heads: evidence stacking, reliability-based expert routing, and candidate-blind reference verification. Development data select one head for each benchmark--backbone condition, and that choice is frozen before testing. Across four benchmarks and two 8B judge backbones, BAER achieves the highest test accuracy among the compared methods in all eight conditions, with full prediction coverage and gains of 0.87--7.32 points over the strongest external baseline. The results show that adapting how evidence is gathered is more reliable than fixing one judging protocol everywhere.

</details>


### [238] [Selective Amortization of Full-Budget Counterfactual Reasoning for Visual Token Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30756)
*Qinglei Qi,Zhihe Liang,Fengzhan Jing,Shenao Zhu,Lei Zhang,Chenyang Zhang,Shuqing He,Jia Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ACV-Gate reduces encoder-side computation in packet-constrained generative image communication by learning to approximate full-budget evaluations for token candidates, using a set-aware student and selective refinement to rank and evaluate candidates, achieving PSNR gains with far fewer evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Estimating the terminal value of each candidate token requires repeated receiver-side reconstructions, which is computationally expensive at the encoder.

Method: ACV-Gate introduces a set-aware student trained on terminal advantages and regrets to predict candidate rankings; a selective refinement mechanism evaluates a bounded candidate set including Local-MDL and direct actions; cost-based thresholds control the average evaluation workload.

Result: On CIFAR-10 at 0.20 bpp, the adaptive configuration improves PSNR by 0.636 dB over LocalMDL with 2.13 candidate evaluations per image (27.60% of the calls required by the Exact-Full expert); matched-candidate comparisons and tests on STL-10 and 384×384 transfer show consistent gains, particularly at low bit rates.

Conclusion: Terminal-value learning combined with selective candidate evaluation provides an effective and controllable mechanism for allocating encoder computation in packet-constrained generative image communication.

Abstract: Generative image communication transmits compact semantic tokens under a limited packet budget, where token selection directly affects the final reconstruction quality after the complete packet is decoded. However, accurately estimating the terminal value of every candidate token requires repeated receiver-side reconstruction, resulting in substantial encoder-side computation. To address this problem, we propose ACV-Gate, an adaptive candidate evaluation framework that learns to approximate full-budget counterfactual evaluation and selectively assigns exact evaluations to the most informative candidates. Specifically, a set-aware student is trained using terminal advantages and regrets to predict candidate rankings directly, while a selective refinement mechanism evaluates only a bounded candidate set containing both Local-MDL and direct actions; cost-based thresholds further enable explicit control of the average evaluation workload. Experiments on CIFAR-10 show that ACV-Gate consistently improves reconstruction quality while substantially reducing candidate evaluations; at 0.20 bpp, the primary adaptive configuration improves PSNR over LocalMDL by 0.636 dB with only 2.13 candidate evaluations per image, corresponding to 27.60% of the calls required by the Exact-Full expert. Matched-candidate comparisons, synchronized GPU measurements, and evaluations on STL-10 and 384 *384 scale transfer further demonstrate consistent quality computation trade-offs, with particularly pronounced gains at low bit rates. These results show that combining terminal-value learning with selective candidate evaluation provides an effective and controllable mechanism for allocating encoder computation in packet-constrained generative image communication.

</details>


### [239] [HCOE: Hyperbolic Clinical Ontology Embeddings from Biomedical Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30763)
*Yixuan Li,Weihao Li,Ziyang Song*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hyperbolic Clinical Ontology Embeddings (HCOE) preserve medical code hierarchies by embedding frozen BioBERT representations into the Poincare ball and applying ontology-guided, contrastive learning with coarse-to-fine path aggregation; it improves ICD/ATC relation prediction, CCS-to-PheCode transfer, and various MIMIC-IV clinical predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Biomedical LMs encode textual semantics but typically ignore hierarchical ontology structure. Hyperbolic geometry is well-suited for representing taxonomic hierarchies, enabling hierarchy-aware clinical concept representations.

Method: Freeze BioBERT embeddings, map into a Poincare ball (hyperbolic space), and train using parent-side and child-side ontology-guided contrastive losses plus coarse-to-fine ontology-path aggregation. Leverages ICD codes organized by CCS and ATC hierarchies to guide embeddings, evaluated on ICD/ATC relation tasks, CCS-to-PheCode transfer, and MIMIC-IV clinical predictions (mortality, readmission, medication recommendation, rare drug prediction).

Result: HCOE achieves state-of-the-art performance on ICD/ATC clinical relation prediction and CCS-to-PheCode hierarchy transfer. On MIMIC-IV, it attains top results for mortality prediction, readmission prediction, medication recommendation, and rare drug prediction.

Conclusion: Hyperbolic ontology embeddings effectively capture hierarchical structure in clinical codes, yielding improved hierarchy-aware representations and downstream clinical prediction performance.

Abstract: Biomedical language models (LMs) encode textual semantics but do not explicitly preserve medical code hierarchies. We present Hyperbolic Clinical Ontology Embeddings (HCOE) for hierarchy-aware clinical concept representation. HCOE maps frozen BioBERT embeddings into a Poincare ball, combining parent-side and child-side ontology-guided contrastive learning with coarse-to-fine ontology-path aggregation. It uses International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes organized by Clinical Classifications Software (CCS) and Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) medication hierarchies. Evaluations show that HCOE performs best on ICD/ATC clinical relation prediction and CCS-to-PheCode hierarchy transfer. On the MIMIC-IV dataset, HCOE also achieves the best performance on mortality prediction, readmission prediction, medication recommendation, and rare drug prediction.

</details>


### [240] [Insurance Reserve Intelligence Platform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30765)
*Anugya A,Saket Mohanty,Abhilash Timmapur,Somya Rai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hybrid Thiele-based reserve evolution with a PINN/KINN to predict standardized reserve ratios for term-life policies, achieving high predictive accuracy and ~120x speed-up over classical solvers, while noting issues with monotonicity and out-of-distribution generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speed and scalability of reserve estimation in sensitivity analysis, optimization, and large-scale scenario evaluation, while preserving physics-based interpretability and numerical stability.

Method: Combine a classical Thiele equation solver with a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) enhanced by Knowledge-Informed Neural Network (KINN) losses. Build a platform with synthetic policy generation, risk-adjusted premium calculation, reserve trajectory generation, reserve-ratio dataset construction, configurable neural training, validation diagnostics, elasticity analysis, prototype optimization workflows, and interest-rate scenario testing. Use seven input features (elapsed time, issue age, pricing rate, scenario rate, premium ratio, sum assured, mortality intensity) to predict a standardized reserve ratio, separating pricing-time and scenario-time interest-rate semantics.

Result: Quantitative performance: R2 = 0.9887, MAE = 785.48, RMSE = 1212.76 on test data. On 200 policies, PINN/KINN inference is ~119.53x faster than the classical solver. Demonstrates strong predictive accuracy, physics consistency, and boundary performance; indicates limitations in monotonicity and out-of-distribution generalization.

Conclusion: The approach delivers accurate, physics-consistent, and substantially faster reserve predictions suitable for sensitivity analysis and scenario evaluation, while highlighting remaining work to ensure monotonicity and robust generalization across unseen policy distributions.

Abstract: Insurance reserve estimation is a fundamental actuarial task supporting premium pricing, solvency assessment, financial reporting, capital planning, and risk management. Classical reserve methods based on Thiele's differential equation provide a rigorous and interpretable foundation for life insurance valuation, but repeated reserve calculations become computationally expensive in sensitivity analysis, optimization, and large-scale scenario evaluation.
  This paper presents an Insurance Reserve Intelligence Platform for term-life reserve modelling that combines a classical Thiele-equation solver with a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) enhanced by Knowledge-Informed Neural Network (KINN) losses. The framework includes synthetic policy generation, risk-adjusted premium calculation, classical reserve trajectory generation, reserve-ratio dataset construction, configurable neural training, validation diagnostics, sensitivity and elasticity analysis, prototype optimization workflows, and interest-rate scenario testing. A key refinement is the use of premium ratio and the explicit separation of pricing-time and scenario-time interest-rate semantics.
  The final model uses seven features: elapsed time, issue age, pricing interest rate, scenario interest rate, premium ratio, sum assured, and mortality intensity. It predicts a standardized reserve ratio instead of raw reserve values, improving numerical stability across policies with different sums assured. The model achieved an R2 of 0.9887, MAE of 785.48, and RMSE of 1212.76 on the test set. On 200 policies, PINN/KINN inference was approximately 119.53 times faster than the classical solver. Results show strong predictive accuracy, physics consistency, and boundary performance, while highlighting remaining limitations in monotonicity and out-of-distribution generalization.

</details>


### [241] [Does Thinking Help Fairness? Reasoning Tokens Resolve Some Biases but Create More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30768)
*Deng Pan,Joe Germino,Yihong Ma,Elizabeth Daly,Nuno Moniz,Ting Hua,Nitesh Chawla*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Thinking in reasoning LMs shows an asymmetric dual effect on counterfactual fairness: it resolves some non-thinking flips but creates many new flips, with created flips outpacing resolved flips by ~5x across models and datasets. CDPG and BTM are proposed to analyze this bias propagation through thinking depth and pair-state transitions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To resolve the debate on whether internal thinking in reasoning language models mitigates or exacerbates bias, by quantifying bias dynamics during reasoning across multiple models and high-stakes tasks.

Method: Within-model ablation comparing thinking vs. non-thinking across three models (QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, Qwen3-32B) on three datasets (Adult, COMPAS, Credit); measure counterfactual flips, and introduce two metrics (CDPG and BTM) to analyze bias evolution and state transitions.

Result: Thinking produces an asymmetric dual effect: it both resolves non-thinking baseline counterfactual flips and generates new flips; in all nine model/dataset pairs, created flips exceed resolved flips by ~5x. Bias propagates and amplifies with thinking as shown by CDPG and the joint transition in BTM.

Conclusion: The thinking trace is a measurable site of fairness change, with an asymmetric dual effect rooted in pair-state transitions during thinking; thus, thinking can amplify bias even as it resolves some flips.

Abstract: Thinking in reasoning language models (RLMs) has been subject to debate on whether it resolves or amplifies bias. Prior works have shown competing conclusions in both directions. Using a within-model thinking-vs.-non-thinking ablation across QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, and Qwen3-32B on three high-stakes decision tasks (Adult, COMPAS, Credit), we show that thinking has an asymmetric dual effect on counterfactual fairness: it both resolves counterfactual flips produced by the non-thinking baseline and creates new flips at near-saturating model confidence. In all nine (model, dataset) combinations, the created flips outnumber the resolved flips by roughly 5 times. To explain the effect, we treat the thinking trace itself as a measurable site of fairness change and study it through two dynamic instruments: 1) We propose Counterfactual Depth Probability Gap (CDPG) to track bias evolution along thinking depth, and observe that bias propagates and amplifies with thinking. 2) We also formulate the Bias Transition Matrix (BTM) to show how predictions of counterfactual pairs change from non-thinking to thinking, and find that the asymmetric dual effect originates in the pair-state joint transition.

</details>


### [242] [ConsultMind:Towards Automated Diagnostic Consultation via Uncertainty-Aware Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30796)
*Xiao Sun,Yuming Yang,Yun Chen,Jiang Zhong,Junnan Zhu,Xinyi Jiang,Haoyang Zeng,Ruirui Chen,Yining Wang,Xinyu Zhou,Rong Tang,Kaiwen Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AutoDisym automatically builds Disorder–Symptom Bayesian Networks from heterogeneous clinical narratives to guide online diagnostic consultations; ConsultMind uses these posteriors with uncertainty-driven queries to improve diagnosis and explanations, achieving substantial gains across multiple medical domains and datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-ended consultations face two challenges: linking diagnostic hypotheses to possible inquiries and translating evolving posteriors into actionable decisions; Bayesian networks offer a principled framework but require adaptation for open-ended, heterogeneous data; need interpretable, uncertainty-aware guidance.

Method: AutoDisym constructs DSBN by integrating diagnostic knowledge with diagnosis-labeled clinical narratives; ConsultMind updates disorder posteriors after each patient response and uses posterior uncertainty to guide inquiry and diagnosis; evaluation on psychiatry, respiratory, fever clinics and three public datasets; uses GPT-5.6-Sol.

Result: AutoDisym achieves macro F1 81.37 for canonical symptoms and 72.19 for manifestations; ConsultMind improves Top-1 and Top-3 accuracy by up to 22.15 and 37.89 percentage points; physician evaluations show improved quality of explanations, differential diagnoses, and rationales across LLM scales.
