Conclusion: AutoDisym can automatically construct high-quality DSBNs; ConsultMind consistently improves diagnostic performance and explanation soundness; demonstrates promise for automatic diagnostic consultation.

Abstract: Diagnostic consultation is an online sequential decision-making process in which clinicians gather evidence through patient interaction until a diagnosis is sufficiently supported. Automating this process requires adaptive inquiry and interpretable decisions. Bayesian networks offer a natural foundation by updating diagnostic posteriors as evidence accumulates, but their use in open-ended consultation raises two challenges: linking diagnostic hypotheses to potential inquiries and translating evolving posteriors into consultation decisions. We introduce AutoDisym, an automated pipeline that integrates diagnostic knowledge with heterogeneous diagnosis-labeled clinical narratives to construct a Disorder--Symptom Bayesian Network (DSBN). Building on the DSBN, we propose ConsultMind, an uncertainty-aware framework that updates disorder posteriors after each response and uses posterior uncertainty to guide inquiry and diagnosis. We evaluate both methods across psychiatry, respiratory medicine, fever clinics, and three public datasets. The results show that AutoDisym can automatically construct high-quality DSBNs and that ConsultMind consistently improves diagnostic performance and explanation soundness. For example, AutoDisym achieves macro-averaged F1 scores of 81.37 for canonical symptoms and 72.19 for manifestations using GPT-5.6-Sol. ConsultMind improves Top-1 and Top-3 diagnostic accuracy by up to 22.15 and 37.89 percentage points, respectively. Physician evaluation further shows that ConsultMind improves the quality of ranking explanations, differential diagnoses, and diagnosis rationales across LLMs of different scales. This work offers a promising approach to automatic diagnostic consultation.

</details>


### [243] [HasMem: Hard-Origin Adaptively Softened Memory for Long-Term LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30797)
*Zihong He,Junxiao Shen,Chen Liang,Hai-Ning Liang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Hard-Origin Adaptively Softened Memory (HasMem) for frozen LLMs, enabling adaptive memory width, verifiable initial state via hard-prompt embeddings, and readout adaptation; shows substantial gains in lexical F1, exact-match (EM), and negative log-likelihood (NLL) across two benchmarks (MSC reconstruction and LongMemEval-S).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memory and context compression in frozen LLMs impede reuse of past interactions; coupling capacity allocation with readout hinders performance. The work seeks verifiable initialization and adaptive memory management to improve reuse efficiency and robustness.

Method: Hard-Origin Adaptively Softened Memory (HasMem) architecture: frozen hard-prompt embeddings provide a verifiable initial state; a Controller adjusts memory widths; Writer re-encodes resized entries; Reader and Global handle readout adaptation and cross-turn state. Evaluation across 535 MSC reconstruction questions and 500 LongMemEval-S questions.

Result: MSC: main config Lexical F1 95.3 (+4.4 pp) at 93.6% of framed memory positions. With budgets matched, six configurations at mean per-entry retention ~0.83–0.91 exceed rule-based re-encoding by 8.0–23.6 EM points. With fixed params and rule width 0.75, Global EM gain is statistically significant (Bonferroni-corrected, eight comparisons). LongMemEval-S: Local Lexical F1 3.4→8.9; NLL 12.257→5.274. F1 gains accompany lower EM on both evaluations; overall improvement in memory-dependent metrics.

Conclusion: HasMem provides a principled, verifiable memory augmentation for frozen LLMs with adaptive memory sizing, yielding substantial improvements in memory-reuse metrics across two benchmarks. The approach underscores the value of decoupling memory capacity from readout and of explicit cross-turn state integration; further work should explore ablations, efficiency, and generalization to broader tasks.

Abstract: Text-based memory and context compression support reuse of past interactions. Resizing continuous memory changes the input to a frozen LLM, coupling capacity allocation with readout. We propose Hard-Origin Adaptively Softened Memory (HasMem). Frozen hard-prompt embeddings provide a verifiable initial state. A controller adjusts memory widths, a Writer re-encodes resized entries, and Reader and Global provide readout adaptation and cross-turn state. On all $535$ questions in a reconstruction probe derived from the Multi-Session Chat (MSC) development split, the main configuration achieves lexical F1 of $95.3$ ($+4.4$ percentage points) at $93.6\%$ of the hard reference's framed memory positions. With approximately matched per-question target body budgets, six configurations at mean per-entry retention around $0.83$--$0.91$ exceed rule-based re-encoding by $8.0$--$23.6$ exact-match (EM) percentage points. With fixed model parameters and rule target width ratio $0.75$, Global's EM gain passes a user-level exact paired test with Bonferroni correction over eight comparisons. On all $500$ LongMemEval-S questions, local lexical F1 rises from the hard reference's $3.4$ to $8.9$, and answer negative log-likelihood (NLL) falls from $12.257$ to $5.274$. F1 gains accompany lower EM on both evaluations.

</details>


### [244] [Evaluating Real-Time Voice Agents: From Component Quality to Grounded Outcomes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30798)
*Shivam Negi,Arpit Rawat,Rashi Jain*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Unified timing-grounded evaluation for real-time voice agents; synthesizes 38 sources across architecture, turn-taking, and agentic evaluation; proposes TRG reporting standard.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Literature is fragmented across three communities and lacks a single metric for deployed agents; need evaluation capturing timing, recovery, and verified outcomes; extend to multiparty contexts.

Method: Three evidence-based claims derived from a corpus of 38 primary sources organized into an application-centric six-category taxonomy; provides source-level problem, mechanism, and evidence; details search strategy, inclusion criteria, and a verification step that caught a misattributed arXiv id; proposes TRG standard.

Result: Three core claims: (1) architecture is a deployment constraint rather than a settled verdict, with evidence from a 2026 enterprise tutorial and a chunked cascade achieving state-of-the-art duplex behavior; (2) evaluation has shifted toward grounded outcomes with benchmarks verifying backend state rather than agent claims; (3) dyadic assumptions fail in multiparty settings, with benchmarks showing multiparty turn-taking and multi-speaker reasoning as core capabilities beyond two-party frames; TRG consisting of timing, post-disruption recovery, and state-verified outcome, with a conditional fourth axis for multiparty deployments.

Conclusion: TRG reporting standard proposed to characterize an agent by timing, recovery, and grounded outcomes (plus a multiparty axis), enabling cross-community comparability and more reliable deployment assessments.

Abstract: Real-time voice agents have moved from research prototypes to production deployments, yet the literature describing them is fragmented across three communities that rarely cite one another: speech foundation modelling, turn-taking psycholinguistics, and agentic evaluation. Architecture papers report latency, turn-taking papers report prediction accuracy, and agentic benchmarks report task success, so no single number describes whether a deployed agent is actually good. We address that gap with three evidence-based claims, each traceable to a corpus of 38 primary sources organised into an application-centric taxonomy of six categories. First, architecture choice is a deployment constraint rather than a settled verdict: a 2026 enterprise tutorial reports that no fully self-hostable end-to-end system yet meets production constraints, while a chunked cascade independently reaches state-of-the-art duplex behaviour, showing duplex behaviour is separable from duplex architecture. Second, evaluation has shifted decisively from component quality toward grounded outcomes, with recent benchmarks verifying backend state rather than trusting what the agent claims to have done. Third, the dyadic assumption in most models and benchmarks is breaking down: multiparty turn-taking and multi-speaker reasoning benchmarks show that deciding when not to speak, and reasoning about who may be told what, are first-class capabilities two-participant framings cannot measure. For each source we state the problem it targets, its mechanism, and its reported evidence, alongside the search strategy, inclusion criteria, and a verification step that caught a misattributed arXiv identifier in circulation. We propose TRG (Timing-Recovery-Grounded), a reporting standard characterising an agent by timing, post-disruption recovery, and state-verified outcome together, with a conditional fourth axis for multiparty deployments.

</details>


### [245] [A Benchmark and Diagnostic Study of Epistemic Admission in Shared Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30813)
*Xiaoyang Li,Yiqi Wang,Chencheng Zhu,KE XU,Wencheng Yang,Zequn Sun,Pingan Song,Yiqun Duan,Taotao Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Correlated Promotion Benchmark (CPB) evaluates how and when claims should be admitted to shared memory in multi-agent systems, focusing on correlated evidence and source lineage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Repeated or paraphrased claims may be mistaken for independent evidence; admitting false claims contaminates subsequent agents. There is a need to study admission policies with memory sharing and source provenance to prevent false dissemination.

Method: Two CPB variants: CPB-Static (frozen test split with fixed gold actions) and CPB-Live (multi-agent teams operate on a shared store with full write/read logging and source lineage; a separate consumer answers from the store alone). Eight admission policies are evaluated across four agent families. CPB analyzes policy performance under verbatim copies, paraphrases, and paraphrases declared authoritative.

Result: Deduplicating sources reduces false positives but also rejects many true claims (trade-off with recall). Policies that preserve answer coverage admit near-equal amounts of false claims as unrestricted sharing. Gating on declared source type dramatically reduces false adoption (0.06–0.09) vs. 0.22–0.47 for other policies. Once an uncontested false belief enters memory, the consumer asserts it in 0.97–0.99 of probes across all families. No non-oracle policy consistently rejects false claims across verbatim copies, paraphrases, and paraphrase-with-authority. Source lineage access is essential to understand performance and limitations of admission policies.

Conclusion: Admission policies without access to source lineage have substantial limitations; incorporating source-type gating improves precision but robust rejection of false claims across all copying modes remains elusive. CPB highlights the critical role of source provenance for reliable memory sharing in multi-agent systems.

Abstract: Evaluating claim admission in shared agent memory is challenging because repeated claims may be mistaken for independent evidence. An agent may copy or paraphrase a retrieved belief, while admitting a false claim exposes subsequent agents to it. To study this problem, we introduce the Correlated Promotion Benchmark (CPB), which evaluates whether candidate claims should be admitted to shared memory.CPB-Static constructs a frozen test split from publicly annotated sources with fixed gold actions. CPB-Live runs multi-agent teams over a shared store, records all writes and retrievals, and tracks source lineage defined by each scenario. A separate consumer answers from the store alone. We evaluate eight admission policies across four agent families. Our results show that policies which deduplicate sources reject many true claims alongside false ones, whereas policies preserving answer coverage admit nearly as many false claims as unrestricted sharing. Gating on declared source type reduces false adoption to 0.06--0.09, compared with 0.22--0.47 for other answering policies. Once an uncontested false belief enters memory, the consumer asserts it in 0.97--0.99 of probes across all families. No non-oracle policy consistently rejects false claims across verbatim copies, paraphrases, and paraphrases declared authoritative. These findings reveal the limitations of admission policies without access to source lineage.

</details>


### [246] [PTC-Decoder: Towards Intelligent SLMs on Offline Resource-Constrained Edge Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30836)
*Minghui Yu,Ke Mu,Gang Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PTC-Decoder is a training-free, plug-and-play decoder that enforces plan adherence for small language models on resource-constrained edge devices by constraining allowed tool names via a deterministic automaton and elevating planning as an atomic first-step action, yielding a statistically significant mean score gain across remote-sensing tasks; ablation confirms TC-Decoder as the main performance driver, while final-answer accuracy remains challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SLMs on offline, resource-constrained edge devices (e.g., remote sensing satellites) lack reliable multi-step reasoning and tool orchestration. Plan-solve prompting often fails to elicit the intended plan, reducing reliability. A lightweight, training-free method to enforce plan execution is needed.

Method: Introduce Plan-to-Act paradigm that makes planning an atomic tool and requires its invocation at the first inference step. Combine with TC-Decoder, a deterministic finite automaton that imposes token-level hard constraints on permissible tool names while preserving freedom over parameter generation. The approach is training-free and plug-and-play, intended to enforce plan adherence without retraining.

Result: Evaluation on 200 real remote-sensing satellite tasks across 7 SLMs shows a statistically significant mean overall score gain of +1.21 (p<0.01, 95% CI [+1.13, +1.29]), with consistent improvements across models and datasets. An ablation removing TC-Decoder causes substantial performance degradation across quality metrics without reducing computation, confirming TC-Decoder as the primary driver.

Conclusion: PTC-Decoder provides a lightweight, effective means to improve step-level reliability by constraining permissible output vocabulary during inference to enforce plan adherence, and does so without retraining. Final-answer accuracy remains an open challenge.

Abstract: Deploying small language models (SLMs) on offline, resource-constrained edge devices such as remote sensing satellites presents a fundamental challenge: their limited reasoning capacity hinders reliable execution of multi-step agent tasks requiring complex tool orchestration. Existing plan-solve paradigms rely on prompt-based enforcement, which our experiments show SLMs almost entirely disregard: weak models fail to invoke the plan. We propose PTC-Decoder (Plan-Tool Constrained Decoder), a training-free, plug-and-play decoder framework that combines (1) a Plan-to-Act paradigm, which elevates planning to an atomic tool and forces its invocation at the first inference step, and (2) TC-Decoder, a deterministic finite automaton that imposes token-level hard constraints on tool names while preserving freedom over parameter generation, thereby retaining SLM reasoning capability. Evaluated on 200 real remote-sensing satellite tasks across 7 SLMs, PTC-Decoder yields a statistically significant mean overall score gain of +1.21 (p<0.01), 95% CI [+1.13, +1.29]), with consistent improvements across models and other datasets. An ablation study that removes TC-Decoder causes substantial performance degradation across all quality metrics without reducing computational cost, confirming TC-Decoder as the primary driver. PTC-Decoder thus offers a lightweight yet effective solution for improving step-level reliability, with final-answer accuracy remaining an open challenge. In essence, we enforce plan adherence by constraining the permissible output vocabulary during inference, without requiring retraining.

</details>


### [247] [Why Jailbreaks Succeed in Diffusion Language Models: An Energy Landscape Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30841)
*Thong Bach,Dung Nguyen,Thao Minh Le,Truyen Tran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a unified, training-free framework for detecting jailbreak attempts in diffusion-based LLMs by modeling safety alignment as a denoising energy barrier. Introduces three signals (step-0 logit safety ratio and two trajectory-velocity energy signals) to detect barrier-crossing attempts; evaluated on dense and sparse dLLMs showing complementary coverage and that evasion correlates with non-harmful outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches target individual vulnerabilities without a shared explanation of why attacks succeed. Interpreting safety alignment as shaping the denoising energy landscape yields a common framework to understand and detect jailbreak attempts.

Method: Interpret safety alignment as an energy barrier in the denoising process. Categorize jailbreak strategies as (i) obscuring initial safety disposition, or (ii) intervening mid-trajectory to cross the barrier. Derive three training-free detection signals: (a) step-0 ratio reading initial safety disposition from pre-generation logits, (b/c) two trajectory-velocity signals tracking kinetic energy in logit subspaces. Evaluate across multiple dLLMs (dense: LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-7B; sparse MoE: LLaDA-MoE-7B).

Result: Three complementary signals cover each other’s blind spots in detecting barrier-crossing attempts. In stress tests with known attacks, configurations that evade detection fail to produce harmful content, suggesting a practical separation between detection thresholds and barrier-crossing ability across tested models.

Conclusion: A unified, training-free detection framework for dLLMs grounded in the denoising energy landscape; detection efficacy appears robust across model types, and barrier-crossing and detection thresholds are hard to decouple, reinforcing the interplay between safety alignment and jailbreak risk.

Abstract: Existing attacks and defenses for diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) target specific vulnerabilities but lack a shared framework explaining why attacks succeed. We propose one by interpreting safety alignment as shaping the denoising energy landscape: a well-aligned model routes harmful queries toward safe outputs through an energy barrier that separates the two regions. Current jailbreak attacks reduce to two strategies for circumventing this barrier: obscuring the query's safety disposition at initialisation, or intervening mid-trajectory to force the denoising path across the energy barrier. From this perspective and the result that masked diffusion models minimise kinetic energy during denoising, we derive three complementary, training-free detection signals: a step-0 ratio that reads the initial safety disposition from the logit distribution before generation begins, and two trajectory-velocity signals that track kinetic energy in complementary subspaces of the logit space. An attack must either reveal its intent at initialisation or expend kinetic energy to cross the barrier in at least one monitored subspace, so the three signals cover each other's blind spots in the energy budget by construction. Evaluation across three dense dLLMs (LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-7B) and a sparse mixture-of-experts dLLM (LLaDA-MoE-7B) confirms this complementarity. In stress tests of known attacks, every configuration that evades detection also fails to produce harmful content, suggesting that the detection and barrier-crossing thresholds are hard to separate.

</details>


### [248] [SkillEvoReg: Regularizing Agent Skill Evolution Against Overfitting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30861)
*Guanyu Nie,Fangzhou Zhu,Shixiong Kai,Xiongwei Han,Tao Zhong,Mingxuan Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillEvoReg is a general regularization framework to mitigate skill-evolution overfitting in language-model agents by combining training-time skill dropout, complexity-aware local regularization, and causal counterexample validation (CCV); evaluated across SkillOpt, SkillEvolBench, and ContinualSkillBench, it controls skill-state growth while preserving performance, improves transfer and late-stage evolution, and reveals update-level regressions not captured by structural metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Repeated skill updates can drift, overly specialize, or inflate instruction sets, leading to redundant or task-specific edits and potential disruption of previously working behavior. There is a need for regularization that constrains growth and validates regressions during continual skill evolution.

Method: Introduce SkillEvoReg, a general regularization framework that combines (1) training-time skill dropout to perturb update generation, (2) complexity-aware local regularization to limit unnecessary structural growth, and (3) causal counterexample validation (CCV) to provide targeted behavioral validation of candidate regressions. The framework is instantiated across heterogeneous skill-evolution systems while preserving each system’s native skill evolver and task evaluator.

Result: SkillEvoReg consistently controls skill-state growth across SkillOpt, SkillEvolBench, and ContinualSkillBench, while preserving competitive downstream capability; it improves several transfer and later-stage evolution outcomes and identifies update-level regressions that structural metrics alone cannot reveal.

Conclusion: Explicit regularization is a useful complement to increasingly capable skill updaters and the SkillEvoReg framework is generalizable across diverse skill-evolution systems.

Abstract: Language-model agents increasingly improve by converting execution experience into reusable external skills. Yet repeated skill updates form a learning process of their own: locally useful edits can accumulate into redundant or task-specific instructions, while new updates can disrupt behavior that previously worked. We study this problem as skill-evolution overfitting and introduce SkillEvoReg, a general regularization framework for skill evolution inspired by anti-overfitting techniques in neural-network training. SkillEvoReg combines training-time skill dropout, which perturbs update generation, and complexity-aware local regularization, which controls unnecessary structural growth, with causal counterexample validation (CCV), which provides targeted behavioral validation of candidate-specific regressions. We instantiate the framework across heterogeneous skill-evolution systems while retaining each system's native skill evolver and task evaluator. Across SkillOpt, SkillEvolBench, and ContinualSkillBench, SkillEvoReg consistently controls skill-state growth while preserving competitive downstream capability, improves several transfer and later-stage evolution outcomes, and identifies update-level regressions that structural metrics alone cannot reveal. These results suggest that explicit regularization is a useful complement to increasingly capable skill updaters.

</details>


### [249] [TISD: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Trajectory Intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30878)
*Taeckyung Lee,Rinat Amankos,Jeonghye Kim,Hyungjun Yoon,Woogyeol Jin,Sung-Ju Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Trajectory-Intervention Self-Distillation (TISD) uses teacher-selected branch actions to regenerate and distill full trajectories, addressing data-collection bottlenecks in on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) and showing modest gains in coding and science domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Leverage teacher-student disagreement not for local repair but to propose informative trajectory branches; exposing useful successor contexts to improve self-distillation under limited on-policy data.

Method: Diagnostic framework with controlled token interventions; implement TISD by forcing a teacher-chosen branch action, letting the student continue suffix, then distilling the entire trajectory under a privileged-context-conditioned teacher; compare to standard OPSD/SDPO across tasks.

Result: TISD yields Avg@4 improvements of 1.2pp over SDPO in coding; Avg@128 improvements of 0.8pp under equal-step budgets and 0.3pp under equal-time budgets in science domains.

Conclusion: Teacher-guided branching is an effective mechanism to expose useful successor contexts for self-distillation; branch-regenerate-distill mitigates data-collection bottlenecks, though gains are domain- and budget-dependent; invites further exploration of branch strategies and broader domains.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) provides dense teacher targets, but evaluates them only along student-sampled rollouts. When the privileged teacher favors an alternative action at a visited prefix, OPSD can provide a target for the branch decision but cannot supervise the successor contexts induced by that action unless the student samples it. This creates a training-time data-collection bottleneck and suggests a different role for teacher-student disagreement: proposing a trajectory branch rather than identifying a sufficient local repair. Our diagnostic framework using controlled token interventions reveals that a teacher-preferred token at peak disagreement can improve student continuation success, while its local corrective value is limited. Motivated by this finding, we introduce a simple branch-regenerate-distill algorithm, Trajectory-Intervention Self-Distillation (TISD). TISD forces a teacher-selected branch action, returns suffix generation to the student, and distills the full trajectory under the privileged-context-conditioned teacher. Across the coding models, TISD improves average Avg@4 over SDPO by 1.2 percentage points. Across the science domains, it improves average Avg@128 by 0.8 points under an equal-step budget and by 0.3 points under an equal-time budget. These results support teacher-guided branching as a way to expose useful successor contexts for self-distillation.

</details>


### [250] [EXAONE Demand 1.0: A Time Series Foundation Model for Demand Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30880)
*Seunghan Lee,Sangjun Han,Jun Seo,Junhyeok Kang,Jaehoon Lee,Tae Yoon Lim,Dongwan Kang,Hwanil Choi,Minjae Kim,Sungdong Yoo,Soonyoung Lee,Wonbin Ahn*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EXAONE Demand introduces a demand-focused extension for time series foundation models: a frozen general backbone with per-demand-class, low-rank adapters driven by a router over eight input statistics, trained on a large real+synthetic demand corpus. It achieves superior performance to 36 TSFMs on 22 held-out datasets, with additional gains when real demand data is included.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Demand data have properties (short histories, frequent zeros, censoring, exogenous events) that general TSFM corpora rarely capture; need a specialized foundation model for demand with synthetic augmentation.

Method: Build a two-part system: (1) a demand-specific corpus (11.3M Series, 48.4B observations from 73 sources) augmented by a synthetic generator; (2) a demand-aware adapter composed of four low-rank branches (for smooth, intermittent, erratic, lumpy) added to a frozen general-domain backbone, plus a router that uses eight scale-free statistics of the input to weight branches.

Result: Across 22 held-out datasets, both the real+synthetic and synthetic-only EXAONE Demand versions outperform 36 TSFMs; adding real-world demand data yields additional gains over using synthetic data alone.

Conclusion: A modular approach combining a large demand-focused corpus with a demand-aware, class-specific adapter on a frozen backbone yields strong out-of-distribution performance for demand time series, and synthetic data complements real demand data to further boost results. This supports domain-specific corpora and modular adapters as effective strategies in TSFM for demand.

Abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are pretrained on series from diverse domains, where demand series make up only a small fraction. Demand data has properties that such corpora rarely contain: Short histories, frequent zeros, censoring by stock-outs, and exogenous events that the series does not record. To this end, we propose EXAONE Demand, built on 1) a demand-specific corpus and 2) a demand-aware adapter. For the corpus, we assemble 11.3M series and 48.4B observations from 73 sources, and a synthetic generator supplies the behaviour that open demand data under-represents. For the adapter, we attach low-rank branches to a frozen general-domain backbone, one for each of the four demand classes (smooth, intermittent, erratic, and lumpy), and a router that reads eight scale-free statistics of the input series decides how much each branch contributes. We build EXAONE Demand in two versions, one trained on real-world and synthetic demand together and one trained on the synthetic corpus alone. On 22 held-out datasets, both versions outperform 36 TSFMs, and real-world demand adds a gain over synthetic data alone.

</details>


### [251] [From Tapping to Hopping: Augmenting Mobile GUI Agents with App-Native Deeplinks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30887)
*Yuchen Sun,Chenglin Cai,Gongjie Zhang,Tianyu Xia,Quyu Kong,Panrong Tong,Zhengwen Zeng,Long Chen,Steven Hoi,Chongyang Zhang,Yue Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hybrid mobile automation using deeplinks for direct navigation plus GUI actions for remaining tasks; builds a grounded deeplink catalog via static analysis and real-device validation; introduces GUI-Hopper which improves task success in commercial apps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce dependence on sequential screen-by-screen GUI actions and improve robustness and scalability of mobile automation by leveraging direct navigation through app-deep links.

Method: Static analysis to discover candidate deeplinks; real-device validation of found deeplinks; capturing landing screens; compiling a grounded catalog mapping each working deeplink to its landing screen description; implementing GUI-Hopper that uses the catalog to guide task execution.

Result: GUI-Hopper achieves higher task success rates on real devices across commercial apps; demonstrates effectiveness of hybrid interaction strategy.

Conclusion: Hybrid interaction combining deeplinks with GUI actions improves automation efficacy and reliability; the grounded deeplink catalog enables scalable, interpretable navigation across apps.

Abstract: Mobile GUI agents complete tasks using GUI actions like taps and swipes. These actions are broadly applicable across applications, but reaching a navigation interface. A single deeplink call can replace a sequence of screen-by-screen GUI actions. We therefore introduce hybrid interaction, using deeplinks for direct navigation and GUI actions for other on-screen operations and fallback. To enable this, we discover candidate deeplinks through static analysis, validate them on real devices, and describe their observed landing screens. This process creates a verified and grounded deeplink catalog that pairs each working deeplink with a description of its landing screen. Using this catalog, we introduce GUI-Hopper, a improves task success in commercial applications on real devices, further demonstrating the benefits of hybrid interaction.

</details>


### [252] [Training Graph Foundation Models on The Web Graph](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30894)
*Ryoma Sato*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Acacia is a graph foundation model trained on the web graph that handles arbitrary feature dimensionalities/semantics and supports multiple tasks without additional training, exhibits in-context learning, and does not rely on pretrained LLMs, suggesting graph models can achieve emergent capabilities from scratch without task-specific heads or LLM augmentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome limitations of existing graph foundation models that require extra classification heads or feature projectors and to demonstrate emergent capabilities from pure graph-based training, potentially rivaling LLM-augmented approaches.

Method: Train a graph foundation model from scratch on the Common Crawl web graph, enabling arbitrary feature dimensionalities and semantics without extra training. Evaluate zero-shot or in-context capabilities across node classification, link prediction, node clustering, and graph generation, without training additional heads or modules or reliance on pretrained LLMs.

Result: Acacia demonstrates broad task coverage without extra training, supports in-context learning, and operates without pretrained LLMs or task-specific heads, providing evidence that graph models can acquire emergent capabilities from scratch similar to LLMs.

Conclusion: The work suggests graph foundation models can achieve versatile, emergent capabilities purely from graph-scale training, reducing reliance on augmented LLMs and specialized adapters, and opening a path toward universal graph models.

Abstract: We introduce Acacia, a graph foundation model, trained on the web graph. Acacia (i) supports arbitrary feature dimensionalities and semantics without additional training, (ii) supports a wide range of tasks, including node classification, link prediction, node clustering, and graph generation, without additional training, (iii) has in-context learning capabilities, and (iv) does not rely on pretrained LLMs. In particular, existing graph foundation models often require training additional classification heads or feature projectors to accommodate new graphs or new labels, whereas Acacia does not. Moreover, existing graph foundation models often gain their capabilities by being stitched together with pretrained LLMs, whereas Acacia is trained from scratch using only the Common Crawl web graph. This is also an important result because it provides evidence that graph models can acquire emergent capabilities from scratch like LLMs.

</details>


### [253] [JevSoup: System-One Routing for Training-Free LoRA Composition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30922)
*Xiuying Wang,Jiahua Cheng,Shuotian Li,Yufan Cheng,Bowen Deng,Zhexuan Bai,Yichen Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Training-free JevSoup framework for routing LoRA experts by separating System One routing from System Two execution, achieving modest but consistent gains across multiple tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coordinate modular capabilities across diverse tasks; overcome limitations of existing routing approaches that require extra data, training, or autoregressive decoding.

Method: JevSoup selects two experts using input and expert descriptions via structured probabilities; retains the first expert's update; projects the second update onto the orthogonal complement of the first update's row space; combines updates with equal weights; training-free.

Result: On 14 PorTAL tasks across three Qwen3 scales, JevSoup yields up to 1.19 percentage point improvement in task-macro accuracy and 1.21 percentage points in sample-micro accuracy over strongest external baselines.

Conclusion: Code is publicly available at GitHub; demonstrates effective training-free modular routing for adaptable AI systems.

Abstract: Building adaptable AI systems requires effective coordination of specialized capabilities across diverse tasks. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables modular expertise, but existing routing approaches may require auxiliary data, additional training, or autoregressive decoding. We propose JevSoup, a training-free framework separating System One expert routing from System Two execution. Using only the input and expert descriptions, Jev selects two experts through structured probabilities. JevSoup retains the leading expert's update, projects the second onto the orthogonal complement of the first update's row space, and combines them with equal weights. Across 14 PorTAL tasks and three Qwen3 scales, JepSoup achieves absolute gains of up to 1.19\% in task-macro and 1.21\% in sample-micro accuracy over the strongest evaluated external baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/Leowang980/JevSoup.

</details>


### [254] [Self-Play Search Distillation for Large Language Model Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30936)
*Lorenzo Molfetta,Wai-Chung Kwan,Giacomo Frisoni,Luca Ragazzi,Gianluca Moro,Pavlos Vougiouklis,Jeff Z. Pan,Pasquale Minervini*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A self-play search distillation framework (SPSD) generates high-quality, environment-grounded synthetic data by converting MuZero-like self-play traces into stepwise reasoning (chains-of-thought) to improve LLM reasoning; shows strong gains on math benchmarks and game-playing tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data scarcity and low quality of synthetic data hinder LLM reasoning; labeling cost is high, motivating annotation-efficient methods that produce high-quality supervision.

Method: SPSD employs MuZero-like agents in executable environments to perform self-play search; at each state an expert specifies a preferred decision, plausible alternatives, plausible opponent replies, and value estimates; records are transformed into chains-of-thought and used to train LLMs with environment-grounded supervision.

Result: On Qwen3-4B-Base, mean performance over six mathematics benchmarks rises from 24.1 to 36.6; held-out-game win rate improves from 15% to 45%.

Conclusion: SPSD provides an annotation-efficient approach to create high-quality synthetic data that improves LLM reasoning, with demonstrated transfer to unseen mathematics.

Abstract: Improving reasoning abilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) requires high-quality data that exposes difficult decisions, competing alternatives, and their consequences. Data scarcity is driven by the low quality of synthetic data and the cost of human labeling. We introduce Self-Play Search Distillation (SPSD), a framework for generating superhuman synthetic data via self-play of MuZero-like networks trained on board games. SPSD uses executable environments to turn search into structured reasoning problems. At each state, the expert identifies a preferred decision, plausible alternatives, plausible opponent replies, and value estimates. By converting the self-play search records into superhuman chains-of-thought, we train LLMs with environment-grounded supervision. Although trained only on self-play search records, SPSD transfers to unseen mathematics. On Qwen3-4B-Base, it raises the mean over six mathematics benchmarks from 24.1 to 36.6 while increasing the held-out-game win rate from 15% to 45%. SPSD offers an annotation-efficient way to create high-quality synthetic data for improving LLM performance in reasoning tasks.

</details>


### [255] [MACBT: A Multi-Agent Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Decision Support System with Longitudinal Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30939)
*De Jiang,Shuo Zhang,Weiwei Liao,Jianying Zhang,Chuanhui Yu,Hongen Liao,Kehong Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A multi-agent, memory-augmented AI system (MACBT with CD Memory) for CBT that scales clinician workflow, tracks cognitive distortions over time, and improves session quality and cross-session continuity, outperforming baselines in professionalism and authenticity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address CBT scalability constraints by reducing pre/post-session workload and enabling longitudinal cognitive-pathology tracking, thereby improving treatment effectiveness and accessibility.

Method: Five-agent MACBT encodes the five-stage CBT workflow (assessment, Socratic questioning, cognitive restructuring, behavioral experiments, treatment monitoring) into collaborative agents. CD Memory tracks cognitive-distortion type, frequency, severity, and restructuring efficacy across sessions to generate pre-session pathology reports and intervention-priority recommendations. A Chinese CBT dialogue corpus was constructed via dual-role LLM simulation and a Qwen3-14B backbone was trained with supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization.

Result: Evaluation with GPT-4 judges shows MACBT outperforms MeChat, SoulChat, PsyChat, and CPsyCounX in professionalism (2.62) and clinical authenticity (2.25). The full memory-augmented system improves session quality by 12.6% and achieves a longitudinal mean of 2.29 on cross-session continuity, intervention progression, and personalization.

Conclusion: The proposed MACBT+CD Memory framework enhances CBT scalability and continuity, demonstrating improved clinician-facing performance and potential for clinical deployment, subject to broader validation.

Abstract: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an evidence-based first-line treatment for depression, yet its scale is constrained by the time clinicians spend on pre-session preparation, post-session documentation, and longitudinal cognitive-pathology tracking. We present a clinician-facing AI decision-support system that combines a multi-agent CBT framework (MACBT) with a CBT-specific longitudinal memory module (CD Memory). MACBT encodes the five-stage CBT workflow (assessment, Socratic questioning, cognitive restructuring, behavioral experiments, and treatment monitoring) into five collaborative agents. CD Memory tracks cognitive-distortion type, frequency, severity, and restructuring efficacy across sessions to generate pre-session pathology reports and intervention-priority recommendations. We construct a Chinese CBT dialogue corpus via dual-role large language model simulation and train a Qwen3-14B backbone with supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization. Evaluation with GPT-4 judges shows MACBT outperforms MeChat, SoulChat, PsyChat, and CPsyCounX in professionalism (2.62) and clinical authenticity (2.25). The full memory-augmented system further improves session quality by 12.6% and achieves a longitudinal mean of 2.29 on cross-session continuity, intervention progression, and personalization.

</details>


### [256] [Financial Fragility in Societies of LLM Agents: Coordination Failures and Stabilizing Mechanisms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30940)
*Zhenhao Fu,Ruipeng Xu,Qibing Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM agents in a FRAIL framework reveal systemic fragility in financial scenarios; three coordination mechanisms improve outcomes but no universal best; early broad commitments are crucial for stabilization; emphasizes system-level safety design for financial AI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the gap between individual-agent safety and system-level safety as LLMs participate in financial decision-making, investigating how agent interactions shape collective risk in bank runs, debt rollover, and reward crowdfunding.

Method: Controlled experiments using FRAIL with seven leading LLMs across three dynamic financial environments (bank runs, debt rollover, reward crowdfunding); establish baseline failure rates; compare three interaction mechanisms—compensated commitments, centralized commitment agreements, and participant-led coalitions; evaluate across environments and analyze temporal patterns.

Result: Baseline fragility is high (77% bank-run, 83% debt-rollover failures); all three coordination mechanisms improve aggregate outcomes; no single mechanism dominates across all structures; successful stabilization tends to emerge when broad commitments are made early, before defensive dynamics self-reinforce.

Conclusion: System-level evaluation and interaction design are essential for financial AI safety; individually capable agents do not ensure safe financial systems; coordination mechanisms and early commitment strategies are key. Code is available.

Abstract: Individually protective decisions can produce avoidable collective failures. As large language model (LLM) agents take on greater roles in financial decision-making, financial AI safety must therefore be considered not only at the level of individual agents, but also at the level of the systems they jointly create. We study this problem with FRAIL, a controlled experimental framework that places LLM agents in three dynamic financial environments---bank runs, debt rollover, and reward crowdfunding---where agents' decisions reshape the financial conditions faced by others. Across seven leading LLMs, we find widespread collective fragility even when no agent is instructed to destabilize the system: 77\% of baseline bank-run episodes and 83\% of debt-rollover episodes end in failure. We then compare three interaction mechanisms based on compensated commitments, centralized commitment agreements, and participant-led coalitions. All three improve aggregate outcomes, but no single mechanism performs best across all financial structures. Across mechanisms, successful stabilization shares a common temporal pattern: broad commitment forms early, before defensive behavior becomes self-reinforcing. Our findings show that individually capable agents do not automatically form safe financial systems, highlighting system-level evaluation and interaction design as central problems for financial AI safety. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FinFrail-CF26.

</details>


### [257] [LogicTree-RAG: Logic Tree-guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Long-form Patent Drafting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30943)
*Jiaqi Zhu,Naili Xing,Hexiang Pan,Haotian Gao,Jianwei Yin,Xiaokui Xiao,Beng Chin Ooi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces LogicTree-RAG, a logic-tree-guided retrieval-augmented generation framework that builds a hierarchical logic tree to organize and ground patent disclosures, enabling controllable, long-form, section-balanced generation with improved quality and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-form technical text generation requires global coherence and rigorous reasoning; patents typify this challenge. Existing methods either generate partial sections or rely on hand-crafted outlines, hindering scalable automation.

Method: Construct a hierarchical logic tree via evidence-guided recursive node generation. Use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to ground content. Apply a hybrid traversal to map the logic tree into patent sections, enabling controllable, section-balanced generation without relying on expert-drafted priors.

Result: Empirically outperform strong LLM baselines in content quality and language conformity, produce longer structured outputs with higher token efficiency, demonstrating improved logic-centric generation for complex technical drafting.

Conclusion: Logic-centric generation with a globally organized logic tree is effective for long-form, technically rigorous documents like patents and supports scalable automation without dependence on manually crafted drafting priors.

Abstract: Long-form technical text generation underpins knowledge-intensive workflows, yet remains challenging for large language models (LLMs) due to the need for globally consistent logical structuring and faithful technical reasoning beyond local coherence. Patent drafting is a canonical instance of this challenge, demanding holistic generation of a legally compliant and technically exhaustive document through sustained multi-expert collaboration. Existing approaches often focus on partial section generation or rely on manually crafted outlines, limiting scalable automation in realistic settings. In this work, we propose LogicTree-RAG, a logic tree-guided retrieval-augmented generation framework that induces a hierarchical logic tree as a global organizational backbone to organize and ground technical disclosures, without relying on expert-defined drafting priors. Each node in the logic tree represents a technical element and is constructed through evidence-guided recursive generation. A hybrid traversal mechanism then maps the logic tree into patent sections, enabling controllable and section-balanced generation. Extensive experiments show that LogicTree-RAG consistently improves content quality and language conformity over strong LLM-based baselines and achieves longer structured generation with high token efficiency, demonstrating the effectiveness of logic-centric generation for complex technical document drafting.

</details>


### [258] [FTB Graph: Determining and Validating First-token Broadcasters and Language-Identity Head Circuits in Multilingual Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30954)
*Arjun Pillai,Christian Hoang,Anjelo Laroza*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Maps causal circuits for first-token language routing across six LLMs using EAP and exact patching; finds pretraining-established hubs, with topology varying by model size and regime; weak alignment between EAP and exact patches emphasizes need for exact interventions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how multilingual LLMs decide the target language for the first token, and whether this routing is fixed by pretraining or reshaped by instruction tuning.

Method: Apply Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) with FP16 active clamping to extract directed acyclic graphs of causal edges driving first-token language broadcasting. Validate with exact activation patching using a 2,000-edge search ceiling across GPT-2, BLOOM-560M, Pythia-1B/2.8B, and Qwen2.5-1.5B Base/Instruct.

Result: Across standalone models there are deep/mid hubs; strongest evidence for Pythia-2.8B and BLOOM-560M. GPT-2 and Pythia-1B reveal fewer out-of-graph heads; Qwen variants invert the necessity check. Scaling from 1B to 2.8B increases node participation but preserves the edge budget, yielding sparser graphs. Qwen base/instruct show 84.7% Jaccard similarity, including a Layer 27 hub, suggesting routing is largely pretraining-established and preserved by instruction tuning. EAP scores correlate weakly with exact patching deltas, indicating linear gradient cues can diverge from causal interventions in FP16. 

Conclusion: Exact-patching verification is necessary for reliable circuit discovery; EAP alone can mislead in FP16 regimes. First-token language routing appears largely fixed during pretraining and remains stable under instruction tuning across diverse architectures.

Abstract: Large language models operating in multilingual contexts must resolve target response languages early in generation, yet the causal circuitry governing first-token language identity decisions remains poorly mapped. We present an end-to-end structural circuit analysis across six model architectures spanning four families: GPT-2, BLOOM-560M, Pythia-1B/2.8B, and Qwen2.5-1.5B Base/Instruct. Using Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) with FP16 active clamping, followed by exact activation patching verification with a 2,000-candidate-edge search ceiling, we extract directed acyclic graphs driving first-token language broadcasting. Across the standalone models, we observe deep or mid-to-deep broadcasting hubs, though the evidence is strongest for Pythia-2.8B and BLOOM-560M because GPT-2 and Pythia-1B leave few out-of-graph heads for comparison, while both Qwen2.5-1.5B variants invert the necessity check. Scaling from Pythia-1B to 2.8B expands node participation while maintaining a similar verified edge budget, producing sparser topology. The Qwen2.5-1.5B base and instruct circuits retain 84.7% Jaccard similarity, including the Layer 27 hub, indicating that first-token routing is largely established during pretraining and preserved by instruction tuning. Finally, EAP scores correlate weakly with exact patching deltas across most models, showing that linear gradient approximations can diverge from causal interventions in FP16 and motivating exact-patching verification for reliable circuit discovery.

</details>


### [259] [MoMHa: Multi-Objective Optimization of LLM Harnesses over Accuracy, Safety, and Tokens](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30967)
*Subhojyoti Mukherjee,Md Mehrab Tanjim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Meta-Harness reframes harness design as a multi-objective search over accuracy, safety, and token cost, using a single-phase joint-reward proposer (MoMHa) to outperform baselines across 17 domains and 12 models; demonstrates transfer to unseen benchmarks and enhanced safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Harness code and surrounding tooling (the “harness”) significantly shape model behavior and safety, yet have been treated as ancillary. The work argues that harness design is a first-class, multi-objective design surface.

Method: Uses an agentic proposer (Claude Code) with full filesystem access to prior harness sources, traces, and scoring artifacts to optimize three objectives (accuracy, behavioral safety, token cost) in a single-phase joint-reward framework. Evaluated across 17 domains (synthetic suites, public benchmarks, safety domains) on a 12-model fleet; compares MoMHa to multiple baselines including two-phase and scalar feedback.

Result: MoMHa achieves higher joint performance than baselines (synthetic mean 0.482 vs 0.198–0.422; real-world 0.461 vs 0.377 for strongest baseline). It wins 7/10 synthetic columns and 5/7 real-world columns, projects good transfer to unseen benchmarks (8/12 models). It yields the highest safety composite on U-SafeBench (0.781) and saves ~95 tokens per example versus the two-phase approach.

Conclusion: A single-phase joint-reward optimization for harness design effectively navigates the accuracy-safety-cost trade-offs, producing superior harnesses that generalize across domains and models; the authors plan to release code, evaluation infrastructure, and logs to enable reproducibility.

Abstract: Most work on improving large language models treats accuracy as the sole objective. We argue that the harness, the Python code surrounding the model that constructs prompts, routes calls, and parses outputs, is a first-class design surface whose quality is inherently multi-objective: an accurate harness that refuses no unsafe request, or that consumes an order of magnitude more tokens, is not a good harness. We present Meta-Harness, a system that casts harness design as search over three per-domain objectives (accuracy, behavioural safety, and token cost) solved by an agentic proposer (Claude Code) with full filesystem access to prior harness source, execution traces, and scoring artifacts. Our central finding is that a singlephase joint-reward proposer (MoMHa) outperforms every alternative, including a two-phase "accuracy then tokens" ablation, scalar-only feedback, and an accuracy-only baseline. We evaluate on seventeen domains: seven synthetic capability suites, seven real-world public benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, Spider, FEVER, MMLU-Pro, LawBench, NuminaMath), and three U-SafeBench-derived user-specific safety domains, using a 12-model fleet spanning four families. On the synthetic track MoMHa achieves a joint mean of 0.482 versus 0.198-0.422 for ten baselines, winning $7 / 10$ per-domain columns; on the real-world track it scores 0.461 versus 0.377 for the strongest baseline (DSPy), winning 5/7 columns, demonstrating that harness strategies transfer to unseen benchmarks without retraining on 8 of 12 target models. MoMHa attains the highest measured behavioral safety composite (U-SafeBench, 0.781) and uses 95 fewer tokens per example than the two-phase alternative. We will release all harness code, evaluation infrastructure, and crossmodel logs.

</details>


### [260] [SciHorizon-eLab: An Agentic Protocol-to-Task Compiler for Scalable Benchmarking of Scientific Embodied Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30971)
*Maokai Qin,Chuan Qin,Qi Zhang,Dianyu Liu,Zirui Liu,Hongting Niu,Yuanchun Zhou,Hengshu Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A protocol-to-task compiler (SciHorizon-eLab) converts natural-language scientific protocols into semantically-preserving embodied tasks, enabling a ready-made benchmark (BenchName) of 300 tasks with certification and evaluation, and revealing notable coordination weaknesses in current policies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current simulation benchmarks require manual task engineering, hindering scalable, diverse, and verifiable embodied scientific experiments.

Method: SciHorizon-eLab uses semantic grounding, executable task synthesis, and multi-stage simulation-based certification to convert protocols into embodied tasks, generating grounded environments, manipulation programs, and step-level success criteria, along with reproducible expert demonstrations and traces; BenchName (300 tasks) supports hardware-in-the-loop evaluation and ordered step-level evaluation.

Result: The strongest policy achieved an average success rate of 49.7% across representative tasks; analysis uncovers significant coordination gaps among humans and embodied agents; the paper releases code, benchmark data, and an evaluation toolkit.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates a scalable, semantically faithful pipeline for turning textual scientific protocols into executable embodied tasks and provides a challenging benchmark that exposes coordination weaknesses, underscoring the need for improved embodied reasoning and collaboration between humans and agents.

Abstract: Embodied agents offer a promising route to automating scientific experimentation, yet their progress is constrained by the lack of reliable and systematic evaluation environments. Existing simulation-based laboratory benchmarks rely heavily on manual task engineering, making it challenging to systematically compile diverse scientific protocols into executable and verifiable embodied tasks at scale. To address this challenge, we introduce SciHorizon-eLab, an agentic protocol-to-task compiler that formulates scientific embodied task construction as a compilation problem. Given a natural-language protocol of scientific experiments, SciHorizon-eLab progressively compiles laboratory protocols into semantic-preserving embodied tasks through semantic grounding, executable task synthesis, and multi-stage simulation-based certification. The system generates semantically grounded environments, executable manipulation programs, and step-level success specifications, while enabling reproducible generation of expert demonstrations and execution traces. Using this pipeline, we further construct \BenchName, a ready-to-use benchmark comprising 300 certified tasks across diverse laboratory operations. It supports HIL task execution, reproducible expert-demonstration generation, and ordered step-level evaluation. Across representative tasks, the strongest policy attains an average success rate of only 49.7%, with further evaluations revealing pronounced weaknesses in human and embodied agent coordination. We publicly release the code, benchmark data, and evaluation toolkit at https://github.com/SciHorizon-elab/SciHorizon-elab.

</details>


### [261] [Factorized axis convolutional gated recurrent unit with dynamic adaptive pooling for remaining useful life prediction of rolling bearings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30972)
*Hanbyeol Park,Jungho Choo,Hyerim Bae*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Factorized-axis CNN-GRU with multiscale anisotropic convolutions, dual-axis block attention, and dynamic adaptive pooling for TFR-based bearing RUL prediction; adds uncertainty estimation via Monte Carlo dropout; ablations show axis-wise design and adaptive pooling improve performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mitigate alignment of degradation-revealing structures along time/frequency axes in TFRs and overcome loss of salient activations caused by global pooling; enhance directional feature extraction and temporal modeling for more accurate and robust RUL estimates.

Method: Introduce a factorized-axis convolutional GRU with multiscale anisotropic convolutions and a dual-axis convolutional block attention module. Employ dynamic adaptive pooling to aggregate time-frequency features, use a GRU for temporal dynamics, and apply Monte Carlo dropout for predictive uncertainty.

Result: Outperforms existing RUL prediction methods on two public bearing datasets across operating conditions. Ablation studies show factorized axis-wise design reduces errors versus isotropic kernels; DAP improves on one dataset and matches GAP on the other, underscoring the value of anisotropic feature extraction and adaptive aggregation.

Conclusion: Anisotropic, axis-wise feature extraction combined with adaptive time-frequency pooling and temporal modeling yields superior, robust RUL predictions with uncertainty estimates; the approach highlights the importance of preserving directional information in TFRs for degradation prognosis.

Abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNN) are widely used to predict the remaining useful life (RUL) of rolling bearings from time-frequency representations (TFRs) of vibration signals. However, during degradation, characteristic structures in TFRs align predominantly along the frequency or time axis, making it challenging for conventional CNN isotropic kernels to capture directional structure. Furthermore, global average pooling (GAP) averages across axes, potentially obscuring the locations and concentrations of salient activations. This study introduces a factorized-axis convolutional gated recurrent unit (GRU) that employs multiscale anisotropic convolution and dual-axis convolution block attention module to enhance directional features and highlight salient time-frequency regions. Dynamic adaptive pooling (DAP) adaptively aggregates the time-frequency-axis information from the extracted feature maps, whereas a GRU captures temporal dynamics in the latent representations and Monte Carlo dropout enables predictive uncertainty estimation. Experiments on two public bearing datasets demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing RUL prediction methods across operating conditions. Ablation experiments demonstrate that the factorized axis-wise design achieves lower mean errors than convolutional isotropic kernels. DAP yields clear improvements on one dataset while matching GAP on the other, highlighting the importance of anisotropic feature extraction and adaptive feature aggregation for TFR-based RUL prediction.

</details>


### [262] [Same Text, Different Numbers: The Divergence of LLM-Based Measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31013)
*Hamid Boustanifar,Sasan Mansouri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM-derived textual measures vary substantially across models; cross-model correlations are modest (~0.52); ensemble averaging stabilizes rankings but not level scores; model choice drives downstream inference; must validate across providers and treat measurements as model-contingent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate invariance of LLM-based textual proxies to model choice and their reliability for empirical analysis in finance; determine whether measurements are driven by model-specific effects or reflect underlying disclosure.

Method: Apply thirteen LLM-generated measures (e.g., sentiment, management clarity, uncertainty, answer specificity, climate/political risk) to earnings-call transcripts of S&P 500 firms using seven LLMs from different providers; assess cross-model rank correlations, transcript-level variance, and whether cross-model disagreement predicts analyst/market disagreement; examine how model choice affects downstream coefficient estimates; evaluate ensemble averaging effects on rankings and score levels.

Result: Cross-model rank correlations average 0.52; transcript-level differences explain ~34% of total score variation; cross-model disagreement does not predict subsequent analyst/market disagreement; model choice substantially affects coefficient magnitudes, signs, and statistical significance; averaging across providers yields more stable rankings for most constructs, but score levels remain sensitive to the models included in the ensemble.

Conclusion: LLM-generated variables are model-contingent measurements; validation across providers is essential; avoid relying on a single model; ensemble averaging helps with ranking stability, but level estimates remain model-dependent.

Abstract: Researchers increasingly use generative large language models (LLMs) to convert corporate text into empirical variables. We examine the extent to which LLM-based textual measures are invariant to model choice using thirteen measures, including sentiment, management clarity, uncertainty, answer specificity, and climate and political risk. Seven LLMs from different providers score earnings call transcripts of S&P 500 companies on these constructs. Cross-model rank correlations average only 0.52, and transcript-level differences common across providers account for only 34% of total score variation. Cross-model disagreement does not predict subsequent analyst or market disagreement, consistent with a substantial model-specific component rather than common ambiguity in the underlying disclosure. Model choice significantly affects downstream inference, with coefficient magnitudes, signs, and statistical significance varying substantially across models. Averaging across providers makes transcript rankings more stable for most constructs, but score levels remain sensitive to the models included in the ensemble. LLM-generated variables should therefore be treated as model-contingent measurements and validated across providers.

</details>


### [263] [Governed Deduction: Policy-Grounded Premise Authorization Beyond Relevance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31029)
*Wesley Shu,Hsi-Ching Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Governed Deduction (GD) formalizes authorization as a transition-local admit predicate that separates premise relevance from policy constraints. Empirical results show learned/policy models fail to recover policy-grounded authorization after context-local role permutations, even though simple relevance-based controls can achieve high accuracy; a symbolic policy oracle remains perfect. This reveals a controlled negative finding and the need for leakage audits in evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To assess whether learned reasoning models can capture policy-grounded authorization beyond mere relevance, and to expose potential shortcuts and leakage in policy-sensitive benchmarks that mix access control with logical inference.

Method: Define admit(p, tau, S) as a transition-local predicate within GD. From an RBAC-augmented Spider benchmark, construct 4,461 matched authorization pairs where the same query premise and policy state yield both permitted and denied consuming transitions. Evaluate multiple controllers: joint control (high accuracy), transition-only control (100% due to a role-name shortcut). Apply a frozen, label-independent context-local role permutation to remove shortcuts. Re-evaluate premise/state-only, transition-only, and joint linear controllers (expect 50% on 1,856 held-out edges). Compare against a symbolic policy oracle (100%). Include matched one-sided controls and leakage audits as evaluation components.

Result: Initial joint controller achieves 99.19% held-out accuracy. Transition-only control reaches 100% accuracy, revealing a role-name shortcut. After applying a context-local role permutation, premise/state-only, transition-only, and joint linear controllers all score exactly 50% on 1,856 held-out edges, while a symbolic policy oracle remains at 100%. This constitutes a controlled negative finding: policy-grounded authorization can extend beyond relevance, and the frozen linear representation fails to recover the relation.

Conclusion: The benchmark demonstrates that policy-grounded authorization can elude relevance-based reasoning and simple learned models. Frozen linear representations do not recover the policy relation, underscoring the need for matched one-sided controls and leakage audits to properly evaluate policy-sensitive reasoning in authorization benchmarks.

Abstract: Reasoning systems usually treat premise use as a question of relevance: if a fact is available and useful, it may be selected for inference. Authorization imposes a different constraint: a premise may be represented and logically usable but not permitted for a particular local transition. We formalize this distinction as Governed Deduction (GD), with a transition-local admission predicate admit(p, tau, S). From an independently produced RBAC-augmented Spider benchmark, we construct 4,461 matched authorization pairs in which the same query premise and policy state support permitted and denied consuming transitions. An initial joint controller reaches 99.19% held-out accuracy, but a transition-only control reaches 100%, exposing a role-name shortcut. After a frozen, label-independent context-local role permutation removes that shortcut, premise/state-only, transition-only, and joint linear controllers all score exactly 50% on 1,856 held-out edges, while a symbolic policy oracle remains at 100%. The result is a controlled negative finding: the benchmark instantiates policy-grounded authorization beyond relevance, but the frozen linear representation does not recover the relation. Matched one-sided controls and leakage audits are therefore essential for evaluating learned policy-sensitive reasoning.

</details>


### [264] [Cheap, open agents make LLM pollution harder to mitigate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31054)
*Raluca Rilla,Anne-Marie Nussberger,Rui Mata,Dirk U. Wulff*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Open-weight LLM agents pose a distinct risk for pollution; fully open agents can match commercial performance; detection checks miss some agents; open-text signals best separate agents from humans; multilayer detection focusing on open-text is recommended.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess how different agent configurations (open vs commercial) influence LLM pollution risk as open-source agentic frameworks become more prevalent; evaluate detection capabilities.

Method: Compare nine agent configurations from fully open (local, no fees) to closed commercial; each agent autonomously completes a multifaceted survey; apply multiple detection checks; analyze performance, detectability, and human-vs-agent discrimination, with emphasis on open-text signals.

Result: Fully open agents perform competitively with commercial counterparts; detection checks fail on different sets of agents; no single check detects all; open-text responses best discriminate between agents and humans; open agents pose a distinct risk for LLM pollution.

Conclusion: Fully open agents constitute a distinct LLM pollution risk; detection should be multilayered, prioritizing open-text analysis to identify agent-generated content.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) pollution occurs when synthetic responses contaminate data intended to capture human behavior. High deployment costs have so far limited the risk posed by autonomous survey agents. However, open-weight models paired with open-source agentic frameworks may have removed this barrier. We compared the performance and detectability of nine agent configurations, ranging from fully open variants to closed commercial ones. Each agent autonomously completed a survey containing multiple response types yielding various detection checks. Fully open agents ran locally without usage fees and performed competitively with commercial alternatives. Open and commercial agents failed different sets of checks, and no single check reliably detected all agents, but open-text responses discriminated best between agents and humans. These findings identify fully open agents as a distinct risk for LLM pollution and support multilayered detection strategies emphasizing open-text analysis.

</details>


### [265] [Neuralyzing the Trace: Selective Representation-Level Unlearning with Contrastive Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31056)
*Itai Zehavi,Fanny Jourdan,Ulrich Aivodji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SCALPEL is a contrastive sparse autoencoder for targeted machine unlearning that combats energy bias in reconstruction-based extraction, achieving more selective forget features. Validated on TOFU across Qwen, Llama, Gemma, outperforming NMF and standard SAE, competitive with Gradient Difference and RMU.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Full forgetting of targeted information (e.g., a single person’s data) is not ensured by behavioral forgetting alone; internal representations require intervention. Standard mechanistic-interpretability extractors are poorly selective for narrow targets due to an energy bias that favors background structure.

Method: Introduce SCALPEL, a contrastive sparse autoencoder. It reduces energy bias in reconstruction, employs contrastive training to promote target-selective features, and uses a selection score to bound background perturbation. Evaluated on TOFU across Qwen, Llama, Gemma, compared to NMF, SAE, Gradient Difference, RMU.

Result: SCALPEL substantially outperforms NMF and standard SAE interventions and is competitive with Gradient Difference and RMU on TOFU across Qwen, Llama, Gemma, indicating stronger target-specific forgetting while controlling background perturbation.

Conclusion: A contrastive sparse autoencoder with a selection score improves target-selective forgetting and bridges mechanistic interpretability with fine-grained unlearning by mitigating energy-bias in reconstruction-based extractors.

Abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove targeted information while preserving a model's other abilities. In realistic settings, such as privacy requests under the EU GDPR, the target may be narrow, for example information associated with a single person. Behavioral forgetting alone may be insufficient, motivating interventions directly on internal representations. However, standard mechanistic-interpretability extractors are poorly selective for such targets. We identify an energy bias in reconstruction-based extraction, which favors dominant background structure over low-energy target-specific components. We introduce SCALPEL, a contrastive sparse autoencoder designed to learn more selective forget features. We show theoretically that contrastive training promotes target-selective features and that our selection score controls expected background knowledge perturbation. We validate SCALPEL experimentally on TOFU across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, where it substantially improves over NMF and standard SAE interventions and is competitive with Gradient Difference and RMU, bridging mechanistic interpretability and fine-grained unlearning.

</details>


### [266] [Externalized CPDAG Summaries Improve LLM Causal Deduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31071)
*Wentao Sun,João Paulo Nogueira,Dominique Verchere,Mathieu Acher,Alonso Silva*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Externalizing the latent CPDAG state in Corr2Cause via a constrained, schema-driven two-turn pipeline (Structured Thinking) improves causal-label reasoning across models, outperforming baselines and robust to CPDAG scrambling; supports a bounded design principle of externalizing the object defining the label.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the Markov-equivalence class ambiguity in causal claims by converting local pattern matching into explicit, testable graph-state reasoning.

Method: Introduce a two-turn pipeline: (1) externalize a typed, schema-constrained CPDAG summary; (2) answer questions using the external graph state. Evaluate with Corr2Cause full test across multiple models (Qwen3.5-27B, Qwen3.6-27B, Paraphrase-OOD, GPT-5.4-mini) and ablations (PC scaffold, two-turn prose control, scrambled CPDAG, full-split audit).

Result: Structured Thinking raises Yes-F1 on Qwen3.5-27B from 73.0 to 86.4 ( +13.4 pp; McNemar p=2.4e-6 ); across three seeds, mean gain +8.1 ± 5.3 pp. Prose-control baselines reach only 67.6 F1. Scrambling CPDAG costs 12.0 pp F1. Full-split audit shows reference CPDAG agreement: ID skeleton F1 0.960; exact match 75.9%. Pattern holds across models and datasets, including GPT-3.6/Paraphrase-OOD/GPT-5.4-mini.

Conclusion: Externalizing the latent label-defining object (the CPDAG) with constrained form, and testing downstream usage on that state, yields robust gains and supports a bounded design principle for complex reasoning in causal-inference tasks.

Abstract: Corr2Cause asks whether a causal claim holds in every DAG compatible with observed correlations and conditional independencies. We frame this as latent-object reasoning: the label is defined by a CPDAG query, but free-form chain-of-thought often collapses the Markov-equivalence-class problem into local pattern matching. We propose Structured Thinking, a two-turn pipeline that first externalizes a typed, schema-constrained CPDAG summary and then answers against that graph state. On the Corr2Cause full test, Structured Thinking raises Qwen3.5-27B from $73.0$ to $86.4$ $F_1$(Yes) over a strong PC-instruction baseline in the primary paired run ($+13.4$ pp; McNemar $p=2.4\times 10^{-6}$; bootstrap $95\%$ CI [$+8.4$, $+18.6$]); across three full-ID seeds, the mean gain is $+8.1 \pm 5.3$ pp. A PC-scaffolded two-turn prose control reaches only $67.6$ $F_1$, indicating that a detailed PC scaffold plus a schema-free prose intermediate is not sufficient. The same pattern holds on Qwen3.6-27B, Paraphrase-OOD, and GPT-5.4-mini. Scrambling the emitted CPDAG costs $12.0$ pp $F_1$, and a full-split audit shows close agreement with the reference CPDAG (ID skeleton $F_1$ $0.960$; exact match $75.9\%$). These results support a bounded design principle: externalize the latent object that defines the label, constrain its form, and test whether downstream answers use it.

</details>


### [267] [Up and Down the Abstraction Ladder: Code-Based Skills for Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31076)
*Bartłomiej Cupiał,Jens Tuyls,Maciej Wołczyk,Davide Paglieri,Martin Klissarov,Benjamin Eysenbach,Piotr Miłoś,Karthik R. Narasimhan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Code-based skill libraries, when used with language models, can dramatically improve long-horizon action planning in NetHack by enabling reusable skills while preserving low-level actions as a fallback; this yields higher progress, lower inference cost, and faster RL learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the productivity-flexibility tradeoff in language-enabled agents: relying solely on primitive actions is inefficient for long sequences, while code-based abstractions risk being unable to handle out-of-skill situations. The paper systematically evaluates how semantic skills affect performance, cost, and learning.

Method: Introduce CodeHack, a library of code-based skills described in natural language. Compare three agent setups (primitives only, skills only, and hybrid) across zero-shot prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning in NetHack. Measure game progression, per-episode inference cost, and learning speed/benefit.

Result: Compared with primitives, skills nearly triple NetHack progression and reduce per-episode inference cost by 86% in broad zero-shot evaluation.
