HybridSkill+Primitives retains most benefits and provides a safe fallback to primitives. In RL, skill-based agents learn much faster, achieving 7.2x larger average dungeon-level gains within the same training budget.

Conclusion: Providing a library of semantic skills improves performance, efficiency, and learning; combining skills with primitives preserves flexibility when the skill library is insufficient. CodeHack and associated code are released for replication.

Abstract: Language agents struggle to act and learn in environments that require long sequences of low-level actions. Code-based abstractions can make these agents more productive by letting them invoke reusable skills instead of repeatedly selecting individual actions. The code handles recurring local decisions, while the language model decides which skills to use and how to combine them. Yet abstractions are leaky, and situations beyond a skill's capabilities may require a return to primitive actions. Motivated by this tradeoff between productivity and flexibility, we systematically study how code-based action abstraction affects the performance, inference cost, and learning of language agents. We study this in NetHack, a challenging, long-horizon game environment, using CodeHack, our library of code-based skills with natural-language descriptions. We use this library to compare agents restricted to primitives with those using semantic skills alone or in combination with primitives. We evaluate these agents in three settings: zero-shot prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. Across a broad zero-shot evaluation on NetHack, we find that compared with primitives, skills nearly triple game progression, while reducing inference cost per episode by 86%. Combining skills with primitives retains much of this benefit while preserving a path back down to low-level actions. Finally, in RL, we find that skill-based agents learn significantly faster than agents acting on primitives, achieving a 7.2x larger average gain in dungeon level over the same training budget. These results show that a supplied skill library can improve performance, efficiency, and learning, while retaining primitives provides flexibility when the library is insufficient. We release CodeHack together with training and evaluation code.

</details>


### [268] [OmouAI: Argumentative Human-AI Policy Deliberation with Simulated Personas](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31078)
*Stylianos Loukas Vasileiou,Antonio Rago,William Yeoh,Georgina Curto*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OmouAI couples LLM-based debates with computational argumentation, enabling multi-agent, human-in-the-loop policy deliberation whose arguments are evaluated against external goals for transparent, goal-aligned recommendations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-stakes human-LLM deliberations (e.g., public policy) risk sycophancy and opaque explanations. A formal, goal-aligned deliberation framework can enhance transparency, fidelity, and accountability.

Method: Simulated personas (stakeholders, domain experts, devil's advocates) each generate arguments; these form a shared argumentation framework. Humans contest, add, or revise arguments. Arguments are evaluated using deterministic argumentative semantics against external goals (e.g., UN SDGs), with goal propagation indicating support for policy recommendations.

Result: Proposes a system and methodology for interactive deliberation that yields interpretable, goal-aligned policy insights, with human oversight guiding argument revision and ensuring faithful explanations.

Conclusion: Integrating LLM-driven argumentation with formal semantics and external-goal evaluation enables transparent, accountable policy deliberations and actionable recommendations, mitigating sycophancy while maintaining stakeholder inclusivity.

Abstract: Debates amongst agents driven by large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated vast potential in various applications, but when these interactions include humans and take place in high-stakes environments, e.g., in public policy deliberations, they are beset with issues such as sycophancy and a lack of faithful explanations. To tackle these issues, we present OmouAI, an interactive and inclusive deliberation system that uses LLMs in combination with computational argumentation, a field which excels in representing and reasoning within debates. OmouAI allows a human user to deliberate policy claims for real-world challenges with simulated personas, e.g., representing stakeholders, domain experts or devil's advocates, towards reducing sycophancy. Each persona generates its own arguments, and the arguments of all parties form a shared argumentation framework. Users can then contest, add and revise arguments, providing crucial human oversight. Then, arguments are evaluated using deterministic argumentative semantics against external goals, such as the UN Sustainable Development Goals, guaranteeing faithful explanations. The advancement or worsening of the goals thus serve as indicators for the policy recommendations.

</details>


### [269] [Monitor Jailbreaking: Evading Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Without Encoded Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31121)
*Julian Schulz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoT monitors can be jailbroken by reformatting prompts; models do not hide reasoning but evade detectors, while humans can read the reasoning. Paraphrasing defenses can restore detection without harming performance. The vulnerability generalizes across models, monitors, tasks, and prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate the reliability of chain-of-thought monitoring under optimization pressure from reinforcement learning and determine whether models hide reasoning or only evade detectors.

Method: Train models on a main task plus a side task, penalizing when a monitor detects side-task reasoning. Test across model sizes, monitor types, and tasks. Assess generalization to unseen monitors and prompts. Evaluate transfer of jailbreaking strategies and a paraphrase-based defense.

Result: Models learn to jailbreak monitors by carefully phrasing their CoT so detectors fail while human readers can still see the reasoning. Jailbreak strategies generalize across models, monitors, tasks, and prompts and transfer to unseen monitors. Paraphrasing jailbroken CoT restores monitor detection without sacrificing task performance.

Conclusion: CoT monitoring is vulnerable under optimization pressure; decoding circuits may not be hidden but formatted to mislead detectors. Robust defenses are needed, with paraphrase-based approaches as a potential remedy, though more robust, detector-agnostic methods are required.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising safety technique for reasoning models, enabling detection of problematic reasoning before models act. A key concern is encoded reasoning, where models hide their true reasoning in ways that monitors and humans cannot interpret. Optimization pressure from CoT monitors during reinforcement learning is considered a likely driver of such behavior. We investigate this by training reasoning models to perform a main task and a side task, while penalizing them when a monitor detects reasoning about the side task. Surprisingly, models learn to evade monitors without encoding their reasoning. Instead, they learn to phrase and format their chains of thought such that monitors fail to flag side task reasoning, while the reasoning remains completely transparent to human readers. We call this phenomenon monitor jailbreaking. We find that monitor jailbreaking arises across different model sizes, monitors, and tasks. Jailbreaks generalize to monitors not seen during training, including both less and more capable monitors, and transfer across different monitor prompts. While jailbreaking strategies appear simple, manually replicating them does not reliably fool monitors. Finally, we show that paraphrasing is an effective defense: paraphrasing a jailbroken CoT allows the same monitor to correctly flag it, while still allowing the model to perform both tasks.

</details>


### [270] [AtomWorld-Mem: Memory-Restored World States for Long-Horizon Atomistic Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31133)
*Tian Luo,Ruge Zhang,Haozhi Han,Yifrng Chen,Yunquan Zhang,Yunxin Liu,Ting Cao,Kun Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Memory-based world-state restoration enables long-horizon, high-fidelity atomistic evolution. AtomWorld-Mem uses memory modules to reconstruct latent states from snapshots, guiding vacancy-mediated events under KMC constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Instantaneous crystal snapshots are ambiguous; different hidden dynamical contexts can lead to different futures. A memory-based restoration of latent world states could enable accurate, transferable long-term evolution.

Method: AtomWorld-Mem builds an AtomWorld where spatial encoders extract multi-scale atomistic keyframes from local topology and defect context. Short-term event memory and long-term structural memory integrate keyframes over time to restore a future-predictive state, which then prioritizes legal vacancy-mediated events under single-event KMC while preserving realism via the underlying simulator.

Result: Empirically, the approach improves long-horizon progress under fixed microscopic event budgets, maintains high-fidelity evolution across energetic, structural, and vacancy-transport observables, and transfers zero-shot to unseen alloy-temperature AtomWorlds, indicating the memory-restoration mechanism captures reusable principles of hidden-state inference.

Conclusion: Memory-restored world-state modeling offers a promising, transferable framework for efficient, physically grounded atomistic evolution.

Abstract: High-fidelity atomistic evolution over long timescales requires more than observing the current crystal configuration. Instantaneous atomistic snapshots are often incomplete: locally similar configurations can correspond to different hidden dynamical contexts, future event preferences, and waiting-time scales. We argue that this snapshot ambiguity makes long-horizon atomistic evolution fundamentally a memory-based world-state restoration problem. To address this, we introduce AtomWorld-Mem, a memory-restored atomistic world model that recovers the latent world state missing from instantaneous crystal snapshots. AtomWorld-Mem treats the evolving alloy as an AtomWorld: spatial encoders write multi-scale atomistic keyframes from dense local topology and sparse long-range defect context, while short-term event memory and long-term structural memory integrate these keyframes across time to restore a future-predictive evolutionary state. The restored state is used to prioritize legal vacancy-mediated events under single-event Kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) constraints, while event legality, physical execution, and residence-time updates remain governed by the underlying simulator. Empirically, AtomWorld-Mem improves long-horizon atomistic progress under fixed microscopic event budgets while maintaining high-fidelity evolution across energetic, structural, and vacancy-transport observables. It further transfers zero-shot across diverse unseen alloy-temperature AtomWorlds, suggesting that the learned memory-restoration mechanism captures reusable principles of hidden-state inference rather than a system-specific local energy heuristic. These results position memory-restored world-state modeling as a promising route toward efficient, physically grounded, and transferable atomistic evolution.

</details>


### [271] [Toward AI-Augmented Cooperative Engineering Workflows: Requirements and Architecture the European Rover Challenge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31136)
*Ahmed R. Sadik,Frank Joublin,Mariusz Bujny,Antonello Ceravola,Joan Smith*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI-augmented cooperative engineering workflows for ERC; empirical bottlenecks and an initial architecture.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill a gap in process-level AI support for cooperative engineering, beyond isolated tasks, in time-constrained, high interdependence contexts.

Method: Role-adaptive 40-question survey of ERC 2025 teams; 104 responses from 14 teams; analyze workflows; derive requirements; propose initial architecture.

Result: Identified bottlenecks: limited documentation, unclear requirements, fragmented communication, informal task monitoring, high integration rework. Derived AI-augmented workflow requirements and a preliminary system architecture linking interfaces, credential management, service selection, AI services, and engineering tools; capabilities include task clarification, requirements/compliance management, communication summarization, integration risk detection, and continuous knowledge capture.

Conclusion: Contributes empirical requirements and architectural direction for AI-augmented cooperative engineering workflows in hybrid human-AI teams; provides foundation for implementation and evaluation.

Abstract: The growing availability of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools creates new opportunities to support engineering design processes, yet their current use often remains limited to isolated tasks such as coding, documentation, or information retrieval. Less attention has been given to how AI can support cooperative engineering workflows at the process level, where teams must coordinate requirements, tasks, communication, knowledge transfer, and subsystem integration. This paper investigates this challenge in the context of the European Rover Challenge (ERC), where student teams design and integrate complex rover systems within a single academic cycle under strict time constraints and high subsystem interdependence. We conducted a role adaptive 40 question survey with ERC 2025 teams, yielding 104 responses from 14 teams. The survey examined team structure, knowledge transfer, task management, integration practices, communication patterns, and current AI usage. The results reveal recurring workflow bottlenecks, including limited documentation, unclear requirements, fragmented communication, informal task monitoring, and substantial integration rework. Based on these findings, we derive requirements for AI augmented cooperative engineering work-flows and propose an initial assistant system architecture that connects user facing interfaces, credential management, service selection, specialized AI services, and external engineering tools. The proposed architecture aims to support task clarification, requirement and compliance management, communication summarization, integration risk detection, and continuous knowledge capture. In doing so, the paper contributes empirical requirements and an architectural direction for AI augmented cooperative engineering workflows in hybrid human AI team settings.

</details>


### [272] [Can Linguistic Reasoning Vectors Enhance Multimodal Reasoning Ability?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31140)
*Ziyi Wang,Li Li,Aolin Zhou,Yankun Shen,Chonghan Liu,Shuxia Lin,Xu Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LIFT injects Reasoning Vectors from a base LLM into a VLM to recover degraded reasoning without retraining the backbone, using explicit reasoning traces to guide language-side activations; LLM-derived vectors outperform those from the VLM, partially recovering reasoning across benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-Language Models often lose base LLM's language-side reasoning when scaled and aligned; leveraging the base LLM could restore this capability without costly retraining.

Method: Define Reasoning Vectors as hidden-state differences between a Reasoner path (with explicit reasoning trace) and a Solver path (without trace). Inject these vectors into language-side activations of target VLM; allow learnable vector adaptation; backbone frozen.

Result: Across two VLMs and six reasoning benchmarks, vectors derived from the base LLM outperform those derived from the aligned VLM; LIFT partially recovers reasoning; analysis indicates vectors influence intermediate reasoning rather than only final outputs.

Conclusion: Language-side intervention via Reasoning Vectors is a viable, lightweight approach to recover degraded reasoning in VLMs and highlights the base LLM as a superior source for reasoning transfer; code will be released.

Abstract: Most Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are built by extending pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) with visual modules and multimodal alignment. However, this multimodal scaling often degrades the language-side reasoning ability originally encoded in the base LLM. While the base LLM retains usable reasoning after scaling, the aligned VLM itself cannot reliably access this ability. Therefore, recovering the degraded reasoning capability in VLMs would benefit more from seeking help from the base LLM than from the VLM alone. Motivated by this, we propose LIFT (Language-side reasonIng Facilitation and Transfer), a lightweight vector-intervention method that transfers reasoning capability from the base LLM to the VLM without retraining the backbone. LIFT defines Reasoning Vectors as answer-token hidden-state differences between a Reasoner path with an explicit reasoning trace and a Solver path without it, and injects these vectors into language-side activations of the target VLM. LIFT further supports learnable vector adaptation while keeping the VLM backbone frozen. We evaluate LIFT on two VLMs across six reasoning benchmarks, comparing Reasoning Vectors extracted from the base LLM and from the aligned VLM under matched protocols. Results show that LLM-derived vectors consistently outperform VLM-derived vectors, confirming that the base LLM is a more effective source for recovering reasoning. LIFT partially recovers degraded reasoning through lightweight language-side interventions. Further analyses show that Reasoning Vectors influence intermediate reasoning behavior rather than merely altering final answers. The source code will be released soon.

</details>


### [273] [Momentum-Guided Federated Split Distillation for Personalized Temporal Edge Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31159)
*Ahmed-Rafik Baahmed,Jean-François Dollinger,Amine Brahmia,Mourad Zghal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A momentum-guided federated split distillation framework for personalized, efficient temporal edge intelligence, featuring TeRR-SAtt for temporal representation and AMGF for client clustering and teacher updates, achieving substantial latency/memory reductions and RMSE improvements on real-world data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable personalized, resource-efficient, autonomous temporal edge intelligence at the network edge with fast inference, low memory usage, and robust local learning in federated settings.

Method: Proposes TeRR-SAtt: a temporal reservoir student attention design that fuses fixed reservoir representations, a lightweight temporal student, and personalized output modules. Proposes AMGF: anticipatory momentum-guided fusion that clusters clients via learned momentum and produces specialized teacher updates. Integrates these into a federated split distillation framework for edge intelligence.

Result: On real-world smart-building data, TeRR-SAtt reduces edge training latency by 65.50%, inference latency by 44.70%, training memory usage by 18.40%, and inference CPU usage by 33.10% compared to baselines. AMGF improves local learning by up to 35.31% in RMSE over global updates.

Conclusion: The proposed TeRR-SAtt with AMGF delivers significant resource efficiency and personalization for temporal edge intelligence in federated settings, with strong empirical gains on real-world data and potential applicability to smart-building scenarios.

Abstract: We propose a momentum-guided federated split distillation framework for personalized, efficient, and autonomous temporal edge intelligence. We introduce TeRR-SAtt, our novel temporal reservoir student attention design that combines fixed reservoir representations, a lightweight temporal student, and personalized output modules. We also present AMGF, our anticipatory momentum-guided fusion mechanism that clusters clients through learning momentum and derives specialized teacher updates. On real-world smart-building data, TeRR-SAtt reduces edge training latency by 65.50%, inference latency by 44.70%, training memory usage by 18.40%, and inference CPU usage by 33.10% over the considered baselines. At the same time, AMGF improves local learning by up to 35.31% in RMSE compared to global updates.

</details>


### [274] [Neural State Prediction: Obstructing Shortcut Learning in EEG Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31167)
*Kieren Yu,Ziyang Liu,Chang Huang,Jintai Chen,Kaishun Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NSP is a latent-predictive framework for EEG foundation models that constrains both latent targets and their context to reduce reliance on local cues, improving transferability across diverse EEG tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Masked prediction in EEG models often exploits stable positional cues and local correlations, hindering transferable representations; a method to constrain targets and context could promote learning from distributed neural structure.

Method: Introduce Neural State Prediction (NSP) with a Target Encoder updated by EMA to define latent supervision, apply identity residualization to remove channel/time additive effects, and enforce topology-separated context that excludes immediate spatial/temporal neighborhoods. Pretrain on 2.2M EEG segments from TUEG; evaluate on 30 downstream datasets; full-parameter multi-task fine-tuning on EEG-FM-Bench.

Result: NSP achieves 63.94 macro balanced accuracy across 14 datasets, outperforming the strongest baseline by 2.35 percentage points. Ablations and controls dissect contributions of mechanisms and context geometry; findings support that joint design of latent targets and context improves learning from distributed signal structure.

Conclusion: Jointly designing latent targets and their context is a promising direction for EEG foundation models to learn from distributed neural signal structure and generalize across diverse cognitive and clinical tasks.

Abstract: EEG foundation models increasingly use masked prediction to learn from unlabeled recordings, but optimizing this objective does not ensure transferable neural representations. A central challenge is that stable positional cues and local correlations can make masked regions predictable without integrating distributed neural context. To reduce this reliance on low-information prediction paths, we introduce Neural State Prediction (NSP), a latent-predictive framework that constrains both the prediction target and the available context. NSP uses a Target Encoder updated by an exponential moving average (EMA) to define latent supervision. Identity residualization removes additive effects associated with channel identity and relative time from the targets, while topology-separated context excludes their immediate spatial and temporal neighborhood from the visible input. We pretrain NSP on 2.2 million EEG segments from TUEG and evaluate it across 30 downstream datasets spanning clinical diagnosis, sleep staging, emotion recognition, motor imagery, event-related potentials, cognitive-state decoding, and language retrieval. Under full-parameter multi-task fine-tuning on EEG-FM-Bench, NSP achieves 63.94 macro balanced accuracy across 14 datasets, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 2.35 percentage points. Controlled component ablations assess the contribution of each mechanism, while matched context controls and held-out interventions characterize the role of context geometry, signal content, and positional information. Jointly designing latent targets and their context offers a promising direction for EEG foundation models that learn from distributed signal structure.

</details>


### [275] [Semantic Navigation for Issue Localization in Code Repository](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31176)
*Yunxiang Wei,Zhenyu Lei,Jundong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SemNav combines deterministic retrieval and iterative, evidence-guided LLM reasoning to localize repo-level issues, using three components (Semantic Navigation Graph, Issue-conditioned Semantic Cards, and a Persistent Candidate Workspace) to seed and refine candidate locations; it achieves strong improvements on SWE-bench Lite and PLocBench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current code-search and issue-localization tools offer limited iterative support: they struggle to identify and relate relevant code locations, reconstruct entity semantics from raw source, and revise candidates without an evidential basis. There is a need for broad initial coverage followed by evidence-based refinement.

Method: 1) Deterministic retrieval seeds a broad candidate set. 2) Semantic Navigation Graph enables on-demand access to program relations via a language server for cross-file navigation. 3) Issue-conditioned Semantic Cards provide compact, source-grounded interpretations of each candidate's role with respect to the issue. 4) Persistent Candidate Workspace records each candidate with its evidential basis to enable grounded verification, revision, and ranking. 5) An LLM agent iteratively revises and ranks candidates using the evidential basis.

Result: Across SWE-bench Lite and PLocBench, SemNav outperforms baselines, increasing File Hit@10 from 68.33% to 82.67% with Gemma 4B. Ablations show complementary roles for the components, and Semantic Cards reduce working-context load by 48.2% relative to full-source reading. SemNav ranks first on all seven evidence-quality metrics on SWE-Explore and improves downstream issue resolution from 44.00% to 52.33%.

Conclusion: SemNav demonstrates that combining deterministic retrieval with evidence-grounded iterative refinement via three components yields stronger, more efficient repository-level issue localization, with clear gains in both retrieval performance and downstream resolution; the components are complementary and reduce context demands while increasing evidential quality.

Abstract: Repository-level issue localization aims to identify and rank the files and functions relevant to resolving a reported issue. LLM agents approach this task iteratively: they identify a set of potentially relevant locations, inspect the corresponding code, and revise their judgments about these candidates as new evidence is acquired. Existing environments, however, provide limited support for this loop: agents must search for unresolved relation targets, reconstruct entity semantics from raw source code, and revise candidates without evidential basis. To address these limitations, we present SemNav, a framework that leverages deterministic retrieval to seed a broad candidate set and an LLM agent to continually refine that set, thereby combining initial coverage with evidence-guided revision. SemNav supports this process through three key components. A Semantic Navigation Graph resolves program relations on demand through a language server, enabling direct navigation to related entities across files. Issue-conditioned Semantic Cards provide compact, source-grounded interpretations of each entity's role and relevance to the issue. A persistent Candidate Workspace records each candidate together with its evidential basis, enabling grounded verification, revision, and ranking. Across SWE-bench Lite and PLocBench, SemNav outperforms existing baselines, improving File Hit@10 from 68.33\% to 82.67\% with Gemma 4B. Component ablations and trajectory analysis support the complementary roles of all three components, while Semantic Cards reduce working-context load by 48.2\% relative to full-source reading. SemNav further ranks first on all seven evidence-quality metrics on SWE-Explore and improves downstream issue resolution from 44.00\% to 52.33\%.

</details>


### [276] [SPO: Discovering Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search Operators via Stackelberg Program Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31179)
*Xinyi Ke,Kai Li,Junliang Xing,Yifan Zhang,Jian Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces SPO, an LLM-based Stackelberg framework to discover adaptive destroy-repair programs in large neighborhood search (LNS). It yields state-dependent, leader-follower operator interactions and demonstrates superior performance on TSP and CVRP with good generalization and behavioral insights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LNS effectiveness hinges on the synergy between destroy and repair operators and their adaptation to evolving search states. Traditional methods lack a principled, automated way to discover state-aware, interacting operators; SPO aims to automate this discovery via an LLM-driven, Stackelberg-informed framework.

Method: Define Stackelberg Program Optimization (SPO) with destroy (leader) and repair (follower) roles. Use an LLM-based generator to propose operator programs conditioned on a compact LNS state. Organize discovery as a Stackelberg interaction over the program space, with role-specific credits guiding an outer evolutionary search over programs. Train through a combination of LLM generator learning and population-based optimization, evaluating on TSP and capacitated VRP.

Result: SPO outperforms strong baselines across diverse settings, and generalizes to larger instances and benchmark sets beyond the discovery scale. Behavioral analyses show state-dependent operator behavior and coupled destroy-repair improvements emerge during discovery.

Conclusion: SPO provides a principled, scalable framework to automatically discover adaptive destroy-repair programs for LNS, enabling improved performance and insights into state-dependent operator dynamics; results motivate further exploration of operator interactions and generalization to broader combinatorial problems.

Abstract: Large neighborhood search (LNS) relies critically on destroy and repair operators, whose effectiveness depends on both adaptation to the evolving LNS state and interaction between the two roles. We introduce Stackelberg Program Optimization (SPO), an LLM-based framework for discovering adaptive executable destroy-repair programs. SPO conditions operator decisions on a compact LNS state, allowing state-dependent behavior to emerge through program discovery, and organizes destroy-repair discovery as a Stackelberg interaction over program space that reflects their asymmetric dependency. Role-specific credits evaluate destroy programs as leaders and repair programs as conditional follower responses, guiding a coupled optimization process that combines LLM generator learning with population-based evolutionary search over programs. Experiments on the traveling salesperson problem and capacitated vehicle routing problem show that SPO outperforms strong baselines across a broad range of settings and generalizes beyond the discovery scale to larger instances and benchmark sets. Behavioral analyses further demonstrate state-dependent operator behavior and coupled destroy-repair improvement during discovery.

</details>


### [277] [Accounting for Bias Enables Sustainable LLM Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31184)
*Harshita Katoch,David Antony Selby,Gerrit Großmann,Sebastian Vollmer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A latent-variable model for LLM-based evaluation that corrects bias and reduces the need for large numbers of comparisons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current leaderboards compensate for systematic measurement bias by increasing comparisons, which is statistically flawed and wasteful. Documented biases (position, verbosity, judge severity, self-enhancement) cannot be eliminated by more data alone; a proper bias-aware model is needed.

Method: A unified latent-variable framework that jointly models pairwise and ordinal judgments, explicitly incorporating bias components and confounders to recover reliable rankings from far fewer comparisons. The approach treats judgments with a bias-correction mechanism and requires negligible compute relative to a single LLM inference.

Result: Produces reliable rankings with substantially fewer comparisons; bias correction is statistically rigorous and more sustainable; compute cost is low relative to LLM inference, enabling scalable trustworthy evaluation.

Conclusion: Bias-aware latent-variable evaluation yields more trustworthy, efficient, and scalable LLM assessments than naïve comparison-heavy methods; the framework can generalize to other sources of bias and measurement noise.

Abstract: LLM-as-a-judge has become the de facto standard for scalable, subjective evaluation, yet current leaderboards compensate for systematic measurement bias by running ever more comparisons, an approach that is both statistically unsound and computationally wasteful. The root cause is an incomplete measurement model, treating LLM judges as neutral, interchangeable instruments ignores documented biases like position bias, verbosity bias, judge severity, and self-enhancement, that no volume of additional data can eliminate. We propose a unified latent variable framework that jointly models pairwise and ordinal data while explicitly correcting for these confounders, recovering reliable rankings from substantially fewer comparisons. Because fitting this model costs negligible compute relative to a single round of LLM inference, bias correction is not only more statistically rigorous but also a more sustainable approach to trustworthy evaluation.

</details>


### [278] [Evolutionary Safety of Recursive Self-Improving AI: Taxonomy, Risk Discovery, and Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31186)
*Chang Gong,Jingping Bi,Di Yao,Xinjian Liang,Chao Xiang,Ruijie Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Evolutionary Safety as a framework to study and govern safety amid persistent RSI, with a taxonomy of states and updates, a risk-discovery approach, and governance principles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI systems undergo recursive self-improvement and persistence, safety cannot be static; safety properties can drift, accumulate, or propagate across generations, requiring a dynamic governance framework.

Method: Develop a taxonomy across persistent agent state, model state, evaluation/environmental feedback, computational substrate, and meta-level update mechanisms; characterize recurring manifestations (intent drift, error accumulation, experience contamination, safety-property erosion, evaluator drift, risk propagation); outline how evolutionary risks can be discovered and evaluated across states, updates, trajectories, and lineages; derive governance principles for modification, selection, authorization, provenance, and recovery; reference project resources for evaluation.

Result: A structured framework for analyzing safety in RSI and initial governance guidelines; identifies open problems and evaluation approaches.

Conclusion: Evolutionary Safety offers a practical lens to maintain safety guarantees as AI systems become more persistent and recursively self-improving, while highlighting the need for further work on measurement, verification, and governance; resources available at the project site.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, with increasingly capable systems taking larger roles in reasoning, decision-making, scientific discovery, and autonomous development. As AI begins to participate in its own improvement, from model training and experience accumulation to agent evolution and automated AI development, the prospect of recursive self-improvement (RSI) is becoming increasingly relevant. This transition raises a fundamental safety question: how can safety be maintained when the system, its accumulated experience, and even the process producing its successors continue to change?
  We introduce Evolutionary Safety as a perspective for studying safety under persistent and recursive self-improvement. It concerns not only whether an AI system is safe at a particular moment, but how safety properties change, persist, accumulate, and propagate throughout evolution. We characterize recurring manifestations, including intent drift, error accumulation, experience contamination, safety-property erosion, evaluator drift, and risk propagation. We then develop a taxonomy spanning persistent agent state, model state, evaluation and environmental feedback, computational substrate, and meta-level update mechanisms. Building on this taxonomy, we examine how evolutionary risks can be discovered and evaluated across states, updates, trajectories, and lineages, and derive governance principles for modification, selection, authorization, provenance, and recovery. Finally, we outline open problems toward maintaining safety guarantees as AI systems become increasingly persistent, adaptive, and recursively self-improving. Project resources and proposed evaluation systems are available at https://chaunceykung.github.io/evolutionary-safety-rsi.

</details>


### [279] [Samples, Sources, Space: Decomposing Data Scale in Spatially Structured Representation Learning of Human Brain Microarchitecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31201)
*Christian Schiffer,Mathis Bode,Thomas Lippert,Katrin Amunts,Timo Dickscheid*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Reframes data scaling as allocation across unique samples, source diversity, and spatial coverage for spatially structured representation learning. In microscopic whole-brain histology, increasing unique samples, spatial coverage, compute, and model capacity improves performance; however, distributing a fixed sample budget across more subjects (1–18) yields no gains, despite better generalization to seen subjects. Inter-subject variation dominates generalization when the budget is fixed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the mismatch between sample count and the structured, multi-source nature of spatial data. The authors seek to decompose data scaling into three axes—unique sample count, source diversity (number of sources/subjects), and spatial coverage—and study their separate effects on representation learning and cross-subject generalization.

Method: Experimentally varied data allocation, compute, and model capacity over 11.6 million spatially anchored patches from 21 human brains across 93 pretraining runs of a contrastive model that uses spatial proximity for supervision. A fixed sample budget was also tested by distributing samples across 1–18 subjects. Evaluation focused on representation quality and generalization to unseen subjects.

Result: - More unique samples, broader spatial coverage, more compute, and larger model capacity consistently improve performance.
- With a fixed sample count, distributing samples across more subjects (1–18) provides no detectable performance gain, though representations generalize better to subjects encountered during pretraining.
- Inter-subject variation strongly affects generalization; adding more subjects offers no benefit under a fixed per-subject budget.
- Distinct axes (sample count, source diversity, spatial coverage) govern data scaling in spatially structured learning.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that sample count, source diversity, and spatial coverage are separable, critical axes of data scaling for spatially structured representation learning. Dataset design should prioritize increasing unique samples and spatial coverage and be mindful that adding subjects under a fixed per-subject budget may not improve, and can even waste, data resources.

Abstract: Scaling studies typically represent training data by a single count of samples. For hierarchically and spatially structured data, however, the same number of samples can be drawn from few or many sources and distributed differently across the underlying domain. We therefore study data scaling as an allocation problem, separating unique sample count, source diversity, and spatial coverage. We study this decomposition in microscopic whole-brain histology, where a source is an individual brain, and a sample is an image patch at a specific spatial location. Across 93 controlled pretraining runs of a contrastive model that uses spatial proximity for supervision, we vary data allocation, compute, and model capacity over 11.6 million spatially anchored image patches from 21 human brains. Performance improves with more unique samples, broader spatial coverage, additional compute, and larger model capacity. At fixed sample count, distributing samples across one to 18 subjects produces no detectable improvement, even though representations generalize substantially better to subjects encountered during pretraining. Inter-subject variation therefore strongly affects generalization, but additional subjects provide no benefit when a fixed sample budget is distributed across more sources. These results establish sample count, source diversity, and spatial coverage as distinct axes of data scaling in spatially structured representation learning.

</details>


### [280] [Which Influence Are We Estimating? The Role of Counterfactual Specifications in Data Attribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31214)
*Zhe Li,Wei Zhao,Peixin Zhang,Jun Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Specification mismatch, not just approximation error, drives disagreements between influence estimators. The paper treats influence as a counterfactual estimand, develops a local decomposition, and shows that spec choices (target behavior, intervention, and training process) significantly affect attributions; aligning specs to the target behavior improves attribution quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing influence estimators often yield incompatible rankings. The root cause is not only approximation error but the specification of what is being attributed, including the behavior surrogate and counterfactual training process.

Method: Formally define influence as a counterfactual estimand; classify estimators by implied specifications; derive a local decomposition showing interaction among behavior signals, training signals, and counterfactual parameters; conduct controlled experiments on noisy label detection and LLM attribution to compare exact vs approximate estimands under varying specifications.

Result: Exact estimands under different specifications can yield different rankings; approximation error grows with perturbation distance from linearization points. Spec choices materially affect attribution quality, with behavior-aligned specifications revealing training examples obscured under default specs.

Conclusion: Specification analysis is essential for interpreting and comparing data influence estimators. Practitioners should align behavior surrogates and interventions with the target attribution task to improve accuracy and interpretability.

Abstract: Estimating the influence of training examples on model behavior is essential for data debugging, valuation, and attribution. Existing influence estimators often produce incompatible rankings, which are commonly ascribed to approximation error. We argue that a more fundamental source of disagreement is specification mismatch: influence depends on the behavior being attributed, the intervention applied to each training example, and the counterfactual training process that maps the intervention to a model response. These choices are especially important when the target behavior requires a tractable surrogate, such as query loss, a logit, or a margin. We formalize influence as a counterfactual estimand, distinguish specification mismatch across estimands from approximation error in estimating a fixed estimand, and organize representative estimators by their implied specifications. We further derive a local decomposition that exposes how behavior signals, training signals, and counterfactual parameter responses interact. Controlled experiments show that exact estimands under different specifications can induce different rankings, whereas approximation error grows as perturbations move farther from their linearization points. Experiments on noisy label detection and LLM attribution show that specification choices significantly affect attribution quality, especially for the choice of behavior surrogate. Behavior-aligned specifications can identify target-specific training examples obscured by default loss-based or similarity-based specifications. These results establish specification analysis as a necessary first step for interpreting and comparing data influence estimators.

</details>


### [281] [DIAL: Position-Debiased LLM Judges with Adaptive Human Preference Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31215)
*Zesheng Cai,Yingqi Fan,Sichang Chen,Jin-Hong Du*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DIAL is a unified framework that debiases LLM-based judgments by separating response-order effects from latent preferences, combining abundant LLM comparisons with limited human input to learn a shared, position-debiased preference structure and calibrate it toward human targets, with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs enable scalable evaluation but judgments are biased by response order and can diverge from human preferences; a data-efficient approach is needed to separate biases, learn shared structure, and align with humans.

Method: DIAL jointly models latent LLM preferences, position effects, and human calibration; adaptive estimation balances LLM anchoring with limited human evidence; fixed-weight uncertainty quantification is used for the calibrated human preference; validated with simulations, three human-preference benchmarks, and a real-data study collecting 410K judgments from 21 LLM judges across display orders.

Result: DIAL shows robustness to unbalanced response order, achieves strong human-aligned rankings with few human labels, and adapts toward human evidence when LLM information is imperfect; the real-data study provides a large resource for studying LLM-judge bias and human alignment.

Conclusion: The framework offers identifiability, adaptive calibration, and reliable uncertainty quantification for aligning LLM judgments with human preferences, delivering both methodological and empirical advances and a valuable data resource for future research.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) as a judge enable scalable evaluation, but their judgments can be sensitive to response order and, even after removing such position effects, can still diverge systematically from human preferences.We introduce DIAL, a unified framework that combines abundant LLM comparisons with limited human comparisons to separate judge-specific position effects, learn shared structure in position-debiased LLM preferences, and adaptively calibrate that structure toward the human preference target. Theoretically, we study three aspects of DIAL: (i) identification of latent LLM preferences, position effects, and human calibration; (ii) adaptive estimation that balances LLM anchoring against limited human evidence; and (iii) fixed-weight uncertainty quantification for the calibrated human preference. Empirically, we evaluate position debiasing and human alignment separately in controlled simulations and on three human-preference benchmarks, showing that DIAL remains robust to unbalanced response order, achieves strong human-aligned rankings with limited labels, and adapts toward human evidence when LLM information is imperfect. Our real-data study collects over 410K judgments from 21 LLM judges in both display orders, providing a resource for future studies of LLM-judge bias, heterogeneity, and human alignment.

</details>


### [282] [Purin: A Biology-inspired Mechanism for Artificial Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31235)
*Zishu Liu,Chunbo Luo,Christos Grecos*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Purin, a biology-inspired synaptic efficacy modulation mechanism for CNNs that uses a time-interval abstraction to enable short- and long-term synaptic changes without discrete time steps, improving accuracy on AlexNet, VGG11, and GoogLeNet after de-confounding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the lack of short-term synaptic changes and the need to model dynamic synaptic efficacy in ANNs without discrete-time simulations, while maintaining compatibility with standard CNN architectures.

Method: Purin adds a bounded efficacy factor and two weight matrices representing input-side and output-side synaptic efficacy. Activity is represented in a time-interval abstraction; update rules via backpropagation interpret these matrices as long-term synaptic modifications, enabling short- and long-term plasticity without discrete timing steps.

Result: Empirical results show consistent classification accuracy improvements across AlexNet, VGG11, and GoogLeNet after removing confounding factors.

Conclusion: Purin provides a biologically-inspired, ANN-compatible mechanism for dynamic synaptic efficacy in CNNs, enabling short- and long-term plasticity without discrete time steps and delivering improved performance.

Abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) usually represent neural transmission with fixed trainable weights during a training batch, which omits short-term changes in synaptic efficacy. In addition, the discrete time-step simulation requires additional temporal processing that many conventional ANN architectures do not use. To overcome these challenges, we propose Purin, a biology-inspired and ANN-compatible mechanism, that introduces synaptic efficacy modulation into conventional convolutional neural networks. Purin uses a time-interval-based abstraction for neural activities, which allows Purin to introduce short- and long-term synaptic efficacy changes without using discrete time-steps. Purin introduces a bounded factor to represent temporary synaptic efficacy changes, together with two weight matrices that represent input-side and output-side efficacy. The weight matrices are updated by backpropagation and interpreted as the long-term synaptic efficacy changes. Experimental results show that after removing the confounding factors in the AlexNet, VGG11, and GoogLeNet architectures, Purin improves the classification accuracies in all three models across the evaluated datasets.

</details>


### [283] [MA-WAM: Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Test-Time Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31281)
*Guowei Zou,Haitao Wang,Guoxin Wang,Beiwen Zhang,Zhiquan Chen,Guojie Wang,Hejun Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Multi-Agent World-Action Model (MA-WAM), a test-time world-model planner for multi-agent flow policies, achieving significant gains with modest overhead across MARL benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-agent world models extended naively to multi-agent settings fail to capture cross-agent action dependencies. A dedicated test-time multi-agent world model is needed to predict team returns from joint actions.

Method: Proposes MA-WAM, a test-time planning framework that uses a frozen multi-agent flow policy and a world-action model to evaluate futures of candidate joint actions, explicitly modeling cross-agent dependencies for joint-action consequences; first test-time world-model planner for multi-agent flow policies.

Result: Across 30 offline MARL settings on MAMuJoCo, SMAC, and MPE, MA-WAM yields mean relative gains of 22.0% over direct execution and 25.6% over uniform action selection; runtime overhead on A100 GPUs is 12.1 ms, about 2.5% of generation-and-scoring time.

Conclusion: MA-WAM effectively enables test-time planning with cross-agent dependencies in multi-agent policies, delivering substantial performance gains with modest computational overhead and establishing a new benchmark for test-time world-model planning in MARL.

Abstract: Multi-agent cooperative tasks require different agents to execute a joint action simultaneously, and each agent's action affects both the observations and responses of the other agents. Hence, a world model is needed to predict the team return resulting from the joint actions of all agents. A naive extension directly applies a single-agent world model to each agent's action when predicting the team return step by step. However, such an extension fails to capture the dependencies among the simultaneous actions of multiple agents. We propose Multi-Agent World-Action Model (MA-WAM), a test-time planning framework that enables a frozen multi-agent flow policy to evaluate futures of candidate joint actions. To our knowledge, MA-WAM is the first test-time world-model planner for multi-agent flow policies. MA-WAM predicts the consequences of each joint action according to cross-agent dependencies and enables efficient candidate scoring. Across 30 offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) settings on MAMuJoCo, SMAC, and MPE, MA-WAM achieves mean relative gains of 22.0% over direct execution and 25.6% over uniform action selection. Under the standard evaluation protocol on an A100 GPU, MA-WAM adds 12.1 ms, accounting for 2.5% of the measured generation-and-scoring time.

</details>


### [284] [G2MAF: Test-Time Gradient Guidance for Multi-Agent Flow Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31286)
*Guowei Zou,Haitao Wang,Guoxin Wang,Zhiquan Chen,Beiwen Zhang,Guojie Wang,Hejun Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A test-time refinement method (G2MAF) for offline MARL using a globally normalized critic gradient to adjust all agents' actions, preserving feasibility and proximity to the frozen policy; shows ~9% gains on MPE/SMAC with ~6% latency increase.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In offline MARL, deployed policies are frozen and a single proposed joint action may be suboptimal. Small policy corrections within the data distribution can yield better performance without environment interaction.

Method: G2MAF (Gradient Guided Multi Agent Flow) applies one globally normalized, projected critic gradient to coordinate and refine all agents' actions at test-time while keeping them feasible and close to the frozen proposal.

Result: Evaluated across 24 MPE and SMAC settings; the canonical variant improves 20 frozen settings with mean relative gains of 9.2% on MPE and 8.9% on SMAC; inference latency increases by about 6%.

Conclusion: G2MAF provides an effective, low-latency test-time refinement mechanism to improve offline MARL policies without additional data collection or online training.

Abstract: Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) learns cooperative policies from fixed datasets without further environment interaction and a learned policy is frozen at deployment. Such a frozen policy typically proposes a single joint action and executes it directly at deployment time. However, this one-shot deployment often commits to a suboptimal proposal, even when better nearby alternatives remain consistent with the behavior data. To address this issue, we propose Gradient Guided Multi Agent Flow (G2MAF), a refinement framework for optimizing joint policies at test-time. G2MAF applies one globally normalized, projected critic gradient to guide and coordinate all agents' corrections while keeping the action both feasible and close to the frozen policy proposal. Across 24 MPE and SMAC settings, its canonical variant improves 20 frozen settings, with mean relative gains of 9.2% on MPE and 8.9% on SMAC, with model inference latency increased by about 6% only.

</details>


### [285] [The Right Information Extraction Pipeline Depends on the Document: Accuracy-Energy Trade-offs for Small, Local Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31341)
*Christoph Walser,Mauricio Fadel Argerich,Jonathan Fürst*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Energy-efficient on-premise information extraction favors text-only models with cheap parsers for near-plain text, and vision-language models for layout-rich documents; batching is the dominant energy lever; neural OCR is costly; FP8 helps mainly without batching; overall guidelines for privacy-preserving, local IE.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Determine whether to process page images or parsed text under privacy constraints and energy efficiency, by evaluating across input representations, model families, and inference configurations on small (≤8B parameter) models.

Method: Evaluate on two datasets (Kleister-NDA contracts: near plain text; VRDU forms: layout-rich) under no-cloud constraints. Explore input representations, model families (text-only vs vision-language), and inference configurations. Measure accuracy and energy. Benchmark batching, FP8 quantization, and OCR preprocessing. Compare neural OCR vs classical OCR for energy cost and Pareto frontier.

Result: Batching reduces energy per page by 38–85% with no accuracy loss. FP8 quantization saves 27–32% when requests are served one at a time, but after batching yields only 9–19% energy savings per page. Neural OCR costs ~17× more energy per page than classical OCR and never reaches the Pareto frontier. The preferred representation depends on document type: vision–language models excel on layout-rich documents; small text-only models with cheap parsers excel on near-plain-text documents, and both outperform any vision–language configuration in accuracy and cost. Provides actionable guidelines for energy-efficient, privacy-preserving local information extraction.

Conclusion: The work delivers concrete guidelines for energy-efficient, privacy-compliant local IE. Key levers are batching (largest energy savings) and choosing the input representation aligned to document layout; avoid neural OCR when energy is critical; use vision-language models for layout-rich content and lightweight text-only models with cheap parsing for plain-text content.

Abstract: Whether an information extraction pipeline should process page images or parsed text depends on the document, and the answer flips across the layout spectrum. We study this trade-off under a constraint that rules out (closed) cloud services: privacy-sensitive documents processed on-premise by small ($\le 8\mathrm{B}$ parameter) text-only and vision--language models, evaluated on both accuracy and energy over a design space spanning input representation, model family, and inference configuration. Benchmarking on the near-plain-text Kleister-NDA contracts and the layout-rich VRDU forms, we find that batching is the dominant energy lever, cutting energy per page by 38-85% at no cost in accuracy, while FP8 quantization saves 27-32% when requests are served one at a time but less than 1mWh per page (9-19%) once batching is applied. Preprocessing dominates what remains: neural OCR costs $17\times$ more energy per page than classical OCR and never reaches the Pareto frontier. Which representation wins flips with the type of document: vision--language models on layout-rich documents and small text-only models with a cheap parser on near-plain text, where they are both more accurate and cheaper than any vision--language configuration. Our work yields concrete guidelines for energy-efficient, privacy-compliant local information extraction.

</details>


### [286] [Mutable Transcripts: Mitigating Context Pollution through Editable Conversation State](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31354)
*Dan Barry,Andrew Hines*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Mutable transcripts enable editing of chat history to reflect evolving user intent, reducing context pollution and improving interaction quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard LLM chat treats history as immutable, causing outdated or irrelevant context to linger as user intent shifts; mutable transcripts address this by allowing edits to the transcript itself.

Method: Developed a prototype integrating transcript-level revisions into a chat interface; conducted a controlled user study (n=17) and transcript analysis of representative interactions; assessed user preferences and interaction metrics.

Result: Users preferred mutable transcripts to standard chat on clarity, confidence, and ease of use; reduced intent to restart conversations; transcript analysis showed shorter conversations and less obsolete context.

Conclusion: User-driven revision of conversational history can improve interaction quality and maintain a current representation of user intent; prototype and source code are publicly available.

Abstract: Contemporary large language model (LLM) chat systems treat conversation history as an immutable sequence of turns that defines the model's working context. However, user intent in real interactions is not static: it evolves through correction, refinement, and shifting constraints. This mismatch between dynamic intent and static transcripts can result in context pollution, where outdated or irrelevant information persists and continues to influence subsequent responses. We introduce mutable transcripts, a new interaction paradigm that enables users to revise prior turns through natural language edit requests, allowing the conversation history itself to be updated rather than appended. This reframes the transcript from a passive record into an editable representation of conversational state. We present a working prototype that integrates transcript-level revision into a standard chat interface and evaluate its feasibility through a controlled user study (n=17) and an illustrative transcript analysis of representative interaction scenarios. Participants significantly preferred mutable transcripts over standard chat across measures of clarity, confidence, and ease of use, with reduced intent to restart conversations. Transcript analysis of representative user study conversations shows that mutable transcripts can reduce conversation length and eliminate obsolete retained context. These findings provide initial evidence that user-driven revision of conversational history can improve interaction quality and help maintain a more current representation of user intent. The source code and prototype can be accessed at https://github.com/QxLabIreland/ReChat

</details>


### [287] [Programs-of-Layers in LLMs through the Lens of Cortical Areas](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31360)
*Justus Westerhoff,Stephan Olbrich,Hatem Oraby,Matthew Evan Larkum,Felix Alexander Gers*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PoLar enables dynamic routing in transformers by treating layers as a function library, allowing adaptive sequences of skipped or repeated blocks. It yields performance gains over fixed-depth forward passes, reproduces several reported findings, and reveals that a small set of generic programs often suffices. The main single-shot router claim does not hold, and error-correcting programs are brittle. A brain-like thalamo-cortical analogy is drawn; code is released for reproducibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To move beyond fixed-depth forward passes by emulating brain-like routing through a library of layer-block programs, assessing whether adaptive, program-like routing can improve performance and generalization, and to scrutinize the robustness and structure of the inferred programs across multiple models.

Method: Reconstruct PoLar's diagnostic Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) in more detail than the original paper and apply it across five transformer models. Systematically evaluate skipping, repeating, and their combination across inputs of varying difficulty, analyze program length vs question difficulty, compare top-1 router predictions to top-k program sets, investigate the existence of a small core of generic programs, and assess robustness by examining edits to programs. Release code publicly.

Result: Reproduced key PoLar findings: skipping outperforms the standard forward pass; repeating outperforms skipping; combining both outperforms either alone. Shorter programs suffice for easy questions; harder ones require more repeats. The main claim about a learned single-shot router failed: the top-ranked router prediction collapses to the standard pass, though top-k programs jointly yielded real accuracy gains. Found that a small number of generic programs solve most questions. Detailed analysis shows that error-correcting programs are highly brittle to edits. The work reinforces a brain-inspired routing analogy (thalamo-cortical coordination) and provides public code release.

Conclusion: PoLar demonstrates that flexible, program-based routing can yield accuracy gains and robustness beyond fixed-depth passes, but单-shot router claims may not generalize; a compact set of generic programs captures much of the benefit, while certain corrections are fragile to edits. The study supports the brain-inspired routing metaphor and highlights areas for improving stability and interpretability of dynamic routing in transformers.

Abstract: Inference in LLMs is conventionally a fixed-depth, fixed-order forward pass through every layer, regardless of how difficult the input is. The human brain does not work this way: using the thalamus as a central hub, it routes information flexibly to all regions of the cortex according to demand. Li et al. (2026) recently showed, with a system they call program-of-layers (PoLar), that transformers can be given an analogous flexibility if their layers are treated as a library of functions rather than a fixed sequence. Performance improves over the standard forward pass when each input is dynamically routed through an adaptive sequence of skipped or repeated contiguous layer blocks. We reconstructed PoLar's diagnostic MCTS in more detail than the original paper and applied it across 5 models. We reproduced several of PoLar's findings: skipping outperformed the standard pass, repeating outperformed skipping, and combining both outperformed either alone. Shorter programs sufficed for easier questions, while harder questions required more layer repeats. However, we failed to replicate the main claim regarding their learned router for single-shot inference: its top-ranked prediction consistently collapsed back to the standard pass, even though its top-k predicted programs, taken together, did show a real accuracy gain. Beyond reproduction, we find that a small number of generic programs are enough to solve most of the questions. We also provide a much deeper analysis of these programs' structure and robustness: for example, we found that programs that correct errors are highly brittle: undoing even a single edit inside a program typically breaks the correction. Connecting this to the brain's routing mechanisms, PoLar mirrors principles of thalamo-cortical coordination between cortical-area-like transformer layers. We publicly release the code at https://datexis.github.io/RE-PoLar/

</details>


### [288] [Completed Pairs Hide Capped Failures: A ReVerPi Case Study of Selective Context Projection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31381)
*Guangzhe Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Projection of archival content into compact excerpts in ReVerPi reduces aggregate logical tokens but may increase suffix requests and impact success rates; careful boundary handling and dual-arm evaluation are essential for fair assessment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantify trade-offs of content projection (archived observations and projected continuations) in a programmable agent (Pi extension) and understand how stopping rules, bounded failures, unexecuted companions, and resource aggregation affect performance.

Method: An 86-run source-reading campaign with 641 model requests, 15 completed pairs (12/15 per arm); 12 boundary runs with suppression of the companion when the first arm fails; analysis with and without boundary runs (27 total boundary runs); comparison of projected versus full continuations across arms; separation of fitting vs evaluation; measurement of success, token usage, and suffix requests.

Result: Projection reduces aggregate logical tokens by 25%; per-pair median tokens increase by 29%; total suffix requests rise from 35 to 55. Restoring all 27 boundary runs bounds projected-minus-full success between -9 and +1 tasks. One omitted, selector-chosen projected continuation retrieves archive text but uses twelve requests; full counterpart answers in three. Eleven jointly correct pairs constitute a fully observed success stratum. The observed framework shows evaluation artifacts: across all data, projection affected token usage and success, and separating fitting from evaluation shifts the selector’s apparent performance (one extra failure and 8.6% more tokens over thirteen runs).

Conclusion: Findings pertain to the recorded campaign and do not claim population-level noninferiority or superiority to unrestricted Pi. Recommendations: retain every intervention boundary in evaluations, run both allocated arms independently of order, and report completion alongside interaction and token expenditure.

Abstract: Context projection replaces older tool observations with compact, addressable excerpts, reducing repeated input while potentially adding evidence-retrieval turns. We study this trade-off in ReVerPi, a Pi extension with archived observations and matched full/projected continuations. In an 86-run source-reading campaign with 641 model requests, the 15 completed pairs show identical success: 12/15 per arm. Twelve further boundary runs stop, with the runner suppressing the companion whenever the first arm fails to complete. Restoring all 27 boundary runs bounds projected-minus-full success between $-$9 and +1 tasks. One omitted, selector-chosen projected continuation successfully retrieves archive text yet exhausts twelve requests; its full counterpart answers in three. The eleven jointly correct pairs form a fully observed success stratum within this recorded frame: projection reduces aggregate logical tokens by 25%, while increasing the median pair's tokens by 29% and total suffix requests from 35 to 55. Separating fitting from evaluation changes the selector's apparent tie: outside its four fitting pairs, it incurs one extra failure and 8.6% more logical tokens over thirteen comparable runs. This methodological case study connects stopping rules, known bounded failures, unexecuted companions, and resource aggregation. Its findings concern the recorded campaign, rather than population noninferiority or superiority over unrestricted Pi. Evaluations should retain every intervention boundary, execute both allocated arms independently of the first arm's completion, and report completion alongside interaction and token expenditure.

</details>


### [289] [Compress What You See, Not What You Say: Anchored Context Distillation for Latent-Observation Software Engineering Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31430)
*Zhensheng Zou,Guoqing Wang,Dan Hao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LOHA-ACD combines latent observations with hard recent text to compress tool-context for SWE agents, maintaining action-critical information via a latent view and anchored distillation, enabling substantial context reduction with competitive performance and throughput gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long interaction histories are costly to maintain; existing context compression can degrade essential information and agent behavior.

Method: LOHA compresses older observations into soft tokens while preserving the agent's turns and the last K observations in text; ACD distills the base model's full-text predictions into the latent view and anchors behavior on plain-text inputs to the same base model; K governs the balance between latent compression and retained text.

Result: Context per call is reduced by 43% (Qwen3-4B) and 57% (SWE-Master-4B-RL) at K=3; resolve rates are 12.1% vs 14.5% and 21.8% vs 27.5% (for the compressed vs uncompressed baselines). A recency sweep with K=8 yields 14.4% and 23.0%. Under 32K tokens, Qwen3 with K=3 resolves 21.1% of a 199-instance subset, versus 11.1% for the full-text adapted agent. Single-GPU throughput is 1.9x that of the full-text agent.

Conclusion: LOHA-ACD demonstrates that latent-context representations with anchored distillation can substantially compress historical context while preserving action-critical performance, delivering meaningful task performance and throughput gains; the benefits scale with the recency window, though larger windows may trade off compression for performance.

Abstract: Tool observations dominate the context of software-engineering agents, making long interaction histories costly to maintain. Existing context compression methods can discard information needed by later actions, while adapting agents to soft-token representations can compromise their original behavior. To reduce context while preserving action-critical information and agent behavior, we combine Latent Observations, Hard Actions (LOHA), a context layout that separates compressed history from text needed for exact reference, with Anchored Context Distillation (ACD), a training method that enables latent reading while constraining behavioral drift. LOHA compresses older tool observations into soft tokens while retaining the agent's own turns and the last K observations in text, providing compact access to historical information and exact access to recent content. To enable the agent to use this representation, ACD distills the base model's full-text predictions into the latent view while anchoring its behavior on plain-text inputs to the same base model. On SWE-bench Verified, K=3 reduces context per call by 43% for Qwen3-4B and 57% for SWE-Master-4B-RL, with resolve rates of 12.1% and 21.8% versus 14.5% and 27.5% for their uncompressed bases. A single-run recency sweep reaches 14.4% and 23.0% at K=8, with larger windows generally favoring task performance over compression. Under a 32K-token limit, Qwen3 with K=3 resolves 21.1% of a 199-instance subset versus 11.1% for the same adapted agent using full text. In concurrent single-GPU serving, it achieves 1.9 times that full-text agent's instance throughput.

</details>


### [290] [Segment-Level Agentic Topic Modeling for Improved Data Exploration and Resource Efficiency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31460)
*Myeongjun Erik Jang,Antonios Georgiadis,Sae Young Moon,Fran Silavong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SeLATM introduces segment-level topic generation with agentic feedback loops to reduce LLM resources while preserving high-quality topic modeling compared to topic-assignment-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based topic models can produce natural, human-readable topics but face (1) no explicit topic distributions per document, (2) topics that are too broad or too narrow, and (3) high resource consumption, which worsens with more/longer documents. This is problematic for industrial-scale analytics requiring precise, scalable solutions.

Method: Segment-level topic generation paired with topic refinement via agentic feedback loops (SeLATM).

Result: Experimental results on multiple datasets show that SeLATM substantially reduces LLM resource usage relative to topic-assignment approaches while maintaining superior performance.

Conclusion: SeLATM offers a scalable, high-quality topic modeling framework suitable for industrial applications by balancing resource efficiency with analytic depth.

Abstract: Topic modeling is an effective technique for discovering hidden themes within documents and is widely used in text mining and data analysis across a variety of industry sectors. Recently, large language model (LLM)-based topic models have been emerged that prompt LLMs to generate topics then assign the topics to documents, producing more natural and human-readable topics than conventional topic modeling algorithms. However, the nature of topic assignment process causes certain drawbacks, such as the incapability to produce topic distributions over a document, too broad or narrow topics, and high resource consumption, which increases with the number and length of of documents being assigned topics. These issues are particularly critical for industrial applications, which require high-quality, in-depth analysis and the processing of large volumes of documents. In this context, this paper introduces a framework called SeLATM, which addresses these concerns by employing segment-level topic generation and topic refinement through agentic feedback loops. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that SeLATM significantly reduces the LLM resources compared to methods based on topic assignment process, while maintaining superior performance.

</details>


### [291] [Game Arena: Strategic LLM Evaluation in Competitive Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31473)
*Bovard Doerschuk-Tiberi,Yao Yan,Justin Chiu,Hann Wang,Timothy Chung,Martyna Plomecka,John Schultz,Jon Lipovetz,Clayton Drazner,Yuchen Zhuang,Jaimie Hwang,Nate Keating,Riley Jones,Andrew Lee,Oran Kelly,Ian Gemp,Michael Aaron,Laurel Prince,Kate Larson,Jeff Moser,Harrison Jobe,Chad Woodford,Siqi Liu,Andrew Wang,Bo Chang,Christopher D'Mello,Diane Chaleff,Addison Howard,Johnny Yip,Chuck Sugnet,Antonio Gulli,Meghan O'Connell,Will Cukierski,Nenad Tomasev,Dima Yeroshenko,Kinjal Parekh,Roxanne Daniel,Marc Lanctot,Domino Weir,Elsa Dong,Daniel Hennes,Melissa Nalubwama,Robert Fraser,Ryan Trostle,Jun Peng,Tom Mason,Lloyd Hightower,Chiamaka Chukwuka,Yuexiang Zhai,Phoebe Kirk,Yi Su,Yuting Han,Jie Ren,Chris Prichard,Sahand Sharifzadeh,Karim Hakimzadeh,DJ Sterling,Meg Risdal,Kate Olszewska,Ya Xu,Orhan Firat,Minmin Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Kaggle Game Arena, a scalable, open platform to evaluate LLMs via competitive games (Chess, Poker, Werewolf) with structured environments, robust evaluation, and head-to-head competitions to study strategic planning, adaptation, and robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Move beyond static benchmarks as models evolve and risk performance saturation; provide a reproducible, transparent, and generalizable framework for evaluating strategic and adaptive capabilities of LLMs.

Method: Describe the platform infrastructure and three pilot environments (Chess, Poker, Werewolf) spanning perfect information, imperfect information, and multiplayer settings; define evaluation metrics; report results from full model competitions to demonstrate reproducibility and generalizability.

Result: Empirical results from head-to-head competitions across multiple models in three games; analysis of strategic planning, adaptation under uncertainty, and robustness; evidence of reproducibility and scalability of the evaluation framework.

Conclusion: Game Arena provides a reproducible, transparent, and extensible benchmarking ecosystem for LLMs that can adapt to new games and variants, enabling ongoing assessment of strategic capabilities.

Abstract: We introduce Kaggle Game Arena, an open and ever-expanding platform to evaluate large language models (LLMs) through competitive games. Different from static benchmarks, game arena enables models to play head-to-head matchups in structured environments where the gameplay strength naturally increases as models evolve, preventing performance saturation. This technical report details the infrastructure behind Game Arena and describes the three pilot game environments: Chess, Poker, and Werewolf. These environments span perfect information, imperfect information, and multiplayer game settings, enabling a systematic study of models' strategic planning, adaptation, and robustness under uncertainty.
