For each game, we provide a detailed description of the environment, evaluation metrics, and results from running full competitions across models. Through robust infrastructure and large-scale ground-truth based evaluation, Game Arena ensures reproducibility, transparency and generalizability to new games and variants over time.

</details>


### [292] ["AI is (not) the new...": A Diagnostic Analogy Framework for Generative AI's Cultural Impacts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31482)
*Rida Qadri,Vinodkumar Prabhakaran,Remi Denton*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A diagnostic framework to analyze how generative AI transforms epistemic/cultural practice by decomposing interventions into three coordinates (epistemic site, governing logic, technical mechanism), differentiating structural versus contingent effects, and applying it to information discovery/knowledge synthesis to reveal traceable cultural shifts and governance levers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the imprecision of historical analogies in describing AI’s epistemic/cultural impact and to equip scholars/policymakers with a precise tool to design targeted governance by identifying the specific property of the technology that drives change.

Method: Propose a diagnostic framework with three coordinates: epistemic site where a technology acts, governing logic that organizes its object, and the technical mechanism that instantiates the logic. Distinguish structural consequences (driven by mechanism) from contingent ones (subject to design/institutional choice). Apply the framework to information discovery and knowledge synthesis to trace consequences and governance levers.

Result: The framework clarifies how shifts from indexicality to inference and from editorial authority to statistical consensus produce specific, traceable cultural effects, and it reveals governance levers that gestalt analogies mask.

Conclusion: Using this diagnostic framework enables precise intervention design by targeting the correct property of the system, revealing structural vs contingent effects and guiding governance in AI-enabled knowledge practices.

Abstract: Generative AI is reshaping the cultural infrastructures through which knowledge is found, synthesized, and held accountable. To make sense of this shift, scholars and policymakers reach for historical analogies of technologies such as the printing press, steam power or electricity. But these comparisons are typically imprecise about which property of the technology carries the comparison, and imprecise analogies produce imprecise governance by designing interventions against the wrong property of the system. This paper offers a diagnostic framework for analyzing how generative AI can transform epistemic and cultural practice. This paper offers a diagnostic framework for analyzing how generative AI can transform epistemic and cultural practice. We decompose each intervention into three coordinates: the epistemic site at which a technology acts, the governing logic by which it organizes its object, and the technical mechanism through which the logic is instantiated. This framework allows us to distinguish between structural cultural consequences, which follow from the mechanism itself, from contingent ones, which remain open to design and institutional choice. Applying the framework to information discovery and knowledge synthesis, we show how the shift from indexicality to inference and from editorial authority to statistical consensus produces specific, traceable cultural effects and reveals governance levers that gestalt analogy obscures.

</details>


### [293] [UQ-LOB: Uncertainty-Aware Limit Order Book Mid-Price Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31491)
*Derrick Gilchrist Edward Manoharan,Eljas Linna,Kestutis Baltakys,Hao Dong,Juho Kanniainen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Uncertainty-aware LOB forecasting with an encoder-agnostic UQ module (UQ-LOB) that attaches to pretrained LOB encoders to produce calibrated predictive distributions for short-horizon mid-price moves and enable selective predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the lack of trust in point forecasts from deep LOB models by providing calibrated uncertainty estimates and a mechanism for selective prediction to improve decision-making in high-frequency settings.

Method: A lightweight, encoder-agnostic UQ module that conditions forecasts on a context set of recent completed windows. Two variants: UQ-regression outputs a calibrated Gaussian predictive distribution over future price displacement; UQ-classification outputs a categorical distribution over down/up/stationary. Both provide a scalar confidence (signal-to-noise ratio or class probability) enabling selective prediction. Inspired by attentive neural processes.

Result: Evaluated on 5.2 billion LOB events across seven cryptocurrency assets at 5/10/15s horizons. UQ-regression achieves near-nominal 68% interval coverage. With the most confident 10% of predictions, macro F1 improves by 0.11–0.15 for regression and 0.05–0.11 for classification across horizons. For large moves, the tightest confidence tier yields directional F1 of 0.88 (down) and 0.83 (up) at 5s.

Conclusion: UQ-LOB offers a lightweight, encoder-agnostic approach to calibrate uncertainty in short-horizon LOB forecasts and enable selective predictions, yielding meaningful accuracy gains and robust calibration across large-scale, real-world crypto data.

Abstract: Forecasting short-horizon mid-price movements from limit order book (LOB) data is central to algorithmic trading, yet most deep LOB forecasters are point predictors: they output a direction or a displacement, but never indicate which of their forecasts can be trusted. We introduce UQ-LOB, a lightweight, encoder-agnostic uncertainty quantification module that attaches to any pretrained LOB encoder and, in the spirit of attentive neural processes, conditions each forecast on a context set of recently completed windows whose outcomes are already realised. The UQ-regression variant outputs a calibrated Gaussian over the future tick displacement, while the UQ-classification variant outputs a categorical distribution over down/up/stationary. Both expose a scalar confidence (predicted signal-to-noise ratio or class probability) that supports selective prediction. On 5.2 billion LOB events across seven cryptocurrency assets and horizons of 5, 10 and 15 seconds, UQ-regression attains near-nominal 68% interval coverage, and restricting to the most confident 10% of predictions raises directional macro F1 by 0.11-0.15 for UQ-regression and 0.05-0.11 for UQ-classification, at every horizon. On large, economically meaningful moves, the tightest confidence tier reaches a directional F1 of 0.88 (down) and 0.83 (up) at the 5-second horizon.

</details>


### [294] [Prompt Minimization: Reducing Input Redundancy Without Sacrificing Output Fidelity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31505)
*Marius F. R. Juston,Kevin A. Karim,Jonathan Gao,Kevin C. Li,Rudhi Bashambu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes prompt minimization for LLMs; shows shorter prompts can match longer ones and reduce overhead; introduces three frameworks to identify minimal prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prompt design is currently heuristic and inefficient; long prompts can waste compute and potentially harm reasoning; uncover what information is essential to elicit desired model behavior.

Method: Three variant frameworks to identify and evaluate minimal prompts; empirical demonstrations comparing minimal prompts with longer prompts; analysis of information density and output fidelity.

Result: Minimal prompts often yield outputs comparable to longer prompts; evidence of redundancy in input space; potential reductions in compute and latency; frameworks provide a means to quantify minimality.

Conclusion: Prompt minimization enables practical efficiency gains and deepens understanding of input compression in LLMs; suggests new directions for prompt engineering.

Abstract: Despite the growing capabilities of large language models (LLMs), prompt design remains largely heuristic and ad hoc. This project will explore $\textit{prompt minimization}$, the process of reducing prompts to their smallest, most information-dense form while preserving output fidelity. Practically, shorter prompts reduce computational overhead and inference latency, especially when large contexts, such as entire documents or codebases, are included unnecessarily. Further, longer prompts can damage LLM reasoning and accuracy. Theoretically, the existence of multiple prompts yielding equivalent outputs suggests a high degree of redundancy in the input space, raising fundamental questions about what information is essential to elicit specific model behaviors. We propose three variant frameworks to identify and evaluate minimal prompts and demonstrate that minimal prompts often produce outputs comparable to those of their longer counterparts. These findings suggest new directions for efficient prompt engineering and deepen our understanding of input compression in LLMs.

</details>


### [295] [A Flow Matching Framework for Neural Representational Dissimilarity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31544)
*Zeyuan Ye,Xue-Xin Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Unifies neural representational dissimilarity metrics via flow matching; shows Jeffreys divergences under velocity constraints; advantageous for complex distributions; enables principled design of new metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide a coherent, principled framework for comparing neural response distributions across stimuli, brain areas, tasks, and models, addressing the patchwork of distance metrics with differing assumptions and estimators.

Method: Develop flow matching framework from deep generative models; demonstrate that various distance metrics are Jeffreys divergences under different velocity constraints; assess benefits for estimating distances between complex, continuous distributions; outline design principles for new metrics.

Result: Flow matching yields a unified approach to estimating neural representational dissimilarity metrics; it is advantageous for complex distributions and continuous variables and enables principled construction of new metrics.

Conclusion: Flow matching offers a unified, principled toolkit for understanding, estimating, and designing neural representational dissimilarity metrics across stimuli, brain areas, tasks, and models.

Abstract: Neural representational dissimilarity quantifies differences between neural response distributions, and is essential for comparing neural codes across stimuli, brain areas, tasks, and models. Commonly used distance metrics involve different assumptions and are estimated with separate methods. Here, we show that a variety of distance metrics can be unified under a flow matching framework developed in deep generative models. That is, these distances arise as Jeffreys divergences under different velocity constraints. We find that flow matching has advantages for estimating distances involving complicated distributions and continuous variables. Furthermore, this framework enables the design of new distance metrics in a principled way. Together, flow matching provides a unified approach for understanding, estimating, and designing neural representational dissimilarity metrics.

</details>


### [296] [Multi-agent Scaling Across Disjunctive and Compensatory Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31563)
*Carolina Fortuna,Blaz Bertalanic*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Taxonomy-based analysis shows that multi-agent LLM scaling depends on task structure; disjunctive tasks show limited gains from simple plurality, but multi-round revision helps; Fermi-estimation yields little benefit from scaling due to high item-level bias; combining models helps only in Fermi tasks, not surpassing the best in disjunctive tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand when increasing team size improves LLM performance by classifying group tasks via Steiner's taxonomy and analyzing disjunctive vs compensatory tasks.

Method: Model independently sampled agents as conditionally independent given the item. Derive large-team limits: plurality voting converges to the modal answer; averaging converges to the model's item-level bias. Empirically test with 13 open-weight models, benchmarks, up to 30 agents.

Result: Disjunctive tasks: probability of at least one correct increases 5–20 points with team size, but plurality voting yields almost no gain (~0–0.5 points). Multi-round revision raises accuracy substantially, but gains saturate similarly with 1 peer as with 29. Fermi estimation: scaling yields little benefit; item-level biases account for ~87% of squared error; averaging reduces error by ~6%. Combining model families helps Fermi but does not beat the strongest member on disjunctive tasks.

Conclusion: Task structure and aggregation mechanism fundamentally determine team scaling. naive aggregation limits scaling benefits; effective utilization requires alignment between task type and aggregation strategy.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems are often expected to improve as team size increases, yet the scaling behavior may depend on task structure. Our central contribution is to introduce Steiner's taxonomy of group tasks as a framework for analyzing multi-agent LLM scaling and focusing the analysis on disjunctive and compensatory tasks. We model independently sampled agents as conditionally independent given the item, which yields their large-team limits: plurality voting converges to the model's modal answer, and averaging converges to the model's item-level bias. Across selected representative benchmarks, 13 open-weight models, and teams of up to 30 agents, we find qualitatively different scaling behavior. On disjunctive tasks, the probability that at least one agent is correct grows by 5-20 points with team size, but plurality voting over agents that answer directly realises almost none of this potential, as the model predicts to within 0.5 points on average. Multi-round revision raises accuracy considerably, yet the gain is nearly the same with one peer as with 29. In contrast, scaling provides little benefit on Fermi estimation, despite its natural suitability for aggregation: item-level biases shared across the samples of a model account for about 87% of the squared error, so averaging reduces error by only about 6%. Combining model families helps on Fermi estimation but does not surpass the strongest member on disjunctive tasks. These results show that task structure, together with the mechanism combining member outputs, is a fundamental determinant of team scaling.

</details>


### [297] [DeepEdu-v1: Efficient and Scalable Agentic LLMs for Vietnamese Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31568)
*Quang Nguyen,Hieu Nguyen,Hien Hoang,Toan Pham,Cong Tran,Nam Vu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DeepEdu-v1 is an on-prem AI-tutoring system for Vietnamese education built on SCALE. It introduces two core innovations: (1) a long-context inference engine that amortizes token selection per cluster, reducing retrieval calls by 7.7x and cutting prefill latency by ~35% while maintaining or improving accuracy; (2) a self-improving agentic layer that curates a verified playbook from past interactions instead of fine-tuning, to reduce reliance on Western priors as local knowledge accumulates. In deployment, it achieves ~2x TTFT speedup over standard vLLM and raises agentic accuracy from 70.0% to 79.5%, with notable gains in financial reasoning and interactive-agent tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses two limitations of AI tutoring in developing regions: (a) data-sovereignty and misalignment issues of cloud-based models like ChatGPT due to data export rules and Western-centric training; (b) memory and latency challenges of self-hosted models when handling long tutoring contexts, alongside persistent hallucinations on region-specific content. The goal is to deliver a scalable, on-premise tutoring solution aligned with Vietnamese curricula.

Method: Two innovations comprise SCALE: (i) long-context inference engine that aggregates token selection from per-sub-chunk to per-cluster granularity, reducing retrieval calls by 7.7x and lowering prefill latency (TTFT) by ~35%; (ii) a self-improving agentic layer that continuously curates a verified playbook from past interactions instead of fine-tuning, aimed at diminishing dependence on dominant-language priors as local knowledge grows.

Result: In deployed configuration, DeepEdu delivers nearly 2x TTFT speedup over standard vLLM serving and improves agentic accuracy from 70.0% to 79.5% on complex tasks, with strongest gains observed in financial-reasoning and interactive-agent benchmarks.

Conclusion: DeepEdu-v1 demonstrates that combining long-context-efficient inference with an agentic, non-finetuning knowledge-curration layer can yield substantial latency reductions and accuracy gains for on-prem AI tutoring in a national curriculum context, supporting data-sovereignty and local-content reliability while approaching or surpassing cloud-based baselines on key tasks.

Abstract: AI tutoring could markedly improve learning outcomes for students in developing regions such as Vietnam, yet the two obvious paths both fall short. Cloud assistants such as ChatGPT route sensitive student data to foreign servers---violating data-sovereignty laws such as Vietnam's Decree 53---and, pre-trained on Western-centric corpora, are not organized around the national textbook curriculum, so their knowledge of local content is unsystematic and frequently hallucinated. Self-hosting an open model keeps data on-premise but hits a two-fold wall: post-training quantization (AWQ, GPTQ) tames the static weight footprint, yet the dynamic KV cache and prefill latency of long tutoring contexts still cause out-of-memory failures and slow responses on consumer GPUs, while the model keeps hallucinating on region-specific material. We present DeepEdu-v1, an AI-tutoring system for Vietnamese education built on SCALE (Self-improving Context-Aware Learning Engine), a framework with two innovations. First, a long-context inference engine amortizes token selection from per-sub-chunk to per-cluster granularity; on long-context retrieval it issues x7.7 fewer retrieval calls than a state-of-the-art selective-attention baseline, cutting prefill latency (TTFT) by roughly 35% while matching or improving task accuracy. Second, a self-improving agentic layer continuously curates a verified playbook from past interactions instead of fine-tuning, a design intended to progressively reduce reliance on dominant-language priors as trustworthy local knowledge accumulates. In its deployed configuration, DeepEdu achieves a nearly x2 TTFT speedup over standard vLLM serving and lifts agentic accuracy from 70.0% to 79.5% on complex tasks, with the strongest per-track gains across financial-reasoning and interactive-agent benchmarks.

</details>


### [298] [Learning to Stop without Learning to Stop: Self-Supervised Confidence Training Improves Reasoning Efficiency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31619)
*Parsa Hosseini,Akasha Tigalappanavara,Sumit Nawathe,Chenrui Fan,Sourya Basu,Genta Indra Winata,Anirban Das,Soheil Feizi,Nima Chitsazan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Fine-tuning reasoning models with self-supervised confidence signals reduces reasoning length during inference without changing the inference procedure, achieving up to ~25% token reduction at matched accuracy across diverse domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce the computational cost of long reasoning traces in chain-of-thought models without relying on explicit length penalties or modified inference-time stopping rules.

Method: Train a model to predict its own confidence at intermediate points along its reasoning via self-supervised targets, using only 600 training problems. The training objective is solely the confidence prediction; no aim to shorten reasoning length. Inference uses standard generation with no confidence elicitation or early stopping.

Result: Fine-tuned models show substantial efficiency gains, reducing generated tokens by up to 25% at matched accuracy across Gemma, Qwen, Nemotron, and GPT-OSS on math, science, and coding benchmarks. Gains are comparable to methods that optimize for shorter reasoning. Confidence supervision largely preserves high-level reasoning composition rather than suppressing specific behaviors.

Conclusion: Efficient reasoning can emerge as a downstream effect of learning metacognitive signals (confidence), without directly optimizing for length or stopping; metacognitive supervision can yield practical efficiency benefits across multiple models and domains.

Abstract: Reasoning models often generate very long reasoning traces, making inference computationally expensive. Existing approaches typically improve efficiency either through inference-time early-stopping mechanisms or by explicitly encouraging shorter reasoning during training, for example through reinforcement learning with length penalties. We show that substantial efficiency gains can instead emerge from a different kind of supervision: \textit{confidence}. Using a self-supervised procedure, we fine-tune reasoning models to predict their confidence in the answer at intermediate points along their own reasoning trajectories using only 600 training problems. Confidence is used only as a training target: the loss contains no objective for reasoning length, efficiency, or stopping. At inference, the fine-tuned models use the standard generation procedure, with no confidence elicitation or early-stopping mechanism. Despite this, self-supervised confidence fine-tuning makes reasoning more efficient, reducing generated tokens by up to 25\% at matched accuracy across Gemma, Qwen, Nemotron, and GPT-OSS models on mathematical, scientific, and coding reasoning benchmarks, with efficiency gains comparable to methods that explicitly optimize for shorter reasoning. Analysis of reasoning episodes further shows that confidence supervision largely preserves the base models' high-level reasoning composition rather than selectively suppressing particular behaviors. Our results suggest that efficient reasoning may emerge as a downstream consequence of learning metacognitive signals, without being directly optimized.

</details>

# cs.RO [[Back]](#toc)

### [299] [TinyCVIO: A Constellation-Aided Visual-Inertial Odometry System for Nanodrones](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30358)
*Derin Ozturk,Kaan Akan,Irwin Wang,Christopher Batten*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: TinyCVIO provides real-time visual-inertial odometry on a commodity microcontroller by co-designing lightweight sensing, visual processing, and estimation around LED constellations and a rigid-board model; it achieves centimeter-scale trajectory accuracy with low latency onboard a tiny quadrotor.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable accurate state estimation for nanodrones under severe computational and sensing constraints without requiring surveyed landmarks or yaw references.

Method: Co-design of miniature sensing, a streaming visual frontend tracking millimeter-scale LED observations (29.2 FPS) under a fixed-filter-state size; use of a rigid-board measurement model that preserves inter-LED constraints and streaming QR bounds for the estimation workspace; LED constellations with known geometry placed on a common level plane to avoid yaw/angular ambiguity.

Result: Across 19 hardware-in-the-loop tests, the rigid-board model reduced mean absolute trajectory error by 27% versus planar-point baselines. Onboard Crazyflie flights (9 flights, 3 speeds) achieved 3.5–3.7 cm MAE and 0.50–0.60% relative pose error over 10 m segments, with 15.7–16.3 ms latency.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates accurate, real-time VIO on constrained hardware through a principled co-design leveraging LED-based landmarks and inter-LED constraints, enabling resilient onboard navigation for nanodrones.

Abstract: Nanodrones require accurate, real-time state estimation under severe sensing and computational constraints. We present TinyCVIO, a visual-inertial odometry system that co-designs miniature sensing, visual processing, and estimation for a commodity dual-core microcontroller with 520 kB SRAM. Lightweight LED constellations provide known geometry without surveyed positions or yaw angles, assuming placement on a common level plane. A streaming visual frontend tracks LED observations from a millimeter-scale camera at 29.2 FPS, while a rigid-board measurement model retains inter-LED constraints and streaming QR bounds estimation workspace for a fixed filter-state size. Across 19 hand-held hardware-in-the-loop datasets, the rigid-board model reduces mean absolute trajectory error by 27% relative to planar points. The complete system runs onboard a Crazyflie across nine flights at three speeds, achieving 3.5-3.7 cm mean absolute trajectory error and 0.50-0.60% relative pose error over 10 m segments, with mean estimate latency of 15.7-16.3 ms.

</details>


### [300] [POIL: Point-based One-Shot Imitation Learning with Stable Dynamical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30404)
*Sang Min Kim,Jinwoo Seo,Hyeongjun Heo,Junho Lee,Yonghyeon Lee,Young Min Kim*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: POIL is a point-based one-shot imitation learning framework that uses a shared set of 3D points on an object's functional part to transfer a demonstrated trajectory and execute it robustly in the presence of scene changes, different grasps, and disturbances, without a full 3D model or pose estimator.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: One-shot imitation learning must generalize a single demonstration across unseen objects, viewpoints, grasp configurations, and disturbances. Traditional methods often rely on full 3D models or accurate pose estimation; POIL proposes a representation grounded in functional parts and stability guarantees to enable cross-object transfer and robust execution.

Method: Define a shared functional-part point set on the object. Use point correspondences to transfer the demonstrated trajectory. Ground the functional-part points with a multi-modal large language model. Transfer trajectory across viewpoint, pose, and object category. During execution, track points online from multiple views and drive them with Point-set BCSDM by projecting per-point velocities onto a single rigid-body twist derived from the tracked points, extending stable dynamical models from SE(3) pose to a point set. The goal dynamics reduce to a gradient flow on the SO(3) potential, implying almost-global convergence under a rigid-object assumption.

Result: Empirical evaluation in both simulation and real-robot experiments shows that POIL can transfer a single demonstration across object category, grasp pose, and goal geometry and recover from external disturbances during execution, achieving robust one-shot manipulation without relying on a full 3D model or pose estimator.

Conclusion: POIL demonstrates that a point-based representation of the object's functional part, combined with stability-driven control and LLM grounding, enables robust one-shot imitation with cross-object generalization and disturbance rejection, extending stable dynamical systems to point sets and enabling almost-global convergence under rigid-object conditions.

Abstract: We present POIL, a point-based one-shot imitation learning framework with stable dynamical systems. While one-shot imitation avoids collecting extensive demonstrations, successful one-shot manipulation requires not only transferring a demonstrated trajectory to a novel object but also executing it robustly under changing scene conditions, grasp configurations, and external disturbances. POIL addresses both problems through a shared representation: a set of 3D points on the object's functional part, used jointly for trajectory transfer and closed-loop execution. The one-shot transfer from the demonstrated trajectory is enabled with point correspondences. POIL grounds the shared functional part with a multi-modal large language model, and transfers the trajectory across viewpoint, pose, and object category changes. During execution, multi-view tracking observes the same points online, and Point-set BCSDM drives them in closed loop by projecting per-point velocities onto a single rigid-body twist computed from the tracked points alone. This extends stable dynamical models from an SE(3) pose to a point set without requiring a known 3D model or pose estimator. We show that at the goal the controller becomes a gradient flow on the classical SO(3) potential, so its terminal phase inherits the almost-global convergence of that potential under a rigid-object assumption. Across simulation and real-robot experiments, POIL transfers a single demonstration across object category, grasp pose, and goal geometry, while recovering from external disturbances during execution. Project page: https://sangminkim-99.github.io/poil

</details>


### [301] [Actively Resolving Contextual Uncertainty for Underspecified Tasks in Natural Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30428)
*Zachary Ravichandran,Jonathan Diller,Fernando Cladera,Varun Murali,George J. Pappas,Vijay Kumar*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A framework named CLUE for resolving contextual uncertainty in language-conditioned robotics through closed-loop hypothesis testing. It uses an LLM-derived policy to hypothesize task concepts and plans, grounds them via an online language-embedded map, and iteratively refines actions through environment interaction. Real-world validation on a Spot shows near-oracle performance and superior results to non-closed-loop baselines; naive language-grounded maps are insufficient and costlier in tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In unfamiliar environments with underspecified tasks, robots face high contextual uncertainty about what constitutes success, what information is relevant, and whether such information exists. Existing language-conditioned policies rely on well-specified goals and upfront maps. There is a need to actively resolve uncertainty through interactive grounding and planning.

Method: CLUE combines: (1) an LLM-derived policy that proposes task-relevant concepts and potential plans, (2) an online, language-embedded map to ground hypotheses, and (3) closed-loop execution that evaluates hypotheses via environment interaction and refines plans as new information is acquired. The approach is deployed on a Boston Dynamics Spot across three indoor/outdoor environments covering 15 tasks (object disambiguation, functional inference, occlusion reasoning).

Result: CLUE achieves a success rate within 7 percentage points of an oracle policy. It outperforms a non-closed-loop LLM-enabled planner by about 4x. Purely building and querying a language-enriched map is substantially worse (≈1/3 the success rate) and requires >10x more VLM tokens. Supporting experiments underscore the necessity of closed-loop grounding for complex contextual planning.

Conclusion: Closed-loop contextual uncertainty resolution enables near-oracle performance in underspecified robotic tasks. The combination of an LLM-driven hypothesis generator with an online language-grounded map and interactive refinement outperforms baselines and highlights the limitations of static language-grounded representations. The framework shows promise for real-world deployment but depends on effective grounding and token efficiency.

Abstract: Foundation models provide robots with the ability to interpret natural language and reason about environmental context, yet most language-conditioned policies assume that goals are well-specified and that task-relevant information is provided upfront via a prior map. Operating in unfamiliar environments with underspecified tasks entails high contextual uncertainty: the robot must jointly infer what constitutes task success, what constitutes relevant information, and where (or whether) that information exists. We address these limitations via CLUE (Closed-Loop contextual Uncertainty rEsolution), a framework for actively resolving contextual uncertainty given underspecified tasks in natural language. CLUE uses an LLM-derived policy to hypothesize task-relevant concepts and potential plans. It then uses a language-embedded map, which is constructed online, to ground these hypotheses into actions. The policy sequentially evaluates hypotheses via closed-loop environment interaction and refines its plans as it gathers new information. We deploy CLUE on a Boston Dynamics Spot across three real indoor and outdoor environments spanning 15 tasks that require object disambiguation, functional inference, and occlusion reasoning. CLUE achieves a success rate within 7 percentage points of an oracle policy and outperforms an LLM-enabled planner without closed-loop feedback by a 4x margin. Supporting experiments demonstrate that simply building and then querying a language-enriched map is insufficient to resolve complex contextual planning tasks; these approaches achieve roughly one third the success rate of CLUE while requiring over 10x more VLM tokens. We provide additional information at https://zacravichandran.github.io/CLUE.

</details>


### [302] [WALT: Learning World-Model-Aligned Latent Trajectories for Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30436)
*Mingkai Jia,Jiaxin Guo,Zhijian Shu,Jiawei Xu,Mingxiao Li,Jintao Cheng,Ping Tan,Wei Yin*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: WALT learns a compact latent trajectory space aligned with a frozen world model to improve planning without modifying the world model, using a dual-branch autoencoder and semantic transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Visual world-state predictions often misalign with actionable geometric trajectories, hindering planning. Aligning latent trajectories with action-relevant semantics can bridge this gap.

Method: Introduce WALT: a dual-branch trajectory autoencoder that maps raw waypoints into a compact latent space and transfers semantic knowledge from a frozen pretrained driving world model. Compare latent-learning paradigms JEPA and REPA; evaluate on NAVSIM benchmarks.

Result: PDMS improves from 89.4 to 89.8 (NAVSIMv1) and EPDMS from 87.3 to 87.9 (NAVSIMv2); trajectory planner FLOPs reduced by 30.5%.

Conclusion: Preserving world representations while extracting action-relevant information provides an effective interface for world-model-based trajectory planning; latent alignment boosts planning efficiency with modest performance gains on NAVSIM.

Abstract: Driving world models learn rich predictive representations of the surrounding environment from visual observations, yet accurate visual prediction does not necessarily translate into effective trajectory planning. We argue that a key bottleneck lies in the mismatch between visual world states and raw geometric trajectories, which may limit the planner's ability to exploit action-relevant semantics encoded by the world model. To address this issue, we propose World-Model Alignment for Latent Trajectories (WALT), which learns a compact generative trajectory latent space by transferring information from a frozen pretrained driving world model without modifying the world model itself. Rather than directly generating raw waypoints, WALT maps them into compact representations through a dual-branch trajectory autoencoder and transfers semantic knowledge from the frozen visual world model into this trajectory space, encouraging the learned action representation to capture scene-level cues relevant to future motion and planning. Beyond our proposed formulation, we systematically study latent learning based on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) and feature alignment following Representation Alignment (REPA) to investigate how trajectory-only representation learning affects downstream planning. We evaluate WALT on the NAVSIM benchmarks. Relative to the raw-waypoint baseline, WALT improves PDMS from 89.4 to 89.8 on NAVSIMv1 and EPDMS from 87.3 to 87.9 on NAVSIMv2 while reducing trajectory planner FLOPs by 30.5%. These results suggest that preserving world representations while extracting action-relevant information provides an effective interface for world-model-based trajectory planning.

</details>


### [303] [VkVIO: Cross-platform GPU Acceleration for Visual-Inertial Odometry with Vulkan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30459)
*Ole Hoffmann,Mateo de Mayo,Daniel Cremers*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: VkVIO is a Vulkan-based, vendor-agnostic GPU-accelerated VIO/VI-SLAM that delivers real-time, state-of-the-art accuracy across devices, outperforming CUDA-based VIO on the same hardware and enabling low-latency, low-power, and low-cost VI-SLAM for robotics and XR.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficient, accurate state estimation is crucial for perception in robotics and XR. While GPUs accelerate VIO/VI-SLAM, CUDA reliance limits deployment options to a single vendor. A cross-platform, vendor-agnostic solution can broaden accessibility and reduce device constraints.

Method: Implement VkVIO using the Vulkan API for GPU acceleration, forming a cross-platform VIO pipeline with causal, real-time estimates. Validate on a workstation, a laptop, and a low-cost single-board computer, and compare performance and accuracy against CUDA-based VIO baselines.

Result: VkVIO achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with causal, real-time estimates and outperforms CUDA-based VIO on the same hardware, across heterogeneous devices.

Conclusion: VkVIO enables low-latency, low-power, and low-cost VIO in robotics and XR via vendor-agnostic GPU acceleration.

Abstract: Perception in robotics and XR fundamentally relies on good state estimation. Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (VI-SLAM) are proven ways of achieving this goal in a cost-effective and accurate manner. Efficiency in these systems allows for smaller, cooler, and lighter devices. GPU acceleration is a natural approach for reducing latency, thanks to their wide availability in platforms like embedded computers, mobile phones, and XR headsets. However, previous works in the literature have limited themselves to the use of CUDA for this task, significantly reducing deployment options to a single vendor. We instead leverage the vendor-agnostic Vulkan API, originally designed for the strict performance requirements of 3D graphics applications. In this work, we present VkVIO, the first, to the best of our knowledge, cross-platform GPU-accelerated VIO method. We provide state-of-the-art accuracy with causal estimates required for real-time operation. We deploy VkVIO on a diverse range of devices spanning a workstation, a laptop, and an extremely inexpensive single-board computer, while outperforming CUDA-based systems on the same hardware. VkVIO enables possibilities for low-latency, low-power, and low-cost VIO in robotics and XR.

</details>


### [304] [Realizability Is Not Enough: Encoding, Liveness, and Auditing of Synthesized Robot Supervisors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30460)
*David C. Conner,Joshua Luzier,William J. Doyle,Emma R. Faith,Aubrie B. Kooiker,Andrew J. Farney,Sebastian Fox,Evangelina Grimes,Ian G. Conner,Kyle Bloom*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Open-source pipeline for ROS 2 FlexBE that generates GR(1) specification-based supervisors, analyzes assumptions, audits strategies, reduces state with a behavior-preservation proof, and emits executable state machines; evaluated via four case studies across two quadcopters, comparing enumerated vs one-hot encodings and two liveness formulations, with recommendations favoring enumerated encoding and System-Goal liveness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge formal realizability from GR(1) synthesis to deployable robot controllers by incorporating assumption analysis, strategy auditing, and state reduction before code emission.

Method: Develop a pipeline that (1) generates capability-based GR(1) specs for FlexBE, (2) analyzes liveness/assumptions prior to synthesis, (3) audits realized strategies, (4) reduces the controller state space via a behavior-preservation proof, and (5) emits executable ROS 2 state-machine controllers. Evaluation uses four case studies (six comparisons) on hardware (two quadcopters), comparing enumerated vs one-hot encodings and two liveness formulations.

Result: Enumerated encoding tends to synthesize faster; fewer propositions do not reliably predict smaller controllers or lower symbolic cost. System-Goal without pending memory is the only liveness formulation that yields executable controllers across encodings; Fair-Outcome can allow realizable cycles without intended completion. The auditor is sound and complete for four structural defect classes but not a general liveness verifier; the reduction preserves capability-level behavior. Overall, the pipeline narrows the gap between formal realizability and deployable controllers.

Conclusion: Recommend using enumerated encoding with System-Goal liveness and auditing every realized strategy for this backend and model; proposition count and realizability alone do not predict deployability.

Abstract: High-level robotic supervisors coordinate capabilities whose reported outcomes determine the robot's next action. Reactive synthesis can generate such supervisors with formal guarantees, but deployment requires more than proving a Generalized Reactivity (1) (GR(1)) specification realizable. Designers must encode failure-prone capabilities, choose liveness assumptions that match retry intent, audit strategies, and translate them into robot software. We present an open-source pipeline for Robot Operating System (ROS) 2 Flexible Behavior Engine (FlexBE) supervisors that generates capability-based GR(1) specifications, analyzes assumptions before synthesis, audits strategies, reduces states with a behavior-preservation proof, and emits executable state machines.
  Across four case studies (six comparisons), including hardware on two quadcopter platforms, we compare enumerated and one-hot encodings and two liveness formulations. Under the tested backend, enumerated encoding usually synthesizes faster, although fewer propositions do not reliably predict smaller controllers or lower symbolic cost. System-Goal without pending memory is the only liveness treatment confirmed to yield executable controllers under both encodings across the reported grid; Fair-Outcome can permit realizable cycles without designer-intended completion. For this backend and model, we recommend enumerated encoding with System-Goal and auditing every realized strategy, since proposition count and realizability do not measure deployability.
  The auditor is sound and complete for four structural defect classes (protocol violations, deadlocks, bounded-failure violations, goal-unreachable traps) but is not a general liveness verifier, and the reduction preserves capability-level behavior. Together, these stages narrow the gap between formal realizability and controllers that pass protocol and structural-progress checks.

</details>


### [305] [DGT-Map: Directional Global Traversability Mapping Utilizing Multi-Task Learning for Heterogeneous Vehicles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30461)
*Jaskrit Singh,Kashif K. Noori,Jing Xiao,Constantinos Chamzas*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: DGT-MAP learns global, directional, and vehicle-conditioned traversability costmaps from RGB-D and locomotion data using a shared backbone with vehicle-specific heads, enabling direction-aware planning and improved navigation across diverse vehicles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Off-road traversability is inherently direction-dependent and vehicle-specific, but traditional maps are isotropic and many learned estimators are vehicle-specific, hindering cross-vehicle generalization and shared terrain representations.

Method: A self-supervised framework with a shared multi-task backbone that extracts common terrain features across training vehicles and vehicle-specific prediction heads for platform-dependent responses. Inference outputs a heading-indexed costmap that can be used by a direction-aware planner (e.g., Hybrid A*). Uses RGB-D observations and locomotion signals during training. 

Result: In simulation, integrating DGT-MAP with a Hybrid A* stack yields the highest or tied-highest navigation success across challenging terrains, including downhill-only slopes and ridge obstacles, compared with geometric, binary, and direction-agnostic learned baselines.

Conclusion: Learning shared terrain representations with vehicle-specific adaptation improves cross-vehicle generalization and enables direction-aware planning, yielding robust navigation performance on terrain where traversability is direction-dependent.

Abstract: Off-road traversability is direction-dependent and vehicle specific, yet most global maps assign a single isotropic cost to each location. Existing learned estimators are also commonly trained independently for each vehicle; this preserves vehicle-specific behavior but prevents vehicles from sharing common terrain representations. DGT-MAP addresses both limitations through a self-supervised framework that learns global, directional, and vehicle-conditioned traversability costmaps from RGB-D observations and locomotion signals. A shared multi-task backbone learns common terrain features across training vehicles while vehicle-specific prediction heads preserve platform-dependent responses. At inference, DGT-MAP produces a heading-indexed costmap that can be used by a direction-aware planner. We evaluate DGT-MAP in simulation by integrating it into a Hybrid A* navigation stack and measuring downstream task success on challenging terrains, including slopes that are traversable downhill but not uphill and a ridge obstacle that is traversable by some vehicles, but not by others. Across evaluated tasks, DGT-MAP achieves the highest or tied-highest navigation success rate when compared against geometric, binary, and learned direction-agnostic baselines.

</details>


### [306] [Policy-Calibrated DAgger: Offline Calibrated Noise Injection for Imitation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30462)
*Jenny Wang,George Kantor*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Introduces Policy-Calibrated DAgger that uses a diffusion policy's predicted action distribution to estimate policy noise offline and guide learning, mitigating covariate shift without sweeping noise levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Imitation learning suffers from compounding errors due to distribution shift between training and deployment. Existing remedies (unsafe failure data collection or noise-hypothesis data collection) are costly or require tuning noise. A method leveraging offline noise estimation from the policy itself could reduce data collection burden.

Method: Estimate the policy's noise offline by analyzing the diffusion policy's action distribution along expert trajectories and its closed-loop error relative to recorded trajectories. Address multimodal action spaces by partial denoising to steer the policy toward the expert trajectory, then unnormalize the measured error using diffusion-model properties to reflect undirected guidance. Train with DAgger-like data augmented by this calibrated noise approach.

Result: Empirical evaluation in a cluttered 3D engine-lever task and a 2D planar reacher shows that Policy-Calibrated DAgger outperforms standard dataset aggregation without added noise and matches the best noisily-tuned baseline in hindsight, without performing a sweep over noise levels.

Conclusion: Offline, diffusion-informed noise calibration enables effective covariate shift mitigation in imitation learning, reducing data-collection burden while achieving competitive performance compared to optimal noisy demonstrations.

Abstract: Policies trained with imitation learning can accumulate errors over time, causing the robot to drift outside the training distribution. Existing methods mitigate this covariate shift by collecting additional data where the policy fails or is likely to fail. The first places the robot in unsafe conditions and the second requires choosing an appropriate noise distribution to collect new expert demonstrations under that noise. We propose Policy-Calibrated DAgger, a method that makes use of the properties of recent generative policies to estimate the policy's noise offline by using its own predicted action distribution. We measure a diffusion policy's spread of predicted actions at observations along the expert trajectory and measure its closed-loop error relative to a recorded trajectory. To address issues with measuring error in a multimodal action space, we guide the policy towards the trajectory during closed-loop control through partial denoising, and use properties of a diffusion model to unnormalize the measured error as if we did not guide it. We experiment in a scenario where a robot is tasked to reach an engine lever in a cluttered and narrow environment and show results in a 3D photorealistic simulator and a 2D planar reacher environment. We show that our method surpasses policies trained with dataset aggregation without noising and matches the performance of the best noise level in hindsight, without requiring a sweep over noise levels.

</details>


### [307] [Learning-Based Pressure Predictive Control of a Vertebraic Soft Robotic Tail](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30479)
*Wenjian Yang,Nan Huang,Yukang Nie,Fang Chen,Wanchao Chi,Jiansheng Dai,Sicong Liu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: LSTM-based PPC improves control and coordination of a vertebraic soft robotic tail with a quadruped, achieving large RMSE reduction and faster computation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modeling soft robot kinematics is challenging due to continuum structure and nonlinear, especially during non-static motions; a data-driven predictive control could simplify control and enhance real-time performance.

Method: Develop LSTM-based pressure predictive control (PPC) comprising inverse Kinematics (IK), forward Kinematics (FK), and pressure compensation (P-comp) models; enable non-static and quasi-static motion control; train with predictive data for tail-quadruped coordination.

Result: Compared to IK-only, PPC reduces trajectory RMSE by 69.8%; in coordinated motions, predictive data training reduces computation time by 60.9% and enables next-moment action prediction; improved real-time responsiveness.

Conclusion: PPC offers a simple, effective approach to model soft tails for non-static and quasi-static control and enables safe interaction with environments in tail-quadruped systems.

Abstract: Soft robots have attracted much attention for their safe human-robot interaction and flexibility, but the typical continuum structure and nonlinear material behavior make the kinematics modelling complex, especially in non-static motions. In this work, we proposed an LSTM-based pressure predictive control (PPC) for the motion control of a vertebraic soft robotic tail and the coordination with a quadruped robot. The PPC consists of an inverse kinematics (IK) model, a forward kinematics (FK) model and a pressure compensation (P-comp) model, and achieves non-static and quasi-static motion control of the tail. Compared with the IK-only model, the average RMSE of the PPC's simulation trajectories reduces by 69.8%, when executing target trajectories. In the coordinated motions of the soft tail quadruped, using a prediction data set to train the PPC enables next-moment action prediction and reduces computation time by 60.9%, which enhances the real-time response of the tail to match the quadruped torso's moving rate. The PPC provides a simple and effective method to model the soft tail for both non-static and quasi-static motion control, and grants the soft tail quadruped with the functionality of interacting with the environment.

</details>


### [308] [Memory-Aware Multi-Sensor Perception for Efficient and Safe Navigation in Dynamic Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30495)
*Jingshuo Li,Yifan Xue,Yifei Li,Shubhodeep Shiv Aditya,Nadia Figueroa*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A memory-aware, multi-sensor navigation framework that combines LiDAR/RGB perception with online distance-field learning and a stage-adaptive MCBF-QP to persistently represent environment and navigate safely in unseen environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Perception-based navigation often depends on static maps or short-horizon data, underutilizing previously observed structure; persistent representation of static infrastructure and tracking dynamic obstacles can improve efficiency and safety during long-horizon navigation.

Method: Fuse LiDAR and RGB perception, learn online distance fields for environment representation, and use a stage-adaptive Modulated Control Barrier Function Quadratic Program to adapt safety constraints and guidance based on local conditions while maintaining a persistent memory of static geometry.

Result: Experiments in complex indoor and outdoor scenes show improved navigation efficiency and goal-reaching performance, with robust collision avoidance in narrow passages and around dynamic obstacles.

Conclusion: The framework enables more efficient, safe, long-horizon navigation by leveraging persistent geometric memory and adaptive safety constraints integrated into the control policy.

Abstract: Autonomous navigation in previously unseen environments requires effective perception, persistent environmental representation, and collision avoidance while maintaining progress toward a goal. Existing perception-based methods often rely on prior maps or short-horizon observations, limiting their ability to exploit previously observed structure. We propose a memory-aware multi-sensor navigation framework that integrates LiDAR and RGB perception, online distance-field representation learning, and a stage-adaptive Modulated Control Barrier Function Quadratic Program (MCBF-QP). The framework persistently represents static infrastructure while tracking dynamic obstacles, enabling the MCBF-QP controller to exploit previously observed geometry for obstacle circumvention and adapt its safety constraints and guidance to local conditions. Experiments in complex indoor and outdoor environments demonstrate improved navigation efficiency and goal-reaching performance while maintaining collision avoidance in narrow passages and around dynamic obstacles.

</details>


### [309] [Tactile Sensing Array for Multi-Phalanx Sensing in Humanoid Hands](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30506)
*Neel Adwani,Muhaiminul Islam Akash,Rituja Bhattacharya,Cong Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A low-cost, distributed tactile sensor array for a humanoid finger using Velostat on seven contact points (fingertip 2x3 matrix plus tip, and proximal/middle phalange lines). A 3D-printed compliant contact structure reduces recovery time by 74% vs a flush baseline. The sensor differentiates contact geometries (flat/edge/corner) and registers contact across all phalanges during grasp. Limitations include hysteresis; software compensation is proposed to address remaining hysteresis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision and proprioception alone cannot provide reliable tactile feedback across the entire finger, especially when self-occlusion by the hand blocks the camera view. A distributed, low-cost tactile array aims to enable robust grasping and manipulation in humanoid hands.

Method: Fabrication of a Velostat-based tactile array on a humanoid finger with seven contact points: a 2x3 contact matrix across the fingertip faces (front, left, right) and a separate tip contact; single front-facing contact lines on the proximal and middle phalanges. Evaluation includes hysteresis and recovery time through repeated loading and release cycles. A 3D-printed compliant contact structure with a gap and a bump is tested against a flush-contact baseline. Additional tests measure activation patterns for different contact geometries (flat, edge, corner) and detect contact across all phalanges during grasp. Discussion includes fabrication limits and potential software-based compensation for residual hysteresis.

Result: The compliant 3D-printed structure reduces recovery time by 74% relative to the flush baseline. The sensor yields distinct activation patterns for different fingertip contact geometries and detects contact across all phalanges during grasp, demonstrating effective distributed tactile sensing. Hysteresis remains a concern, but the authors suggest software compensation as a promising mitigation route.

Conclusion: A low-cost, distributed tactile sensing solution for humanoid fingers is demonstrated, enabling geometry-dependent tactile signatures and multi-phalange contact sensing. While hysteresis limits persist, the work identifies practical fabrication improvements and points to software-based compensation as a viable path to further performance gains.

Abstract: Humanoid hands require tactile feedback across the whole finger, not just the fingertip, to grasp and manipulate objects properly. Vision and proprioception alone cannot reliably provide this information, particularly when the hand's own fingers occlude the camera's view of the grasp. We present a low-cost tactile array for a humanoid finger, made from Velostat and conductive tape. The fingertip carries seven contact points including a 2x3 matrix wrapped across its front, left, and right faces, and a separate contact point at the tip. The proximal and middle phalanges each carry a single front-facing contact line. We measure the sensor's hysteresis and recovery time after release, through repeated loading and press-release tests. We also test a compliant, 3D-printed contact structure with a gap and a bump, inspired by similar designs in prior work, and show it cuts recovery time by 74% compared to a flush-contact baseline. We then show the sensor can produce distinct activation patterns for different contact geometries (flat, edge, corner) at the fingertip, and that it registers contact across all three phalanges during a grip. Finally, we discuss the limits of our fabrication changes and point to software-based compensation as a promising way to more directly fix the remaining hysteresis in the future.

</details>


### [310] [Aerial Manipulation in the Wild with Onboard Perception, Policy Learning, and Whole-Body Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30521)
*Yuanzhu Zhan,Yufei Jiang,Zemu Zhang,Junyi Geng*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A real-world outdoor aerial manipulation framework combining imitation learning, onboard LiDAR–inertial state estimation, and whole-body MPC to perform robust end-effector manipulation without external motion capture; validated on a physical aerial manipulator.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Outdoor aerial manipulation faces challenges in reliable state estimation, stable flight, and precise manipulation under disturbances, exacerbated by the lack of external motion capture infrastructure.

Method: Train a Diffusion Policy from manipulation demonstrations to generate end-effector commands from onboard observations; execute commands via a whole-body model predictive controller that jointly coordinates the aerial platform and manipulator; use onboard LiDAR–inertial odometry for state estimation during outdoor operation.

Result: Demonstrated successful outdoor manipulation on a physical aerial manipulator; shows that demonstration-driven policies can be effectively integrated with onboard state estimation and model-based whole-body control to extend aerial manipulation beyond indoor environments.

Conclusion: The work validates the viability of integrating imitation-learning-based end-effector policies with onboard state estimation and whole-body MPC for outdoor aerial manipulation, reducing reliance on external motion capture and enabling real-world deployment.

Abstract: Aerial manipulation in outdoor environments remains challenging due to the simultaneous requirements of reliable state estimation, stable aerial motion, and precise manipulation under external disturbances. In this work, we present a real-world outdoor aerial manipulation framework that integrates imitation learning, onboard LiDAR-inertial state estimation, and whole-body model predictive control. A Diffusion Policy is trained from manipulation demonstrations to generate desired end-effector motions from onboard observations. These learned commands are executed by a whole-body MPC that jointly coordinates the aerial platform and manipulator to realize the desired end-effector trajectory. To eliminate reliance on external motion-capture infrastructure, the platform employs onboard LiDAR-inertial odometry for state estimation during outdoor operation. We validate the complete framework on a physical aerial manipulator and demonstrate successful execution of outdoor manipulation tasks. The experimental results show that demonstration-driven manipulation policies can be effectively integrated with onboard state estimation and model-based whole-body control to enable aerial manipulation beyond controlled indoor environments.

</details>


### [311] [Containing Behavioral Cascades from Manipulated Claims in LLM-Powered Multi-Robot Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30523)
*Waleed Bin Khalid,Byung-Cheol Min*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: An active verification framework (Verify-Adapt-Hold) mitigates semantic manipulation in LLM-powered multi-robot systems by containing cascades through selective inspection, provisional adaptation, and trusted planning; evaluated on false obstacle injections showing reduced cascade, cost, makespan, and improved coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semantic manipulation of LLM-based fleets can trigger fleet-wide inefficiencies and unsafe behaviors. Binary trust decisions are insufficient; a proactive, team-level planning approach is needed to bound downstream effects.

Method: Propose a Verify-Adapt-Hold plan: a verification module selects regions of consequence for inspection by certain robots, a limited subset provisionally adapts as needed, and remaining robots retain trusted plans. Evaluation in a multi-robot transportation setting with injected false obstacle claims across varying impact levels and team sizes; metrics include cascade containment, Sum-of-Costs, makespan, and coverage ratio.

Result: Treating post-compromise verification as a team-level planning problem constrains cascading physical consequences more effectively than binary trust decisions, demonstrated across different manipulation impacts and team sizes.

Conclusion: Active, fleet-level verification can robustly bound downstream effects of semantic manipulation in LLM-powered multi-robot systems, enabling safer and more efficient coordinated operation.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-powered multi-robot systems are vulnerable to semantic manipulation: an accepted false world-state claim can trigger a fleet-wide behavioral cascade, causing unnecessary replanning, increased path costs, congestion, or apparent mission infeasibility. Conditioning on a successful manipulation, we propose an active verification framework that contains its downstream effects before they propagate across the fleet. A dedicated verification module generates a structured Verify-Adapt-Hold plan: selected robots inspect consequential regions, a limited subset provisionally adapts when necessary, and the remaining robots retain their trusted plans. We evaluate the framework in a multi-robot transportation environment using injected false obstacle claims across different impacts and team sizes. Evaluation measures cascade containment, Sum-of-Costs, makespan, and coverage ratio. Results show that treating post-compromise verification as a team-level planning problem, rather than a binary trust decision, effectively limits the cascading physical consequences of semantic manipulation.

</details>


### [312] [A Long-Legged, Direct-Drive Monopedal Robot Achieves Exceptional Jump Height](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30530)
*Gihyeok Na,Justin K. Yim*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: High-jump, spring-free, electrically actuated robot with a single long leg achieves 7.6 m jumps at 281 g using a fabric-wrap, variable-transmission and a top-station attitude-control module with micro-propellers; validated outdoors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explore high-performance jumping without elastic energy storage by combining direct-drive actuation with a variable mechanical advantage transmission and active attitude/orientation control to enhance stability and jump capability.

Method: Design a single long leg driven by a direct-drive motor via a fabric-wrap transmission providing variable mechanical advantage; brace the leg to resist buckling; add a top balancing module with small propellers to control leg orientation on the ground and in flight; validate through outdoor experiments including vertical jumps, attitude control on ground and in air, and tilted jumps.

Result: Achieves 7.6 m jump height with 281 g prototype and 190 ms stance time; the highest jump reported for an electrically actuated, spring-free system; outdoor validation of vertical jumps, attitude control, and tilted jumps.

Conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of high, controlled jumps in spring-free, electrically actuated robots by integrating variable-transmission actuation with active attitude control, enabling stable, large-magnitude jumps with a long leg and minimal energy storage.

Abstract: We demonstrate a jumping robot that reaches high (7.6 m) and fast (190 ms stance time) jumps from a single long leg driven by a direct-drive transmission, without elastic energy storage. At 281 g, it achieves the highest jump yet reported for an electrically actuated, spring-free system. The leg uses a new fabric-wrap transmission that provides a variable mechanical advantage, keeping a small electric motor near its peak power output through the stroke while bracing the long, lightweight leg against buckling. A balancing module at the top of the leg uses small propellers to control the leg's orientation on the ground and in the air, where the long leg provides a large moment arm for the control torques. The robot is validated outdoors with vertical jumps, attitude control on the ground and in flight, and tilted jumps.

</details>


### [313] [ST-pRRTC: Parallel Space-Time RRT-C with Adaptive Goal-Time Forests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30533)
*Duo Zhang,Jintong Li,Junshan Huang,Jingjin Yu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A GPU-accelerated, space-time RRT-Connect variant (ST-pRRTC) for dynamic environments with known obstacle trajectories; uses a shared forward tree and an adaptive backward-time forest with interval root sampling to achieve probabilistic completeness and asymptotic arrival-time optimality in bounded time, plus a practical root-recycling variant; experimentally faster and earlier arrivals than ST-RRT* and SI-RRT, including real-robot demos.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable efficient motion planning in dynamic environments with moving obstacles and unconstrained arrival times, leveraging GPU parallelism and a flexible temporal expansion strategy while preserving theoretical guarantees.

Method: ST-pRRTC builds a shared forward tree and an adaptive forest of backward goal-time trees. It uses an interval root formulation to sample goal arrival times continuously, achieving probabilistic completeness and asymptotic arrival-time optimality under a bounded time domain. A root recycling policy maintains progress with a fixed number of backward trees, trading guarantees for practicality. Extensive experiments compare variants against ST-RRT* and SI-RRT; real-robot demonstrations validate feasibility.

Result: Both ST-pRRTC variants reduce mean first-solution time and shorten mean final arrival times relative to ST-RRT* and SI-RRT on problems solvable by all methods. Root recycling improves performance over broad arrival-time ranges. Real-robot tests show planning motions for a UR5e navigating among moving Crazyflie drones.

Conclusion: ST-pRRTC provides theoretically grounded, GPU-accelerated motion planning in dynamic environments with known obstacle trajectories and uncertain arrival time, offering faster planning and earlier arrivals than strong baselines; a practical root-recycling variant enhances applicability when strict guarantees are relaxed.

Abstract: We propose ST-pRRTC, a GPU-parallel space- time RRT-Connect motion planner for problems with known obstacle trajectories and unspecified arrival time. Searching over many arrival times broadens temporal coverage but divides a finite planning budget among more backward trees. To address the challenge, ST-pRRTC builds a shared forward tree and an adaptive forest of backward goal-time trees. Its interval root formulation samples goal arrival times continuously and guarantees probabilistic completeness and asymptotic arrival- time optimality under the stated assumptions in a bounded time domain. The practical root recycling policy has no such guar- antees. It adapts a fixed number of backward trees, replacing later roots while retaining useful search progress. Experiments on three dynamic benchmarks show that both variants achieve lower mean first-solution times and earlier mean final arrivals than ST-RRT* and SI-RRT on problems solved by all compared methods. Further experiments demonstrate the benefit of recy- cling over broad arrival-time ranges. Real-robot demonstrations show root-recycling ST-pRRTC planning motions for a UR5e among moving Crazyflie quadrotors.

</details>


### [314] [GraspTwin: Zero-Shot Task-Oriented Grasp Optimization via a Digital Twin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30543)
*Daniel J. Evans,Yinlong Dai,Simon Stepputtis,Dylan P. Losey*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A real-to-sim-to-real framework (GraspTwin) uses foundation-models to propose task-aligned grasps, refined by Bayesian optimization and physics rollouts for robust, zero-shot task-oriented grasping in homes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robots in homes must grasp objects with task intent (e.g., grasp mug by handle for pouring). Prior work either ignores task context or lacks physical grounding; a method that combines semantic task priors with physically plausible optimization is needed.

Method: From a single RGB-D observation, construct a digital twin of the scene, query a large foundation model for grasps aligned with object affordances and the task, then treat these proposals as semantic priors and optimize via Bayesian optimization with Thompson sampling to sample nearby poses. Evaluate candidates in parallel through domain-randomized physics rollouts and execute the best feasible grasp on the real robot.

Result: Zero-shot real-world transfer completes in minutes and improves task-oriented grasping success by up to 33% over state-of-the-art pipelines.

Conclusion: The approach effectively bridges semantic task grounding and physical feasibility in a real-to-sim-to-real loop, enabling fast, task-aware, robust grasps with publicly released code.

Abstract: As robots transition from structured factory settings into homes, they are required to interact with an ever-increasing variety of objects. Many tasks require grasping, and often it is not sufficient to just pick up the target object. Consider a task like "pouring coffee" --- to facilitate the subsequent pouring, the robot should grasp the mug by its handle. Existing learning-based approaches for grasping either find robust and collision-free grasps that are largely agnostic to the task (e.g., picking up the mug by its rim), or leverage foundation models to propose task-appropriate grasp locations that lack fine-grained physical grounding (e.g., reaching for and missing the handle). In this work, we bridge these approaches with a real-to-sim-to-real framework. Based on a single RGB-D observation, we construct a digital twin of the environment, query a large foundation model to propose grasps that align with the object's affordances and task description, and then optimize the proposals to ensure robustness and plausibility before executing the result on the real robot. Our key insight is that the grasp proposals of the foundation model should be regarded as semantic priors that serve as seeds for local, gradient-free optimization. We leverage Bayesian optimization with Thompson sampling to draw batches of nearby poses, which are subsequently evaluated in parallel under domain-randomized physics rollouts. The resulting grasp is both task-oriented and physically feasible for execution by the robot arm. Our full zero-shot real-world transfer only takes a few minutes and improves task-oriented grasping success by up to 33% as compared to other state-of-the-art pipelines. Our code is available here: https://github.com/VT-Collab/GraspTwin/

</details>


### [315] [Privacy-Preserving Prompted Policy Search for Robotic Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30554)
*Ali Irshayyid,Feng Lin,Chong Li,Jun Chen*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: PP-ProPS introduces privacy-preserving prompts for LLM-guided policy search in RL by encoding policy parameters and rewards client-side, keeping raw data hidden from the LLM provider. It also adds per-component reward feedback and a bounded history to improve search, enabling open-weight LLM use. Empirically, it outperforms Vanilla ProPS on 7/10 tasks and outperforms several standard RL methods on 5/6 tasks across MuJoCo, classic control, highway driving, and robotic manipulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Protect proprietary optimization strategies and confidential data when leveraging cloud-based LLMs for in-context policy search; avoid disclosing true optimal returns; enable use of open-weight LLMs; improve feedback granularity and prompt efficiency.

Method: Client-side secret transformations encode policy parameters and reward values before API transmission; the LLM observes encoded policy parameters and scaled rewards rather than raw data; provides individual reward components instead of only total return; uses a bounded history to cap prompt size; does not require disclosure of the true optimal episodic return; applicable to both continuous and discrete control tasks.

Result: PP-ProPS outperforms Vanilla ProPS in 7 of 10 tasks and surpasses conventional RL methods (PPO, SAC, TRPO) in 5 of 6 tasks, evaluated on MuJoCo locomotion, classic control, highway driving, and robotic arm manipulation.

Conclusion: A privacy-preserving, information-rich, and history-bounded LLM-guided policy search framework is feasible and beneficial, enabling confidential optimization while maintaining competitive or superior performance compared with strong RL baselines; future work may address security of transformations, scalability, and broader task domains.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated promising capabilities as in-context policy optimizers for Reinforcement Learning (RL), enabling policy search driven by both numerical reward signals and natural language reasoning. However, deploying such methods in practice requires transmitting raw policy parameters and rewards history to cloud-based LLM APIs, exposing proprietary control strategies to third-party service providers. To address this issue, this paper introduces Privacy-Preserving Prompted Policy Search (PP-ProPS), a framework that enables LLM-guided policy optimization while keeping policy and environmental parameters confidential. PP-ProPS encodes policy parameters and reward values using secret client-side transformations before they are included in each API request, ensuring that the LLM provider observes only encoded policy parameters and scaled reward information. Furthermore, unlike Vanilla ProPS, the proposed framework does not require the true optimal episodic return to be known or disclosed to the LLM. Beyond protecting the optimization data, PP-ProPS improves the search process in two ways. First, it provides the LLM with individual reward components instead of only a single total return, offering more informative feedback about each candidate policy. Second, it uses a bounded history that prevents the prompt from growing indefinitely, improving search with high-dimensional policies and supporting the use of open-weight LLMs. The proposed PP-ProPS is evaluated on both continuous and discrete control problems spanning Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact (MuJoCo) locomotion, classic control, highway driving, and robotic arm manipulation. Compared to Vanilla ProPS, the proposed PP-ProPS outperforms ProPS in seven of the ten evaluated tasks, and surpasses conventional RL methods including PPO, SAC, and TRPO, in five of the six tasks.

</details>


### [316] [Auditing Latent-Space Monitors for Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30557)
*Nikhil Kamalkumar Advani,Vishwajeet Shivaji Hogale,Saurav Kumar*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Post-hoc probes on internal representations can predict frame-level failures in autonomous driving tasks, but latent access may not outperform observable inputs/outputs; results show AUROC improvements on LaneSegNet and VAD, yet baseline non-latent performance is strong; authors propose an evaluation protocol to test incremental latent value and release failure endpoint labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether access to a model's internal representations provides predictive power for runtime failure monitoring beyond traditional inputs and outputs, and whether latent features add value.

Method: Train supervised probes on latent features from LaneSegNet and VAD to predict per-frame failures (Chamfer error for LaneSegNet; mean-ADE for VAD). Compare against baselines using only model predictions/inputs. Report AUROC across multiple endpoints and release per-frame failure endpoint labels; propose an evaluation protocol for latent-value assessment.

Result: Latent probes achieve AUROC 0.780 for LaneSegNet high Chamfer error; AUROC 0.868 for VAD mean-ADE failure. Non-latent baselines reach AUROC 0.825 (LaneSegNet) and 0.924 (VAD) on mean-ADE. Adding latent features yields no statistically detectable improvement. Findings hold across various planning-failure endpoints, including geometry-dependent labels inaccessible to non-latent baselines.

Conclusion: Informant representations do not automatically confer additional predictive value beyond observable inputs/outputs for per-frame failure monitoring. The authors propose an evaluation protocol to test incremental latent value and release per-frame failure endpoint labels.

Abstract: Runtime failure monitors can use a model's internal representations to anticipate failures. We audit this monitoring strategy across two autonomous-driving tasks: online vectorized map generation with LaneSegNet and end-to-end planning with VAD. We find that frame-level errors are predictable at inference in both tasks.
