For LaneSegNet, a supervised latent probe reaches Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC) 0.780 for high Chamfer error; to our knowledge, this is the first post-hoc frame-level failure monitor for online vectorized map generation. For VAD, a supervised planning-latent probe reaches AUROC 0.868 for mean-ADE failure.
  Our audit shows that internal access is not necessary for strong failure prediction. A monitor using only LaneSegNet's prediction outputs reaches AUROC 0.825, while for VAD, ego state, driving command, and the planner's predicted trajectory reach 0.924 on the same mean-ADE endpoint. Adding latent features to either baseline yields no statistically resolved improvement. This observation persists across a broad suite of planning failure endpoints, including endpoints whose labels depend on geometry unavailable to the non-latent baseline. Thus, predicting failure from an internal representation does not establish that the representation provides useful information beyond observable inputs and outputs. We propose an evaluation protocol for testing the incremental value of latent access and release our per-frame failure endpoint labels.

</details>


### [317] [SoGuDiff: Socially Guided Diffusion for Steerable, Norm-Grounded Robot Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30560)
*Christian Schaible,Haoran Ji,Yash Vardhan Pant,Stephen L. Smith*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Diffusion-based navigation with tunable social style; continuous style axes; feasibility layer; beats fixed baselines; validated in real-world demos.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable runtime adjustment of social conventions in robot navigation to accommodate contextual/cultural variations and deployment constraints.

Method: Diffusion-based planner with continuous, composable social style axes; separation of learned social behavior from kinematic feasibility and collision avoidance via a feasibility projection layer; demonstrates via a single-axis sweep and real-world demonstrations.

Result: Trade-off curve from the single-axis sweep strictly dominates evaluated fixed-behavior baselines; stylistic differences reproduced in real-world robot demonstrations.

Conclusion: Continuous, composable social style control in diffusion-based navigation yields more adaptable and deployment-friendly behavior than traditional single-policy approaches.

Abstract: Beyond collision avoidance, socially competent robot navigation requires adherence to implicit social conventions that vary across contexts, cultures, and deployment requirements. Many conventional navigation policies learn a single normative behavior, either through reinforcement learning against a fixed reward function or imitation of human demonstrations, exposing no interface for adjusting that conduct at runtime. We present a diffusion-based navigation framework whose social behavior can be tuned at deployment: a desired style is specified, such as how closely the robot passes, which side it yields to, or how much it defers to groups, and the planner adapts accordingly. Continuous style axes can be followed independently or composed, spanning a behavioral space rather than discrete, primitive-based specifications. A feasibility projection layer separates learned social behavior from kinematic feasibility and collision avoidance. A single-axis sweep illustrates a tradeoff curve that strictly dominates the evaluated fixed-behavior baseline configurations, and stylistic differences are replicated in real-world demonstrations.

</details>


### [318] [MOCHA: Multi-Objective Co-Design using Hypernetwork Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30570)
*Varun Madabushi,Neil Janwani,Maegan Tucker*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: MOCHA introduces a reinforcement learning framework that uses a multi-objective design hypernetwork (MDH) to generate design-conditioned policy networks, enabling a single model to represent Pareto-optimal design-policy families, derive Design Pareto sets via evolutionary search, and compute generalist designs across objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficiently represent and compute Pareto-optimal policies across robot design spaces and multiple objectives with a single learned model, reducing search complexity and enabling rapid design-policy provisioning.

Method: Train a hypernetwork that outputs specialized policy network parameters conditioned on a robot design vector and objective priorities, forming a multi-objective design hypernetwork (MDH). Demonstrate on two robot morphologies with six design dimensions and 2–3 objectives. Use evolutionary search over the learned policy to assemble the Design Pareto set for different objective weightings, and derive generalist designs by maximizing cumulative performance across objectives.

Result: MDHs can represent a complex family of design-dependent strategies across two morphologies and multiple objectives. The approach enables efficient generation of Design Pareto sets and computation of generalist designs that perform well across the objective spectrum.

Conclusion: MDHs enable a scalable, single-network solution for multi-objective robotics design, producing design-conditioned policies, pareto-front representations, and robust generalist designs, with potential broad applicability to design optimization in RL-driven robotics.

Abstract: In this work, we present MOCHA, the first, to our knowledge, reinforcement learning based approach to computing a family of Pareto-optimal policies across the design space of a robot using a single network. Specifically, MOCHA leverages the hypernetwork architecture to learn a network that produces specialized network parameters optimized for a given objective and parameterized robot design; we term this a multi-objective design hypernetwork (MDH). We demonstrate the capabilities of MDHs to represent a complex family of design-dependent strategies on two distinct robot morphologies, each with six design dimensions and across 2-3 objectives. Moreover, we propose an approach for efficiently producing a Design Pareto set using evolutionary search of the learned policy network, generating the optimal design-policy combination for each objective prioritization. Lastly, we provide an efficient method for computing generalist robot designs which achieve the best cumulative performance across the entire set of objectives.

</details>


### [319] [HuGo: LLMs as Whole-Body Policy Code Designers for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30594)
*Seoyeon Choi,Shizhao Ye,Nicholas Bui,Aayushi Shrivastava,Kanghyun Ryu,Dhruva Tirumala,Markus Wulfmeier,Negar Mehr*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: HuGo is a hierarchical loco-manipulation framework where an LLM generates executable high-level policy code atop a frozen low-level whole-body policy, refined via rollouts and video frames. It achieves strong sim performance and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without task-specific rewards or demonstrations, approaching demonstration-based baselines across five tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable scalable humanoid loco-manipulation across diverse tasks without per-task reward engineering or demonstration data; reduce the cost and complexity of training new task policies.

Method: Use an LLM to produce task-specific, closed-loop high-level policy code from a task description, observations, and commands, running on top of a fixed low-level policy. The policy is refined iteratively using numerical trajectory data and selected video frames to generate targeted code updates. Evaluate across five simulation tasks with two low-level policies; test zero-shot transfer to hardware and real-world refinement without expert demonstrations.

Result: HuGo substantially outperforms a high-level RL baseline and approaches a demonstration-based baseline across five simulation tasks, despite no task-specific reward design or demonstrations. The approach also demonstrates zero-shot transfer to hardware, with further improvements when refining real-world rollouts, without retraining policies or using demonstrations.

Conclusion: Hierarchical, LLM-driven generation of high-level loco-manipulation policies on top of a frozen low-level policy offers scalable, task-agnostic learning capable of strong sim performance and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, though performance may depend on LLM quality and low-level policy effectiveness.

Abstract: For humanoids to be useful in everyday environments, they must perform a wide range of tasks that couple locomotion and manipulation. Existing approaches commonly acquire a loco-manipulation policy through reward engineering or demonstrations followed by task-specific training, making it costly to scale to new tasks. In this work, we propose a hierarchical approach to humanoid loco-manipulation that eliminates these per-task requirements. HuGo, Humanoid policy code Generation, uses a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate executable, closed-loop high-level policy code from a task description on top of a frozen low-level whole-body policy. Given the task, observation, and command specifications, the LLM constructs the task logic in code. HuGo then refines the policy from its rollouts using numerical trajectories and selected video frames to produce feedback and targeted code updates. Across five simulation tasks, using two different low-level policies, HuGo substantially outperforms a high-level reinforcement learning baseline and approaches the performance of a demonstration-based baseline. We achieve this level of performance without task-specific reward design or demonstration collection. We further demonstrate zero-shot transfer of simulation-generated policies to hardware and show that applying the same refinement loop to real-world rollouts can further improve transfer performance without expert demonstrations or policy retraining. Project website is https://iconlab.negarmehr.com/HuGo/

</details>


### [320] [Learning-Accelerated Narrow-Phase Collision Detection via Check Ordering for Sampling-Based Motion Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30599)
*Hao Jiang,Yinghan Wang,Jianping He,Xiaoming Duan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A learning-based approach optimizes the narrow-phase check order in phase-based collision detection by predicting per-pair collision probabilities with a hypernetwork to minimize expected check time, yielding faster collision checks and improved sampling-based planner performance in cluttered scenes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Collision detection is a major computational bottleneck in motion planning. Phase-based methods reduce work via broad-phase pruning, but the narrow phase is often processed in a fixed order, which is suboptimal in cluttered environments where many pairs remain and dominate runtime.

Method: Formulate the expected time cost of the narrow phase and derive an optimal check-ordering criterion. Since priors are hard to obtain, train a hypernetwork to predict collision probabilities for object pairs and use these probabilities to approximate the optimal check order. Execute exact mesh checks in the resulting order without changing the underlying collision checker.

Result: Simulation results show that the proposed method accelerates phase-based collision detection and improves the efficiency and success rate of sampling-based motion planning, especially in cluttered environments.

Conclusion: The learned check-ordering approach reduces collision-detection time without altering the geometric collision checker, offering practical gains for planners in cluttered scenes; effectiveness hinges on accurate probability predictions and integration with existing broad/narrow-phase workflows.

Abstract: Collision detection is critical for ensuring the safety of planned paths. However, it imposes a non-negligible computational burden on motion planners, motivating extensive studies on collision-detection acceleration. In commonly used phase-based collision-detection methods, the broad phase employs hierarchical structures to rapidly discard object pairs that are clearly collision-free, while the subsequent narrow phase performs detailed collision checks on the remaining object pairs whose collision status cannot be determined by the broad phase. Although these methods effectively reduce the number of detailed checks through broad-phase pruning, the narrow phase is usually executed in the default order returned by the broad phase, with little explicit optimization of the check order. This leaves room for further acceleration, especially in cluttered environments where many object pairs may remain after the broad phase and the narrow phase can account for a significant portion of the total detection time. In this work, we propose a learning-based method to accelerate phase-based collision detection by optimizing the check order in the narrow phase. We first formulate the expected time cost of the narrow phase and derive an optimal check-ordering criterion that minimizes this expectation. Since the priors required by this criterion are difficult to obtain in advance, we design a hypernetwork-based model to predict collision probabilities, which are then used to approximate the optimal check order. The resulting order guides the execution of exact mesh checks in the narrow phase, thereby reducing detection time without replacing the underlying geometric collision checker. Simulation results show that our method effectively accelerates phase-based collision detection and improves the efficiency and success rate of sampling-based motion planning, especially in cluttered environments.

</details>


### [321] [Audit Before You Commit: Locating Belief Failures in Active Identification for One-Shot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30608)
*Mohamed Abouagour,Byung-Cheol Min*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Auditable separation of belief adequacy and failure scoring reveals where commit decisions fail; correcting a single observation-model error improves outcomes and uncovers execution-model issues across engines and tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand when to commit after a few probes for irreversible actions and diagnose which component governs misdecisions.

Method: Deploy a probe-then-commit pipeline (particle belief, scenario failure score, one commit) and audit offline with ground truth across simulated and physical tasks, using conformal calibration and cross-engine/task analysis to localize failures to observation vs execution models.

Result: In simulation, more taps sharpen belief; truth leaves support in 16.9% of episodes and failure score becomes optimistic by 0.31. Conformal calibration recovers coverage but not decision; audit points to observation-model error: a 2.1 mm tap-boundary error. Correcting it reduces failure from 0.354 to 0.112 and shifts unrefitted to a second engine; another engine reveals an execution-model mismatch. Across seven task families in three engines, a few probes at fixed executor reduce miss/failure. Physical-arm experiments reproduce the gain and audit signatures; replay under injected model error shows the audit signal on real data.

Conclusion: Separating belief and failure-model diagnostics enables targeted fixes (observation vs execution models) and validates the audit as a general tool across tasks and physical systems, with substantial impact from small model corrections.

Abstract: A robot that probes a few times before one irreversible action, such as tapping a surface before inserting a peg, must decide when the evidence is enough to commit. We argue that this decision rests on two conditions that existing methods do not separate: the belief must still cover the truth in the coordinate that decides the action, and the failure model that scores actions must track realized failure. We audit both conditions separately, offline and with ground truth, on a deployed probe-then-commit pipeline: a particle belief, a scenario failure score, and one commit. On simulated insertion, more taps sharpen the belief while the truth leaves its support on 16.9% of episodes and the failure score turns optimistic by 0.31. Conformal calibration restores coverage but not the decision: confidently wrong instances still pass a confidence gate. The audit's signatures instead point at the observation model, where a hand scan finds a 2.1 mm error in the tap boundary. Correcting that one number cuts failure from 0.354 to 0.112 on untouched instances and transfers unrefitted to a second engine, while in a third engine the same audit suggests an execution-model mismatch instead. Across seven task families in three engines, a few probes at a fixed executor reduce miss or failure. On a physical arm inserting a tool into a rigid pocket by touch, the gain and the audit's two conditions reproduce, and replaying the recorded taps under an injected model error shows the audit's signature on real data. Additional materials are available at https://sites.google.com/view/auditbeforeyoucommit.

</details>


### [322] [Frequency-Modulated Piezoelectric Haptic Display](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30626)
*Boyuan Liang,Lingfeng Sun,Masayoshi Tomizuka*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: FM haptic display using piezo actuators; introduces Shared-Source Frequency Modulation (SSFM) to drive many pixels from a single amplifier, encoding intensity via vibration frequency rather than amplitude; proof-of-concept shows feasible distributed haptic rendering for high-density wearables.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome scaling limits of amplitude-modulated (AM) haptic pixels, where per-pixel high-power amplification becomes bulky; enable compact, scalable driving for large-area wearable haptics.

Method: Apply frequency modulation to encode haptic intensity; develop SSFM where multiple haptic pixels share a common power amplifier while their vibration spectra are individually controlled; fabricate a proof-of-concept piezoelectric haptic display and evaluate spatial/temporal rendering via user tests.

Result: Participants reliably distinguished spatial and temporal patterns encoded through FM within the operating range; demonstrates feasibility of FM-based distributed haptic rendering and supports a path toward compact driving architectures for high-density wearables.

Conclusion: FM-based distributed haptic rendering is feasible and scalable; SSFM reduces per-pixel amplification needs, enabling compact driving architectures for future high-density, large-area wearable haptic displays.

Abstract: We present a frequency-modulated (FM) haptic display based on piezoelectric vibrating actuators. Existing haptic displays commonly encode haptic intensity through the deformation amplitude of individual haptic pixels. Although amplitude-modulated (AM) approaches have enabled compact haptic pixels, independently controlling the deformation amplitude of a large number of pixels can require increasingly complex and bulky driving systems, posing challenges for scaling toward high-density, large-area wearable displays. To address this scaling challenge, we investigate an FM design principle in which haptic intensity is encoded through vibration frequency. We further develop a \textit{Shared-Source Frequency Modulation} (SSFM) structure in which multiple haptic pixels are powered by a common power amplifier while their vibration spectrum are controlled individually, reducing the need for independent high-power amplification at each pixel. A proof-of-concept piezoelectric haptic display was built and evaluated on rendering spatial and temporal haptic patterns through volunteer tests. The results show that participants reliably distinguished spatial and temporal patterns encoded using FM principles within the investigated operating range. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of FM-based distributed haptic rendering and suggest a potential pathway toward more compact driving architectures for future high-density, large-area wearable haptic displays.

</details>


### [323] [MR. POP: Multi-Robot Parallel Optimizing Planner for Almost-Surely Asymptotically Optimal Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30644)
*Chih H. Huang,Roy Xing,Brian Plancher,Zachary Kingston*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GPU-driven, asymptotically optimal multi-robot planner MR. POP combines dRRT and AO-x to achieve 100% solve rate and faster performance (up to 35-DOF), while significantly improving downstream optimizer successes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scale probabilistically guaranteed multi-robot planning to practical problem sizes by leveraging GPU parallelism to overcome CPU-bound limitations and improve solvability across larger DOF counts.

Method: MR. POP uses large-scale SIMT GPU parallelism to run hundreds of roadmap construction and tree search iterations with parallel nearest-neighbor search and collision checking, built on the dRRT and AO-x meta-algorithm, producing high-quality diverse seeds for downstream optimizers.

Result: Achieves 100% solve rate in multi-robot planning tests up to 35-DOF and outperforms state-of-the-art a.s.a.o. planners on this scale; increases downstream motion optimizer success from about 4% to 72% by providing better seeds.

Conclusion: Demonstrates that GPU-based parallelism can deliver both probabilistic convergence guarantees and strong computational performance for multi-robot planning, enabling scalable planning with improved seed quality for downstream optimizers.

Abstract: Finding globally optimal paths remains a fundamental challenge in multi-robot motion planning. Despite acceleration of almost-surely asymptotically optimal (a.s.a.o.) planners via CPU-based parallelism, achieving both probabilistic convergence guarantees and strong computational performance, these algorithms still struggle to scale to multi-robot settings. As such, we introduce MR. POP, a GPU-based a.s.a.o. multi-robot planner based on dRRT and the AO-x meta-algorithm. MR. POP uses large-scale GPU-based SIMT-parallelism to simultaneously run hundreds of roadmap construction and tree search iterations with underlying parallel nearest neighbor search and collision checking operations. We show that this enables MR. POP to become the only planner achieving a 100% solve rate while being faster than state-of-the-art a.s.a.o. planners in multi-robot systems up to 35-DOF. MR. POP also raises the success rate of downstream motion optimizers (e.g., from 4% to 72%), by creating high-quality, diverse seeds that help avoid local minima.

</details>


### [324] [Can a Robot Read Braille? - Learning to Adapt Contact via Imitation Learning for Tactile Braille Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30676)
*Xi Chen,Yunlong Shan,Sihan Chen,Jun Hu,Zhongxuan Li,Shiyao Zhang,Sichao Liu,Zhong Zhao,Kosta Jovanovic,Peng Zhou*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: An adaptive-contact robotic Braille reader that actively establishes readable contact using Multi-Head Policy Learning; achieves high tactile quality and reconstruction across multiple plates, outperforming recognition-only approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To move beyond post-contact recognition by ensuring contact quality to read tactile Braille, addressing the gap where robots fail to establish readable contact.

Method: Adaptive-contact framework with contact quality assessment and physical correction; Multi-Head Policy Learning trained on expert demonstrations to learn contact acceptability and pose corrections; iterative contact re-establishment and pose-aware fusion for Braille reconstruction.

Result: Evaluated on 20 physical Braille plates (learning and evaluation) with ten online-evaluation plates; achieves 94.0% tactile quality and 88.6% tactile reconstruction on online plates.

Conclusion: Active contact establishment is crucial for reliable robotic Braille reading; leveraging adjustable contact and pose correction improves robustness beyond post-contact recognition.

Abstract: For people who are blind, touch provides an essen-tial channel for accessing written information through Braille. Bringing a similar capability to robots requires them not only to recognize tactile patterns, but also to actively establish physical contact that makes those patterns readable. Yet existing robotic Braille readers largely focus on recognition after contact, leaving contact establishment itself insufficiently addressed. We present an adaptive-contact framework for robotic tactile Braille reading that assesses contact quality and physically corrects unsuitable contact before recognition and reconstruc-tion. Multi-Head Policy Learning uses expert-guided contact-adjustment demonstrations to jointly learn contact acceptability and pose corrections. During deployment, the robot iteratively evaluates and re-establishes contact, retaining reliable tactile observations for pose-aware fusion and Braille reconstruction. Across 20 physical Braille plates used for learning and eval-uation, the proposed approach achieves 94.0% tactile quality and 88.6% tactile reconstruction on the ten online-evaluation plates. These results demonstrate the importance of actively establishing readable contact, rather than relying solely on recognition under imperfect tactile observations, for reliable robotic Braille reading.

</details>


### [325] [Multi-Objective Human-in-the-Loop Bayesian Optimization of a Lower-Limb Exoskeleton](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30695)
*Neil Janwani,Matthew T. Lerner,Aaron J. Young,Maegan Tucker*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: MO-HILBO extends explicit multi-objective Bayesian optimization to human-in-the-loop control, enabling personalized Pareto-optimal controllers for wearables; validated on a lower-limb exoskeleton with metabolic cost and comfort; code released as mohilo.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: HILO often optimizes a single objective or uses fixed objective weights, failing to capture time-varying, user-specific preferences over objectives.

Method: Employs explicit multi-objective Bayesian optimization to infer a personalized Pareto set; compares against an existing MO-HILO method; evaluates on a two-objective setup (metabolic cost, ordinal comfort) and validates Pareto ordering with trials; provides mohilo Python package.

Result: MO-HILBO identifies Pareto-optimal controllers and the Pareto-front point orderings align with validation trials; demonstrates feasibility of personalized, MO-HILO control for assistive devices.

Conclusion: MO-HILBO is an effective framework for user-preference-aware HILO in wearable devices and is readily usable via the mohilo package.

Abstract: Human-in-the-loop optimization (HILO) is a common approach for optimizing the control of assistive devices to account for the wearer's unique biomechanics and subjective preferences. However, despite research suggesting that a person may have a different prioritization of objectives depending on time-varying factors such as the environment, their mood, or energy levels, existing HILO approaches only consider a single objective or enforce a fixed weighting on a set of objectives. Neither approach is capable of representing an individual's preferences over objectives. In this work, we propose Multi-Objective Human-in-the-loop Bayesian Optimization (MO-HILBO), which builds on explicit multi-objective Bayesian optimization to efficiently infer a personalized set of Pareto-optimal controllers. We compare our approach with an existing multi-objective HILO method and experimentally demonstrate MO-HILBO on a lower-limb exoskeleton across two objectives: metabolic cost (efficiency) and ordinal human feedback (comfort). We find that MO-HILBO (1) discovers Pareto-optimal controllers, and (2) that the pairwise ordering of points on the Pareto front itself is consistent with validation trials. Lastly, we open-source mohilo, a Python package for running both HILO and MO-HILBO on wearable devices: https://dynamicmobility.github.io/mohilo/.

</details>


### [326] [Learning Vision-Based Agile Gap Traversal: Differentiable Simulation with a Warm-Started Critic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30696)
*Nuthasith Gerdpratoom,Tianchen Sun,Yichao Gao,Lin Zhao*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A two-stage RL framework for ego-centric visuomotor gap traversal using quasi-analytical policy gradients (QPG) and critic warm-starting. Stage 1 trains an expert actor/critic with privileged data; stage 2 trains a visual policy with binary gap masks while initializing its critic from stage 1, improving efficiency and generalization over backprop-through-time methods and non-warm-started critics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficiently learning high-DoF visuomotor policies for tight-gap traversal is challenging due to high computational/ memory costs of differentiable rendering and full BPTT, and poor sample efficiency of pure end-to-end methods. The goal is to leverage privileged information during training, reduce reliance on backprop through rendering, and enable fast transfer across drone platforms.

Method: A two-stage RL pipeline. Stage 1: train an expert actor/critic using privileged observations (including gap geometry) with quasi-analytical policy gradients in differentiable simulation; no requirement to reset along optimized reference trajectories. Stage 2: train a visual policy using binary gap masks from ego-centric cameras and low-dimensional observations, with its privileged critic warm-started from Stage 1. The framework avoids backprop through rendering, reduces computation, and improves sample efficiency. Generalization across platforms is enhanced since the expert policy is not retrained for parameter changes; the visual policy transfers to unseen gap shapes.

Result: According to the abstract, the approach yields substantially better training efficiency and traversal success compared with cold-started critics or full-rollout BPTT. Real-world experiments show robust gap traversal using online-rendered binary masks. The method also generalizes to unseen gap shapes and is claimed to be extendable to other visuomotor tasks, without retraining the expert actor when system parameters change.

Conclusion: The proposed two-stage QPG-based framework provides sample-efficient, computation-friendly training for ego-centric visuomotor gap traversal, with good real-world performance and cross-platform generalization. It offers a generic extension to other visuomotor robotics problems beyond gap traversal.

Abstract: Traversing narrow gaps is challenging for autonomous quadrotors, especially when control commands come directly from high-dimensional visual observations. Existing end-to-end methods often rely on behavior cloning or full-rollout backpropagation through time (BPTT) via differentiable simulation, which can limit policy performance or incur high training costs. We propose a two-stage reinforcement learning framework for more efficient ego-centric visuomotor gap-traversal policy training, leveraging quasi-analytical policy gradients (QPG) via differentiable simulation and critic warm-starting. The framework utilizes QPG to avoid backpropagation through visual rendering, reducing computation and memory costs while improving sample efficiency. In the first stage, an expert actor and critic are trained using privileged observations, including gap geometry. Unlike prior gap-traversal approaches, our training utilizing QPG does not require resetting the agent along optimized reference trajectories. In the second stage, a visual policy is trained using binary gap masks from two ego-centric cameras and low-dimensional observations, while its privileged critic is warm-started from the first stage. This substantially improves training efficiency and traversal success compared with cold-starting the critic or using full-rollout BPTT. Our framework does not require retraining the expert actor when system parameters change, enabling more efficient generalization across drone platforms than state-of-the-art visual gap-traversal methods based on action supervision. The learned visual policy also generalizes to gaps with unseen shapes. Extensive real-world experiments further demonstrate robust gap traversal using binary masks rendered online. Beyond gap traversal, the proposed framework is generic and can be extended to other visuomotor robot learning tasks.

</details>


### [327] [From Visual Search to Movement Control: A Priority Field for Artificial Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30704)
*Han Zhang,Zhong Cao*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A priority-map framework for movement control in artificial agents, extending vision search to action. Shows efficient learning and strong generalization in reach-avoid tasks; memory adds history-driven goal anticipation; suggests priority-based computation as a foundation for motor control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extend priority-based spatial attention models to movement control in artificial agents by building on an integrated priority map used for visual search and saccade data.

Method: 1) Develop a lightweight visual search model based on an integrated priority map, trained on human saccades. 2) Extend this by giving an artificial agent a priority field and test in a reach-avoid task with moving obstacles. 3) Compare against alternative architectures. 4) Add a simple memory mechanism to induce history-driven anticipation of future goal locations.

Result: The model reproduced oculomotor suppression and history-driven selection. Priority-field agents trained more efficiently and generalised better to unseen, complex scenarios, even from simple demonstrations. The memory mechanism produced human-like history-driven anticipation of the upcoming goal.

Conclusion: Priority-based computation is a promising foundation for movement control in artificial agents, enabling efficient learning, robust generalisation, and human-like anticipatory behavior.

Abstract: Human spatial attention is widely conceptualized as being guided by a priority map that integrates perceptual salience, current goals, and past experiences. Here, we extend priority-based computation to movement control in artificial agents. We first introduce a lightweight model of visual search based on an integrated priority map. Trained on human saccades, it reproduced key behavioral patterns, including oculomotor suppression and history-driven selection. Extending the search model, we equipped an artificial agent with a priority field and evaluated its performance in a reach-avoid task that required reaching a goal destination while avoiding moving obstacles. Compared with alternative architectures, priority-field agents trained more efficiently and performed better in unseen, complex scenarios, even from simple demonstrations. Adding a simple memory mechanism also produced human-like, history-driven effects in anticipating the likely location of the upcoming goal. These findings suggest that priority-based computation may provide a promising foundation for movement control in artificial agents.

</details>


### [328] [RoboMonitor: Label-Efficient Runtime Monitoring of Robot Task Execution via Predictive Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30715)
*Abhiroop Ajith,Gokul Narayanan,Kyle Coelho,Tingji Zhao,Yash Shahapurkar,Brian Zhu,Melih Erdogan,Ted Krubasik,Constantinos Chamzas,Eugen Solowjow*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: RoboMonitor is a label-efficient vision-language execution monitor for robot policies. It pre-trains on multi-camera robot trajectories with action-conditioned future-feature prediction, inverse dynamics, and masked-present prediction, then transfers to a causal monitor and applies Temporal SFT. It achieves high phase accuracy and macro recall on a four-task benchmark and succeeds in closed-loop trials in simulated and real settings, with no false recovery triggers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Execution monitoring for robot policies requires identifying the current phase, detecting failures, and recognizing completion from observations, but annotated data for monitoring are scarce in robot-policy datasets. A label-efficient, generalizable monitor is needed that can leverage existing policy data.

Method: Pre-train on 25 hours of multi-camera robot trajectories across 12 manipulation tasks and two embodiments using action-conditioned future-feature prediction, inverse dynamics, and masked-present prediction. Transfer learned visual and context encoders to a causal monitor and apply Temporal Supervised Fine-Tuning (Temporal SFT) that supervises across each observation window and enforces consistency within and across overlapping windows. Deployment uses only task instruction and camera observations.

Result: On a four-task monitoring benchmark, RoboMonitor with 52 labeled episodes achieves 93.1% mean phase accuracy and 85.9% macro recall over two fine-tuning seeds, outperforming Qwen3-VL and Robometer trained with the same supervision. Temporal SFT reduces mean spurious phase switching from 15.23% to 4.95% in ablation. In closed-loop deployment, the system completes 39/40 simulated Toolbox Sorting trials and 35/40 Reel Packing trials in the real world, with no false recovery triggers.

Conclusion: A label-efficient, transferrable vision-language monitor can deliver accurate execution phase estimation and robust closed-loop performance across multiple tasks and embodiments, with Temporal SFT providing notable reductions in spurious phase switching and improved consistency across observation windows.

Abstract: Learned robot policies produce actions, but their outputs alone do not establish whether execution is progressing as intended. Robot execution monitoring requires identifying the current execution phase, detecting failures, and recognizing task completion from observations available during execution. Training such monitors requires annotations that are scarce in datasets collected for robot-policy learning. We present RoboMonitor, a label-efficient vision--language execution monitor that learns from these datasets before introducing monitoring supervision. We pre-train on 25 hours of multi-camera trajectories spanning 12 manipulation tasks and two robot embodiments, using action-conditioned future-feature prediction, inverse dynamics, and masked-present prediction. We then transfer the learned visual and context encoders to a causal monitor and apply temporal supervised fine-tuning (Temporal SFT), which combines supervision throughout each observation window with consistency objectives within and across overlapping windows. At deployment, RoboMonitor requires only the task instruction and camera observations.
  On a four-task monitoring benchmark, RoboMonitor trained with 52 labeled episodes achieves 93.1% mean phase accuracy and 85.9% macro recall over two fine-tuning seeds, exceeding Qwen3-VL and Robometer trained with the same monitoring supervision. Its phase accuracy also exceeds that of both Qwen3-VL and Robometer trained with 100 episodes. A Qwen3-VL ablation shows that Temporal SFT reduces mean spurious phase switching from 15.23% to 4.95%. In closed-loop deployment, the integrated system completes 39 of 40 simulated Toolbox Sorting trials and 35 of 40 real-world Reel Packing trials, with no false recovery triggers observed.

</details>


### [329] [Praxis: Distilling Physical Interaction Priors from Egocentric Videos for Generalizable Whole-Body Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30735)
*Shuliang He,Ruiyan Xu,Bo Yue,Hengming Zhang,Huayi Zhou,Shuai Wang,Wei-Shi Zheng,Guiliang Liu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Praxis enables generalizable whole-body manipulation from a single demonstration by combining one-shot egocentric priors with online perception and tactile feedback across navigation, posture calibration, and dexterous manipulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learn dexterous, whole-body manipulation from minimal task-specific data by leveraging physical interaction priors from one-shot demonstrations and online re-grounding under varying object poses and contacts.

Method: Three-stage framework: vision-language guided navigation to target objects; closed-loop posture calibration to align the arm-hand workspace with the scene; and dexterous manipulation with synchronized upper- and lower-body control. Uses online visual feedback to re-ground the demonstrated interaction geometry and tactile feedback to adapt to contact conditions. Each skill is specified by a single human demonstration without retraining task-specific policies.

Result: Validated on five long-horizon manipulation tasks, demonstrating spatial, visual, and cross-object generalization and recovery from external disturbances across all stages.

Conclusion: Shows that robust, generalizable whole-body manipulation can be achieved from minimal demonstrations by integrating priors, perception, and tactile feedback without task-specific policy training.

Abstract: Mobile humanoid manipulation requires both reaching a usable workspace and preserving precise hand-object interactions as object poses and contact conditions change. Learning these behaviors from limited task-specific data remains challenging. To bridge this gap, we introduce Praxis, a whole-body manipulation framework that combines physical interaction priors from one-shot egocentric video demonstrations with closed-loop posture calibration and online perception. The framework coordinates three stages: vision-language-guided navigation toward target objects, closed-loop posture calibration to align the arm-hand workspace, and dexterous manipulation with synchronized upper- and lower-body control. Online visual feedback re-grounds demonstrated interaction geometry under new object poses and scene configurations, while tactile feedback adapts hand motions to actual contact conditions. Each manipulation skill is specified by one human demonstration, without task-specific manipulation-policy retraining. Experiments across five long-horizon manipulation tasks demonstrate spatial, visual, and cross-object generalization, as well as recovery from external physical disturbances across all three stages.

</details>


### [330] [Anatomy-Aware Dexterity-Driven Design Optimization of Surgical Continuum Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30745)
*Tony Qin,Peter Connor,Khoa Dang,Carter Hatch,Caleb Rucker,Robert J. Webster,Ron Alterovitz*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Introduces Reachable Volumetric Dexterous Solid Angle (RVDSA) as an objective for optimizing continuum robot design to maximize collision-free, multi-direction reachability within a goal volume, validated on a bimanual dexterous sheaths robot for colon polyp procedures with simulated annealing optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To design continuum robots that are highly dexterous within the constraints of human anatomy, requiring an objective that captures directional reachability and collision-free paths rather than simple coverage metrics.

Method: Define RVDSA as the set of directions from start configuration to the goal volume that yield collision-free, reachable points; compute this efficiently with a dedicated motion planner; optimize design using an asymptotically optimal simulated annealing algorithm; apply to a bimanual dexterous sheaths robot for colon cancer polyp procedures and compare against 3D voxel coverage objectives.

Result: Achieved on average 78% higher RVDSA than optimization focused solely on 3D voxel coverage, indicating improved dexterity distribution within the anatomical context.

Conclusion: RVDSA is an effective objective for geometry-to-anatomy design optimization of dexterous continuum robots, enabling substantial gains in reachability dexterity within target anatomies; supports future work on broader anatomical applications and real-time planning.

Abstract: Performing complex medical procedures with continuum robots requires careful selection of their geometric design parameters. The robot should have high dexterity in the specific anatomical environment of its procedure. This work presents a design optimization method that considers both dexterity and anatomy. We introduce the Reachable Volumetric Dexterous Solid Angle (RVDSA) metric as our objective, which measures the ability of a robot's end effector to reach the points in a goal volume from different directions via collision-free paths from a start configuration. We present a computationally efficient motion planner to compute this objective function for a given robotic design, and we use an asymptotically optimal simulated annealing optimizer to compute an optimized design. We applied our new method to optimize the design of a bimanual dexterous sheaths robot for performing procedures on cancerous polyps in colon anatomies, achieving a 78% higher RVDSA on average than optimizing for 3D voxel coverage alone.

</details>


### [331] [Design and Characterization of a Variable-Length Continuum Mechanism with Force Locking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30759)
*Katelyn King,Veronica Fish,Allison M. Okamura*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A rod-driven continuum helical mechanism achieving flexible-to-rigid behavior via force locking and antagonistic drive, with experimental validation of large bending range, low positioning error, and tunable stiffness (rod tension yields 0.56 stiffness gain).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Flexible continuum robots suffer from low stiffness in high-force tasks; a mechanism that combines dexterity with controllable stiffness would enable reliable manipulation under varying load.

Method: Design of a rod-driven continuum helical structure with antagonistic extension/contraction and force-locking to enable variable-length workspace and enhanced stiffness; experimental characterization of bending range, positional accuracy, and stiffness under force-locked and tensioned conditions.

Result: Demonstrated 180° bending range with average distal positioning error <10%; force locking improves axial stiffness and increases bending stiffness anisotropically; maximum bending stiffness aligns with load paths having large axial components; applying rod tension in the force-locked state yields additional stiffness tunability with a dimensionless gain of 0.56.

Conclusion: The proposed mechanism provides tunable stiffness and dexterity, enabling effective manipulation across flexible and rigid regimes; force locking and rod tension offer predictable stiffness control for high-force tasks.

Abstract: The utility of flexible continuum mechanisms for dexterous navigation is often impaired by their low stiffness, making them ineffective at manipulation in high-force scenarios. To address this challenge, we propose a novel continuum mechanism that achieves both flexible and rigid behavior by antagonistic extension and contraction of a rod-driven continuum helical structure. The helical design combines variable-length capacity with force locking for workspace and stiffness enhancement. In this article, we present the detailed design of the proposed mechanism and characterize its performance through experiments that quantify bending and stiffness. The results demonstrate 180 degree bending range of motion with an average distal positioning error of <10%. Further tests demonstrate that force locking directly improves axial stiffness and thus indirectly increases bending stiffness anisotropically, with maximum bending stiffness along load paths with a large axial component. Tensioning the driving rods provides additional stiffness tunability in the force-locked state, where increasing rod tension proportionally increases bending stiffness with a dimensionless gain of 0.56.

</details>


### [332] [NavGen: Visual Generative Models as a Scalable Data Engine for Embodied 3D Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30770)
*Xijie Huang,Yongyang Wan,Chengbin Dong,Zimo Ding,Mo Zhu,Yijin Wang,Zhiyang Liu,Fei Gao,Yuze Wu,Xin Zhou*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: NavGen uses a text-to-video generator to create ~400k diverse VLN episodes, with style-diversification to cover long-tail data; leads to improved UAV navigation models and 75% success in real-world tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the data bottleneck in embodied 3D navigation by leveraging high-fidelity generative models to synthesize scalable, diverse, and realistic vision-language navigation data, reducing reliance on costly real-world collection and mitigating the visual sim-to-real gap.

Method: 1) Build NavGen, a text-to-video data generation pipeline producing diverse indoor/outdoor VLN episodes. 2) Apply style-diversification to augment long-tail data. 3) Assemble ~400k episodes. 4) Evaluate against existing UAV navigation datasets across metrics. 5) Validate real-world transfer using a world-action-model paradigm on flying experiments. 6) Report 75% success in varied tasks/environments.

Result: The dataset, when scaled, improves model performance relative to training on existing datasets. The trained model achieves notable real-world performance, with 75% success across tasks/environments.

Conclusion: High-fidelity generative data can serve as a scalable engine for embodied 3D navigation, enabling better performance and real-world transfer; further work should address realism, bias, and domain gaps in synthetic-to-real transfer.

Abstract: General-purpose robot models increasingly rely on large and diverse datasets. For embodied 3D navigation, however, existing data sources face a fundamental trade-off: simulated data can be generated at scale but often suffer from the visual sim-to-real gap, whereas real-world flight data provide realistic observations but are costly to collect. This paper studies another direction: the use of high-fidelity visual generative models as scalable data engines for embodied 3D navigation. We introduce NavGen, a text-to-video data generation pipeline that produces diverse vision-language navigation (VLN) episodes across indoor and outdoor scenes. We also propose a style-diversification method that scales up long-tail data that are difficult and costly to collect. The resulting dataset contains approximately 400K navigation episodes. We evaluate our dataset against existing UAV navigation datasets across multiple metrics, and find that the model trained on our data generally improves with scale, outperforming those trained on existing datasets. To validate real-world transferability, we deploy the trained model in world-action-model paradigm to real-world flying experiments. The final model achieves a 75\% success rate across different navigation tasks and environments.

</details>


### [333] [Moving Horizon Estimation for Quadrotors: An $\mathcal{L}_1$ Adaptive Optimizer Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30777)
*Thinh Nguyen,Minkyung Kim,Sandeep Banik,Jinrae Kim,Naira Hovakimyan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Time-varying MHE solver using continuous-time Newton's method with L1 adaptive augmentation improves efficiency and accuracy over time-invariant solvers, as demonstrated on a quadrotor against EKF and standard MHE.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MHE offers higher accuracy than Kalman filters but is computationally intensive. Time-varying solvers can exploit problem evolution to reduce iterations. The L1 Adaptive Optimizer augmentation aims to counteract prediction inaccuracy from noisy sensors and limited system knowledge.

Method: Formulates a linear smoothing MHE as a dense QP. Develops a time-varying solver based on a continuous-time Newton method augmented with L1-AO. The solver tracks the optimal solution over time to reduce iterations. Evaluated in simulation on a quadrotor, comparing against EKF and standard MHE.

Result: The L1-AO augmented time-varying solver solves the MHE optimization more efficiently than the baseline time-invariant solver and achieves higher estimation accuracy under challenging conditions compared with EKF and standard MHE.

Conclusion: A time-varying, L1-AO-augmented MHE solver can enhance both computational efficiency and estimation accuracy in nonlinear, noisy sensing scenarios, with quadrotor experiments supporting the approach. This motivates broader adoption of temporal-solver strategies for MHE.

Abstract: Moving Horizon Estimation (MHE) is a state estimation method based on finite-horizon optimization that can offer higher accuracy at the cost of increased computation compared to Kalman filter-based approaches. We present a linear smoothing MHE formulation as a dense Quadratic Program (QP), and a solver consisting of a continuous-time Newton's method augmented with the $\mathcal{L}_1$ Adaptive Optimizer ($\mathcal{L}_1$-AO). While MHE is inherently time-varying, conventional approaches treat it as a sequence of independent, time-invariant problems and employ iterative solvers at each time step, which can be both inaccurate and computationally burdensome. In contrast, time-varying solvers track the optimal solution with fewer iterations by exploiting the temporal evolution of the problem, thereby reducing the computational load. In this research, we enhance both the performance and efficiency of MHE through a time-varying solver with an $\mathcal{L}_1$-AO augmentation that compensates for the prediction inaccuracy, which is common in practice due to noisy sensors and the lack of prior knowledge of the system. Simulation results on a quadrotor platform show that the $\mathcal{L}_1$-AO-augmented approach solves the MHE optimization problem more efficiently than the baseline time-invariant solver and achieves higher estimation accuracy under challenging conditions, compared with both the Extended Kalman Filter and the standard MHE.

</details>


### [334] [SeA-RVINS: Semantic-Aware Tightly Coupled RTK-Visual-Inertial System with Correlation-Preserving Robust Estimation for Urban Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30814)
*Wang Hu,Bo Wu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Robust, semantic-aware RTK-VINS for urban pose estimation that mitigates outliers in GNSS and visual data via dynamic covariance scaling and a hybrid ambiguity-continuation strategy; achieves sub-meter accuracy and full availability on challenging urban routes; open-source.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Urban localization suffers from multipath GNSS, false visual associations, and mis-timed data associations in tightly coupled estimators. A robust, semantically filtered fusion with flexible GNSS robustness is needed.

Method: Semantic-aware learned stereo frontend to filter unreliable visual tracks; Dynamic Covariance Scaling with double-differenced GNSS and configurable robust formulations; shared-pivot correlation; hybrid ambiguity-continuation sharing an ambiguity state across short arcs with verified continuity and random-walk links; fixed-lag factor-graph RTK-VINS; open-source.

Result: On a ~20 km TEX-CUP route with ~50% deep-urban driving, latent-pivot configuration yields 100% availability, 1.6 m max horizontal error; 96.16% of epochs <1 m; 99.90% <1.5 m.

Conclusion: Shows strong robustness and accuracy for urban pose estimation, validating the combination of semantic filtering, robust GNSS modeling, and ambiguity management within a fixed-lag RTK-VINS framework; implementation released as open-source.

Abstract: Reliable absolute pose estimation in urban environments is undermined by outlier measurements and incorrect temporal associations that can persist in tightly coupled estimators. Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) observations provide globally referenced measurements but are prone to multipath effects. Visual-inertial sensing supplies local motion constraints, but false visual associations can corrupt the estimator. We present SeA-RVINS, a fixed-lag factor-graph Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) visual-inertial system for robust urban pose estimation. A semantic-aware learned stereo frontend rejects unreliable tracks before persistent landmarks enter the graph. For double-differenced GNSS measurements, SeA-RVINS applies Dynamic Covariance Scaling through configurable batch, scalar, and latent-pivot robust formulations while retaining the shared-pivot correlation structure. We propose a hybrid ambiguity-continuation strategy that shares one ambiguity state over short arcs with verified continuity and softly links successive arcs through random-walk factors. On an approximately 20-km route from the public TEX-CUP dataset, including about 50\% deep-urban driving, the latent-pivot configuration achieves 100\% availability and a 1.6-m maximum horizontal error, with 96.16\% and 99.90\% of epochs below 1.0 and 1.5 m, respectively. The implementation is released as open-source software

</details>


### [335] [Evaluation Is All You Need for Multi-Modal Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30818)
*Zeyu He,Shiqi Liu,Ke Chen,Yun Yan,Jinzi Wu,Dianqiao Lei,Sirui Wang,ShuRui Peng,Tao Chen,Zhuo Huang,Yu Wu,Yadong Shao,Zhichao Li,Ke Sun,Yang Guan,Keqiang Li,Shengbo Eben Li*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: iDriveVLA introduces a unified trajectory evaluator and VLM-guided modulation to address generation-evaluation asymmetry in multi-modal planning for autonomous driving, coupled with a progressive training strategy; it sets a new SOTA at 94.95 PDMS on NAVSIM v1.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-modal planners show strong oracle performance yet fail to reliably select the best candidate due to generation-evaluation asymmetry. There is a need to both expand the candidate trajectory space and develop context-aware evaluation that aligns with human/expert judgments.

Method: A unified trajectory evaluator combining a Safety-aware Scorer (quality and risk estimation) and a VLM-guided Modulator for scene-adaptive criterion weighting; and an oracle-aligned progressive training pipeline with candidate imitation pretraining, candidate space refinement, and semantic ranking alignment.

Result: Achieves 94.95 PDMS on the NAVSIM v1 leaderboard, surpassing human-expert reference and establishing state-of-the-art performance.

Conclusion: The framework effectively broadens the candidate trajectory space while improving evaluation reliability, addressing the generation-evaluation gap and yielding superior performance in challenging, long-tail driving scenarios.

Abstract: Multi-modal planning is promising for autonomous driving by representing multiple plausible behaviors in ambiguous and long-tail scenarios. Existing methods mainly focus on improving trajectory multi-modality, enhancing trajectory representations, or reshaping the candidate distribution. Nevertheless, we identify a pronounced generation-evaluation asymmetry in multi-modal planning: despite strong oracle performance, existing planners often fail to reliably select the best available candidate, leaving substantial planning potential unrealized. To address this challenge, we propose iDriveVLA, a multi-modal planning framework that improves the candidate trajectory space while enabling more reliable and context-aware trajectory evaluation. Specifically, iDriveVLA introduces a unified trajectory evaluator comprising a Safety-aware Scorer for quality and risk estimation, together with a VLM-guided Modulator for scene-adaptive criterion weighting. We further develop an oracle-aligned progressive training strategy consisting of candidate imitation pretraining, candidate space refinement, and semantic ranking alignment. On the public NAVSIM v1 leaderboard, iDriveVLA achieves a new state-of-the-art performance of 94.95 PDMS, surpassing the human-expert reference.

</details>


### [336] [HIRE: History-Conditioned Interaction Reasoning and High-Rate Execution for Visually Aliased Precision Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30828)
*Rongji Li,Wenhao He,Cewu Lu,Xingyu Chen,Xu-Yao Zhang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: HIRE integrates history-conditioned reasoning with high-rate execution for history-dependent, contact-rich manipulation, using a two-component architecture (ISR and IME) with a cross-rate loop to leverage wrench history for improved disambiguation and precision, achieving ~90% completion across tasks; code release planned.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limitations of visual-only, history-agnostic policies in precision manipulation, where visually similar observations map to different latent states and small errors affect outcomes; integrate memory/force context and high-rate execution to enable reliable long-horizon planning under partial observability.

Method: Two-part framework: (1) ISR — history-conditioned Interaction-State Reasoner that encodes ordered wrench history with a temporal wrench encoder and a Force Perceiver to provide persistent physical evidence for state-consistent action generation; (2) IME — Interaction-Manifold Executor that structures contact-critical motion into intrinsic progress and transverse correction at a high rate; a cross-rate loop allows physical traces to inform subsequent reasoning.

Result: In real-robot experiments across surface, insertion, and rotational interactions, HIRE achieves at least 90% completion across all evaluated task stages, with improvements in interaction-state disambiguation, execution precision, and generalization.

Conclusion: HIRE provides a unified reasoning–execution perspective for precision manipulation under history-dependent partial observability, where physical interaction both realizes task intent and reveals latent-state evidence for future decisions; code will be released upon publication.

Abstract: Precision manipulation with contact-critical interactions is often history-dependent: visually similar observations can correspond to different latent interaction states and therefore require different actions, while small execution errors can alter task outcomes. Policies relying on the current visual observation alone cannot resolve such ambiguity; force-aware and memory-augmented methods enrich physical or temporal context, while reactive high-rate policies improve local contact response, yet long-horizon temporal reasoning and precision execution remain largely decoupled in existing methods, limiting reliable progression in visually aliased precision manipulation. To bridge this gap, we introduce History-Conditioned Interaction Reasoning and Execution (HIRE), a cross-rate framework comprising a history-conditioned Interaction-State Reasoner (ISR) and a high-rate Interaction-Manifold Executor (IME). ISR encodes ordered wrench history with a temporal wrench encoder and Force Perceiver as persistent physical evidence for state-consistent action generation, while IME structures contact-critical motion into intrinsic progress and transverse correction for precise execution; their cross-rate loop allows the resulting physical traces to inform subsequent reasoning. In real-robot experiments across surface, insertion, and rotational interactions, HIRE achieves at least 90% completion across all evaluated task stages while improving interaction-state disambiguation, execution precision, and generalization. More broadly, HIRE provides a unified reasoning--execution perspective on precision manipulation under history-dependent partial observability, where physical interaction both realizes task intent and reveals latent-state evidence for future decisions. Code will be released upon publication.

</details>


### [337] [Fast Plans, Faithful Actions: Closing the Planning-Execution Gap in Hierarchical Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30833)
*Chuanliang Xie,Boyu Ma,Gen Li,Yizhou Liu,Houwang Chen,Xinyu Zhou,Jianfei Yang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A hierarchical VLA system suffers real-time planning latency and misalignment between planner and executor. A_Block-AR with normalized goal modulation (NGM) reduces VLM calls and improves plan-to-action influence, achieving substantial latency reduction and higher success rates on LIBERO benchmarks and bimanual tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-time control requires fast, informative plans that meaningfully constrain action. The baseline Token-AR planner is too slow (57 VLM passes) and produces overly fine-grained plans with limited executor influence.

Method: Introduce waypoint-aligned block-autoregressive decoding (Block-AR) to reduce planning steps and latency; apply Normalized Goal Modulation (NGM) with phase gating and anti-shortcut training to ensure the waypoint plan meaningfully guides action; evaluate on LIBERO benchmarks and Rokae dual-arm robot; report VLM forward passes, planning latency, and success rates across tasks.

Result: Max VLM passes reduced from 57 to 8 (plus one prefix). 8.7x faster planning latency on Rokae dual-arm robot. LIBERO-Long success rate improved from 91.0% to 96.2%; average across four suites from 95.85% to 98.45%. Three bimanual tasks show comparable success across methods.

Conclusion: Misalignment between planner and executor stems from overly fine-grained outputs and underutilization of plans. Block-AR with NGMs alleviates latency and improves plan efficacy, with substantial gains in real-time performance and success rates across benchmarks.

Abstract: Hierarchical vision-language-action (VLA) systems consist of a high-level vision-language planner and a low-level action expert that generates continuous actions. This hierarchical design has practical value only if the planner can generate plans fast enough to meet real-time control requirements, and the resulting plans actually contribute to the generation of action. We study one such system, a waypoint hierarchy pipeline adapted from $π_{0.5}$, and find that neither requirement is satisfied. This baseline relies on token-level autoregressive decoding (Token-AR) to generate a waypoint plan, requiring 57 very expensive vision-language model (VLM) forward passes. However, we find that erasing the waypoint endpoints has little effect on task success. Two findings reveal the misalignment of planner-executor: the planner generates outputs at an excessively fine granularity, and the executor underuses plans as a control condition. We address the latency issue with waypoint-aligned block-autoregressive decoding (Block-AR), and plan underuse issue with normalized goal modulation (NGM), a layer-wise goal path constrained by phase gating and anti-shortcut training so that the waypoint influences action generation maintaining other signals. Our method reduces the maximum number of VLM forward passes from 57 to 8 on LIBERO, including one prefix prefill, and achieves an $8.7\times$ reduction in planning latency on a Rokae dual-arm robot. With normalized goal modulation and anti-shortcut training, Block-AR's success rate on LIBERO-Long increases from 91.0% to 96.2%, while its average success rate across the four suites increases from 95.85% to 98.45%. On three bimanual tasks with this robot, success rates remain comparable across methods.

</details>


### [338] [Impedance Cloning: Learning Equilibrium Point Parameters for Contact-Rich Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30842)
*Hayato Takahashi,Ryoga Oishi,Yuki Kasuga,Toshiaki Tsuji*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Impedance Cloning extracts biomechanical priors (stiffness and equilibrium) from teleoperation to generalize contact-rich manipulation across unseen surface geometries, outperforming fixed-impedance baselines and matching variable-impedance performance without force sensors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Trajectory-based imitation learning reproduces outcomes but fails under surface geometry shifts; encoding intent via passive impedance priors enables robust contact handling across varying geometries.

Method: Extract stiffness and equilibrium from bilateral teleoperation demonstrations using a particle filter without force/torque sensors; apply to CRANE-X7 manipulators; evaluate on wiping (joint-space and Cartesian-space actions) and pick-and-place with 10 cups; compare to fixed-impedance and variable-impedance baselines; test grasping on ILBiT and Mamba backbones.

Result: Wiping (joint-space): maintains ~4–5 N contact below -6 cm where baseline loses contact; Cartesian-space: force-height slope 0.13±0.03 N/cm vs 0.34–0.83 N/cm for fixed baselines; Pick-and-place (10 cups, 100 trials): 84/100 success, surpassing fixed-impedance 74/100 and close to variable-impedance 82/100 with one demo vs ten; Grasping: torque-tracking error reduced across ILBiT and Mamba backbones.

Conclusion: Impedance Cloning provides robust generalization to surface geometry changes by encoding intent as passive impedance priors; reduces reliance on force sensing and is effective across task domains and backbones, achieving competitive performance with minimal demonstrations.

Abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires robots to regulate force against surfaces whose geometry deviates unpredictably from training conditions. Trajectory-based imitation learning, which reproduces observable outputs, breaks down under such shifts. We propose Impedance Cloning, which instead imitates the biomechanical priors that generate motion -- the stiffness and equilibrium point -- and thereby passively absorbs contact uncertainty. Because these parameters encode intent rather than outcome, they generalize across surface geometries where trajectory reproduction does not. We extract them from bilateral teleoperation demonstrations via a particle filter without force/torque sensors and evaluate the framework on two CRANE-X7 manipulators. In a wiping task with joint-space actions, the trajectory-based baseline loses contact below -6 cm, whereas the proposed method maintains a consistent 4-5 N contact force above -6 cm, with a gradual decrease below; with Cartesian-space actions, its force-height slope over 0 to +8 cm is 0.13 +/- 0.03 N/cm, versus 0.34-0.83 N/cm for fixed-impedance baselines. In a pick-and-place task with 10 diverse cups (100 trials), the proposed method succeeds in 84 trials, outperforming the fixed-impedance baseline (74/100) and performing comparably to a variable impedance control baseline (82/100) with one demonstration instead of ten. In a grasping task, the representation reduces torque tracking error with both ILBiT and Mamba backbones, confirming its generality across architectures.

</details>


### [339] [VLaRL: Augmenting Vision-Language-Action Models with Simulation-Trained Latent-Conditioned Residual RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30868)
*Namiko Saito,Kinam Kim,Heecheol Kim,Katsushi Ikeuchi,Yasuyuki Matsushita*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: VLaRL enables residual RL for frozen vision-language-action models by conditioning on the VLA's latent representations and learning a lightweight latent mapper to align simulation and real latents, allowing safe, simulation-trained policy transfer to real robots with no online RL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address imprecision in contact-rich manipulation of VLA systems and the cost/safety of real-world RL; need effective sim-to-real transfer that does not rely on pixel-level visual correspondence.

Method: Use internal latent representations as conditioning for a residual controller; train residual RL in simulation; learn a lightweight latent mapper to translate sim latents to real latents; no pixel-level alignment required; test across four tasks and two VLA backbones.

Result: Consistent improvements in real-world success across all task-backbone combinations; ablations show latent conditioning and latent alignment are essential for transfer.

Conclusion: Latent-conditioned residual RL is effective for bridging sim-to-real for frozen VLA; leveraging VLA latent space reduces transfer difficulty and improves robustness; latent alignment is a key factor.

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide broad, instruction-conditioned manipulation behaviors, but their physical execution can remain imprecise during contact-rich interaction. Residual reinforcement learning (RL) can correct such errors while keeping the VLA frozen, but real-robot RL is costly and safety-critical. We propose VLA Latent-Conditioned RL (VLaRL), which enables residual RL for frozen VLAs to be trained in simulation and deployed on real robots without real-world RL or online adaptation. The key challenge is transferring the learned residual policy despite the visual gap between simulation and reality. Rather than requiring pixel-level visual correspondence, VLaRL uses the VLA's internal vision-language latent representation to condition residual control and as the sim-to-real transfer interface, and learns a lightweight mapper that transforms simulation-derived latents toward the real latent distribution. Across four contact-rich manipulation tasks and two VLA backbones, VLaRL improves real-world success in all task-backbone combinations, while controlled ablations demonstrate the importance of both latent conditioning and latent alignment for transferring simulation-trained residual control.

</details>


### [340] [A Second Torque Port for Series Elastic Actuators: Parallel-Integrated Design and Time-Scale Torque Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30873)
*Donghao Jia,Xiubo Xia,Junhang Liu,Zeyu Zhu,Xiaoyu Geng,Jian Sun*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Pi-SEA adds a second torque port by paralleling a frameless direct-drive micro motor with a fixed-stiffness spring, in parallel to a traditional SEA, enabling time-scale separation to divide commanded torque. This expands bandwidth, improves small-amplitude tracking, and reduces environmental residuals, with a closed-form sizing rule and sensorless torque readout from spring deflection and micro current.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome the amplitude and bandwidth limitations of a single-tork-port SEA caused by reflected inertia, transmission friction, and low-frequency saturation; enable stable, fast torque delivery across a wider operational band without relying on filter-based tuning.

Method: Implement a parallel-integrated SEA (Pi-SEA) with two torque channels: a fast micro motor loop and a slower spring/gear loop. Torque is divided by time-scale separation rather than filtering. The micro torque loop stabilizes the fast dynamics; a leaky integrator shapes steady-state torque; a closed-form sizing rule links spring, geared motor, and micro motor to target amplitudes and frequencies. Torque readout is sensorless, inferred from spring deflection and micro motor current.

Result: The Pi-SEA broadens the tracked torque band at small amplitudes and reduces the environmental residual by about an order of magnitude compared to conventional SEAs.

Conclusion: Using time-scale separation and a parallel fast actuating channel, Pi-SEA offers wider bandwidth at low amplitudes, easier tuning via a closed-form sizing rule, and improved torque delivery with reduced environmental interaction, at the cost of integrating a micro motor and managing two coupled control loops.

Abstract: A series elastic actuator has a single torque port and pays for it twice: the geared motor must swing its own reflected inertia through the spring, so the amplitude it delivers collapses as $ω^{-2}$ in the command frequency $ω$ once it saturates, while commands below the transmission's breakaway friction never arrive at all. This letter opens a second torque port on the load side, placing a frameless direct-drive micro motor in parallel with a fixed-stiffness spring -- a parallel-integrated SEA, or Pi-SEA, whose delivered torque is read from spring deflection and micro current without a sensor -- and dividing the commanded torque between the two channels by time scale rather than by filter design. The micro torque loop is the fast subsystem, which makes the closed loop singularly perturbed and turns the separation the channels need into a bound to check rather than a crossover to tune; a leaky mid-ranging integrator returns the steady load to the spring; and the amplitude ceiling, read backwards, becomes a closed-form sizing rule that matches spring, geared motor and micro motor to the amplitudes and frequencies an application asks for. Against SEAs, the Pi-SEA widens the tracked band at small amplitudes and lowers the residual the joint imposes on its environment, each by an order of magnitude.

</details>


### [341] [PHASE: Compliance-Enabled Tactile Phase Retrieval for Few-Shot Insertion Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30889)
*Jeremy Siburian,Cristian C. Beltran-Hernandez,Tatsuya Matsushima,Yusuke Iwasawa,Masashi Hamaya,Mai Nishimura*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: PHASE introduces phase-aware, phase-consistent retrieval for contact-rich peg-in-hole using compliant wrist tactile signals; achieves notable improvements in few-shot learning across multiple geometries and unseen starts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning contact-rich insertion from limited demonstrations is challenging; existing retrieval-based imitation learning lacks principled phase-specific retrieval. Phase structure revealed by tactile signals through compliance offers a path to robust learning.

Method: PHASE integrates (1) multimodal contact-aware representation learning, (2) variable-length phase segmentation from tactile signals, and (3) phase-consistent retrieval for policy learning, leveraging a compliant wrist to sustain contact and reveal phase information.

Result: PHASE improves overall success rate by 13 percentage points over the strongest non-phase-aware baseline and 30 percentage points for unseen initial positions in real-world peg-in-hole across five peg geometries, outperforming state-of-the-art retrieval baselines under a shared policy architecture.

Conclusion: Aligning retrieval with interaction-defined contact phases substantially improves robustness in few-shot insertion learning; phase-aware tactile retrieval is effective for contact-rich manipulation.

Abstract: Contact-rich assembly tasks such as peg-in-hole insertion remain difficult to learn from limited demonstrations. While retrieval-augmented imitation learning, which augments target demonstrations with relevant prior data, offers a promising direction, its applicability to contact-rich manipulation remains largely unexplored. Contact-rich insertion unfolds over multiple phases from search to insert, and retrieving phase-specific experience from prior data in principled ways remains an open question. Our key insight is that a compliant wrist enables the robot to sustain contact throughout execution, producing rich tactile and force signals that naturally reveal the phase structure of insertion and inform what should be retrieved. Based on this insight, we present PHASE (PHase-Aware Segmentation and REtrieval), a framework for compliance-enabled tactile phase retrieval that integrates multimodal contact-aware representation learning, variable-length phase segmentation from tactile signals, and phase-consistent retrieval for policy learning. We evaluate PHASE on real-world peg-in-hole insertion across five peg geometries, comparing against retrieval strategies drawn from state-of-the-art methods under a shared policy architecture. PHASE improves the overall success rate by 13 percentage points over the strongest non-phase-aware baseline, and improves performance under unseen initial positions by 30 percentage points.
