These results demonstrate that aligning retrieval with interaction-defined contact phases substantially improves robustness in few-shot insertion learning.

</details>


### [342] [Causeway: Restoring Task Accessibility for Instruction Switching in VLA Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30913)
*Qingzi Wang,Kaixi Feng,Guangyao Shi,Xiyang Wu,Ang Li,Dinesh Manocha*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Causeway is a training-free, inference-time intervention that recovers success for vision-language-action policies when instruction switches lead to task islands. It back-propagates through the frozen decoder to perform a state-directed write in the action stream, enabling the VLA to decode the return motion without updates or new heads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: During instruction switching, a target task can become inaccessible from the state produced by a preceding task, creating task islands that standard policies struggle to re-enter.

Method: Given the current state and a re-entry pose for the target task, Causeway back-propagates through the frozen decoding computation and writes into the action-stream representation in a state-directed manner. No parameter updates, new action heads, or external action generation are required; the VLA decodes the return motion itself.

Result: On LIBERO-Goal across 71 cross-object pairs, three switch timings, and three VLA architectures, bare-switch success rises from 3–26% to 47–65%, and the rate of reaching the handoff neighborhood increases by 42–72 percentage points across models. Additional experiments on LIBERO-Object and a real xArm demonstrate recovery beyond LIBERO-Goal, in both simulation and hardware.

Conclusion: Causeway provides a training-free, inference-time correction mechanism that mitigates task islands by editing the action stream during decoding, yielding substantial performance gains and broader generalization to different tasks and real-world robotics.

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can execute many tasks from standard initial states, yet a new instruction may fail after another task has altered the robot's physical state. We study instruction switching, where a new task is issued during or after the execution of a different one. We observe that a target task that is reliably completed from its standard initial states can become inaccessible from states produced by a preceding task. We call such states task islands. We propose Causeway, a training-free inference-time intervention. Given the current state and a re-entry pose for the target task, Causeway back-propagates through the frozen decoding computation and applies a state-directed write within the action-stream representation. The VLA decodes the return motion itself, without parameter updates, a new action head, or external action generation. Across 71 cross-object pairs, three switch timings, and three VLA architectures on LIBERO-Goal, Causeway raises bare-switch success from 3-26% to 47-65% and increases the rate of reaching the handoff neighborhood by 42-72 percentage points across models. Additional experiments on LIBERO-Object and a real xArm platform show that the recovery extends beyond the main LIBERO-Goal setting, both in simulation and on a robot.

</details>


### [343] [Bundled Contact Gradients: Stabilizing Differentiable Simulation for Deployable Dynamic Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30951)
*Dyuman Aditya,Jin Cheng,Clemens Schwarke,Quan Nguyen,Gaurav Sukhatme,Stelian Coros,Gabriele Fadini*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Bundled Contact Gradients (BCG) is a contact-local randomized smoothing technique for differentiable simulation that reduces gradient variance in stiff-contact regimes by aggregating gradients from a local bundle of randomized perturbations, improving sample efficiency and enabling zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for dynamic humanoids.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rigid-body differentiable simulators with stiff contact yield high-variance gradients, hindering first-order policy optimization and real-world transfer. Softened contact models trade fidelity, so a method that preserves rigidity while stabilizing gradients is needed.

Method: Detect stiff contact; sample a local bundle of perturbations around the contact configuration; perform rollouts for each perturbation; compute and aggregate gradients from these rollouts to produce a smoothed gradient used for policy optimization.

Result: Demonstrated successful training and zero-shot transfer of dynamic motions to a Unitree G1 humanoid in the real world; supplementary materials and video available.

Conclusion: BCG provides a practical, contact-local smoothing mechanism that mitigates gradient variance without sacrificing contact fidelity, enabling more robust differentiable policy learning and sim-to-real transfer for high-dynamics humanoid control.

Abstract: Differentiable simulation provides analytic gradients of robot dynamics, enabling fast and sample-efficient first-order policy optimization. However, obtaining smooth and informative gradients through rigid-body contact typically requires softened contact models, often at the expense of physical fidelity and thereby limiting learned policies largely to simulation. This trade-off becomes particularly consequential for dynamic humanoid motions, where accurate contact dynamics are critical for transferring policies to the real world. Increasing contact stiffness in rigid-body simulation improves the fidelity of interactions, but also makes the dynamics increasingly sensitive to small state perturbations, producing high-variance gradients that can destabilize first-order policy learning. To address this, we propose \emph{Bundled Contact Gradients (BCG)}, a contact-local randomized smoothing framework for differentiable policy learning. When stiff contact is detected, our method evaluates a local bundle of randomized perturbation rollouts around the stiff contact configuration and aggregates their gradient signal thereby reducing gradient variance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by successfully training and transferring dynamic motions zero-shot onto a real-world Unitree G1 humanoid platform. Videos and supplementary information can be found at https://bundledcontactgradients.github.io/

</details>


### [344] [VisTacAlign: Co-Training Dexterous Policies on Tactile Human and Robot Demonstrations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30959)
*Julien Poffet,Matthew Strong,Ankush Dhawan,Baiyu Shi,Shalika Neelaveni,Yujia Yuan,Zhenan Bao,Monroe Kennedy*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: VisTacAlign co-trains 3D visual–tactile dexterous policies by aligning human and robot demonstrations through multi-step visual and tactile alignment, then fusing modalities with a diffusion transformer; it improves performance on real tasks over robot-only data, with ablations highlighting the necessity of both tactile input and visual alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge the human–robot modality gap in dexterous manipulation by leveraging abundant human demonstrations while ensuring the robot policy consumes the same sensory modalities (vision, proprioception, tactile signals).

Method: Map human hand motions to a 17-DoF tactile robot hand; perform a one-time fingertip correction. Erase the human hand in stereo data and replace with a posed robot-hand mesh coated with robot-recorded pixels. Re-run a real-time stereo foundation model on the composite so human-point clouds inherit robot-like stereo errors/visibility. Align a capacitive tactile glove to the robot fingertips, forming per-finger force signals. Use a diffusion transformer to fuse point-cloud, proprioceptive, and tactile tokens. Evaluate on Lego assembly, strawberry plucking, and activating/lifting a power drill, comparing robot-only vs. mixed demonstrations and performing ablations.

Result: Incorporating aligned human demonstrations yields performance gains over robot-only policies across all three tasks; ablations show that both tactile input and visual alignment are necessary for the improvements.

Conclusion: Multi-modal alignment of vision and touch, together with human demonstrations, effectively narrows the sim-to-real and modality gaps in dexterous manipulation, enabling better policy learning from heterogeneous data.

Abstract: Human demonstrations are a cheap source of data for dexterous manipulation, but co-training a robot policy on them requires closing the human--robot gap in every modality the policy consumes. We present VisTacAlign, a framework for co-training 3D-visual-tactile dexterous policies on human and robot demonstrations. Glove-tracked human hand motion is retargeted to a 17-DoF tactile robot hand with a one-time fingertip correction. The human hand is then erased from both stereo views and replaced by a posed robot-hand mesh painted with pixels from robot recordings, and a real-time stereo foundation model is re-run on the composite, so the human point clouds carry the same stereo errors and visibility as the robot ones. Finally, a capacitive tactile glove is aligned to the robot's fingertip sensors in its signal space, giving one interpretable per-finger force representation. A diffusion transformer consumes point-cloud, proprioceptive, and per-finger tactile tokens. On three real-world tasks requiring precise force -- Lego assembly, plucking strawberries of varying size, and activating and lifting a power drill -- adding aligned human demonstrations to existing robot data improves over robot-only policies, and ablations show that both tactile input and visual alignment are necessary. Project page: https://vis-tac-align.github.io

</details>


### [345] [FRAM: Trajectory-Guided Visual Feature Selection for Compact Language-Conditioned Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30965)
*Hiroshi Ito,Hyogo Hiruma,Yoshiki Kanai,Takahiro Yoshida,Akira Kanazawa,Hiroki Yamada*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: FRAM is a small policy (138.7M params) that links future end-effector trajectories to current vision by using predicted trajectory coordinates as spatial pointers to read local visual features, achieving near-state performance on LIBERO suites and strong real-robot results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce model size and compute while preserving strong performance in vision-language-action for robot manipulation; enable high robustness by grounding actions in predicted future motion; automate supervision via trajectory labels inferred from demonstrations and camera geometry.

Method: The model reads the image coordinates of a predicted end-effector trajectory as spatial pointers and gathers local visual features related to the motion from the current image. It organizes information into Where (reference position), What (visual state), and Future (future motion). Trajectory labels are automatically generated using demonstrations and camera geometry, eliminating manual annotation. Evaluated on LIBERO suites (average 92.2% with 138.7M params; close to π0’s 94.2% with 3.3B params) and LIBERO-Plus (67.3% without extra training). Real-robot validation on a dual-arm UR5e stacks cups using wrist cameras and arm switching.

Result: FRAM achieves high success rates with substantially fewer parameters than state-of-the-art large models; ablations show contributions from both predicted future trajectory and local visual features; demonstrates feasibility of small, robust policies in both simulated benchmarks and real hardware.

Conclusion: Explicitly conditioning action on future motion via spatial pointers to local visual features yields strong performance with significantly fewer parameters, offering a practical route toward efficient, robust vision-language-action policies for manipulation tasks.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action models achieve strong performance in robot manipulation, but often require large numbers of parameters. In this work, we propose the Future Representation Action Model (FRAM), a small policy that explicitly links the future end-effector trajectory to the current visual input. FRAM uses the image coordinates of the predicted trajectory as spatial pointers and reads local visual features related to the motion from the current image. This organizes the information for action generation into the reference position (Where), the visual state (What), and the future motion (Future). Trajectory labels are generated automatically from demonstrations and camera geometry, so no manual annotation is needed. With 138.7M parameters, including a frozen language encoder, FRAM reaches an average success rate of 92.2% over the four standard LIBERO suites, close to the 94.2% of $π_0$ with 3.3B parameters. Without extra training, it also reaches an average of 67.3% on LIBERO-Plus. Ablations confirm that both the future trajectory and the local visual features improve performance and robustness. On a real dual-arm UR5e, FRAM stacks cups using only wrist cameras, including choosing and switching between the left and right arms. These results show that selecting visual information based on future motion is an effective way to obtain both high performance and robustness in a small robot policy.

</details>


### [346] [TACTIC: Understanding Tactile Encoders and Conditioning for Contact-rich Robot Manipulation Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30969)
*Seongjin Bien,Débora Oliveira Makowski,Carlo Kneissl,Reihaneh Mirjalili,Pankhuri Vanjani,Rudolf Lioutikov,Gitta Kutyniok,Florian Walter,Wolfram Burgard*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A real-world, large-scale comparative study of vision-based tactile encoders and fusion methods shows task-dependent performance with no universal best choice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a proliferation of architectures, datasets, and evaluation protocols in vision-based tactile sensing; a controlled real-world comparison is needed to identify robust design choices.

Method: Train and evaluate a broad set of tactile encoders and fusion strategies within the same pipeline; perform more than 2000 real-world rollouts across multiple contact-rich manipulation tasks to enable fair comparison.

Result: No single encoder or fusion strategy universally outperforms others; performance strongly depends on the task;simulation-based assessments may not reflect real-world performance; large-scale real-world evaluation yields reliable statistics.

Conclusion: Encoder and fusion choices should be task-driven; large-scale real-world testing is essential; future work could focus on developing guidelines or meta-learning approaches to select architectures per task.

Abstract: Tactile information is essential for contact-rich manipulation tasks in robotics. Vision-based tactile sensors make it particularly easy to design end-to-end manipulation policies with tactile sensing, as they enable the use of existing encoders from computer vision. However, this has led to a huge variety of architectures, training datasets, and evaluation protocols, making it difficult to determine which design choices best encode touch. In this work, we address this gap and present a comprehensive study of tactile encoders and fusion strategies across various contact-rich manipulation tasks in real-world experiments. To enable a controlled comparison, we train and evaluate all models under the same pipeline and experimental setup, comprising more than 2000 real-world rollouts. Our results go beyond other studies that only compare simulation performance, which does not necessarily translate to real-world settings, where large-scale evaluations are needed to obtain reliable statistics. Our key finding is that there is no universally optimal representation or fusion strategy for encoding visual-tactile. Instead, the best encoder backbone and fusion scheme depend strongly on the task.

</details>


### [347] [Quadruped Obstacle Avoidance and Footstep Planning with Distributed Low-cost Time-of-Flight Sensors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31008)
*Giammarco Caroleo,Timothée Mahamoodally,Matteo Manzardo,Jin Jin,Marco Pontin,Matias Mattamala,Renato Vidoni,Perla Maiolino,Maurice Fallon*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Distributed Time-of-Flight (ToF) sensors can substitute for depth cameras for near-field mapping on quadrupeds, achieving centimeter-level local accuracy at lower cost and energy, despite lower resolution and higher noise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limitations of depth cameras and LiDAR (cost, power, limited close-range coverage, blind spots) to enable reliable perceptual locomotion for quadrupeds in near-field environments.

Method: Design and deploy a distributed ToF sensing architecture on the ANYbotics ANYmal quadruped; assess environment reconstruction accuracy and benchmark against depth cameras for terrain mapping and obstacle avoidance; analyze how sensor distribution around the robot mitigates blind spots.

Result: Distributed ToF sensors yield centimeter-level local mapping accuracy and support reliable perceptual locomotion for near-field obstacle avoidance and footstep planning, despite lower resolution and higher noise; significant reductions in cost, energy consumption, and system complexity compared to depth cameras.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates the viability of distributed ToF sensing as a low-cost alternative for near-field perception in quadruped locomotion. Trade-offs include resolution and noise, which may be mitigated with calibration, fusion, and smarter algorithms; future work could enhance range, resolution, and integration with planning modules.

Abstract: Quadruped robots typically rely on depth cameras and LiDAR sensors to map their local environment. However, these sensors have limited close-range coverage, are relatively expensive, and consume significant power. This study investigates whether distributed Time-of-Flight (ToF) sensors can serve as a low-cost alternative to depth cameras for near-field terrain mapping for locomotion and local navigation. We designed a distributed ToF sensing architecture for the ANYbotics ANYmal quadruped, assessed its environment reconstruction accuracy, and benchmarked it against depth cameras for terrain mapping and obstacle avoidance. Distributing these sensors around the robot can also avoid the blind spots of traditional sensors. Our results show that, despite their low resolution and higher measurement noise, distributed ToF sensors can support reliable perceptual locomotion with centimeter-level local mapping accuracy. The proposed sensing strategy provides sufficient geometric information for near-field obstacle avoidance and footstep planning, at substantially lower cost, energy consumption, and system complexity than depth cameras.

</details>


### [348] [Co-design of trajectory and morphology for a vertical jump-climbing robot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31014)
*Christopher Y. Xu,Elliot W. Hawkes*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A 290 g robot demonstrates vertical climbing by bounding that includes an aerial phase, achieved through co-optimized morphology and trajectory under adhesion constraints, enabling continuous climb at 0.375 m/s and enabling aerial reorientation using the rear leg as an inertial tail.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Animal-like agility on vertical terrain remains challenging for robots; existing platforms use conservative contact-based gaits limiting dynamic maneuvers. This work aims to achieve faster, more agile vertical climbing via a jump-climb strategy.

Method: Co-design workflow that jointly optimizes morphology and trajectory under adhesion-force limits from spined grippers; development of a bounding (aerial) climb with an aerial phase and reorientation using the rear leg as an inertial tail; evaluation of jump-force trajectories in 2D force space; demonstration of continuous climbing and surface transitions.

Result: The optimized morphology enables continuous vertical climbing at 0.375 m/s (1.97 body lengths/s); the robot can perform ground locomotion and transition to vertical surfaces; jump forces analyzed in 2D force space; provides design insights for jump-climbing.

Conclusion: Co-optimized morphology and trajectory enable agile vertical climbing via a bounding jump with an aerial phase; the approach provides design guidance toward animal-like climbing robots and highlights the value of integrating propulsion, adhesion limits, and inertial reorientation.

Abstract: Animals such as squirrels and even bears have adapted to rapidly climb up trees and other complex vertical terrain, but achieving comparable agility has been a challenge for climbing robots. Existing robots often use walking gaits and move conservatively to stay in contact with the surface, which limits the range of dynamic maneuvers. In this paper we present a 290 g robot that, to our knowledge, is the first to climb vertically by bounding (with an aerial phase). We leverage a co-design workflow, in which the morphology and trajectory are jointly optimized for fast locomotion, subject to adhesion force limitations seen in spined grippers. The resulting trajectory includes a rapid maneuver that launches the robot vertically, and an aerial reorientation that brings the front grippers back to the surface using the rear leg as an inertial tail. We evaluate the resulting jump forces in 2D force space and demonstrate that the optimized morphology is capable of continuous climbing at a speed of 0.375 m/s (1.97 body lengths/s), and can also achieve ground locomotion and transition to a vertical surface. Our work proposes design insights for the jump-climbing maneuver and serves as an important step toward creating climbing robots with agility on par with that of animals.

</details>


### [349] [Precision at Speed: Sample-Efficient Online Model-Based Reinforcement Learning for Hydraulic Excavator Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31025)
*Claudio Canales,Fang Nan,Marco Hutter,Javier Ruiz-del-Solar*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Online model-based RL with a probabilistic dynamics ensemble and a precision-gated contouring objective enables data-efficient, high-precision path tracking for an 11.5-ton hydraulic excavator, achieving comparable performance to longer training after ~20 minutes and sub-centimeter accuracy after ~40 minutes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the challenge of precise, high-speed control for robots with complex actuation dynamics while reducing real-world data requirements and the cost of hardware interaction.

Method: Online model-based reinforcement learning that learns a probabilistic dynamics ensemble for sampling-based model predictive control, guided by a precision-gated contouring objective that emphasizes path accuracy. Evaluation includes a data-driven excavator simulator and real-world testing on an 11.5-ton excavator with no demonstrations or pretraining.

Result: In simulation, higher sample efficiency than evaluated model-based RL baselines. Real-world validation shows after 20 minutes of interaction the controller reaches tracking accuracy comparable to prior learned controllers trained on 100–150 minutes; after 40 minutes it sustains sub-centimeter mean path error at high speeds.

Conclusion: Demonstrates data-efficient, hardware-learned control for heavy actuators using online, model-based RL with a probabilistic dynamics ensemble and precision-focused rewards, achieving rapid convergence and high-precision performance without demonstrations.

Abstract: Precise, high-speed control remains challenging for robots with complex actuation dynamics. Learning directly on hardware is further constrained by the cost of real-world interaction. We present an online model-based reinforcement learning framework that learns a probabilistic dynamics ensemble model from scratch for sampling-based model predictive control. A precision-gated contouring objective conditions the progress reward on path accuracy, prioritizing precision over speed. In a data-driven excavator simulator, the framework achieves higher sample efficiency than the evaluated model-based reinforcement learning baselines. We validate the framework by learning directly on an 11.5-ton Menzi Muck M445 hydraulic excavator, without demonstrations or simulation pretraining. After 20 minutes of interaction, the controller reaches tracking accuracy comparable to prior learned controllers trained on 100-150 minutes of data. After 40 minutes, it sustains sub-centimeter mean path error at high operating speeds.

</details>


### [350] [Compact Force Sensor for Dual-UAV Cable-Suspended Payload Transport with Tension-Aware Outer-Loop Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31035)
*Andrea Delbene,Giorgio Cannata,Giorgio Carlini,Filippo Sante,Marco Baglietto*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Dual-UAV payload transport with a custom force sensor at the cable anchor enables cascade control for improved stabilization and disturbance rejection, validated by simulations and indoor experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Stability, coordination, and robustness gaps in cooperative UAV payload transport under disturbances and unmodeled dynamics.

Method: Introduce a compact force sensor at the UAV cable anchor, develop a mathematical model, and implement a cascade control architecture: fast inner loops for stabilization and outer loops compensating measured forces. Validate via simulations and indoor experiments, including payload-drop and constrained-space tests, and compare against literature-based distributed references.

Result: Sensor characterization shows linearity, hysteresis, repeatability, and cross-load properties. The control framework yields improved stabilization, coordination, and disturbance rejection relative to reference methods; outcomes supported by simulations and indoor experiments; demonstration video provided.

Conclusion: The integrated sensing and control framework enhances performance in cooperative payload transport with dual UAVs and is validated experimentally; the approach offers robust disturbance rejection and better coordination under constrained conditions.

Abstract: Cooperative payload transportation using multiple \textit{Unmanned Aerial Vehicles} (UAVs) poses challenges in stability, coordination, and robustness, especially under external disturbances and unmodeled dynamics. This work proposes a dual-UAV payload transportation framework supported by a compact, custom-designed force sensor measuring the interaction force at the UAV cable anchor point. The sensor design and mathematical model are presented, and its performance is characterized through static and dynamic tests evaluating linearity, hysteresis, repeatability, and crossload. The control architecture follows a cascade structure: fast inner loops handle vehicle stabilization, while outer loops are designed to compensate for the measured forces. The approach is validated through simulations and indoor experiments under position uncertainty. Payload-drop and constrained-space tests assess the proposed sensing and control architecture against literature-based distributed references, showing improved stabilization, coordination, and disturbance rejection. A video of the experiments is available at: https://youtu.be/rIw9-fvV8Qw.

</details>


### [351] [Kintsugi-VLA: Turning Failed Robot Rollouts into Recovery Data through Interventional Recoverability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31048)
*Ivan Snegirev,Elizaveta Semenyakina,Dmitrii Maliukov,Miguel Altamirano Cabrera,Dzmitry Tsetserukou*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Kintsugi-VLA converts failed simulator rollouts into targeted recovery data by measuring interventional recoverability through state restoration; it identifies a recoverability frontier to guide recovery data selection, yielding improved recovery success in a simulated Franka manipulation task compared with uniform sampling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current simulation-based VLA training discards failed rollouts, wasting off-nominal states needed for recovery. A principled method to reuse failure data could improve sample efficiency and robustness of learned policies.

Method: Define interventional recoverability as the probability of completing the original task when the simulator is restored to a given state. Estimate it with adaptive Monte Carlo continuations and pointwise Wilson intervals, and analyze its non-monotonic evolution along failed trajectories to find a terminal low-recoverability frontier. Use this frontier to select informative recovery starting states and generate targeted synthetic recovery data for training SmolVLA.

Result: On a simulated Franka manipulation task, targeted recovery data yield aggregate SmolVLA recovery successes of 34.6% (difficulty-matching) and 38.4% (frame-budget matching), improving by 5.8 and 6.7 percentage points over uniform sampling within the same recovery window. These gains persist under disturbed end-to-end execution and altered clutter/physics, though clean-task success falls from 76.8% to 74.7%.

Conclusion: Kintsugi-VLA shows that failed simulator rollouts can be repurposed into structured, informative recovery-training data via direct interventional measurement, offering data-efficiency and robustness benefits for simulation-based VLA policies.

Abstract: Simulation enables scalable training of Vision-Language-Action policies by using privileged experts to generate visual demonstrations without requiring every trajectory to be collected through manual teleoperation. However, such pipelines typically retain successful demonstrations while failed rollouts are discarded, even though they expose precisely the off-nominal states from which recovery must be learned.
  We introduce Kintsugi-VLA, a framework for converting failed rollouts into targeted synthetic recovery data by exploiting exact state restoration and branching in simulation. For a fixed privileged expert, we define interventional recoverability as the probability of completing the original task after the simulator is restored to a given state, estimate it using adaptive Monte Carlo continuations with pointwise Wilson intervals, and characterize its non-monotonic evolution along failed trajectories. These estimates identify an observed terminal low-recoverability frontier-the point after which measured recoverability remains below a threshold-which is then used to select informative recovery starting states.
  In a simulated Franka manipulation task, targeted recovery data yield aggregate SmolVLA recovery success of 34.6\% and 38.4\% under difficulty- and frame-budget matching, respectively, 5.8 and 6.7 percentage points above uniform sampling within the same recovery window. The same ordering is observed under disturbed end-to-end execution and shifted clutter and physics conditions, while clean-task success decreases from 76.8\% to 74.7\%. Kintsugi-VLA demonstrates how failed simulator rollouts can be transformed from discarded experience into structured recovery-training data through direct interventional measurement.

</details>


### [352] [Accuracy Evaluation of INS/ZUPT Filtering Methods Based on Different Geometric Error Definitions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31057)
*Wei Ouyang,Jiale Han,Yarong Luo,Maoran Zhu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Geometric filtering for inertial navigation shows theoretical consistency but practical gains over IEKF are limited; IEKF remains competitive for INS with ZUPT in the tested scenario.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensure filter consistency by leveraging the system's Lie-group structure; address limitations of additive error in indirect Kalman filters for inertial navigation with zero-velocity updates.

Method: Derive left-error process and measurement models using invariant filtering, two-frame-group filtering, and equivariant filtering for zero-velocity updates; introduce a new left tangent-group operation; compare TF-IEKF, TG-EqF, and IEKF theoretically and via INS/ZUPT experiments.

Result: Analytical results indicate TF-IEKF and TG-EqF do not offer meaningful consistency gains over IEKF; experiments show the three geometric filters reach comparable positioning accuracy, while a conventional indirect EKF with small initial attitude errors achieves loop-closure errors below 0.1% of distance.

Conclusion: Geometric filters provide a principled approach to error modeling, but in this setup they do not outperform IEKF in consistency; selection should consider modeling complexity and computational cost; further evaluation under larger errors or dynamic conditions is suggested.

Abstract: Geometric filters have recently been introduced to improve the accuracy and consistency of inertial-based integrated navigation systems. Error states were defined through specific group operations, introducing state correlations in error definition, which were lacked in the additive error used by a conventional indirect Kalman filter. The desirable consistent filtering models can be obtained based on specific geometric errors. For zero-velocity measurements expressed in the reference frame, this paper derives left-error process and measurement models from invariant filtering, two-frame-group filtering, and equivariant filtering. Importantly, a new group operation is introduced for the left tangent-group equivariant error. The analysis shows that the two-frame-group invariant extended Kalman filter (TFG-IEKF) and the tangent-group equivariant filter (TG-EqF) do not offer a significant consistency advantage over the invariant extended Kalman filter (IEKF). Experiments with an INS/ZUPT measurement system show that, under small initial attitude errors, the conventional indirect extended Kalman filter (EKF) achieves loop-closure position errors below $0.1\%$ of the traveled distance, while the three geometric filters achieve comparable positioning accuracy.

</details>


### [353] [AuthGuard-R: Safety-Compliant Mission Hijacking and Dual-Gate Defense for LLM-Controlled Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31110)
*Saidattu Chepuri,Vikas Srivastava*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes MissionPAIR as an adaptive attacker framework for safety-compliant mission hijacking and introduces AuthGuard-R, a deterministic authorization layer with dual gates that binds executable actions to signed missions and provenance; empirical eval shows AuthGuard-R blocks all unauthorized actions in live attacks across two planners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To tackle safety-safe yet mission-violating actions in LLM-guided robotic control, where an action can be physically safe but outside the authenticated mission, a vulnerability not addressed by traditional safety gates.

Method: Introduce MissionPAIR to search for executable plans that pass a safety gate yet violate the authenticated mission. Propose AuthGuard-R, an independent safety gate that binds each executable action to a signed mission, robot identity, object/region scope, current state, time, and input provenance. Formalize mission policies over robot traces, define security games, and prove properties including authorization soundness, non-escalation, replay resistance, robot binding, provenance separation, threshold-approval security, audit-log tamper evidence, and trace-level composition. Conduct cross-model evaluation with Claude Haiku 4.5 and Qwen2.5 7B planner over 240 live attack trials (109 succeeded hijacks); AuthGuard-R rejected all unauthorized actions. A separate suite of eleven attacks was also blocked completely.

Result: AuthGuard-R achieved complete protection against the tested safety-compliant mission hijacking attempts; 109 hijacking attempts were blocked out of 109 in the live attacks; the additional protocol- and policy-level attacks were also blocked.

Conclusion: The dual-gate AuthGuard-R approach, together with formalized policies and security proofs, provides strong protection against safety-compliant mission hijacking in LLM-guided robotic planning, demonstrating practical effectiveness across multiple planners; future work could explore scalability, real-world deployment, and broader attack surfaces.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as high-level planners for mobile robots, robot manipulators, and autonomous vehicles. Recent studies show that these systems can be influenced through malicious text, speech, visual instructions, retrieved documents, and poisoned sensory context. Most defenses ask whether a proposed action is physically safe. This paper studies a different problem: an action may be physically safe and still violate the mission authorized by the user. An attacker may redirect a delivery robot, replace an approved object, extend a robot's operating region, activate an unnecessary sensor, or delay a mission without creating an immediate physical hazard. We call this attack \emph{safety-compliant mission hijacking}. We propose MissionPAIR, an adaptive attack framework that searches for executable plans that pass a safety gate while violating an authenticated mission. We also propose AuthGuard-R, a deterministic authorization layer that binds every executable action to a signed mission, robot identity, object and region scope, current state, time, and input provenance. AuthGuard-R operates with an independent safety gate, giving a dual-gate architecture. We formalize mission policies over robot traces, define security games, and prove authorization soundness, mission non-escalation, replay resistance, robot binding, provenance separation, threshold-approval security, audit-log tamper evidence, and trace-level composition. We report a preliminary cross-model evaluation with Claude Haiku~4.5 and the open-source Qwen2.5~7B planner. Across 240 live attack trials, the planners followed an injected mission deviation in 109 trials; AuthGuard-R rejected all 109 resulting unauthorized actions. A separate hand-constructed suite of eleven protocol- and policy-level attacks was also blocked completely.

</details>


### [354] [DualManip: Agentic Dynamic Manipulation via Dual-Path Semantic Reasoning and Geometric Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31112)
*Chengxi Li,Yan Di,Yingyue Li,Ruida Zhang,Mingyang Li,Xiangyang Ji*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: DualManip introduces a dual-path framework for robot manipulation using vision-language models, decoupling semantic reasoning from fast geometric adaptation to handle dynamic scenes efficiently.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLMs enable open-vocabulary manipulation but suffer high latency; dynamic scenes cause geometry changes while task intent persists, necessitating fast, robust adaptation and replanning.

Method: A semantic path grounds task-relevant interactions and performs constraint-based pose optimization; a geometric path updates template-to-observation correspondences via a shape-adaptive network from live RGB-D; an Information Interaction Module links both, initializing grasps from semantic grounding, validating updates, and triggering semantic replanning on failures.

Result: Evaluated on six manipulation tasks (non-rigid, articulated, rigid, high-precision) across static, single-change, and continuous dynamic scenes; shows superior robustness under scene changes and ~46x faster geometric adaptation than agentic verification and semantic replanning.

Conclusion: Demonstrates the viability of decoupled semantic and geometric reasoning for real-time manipulation with VLMs and provides a scalable path toward robust, dynamic manipulation in real-world settings.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable open-vocabulary reasoning for robot manipulation, but their high inference latency limits responsiveness in dynamic scenes. Many scene changes, however, alter object geometry without invalidating task intent. We present DualManip, a dual-path framework that decouples infrequent semantic reasoning from responsive geometric adaptation. The semantic path decomposes the task and grounds task-relevant interactions, followed by a constraint-solving module for pose optimization. During execution, the geometric path continuously updates template-to-observation correspondences from live RGB-D observations via a shape-adaptive network. These correspondences transfer task-relevant grasp contacts across observations, enabling online grasp reconstruction under object motion and non-rigid deformation. The Information Interaction Module bridges the two paths by initializing task-relevant grasps from semantic grounding, validating geometric updates, and triggering semantic replanning upon update failures. Real-world evaluation spans six manipulation tasks covering non-rigid deformation, articulated reconfiguration, rigid motion, and high-precision assembly across three settings: static, single-change, and continuous dynamic. DualManip demonstrates superior manipulation robustness, particularly under continuous scene changes, while achieving geometric adaptation approximately 46$\times$ faster than agentic verification and semantic replanning. Our project page: https://lichengxi1.github.io/Dualmanip.

</details>


### [355] [Comparative Evaluation of an XR Pen-based Control Interface for Semi-Autonomous Mobile Robot Navigation in Service Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31117)
*Alicia Torc,Carl Tornberg,Eric Piette,Renaud Ronsse,Benoit Macq,Gustavo Alfonso Garcia Ricardez,Lotfi El Hafi,Tadahiro Taniguchi*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: XR-based control interface for a semi-autonomous home robot evaluated against XR pen, XR motion controllers, hand gestures, and RViz; XR pen offers fastest task selection, XR controllers yield best usability/workload; overall XR approaches show promise, but XR pen integration limits remain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable intuitive, novice-friendly control of service robots in domestic environments by leveraging XR overlays, addressing the gap where traditional interfaces are unintuitive or inaccessible.

Method: Implemented four AR/VR control interfaces within a common framework, including a novel XR pen-based interaction (point-select-drag arrow for orientation), plus motion controllers and gestures; compared against RViz in a user study with 10 participants performing navigation tasks in a home-like environment; metrics include task selection time, consistency, workload, and usability.

Result: XR pen yielded fastest and most consistent task selection; XR motion controllers achieved the best perceived workload and usability; RViz lagged behind; overall, XR-based control is a viable intuitive option for novices; XR pen faces integration limitations affecting user experience.

Conclusion: XR-based control shows promise for novice-friendly robot operation in domestic contexts; to realize its potential, improvements in XR pen integration and robustness are needed; future work could optimize interaction latency, reliability, and ease of use.

Abstract: Service robots remain difficult to deploy in domestic environments, partly because fully autonomous operation is not yet reliable in unpredictable surroundings, and partly because conventional control methods remain inaccessible to novice users. Extended Reality (XR) enables operators to visualize robot information overlaid onto the real world and to interact with augmented elements. Yet, common XR control methods, such as motion controllers and hand gestures, are still perceived as unintuitive. This paper presents a control interface that uses a commercial XR pen to command a semi-autonomous mobile robot in Augmented Reality (AR): the operator points at a position in the room, selects it, and drags an augmented arrow to set the desired orientation of the robot at this destination. Two additional interfaces, based on the XR motion controllers and hand gestures, were developed within the same framework. To assess the performance and users' perception of these interfaces, and of the XR pen in particular, a study with 10 participants compared four control methods, i.e., the XR pen, the XR motion controllers, hand gestures, and a computer-based baseline RViz, in navigation tasks performed in a home-like environment. Results show that the XR pen significantly outperforms the other methods in task selection time with the most consistent selections, and that the XR motion controllers obtain the best perceived workload and usability scores, ahead of the computer-based baseline, supporting XR-based control as an intuitive alternative for novice users. However, technical limitations in the integration of the recently released XR pen currently hold back its user experience.

</details>


### [356] [INTERACT: Interactive Planning for Autonomous Driving via Anchor-Conditioned Prediction and Trust-Region Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31137)
*Aron Distelzweig,Andreas Look,Faris Janjoš,Steffen Hagedorn,Luigi Palmieri,Joschka Boedecker*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes INTERACT, an anchor-conditioned interactive planner that decouples prediction from planning by querying a conditioned predictor per anchor and refining each anchor with trust-region constrained Cross-Entropy Method, achieving state-of-the-art results on nuPlan and interPlan especially in interactive scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In dense urban driving, surrounding agents respond to the intent expressed by a vehicle's trajectory rather than its exact path. Traditional planners either couple prediction and planning (causing task interference) or rely on a fixed proposal set. A decoupled approach with anchor-driven conditioning aims to capture interactions with low computational cost.

Method: Define a small set of anchors derived from map geometry representing driving intents. Query an ego-conditioned predictor once per anchor to forecast responses. For each anchor, refine the plan using Cross-Entropy Method with a trust-region penalty to keep it close to the anchor, ensuring the conditioned reaction remains applicable. Process all anchors in parallel, enabling a single predictor query per anchor and allowing continuous refinement beyond the anchor set.

Result: On nuPlan and interPlan benchmarks, INTERACT achieves state-of-the-art performance, with the largest gains in interactive scenarios that motivated the method. The approach reduces dependency on large numbers of planner proposals by leveraging anchor-conditioned prediction and parallel refinement.

Conclusion: Prediction remains a separate module, avoiding task interference; anchoring preserves the dependency between intent and reaction; continuous refinement yields flexible, high-quality plans not restricted to the anchor set, with efficient computation by limiting predictor queries to one per anchor.

Abstract: Driving in dense urban traffic is interactive: whether a merge or an unprotected turn succeeds depends on how surrounding agents respond to the ego vehicle. Conventional planners predict first and plan second and, therefore, cannot account for this dependency. Methods that integrate prediction and planning either train both jointly, which introduces task interference, or keep them separate and are restricted to a predefined set of proposals. We present INTERACT: Interactive Planning for Autonomous Driving via Anchor-Conditioned Prediction and Trust-Region Refinement. Our key insight is that surrounding agents react to the intent a trajectory expresses rather than to its exact realization, so a single reactive prediction stays valid across an entire family of plans. INTERACT therefore decomposes interactive planning into prediction across driving intents and optimization within each intent. We derive a small set of diverse intents, which we call anchors, from map geometry, query a dedicated ego-conditioned prediction model once per anchor, and refine every anchor with the Cross-Entropy Method under a trust-region penalty that keeps the refined plan close enough to its anchor for the conditioned reaction to still apply. Prediction thus remains a separate model, avoiding task interference, while conditioning on anchors preserves the dependency. Because each anchor is refined continuously, the final plan is not restricted to the anchor set, yet INTERACT requires only one predictor query per anchor rather than one per candidate plan, with all anchors processed in parallel. On the nuPlan and interPlan closed-loop benchmarks, INTERACT sets a new state of the art, with the largest gains precisely in the interactive scenarios that motivate the method. The code will be released upon acceptance.

</details>


### [357] [Evaluating the Impact of Adaptive Extended Reality on Human-Robot Interaction Across the Reality-Virtuality Continuum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31138)
*Carl Tornberg,Alicia Torck,Lotfi El Hafi,Tadahiro Taniguchi*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Adaptive XR modality along the Reality-Virtuality Continuum improves HRI performance with Cybernetic Avatars; fixed AR/AV/VR modes differ in user workload outcomes, and runtime, dynamic modality switching yields the best performance with lower workload.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address aging populations and labor shortages by evaluating how XR modalities and runtime adaptation affect Human-Robot Interaction, aiming to optimize interfaces for cybernetic avatars and robotic control.

Method: Within-subjects design in a multi-room pick-and-place task using a custom XR app linked to a mobile manipulator. Compare fixed AR, AV, VR modalities with a dynamic RVC condition that switches modality at runtime. Assess task metrics, NASA-TLX, and SUS; implementation is publicly available (GitHub).

Result: Fixed reality modality significantly influences HRI performance; the adaptive dynamic RVC condition produced the highest throughput and lowest workload. AR yielded lower mental demand, effort, and frustration than AV or VR.

Conclusion: Adaptive XR interfaces along the Reality-Virtuality Continuum improve human-robot symbiosis. Runtime modality adaptation can enhance performance and reduce workload in HRI tasks; the approach is practical and reproducible via the provided implementation.

Abstract: As populations in developed countries age and labor shortages intensify, Cybernetic Avatars (CAs) are proposed to extend human capabilities through robotic embodiments, requiring effective Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) frameworks. Extended Reality (XR), an umbrella term for Augmented Reality (AR), Augmented Virtuality (AV), and Virtual Reality (VR), offers such interfaces, but prior research typically fixes the XR modality without evaluating its effect on task outcomes. This study examines whether the XR modality impacts HRI performance and whether an adaptive interface adjusting the level of virtuality along the Reality-Virtuality Continuum (RVC) at runtime improves it. A custom XR application interfaced with a mobile manipulator supports immersive control and runtime modality switching. In a within-participant multi-room pick-and-place experiment comparing fixed AR, AV, and VR with dynamic RVC through task metrics, the NASA-TLX, and the System Usability Scale (SUS), this study demonstrates that 1) the fixed reality modality affects HRI results, and 2) dynamically changing the modality along the RVC improves them. AR yielded significantly lower mental demand, effort, and frustration than AV and VR, while the dynamic RVC condition achieved the highest throughput and lowest workload, highlighting the value of adaptive XR interfaces for human-robot symbiosis. The implementation is available at https://github.com/CarlTornberg/XR-HRI.

</details>


### [358] [Onboard Wind-Preview Model Predictive Control Using Pitot-Static Sensing for Multirotor UAVs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31185)
*Bas Meere,Eline Wisse,Laurens Vousten,Sander Doodeman,Elena Torta,Paula Chanfreut,Duarte Antunes*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Wind preview via a pitot-static boom is integrated into nonlinear MPC to anticipate gusts, improving hover stability; optimal boom length depends on wind speed and actuation latency; outdoor tests show substantial wind-aligned error reduction (54%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome reactive gust rejection by measuring wind disturbances after they affect the drone, leveraging a forward wind preview to enhance hover in outdoor environments.

Method: Mount a low-cost pitot-static sensor on a boom to measure wind ahead; feed this preview into a nonlinear MPC that optimizes drone motion considering predicted disturbances; analyze trade-offs with boom length via simulation; validate with indoor hardware experiments and outdoor flights comparing against a PX4 baseline and a wind-unaware MPC.

Result: The optimal wind preview distance is not fixed; it shifts with wind speed and drone responsiveness. Indoor tests show substantial improvement over baselines; outdoor tests report a 54% reduction in wind-direction error compared to baseline.

Conclusion: A single wind-aligned, forward-facing sensor can significantly enhance hover performance in gusty outdoor conditions when integrated into MPC, with the preview horizon governed by wind speed and actuation bandwidth; design must balance preview time against added inertia from a longer boom.

Abstract: Effective wind gust rejection and stable hovering are critical for the outdoor operation of autonomous drones. However, existing gust rejection methods are primarily reactive, inferring the disturbance from the resulting motion or measuring it at the airframe. Either way, the wind has already begun to act before it can be compensated. In this work, we anticipate the gust instead by measuring the wind ahead of the drone with a low-cost, low-weight pitot-static sensor mounted on a boom. The resulting wind preview is incorporated into a nonlinear model predictive controller (MPC), which optimizes the drone motion while anticipating wind disturbances. A longer boom offers more preview time but adds inertia and degrades flight performance. We characterize this trade-off in simulation and show that the optimal preview distance is not a fixed property of the platform, but shifts with the wind speed and with how quickly the drone can respond. Indoor hardware experiments confirm the trend and show that the proposed controller substantially improves hover performance against a PX4 baseline and an otherwise identical wind-unaware MPC. Outdoor experiments show that the error along the wind direction is reduced by 54 percent with respect to the baseline, demonstrating that a single wind-aligned sensor can significantly improve hovering performance.

</details>


### [359] [Enabling a Unified Cross-Domain Representation for Two-Finger Gripper Manipulation via Interaction-Centric Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31207)
*Guanlin Li,Shifeng Bao,Yihan Zhao,Haitao Shen,Haoyang Li,Chen Zhao,Tong Yang,Jie Tang,Jing Zhang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: An interaction-centric framework with a universal gripper abstraction and grounded subtask reasoning enables cross-embodiment imitation learning; it uses VLM+SAM grounding, hybrid global-local features, and a Flow-Matching Transformer to predict 7-DoF actions, achieving competitive scores and extreme zero-shot sim-to-real transfer across heterogeneous robots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the entanglement of task semantics with hardware-specific visual geometry that hinders cross-embodiment generalization and sim-to-real transfer in imitation learning.

Method: 1) Define a parameterized universal gripper abstraction to yield a canonical gripper-frame representation. 2) Use language and RGB-D inputs to infer subtasks and ground an interaction triplet (gripper, held, target) via a vision-language model, with SAM 2.1 masks to reduce queries. 3) Build concise hybrid features by combining target/cotential-field guidance with segmented gripper-frame point clouds for local geometry. 4) Apply a Flow-Matching Transformer to predict smooth 7-DoF action chunks.

Result: In both simulation and real-world tasks, the approach achieves competitive benchmark scores while exhibiting extreme cross-embodiment/cross-viewpoint zero-shot sim-to-real transfer to completely distinct, heterogeneous robot platforms.

Conclusion: The proposed interaction-centric, canonical-gripper framework with VLM grounding and Flow-Matching enables robust cross-embodiment generalization and zero-shot transfer across heterogeneous robots, marking a significant advance in imitation learning.

Abstract: Achieving robust cross-embodiment generalization in imitation learning demands overcoming a critical representation flaw that inextricably entangles task semantics with hardware-specific visual geometry. We propose an interaction-centric framework that leverages the shared structure of two-finger grippers via a parameterized universal gripper abstraction, yielding a canonical gripper-frame representation. Given language and RGB-D observations, a VLM infers the subtask and grounds an interaction triplet (gripper, held, target), while SAM~2.1 tracks masks to reduce VLM queries. We design concise hybrid features that combine target/collision artificial potential fields for global guidance with segmented gripper-frame point clouds for local geometry, and use a Flow-Matching Transformer to predict smooth 7-DoF action chunks. Experiments in simulation and real-world tasks demonstrate that ours is the first imitation learning approach to simultaneously achieve competitive benchmark scores and extreme cross-embodiment/cross-viewpoint zero-shot sim-to-real transfer to completely distinct, heterogeneous robot platforms.

</details>


### [360] [CoralPlan: Observation Skill Selection and Execution for Underwater Robotic Inspection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31211)
*Yuer Gao,Yu Zhao,Yi Cai*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Vision-language CoralPlan selects target-relative observation skills for underwater inspection, linking perception to action; evaluated in simulation/hardware with partial success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Underwater inspection of structurally complex coral requires task-directed viewing motions beyond static target recognition; bridging perception and action to improve data acquisition and task success.

Method: CoralPlan uses a vision-language interface to pick an observation skill (orbit, patch, or survey) from a current camera image and task text; a shared motion interface executes target-relative trajectories; evaluation across 144 simulated episodes and 36 sim–hardware pairs with target-reference poses in a clear-water pool.

Result: Hardware observation completion: 77.8%; joint success: 63.9%; identifies issues with reference mismatch and incomplete observations after skill selection; demonstrates link between observation-skill choice and execution outcomes.

Conclusion: Task-directed observation selection improves measurable underwater acquisition outcomes and reveals where and why acquisition succeeds or fails; highlights need for robust reference matching and observation completeness to improve task success.

Abstract: Underwater robotic inspection depends on acquiring views that reveal task-relevant structure. For a structurally complex coral colony, recognising the target is only the starting point: the robot must select and execute a viewing motion suited to the inspection task. We present CoralPlan, a vision-language system that selects an observation skill from a current camera image and task text supplied by an episode manifest. A shared motion interface executes orbit, patch, or survey as target-relative trajectories; the remaining plan fields provide operator guidance. Observation completion requires target keeping and primitive-specific coverage, while joint success also requires selection to match the recorded reference. We evaluate this interface in 144 simulated episodes and 36 matched simulation-hardware pairs. In a clear-water pool with external target-reference poses, hardware observation completion reaches 77.8% and joint success reaches 63.9%. The experiments identify both reference-mismatched completions and incomplete observations after a matching skill selection. These results connect observation-skill choice to measurable underwater execution outcomes and identify where task-directed acquisition succeeds or fails.

</details>


### [361] [Imp-ACT: Adaptive Impedance Control and Action Chunking with Transformers to Learn Contact-Rich Manipulation from Demonstrations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31225)
*Luca Zanetti,Doganay Sirintuna,Idil Ozdamar,Pietro Balatti,Heng Zhang,Arash Ajoudani*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Direction-dependent stiffness via self-tuning impedance during teleoperation, recorded with visual/motion data, enabling ACT to predict pose, action, and stiffness; improves handling of contact while maintaining task success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the trade-off between accurate motion tracking and compliant interaction in contact-rich manipulation; fixed stiffness at the controller level limits adaptability during contacts.

Method: Self-tuning impedance controller modulates stiffness along the instantaneous direction of motion during teleoperation; adapted stiffness is recorded with visual observations and motion commands; data is used to train Action Chunking with Transformer (ACT) to predict end-effector pose, gripper action, and direction-specific stiffness from multimodal inputs (visual, proprioceptive, wrench).

Result: Compared with fixed low- and high-stiffness baselines, Imp-ACT achieves comparable or higher success while maintaining lower interaction forces; in wiping, reduces contact-force vibration by ~29x vs compliant baseline and ~180x vs stiff baseline; in plug insertion, reduces orthogonal insertion forces by ~43% relative to the better fixed-stiffness baseline.

Conclusion: Incorporating direction-dependent stiffness into demonstration collection and the learning pipeline enables more compliant yet effective contact-rich manipulation, demonstrated on wiping and plug insertion.

Abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires robots to balance accurate motion tracking with compliant interaction, yet most visual-action policies leave compliance fixed at the controller level. We present Imp-ACT, a methodologically grounded and practical approach to incorporating direction-dependent Cartesian stiffness modulation directly into demonstration collection, without manual stiffness selection or offline target reconstruction. During teleoperation, a self-tuning impedance controller adapts stiffness along the instantaneous direction of motion while maintaining compliance in orthogonal directions. The adapted stiffness is applied and recorded alongside visual observations and motion commands, capturing motion and compliance under the same dynamics. We implement this pipeline using Action Chunking with Transformer (ACT) to predict end-effector pose, gripper action, and motion-direction stiffness from visual, proprioceptive, and wrench observations. The performance of Imp-ACT is evaluated on wiping and plug insertion using both success rate and quantitative measures of contact behavior. Compared with fixed low- and high-stiffness baselines, Imp-ACT achieves comparable or higher success while maintaining low interaction forces. In wiping, it reduces contact-force vibration by approximately $29\times$ relative to the compliant baseline and $180\times$ relative to the stiff baseline. In plug insertion, it reduces forces orthogonal to the insertion direction by $43\%$ relative to the better fixed-stiffness baseline. These results highlight the benefit of maintaining sufficient stiffness along the direction needed for task execution while preserving compliance in other directions to limit contact forces and accommodate environmental constraints.

</details>


### [362] [Cybflight: An Embedded Rust Autopilot for Aerial Robotics Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31232)
*Yifan Lin,Chao Qin,H S Helson Go,Hugh H. -T. Liu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Open-source embedded Rust autopilot (Cybflight) that runs MPCTC and INDI entirely on a single STM32H743, enabling indoor flight at 12.38 m/s and outdoor GNSS-enabled flight at 31.4 m/s, without a companion computer; demonstrates a modular, compile-time-optimized autopilot architecture.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lower the barrier for translating aerial robotics from simulation to flight by avoiding the need to rebuild mature autopilots or add companion computers; provide typed, replaceable interfaces for hardware access, perception, estimation, planning, and control.

Method: Develop replaceable Rust implementations of model predictive contour-tracking control (MPCTC) and incremental nonlinear dynamic inversion (INDI) running on one STM32H743 MCU without a companion computer, connected via typed interfaces to a modular autopilot stack.

Result: Demonstrates feasible onboard computation for demanding estimation and nonlinear control on a flight-controller MCU while preserving modular autopilot structure; indoor flight at 12.38 m/s and outdoor GNSS-enabled flight at 31.4 m/s.

Conclusion: Shows that a fully onboard, modular autopilot architecture with on-MCU estimation and nonlinear control is feasible and practical for aerial robotics, aided by Rust’s type-safe, replaceable components.

Abstract: Bringing an aerial robotics method from simulation to flight should not require rebuilding a mature autopilot or adding a companion computer. Cybflight is an open-source embedded Rust research autopilot whose typed, replaceable interfaces connect hardware access, perception, state estimation, trajectory planning, and control. This modular development and compile-time optimization workflow is demonstrated with replaceable Rust implementations of model predictive contour-tracking control (MPCTC) and incremental nonlinear dynamic inversion (INDI) running on one STM32H743 without a companion computer. Using this configuration, the vehicle reaches 12.38 m/s during indoor flight, while an outdoor flight using global navigation satellite system (GNSS) position updates reaches 31.4 m/s. These flights show that running demanding estimation and nonlinear control entirely on a flight-controller microcontroller need not come at the expense of a modular autopilot structure.

</details>


### [363] [Towards VLA-Dreamer: Refining VLA Behavior Using World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31313)
*Parsa Mastouri Kashani,Jan-Gerrit Habekost,Stefan Wermter*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes a sample-efficient Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architecture by learning a predictive world model in the vision encoder's embedding space, enabling short-term planning and reduced data needs; aims to test whether embeddings carry action-relevant dynamics for future prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLAs typically require large imitation datasets and lack an explicit world model; using a non-lossy implicit dynamics model in embedding space could improve sample efficiency and planning.

Method: Train a predictive world model on the VLA vision-embedding space (not raw pixels), leveraging joint embedding predictive architectures; evaluate whether the embeddings are action-relevant for forecasting future states; use the world model to sample actions toward goal images for planning.

Result: No empirical results are reported here as this is a concept paper; the work outlines intended experiments to assess embedding richness and predictive capability for planning and data efficiency.

Conclusion: If vision embeddings capture action-relevant dynamics, embedding-space world models can provide implicit dynamics and short-term planning, potentially reducing data requirements for VLAs.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs), while showing strong potential for robot control, require massive amounts of high-quality imitation learning data. Moreover, the absence of an explicit world model casts further doubt on their control capabilities. In this concept paper, we propose a novel architecture that addresses sample efficiency in VLAs by training a predictive world model on the embedding space of the VLA's vision encoder. We hypothesize that these embeddings are action-relevant and usable for future prediction. To this end, we propose using the suggested architecture to investigate how well these embeddings predict the future based on actions, as the inability to do so would mark a key limitation of VLA architectures: the lack of a non-lossy implicit world model to simulate real-world dynamics. The proposed architecture differs from the standard world model dynamics as the loss comes from the embedding space rather than the pixel space, similar to joint embedding predictive architectures. Furthermore, the trained world model can be utilized for short-term planning tasks by sampling VLA actions given goal images. We intend to examine the richness of vision embeddings in VLAs and reduce their high data requirements through a world model that can also generate plans during inference.

</details>


### [364] [See to Reach, Feel to Grasp: Learning A Blind Grasp Reflex for Anthropomorphic Robotic Hands](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31323)
*Alexander Alexiev,Tzu-Yuan Lin,Sang Min Kim,Ho Jae Lee,Yonghyeon Lee,Sangbae Kim*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes a vision-free, proprioception-only grasping framework that separates global arm motion from local hand contact control. Introduces a blind grasp reflex and a learned stability score, validated in simulation and on hardware, and shown to be composable with diverse arm controllers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the need for robust grasping without visual data or object geometry, enabling a reusable hand-level skill that can be integrated with various arm controllers and reducing reliance on perception-based pose estimation.

Method: A modular architecture with a separate arm controller guiding reach and a hand policy that uses only hand proprioception to grasp and stabilize the object. A learned stable-grasp score determines when the grasp is secure. Training and evaluation occur in both simulation and hardware, with experiments across diverse objects and tests of composition with different arms.

Result: Demonstrates robust blind grasping across diverse objects in both simulation and hardware, and shows seamless composition with a range of arm controllers. The learned grasp score correlates with a physics-based stability measure despite no exposure to contact geometry.

Conclusion: The approach embodies the principle see to reach, feel to grasp, by delivering a reusable hand-level grasp capability that can be integrated with various arm controllers, enabling modular and robust manipulation without vision.

Abstract: In this work we study if a robotic hand using proprioception alone can grasp diverse objects with no visual observation. We present a modular dexterous grasping architecture that separates global arm motion from local contact control. An independently controlled arm guides the hand toward the object, while a reinforcement learning policy grasps and stabilizes it using only hand proprioceptive feedback. We call this \textit{a blind grasp reflex}: grasping without images, object poses, or geometric observations. A learned stable-grasp score determines when the object is securely held, allowing the arm to begin post-grasp manipulation. This separation makes grasping a reusable hand-level skill that can be combined with independently designed arm controllers for various manipulation tasks. Experiments in simulation and on hardware demonstrate robust blind grasping across diverse objects and seamless composition with a range of arm controllers. Moreover, despite never observing contact geometry, the learned grasp score closely aligns with an independent physics-based measure of grasp stability. The resulting approach follows a simple principle: see to reach, feel to grasp. Project page: https://blindgraspreflex.github.io.

</details>


### [365] [Representation-Guided Generation and Integration of Executable Programs for Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31337)
*Ruixiao Yang,Mingxin Yu,Chuchu Fan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: RIVET integrates VLM-generated executable task programs around a shared object-centric representation to create reusable robotic manipulation systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge the gap between independently generated perception, planning, and control components that misalign in geometry and task-level information by providing a unified representation.

Method: Introduce an object-centric representation combining per-object 6D poses and a relation graph; use VLM to generate cooperating perception, rendering, relation-inference, and planning programs that leverage existing packages; author programs once for a domain and reuse them on unseen configurations without regeneration.

Result: Evaluated on cube stacking, tangram rearrangement, and 3D assembly in simulation and on a real robot; 83% overall real-world success by reusing offline-generated systems.

Conclusion: Representation-guided program generation can adapt a common manipulation framework to tasks with varying geometric, relational, and sequential requirements, enabling reusable end-to-end systems without per-task code regeneration.

Abstract: Building a robotic manipulation system requires connecting perception, planning, and control through carefully designed representations and interfaces. VLM code generation offers a way to automate this construction, but independently generated components may operate on incompatible geometric and task-level information. We present Representation-guided Integration of VLM-generated Executable Task programs (RIVET), a framework for generating complete manipulation systems around a shared object-centric representation. The representation combines per-object 6D poses, which preserve the metric information required for action grounding, with a relation graph that exposes the task-level structure required for planning. Guided by this representation, a VLM generates cooperating perception, rendering, relation-inference, and planning programs, each combining task-specific computation with available packages where useful. The resulting programs are authored once for a manipulation domain and reused on unseen start and goal configurations without code regeneration. We evaluate RIVET on cube stacking, tangram rearrangement, and three-dimensional assembly in simulation and on a physical robot, where we achieve 83% overall success rate in the real world by reusing offline-generated systems. Our results demonstrate that representation-guided program generation can adapt a common manipulation framework to tasks with different geometric, relational, and sequential requirements.

</details>


### [366] [Transformer-based Monte Carlo Localization in Construction Meshes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31357)
*Linus Kramer,William Talbot,Olga Vysotska,Marco Hutter*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: LiDAR-based global relocalization for construction robots using synthetic training data, integrating a PointNet++ encoder with a place-recognition decoder to form a learned observation model for Monte Carlo Localization; robust via an uncertainty-aware decoder and resampling; exceeds diffusion-based and ScanContext++ baselines with fast 18 ms inference; validates synthetic-data training for mesh-referenced global localization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Localization on construction sites requires reliable global positioning relative to a building mesh in environments with repeated room layouts and low-texture surfaces, where traditional LiDAR/vision methods fail. The work aims to enable robust, real-time global relocalization by leveraging synthetic training data to model observations within a mesh context.

Method: A LiDAR-based global relocalization pipeline that uses a PointNet++ encoder coupled with a place recognition decoder to produce a learned observation model for Monte Carlo Localization (MCL). The system is trained exclusively on synthetic LiDAR scans generated inside the building mesh. It employs an uncertainty-aware decoder to scale positional likelihoods and a resampling strategy to reintroduce hypotheses, mitigating particle depletion.

Result: On real-world datasets, the method outperforms diffusion-based and ScanContext++ baselines while maintaining fast inference (approximately 18 ms per call). This demonstrates the practicality of synthetic-data training for mesh-referenced global localization in construction robotics.

Conclusion: Synthetic-data training for mesh-referenced global localization is effective; the proposed approach provides robust, fast localization in challenging, low-texture environments and supports practical deployment on construction sites.

Abstract: To be able to perform inspection or digitization tasks, mobile robots on construction sites must be able to localize themselves reliably with respect to a global reference frame that is shared with a building map. Similar room layouts and low-texture surfaces pose a challenge for existing LiDAR- and vision-based localization methods. We approach this problem with a LiDAR-based global relocalization system that estimates the robot's pose relative to a building mesh and combines a PointNet++ encoder with a place recognition decoder, whose outputs serve as a learned observation model within a Monte Carlo Localization (MCL) framework. The pipeline is trained exclusively on synthetic LiDAR scans obtained by simulating the robot's sensors inside the building mesh. Our approach is robust in ambiguous environments due to an uncertainty-aware decoder that scales positional likelihoods and a resampling strategy that injects model hypotheses into the particle set, enabling recovery from potential particle depletion. Evaluations on real-world datasets show that our method outperforms both diffusion-based and ScanContext++ baselines while maintaining fast inference (18 ms per call), demonstrating the practicality of synthetic-data training for mesh-referenced global localization in construction robotics.

</details>


### [367] [RECAST: From Log Replay to Closed-Loop Driving Simulation with View-Complete Actors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31374)
*Zijun Zhao,Liewen Liao,Kang Shen,Songan Zhang,Ming Yang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: RECAST uses 3D Gaussian Splatting to reconstruct a view-complete actor from a single vehicle observation for closed-loop driving simulation; RECAR provides real-vehicle image data; two-stage adaptation improves realism; experiments show reduced inception-face-distance-like metrics and improved planner safety metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To maintain reliable, view-consistent rendered observations in closed-loop driving simulation when ego and surrounding actors move beyond recorded trajectories, where log-derived reconstructions often produce artifacts.
