Method: Generate a view-complete actor from a single segmented vehicle observation using 3D Gaussian Splatting and register it in the scene; support planner-in-the-loop rendering with ego-actor interactions; introduce RECAR, a dataset of ~20k real vehicles with 600k background-free RGBA images; apply two-stage adaptation to improve vehicle generation from real driving-log observations.

Result: Actor-level FD_incep reduced from 9.788 to 7.992 (relative to unadapted TRELLIS); scene-level FD_incep reduced from 129.35 to 112.10; CLIP_margin (×1000) increased from 0.14 to 3.47 relative to Street Gaussians. Planner-in-loop with GTRS-Dense: no-collision rate 63.0% (34/54) vs 22.2% (12/54) and minimum predicted TTC improved from 0.798 s to 2.150 s.

Conclusion: RECAST enables closed-loop planner evaluation beyond log replay by reconstructing controllable 3D actors; two-stage adaptation improves realism for real-vehicle data via RECAR; demonstrates improved safety metrics in planner-in-loop experiments.

Abstract: Closed-loop driving simulation requires rendered observations to remain reliable as the ego vehicle and surrounding actors move beyond their recorded trajectories, exposing views absent from the source log. Existing data-driven simulators reconstruct dynamic actors from sparse observations, which can result in rendering artifacts under these viewpoint changes. We introduce RECAST (REconstructing Controllable Actors for Simulation and Testing), a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that generates a view-complete actor from a single segmented vehicle observation in a driving log and registers the generated actor in the reconstructed scene. RECAST supports planner-in-the-loop rendering under controlled ego-actor interactions. To adapt an image-to-3D prior to real vehicles, we further introduce RECAR, a dataset of approximately 20K real vehicles with 600K background-free RGBA images spanning diverse vehicle colors and types. We use two-stage adaptation to improve vehicle generation from real driving-log observations. At the actor level, RECAST reduces $\mathrm{FD}_{\mathrm{incep}}$ from 9.788 to 7.992 relative to unadapted TRELLIS. At the scene level, under actor motion beyond logged trajectories, RECAST reduces $\mathrm{FD}_{\mathrm{incep}}$ from 129.35 to 112.10 and increases $\mathrm{CLIP}_{\mathrm{margin}}$ ($\times1000$) from 0.14 to 3.47 relative to Street Gaussians. We demonstrate planner-in-the-loop simulation with the image-conditioned planner GTRS-Dense. Compared with native Street Gaussians actors, RECAST increases the no-collision (NC) rate from 22.2% (12/54) to 63.0% (34/54) and the mean minimum predicted time-to-collision (TTC) from 0.798 s to 2.150 s. These experiments show that RECAST supports closed-loop planner evaluation under controlled ego-actor interactions beyond log replay. Visit our project page at https://zijunkr.github.io/RECAST/

</details>


### [368] [Guiding End-to-End Driving Models with Endpoint-Constrained Trajectory Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31383)
*Brayden Zhang,Mahsa Golchoubian,Igor Gilitschenski,Boris Ivanovic,Kashyap Chitta*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: ECO is a postprocessing layer that fixes intermediate trajectory geometry in end-to-end driving without retraining or maps, improving closed-loop performance across multiple policies and simulators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-loop training. the open-loop–closed-loop gap arises not only from covariate shift and causal confusion but also from waypoint-based supervision that yields incoherent intermediate trajectories; endpoints are relatively reliable. Fixing intermediate geometry can improve controller feasibility and closed-loop scores.

Method: Endpoint-Constrained Optimization (ECO) anchors the trajectory to the vehicle's executed history, preserves the policy's predicted endpoint, and reshapes intermediate waypoints to improve feasibility. It requires no map, no privileged simulator state, and no additional training, and can be inserted between waypoint-emitting policies and their controllers.

Result: Across two closed-loop simulators and six evaluated policies, ECO improves aggregate closed-loop scores. On HUGSIM, VaVAM improved from 18.1 to 31.0 HD-Score (+71%), achieving 1st place on the HUGSIM Closed-Loop Driving Challenge. On AlpaSim, VaVAM and DiffusionDrive scene scores increased by 123% and 22%, respectively, demonstrating that repairing intermediate trajectory geometry can substantially improve closed-loop performance without altering the policy endpoint.

Conclusion: Repairing intermediate trajectory geometry via a lightweight postprocessing step yields substantial closed-loop gains across diverse end-to-end driving models, validating ECO as a general plug-in to improve controller feasibility without retraining or additional data.

Abstract: End-to-end driving policies are commonly trained through open-loop behavior cloning, yet they must ultimately operate in closed-loop when deployed on a vehicle, creating a fundamental mismatch between training and execution. Beyond the commonly studied effects of covariate shift and causal confusion, we identify a complementary factor for this open-loop/closed-loop gap: waypoint-based supervision and displacement metrics do not ensure that the intermediate trajectory is physically coherent or easy for the controller to track. We observe that these inconsistencies concentrate primarily at intermediate waypoints, while the predicted endpoint remains comparatively reliable. Based on this observation, we introduce Endpoint-Constrained Optimization (ECO), a lightweight postprocessing layer that anchors the trajectory to the vehicle's executed history, preserves the policy's predicted endpoint, and reshapes the intermediate waypoints to improve feasibility. ECO requires no map, privileged simulator state, or additional training, and can be inserted between a broad range of waypoint-emitting policies and their controllers. Across two closed-loop simulators, it improves the aggregate closed-loop score of all six evaluated generative and regression-based driving policies, and the gains tend to increase with how often the base plans violate motion limits. On HUGSIM, ECO improves VaVAM from 18.1 to 31.0 HD-Score (+71%), achieving 1st place on the HUGSIM Closed-Loop Driving Challenge. Similarly, on AlpaSim, ECO increases the scene scores of VaVAM and DiffusionDrive by 123% and 22%, respectively. These results show that for a broad collection of end-to-end driving models, repairing the intermediate geometry of predicted trajectories without changing the policy's predicted endpoint can substantially improve closed-loop performance.

</details>


### [369] [Modeling and Generative-AI-Based Design of Load-Adaptive Gravity Balancing Mechanisms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31386)
*Ryotaro Kayawake,Kazuki Abe,Shota Miyake,Masahiro Watanabe,Kenjiro Tadakuma*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: LA-GBMs adapt to payload by using general potential-field design forms that are architecture-agnostic. Two core forms are derived: an affine form for payload mass and a factorized form for load-adaptation/state transitions. Generative AI is used to propose candidate potential functions, which are analytically checked against the forms and validity conditions. The potentials are decomposed into terms, and an example construction using springs, counterweights, and function-generating linkages is shown. The approach enables design without pre-specifying mechanisms, but practical realizability and manufacturability remain future work.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The design of load-adaptive gravity balancing mechanisms is difficult because required motion and static balance must hold under varying payloads. A general, architecture-agnostic framework is needed to generate viable candidate designs.

Method: Formulate necessary conditions for LA-GBM potential fields. Derive two general forms: (i) an affine form capturing payload mass effects, and (ii) a factorized form capturing state transitions during load adaptation and gravity balancing. Provide these forms as design requirements to generative AI to produce candidate potential functions. Analytically verify that generated potentials conform to the forms and validity conditions. Decompose verified potentials into terms. Present a constructive example combining springs, counterweights, and function-generating linkages.

Result: Generated potential functions are analytically shown to satisfy the two general forms and related conditions. Potentials are decomposed into constitutive terms. An example construction method integrating springs, counterweights, and linkage-based function generation is demonstrated.

Conclusion: Using potential fields as an intermediate representation allows generating LA-GBM design candidates without fixing a mechanism architecture in advance; however, mechanical realizability and manufacturability of the generated potential fields require future work.

Abstract: Load-adaptive gravity balancing mechanisms (LA-GBMs) can accommodate various loading conditions by passively changing their characteristics in response to payload variations. However, their design is difficult because both the desired mechanism motion and static equilibrium under variable payloads must be satisfied simultaneously. This study proposes a general design methodology for LA-GBMs that does not depend on specific mechanism architectures or mechanical elements. The necessary conditions for the potential fields of LA-GBMs are formulated, and two general forms are derived: an affine form representing the effect of payload mass and a factorized form representing state transitions associated with load adaptation and gravity balancing. These forms are then provided to generative AI as design requirements to generate candidate potential functions. The generated functions are analytically verified in terms of their conformity to the two general forms and the conditions required for valid LA-GBMs. Furthermore, the obtained potential functions are decomposed into individual terms, and an example of a method for constructing an LA-GBM by combining springs, counterweights, and function-generating linkage mechanisms is presented. By using potential functions as an intermediate representation, the proposed framework enables the generation of LA-GBM design candidates without prescribing a mechanism architecture in advance. Mechanical realizability and manufacturability of the generated potential fields remain important issues for future work.

</details>


### [370] [InternW0-$Δ$: A World Action Model Bridging Predictive Dynamics and Actions with 20K+ Hours of Open Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31394)
*Xingyu Miao,Zizun Li,Baole Fang,Kaiwen Song,Tenghui Wang,Hanxue Zhang,Yating Wang,Xudong Li,Yuping He,Xueyuan Wei,Chao Gao,Xijie Yang,Yingxiang Xu,Kerui Ren,Wenqi Guo,Jianjun Zhou,Xinzhe Wang,Weiguang Zhao,Ni Yang,Zetao Cai,Yufei Xue,Hengjie Li,Zeyu He,Yuanzhen Zhou,Rong Fu,Jianyang Zhang,Siwei Cui,Fuxian Huang,Yunsong Zhou,Xing Gao,Yifei Yao,Qiaojun Yu,Kailin Li,Ming Zhou,Mu Huang,Xinyue Li,Wenze Cui,Bingqi Jiang,Xueyue Zhu,Junting Dong,Haoyu Guo,Tao Lu,Mulin Yu,Bowen Zhou,Bin Zhao,Tianfan Xue,Weinan Zhang,Chunhua Shen*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: InternW0-Δ introduces a unified World Action Model pretrained on a heterogeneous, multi-modal corpus, combining visual dynamics, semantics, 4D geometry and motion priors with action generation via a Mixture-of-Transformers. It adds Causal Imprint for future-relevant scene changes, and shows strong sim and real-robot performance; open-sourcing planned.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the integration gap for priors derived from large-scale pretrained models in robot manipulation, by unifying visual dynamics, scene semantics, geometry, and motion priors into a single action-generation framework.

Method: A Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture with a video expert and an action expert interacting under guidance from a frozen vision-language model (VLM), plus a 4D foundation model infused via training-time distillation. Causal Imprint provides predictive scene-change representations from training-only future supervision without relying on future-video rollout at inference. Training uses a heterogeneous corpus (~20k hours) of robot demonstrations, UMI data, egocentric human demonstrations, and Ego2Robot data, aligned under a common state-action space. Pretraining on this corpus yields InternW0-Δ, with planned open-source release of code, weights, data pipelines, and processed data.

Result: Outperforms prior methods on both simulation benchmarks and real-robot platforms; demonstrates the benefits of large-scale cross-modal priors and 4D priors in unified action generation; claims the largest open-source multi-source corpus for this domain (~20k hours).

Conclusion: Shows the promise of large-scale, cross-modal pretraining for unified robot action generation, and positions InternW0-Δ as a versatile foundation for generalist manipulation, with open-source contributions enabling broader adoption and benchmarking.

Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly model visual dynamics and action generation for generalist robot manipulation. A central challenge is to integrate priors from large-scale pretrained models---including visual dynamics, scene semantics, geometry, and motion---into a unified framework for robot action generation. We introduce InternW0-$Δ$, a unified WAM pretrained on a heterogeneous corpus that outperforms prior methods across simulation benchmarks and real-robot platforms.
  InternW0-$Δ$ combines pretrained visual dynamics, scene-level semantics, 4D geometric and motion priors, and action generation within a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) framework. A pretrained video expert and an action expert interact under semantic guidance from a frozen VLM, while a pretrained 4D foundation model injects geometric and motion priors through training-only distillation. We further introduce Causal Imprint, which learns future-relevant scene changes from training-only future supervision and provides predictive representations directly to the action expert without future-video rollout at inference.
  For large-scale joint training, we construct a heterogeneous corpus of robot demonstrations, UMI data, egocentric human demonstrations, and Ego2Robot data, curated and aligned under a common state-action representation. The resulting corpus contains over 20K hours of processed training data, to our knowledge the largest open-source corpus of its kind. We pretrain InternW0-$Δ$ on this corpus and demonstrate strong performance across simulation benchmarks and real-robot platforms. We will open source the training code, model weights, infrastructure, data-processing pipeline, and processed data where licenses permit. Project page: https://internrobotics.github.io/InternW0-Delta/

</details>


### [371] [Augmented Reality Interfaces for Human-Robot Collaboration: Development of a ROS 2-Based Sensor Streaming Framework and Validation via SLAM Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31396)
*Alessandro Rubert,Stefano Ghidoni,Matteo Terreran*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A sensor streaming framework links Magic Leap 2 AR headset with ROS 2 to enable real-time, bidirectional sensing for HRC, validated with SLAM to assess accuracy, latency, and robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge AR visualization and spatial data gathering with robotic control in Industry 4.0 HRC, enabling real-time interaction and shared spatial awareness through a robust data pipeline.

Method: Develop on-board AR headset application in Unity using the ROSTCP-Connector to publish real-time sensor data (pose, cameras, env sensors) to ROS 2 topics; test framework with SLAM algorithms to evaluate accuracy, latency, and robustness of data streams.

Result: Achieved stable data transmission between the Magic Leap 2 headset and ROS 2; demonstrated viability for safe real-time interaction and shared spatial awareness; opens pathways for improved control and supervision in complex HRC scenarios.

Conclusion: The proposed AR-ROS 2 sensor streaming architecture provides reliable real-time multi-sensor data integration for HRC, enabling enhanced control, monitoring, and collaboration in Industry 4.0 environments.

Abstract: In recent years, Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) has taken on a central role in Industry 4.0 and collaborative robotics, demanding communication channels that are increasingly bidirectional, intuitive, and efficient. In this context, Augmented Reality (AR) presents itself as a fundamental enabling technology, capable of both displaying information to the operator and gathering spatial data about the surrounding environment. This thesis presents the development of a sensor streaming framework that connects the Magic Leap 2 AR headset with the ROS 2 (Robot Operating System) ecosystem. Using the Unity development environment and the ROSTCP-Connector package, an on-board application for the headset was developed, capable of acquiring real-time data from the integrated sensors (pose tracking, cameras, and environmental sensors) and publishing it to dedicated ROS 2 topics. In order to test the accuracy, latency, and robustness of the generated data stream, the framework was validated using SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) algorithms known in the literature. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed architecture ensures stable data transmission, laying the groundwork for safe real-time interaction and shared spatial awareness, and opening up new perspectives for the control and supervision of robotic systems in complex HRC scenarios.

</details>


### [372] [dRVG: Quadtree-Guided, Resolution-Complete Online Motion Planning for Polygonal Robots in Unknown Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31412)
*Duo Zhang,Hechen Zhang,Junshan Huang,Jingjin Yu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: An online motion planner (dRVG) for polygonal robots in unknown static environments merges local roadmaps from successive observations with a rotation-aware visibility graph, using a spatial quadtree to schedule sensing while preserving orientation configurations. It is resolution-complete relative to a full-map RVG under certain assumptions and shows strong empirical performance (140 cases, 20 maps, 7 angular resolutions, 20 s budget; median 1.18 s at 360 orientations) with demonstrations on a real robot.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable efficient online planning for polygonal robots requiring both translation and rotation in unknown, static environments, without relying on a uniform position grid, while ensuring completeness relative to an ideal full-map planner.

Method: Introduce dynamic rotation-stacked visibility graph (dRVG) that incrementally merges local roadmaps from successive observations. Use a spatial quadtree to distribute sensing goals across regions to reduce revisits while preserving all orientation configurations for routing. Plan via center scans; assume exact sensing and geometric computation and star-shaped robot and envelope; achieve resolution completeness relative to full-map RVG at the same angular resolution.

Result: Empirically strong performance: all 140 cases across 20 difficult maps and seven angular resolutions solved within 20 seconds, median planning time 1.18 seconds at 360 orientation layers. Six microMVP demonstrations on a real robot illustrate the complete online planning loop.

Conclusion: dRVG provides a practical, rotation-aware online planning framework with no uniform position grid, achieving resolution-completeness under stated assumptions and demonstrated effectiveness in simulation and on hardware; it offers a scalable approach to planning translations and rotations in unknown environments.

Abstract: We present the dynamic rotation-stacked visibility graph (dRVG), an online motion planner that guides polygonal robots to specified goals in initially unknown, static environ- ments. It merges local roadmaps from successive observations to plan collision-free translations and rotations without a uniform position grid. A spatial quadtree schedules sensing goals across regions to reduce repeated visits while retaining all orientation configurations for routing. Under exact sensing and geometric computation and star-shaped robot and envelope assumptions, dRVG with center scans is resolution-complete relative to full- map RVG at the same angular resolution. In experiments using footprint scans, dRVG solves all 140 cases across 20 difficult maps and seven angular resolutions within a 20 s planning budget, with a median planning time of 1.18 s at 360 orientation layers. Six microMVP demonstrations illustrate the complete online planning loop on a physical robot.

</details>


### [373] [CognitiveReality: Robot-Agnostic Semantic Gaussian Mapping with an LLM Agent for Immersive Collaborative VR Teleoperation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31418)
*Timofei Kozlov,Dmitrii Maliukov,Andrey Marchenko,Dmitrii Plotnikov,Miguel Altamirano Cabrera,Dzmitry Tsetserukou*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: CognitiveReality is a platform-agnostic, semantically indexed Gaussian-TSDF mapping pipeline that fuses a robot's perception with VR operator interfaces and language-grounded tools, enabling robust object awareness, action grounding, and improved performance under SLAM outages, validated on simulated and real robots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge the gap between photorealistic 3D views and semantic scene understanding for teleoperation, enabling open-vocabulary object identities, reliable tool use, and grounding of human actions (speech, pointing) into robot actions despite localization outages.

Method: A mapper binary ingests multiple pose streams (robot SLAM, joint kinematics, motion capture, inline visual tracker), maintains a Gaussian-TSDF map with semantic indexing and per-object quality; uses a shadow tracker and keyframe-anchored PnP to bridge localization outages; supports open-vocabulary instance identities with per-object quality at 2 Hz; grounds speech and controller rays to persistent scene objects via validated typed tools and operator-confirmed robot actions; platform-agnostic, VR operator interface, local reasoning with Qwen3-VL-8B router; merge-aware replay to redirect absorbed object identifiers; deployed on two quadrupeds.

Result: Controlled agent evaluation shows 81.24% tool exact match; 101 absorbed object identifiers correctly redirected via merge-aware replay; on robot data, CognitiveReality improves Gaussian+SDF baseline by 2–8 dB; pose error during 5–40 s SLAM outages remains 1–8 cm; live deployment on two quadrupeds yields 26/30 navigation requests and 20/20 re-observation requests, with object quality improving by 2–5 dB.

Conclusion: CognitiveReality delivers robust, semantically enriched 3D mapping and grounding for teleoperation across platforms, maintaining high tool grounding accuracy and resilience to localization outages, and enabling measurable improvements in perception and navigation in real-world deployments.

Abstract: A photorealistic 3D view tells a teleoperator where a robot is, but not what the scene contains, how well each object has been observed, or how to turn pointing and speech into robot action. CognitiveReality turns a robot's RGB-D stream into a live, semantically indexed Gaussian-TSDF map shared by an operator in virtual reality and a tool-using language agent. One mapper binary serves any platform through configuration alone: it ingests poses from robot SLAM, joint kinematics, motion capture or an inline visual tracker, bridges localization outages with a shadow tracker and keyframe-anchored PnP, and maintains open-vocabulary instance identities with per-object quality at 2 Hz. Speech and controller rays are grounded against persistent scene objects through validated typed tools and operator-confirmed robot actions. In the controlled agent evaluation, the deployed local Qwen3-VL-8B router reaches 81.24\% tool exact match, while merge-aware replay correctly redirects 101 absorbed object identifiers. On robot data CognitiveReality exceeds a Gaussian-plus-SDF baseline by 2-8 dB; pose error through 5-40 s SLAM outages stays within 1-8 cm. Deployed live on two quadrupeds, the agent executed 26 of 30 navigation requests and 20 of 20 re-observation requests, raising object quality by 2-5 dB.

</details>


### [374] [ExoLaN: Physics-Consistent Context-Aware Dynamics Learning for Exoskeletons](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31434)
*Lucas Schulze,Maximilian Schwarz,Jona Hoppe,Jan Peters,Oleg Arenz*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: ExoLaN extends Deep Lagrangian Networks to be context-aware for human-exoskeleton interaction, enabling task-agnostic control by fusing temporal context and partial contact-force data to infer latent dynamics and estimate generalized contact torques; shows improvements in torque estimation and forward prediction on unseen users/tasks, and reveals latent task information without explicit labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need for flexible, task-agnostic assistive control that adapts to individual users and intermittent contacts without retraining on each new user or task. Physics-informed methods like DeLaN struggle with adaptation and contact intermittency.

Method: Introduce ExoLaN, a Context-Aware DeLaN that learns the full coupled human-exoskeleton dynamics and adapts to interaction context. Combines temporal context with partial contact-force measurements from force-sensitive insoles to infer latent dynamics embeddings and estimate generalized contact torques. Enables unified inverse and forward dynamics modeling; uses multi-step prediction loss to improve long-horizon predictions.

Result: Torque estimation MSE on seven unseen users performing 21 unseen tasks improves by 7% over a black-box baseline. Forward prediction benefits: multi-step prediction reduces acceleration MSE by 59% and long-horizon position/velocity errors by 60% and 93% respectively compared with single-step loss. The latent context captures task information without explicit task labels.

Conclusion: ExoLaN provides a unified, context-aware model for inverse and forward dynamics in human-exoskeleton interaction, enabling task-aware assistive control without explicit task labeling; promising for robust, adaptive exoskeleton assistance.

Abstract: Task-agnostic assistive exoskeleton control based on human intention offers greater flexibility than conventional approaches that rely on predefined tasks or motion patterns. Human joint torque estimation enables task-agnostic assistance by characterizing user actions. Physics-consistent methods such as Deep Lagrangian Networks (DeLaN) have been applied to estimate the human torques in multi-user settings, but existing approaches cannot adapt to a specific user without retraining, and do not account for intermittent contacts during locomotion. We propose ExoLaN, a Context-Aware DeLaN for human-exoskeleton interaction that learns the full coupled system dynamics while adapting to changes in interaction context. ExoLaN combines temporal context with partial contact-force measurements from force-sensitive insoles to infer latent dynamics embeddings and estimate generalized contact torques. On seven unseen users performing 21 unseen tasks, ExoLaN reduces torque estimation MSE by 7% compared to a black-box baseline. Beyond inverse dynamics, ExoLaN serves as a unified model that also enables accurate forward prediction: training with a multi-step prediction loss reduces acceleration MSE by 59% and long-horizon position and velocity errors by 60% and 93%, respectively, compared with a single-step loss. Moreover, the learned latent context captures task information without explicit task labels, making it a promising signal for task-aware assistive control.

</details>


### [375] [Learning to Leverage Compliance: A Policy-Admittance Learning Framework for Robotic Insertion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31439)
*Chongren Wang,Minghe Li,Honghua Dai,Zhicheng Lin,Shiyang Wei,Xiaokui Yue*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: LeCo learns to leverage fixed mechanical compliance by turning multirate policy-admittance interactions into reward signals, reducing loading and improving success in contact-rich assembly (94% success across four tasks; ~30% force and ~64% torque peak reductions).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In contact-rich autonomous assembly, a learning policy and a compliant controller can conflict (policy pushes, controller yields), causing sustained loading with little progress. A coordinating framework is needed to exploit compliance and ensure productive interaction.

Method: LeCo (Leverage Compliance) is a policy-admittance learning framework with fixed admittance. It uses a multirate feedback mechanism to translate high-rate contact-interaction records into policy-transition rewards. An integrated conflict cost penalizes sustained policy-loading/controller-unloading opposition, and a directional high-force tail cost penalizes continued-loading events within a transition. Task completion is also rewarded. Evaluated on four real connector-assembly tasks.

Result: Aggregate success rate: 94%. Across tasks, mean successful-trial resultant-force peaks decreased by ~30% and torque peaks by ~64% relative to a baseline. Reward ablation shows conflict shaping reduces median successful-trial contact-conditioned conflict density by ~53%.

Conclusion: Learning to leverage fixed compliance via reward design and multirate policy-admittance interaction yields effective, lower-load insertions in contact-rich assembly tasks.

Abstract: Policy learning and compliant control offer a promising route to reliable autonomous assembly under pose errors and contact uncertainty. However, combining them does not ensure coordination: the policy may continue pushing against contact while the controller yields, producing sustained loading with limited progress. To address this problem, we propose LeCo (Leverage Compliance), a policy-admittance learning framework that guides a visual policy through execution-time interaction under fixed admittance. A multirate feedback mechanism aggregates high-rate contact-interaction records into policy-transition rewards. An integrated conflict cost then characterizes sustained policy-loading/controller-unloading opposition, while a directional high-force tail cost captures continued-loading events within a transition. Together with task completion, these costs encourage the policy to leverage compliance with less unproductive loading. We evaluate LeCo on four real connector-assembly tasks, obtaining an aggregate success rate of 94%. Across tasks, mean successful-trial resultant-force and torque peaks decrease by approximately 30% and 64% relative to the comparison baseline. Reward ablation further shows that adding conflict shaping reduces median successful-trial contact-conditioned conflict density by approximately 53%. These results support learning to leverage fixed compliance by turning multirate policy-admittance interaction into complementary reward signals for effective, lower-load insertion.

</details>


### [376] [Vision-Based 6-DoF Grasp Pose Estimation for Robot Cloth Unfolding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31452)
*Domen Tabernik,Peter Nimac,Jan Jerićević,Danijel Skočaj,Andrej Gams*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: CeDiRNet-6DoF proposes a joint 6-DoF grasp pose and optimal grasp point predictor for cloth unfolding in a bimanual setup, using dense 3D grasp regression plus segmentation and sine-cosine-encoded Euler angles; achieves state-of-the-art on ICRA 2024 Cloth Competition with ablations validating key components.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cloth manipulation is highly challenging due to deformability, high-dimensional state, and perceptual ambiguity from occlusions (folds, edges, grasp points). An in-air regrasping strategy requires reliable prediction of where to grasp to unfold cloth effectively.

Method: A deep learning framework (CeDiRNet-6DoF) that jointly predicts the optimal grasp point and the complete 6-DoF grasp pose from observed cloth configuration. Integrates dense 3D grasp regression with segmentation and sine-cosine-encoded Euler angles. Includes ablations on joint segmentation, background randomization, and image cropping; evaluated in a bimanual setup.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ICRA 2024 Cloth Competition framework; ablation study confirms benefits of key components, showing robustness and reliability in unstructured environments.

Conclusion: CeDiRNet-6DoF provides a robust and versatile foundation for reliable robotic cloth manipulation in unstructured environments, with strong potential for generalization to related deformable-object manipulation tasks.

Abstract: Cloth manipulation is a challenging task due to the deformable and high-dimensional nature of cloth, which leads to complex interaction dynamics and perceptual ambiguity arising from frequent occlusions of critical visual cues such as folds, edges, and grasp points. In this work, we tackle cloth unfolding using a regrasping-in-the-air strategy, where one manipulator holds the cloth while the other grasps it at an optimally selected point to unfold it. To this end, we propose CeDiRNet-6DoF, a deep learning framework that jointly predicts effective grasp points and the complete 6-DoF grasp pose from the observed cloth configuration. By integrating dense 3D grasp regression with segmentation and sine-cosine-encoded Euler angles, the proposed method reliably estimates the grasp configuration that maximizes the unfolded cloth area. We extensively evaluated CeDiRNet-6DoF on a bimanual robotic setup within the ICRA 2024 Cloth Competition framework, achieving state-of-the-art performance. An ablation study further validates the benefits of key design components, including joint segmentation, background randomization, and image cropping. These results establish CeDiRNet-6DoF as a robust and versatile foundation for reliable robotic cloth manipulation in unstructured environments.

</details>


### [377] [Generate, Track, Improve: Perceptive Multi-Skill Humanoid Locomotion with RL-Fine-Tuned Motion Generators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31577)
*Zachary Olkin,William D. Compton,Aaron D. Ames*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A two-layer perceptive locomotion system using a depth-based motion generator and tracking policy, trained on terrain-consistent human-derived motion clips, with an off-policy RL fine-tuning loop that improves terrain performance and skill selection for outdoor humanoid locomotion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Create versatile, robust humanoid locomotion that operates across diverse terrains using perception from depth sensors, without reliance on odometry or height maps, and with sample-efficient learning to enhance motion generation and skill composition.

Method: (1) A perceptive flow-matching motion generator plans full-body trajectories from raw depth images. (2) A perceptive tracking policy, trained with control-guided RL, follows these motions. Training data come from a library of terrain-consistent motion clips generated from dynamically optimized human data. A central off-policy fine-tuning loop improves the motion generator via a structured search method to collect data for advantage-weighted regression (AWR). This loop is more sample-efficient than on-policy residual fine-tuning and enhances terrain consistency for unseen geometries and skill compositions. (3) The system uses raw depth imagery (no odometry/height maps); two cameras extend lookahead; a single policy pair enables a Unitree G1 to perform walking, running, standing, jumping on/off boxes, and stair traversal outdoors.

Result: The approach yielded up to 25 percentage points improvement in successful terrain traversals and up to 80 percentage points improvement in skill selection. It enables outdoor deployment without odometry, with depth-based perception. The policy, with two cameras, can anticipate terrain and adjust velocity to traverse varied terrains, demonstrating broad skill coverage on the Unitree G1."

Conclusion: A data-efficient, perception-driven two-layer locomotion framework with an off-policy fine-tuning loop enhances terrain-adaptive gait generation and skill composition, enabling robust outdoor humanoid locomotion using depth perception and a single policy pair.

Abstract: General purpose humanoids require locomotion controllers that are multi-skill, perceptive, dynamic, and robust enough to go anywhere humans can. In this work, we present a two layer locomotion architecture: (1) a perceptive flow matching motion generator plans whole body trajectories from raw depth images while a (2) perceptive tracking policy trained with control-guided RL follows these motions. Both policies are trained on a library of terrain consistent motion clips created with dynamically optimized human data which yields both accurate velocity tracking and terrain consistent references. Our central contribution is a simple yet effective off-policy RL fine tuning loop that improves the motion generator. A structured search method is used with the generator to gather data for advantage weighted regression. This off-policy loop is much more sample efficient than on-policy residual fine tuning and improves terrain consistency on unseen geometries and skill compositions. We find that successful terrain traversals increased by up to 25 percentage points and skill selection improved by up to 80 percentage points. By using raw depth images to perceive the environment no odometry or height maps are needed, and outdoor deployment is easy. With two cameras, the policy can see terrain coming from further away and adjust its velocity regardless of the commanded speed so it can traverse the terrain. A single policy pair enables a Unitree G1 humanoid to walk, run, stand, jump on and off of boxes, and traverse stairs in outdoor environments. Project page: https://zolkin1.github.io/generate-track-improve/

</details>


### [378] [Learning Robot Policies from Sparse Success Signals via STL-Guided Stein Variational Policy Gradient](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31606)
*Hongrui Zheng,Cristian Ioan Vasile,Antonio Loquercio,Rahul Mangharam*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: STL-SVPG uses Signal Temporal Logic robustness as a trajectory-level objective in a SVPG framework to learn policies for sparse, temporally structured robotics tasks, achieving strong success and sim-to-real transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning robot policies under sparse success signals is challenging when success depends on coordinated actions, precise contacts, or satisfying several conditions; conventional reward shaping may misalign local progress with task completion.

Method: Integrate smooth STL robustness as a trajectory-level training objective within Stein Variational Policy Gradient (SVPG), differentiating through the dynamics to credit actions by their contribution to the full task specification; evaluate on six quadcopter and manipulator tasks with event-triggered, ordered, deadline-bound, and contact requirements; demonstrate sim-to-real transfer.

Result: STL-SVPG attains the highest mean success rate among compared methods on five of six benchmarks; policies trained in simulation transfer temporal and contact-task behavior to the real world.

Conclusion: Formal temporal-logic-guided, population-based policy search effectively handles sparse, temporally constrained robotic tasks and transfers from simulation to real hardware.

Abstract: Learning robot policies for tasks with sparse success signals is challenging when completion depends on coordinated actions, precise contact outcomes, or satisfying several conditions together. Intricate physical interactions with the world further complicate these requirements. Prior work using conventional reward shaping mechanisms provides dense feedback but local progress might not translate into eventual task completion. We present Signal Temporal Logic-guided Stein Variational Policy Gradient (STL-SVPG), a population-based method that uses smooth STL robustness as a trajectory-level training objective. Differentiating this objective through the dynamics assigns credit to policy actions according to their effect on the complete task specification, rather than local progress alone. We evaluate the approach on six quadcopter and manipulator tasks that involves event-triggered responses, strictly ordered behavior, responses within specified deadlines, and physical interaction with the world. STL-SVPG achieves the highest mean success rate among the compared methods on five of six benchmarks. Simulation-trained policies trained in simulation transfer temporal and contact task behavior to the real world.

</details>

### [379] [Geometric Optimization Parameterized by Piercing Complexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30829)
*Aritra Banik,Rajiv Raman,Saurabh Ray*

Main category: cs.CG

TL;DR: PTAS and approximation guarantees for geometric packing/covering under a bounded piercing degree, via a sublinear separator and local-search analysis; applies to weighted Set Cover and Discrete Independent Set, including axis-aligned rectangles with bounded piercing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Explore how piercing degree, a combinatorial-geometric property, affects the tractability of classic NP-hard problems (Set Cover, Independent Set) in geometric settings; extend non-piercing results to bounded-piercing families.

Method: Develop a locality graph whose structure is governed by piercing degree; prove a sublinear balanced separator exists depending only on the fixed piercing degree; use adaptive recursive local-search with this separator; derive a polynomial shallow-trace bound; obtain deterministic approximation ratios for weighted problems.

Result: - PTAS for unweighted Discrete Independent Set and Set Cover when piercing degree is fixed.
- Polynomial shallow-trace bound depending on piercing degree.
- Weighted Set Cover: deterministic Cr_r-approximation.
- Weighted Discrete Independent Set: deterministic O(r+1)-approximation.
- Applicability to axis-parallel rectangles with bounded piercing degree.

Conclusion: Piercing degree is a robust complexity parameter: fixed bounds enable PTAS and strong approximations for a broad class of geometric packing/covering problems, extending results from non-piercing families to bounded-piercing ones.

Abstract: Packing and covering problems for geometric regions have been studied under many notions of complexity, including VC-dimension, union complexity, shallow-cell complexity, and fatness. Although these restrictions often yield constant-factor approximation algorithms, they do not by themselves generally lead to PTASs. A recurring feature of known hardness constructions is that one region may be \emph{pierced} by many others: a region $B$ pierces $A$ when $A\setminus B$ is disconnected.
  We study geometric instances through the \emph{piercing degree}. Since piercing is symmetric for Jordan regions, this is the maximum degree of the corresponding piercing graph. Our main result is that, for every fixed piercing degree, the standard local-search algorithms give PTASs for the unweighted \emph{Discrete Independent Set} and \emph{Set Cover} problems. The proof constructs a sublinear balanced separator for an appropriate locality graph and applies it adaptively throughout the recursive local-search analysis. This guarantee depends only on the piercing degree; in particular, it places no bound on the number of components created by an individual piercing pair.
  We also prove a polynomial shallow-trace bound depending only on the piercing degree. As consequences, for every fixed piercing degree, weighted Set Cover admits a deterministic $C_r$-approximation and weighted Discrete Independent Set admits a deterministic $O(r+1)$-approximation. These results extend the known guarantees for non-piercing families and apply, for example, to axis-parallel rectangles when every rectangle is pierced by only a bounded number of other rectangles.

</details>


### [380] [Flow-TAG: Flow-based conditional latent transport for accurate spline approximation and data compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30955)
*Roman Pavelkin,Luis A. Zavala-Mondragon,Fons van der Sommen*

Main category: cs.CG

TL;DR: Introduces flow-TAG, a data-driven framework using a 1D U-Net generative flow to map curve geometry to optimal cubic B-spline parametrizations, improving parameterization robustness to noise and generalization across 2D/3D curves; also explores ECG signal compression with a 13:1 ratio and ~5% distortion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robust, accurate parameterization of noisy discrete curve data is crucial for CAD workflows, where local control and smoothness of B-spline representations are desirable; improving data-driven parameterization can enhance numerical stability and downstream processing.

Method: A generative flow model with a 1D U-Net backbone that maps curve geometry to optimal B-spline parametrization for cubic B-splines. The framework is trained to learn geometric patterns and produce parameterizations that minimize alignment errors. Evaluation includes regression-style metrics (RMSE) and geometric metrics (Hausdorff distance). A secondary study applies the framework to ECG signal compression on wearables, aiming for high compression with acceptable distortion.

Result: Flow-TAG yields fitted curves with ~55% lower RMSE and ~52% lower Hausdorff distance than state-of-the-art data-driven methods on unseen 2D/3D curves. The ECG compression setup achieves a 13:1 compression ratio with around 5% distortion, deemed acceptable in practice.

Conclusion: The proposed generative, flow-based parameterization approach improves accuracy and robustness of B-spline curve fitting and demonstrates practical viability in resource-constrained signal compression, suggesting broad applicability to CAD data pipelines and wearable sensing.

Abstract: Robust curve fitting is essential in computer-aided design for transforming noisy, discrete data into accurate geometric models that ensure numerical stability across engineering workflows. B-spline models have become the industry standard for this task, offering a flexible and reliable framework characterized by local control and smooth shape representation. This paper presents flow-TAG--a data-driven framework based on a generative flow model with a 1D U-Net backbone capable of mapping the geometry of a curve to the optimal parametrization for cubic B-splines. By leveraging learned geometric patterns, flow-TAG exhibits superior parameterization performance, robustness to noise in the input data, and strong generalization capability to previously unseen 2D and 3D curves drawn from distinct data distributions. Flow-TAG yields fitted curves that achieve the lower root-mean-square error (55% lower on average) and Hausdorff distance (52% lower on average) relative to state-of-the-art data-driven methods. In addition, we investigate the practical applicability of our generative framework in the compression of ECG signals for wearable devices. The proposed compression setup provides a compression ratio of 13 with the signal distortion of around 5%, which is acceptable in the field.

</details>


### [381] [Polychromatic 2-colorings with Bounded Discrepancy for Triangulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31574)
*Alma Arevalo Loyola,Ahmad Biniaz,Prosenjit Bose,Thomas Shermer*

Main category: cs.CG

TL;DR: Improved upper bound (3n-16)/7 for polychromatic 2-coloring discrepancy in triangulations; quadratic-time algorithm; discrepancy bounds tied to matching size M; Delaunay triangulations get ≤ n/3; linear-time algorithm achieving ≤ (5n-24)/7; and a connection to a recent result on proper 4-colorings yielding discrepancy at most n/3.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tighten discrepancy bounds for polychromatic 2-colorings of triangulations and provide efficient algorithms; explore dependence on matching structure and connect to known coloring results.

Method: Constructive combinatorial analysis of triangulations; derive bounds using matching size; give algorithms (quadratic- and linear-time) for producing 2-colorings with desired discrepancy; relate results to Delaunay triangulations and to proper 4-colorings.

Result: Upper bound improved to (3n-16)/7 with quadratic-time computability; discrepancy for triangulations with a matching of size M is at most n-4M/3; in particular Delaunay triangulations have discrepancy ≤ n/3; linear-time algorithm yields discrepancy ≤ (5n-24)/7; a conditional link shows that a proper four-coloring with the largest color class size n/2 implies discrepancy ≤ n/3, together with a recent result confirming such coloring.

Conclusion: The discrepancy for triangulations is at most n/3; the work advances bounds and provides efficient algorithms, aligning with concurrent results on colorings.

Abstract: A polychromatic $2$-coloring of a triangulation is a $2$-coloring of the vertices such that no face is monochromatic. The discrepancy of a coloring is the maximum difference between the sizes of the color classes. Asayama and Matsumoto (Graphs and Combinatorics, 2022) proved that every triangulation admits a polychromatic $2$-coloring with discrepancy at most $\tfrac{5n-16}{9}$, and that there exists a class of triangulations for which every polychromatic $2$-coloring has discrepancy at least $\tfrac{n}{3} - 2$, where $n$ is the number of vertices. We improve the upper bound, showing that every triangulation admits a polychromatic $2$-coloring with discrepancy at most $\tfrac{3n-16}{7}$ and such a $2$-coloring can be computed in quadratic time. We also show a discrepancy of at most $n-\tfrac{4M}{3}$ for triangulations with a matching of size $M$. This implies, for example, that Delaunay triangulations admit a discrepancy of at most $\tfrac{n}{3}$. We provide a linear-time algorithm to compute a $2$-coloring whose discrepancy is at most $\tfrac{5n-24}{7}$.
  One of our results shows that any proper four coloring with the largest color class of size $\frac{n}{2}$ would imply a $2$-coloring with discrepancy at most $\frac{n}{3}$. The existence of such a proper coloring has been recently confirmed by Kawarabayashi, Yoneda, and Yoneda (arXiv 2026). Therefore the two results together confirm the discrepancy of at most $\frac{n}{3}$ for triangulations.

</details>
